Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa

Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One.

Vinayapiṭake

In the Vinaya Piṭaka

Vinayasaṅgaha-aṭṭhakathā

The Commentary on the Vinayasaṅgaha

Ganthārambhakathā

Introduction to the Text

Vatthuttayaṃ [M 0.0001][V 0.0001] namassitvā, saraṇaṃ sabbapāṇinaṃ;

Vinaye pāṭavatthāya, yogāvacarabhikkhunaṃ.

Having paid homage to the Triple Gem, the refuge of all beings, [this is written] for the sake of proficiency in the Vinaya for monks devoted to the practice.

Vippakiṇṇamanekattha, pāḷimuttavinicchayaṃ;

Samāharitvā ekattha, dassayissamanākulaṃ.

Having gathered into one place the judgments on the Vinaya that are apart from the Pāli Canon and scattered throughout many treatises, I shall present them without confusion.

Tatrāyaṃ mātikā –

Therein, this is the table of contents:

“Divāseyyā parikkhāro, bhesajjakaraṇampi ca;

Parittaṃ paṭisanthāro, viññatti kulasaṅgaho.

Daytime lying down; requisites; and the preparation of medicine; recitation of paritta; friendly welcome; asking; and the support of families.

“Macchamaṃsaṃ [V 0.0002] anāmāsaṃ, adhiṭṭhānavikappanaṃ;

Cīvarenavināvāso, bhaṇḍassa paṭisāmanaṃ.

Fish and meat; things not to be touched; determination and sharing; dwelling without the robes; and the putting away of goods.

“Kayavikkayasamāpatti, rūpiyādipaṭiggaho;

Dānavissāsaggāhehi, lābhassa pariṇāmanaṃ.

Engaging in buying and selling; acceptance of money and so forth; giving and taking through familiarity; and the directing of gains.

“Pathavī bhūtagāmo ca, duvidhaṃ sahaseyyakaṃ;

Vihāre saṅghike seyyaṃ, santharitvāna pakkamo.

The earth and plant life; the two kinds of lying down together; and departing from a Saṅgha dwelling after having spread out bedding.

“Kālikānipi cattāri, kappiyā catubhūmiyo;

Khādanīyādipaṭiggāho, paṭikkhepapavāraṇā.

The four kinds of time-limited items; the four suitable grounds; acceptance of edibles and so forth; and refusal and invitation.

“Pabbajjā nissayo sīmā, uposathapavāraṇaṃ;

Vassūpanāyikā vattaṃ, catupaccayabhājanaṃ.

Ordination; dependence; boundary; Uposatha and Pavāraṇā; the rains-residence; duties; and the distribution of the four requisites.

“Kathinaṃ garubhaṇḍāni, codanādivinicchayo;

Garukāpattivuṭṭhānaṃ, kammākammaṃ pakiṇṇaka”nti.

The Kathina; heavy goods; judgments concerning accusation and so forth; rising from a grave offense; valid and invalid formal acts; and miscellaneous matters.

1. Divāseyyavinicchayakathā

The Discourse on the Judgment Concerning Daytime Lying Down

1. Tattha [M 0.0002][V 0.0003] divāseyyāti divānipajjanaṃ. Tatrāyaṃ vinicchayo – “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, divā paṭisallīyantena dvāraṃ saṃvaritvā paṭisallīyitu”nti (pārā. 77) vacanato divā nipajjantena dvāraṃ saṃvaritvā nipajjitabbaṃ. Ettha ca kiñcāpi pāḷiyaṃ “ayaṃ nāma āpattī”ti na vuttā, vivaritvā nipannadosena pana uppanne vatthusmiṃ dvāraṃ saṃvaritvā nipajjituṃ anuññātattā asaṃvaritvā nipajjantassa aṭṭhakathāyaṃ dukkaṭaṃ (pārā. aṭṭha. 1.77) vuttaṃ. Bhagavato hi adhippāyaṃ ñatvā upālittherādīhi aṭṭhakathā ṭhapitā. “Atthāpatti divā āpajjati, no ratti”nti (pari. 323) imināpi cetaṃ siddhaṃ.

Therein, 'daytime lying down' (divāseyyā) means lying down during the day. In that regard, this is the judgment: “I allow, monks, one who is secluding oneself during the day to seclude oneself by closing the door.” According to this, one who lies down during the day should lie down after closing the door. And in this matter, although it is not stated in the Pāli, “This is such-and-such an offense,” a dukkaṭa offense is stated in the commentary for one who lies down without closing the door, because permission to lie down after closing the door was given when the matter arose concerning the fault of lying down with the door open. For the commentary was established by the Elder Upāli and others, having understood the Blessed One’s intention. This is also established by the following: “There is an offense that one commits during the day, not at night.”

2. Kīdisaṃ pana dvāraṃ saṃvaritabbaṃ, kīdisaṃ na saṃvaritabbaṃ? Rukkhapadaraveḷupadarakilañjapaṇṇādīnaṃ yena kenaci kavāṭaṃ katvā heṭṭhā udukkhale upari uttarapāsake ca pavesetvā kataṃ parivattakadvārameva saṃvaritabbaṃ. Aññaṃ gorūpānaṃ vajesu viya rukkhasūcikaṇṭakadvāraṃ, gāmathakanakaṃ cakkalakayuttadvāraṃ, phalakesu vā kiṭikāsu vā dve tīṇi cakkalakāni yojetvā kataṃ saṃsaraṇakiṭikadvāraṃ, āpaṇesu viya kataṃ ugghāṭanakiṭikadvāraṃ, dvīsu tīsu ṭhānesu veḷusalākā gopphetvā paṇṇakuṭīsu kataṃ salākahatthakadvāraṃ, dussasāṇidvāranti evarūpaṃ dvāraṃ na saṃvaritabbaṃ. Pattahatthassa kavāṭappaṇāmane pana ekaṃ dussasāṇidvārameva anāpattikaraṃ, avasesāni paṇāmentassa āpatti. Divā paṭisallīyantassa pana parivattakadvārameva āpattikaraṃ, sesāni saṃvaritvā vā asaṃvaritvā vā nipajjantassa āpatti natthi, saṃvaritvā pana nipajjitabbaṃ, etaṃ vattaṃ.

1. What kind of door, then, should be secured, and what kind should not be secured? Only a revolving door should be secured—one made from any kind of wood planks, bamboo strips, mats, leaves, or the like, by making a door panel and inserting it below into a socket and above into a lintel loop. Other kinds of doors should not be secured, such as a wooden-bolt door or a thorn door like those in cattle pens; a village gate fitted with a wheel; a sliding lattice door made by attaching two or three wheels to planks or panels; a lift-up lattice door made like those in shops; a bamboo-strip handle door made in leaf huts by weaving bamboo strips in two or three places; or a cloth-screen door. However, for one with a bowl in hand, in opening a door, only a cloth-screen door is a cause for no offense; opening the remaining ones is an offense. For one secluding oneself during the day, however, only the revolving door is a cause for an offense. For one lying down after securing or without securing the remaining doors, there is no offense. However, one should lie down after securing them; this is the duty.

3. Parivattakadvāraṃ kittakena saṃvutaṃ hoti? Sūcighaṭikāsu dinnāsu saṃvutameva hoti. Apica kho sūcimattepi dinne vaṭṭati, ghaṭikāmattepi dinne vaṭṭati, dvārabāhaṃ phusitvā ṭhapitamattepi vaṭṭati, īsakaṃ aphusitepi vaṭṭati, sabbantimena vidhinā yāvatā sīsaṃ nappavisati, tāvatā aphusitepi vaṭṭati. Sace bahūnaṃ vaḷañjanaṭṭhānaṃ hoti, bhikkhuṃ vā sāmaṇeraṃ vā “dvāraṃ, āvuso, jaggāhī”ti vatvāpi nipajjituṃ vaṭṭati. Atha bhikkhū cīvarakammaṃ vā aññaṃ vā kiñci karontā nisinnā honti, “ete dvāraṃ jaggissantī”ti [M 0.0003] ābhogaṃ katvāpi nipajjituṃ vaṭṭati. Kurundaṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana “upāsakampi āpucchitvā vā ‘esa [V 0.0004] jaggissatī’ti ābhogaṃ katvā vā nipajjituṃ vaṭṭati, kevalaṃ bhikkhuniṃ vā mātugāmaṃ vā āpucchituṃ na vaṭṭatī”ti vuttaṃ, taṃ yuttaṃ. Evaṃ sabbatthapi yo yo theravādo vā aṭṭhakathāvādo vā pacchā vuccati, so sova pamāṇanti gahetabbaṃ.

1. How much must a revolving door be secured for it to be considered secured? It is considered secured when the pin and the latch are set. Moreover, it is permissible even if only the pin is inserted, and it is permissible even if only the latch is inserted. It is permissible if it is merely placed touching the doorpost, and permissible even if slightly not touching. By the very last method, it is permissible even if it does not touch, as long as a head cannot enter. If it is a place frequented by many, it is permissible to lie down even after saying to a bhikkhu or a sāmaṇera, “Friend, watch the door.” Furthermore, if bhikkhus are sitting doing robe-work or some other task, it is permissible to lie down even after making the reflection, “These will watch the door.” In the Kurundaṭṭhakathā, however, it is said: “It is permissible to lie down after asking a layman, or after making the reflection, ‘This one will watch.’ But it is not permissible to ask a bhikkhunī alone or a woman alone.” That is proper. Thus, in all cases, whichever Theravāda view or commentary view is stated later should be taken as the authority.

4. Atha dvārassa udukkhalaṃ vā uttarapāsako vā bhinno hoti aṭṭhapito vā, saṃvarituṃ na sakkoti, navakammatthaṃ vā pana iṭṭhakapuñjo vā mattikādīnaṃ vā rāsi antodvāre kato hoti, aṭṭaṃ vā bandhanti, yathā saṃvarituṃ na sakkoti. Evarūpe antarāye sati asaṃvaritvāpi nipajjituṃ vaṭṭati. Yadi pana kavāṭaṃ natthi, laddhakappameva. Upari sayantena nisseṇiṃ āropetvā nipajjitabbaṃ. Sace nisseṇimatthake thakanakaṃ hoti, thaketvāpi nipajjitabbaṃ. Gabbhe nipajjantena gabbhadvāraṃ vā pamukhadvāraṃ vā yaṃ kiñci saṃvaritvā nipajjituṃ vaṭṭati. Sace ekakuṭṭake gehe dvīsu passesu dvārāni katvā vaḷañjanti, dvepi dvārāni jaggitabbāni, tibhūmakepi pāsāde dvāraṃ jaggitabbameva. Sace bhikkhācārā paṭikkamma lohapāsādasadisaṃ pāsādaṃ bahū bhikkhū divāvihāratthaṃ pavisanti, saṅghattherena dvārapālassa “dvāraṃ jaggāhī”ti vatvā vā “dvārajagganaṃ nāma etassa bhāro”ti ābhogaṃ katvā vā pavisitvā nipajjitabbaṃ. Yāva saṅghanavakena evameva kātabbaṃ. Pure pavisantānaṃ “dvārajagganaṃ nāma pacchimānaṃ bhāro”ti evaṃ ābhogaṃ kātumpi vaṭṭati. Anāpucchā vā ābhogaṃ akatvā vā antogabbhe vā asaṃvutadvāre bahi vā nipajjantānaṃ āpatti. Gabbhe vā bahi vā nipajjanakālepi “dvārajagganaṃ nāma mahādvāre dvārapālassa bhāro”ti ābhogaṃ katvā nipajjituṃ vaṭṭatiyeva. Evaṃ lohapāsādādīsu ākāsatale nipajjantenapi dvāraṃ saṃvaritabbameva.

4. Now, if the door's socket or upper latch-ring is broken or not in place, so that it cannot be secured; or if for new construction a pile of bricks or a heap of clay and the like is made inside the doorway, or a scaffold is being bound in such a way that the door cannot be secured—in such a case of obstruction, it is permissible to lie down even without securing it. If, however, there is no door-leaf, it is allowable as if permission had been obtained. One lying down upstairs should lie down after raising the ladder. If there is a cover at the top of the ladder, one should lie down after closing it. When lying down in a chamber, one may lie down after securing the chamber's door, the main entrance, or any such door. If in a single-chambered house, doors are made and used on two sides, both doors must be secured. Even in a three-story palace, the door must be secured. If, after returning from the alms-round, many monks enter a palace such as the Lohapāsāda for their day-sojourn, the senior monk of the community should enter and lie down after either telling the doorkeeper, 'Secure the door,' or making the reflection, 'The responsibility for securing the door is his.' This should be done by all, down to the most junior monk of the community. For those entering earlier, it is also permissible to make the reflection, 'The responsibility for securing the door falls on those who come last.' An offense is incurred by those who lie down without asking, or without making the reflection, or inside a chamber with an unsecured door, or outside. Even when lying down inside or outside, it is indeed permissible to lie down after making the reflection, 'The responsibility for securing the main door lies with the doorkeeper.' Thus, in places such as the Lohapāsāda, even when one is lying down on an open-air terrace, the door must still be secured.

Ayañhettha saṅkhepo – idaṃ divāpaṭisallīyanaṃ yena kenaci parikkhitte sadvārabandhe ṭhāne kathitaṃ, tasmā abbhokāse vā rukkhamūle vā maṇḍape vā yattha katthaci sadvārabandhe nipajjantena dvāraṃ saṃvaritvāva nipajjitabbaṃ. Sace mahāpariveṇaṃ hoti mahābodhiyaṅgaṇalohapāsādaṅgaṇasadisaṃ bahūnaṃ osaraṇaṭṭhānaṃ, yattha dvāraṃ saṃvutampi saṃvutaṭṭhāne na tiṭṭhati, dvāraṃ alabhantā pākāraṃ āruhitvāpi vicaranti, tattha saṃvaraṇakiccaṃ natthi. Rattiṃ dvāraṃ vivaritvā nipanno aruṇe uggate vuṭṭhāti, anāpatti. Sace pana pabujjhitvā [M 0.0004] puna supati, āpatti. Yo pana “aruṇe uggate vuṭṭhahissāmī”ti paricchinditvāva dvāraṃ asaṃvaritvā rattiṃ nipajjati, yathāparicchedameva vuṭṭhāti, tassa āpattiyeva. Mahāpaccariyaṃ pana “evaṃ nipajjanto anādariyadukkaṭāpi na muccatī”ti vuttaṃ.

Herein is the summary: This daytime seclusion has been described as being in any enclosed place with a secured door. Therefore, whether in the open air, at the foot of a tree, or in a pavilion—wherever one lies down in a place with a secured door—one must lie down only after securing the door. If it is a large monastic compound, like the courtyard of the Great Bodhi Tree or the Lohapāsāda courtyard—a place where many people gather—where a door, even if closed, does not remain so, and where people, finding the door unavailable, even climb over the walls to move about, in such a place there is no duty to secure it. If one lies down at night with the door open and rises at dawn, there is no offense. But if, after waking up, one goes back to sleep, there is an offense. However, if one lies down at night without securing the door, having determined, 'I will rise at dawn,' and rises exactly as determined, there is indeed an offense. But in the Mahāpaccarī it is said: 'One who lies down in this manner is not free even from an offense of disrespect.'

5. Yo [V 0.0005] pana bahudeva rattiṃ jaggitvā addhānaṃ vā gantvā divā kilantarūpo mañce nisinno pāde bhūmito amocetvāva niddāvasena nipajjati, tassa anāpatti. Sace okkantaniddo ajānantopi pāde mañcakaṃ āropeti, āpattiyeva. Nisīditvā apassāya supantassa anāpatti. Yopi ca “niddaṃ vinodessāmī”ti caṅkamanto patitvā sahasā vuṭṭhāti, tassapi anāpatti. Yo pana patitvā tattheva sayati, na vuṭṭhāti, tassa āpatti.

5. But for a monk who, having stayed awake for much of the night or having traveled a long distance and being weary during the day, sits on a bed and lies down due to sleepiness without lifting his feet from the ground, there is no offense. If, overcome by sleep, he even unknowingly places his feet on the bed, there is indeed an offense. For one who sits and sleeps while leaning on a support, there is no offense. And for one who, thinking, 'I will dispel sleepiness,' is walking back and forth, falls, and suddenly gets up, there is also no offense. But for one who falls and lies down right there without getting up, there is an offense.

Ko muccati, ko na muccatīti? Mahāpaccariyaṃ tāva “ekabhaṅgena nipannako eva muccati. Pāde pana bhūmito mocetvā nipannopi yakkhagahitakopi visaññībhūtopi na muccatī”ti vuttaṃ. Kurundaṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana “bandhitvā nipajjāpitova muccatī”ti vuttaṃ. Mahāaṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana “yo caṅkamanto mucchitvā patito tattheva supati, tassapi avisayatāya āpatti na dissati. Ācariyā pana evaṃ na kathayanti, tasmā āpattiyevāti mahāpadumattherena vuttaṃ. Dve pana janā āpattito muccantiyeva, yo ca yakkhagahitako, yo ca bandhitvā nipajjāpito”ti.

Who is released? Who is not released? First, in the Mahāpaccarī, it is said: 'Only one who lies down with one side bent is released. However, one who lies down having lifted the feet from the ground, one seized by a yakkha, or one who has become unconscious is not released.' In the Kurundaṭṭhakathā, however, it is said: 'Only one who is bound and made to lie down is released.' In the Mahāaṭṭhakathā, however, it is said: 'For a bhikkhu who, while walking in meditation, faints, falls, and sleeps right there, no offense is seen because it is beyond his control. The teachers, however, do not say thus; therefore, it is indeed an offense,' so it was said by the Elder Mahāpaduma. 'But two persons are indeed released from the offense: one who is seized by a yakkha, and one who is bound and made to lie down.'

Iti pāḷimuttakavinayavinicchayasaṅgahe

Thus, in the Compendium of Vinaya Decisions Independent of the Pāḷi Canon,

Divāseyyavinicchayakathā samattā.

The Discussion on the Decision Concerning Daytime Lying Down is complete.

2. Parikkhāravinicchayakathā

2. Discourse on the Determination of Requisites

6. Parikkhāroti [V 0.0006] samaṇaparikkhāro. Tatrāyaṃ kappiyākappiyaparikkhāravinicchayo (pārā. aṭṭha. 1.85) – keci tālapaṇṇacchattaṃ anto vā bahi vā pañcavaṇṇena suttena sibbitvā vaṇṇamaṭṭhaṃ karonti, taṃ na vaṭṭati. Ekavaṇṇena pana nīlena vā pītakena vā yena kenaci suttena anto vā bahi vā sibbituṃ[M 0.0005], chattadaṇḍaggāhakaṃ salākapañjaraṃ vā vinandhituṃ vaṭṭati, tañca kho thirakaraṇatthaṃ vaṭṭati, na vaṇṇamaṭṭhatthāya. Chattapaṇṇesu makaradantakaṃ vā aḍḍhacandakaṃ vā chindituṃ na vaṭṭati. Chattadaṇḍe gehatthambhesu viya ghaṭako vā vāḷarūpakaṃ vā na vaṭṭati. Sacepi sabbattha āraggena lekhā dinnā hoti, sāpi na vaṭṭati. Ghaṭakaṃ vā vāḷarūpakaṃ vā bhinditvā dhāretabbaṃ, lekhāpi ghaṃsitvā vā apanetabbā, suttakena vā daṇḍo veṭhetabbo. Daṇḍabunde pana ahicchattakasaṇṭhānaṃ vaṭṭati. Vātappahārena acalanatthaṃ chattamaṇḍalikaṃ rajjukehi gāhetvā daṇḍe bandhanti, tasmiṃ bandhanaṭṭhāne valayamiva ukkiritvā lekhaṃ ṭhapenti, sā vaṭṭati.

6. The requisites are the requisites of a monk. Herein is the determination of allowable and unallowable requisites. Some make a palm-leaf umbrella, stitching it inside or outside with thread of five colors and then embellishing it with color; this is not allowable. However, it is allowable to stitch it inside or outside with thread of a single color, such as blue or yellow, or any other, or to bind the handle-holder or the framework of ribs; and this is for the purpose of making it sturdy, not for the sake of embellishment. It is not allowable to cut the umbrella leaves into shapes like crocodile teeth or half-moons. On the umbrella handle, a pot-shaped ornament or a wild animal figure, like those on house pillars, is not allowable. Even if lines are incised all over with an awl, that too is not allowable. A pot-shaped ornament or a wild animal figure should be broken off before it is used; any lines should be scraped away or removed, or the handle should be wrapped with thread. On the handle’s knob, however, a mushroom-like shape is allowable. To prevent the umbrella from being shaken by the wind, they fasten the umbrella’s circular frame with strings to the handle; at the fastening point, they may raise a ring-like design—this is allowable.

7. Cīvaramaṇḍanatthāya nānāsuttakehi satapadisadisaṃ sibbantā āgantukapaṭṭaṃ ṭhapenti, aññampi yaṃ kiñci sūcikammavikāraṃ karonti, paṭṭamukhe vā pariyante vā veṇiṃ vā saṅkhalikaṃ vā muggaraṃ vā evamādi sabbaṃ na vaṭṭati, pakatisūcikammameva vaṭṭati. Gaṇṭhikapaṭṭakañca pāsakapaṭṭakañca aṭṭhakoṇampi soḷasakoṇampi karonti, tattha agghiyagayamuggarādīni dassenti, kakkaṭakkhīni ukkiranti, sabbaṃ na vaṭṭati, catukoṇameva vaṭṭati, koṇasuttapīḷakā ca cīvare ratte duviññeyyarūpā vaṭṭanti. Kañjikapiṭṭhakhaliaalakādīsu cīvaraṃ pakkhipituṃ na vaṭṭati, cīvarakammakāle pana hatthamalasūcimalādīnaṃ dhovanatthaṃ kiliṭṭhakāle ca dhovanatthaṃ vaṭṭati, gandhaṃ vā lākhaṃ vā telaṃ vā rajane pakkhipituṃ na vaṭṭati.

7. For the purpose of decorating a robe, they sew patterns resembling a centipede with threads of various colors and attach an extra patch. Or they do any other kind of fancy needlework. On the corner of the robe or on the border, they make patterns like a braid, a chain, or a mallet. All such things are not allowable; only plain needlework is allowable. They also make the patch for the loop and the patch for the fastener eight-cornered or sixteen-cornered. Therein, they create designs like a stupa, a spike, a mallet, and so on; they make raised patterns like crab's eyes. All of this is not allowable; only a four-cornered design is allowable. And small tassel-threads at the corner, if they are indistinct after the robe is dyed, are allowable. It is not allowable to put a robe into rice-gruel, flour-paste, oil-cake, and the like. However, at the time of making the robe, it is allowable for washing off dirt from the hands, rust from the needle, and so on, and for washing it when it is soiled. It is not allowable to put perfume, lac, or oil into the dye.

Rajanesu ca haliddiṃ ṭhapetvā sabbaṃ mūlarajanaṃ vaṭṭati, mañjiṭṭhiñca tuṅgahārañca ṭhapetvā sabbaṃ khandharajanaṃ vaṭṭati. Tuṅgahāro nāma eko sakaṇṭakarukkho, tassa haritālavaṇṇaṃ khandharajanaṃ hoti. Loddañca kaṇḍulañca ṭhapetvā sabbaṃ tacarajanaṃ vaṭṭati. Allipattañca nīlipattañca ṭhapetvā sabbaṃ pattarajanaṃ vaṭṭati. Gihiparibhuttakaṃ pana allipattena ekavāraṃ rajituṃ [V 0.0007] vaṭṭati. Kiṃsukapupphañca kusumbhapupphañca ṭhapetvā sabbaṃ puppharajanaṃ vaṭṭati. Phalarajane pana na kiñci na vaṭṭati (mahāva. aṭṭha. 344).

And among dyes, excepting turmeric, all root-dyes are allowable. Excepting madder and tuṅgahāra, all stem-dyes are allowable. Tuṅgahāra is the name of a certain thorny tree; its stem-dye has the color of orpiment. Excepting lodda and kaṇḍula, all bark-dyes are allowable. Excepting allipatta leaf and nīlipatta leaf, all leaf-dyes are allowable. But a cloth used by a householder is allowed to be dyed once with allipatta leaf. Excepting kiṃsuka flowers and kusumbha flowers, all flower-dyes are allowable. As for fruit-dyes, however, all are allowable.

8. Cīvaraṃ rajitvā saṅkhena vā maṇinā vā yena kenaci na ghaṭṭetabbaṃ, bhūmiyaṃ jāṇukāni nihantvā hatthehi gahetvā doṇiyampi na ghaṃsitabbaṃ. Doṇiyaṃ vā phalake vā ṭhapetvā ante gāhāpetvā hatthena paharituṃ pana [M 0.0006] vaṭṭati, tampi muṭṭhinā na kātabbaṃ. Porāṇakattherā pana doṇiyampi na ṭhapesuṃ. Eko cīvaraṃ gahetvā tiṭṭhati, aparo hatthe katvā hatthena paharati. Cīvarassa kaṇṇasuttakaṃ na vaṭṭati, rajitakāle chinditabbaṃ. Yaṃ pana “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, kaṇṇasuttaka”nti (mahāva. 344) evaṃ anuññātaṃ, taṃ anuvāte pāsakaṃ katvā bandhitabbaṃ rajanakāle lagganatthāya. Gaṇṭhikepi sobhākaraṇatthaṃ lekhā vā pīḷakā vā na vaṭṭati, nāsetvā paribhuñjitabbaṃ.

8. After dyeing a robe, it should not be rubbed with anything, such as a conch shell or a gemstone. One should not rub it in a trough, having placed one's knees on the ground and taken it with the hands. However, it is allowable to place it in a trough or on a board, and having another person hold it at the edge, to strike it with the hand; but even that should not be done with a clenched fist. The ancient elders, however, did not even place it in a trough. One person stands holding the robe, while another strikes it with his hand, having placed it on his hand. A corner-string on a robe is not allowable; it should be cut off after dyeing. As for the corner-string that was permitted thus: “I allow, O monks, a corner-string,” that should be made into a loop at the lengthwise border-edge and tied for the purpose of hanging it up at the time of dyeing. Also on a knot, lines or small beads for the purpose of beautification are not allowable; they should be destroyed before use.

9. Patte vā thālake vā āraggena lekhaṃ karonti anto vā bahi vā, na vaṭṭati. Pattaṃ bhamaṃ āropetvā majjitvā pacanti “maṇivaṇṇaṃ karissāmā”ti, na vaṭṭati, telavaṇṇo pana vaṭṭati. Pattamaṇḍale bhittikammaṃ na vaṭṭati, makaradantakaṃ pana vaṭṭati.

9. Making lines on a bowl or a plate with an awl, whether inside or outside, is not allowable. Mounting a bowl on a lathe, polishing it, and firing it with the intention, “We will make it jewel-colored,” is not allowable; however, an oil-colored finish is allowable. On a bowl-stand, pictorial designs are not allowable, but a makara-tooth design is allowable.

Dhamakaraṇachattakassa upari vā heṭṭhā vā dhamakaraṇakucchiyaṃ vā lekhā na vaṭṭati, chattamukhavaṭṭiyaṃ panassa lekhā vaṭṭati.

On the upper part, the lower part, or in the cavity of a water-strainer, lines are not allowable. However, on the rim of its lid, a circular line is allowable.

10. Kāyabandhanassa sobhanatthaṃ tahiṃ tahiṃ diguṇaṃ suttaṃ koṭṭenti, kakkaṭakkhīni uṭṭhāpenti, na vaṭṭati, ubhosu pana antesu dasāmukhassa thirabhāvāya diguṇaṃ koṭṭetuṃ vaṭṭati. Dasāmukhe pana ghaṭakaṃ vā makaramukhaṃ vā deḍḍubhasīsaṃ vā yaṃ kiñci vikārarūpaṃ kātuṃ na vaṭṭati, tattha tattha acchīni dassetvā mālākammādīni vā katvā koṭṭitakāyabandhanampi na vaṭṭati, ujukameva pana macchakaṇṭakaṃ vā khajjūripattakaṃ vā maṭṭhakapaṭṭikaṃ vā katvā koṭṭetuṃ vaṭṭati. Kāyabandhanassa dasā ekā vaṭṭati, dve tīṇi cattāripi vaṭṭanti, tato paraṃ na vaṭṭanti. Rajjukakāyabandhanaṃ ekameva vaṭṭati, pāmaṅgasaṇṭhānaṃ pana ekampi na vaṭṭati, dasā pana pāmaṅgasaṇṭhānāpi vaṭṭati, bahurajjuke ekato katvā ekena nirantaraṃ veṭhetvā kataṃ bahurajjukanti na vattabbaṃ, taṃ vaṭṭati.

10. For the sake of beautifying a belt, they braid a doubled thread in various places and create crab-eye-like patterns; this is not allowable. However, at both ends, for the stability of the base of the fringe, it is allowable to braid a doubled thread. On the fringe, however, it is not allowable to make any kind of fancy shape, such as a water-pot shape, a makara-mouth shape, or a water-snake-head shape. A braided belt made by showing elephant-eye-socket-like patterns in various places or by adding floral work and the like is also not allowable. However, it is allowable to braid it straight, having made it in the shape of a fish bone, a date-palm leaf, or a smooth plank. For a belt, one fringe is allowable; two, three, or four are also allowable, but more than that are not allowable. Only one rope belt is allowable. But a belt with a chisel-handle shape, even one, is not allowable. The fringe, however, is allowable even with a chisel-handle shape. A belt made by gathering many ropes together and wrapping them continuously with one rope should not be called 'a many-roped belt'; such a belt is allowable.

Kāyabandhanavidhe [V 0.0008] aṭṭhamaṅgalādikaṃ yaṃ kiñci vikārarūpaṃ na vaṭṭati, paricchedalekhāmattaṃ vaṭṭati. Vidhakassa ubhosu antesu thirakaraṇatthāya ghaṭakaṃ karonti, ayampi vaṭṭati.

On the border of a belt, any kind of fancy shape, such as the eight auspicious symbols and so on, is not allowable; only a mere dividing line is allowable. At both ends of the border, for the purpose of making it firm, they make a water-pot shape; this is also allowable.

11. Añjaniyaṃ itthipurisacatuppadasakuṇarūpaṃ vā mālākammalatākammamakaradantakagomuttakaaḍḍhacandakādibhedaṃ vā vikārarūpaṃ na vaṭṭati, ghaṃsitvā vā [M 0.0007] bhinditvā vā yathā vā na paññāyati, tathā suttakena veṭhetvā vaḷañjetabbā. Ujukameva pana caturaṃsā vā aṭṭhaṃsā vā soḷasaṃsā vā añjanī vaṭṭati. Heṭṭhatopissā dve vā tisso vā vaṭṭalekhāyo vaṭṭanti, gīvāyampissā pidhānakabandhanatthaṃ ekā vaṭṭalekhā vaṭṭati.

11. On a collyrium container, the form of a woman, man, quadruped, or bird, or a fancy shape with varieties such as floral work, creeper work, a makara-tooth pattern, a cow's urine pattern, a half-moon shape, and so on, is not allowable. Having ground it down or broken it in such a way that it is not recognizable, it should be wrapped with thread and then used. However, a straight collyrium container that is four-sided, eight-sided, or sixteen-sided is allowable. Below it, two or three circular lines are allowable. On its neck, one circular line for the purpose of tying the lid is allowable.

Añjanīsalākāyapi vaṇṇamaṭṭhakammaṃ na vaṭṭati, añjanīthavikāyapi yaṃ kiñci nānāvaṇṇena suttena vaṇṇamaṭṭhakammaṃ na vaṭṭati. Eseva nayo kuñcikakosakepi. Kuñcikāya vaṇṇamaṭṭhakammaṃ na vaṭṭati, tathā sipāṭikāya. Ekavaṇṇasuttena pana yena kenaci yaṃ kiñci sibbituṃ vaṭṭati.

On a collyrium stick also, elaborate color work is not allowable. On a bag for a collyrium container also, any elaborate color work with thread of various colors is not allowable. This same principle applies to a key case. On a key, elaborate color work is not allowable; likewise on a razor case. However, with a single-colored thread, it is allowable to do any kind of sewing.

12. Ārakaṇṭakepi vaṭṭamaṇikaṃ vā aññaṃ vā vaṇṇamaṭṭhaṃ na vaṭṭati, gīvāyaṃ pana paricchedalekhā vaṭṭati. Pipphalikepi maṇikaṃ vā pīḷakaṃ vā yaṃ kiñci uṭṭhāpetuṃ na vaṭṭati, daṇḍake pana paricchedalekhā vaṭṭati. Nakhacchedanaṃ valitakaṃyeva karonti, tasmā taṃ vaṭṭati. Uttarāraṇiyaṃ vāpi araṇidhanuke vā uparipellanadaṇḍake vā mālākammādi yaṃ kiñci vaṇṇamaṭṭhaṃ na vaṭṭati. Pellanadaṇḍakassa pana vemajjhe maṇḍalaṃ hoti, tattha paricchedalekhāmattaṃ vaṭṭati. Sūcisaṇḍāsaṃ karonti, yena sūciṃ ḍaṃsāpetvā ghaṃsanti, tattha makaramukhādikaṃ yaṃ kiñci vaṇṇamaṭṭhaṃ na vaṭṭati, sūciḍaṃsanatthaṃ pana mukhamattaṃ hoti, taṃ vaṭṭati.

12. On a stylus with a long point also, a large round bead or other elaborate color work is not allowable, but on its neck, a demarcation line is allowable. On a razor also, it is not allowable to affix a large bead, a small bead, or anything whatsoever, but on the handle, a demarcation line is allowable. As for a small nail-cutting knife, they make it as a folded one; therefore, that is allowable. On an upper fire-stick, or on a fire-bow, or on an upper turning-stick, any elaborate color work such as garland work and so on is not allowable. But on the turning-stick, there is a circle in the middle; there, only a line to demarcate it is allowable. They make needle-tongs, with which they clamp a needle and sharpen it. Thereon, any elaborate color work such as the shape of a makara's mouth and so on is not allowable. But for the purpose of gripping the needle, there is a mere opening; that is allowable.

Dantakaṭṭhacchedanavāsiyampi yaṃ kiñci vaṇṇamaṭṭhaṃ na vaṭṭati, ujukameva kappiyalohena ubhosu vā passesu caturaṃsaṃ vā aṭṭhaṃsaṃ vā bandhituṃ vaṭṭati. Kattaradaṇḍepi yaṃ kiñci vaṇṇamaṭṭhaṃ na vaṭṭati, heṭṭhā ekā vā dve vā vaṭṭalekhā upari ahicchattakamakuḷamattañca vaṭṭati.

On the handle of a small adze for cutting tooth-sticks also, any elaborate color work is not allowable; it is allowable only to bind it straight on both sides with allowable metal in a four-cornered or eight-cornered shape. On a walking stick also, any elaborate color work is not allowable; however, below, one or two round lines are allowable, and above, something the size of a mushroom bud is also allowable.

13. Telabhājanesu visāṇe vā nāḷiyaṃ vā alābuke vā āmaṇḍasārake vā ṭhapetvā itthirūpaṃ purisarūpañca avasesaṃ sabbampi vaṇṇamaṭṭhakammaṃ vaṭṭati. Mañcapīṭhe bhisibimbohane bhūmattharaṇe pādapuñchane caṅkamanabhisiyā sammuñjaniyaṃ kacavarachaḍḍanake rajanadoṇikāya pānīyauḷuṅke [V 0.0009] pānīyaghaṭe pādakathalikāya phalakapīṭhake valayādhārake daṇḍādhārake pattapidhāne tālavaṇṭe bījaneti etesu sabbaṃ mālākammādi vaṇṇamaṭṭhakammaṃ vaṭṭati.

13. In oil containers—whether an animal horn, a coconut tube, a gourd, or a container made from the heartwood of the castor-oil plant—excepting the form of a woman and the form of a man, all remaining polished ornamental work is allowable. On beds and stools, mattresses and cushions, floor coverings, foot-wipers, cushions for the walking path, brooms, baskets for disposing of rubbish, dyeing troughs, drinking water ladles, drinking water pots, potsherds for rubbing the feet, plank-stools, ring-stands, staff-stands, bowl-lids, palm-leaf fans, and fans—on all these, all polished ornamental work, such as garland-work and so forth, is allowable.

14. Senāsane pana dvārakavāṭavātapānakavāṭādīsu sabbaratanamayampi vaṇṇamaṭṭhakammaṃ vaṭṭati. Senāsane kiñci paṭisedhetabbaṃ natthi aññatra viruddhasenāsanā[M 0.0008]. Viruddhasenāsanaṃ nāma aññesaṃ sīmāya rājavallabhehi katasenāsanaṃ vuccati. Tasmā ye tādisaṃ senāsanaṃ karonti, te vattabbā “mā amhākaṃ sīmāya senāsanaṃ karothā”ti. Anādiyitvā karontiyeva, punapi vattabbā “mā evaṃ akattha, mā amhākaṃ uposathapavāraṇānaṃ antarāyamakattha, mā sāmaggiṃ bhindittha, tumhākaṃ senāsanaṃ katampi kataṭṭhāne na ṭhassatī”ti. Sace balakkārena karontiyeva, yadā tesaṃ lajjiparisā ussannā hoti, sakkā ca hoti laddhuṃ dhammiko vinicchayo, tadā tesaṃ pesetabbaṃ “tumhākaṃ āvāsaṃ harathā”ti. Sace yāvatatiyaṃ pesite haranti, sādhu. No ce haranti, ṭhapetvā bodhiñca cetiyañca avasesasenāsanāni bhinditabbāni, no ca kho aparibhogaṃ karontehi, paṭipāṭiyā pana chadanagopānasīiṭṭhakādīni apanetvā tesaṃ pesetabbaṃ “tumhākaṃ dabbasambhāre harathā”ti. Sace haranti, sādhu. No ce haranti, atha tesu dabbasambhāresu himavassavātātapādīhi pūtibhūtesu vā corehi vā haṭesu agginā vā daḍḍhesu sīmasāmikā bhikkhū anupavajjā, na labbhā codetuṃ “tumhehi amhākaṃ dabbasambhārā nāsitā”ti vā “tumhākaṃ gīvā”ti vā. Yaṃ pana sīmasāmikehi bhikkhūhi kataṃ, taṃ sukatameva hoti. Yopi bhikkhu bahussuto vinayaññū aññaṃ bhikkhuṃ akappiyaparikkhāraṃ gahetvā vicarantaṃ disvā chindāpeyya vā bhindāpeyya vā, anupavajjo, so neva codetabbo na sāretabbo, na taṃ labbhā vattuṃ “ayaṃ nāma mama parikkhāro tayā nāsito, taṃ me dehī”ti.

14. In a dwelling, however, on door-leaves, window-leaves, and the like, even polished decorative work made of all jewels is allowable. In a dwelling, there is nothing that should be prohibited except for a hostile dwelling. A hostile dwelling, by name, is said to be a dwelling built by shameless monks who are royal favorites within the boundary of others. Therefore, those monks who build such a dwelling should be told, 'Do not build a dwelling within our boundary.' If, without heeding their words, they still build, they should be told again, 'Do not act thus. Do not create an obstacle for our Uposatha and Pavāraṇā. Do not break the harmony. Your dwelling, even if built, will not stand in the place where it is built.' If they still build by force, when the assembly of scrupulous monks becomes numerous and it is possible to obtain a lawful decision, then a message should be sent to them: 'Take away your residence.' If, when the message has been sent up to the third time, they take it away, it is good. If they do not take it away, then, setting aside the Bodhi tree and the cetiya, the remaining dwellings should be demolished—but not by those making it unusable. But in sequence, the roofing, rafters, bricks, and so forth should be removed, and a message should be sent to them: 'Take away your materials.' If they take them away, it is good. If they do not take them away, then, when those materials have become rotten due to snow, rain, wind, sun, and so forth, or are carried away by thieves, or are burned by fire, the monks who are owners of the boundary are blameless. It is not possible to accuse them, saying, ‘Our materials were destroyed by you,’ or, ‘It is your liability.’ Whatever is done by the monks who are owners of the boundary is indeed well done. Furthermore, whatever monk who is learned and an expert in the Vinaya, having seen another monk wandering about having taken an unsuitable requisite, should have it cut or broken, he is blameless. He should neither be accused nor reminded. It is not possible to say to him, 'This requisite of mine was destroyed by you; give it to me.'

Iti pāḷimuttakavinayavinicchayasaṅgahe

In the Vinayasaṅgaha-aṭṭhakathā, a compilation of Vinaya decisions independent of the Pāḷi Canon:

Parikkhāravinicchayakathā samattā.

The Discourse on the Decision Concerning Requisites is Concluded.

3. Bhesajjādikaraṇavinicchayakathā

3. The Discourse on the Decision Concerning Medicines and the Like

15. Bhesajjakaraṇaparittapaṭisanthāresu [V 0.0010] pana bhesajjakaraṇe tāva ayaṃ vinicchayo (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.185-7) – āgatāgatassa parajanassa bhesajjaṃ na kātabbaṃ, karonto dukkaṭaṃ āpajjati. Pañcannaṃ pana sahadhammikānaṃ kātabbaṃ bhikkhussa bhikkhuniyā [M 0.0009] sikkhamānāya sāmaṇerassa sāmaṇeriyāti. Samasīlasaddhāpaññānañhi etesaṃ tīsu sikkhāsu yuttānaṃ bhesajjaṃ akātuṃ na labbhati. Karontena ca sace tesaṃ atthi, tesaṃ santakaṃ gahetvā yojetvā dātabbaṃ, sace natthi, attano santakaṃ kātabbaṃ. Sace attanopi natthi, bhikkhācāravattena vā ñātakapavāritaṭṭhānato vā pariyesitabbaṃ, alabhantena gilānassa atthāya akataviññattiyāpi āharitvā kātabbaṃ.

15. Now, regarding the administering of medicine, the reciting of protective chants, and making arrangements: in the matter of administering medicine, first, this is the decision. Medicine should not be administered for any outsider who comes; one who does so incurs a dukkaṭa offense. However, it should be administered for the five co-religionists: a bhikkhu, a bhikkhunī, a sikkhamānā, a sāmaṇera, and a sāmaṇerī. Indeed, for these co-religionists who possess equal virtue, faith, and wisdom, and are engaged in the three trainings, it is not permissible to refrain from administering medicine. And when administering it, if they have possessions, one should take their possessions, prepare it, and give it. If they do not have, it should be prepared with one's own possessions. If one oneself also does not have, it should be sought either by the practice of the alms-round or from relatives or from those who have extended an invitation. If one is unable to obtain it, for the sake of the sick person, one should bring and prepare it even by making an inappropriate request.

16. Aparesampi pañcannaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭati mātu pitu tadupaṭṭhākānaṃ attano veyyāvaccakarassa paṇḍupalāsassa cāti. Paṇḍupalāso nāma yo pabbajjāpekkho yāva pattacīvaraṃ paṭiyādiyati, tāva vihāre vasati. Tesu sace mātāpitaro issarā honti na paccāsīsanti, akātuṃ vaṭṭati. Sace pana rajjepi ṭhitā paccāsīsanti, akātuṃ na vaṭṭati. Bhesajjaṃ paccāsīsantānaṃ bhesajjaṃ dātabbaṃ, yojetuṃ ajānantānaṃ yojetvā dātabbaṃ. Sabbesaṃ atthāya sahadhammikesu vuttanayeneva pariyesitabbaṃ. Sace pana mātaraṃ vihāraṃ ānetvā jaggati, sabbaṃ parikammaṃ anāmasantena kātabbaṃ, khādanīyabhojanīyaṃ sahatthā dātabbaṃ. Pitā pana yathā sāmaṇero, evaṃ sahatthena nhāpanasambāhanādīni katvā upaṭṭhātabbo. Ye ca mātāpitaro upaṭṭhahanti paṭijagganti, tesampi evameva kātabbaṃ. Veyyāvaccakaro nāma yo vetanaṃ gahetvā araññe dārūni vā chindati, aññaṃ vā kiñci kammaṃ karoti, tassa roge uppanne yāva ñātakā na passanti, tāva bhesajjaṃ kātabbaṃ. Yo pana bhikkhunissitakova hutvā sabbakammāni karoti, tassa bhesajjaṃ kātabbameva. Paṇḍupalāsepi sāmaṇere viya paṭipajjitabbaṃ.

16. It is also permissible to prepare medicine for five other persons: one’s mother, father, those who attend to them, one’s own attendant, and a paṇḍupalāsa. A paṇḍupalāsa is one who, aspiring for ordination, resides in the monastery for as long as it takes to prepare a bowl and robes. Among these, if one’s parents are independent and do not expect it, it is permissible not to prepare medicine for them. But if they do expect it, even if they hold royal status, it is not permissible to refrain. Medicine should be given to those who expect it; if they do not know how to prepare it, it should be prepared and then given. For all these cases, resources should be sought in the same manner as described for fellow monastics. If one brings one's mother to the monastery to care for her, all services should be performed without touching her, and food should be given with one's own hand. The father, however, should be attended to in the same way as a novice, by personally bathing and massaging him, and so on. The same applies to those who attend and care for one's parents. An attendant is one who, in exchange for wages, cuts wood in the forest or performs some other task. If such an attendant falls ill, medicine should be prepared for them for as long as their relatives do not look after them. But for one who, being solely dependent on a bhikkhu, performs all tasks, medicine must indeed be prepared for them. For a paṇḍupalāsa, one should act as one would for a novice.

17. Aparesampi dasannaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭati jeṭṭhabhātu kaniṭṭhabhātu jeṭṭhabhaginiyā kaniṭṭhabhaginiyā cūḷamātuyā mahāmātuyā cūḷapituno mahāpituno pitucchāya mātulassāti. Tesaṃ pana sabbesampi karontena tesaṃyeva santakaṃ bhesajjaṃ gahetvā kevalaṃ yojetvā dātabbaṃ. Sace [V 0.0011] pana nappahonti yācanti ca “detha no, bhante, tumhākaṃ paṭidassāmā”ti, tāvakālikaṃ dātabbaṃ. Sacepi na yācanti, “amhākaṃ bhesajjaṃ atthi, tāvakālikaṃ gaṇhathā”ti vatvā vā [M 0.0010] “yadā tesaṃ bhavissati, tadā dassantī”ti ābhogaṃ vā katvā dātabbaṃ. Sace paṭidenti, gahetabbaṃ. No ce denti, na codetabbā. Ete dasa ñātake ṭhapetvā aññesaṃ na kātabbaṃ.

17. It is permissible to prepare [medicine] for ten others as well: an elder brother, a younger brother, an elder sister, a younger sister, a stepmother, a great mother (mother's elder sister), a lesser father (father's younger brother), a great father (father's elder brother), a paternal aunt, and a maternal uncle. However, when preparing for any of them, having taken medicine that is their own property, it should be prepared and given using only that. If, however, they do not have enough and they ask, saying, 'Venerable sir, give us what is yours; we will repay,' it should be given as a temporary loan. Even if they do not ask, it should be given either after saying, 'We have medicine; take it as a temporary loan,' or after making the reflection, 'When they have [the means], they will give [it back].' If they give it back, it should be accepted. If they do not give, they should not be pressed. Setting aside these ten relatives, it should not be prepared for others.

Etesaṃ puttaparamparāya pana yāva sattamā kulaparivaṭṭā, tāva cattāro paccaye āharāpentassa akataviññatti vā bhesajjaṃ karontassa vejjakammaṃ vā kuladūsakāpatti vā na hoti. Sace bhātu jāyā, bhaginiyā sāmiko vā gilāno hoti, ñātakā ce, tesampi vaṭṭati. Aññātakā ce, bhātu ca bhaginiyā ca katvā dātabbaṃ “tumhākaṃ jagganaṭṭhāne dethā”ti. Atha vā tesaṃ puttānaṃ katvā dātabbaṃ “tumhākaṃ mātāpitūnaṃ dethā”ti. Etenupāyena sabbapadesu vinicchayo veditabbo.

However, regarding their descendants up to the seventh family generation, for a monk who causes the four requisites to be brought, there is no [offense of] improper request; for one who prepares medicine, there is no [offense of] medical practice; and there is no offense of corrupting families. If a brother's wife or a sister's husband is sick, and if they are [considered] relatives, it is permissible for them also. If they are not [considered] relatives, it should be given after making it the property of the brother and the sister, saying, 'Give this for the care of your charge.' Or alternatively, it should be given after making it the property of their children, saying, 'Give this to your mother and father.' By this method, the ruling should be understood in all such cases.

Tesaṃ atthāya ca sāmaṇerehi araññato bhesajjaṃ āharāpentena ñātisāmaṇerehi vā āharāpetabbaṃ, aññātakehi attano atthāya vā āharāpetvā dātabbaṃ. Tehipi “upajjhāyassa āharāmā”ti vattasīsena āharitabbaṃ. Upajjhāyassa mātāpitaro gilānā vihāraṃ āgacchanti, upajjhāyo ca disāpakkanto hoti, saddhivihārikena upajjhāyassa santakaṃ bhesajjaṃ dātabbaṃ. No ce atthi, attano bhesajjaṃ upajjhāyassa pariccajitvā dātabbaṃ. Attanopi asante vuttanayeneva pariyesitvā upajjhāyassa santakaṃ katvā dātabbaṃ. Upajjhāyenapi saddhivihārikassa mātāpitūsu evameva paṭipajjitabbaṃ. Eseva nayo ācariyantevāsikesupi. Aññopi yo āgantuko vā coro vā yuddhaparājito issaro vā ñātakehi pariccatto kapaṇo vā gamiyamanusso vā gilāno hutvā vihāraṃ pavisati, sabbesaṃ apaccāsīsantena bhesajjaṃ kātabbaṃ.

For their sake, when causing novices to bring medicine from the forest, one should have it brought by relative-novices; or, one should have it brought by non-relative novices for one's own sake and then give it. They too should bring it with duty as the basis, thinking, 'We are bringing it for our preceptor.' If the preceptor's parents come to the monastery sick, and the preceptor has gone to another region, the co-resident disciple should give the medicine belonging to the preceptor. If there is none, having relinquished his own medicine for the preceptor, it should be given. If he himself has none, having searched for it in the manner already stated, he should make it the preceptor's property and then give it. The preceptor, too, should act in this very same way towards the parents of the co-resident disciple. This same method is to be understood also in the case of teachers and their resident pupils. Furthermore, if any visitor, or thief, or ruler defeated in battle, or one abandoned by relatives, or a destitute person, or a traveler, being sick, enters the monastery, medicine should be prepared for all of them without expecting any gain.

18. Saddhaṃ kulaṃ hoti catūhi paccayehi upaṭṭhāyakaṃ bhikkhusaṅghassa mātāpituṭṭhāniyaṃ, tatra ce koci gilāno hoti, tassatthāya vissāsena “bhesajjaṃ katvā bhante dethā”ti vadanti, neva dātabbaṃ na kātabbaṃ. Atha pana kappiyaṃ ñatvā evaṃ pucchanti “bhante, asukassa nāma rogassa kiṃ bhesajjaṃ karontī”ti, “idañcidañca gahetvā karontī”ti vattuṃ vaṭṭati. “Bhante, mayhaṃ mātā gilānā, bhesajjaṃ tāva ācikkhathā”ti evaṃ pucchite pana na ācikkhitabbaṃ, aññamaññaṃ pana kathā kātabbā [M 0.0011] “āvuso, asukassa nāma bhikkhuno imasmiṃ [V 0.0012] roge kiṃ bhesajjaṃ kariṃsū”ti. Idañcidañca bhesajjaṃ bhanteti. Taṃ sutvā itaro mātu bhesajjaṃ karoti, vaṭṭati. Mahāpadumatthero kira vasabharaññopi deviyā roge uppanne ekāya itthiyā āgantvā pucchito “na jānāmī”ti avatvā evameva bhikkhūhi saddhiṃ samullapesi. Taṃ sutvā tassā bhesajjamakaṃsu. Vūpasante ca roge ticīvarena tīhi ca kahāpaṇasatehi saddhiṃ bhesajjacaṅkoṭakaṃ pūretvā āharitvā therassa pādamūle ṭhapetvā “bhante, pupphapūjaṃ karothā”ti āhaṃsu. Thero “ācariyabhāgo nāma aya”nti kappiyavasena gāhāpetvā pupphapūjamakāsi. Evaṃ tāva bhesajje paṭipajjitabbaṃ.

18. A faithful family is a supporter of the community of bhikkhus with the four requisites, standing in the place of mother and father. If someone in that family is sick, and for their benefit they say with familiarity, 'Venerable Sir, having prepared the medicine, please give it,' it should neither be given nor prepared. However, if, knowing what is allowable, they then ask thus, 'Venerable Sir, for such-and-such a disease, what medicine do they make?' it is allowable to say, 'Having taken this and that, they make it.' But when asked thus, 'Venerable Sir, my mother is sick; please instruct me about the medicine,' it should not be told. Instead, a conversation should be had among one another: 'Friend, for the bhikkhu named so-and-so, what medicine did they make for this disease?' 'Venerable Sir, they made this and that medicine.' Having heard that, the other person makes the medicine for his mother; this is allowable. It is said that when a disease arose in the queen of King Vasabha, the Elder Mahāpaduma, having been approached and questioned by a certain woman, did not say, 'I do not know,' but instead conversed with the bhikkhus in this very same manner. Hearing that, they made the medicine for her. And when the disease had subsided, having filled a medicine basket with the three robes and three hundred kahāpaṇas, they brought it, placed it at the Elder's feet, and said, 'Venerable Sir, please make a flower offering.' The Elder, thinking, 'This is called the teacher's portion,' had it accepted by way of what is allowable and made the flower offering. Thus, in the matter of medicine, should one practice.

19. Paritte pana “gilānassa parittaṃ karotha, bhante”ti vutte na kātabbaṃ, “parittaṃ bhaṇathā”ti vutte pana bhaṇitabbaṃ. Sacepissa evaṃ hoti “manussā nāma na jānanti, akariyamāne vippaṭisārino bhavissantī”ti, kātabbaṃ. “Parittodakaṃ parittasuttaṃ katvā dethā”ti vutte pana tesaṃyeva udakaṃ hatthena cāletvā suttaṃ parimajjitvā dātabbaṃ. Sace vihārato udakaṃ attano santakaṃ vā suttaṃ deti, dukkaṭaṃ. Manussā udakañca suttañca gahetvā nisīditvā “parittaṃ bhaṇathā”ti vadanti, kātabbaṃ. No ce jānanti, ācikkhitabbaṃ. Bhikkhūnaṃ nisinnānaṃ pādesu udakaṃ ākiritvā suttañca ṭhapetvā gacchanti “parittaṃ karotha, parittaṃ bhaṇathā”ti, na pādā apanetabbā. Manussā hi vippaṭisārino honti. Antogāmepi gilānassa atthāya vihāraṃ pesenti “parittaṃ bhaṇantū”ti, bhaṇitabbaṃ. Antogāme rājagehādīsu roge vā upaddave vā uppanne pakkosāpetvā bhaṇāpenti, āṭānāṭiyasuttādīni bhaṇitabbāni. “Āgantvā gilānassa sikkhāpadāni dentu, dhammaṃ kathentu, rājantepure vā amaccagehe vā āgantvā sikkhāpadāni dentu, dhammaṃ kathentū”ti pesitepi gantvā sikkhāpadāni dātabbāni, dhammo kathetabbo. “Matānaṃ parivāratthaṃ āgacchantū”ti pakkosanti, na gantabbaṃ. “Sīvathikadassane asubhadassane ca maraṇassatiṃ paṭilabhissāmā”ti kammaṭṭhānasīsena gantuṃ vaṭṭati. “Pahāredinne matepi amaraṇādhippāyassa anāpatti vuttā”ti na ettakeneva amanussagahitassa pahāro dātabbo[M 0.0012], tālapaṇṇaṃ pana parittasuttaṃ vā hatthe vā pāde vā bandhitabbaṃ, ratanasuttādīni parittāni bhaṇitabbāni, “mā sīlavantaṃ bhikkhuṃ viheṭhehī”ti dhammakathā kātabbā, āṭānāṭiyaparittaṃ vā bhaṇitabbaṃ.

19. However, in the matter of protection, when asked, 'Venerable sir, perform a protection for the sick,' it should not be done. But when told, 'Recite the protection,' it should be recited. If it occurs to one thus, 'People do not know; if it is not done, they will become regretful,' it should be done. When told, 'Prepare protection water and a protection thread and give them,' one should stir their own water with the hand, rub the thread, and give it. If one gives water from the monastery or one's own thread, it is an offense of wrong-doing. If people, having taken water and thread, sit down and say, 'Recite the protection,' it should be done. If they do not know, it should be explained to them. If, while bhikkhus are seated, people pour water on their feet, place a thread, and leave, saying, 'Perform the protection, recite the protection,' the feet should not be moved away, for people become regretful. Even within the village, if they send a message to the monastery for the sake of a sick person, saying, 'Let them recite the protection,' it should be recited. If, within the village, in a royal house or the like, a disease or calamity arises and they have bhikkhus summoned and have them recite, suttas such as the Āṭānāṭiya Sutta should be recited. Even when sent with the message, 'Having come, let them give the training precepts to the sick person and speak the Dhamma,' or 'Having come to the royal inner quarters or a minister's house, let them give the training precepts and speak the Dhamma,' one should go, and the training precepts should be given and the Dhamma should be spoken. If they summon, saying, 'Let them come for the sake of an entourage for the dead,' one should not go. It is proper to go with the meditation subject as the basis, thinking, 'By seeing a charnel ground and by seeing the unattractive, we will obtain mindfulness of death.' Just because it is said, 'There is no offense for one who strikes without the intention to kill, even if the other person dies from the blow,' a blow should not be given to one seized by a non-human. Rather, a palm leaf or a protection thread should be tied on the hand or on the foot, protections such as the Ratana Sutta should be recited, a Dhamma talk should be given, saying, 'Do not harass a virtuous bhikkhu,' or the Āṭānāṭiya protection should be recited.

Idha pana āṭānāṭiyaparittassa parikammaṃ veditabbaṃ (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 3.282). Paṭhamameva hi āṭānāṭiyasuttaṃ na bhaṇitabbaṃ, mettasuttaṃ (khu. pā. 9.1 ādayo; su. ni. 143 ādayo) dhajaggasuttaṃ (saṃ. ni. 1.249) ratanasuttanti (khu. pā. 6.1 ādayo; su. ni. 224 ādayo) imāni [V 0.0013] sattāhaṃ bhaṇitabbāni. Sace muñcati, sundaraṃ. No ce muñcati, āṭānāṭiyasuttaṃ bhaṇitabbaṃ. Taṃ bhaṇantena ca bhikkhunā piṭṭhaṃ vā maṃsaṃ vā na khāditabbaṃ, susāne na vasitabbaṃ. Kasmā? Amanussā otāraṃ labhanti. Parittakaraṇaṭṭhānaṃ haritūpalittaṃ kāretvā tattha parisuddhaṃ āsanaṃ paññapetvā nisīditabbaṃ. Parittakārako bhikkhu vihārato gharaṃ nentehi phalakāvudhehi parivāretvā netabbo. Abbhokāse nisīditvā na vattabbaṃ, dvāravātapānāni pidahitvā nisinnena āvudhahatthehi samparivāritena mettacittaṃ purecārikaṃ katvā vattabbaṃ, paṭhamaṃ sikkhāpadāni gāhāpetvā sīle patiṭṭhitassa parittaṃ kātabbaṃ. Evampi mocetuṃ asakkontena vihāraṃ netvā cetiyaṅgaṇe nipajjāpetvā āsanapūjaṃ kāretvā dīpe jālāpetvā cetiyaṅgaṇaṃ sammajjitvā maṅgalakathā vattabbā, sabbasannipāto ghosetabbo, vihārassa upavane jeṭṭhakarukkho nāma hoti, tattha “bhikkhusaṅgho tumhākaṃ āgamanaṃ patimānetī”ti pahiṇitabbaṃ. Sabbasannipātaṭṭhāne anāgantuṃ nāma na labhati, tato amanussagahitako “tvaṃ konāmosī”ti pucchitabbo, nāme kathite nāmeneva ālapitabbo, “itthannāma tuyhaṃ mālāgandhādīsu patti, āsanapūjāyaṃ patti, piṇḍapāte patti, bhikkhusaṅghena tuyhaṃ paṇṇākāratthāya mahāmaṅgalakathā vuttā, bhikkhusaṅghe gāravena etaṃ muñcāhī”ti mocetabbo. Sace na muñcati, devatānaṃ ārocetabbaṃ “tumhe jānātha, ayaṃ amanusso amhākaṃ vacanaṃ na karoti, mayaṃ buddhaāṇaṃ karissāmā”ti parittaṃ kātabbaṃ. Etaṃ tāva gihīnaṃ parikammaṃ. Sace pana bhikkhu amanussena gahito hoti, āsanāni dhovitvā sabbasannipātaṃ ghosāpetvā gandhamālādīsu [M 0.0013] pattiṃ datvā parittaṃ bhaṇitabbaṃ, idaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ parikammaṃ. Evaṃ paritte paṭipajjitabbaṃ.

Here, the preliminary procedure for the Āṭānāṭiya protective discourse should be understood. First, the Āṭānāṭiya Sutta should not be recited. The Mettā Sutta, the Dhajagga Sutta, and the Ratana Sutta—these should be recited for seven days. If the afflicted is released, it is excellent. If not released, the Āṭānāṭiya Sutta should be recited. While reciting it, a monk should not eat flour cake or meat, nor should he dwell in a charnel ground. Why? Non-human beings gain an opening. The place for performing the protective discourse should be prepared by having it smeared with fresh cow-dung, and a clean seat should be arranged there to sit upon. The monk performing the protection should be led from the monastery to the house, surrounded by men bearing shields and weapons. One should not recite while sitting in an open space. The doors and windows should be closed, and one should sit surrounded by armed men, having made loving-kindness the forerunner, and then recite. First, after making the person undertake the training precepts and establishing them in virtue, the protective discourse should be performed. If even then one is unable to free them, the afflicted should be taken to the monastery and made to lie down in the shrine courtyard. An offering of seats should be performed, lamps should be lit, the shrine courtyard should be swept, and an auspicious discourse should be spoken. A general assembly should be proclaimed. In the monastery’s grove, there is a principal tree. A message should be sent there: “The community of monks awaits your coming.” At the place of the general assembly, it is not possible for them not to come. Then, the one seized by a non-human being should be asked, “What is your name?” When the name is stated, they should be addressed by that name: “So-and-so, a share in garlands, perfumes, and so forth has been given to you; a share in the offering of seats; a share in the almsfood. For your sake as a gift, the community of monks has spoken a great auspicious discourse. Out of respect for the community of monks, release this one.” Thus, they should be made to release the person. If they do not release, it should be announced to the deities: “You should know that this non-human being does not heed our words. We will act by the Buddha’s command.” Then the protective discourse should be performed. This is the preliminary procedure for laypersons. But if a monk is seized by a non-human being, the seats should be washed, a general assembly should be proclaimed, a share in perfumes, garlands, and so forth should be given, and the protective discourse should be recited. This is the preliminary procedure for monks. Thus, one should proceed with the protective discourse.

20. Paṭisanthāre pana ayaṃ vinicchayo (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.185-7) – anāmaṭṭhapiṇḍapāto kassa dātabbo, kassa na dātabbo? Mātāpitūnaṃ tāva dātabbo. Sacepi kahāpaṇagghanako hoti, saddhādeyyavinipātanaṃ natthi. Mātāpituupaṭṭhākānaṃ veyyāvaccakarassa paṇḍupalāsassa cāti etesampi dātabbo. Tattha paṇḍupalāsassa thālake pakkhipitvāpi dātuṃ vaṭṭati, taṃ ṭhapetvā aññesaṃ agārikānaṃ mātāpitūnampi na vaṭṭati. Pabbajitaparibhogo hi agārikānaṃ cetiyaṭṭhāniyo. Apica anāmaṭṭhapiṇḍapātho nāmesa sampattassa dāmarikacorassapi issariyassapi dātabbo. Kasmā? Te hi adīyamānepi “na dentī”ti āmasitvā dīyamānepi “ucchiṭṭhakaṃ dentī”ti kujjhanti, kuddhā jīvitāpi voropenti, sāsanassapi antarāyaṃ karonti. Rajjaṃ patthayamānassa vicarato coranāgassa vatthu cettha kathetabbaṃ. Evaṃ anāmaṭṭhapiṇḍapāte paṭipajjitabbaṃ.

20. Now, regarding hospitality, this is the determination to be known concerning untouched almsfood: To whom should it be given? To whom should it not be given? First, it should be given to one’s mother and father. Even if it is worth a kahāpaṇa, there is no destruction of an offering given in faith. It should also be given to those who attend on one's mother and father, to one's attendant, and to a postulant. Among them, it is permissible to give to a postulant even by placing it in his bowl. Setting him aside, it is not permissible to give to other householders—even to one's mother and father—by placing it in the bowl. For, to householders, a requisite of one who has gone forth stands in the place of a shrine. Moreover, this so-called untouched almsfood should be given to a rebel robber or a ruler who has arrived. Why? For if it is not given, they become angry, saying, 'They do not give'; and if it is given after having been handled, they become angry, saying, 'They give leftovers.' Being angry, they may even deprive one of life and may cause harm to the Dispensation. Here, the story of the robber Nāga, who, desiring kingship, was wandering about, should be told. Thus should one practice with regard to untouched almsfood.

Paṭisanthāro [V 0.0014] ca nāmāyaṃ kassa kātabbo, kassa na kātabbo? Paṭisanthāro nāma vihāraṃ sampattassa yassa kassaci āgantukassa vā daliddassa vā corassa vā issarassa vā kātabboyeva. Kathaṃ? Āgantukaṃ tāva khīṇaparibbayaṃ vihāraṃ sampattaṃ disvā “pānīyaṃ pivā”ti dātabbaṃ, pādamakkhanatelaṃ dātabbaṃ, kāle āgatassa yāgubhattaṃ, vikāle āgatassa sace taṇḍulā atthi, taṇḍulā dātabbā. Avelāya sampattopi “gacchāhī”ti na vattabbo, sayanaṭṭhānaṃ dātabbaṃ. Sabbaṃ apaccāsīyanteneva kātabbaṃ. “Manussā nāma catupaccayadāyakā, evaṃ saṅgahe kariyamāne punappunaṃ pasīditvā upakāraṃ karissantī”ti cittaṃ na uppādetabbaṃ. Corānaṃ pana saṅghikampi dātabbaṃ. Paṭisanthārānisaṃsadīpanatthañca coranāgavatthu, bhātarā saddhiṃ jambudīpagatassa mahānāgarañño vatthu, piturājassa rajje catunnaṃ amaccānaṃ vatthu, abhayacoravatthūti evamādīni bahūni vatthūni mahāaṭṭhakathāyaṃ vitthārato vuttāni.

And this hospitality—to whom should it be shown, and to whom should it not be shown? Hospitality should indeed be shown to anyone who has arrived at the monastery, whether a guest, a poor person, a robber, or a ruler. How? Upon seeing a guest who has arrived at the monastery with exhausted provisions, water to drink should be given, and oil for anointing the feet should be given. If one has arrived at the proper time, gruel and a meal should be given; if one has arrived at an improper time, and if there are rice grains, rice grains should be given. Even one who has arrived at an inconvenient time should not be dismissed with, 'Go away'; a sleeping place should be given. All this should be done without expecting anything in return. The thought should not arise, 'People are donors of the four requisites; when such support is given, they will be pleased again and again and will render assistance in return.' To robbers, even what belongs to the Sangha should be given. And for the purpose of illustrating the benefits of hospitality, the story of the robber Nāga, the story of King Mahānāga who went to Jambudīpa with his brother, the story of the four ministers in the kingdom of the father-king, the story of the robber Abhaya, and many other such stories are told in detail in the Great Commentary.

Tatrāyaṃ ekavatthudīpanā – sīhaḷadīpe kira abhayo nāma coro pañcasataparivāro ekasmiṃ ṭhāne khandhāvāraṃ bandhitvā samantā tiyojanaṃ ubbāsetvā [M 0.0014] vasati. Anurādhapuravāsino kadambanadiṃ na uttaranti, cetiyagirimagge janasañcāro upacchinno. Athekadivasaṃ coro “cetiyagiriṃ vilumpissāmī”ti agamāsi. Ārāmikā disvā dīghabhāṇakaabhayattherassa ārocesuṃ. Thero “sappiphāṇitādīni atthī”ti pucchi. “Atthi, bhante”ti. “Corānaṃ detha”. “Taṇḍulā atthī”ti. “Atthi, bhante, saṅghassatthāya āhaṭā taṇḍulā ca pakkasākañca goraso cā”ti. “Bhattaṃ sampādetvā corānaṃ dethā”ti. Ārāmikā tathā kariṃsu. Corā bhattaṃ bhuñjitvā “kenāyaṃ paṭisanthāro kato”ti pucchiṃsu. “Amhākaṃ ayyena abhayattherenā”ti. Corā therassa santikaṃ gantvā vanditvā āhaṃsu “mayaṃ ‘saṅghassa ca cetiyassa ca santakaṃ acchinditvā gahessāmā’ti āgatā, tumhākaṃ pana iminā paṭisanthārena mayaṃ pasannā, ajja paṭṭhāya vihāre dhammikārakkhā amhākaṃ āyattā hotu, nāgarā āgantvā dānaṃ dentu, cetiyaṃ vandantū”ti. Tato paṭṭhāya ca nāgare dānaṃ dātuṃ āgacchante nadītīreyeva paccuggantvā rakkhantā vihāraṃ nenti, vihārepi dānaṃ dentānaṃ rakkhaṃ katvā tiṭṭhanti. Tepi bhikkhūnaṃ bhuttāvasesaṃ corānaṃ denti. Gamanakālepi te corā nadītīraṃ pāpetvā nivattanti.

Herein is the exposition of a single story: In the island of Sīhaḷa, it is said, a robber named Abhaya with a retinue of five hundred established a stronghold in one place and dwelt, having terrorized an area of three yojanas all around. The inhabitants of Anurādhapura did not cross the Kadamba River, and the movement of people on the road to Cetiyagiri was cut off. Then one day, the robber went, thinking, 'I will plunder Cetiyagiri.' The monastery attendants saw this and reported it to the Elder Abhaya, the reciter of the Dīgha Nikāya. The Elder asked, 'Are there ghee, molasses, and so forth?' 'There are, venerable sir.' 'Give them to the robbers.' 'Are there rice grains?' 'There are, venerable sir: rice grains brought for the sake of the Saṅgha, cooked vegetables, and dairy products.' 'Prepare a meal and give it to the robbers.' The attendants did so. The robbers, having eaten the meal, asked, 'By whom was this friendly reception provided?' 'By our master, the Elder Abhaya.' The robbers went to the Elder’s presence, paid homage, and said, 'We came thinking, “We will seize what belongs to the Saṅgha and the cetiya,” but we are pleased by this friendly reception of yours. From today onwards, let the righteous protection of the monastery be our responsibility. Let the townspeople come and give alms, and let them worship the cetiya.' And from then on, when townspeople came to give alms, the robbers would meet them at the very riverbank and, while protecting them, lead them to the monastery. In the monastery too, they would stand providing protection for those giving alms. And those townspeople also gave the leftovers from the monks' meal to the robbers. At the time of departure, those robbers would escort them to the riverbank and then return.

Athekadivasaṃ bhikkhusaṅghe khīyanakakathā uppannā “thero issaravatāya saṅghasantakaṃ corānaṃ adāsī”ti. Thero sannipātaṃ kārāpetvā āha “corā ‘saṅghassa pakativaṭṭañca cetiyasantakañca acchinditvā gaṇhissāmā’ti āgamiṃsu, atha tesaṃ mayā ‘etaṃ na harissantī’ti ettako nāma paṭisanthāro kato, taṃ sabbampi ekato sampiṇḍetvā agghāpetha, tena [V 0.0015] kāraṇena aviluttaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ ekato sampiṇḍetvā agghāpethā”ti. Tato sabbampi therena dinnakaṃ cetiyaghare ekaṃ varapotthakacittattharaṇaṃ na agghati. Tato āhaṃsu “therena kato paṭisanthāro sukato, codetuṃ vā sāretuṃ vā na labbhati, gīvā vā avahāro vā natthī”ti. Evaṃ mahānisaṃso paṭisanthāroti sallakkhetvā kattabbo paṇḍitena bhikkhunāti.

Then, one day, a talk of criticism arose in the community of monks: 'The Elder, by his authority, gave the Saṅgha's property to robbers.' The Elder, having caused an assembly to be convened, said: 'The robbers came thinking, “We will plunder and take the Saṅgha's regular requisites and the cetiya's property.” Then, a certain conciliatory gesture was made by me to them, thinking, “They will not take this away.” Having gathered all of that together, you should assess its value. For that reason, having gathered the unplundered goods together, you should assess their value.' Then, all that was given by the Elder was not worth even a single excellent, variegated cloth-covering decorated with figures in the cetiya-house. Then they said: 'The conciliatory gesture made by the Elder was well done. It is not possible to accuse or to remind him of a fault. There is neither restitution nor theft.' Thus, having recognized that a conciliatory gesture is of great benefit, it should be done by a wise monk.

Iti pāḷimuttakavinayavinicchayasaṅgahe

Thus in the Compilation of Vinaya Decisions Independent of the Pāḷi Canon,

Bhesajjādikaraṇavinicchayakathā samattā.

The Discourse on Decisions Concerning Matters of Medicine and So Forth is concluded.

4. Viññattivinicchayakathā

4. The Discourse on Decisions Concerning Intimation

21. Viññattīti [M 0.0015][V 0.0016] yācanā. Tatrāyaṃ vinicchayo (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.342) – mūlacchejjāya purisaṃ yācituṃ na vaṭṭati, “sahāyatthāya kammakaraṇatthāya purisaṃ dethā”ti yācituṃ vaṭṭati, purisena kattabbaṃ hatthakammasaṅkhātaṃ purisattakaraṃ yācituṃ vaṭṭatiyeva. Hatthakammañhi kiñci vatthu na hoti, tasmā taṃ ṭhapetvā migaluddakamacchabandhanakādīnaṃ sakakammaṃ avasesaṃ sabbaṃ kappiyaṃ. “Kiṃ, bhante, āgatāttha kena kammenā”ti pucchite vā apucchite vā yācituṃ vaṭṭati, viññattipaccayā doso natthi. Migaluddakādayo pana sakakammaṃ na yācitabbā, “hatthakammaṃ dethā”ti aniyametvāpi na yācitabbā. Evaṃ yācitā hi te “sādhu, bhante”ti bhikkhū uyyojetvā migepi māretvā āhareyyuṃ. Niyametvā pana “vihāre kiñci kattabbaṃ atthi, tattha hatthakammaṃ dethā”ti yācitabbā, phālanaṅgalādīni upakaraṇāni gahetvā kasituṃ vā vapituṃ vā lāyituṃ vā gacchantaṃ sakakiccapasutampi kassakaṃ vā aññaṃ vā kiñci hatthakammaṃ yācituṃ vaṭṭateva. Yo pana vighāsādo vā añño vā koci nikkammo niratthakakathaṃ kathento niddāyanto vā viharati, evarūpaṃ ayācitvāpi “ehi re idaṃ vā idaṃ vā karohī”ti yadicchakaṃ kārāpetuṃ vaṭṭati.

21. "Viññatti" means requesting. Herein is the decision: It is not allowable to ask for a person for the purpose of uprooting. It is allowable to ask, "Give a person for the purpose of assistance or for the purpose of performing work." It is indeed allowable to ask for manual labor to be performed by a person. For manual labor is not a material object; therefore, setting aside the personal work of hunters, fishermen, and the like, all the remaining types of manual labor are allowable. Whether one is asked, "Venerable sirs, for what reason have you come? What work is there?" or not, it is allowable to ask for it. There is no fault on account of the request. However, hunters and the like should not be asked for their own work; even without specifying, they should not be asked, "Give manual labor." For if asked in this way, they might say, "Very well, venerable sirs," send the bhikkhus away, and then kill deer and bring them. However, by specifying, they should be asked, "There is something to be done in the monastery; give manual labor there." It is indeed allowable to ask for some manual labor from a farmer or another person, even one who is engaged in their own task, who is on their way to plow, sow, or reap, having taken up implements such as a plowshare and plow. But as for someone who is an eater of leftovers, or some other idle person who dwells speaking useless talk or sleeping, it is allowable to have such a person do whatever one wishes, even without asking, saying, "Come, do this or that."

Hatthakammassa pana sabbakappiyabhāvadīpanatthaṃ imaṃ nayaṃ kathenti. Sace hi bhikkhu pāsādaṃ kāretukāmo hoti, thambhatthāya pāsāṇakoṭṭakānaṃ gharaṃ gantvā vattabbaṃ “hatthakammaṃ laddhuṃ vaṭṭati upāsakā”ti. “Kiṃ kātabbaṃ, bhante”ti? “Pāsāṇatthambhā uddharitvā dātabbā”ti. Sace te uddharitvā vā denti, uddharitvā nikkhitte attano thambhe vā denti, vaṭṭati. Athāpi vadanti “amhākaṃ, bhante, hatthakammaṃ kātuṃ khaṇo natthi, aññaṃ uddharāpetha, tassa mūlaṃ dassāmā”ti, uddharāpetvā “pāsāṇatthambhe uddhaṭamanussānaṃ mūlaṃ dethā”ti vattuṃ vaṭṭati. Eteneva upāyena pāsādadārūnaṃ atthāya vaḍḍhakīnaṃ santikaṃ, iṭṭhakatthāya iṭṭhakavaḍḍhakīnaṃ, chadanatthāya gehacchādakānaṃ, cittakammatthāya cittakārānanti yena yena attho hoti, tassa tassa atthāya tesaṃ tesaṃ sippakārakānaṃ santikaṃ gantvā hatthakammaṃ yācituṃ vaṭṭati, hatthakammayācanavasena ca mūlacchejjāya vā bhattavetanānuppadānena vā laddhampi sabbaṃ gahetuṃ vaṭṭati. Araññato āharāpentena ca sabbaṃ anajjhāvutthakaṃ āharāpetabbaṃ.

Furthermore, to show that manual labor is entirely permissible, the teachers state this method. Indeed, if a bhikkhu wishes to have a mansion built, he should go to the house of stonecutters for the purpose of pillars and say, 'Lay devotees, it is permissible to receive manual labor.' When they ask, 'Venerable sir, what is to be done?' he should reply, 'Stone pillars are to be extracted and given.' If they extract and give them, or give their own pillars that have been extracted and set aside, it is permissible. And if they say, 'Venerable sir, we have no time to perform manual labor; have someone else extract them, and we will give the payment to that person,' it is permissible to have them extracted and then say, 'Give the payment to the people who extracted the stone pillars.' By this very method, for the purpose of timber for the mansion, he may go to carpenters; for bricks, to brickmakers; for roofing, to roofers; for decorative work, to painters—thus for whatever is needed, he may go to the respective craftsmen for that purpose and request manual labor. And by means of requesting manual labor, it is permissible to accept everything received, whether as an outright acquisition or through the provision of food and wages. And when having things brought from the forest, everything that is caused to be brought must be un-owned.

22. Na [M 0.0016][V 0.0017] kevalañca pāsādaṃ kāretukāmena, mañcapīṭhapattaparissāvanadhamakaraṇacīvarādīni kārāpetukāmenapi dārulohasuttādīni labhitvā te te sippakārake upasaṅkamitvā vuttanayeneva hatthakammaṃ yācitabbaṃ. Hatthakammayācanavasena ca mūlacchejjāya vā bhattavetanānuppadānena vā laddhampi sabbaṃ gahetabbaṃ. Sace pana kātuṃ na icchanti, bhattavetanaṃ paccāsīsanti, akappiyakahāpaṇādi na dātabbaṃ, bhikkhācāravattena taṇḍulādīni pariyesitvā dātuṃ vaṭṭati. Hatthakammavasena pattaṃ kāretvā tatheva pācetvā navapakkassa pattassa puñchanatelatthāya antogāmaṃ paviṭṭhena “bhikkhāya āgato”ti sallakkhetvā yāguyā vā bhatte vā ānīte hatthena patto pidhātabbo. Sace upāsikā “kiṃ, bhante”ti pucchati, “navapakko patto, puñchanatelena attho”ti vattabbaṃ. Sace sā “dehi, bhante”ti pattaṃ gahetvā telena puñchitvā yāguyā vā bhattassa vā pūretvā deti, viññatti nāma na hoti, gahetuṃ vaṭṭati.

22. And not only by one who wishes to have a mansion constructed, but also by one who desires to have beds, chairs, bowls, water-strainers, robes, and other such items made, having obtained wood, metal, thread, and so on, one should approach the respective craftsmen and request manual labor in the very manner that has been stated. And by means of requesting manual labor, everything received is to be accepted, whether as an outright acquisition or through the provision of food and wages. If, however, they do not wish to make it and they expect food and wages, impermissible items such as kahāpaṇas are not to be given; it is permissible to seek rice and so on by the practice of the alms-round and give it. Having had a bowl made by means of manual labor and having had it fired in the same way, when entering a village for the purpose of obtaining oil for wiping the newly fired bowl, if, after one has indicated, 'I have come for alms,' gruel or cooked rice is brought, the bowl should be covered with the hand. If a laywoman asks, 'What is it, venerable sir?' one should say, 'The bowl is newly fired; there is a need for oil for wiping.' If she says, 'Give it, venerable sir,' takes the bowl, wipes it with oil, fills it with gruel or cooked rice, and gives it, this is not what is called a request—it is permissible to accept.

23. Bhikkhū pageva piṇḍāya caritvā āsanasālaṃ gantvā āsanaṃ apassantā tiṭṭhanti. Tatra ce upāsakā bhikkhū ṭhite disvā sayameva āsanāni āharāpenti, nisīditvā gacchantehi āpucchitvā gantabbaṃ, anāpucchā gatānampi naṭṭhaṃ gīvā na hoti, āpucchitvā gamanaṃ pana vattaṃ. Sace bhikkhūhi “āsanāni āharathā”ti vuttehi āhaṭāni honti, āpucchitvāva gantabbaṃ, anāpucchā gatānaṃ vattabhedo ca naṭṭhañca gīvā. Attharaṇakojavakādīsupi eseva nayo.

23. Bhikkhus, having gone for alms quite early and having gone to the seating hall, stand when not seeing a seat. There, if lay devotees, seeing the bhikkhus standing, have seats brought of their own accord, having sat down, those who are leaving should go after asking permission. Even for those who have gone without asking permission, if a seat is lost, no compensation is required; but going after asking permission is the proper conduct. If the seats are those that were brought by people who were told by the bhikkhus, 'Bring seats,' one must certainly go only after asking permission. For those who go without asking permission, there is both a breach of proper conduct and, if a seat is lost, compensation is required. This very same principle is to be understood also in the case of floor-coverings, rugs, and so on.

Makkhikā bahukā honti, “makkhikabījaniṃ āharathā”ti vattabbaṃ, pucimandasākhādīni āharanti, kappiyaṃ kārāpetvā paṭiggahetabbāni. Āsanasālāyaṃ udakabhājanaṃ rittaṃ hoti, “dhamakaraṇaṃ gaṇhāhī”ti na vattabbaṃ. Dhamakaraṇañhi rittabhājane pakkhipanto bhindeyya, “nadiṃ vā taḷākaṃ vā gantvā udakaṃ āharā”ti pana vattuṃ vaṭṭati, “gehato āharā”ti neva vattuṃ vaṭṭati, na āhaṭaṃ paribhuñjituṃ. Āsanasālāya vā araññe vā bhattakiccaṃ karontehi tattha jātakaṃ anajjhāvutthakaṃ yaṃ kiñci uttaribhaṅgārahaṃ pattaṃ vā phalaṃ vā sace kiñci kammaṃ karontaṃ āharāpeti, hatthakammavasena āharāpetvā paribhuñjituṃ vaṭṭati, alajjīhi pana bhikkhūhi vā sāmaṇerehi vā hatthakammaṃ na kāretabbaṃ. Ayaṃ tāva purisattakare nayo.

If there are many flies, it should be said, 'Bring a fly-whisk.' If they bring neem branches and so on, having had them made permissible, they are to be accepted. In the dining hall, if the water pot is empty, it should not be said, 'Take the water-strainer.' For one putting the water-strainer into an empty pot might break it. But it is permissible to say, 'Go to the river or the lake and fetch water.' It is not at all permissible to say, 'Bring it from the house,' nor is it permissible to use what has been brought. When scrupulous bhikkhus or novices are performing their meal-duty in a dining hall or in the forest, if they have any leaf or fruit whatsoever—which has grown there, is un-owned, and is suitable for an extra dish—brought by someone who is doing some work, it is permissible to have it brought by means of manual labor and to use it. However, shameless bhikkhus or novices should not have manual labor performed. This, for now, is the method concerning human labor.

24. Goṇaṃ [M 0.0017] pana aññātakaappavāritaṭṭhānato āharāpetuṃ na vaṭṭati, āharāpentassa dukkaṭaṃ. Ñātakapavāritaṭṭhānatopi mūlacchejjāya yācituṃ na vaṭṭati, tāvakālikanayena sabbattha vaṭṭati. Evaṃ āharāpitañca goṇaṃ rakkhitvā jaggitvā sāmikā paṭicchāpetabbā. Sacassa pādo [V 0.0018] vā siṅgaṃ vā bhijjati vā nassati vā, sāmikā ce sampaṭicchanti, iccetaṃ kusalaṃ. No ce sampaṭicchanti, gīvā hoti. Sace “tumhākaṃyeva demā”ti vadanti, na sampaṭicchitabbaṃ. “Vihārassa demā”ti vutte pana “ārāmikānaṃ ācikkhatha jagganatthāyā”ti vattabbā.

24. However, it is not permissible to have an ox brought from non-relatives or from those who have not given an invitation; for one who has it brought, there is an offense of wrong-doing. Even from relatives and those who have given an invitation, it is not permissible to request it for permanent acquisition; it is permissible everywhere only on a temporary basis. An ox brought in this way should be guarded, tended, and returned to the owners. If its foot or horn is broken or it is lost, and if the owners forbear, this is blameless. If they do not forbear, compensation is required. If they say, 'We give it only to you,' it should not be accepted. But when it is said, 'We give it to the monastery,' they should be told, 'Inform the monastery attendants for the purpose of tending it.'

25. “Sakaṭaṃ dethā”tipi aññātakaappavārite vattuṃ na vaṭṭati, viññatti eva hoti, dukkaṭaṃ āpajjati. Ñātakapavāritaṭṭhāne pana vaṭṭati, tāvakālikaṃ vaṭṭati, kammaṃ pana katvā puna dātabbaṃ. Sace nemiādīni bhijjanti, pākatikāni katvā dātabbaṃ, naṭṭhe gīvā hoti. “Tumhākameva demā”ti vutte dārubhaṇḍaṃ nāma sampaṭicchituṃ vaṭṭati. Esa nayo vāsipharasukuṭhārīkudālanikhādanesu valliādīsu ca parapariggahitesu. Garubhaṇḍappahonakesuyeva valliādīsu viññatti hoti, na tato oraṃ.

25. It is not permissible to say, 'Give a cart,' to non-relatives or those who have not given an invitation; it is simply a request (viññatti), and one incurs a dukkaṭa offense. In the case of relatives and those who have given an invitation, however, it is permissible. To ask for temporary use is also permissible; however, after the work is done, it must be given back. If the rims or other parts should break, they must be restored to their original condition and given back. If it is lost, compensation is required. When it is said, 'We give it to you only,' it is permissible to accept what is called a wooden article. This same principle is to be understood regarding an adze, axe, hatchet, hoe, digging spade, and vines, etc., that are in the possession of others. Regarding vines, etc., a request (viññatti) occurs only when they are sufficient to be heavy goods, not for anything less than that.

26. Anajjhāvutthakaṃ pana yaṃ kiñci āharāpetuṃ vaṭṭati. Rakkhitagopitaṭṭhāneyeva hi viññatti nāma vuccati. Sā dvīsu paccayesu sabbena sabbaṃ na vaṭṭati. Senāsanapaccaye pana “āhara dehī”ti viññattimattameva na vaṭṭati, parikathobhāsanimittakammāni vaṭṭanti. Tattha uposathāgāraṃ vā bhojanasālaṃ vā aññaṃ vā kiñci senāsanaṃ icchato “imasmiṃ vata okāse evarūpaṃ senāsanaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti vā “yutta”nti vā “anurūpa”nti vātiādinā nayena vacanaṃ parikathā nāma. Upāsakā tumhe kuhiṃ vasathāti. Pāsāde, bhanteti. “Kiṃ bhikkhūnaṃ pana upāsakā pāsādo na vaṭṭatī”ti evamādivacanaṃ obhāso nāma. Manusse disvā rajjuṃ pasāreti, khīle ākoṭāpeti, “kiṃ idaṃ, bhante”ti vutte “idha āvāsaṃ karissāmā”ti evamādikaraṇaṃ pana nimittakammaṃ nāma. Gilānapaccaye pana viññattipi vaṭṭati, pageva parikathādīni.

26. However, it is proper to have brought anything whatsoever that is not taken possession of by an owner. Indeed, what is called a 'request' (viññatti) is spoken of only in a guarded and protected place. That request is not proper in any way at all regarding the two requisites of robes and almsfood. However, regarding the requisite of lodging, merely a request such as, 'Bring it; give it,' is not proper; allusive talk (parikathā), hinting (obhāsa), and making a sign (nimittakamma) are proper. Therein, for one who desires an Uposatha hall, a dining hall, or any other lodging, speech in the manner of, 'Indeed, in this spot it is proper to build such a lodging,' or 'It is suitable,' or 'It is appropriate,' and so on, is called allusive talk. When asked, 'Lay supporters, where do you live?' and they reply, 'In a mansion, venerable sir,' speech such as, 'Lay supporters, but is a mansion not proper for monks?' is called a hint. Seeing people, one stretches out a rope or has stakes hammered in; when asked, 'Venerable sir, what is this?' an act such as replying, 'We will make a dwelling here,' is called making a sign. However, regarding the requisite for the sick, even a request is proper, let alone allusive talk and the others.

Iti pāḷimuttakavinayavinicchayasaṅgahe

Thus in the Compilation of Vinaya Determinations Independent of the Canon,

Viññattivinicchayakathā samattā.

The Discourse on the Determination of Requests is concluded.

5. Kulasaṅgahavinicchayakathā

5. The Discourse on the Determination of Supporting Families

27. Kulasaṅgahoti [M 0.0018][V 0.0019] pupphaphalādīhi kulānaṃ saṅgaho kulasaṅgaho. Tatrāyaṃ vinicchayo (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.431) – kulasaṅgahatthāya mālāvacchādīni ropetuṃ vā ropāpetuṃ vā siñcituṃ vā siñcāpetuṃ vā pupphāni ocinituṃ vā ocināpetuṃ vā ganthituṃ vā ganthāpetuṃ vā na vaṭṭati. Tattha akappiyavohāro kappiyavohāro pariyāyo obhāso nimittakammanti imāni pañca jānitabbāni.

27. Supporting families means the winning over of families by means of flowers, fruits, and so on.
