In that regard, this is the determination: For the purpose of supporting families, it is not allowable to plant or have planted flower saplings and so on, to water or have watered, to pluck or have plucked flowers, or to string or have strung them. In this connection, these five should be understood: unallowable expression, allowable expression, circumlocution, giving a hint, and making a sign.

28. Tattha akappiyavohāro nāma allaharitānaṃ koṭṭanaṃ koṭṭāpanaṃ, āvāṭassa khaṇanaṃ khaṇāpanaṃ, mālāvacchassa ropanaṃ ropāpanaṃ, āḷiyā bandhanaṃ bandhāpanaṃ, udakassa secanaṃ secāpanaṃ, mātikāya sammukhakaraṇaṃ, kappiyaudakasiñcanaṃ, hatthapādamukhadhovananahānodakasiñcanaṃ. Kappiyavohāro nāma “imaṃ rukkhaṃ jāna, imaṃ āvāṭaṃ jāna, imaṃ mālāvacchaṃ jāna, ettha udakaṃ jānā”tiādivacanaṃ sukkhamātikāya ujukaraṇañca. Pariyāyo nāma “paṇḍitena mālāvacchādayo ropāpetabbā, nacirasseva upakārāya saṃvattantī”tiādivacanaṃ. Obhāso nāma kudālakhaṇittādīni ca mālāvacche ca gahetvā ṭhānaṃ. Evaṃ ṭhitañhi sāmaṇerādayo disvā “thero kārāpetukāmo”ti gantvā karonti. Nimittakammaṃ nāma kudālakhaṇittivāsipharasuudakabhājanāni āharitvā samīpe ṭhapanaṃ.

28. Herein, 'unallowable expression' means: pounding or causing to be pounded fresh green plants; digging or causing to be dug a pit; planting or causing to be planted a flower sapling; building or causing to be built an embankment; sprinkling or causing to be sprinkled water; directing a water channel towards something; sprinkling with allowable water; and sprinkling with water for washing hands, feet, and face, or for bathing. 'Allowable expression' means statements such as, 'Know this tree,' 'Know this pit,' 'Know this flower sapling,' 'Know the water here,' and also straightening a dry channel. 'Circumlocution' means statements such as, 'Flower saplings and so on should be caused to be planted by a wise person; they become beneficial before long.' 'Giving a hint' means taking a hoe, a digging spade, and so on, and flower saplings, and standing there. For, seeing one standing thus, novices and others go and do it, thinking, 'The elder wishes to have it done.' 'Making a sign' means bringing a hoe, a digging spade, an adze, an axe, a water pot, and so on, and placing them nearby.

29. Imāni pañcapi kulasaṅgahatthāya ropanaropāpanādīsu na vaṭṭanti. Phalaparibhogatthāya kappiyākappiyavohāradvayameva na vaṭṭati, itarattayaṃ vaṭṭati. Mahāpaccariyaṃ pana “kappiyavohāropi vaṭṭati, yañca attano paribhogatthāya vaṭṭati, taṃ aññapuggalassa vā saṅghassa vā cetiyassa vā atthāyapi vaṭṭatī”ti vuttaṃ. Ārāmatthāya pana vanatthāya chāyatthāya ca akappiyavohāramattameva na vaṭṭati, sesaṃ vaṭṭati. Na kevalañca sesaṃ, yaṃ kiñci mātikampi ujuṃ kātuṃ kappiyaudakaṃ siñcituṃ nahānakoṭṭhakaṃ katvā nahāyituṃ hatthapādamukhadhovanaudakāni ca tattha chaḍḍetumpi vaṭṭati. Mahāpaccariyaṃ pana kurundiyañca “kappiyapathaviyaṃ sayaṃ ropetumpi vaṭṭatī”ti vuttaṃ. Ārāmādiatthāya pana ropitassa vā ropāpitassa vā phalaṃ paribhuñjitumpi vaṭṭati.

29. These five are not allowable for the purpose of supporting families, in matters of planting, causing to be planted, and so on. For the purpose of consuming the fruit, only the pair of expressions—allowable and unallowable—is not allowable; the other three are allowable. However, in the Mahāpaccariya it is stated: 'Even an allowable expression is allowable, and that which is allowable for one's own consumption is also allowable for the benefit of another person, or of the Saṅgha, or of a cetiya.' Furthermore, for the purpose of a monastery, for the purpose of a forest, and for the purpose of shade, only an unallowable expression is not allowable; the rest is allowable. And not only is the rest allowable, but it is also allowable to straighten any water channel, to sprinkle it with allowable water, to make a bathing enclosure and bathe, and also to discard there water for washing hands, feet, and face. However, in the Mahāpaccariya and the Kurundī it is stated: 'It is allowable to plant oneself on allowable ground.' Furthermore, for the purpose of a monastery and so on, it is also allowable to consume the fruit of that which has been planted or caused to be planted.

30. Ayaṃ [M 0.0019][V 0.0020] pana ādito paṭṭhāya vitthārena āpattivinicchayo – kuladūsanatthāya akappiyapathaviyaṃ mālāvacchaṃ ropentassa pācittiyañceva dukkaṭañca, tathā akappiyavohārena ropāpentassa. Kappiyapathaviyaṃ ropanepi ropāpanepi dukkaṭameva. Ubhayatrāpi sakiṃ āṇattiyā bahūnampi ropane ekameva sapācittiyadukkaṭaṃ vā suddhadukkaṭaṃ vā hoti. Paribhogatthāya kappiyabhūmiyaṃ vā akappiyabhūmiyaṃ vā kappiyavohārena ropāpane anāpatti. Ārāmādiatthāyapi akappiyapathaviyaṃ ropentassa vā akappiyavacanena ropāpentassa vā pācittiyaṃ. Ayaṃ pana nayo mahāaṭṭhakathāyaṃ na suṭṭhu vibhatto, mahāpaccariyaṃ pana vibhattoti.

30. Now, this is the detailed determination of offenses, beginning from the start: For one who plants a flower sapling on unallowable ground for the purpose of corrupting a family, there is both a pācittiya and a dukkaṭa offense; likewise for one who causes it to be planted with an unallowable expression. On allowable ground, for both planting and causing to be planted for the purpose of corrupting a family, there is only a dukkaṭa offense. In both cases, with a single command to plant many, there is only one offense, either a dukkaṭa together with a pācittiya, or a simple dukkaṭa. For the purpose of consumption, in causing something to be planted with an allowable expression, whether on allowable ground or unallowable ground, there is no offense. Also, for the purpose of a monastery and so on, for one who plants on unallowable ground or for one who causes it to be planted with unallowable speech, there is a pācittiya offense. However, this method is not well analyzed in the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā, but it is analyzed in the Mahāpaccariya.

Siñcanasiñcāpane pana akappiyaudakena sabbattha pācittiyaṃ, kuladūsanaparibhogatthāya dukkaṭampi. Kappiyena tesaṃyeva dvinnaṃ atthāya dukkaṭaṃ, paribhogatthāya cettha kappiyavohārena siñcāpane anāpatti. Āpattiṭṭhāne pana dhārāvacchedavasena payogabahulatāya ca āpattibahulatā veditabbā.

Furthermore, regarding watering or causing another to water with unallowable water, in all cases there is a pācittiya offense; for the purpose of corrupting a family or for consumption, there is also a dukkaṭa offense. With allowable water, for those same two purposes, there is a dukkaṭa offense. However, in this case, for the purpose of consumption, in causing another to water by means of an allowable expression, there is no offense. Furthermore, in the case of an offense, the multiplicity of offenses should be understood by means of the breaking of the stream and by the multiplicity of efforts.

Kulasaṅgahatthāya ocinane pupphagaṇanāya dukkaṭapācittiyāni, aññattha pācittiyāneva. Bahūni pana pupphāni ekapayogena ocinanto payogavasena kāretabbo. Ocināpane kuladūsanatthāya sakiṃ āṇatto bahumpi ocināti, ekameva sapācittiyadukkaṭaṃ, aññatra pācittiyameva.

In picking for the purpose of supporting families, there are dukkaṭa and pācittiya offenses according to the count of the flowers; for other purposes, there are only pācittiya offenses. Furthermore, one picking many flowers with a single effort should be dealt with according to the effort. In causing flowers to be picked, if one who is ordered once for the purpose of corrupting a family picks many, there is only one offense of a dukkaṭa together with a pācittiya; in other cases, there is only a pācittiya offense.

31. Ganthanaganthāpanesu pana sabbāpi cha pupphavikatiyo veditabbā – ganthimaṃ gopphimaṃ vedhimaṃ veṭhimaṃ pūrimaṃ vāyimanti. Tattha ganthimaṃ nāma sadaṇḍakesu vā uppalapadumādīsu aññesu vā dīghavaṇṭesu pupphesu daṭṭhabbaṃ. Daṇḍakena vā daṇḍakaṃ, vaṇṭena vā vaṇṭaṃ ganthetvā katameva hi ganthimaṃ. Taṃ bhikkhussa vā bhikkhuniyā vā kātumpi akappiyavacanena kārāpetumpi na vaṭṭati, “evaṃ jāna, evaṃ kate sobheyya, yathā etāni pupphāni na vikiriyanti, tathā karohī”tiādinā pana kappiyavacanena kārāpetuṃ vaṭṭati.

31. Furthermore, regarding tying or causing to be tied, all six kinds of flower-work should be known: tying (ganthima), braiding (gopphima), piercing (vedhima), wrapping (veṭhima), overlapping (pūrima), and weaving (vāyima). Among these, what is called ‘tying’ should be understood in relation to flowers with stalks, such as blue lotuses, white lotuses, and so on, or other flowers with long stems. For ‘tying’ is indeed that which is made by tying stalk to stalk or stem to stem. It is not allowable for a monk or a nun to make it themselves or to cause it to be made with an impermissible expression. However, it is allowable to cause it to be made with a permissible expression, such as: ‘Know it to be like this,’ ‘If made this way, it would be beautiful,’ or ‘Do it in such a way that these flowers do not scatter,’ and so on.

Gopphimaṃ nāma suttena vā vākādīhi vā vassikapupphādīnaṃ ekatovaṇṭikaubhatovaṇṭikamālāvasena gopphanaṃ, vākaṃ vā rajjuṃ vā diguṇaṃ katvā tattha avaṇṭakāni nīpapupphādīni pavesetvā paṭipāṭiyā bandhanti, etampi gopphimameva. Sabbaṃ purimanayeneva na vaṭṭati.

What is called ‘braiding’ is the braiding of jasmine flowers and so on with thread or with bark strips, etc., by way of a garland with stems on one side or with stems on both sides. Or, having doubled a bark strip or a rope, they insert stemless flowers such as Kadamba flowers into it and bind them in sequence; this too is indeed ‘braiding’. All of this is not allowable, according to the preceding principle.

Vedhimaṃ [M 0.0020][V 0.0021] nāma savaṇṭakāni vassikapupphādīni vaṇṭe, avaṇṭakāni vakulapupphādīni attano chiddesu sūcitālahīrādīhi vinivijjhitvā āvunanti, etaṃ vedhimaṃ nāma. Taṃ purimanayeneva na vaṭṭati. Keci pana kadalikkhandhamhi kaṇṭake vā tālahīrādīni vā pavesetvā tattha pupphāni vinivijjhitvā ṭhapenti, keci kaṇṭakasākhāsu, keci pupphachattapupphakūṭāgārakaraṇatthaṃ chatte ca bhittiyañca pavesetvā ṭhapitakaṇṭakesu, keci dhammāsanavitāne baddhakaṇṭakesu, keci kaṇikārapupphādīni salākāhi vijjhanti, chattādhichattaṃ viya karonti, taṃ atioḷārikameva. Pupphavijjhanatthaṃ pana dhammāsanavitāne kaṇṭakampi bandhituṃ kaṇṭakādīhi vā ekapupphampi vijjhituṃ puppheyeva vā pupphaṃ pavesetuṃ na vaṭṭati. Jālavitānavedikanāgadantakapupphapaṭicchakatālapaṇṇaguḷakādīnaṃ pana chiddesu asokapiṇḍiyā vā antaresu pupphāni pavesetuṃ na doso. Na hetaṃ vedhimaṃ hoti. Dhammarajjuyampi eseva nayo.

‘Piercing’ is when they string stemmed flowers, such as jasmine flowers, by piercing them on the stem, or stemless flowers, such as Spanish cherry flowers, by piercing them through their own holes with needles, palm-leaf fibers, and so on; this is called ‘piercing’. That is not allowable by the preceding method. Furthermore, some insert thorns or palm-leaf fibers and so on into a banana trunk and then pierce flowers onto them and place them there. Some pierce flowers on thorny branches. Some, for the purpose of making a flower-umbrella or a flower-pinnacled mansion, pierce flowers onto thorns that have been inserted and placed in a canopy and on a wall. Some pierce flowers onto thorns fastened to the canopy of a Dhamma-seat. Some pierce flowers like Golden Shower Tree flowers with splinters, making them like a tiered umbrella. All of that is indeed very coarse. Furthermore, for the purpose of piercing flowers, it is not allowable to fasten even a thorn to the canopy of a Dhamma-seat, nor to pierce even a single flower with thorns and so on, nor to insert a flower into a flower itself. However, there is no fault in inserting flowers into the holes of a net-canopy, a railing, a peg, a flower-receptacle, a ball of young palm leaves, and so on, or between clusters of Asoka flowers. Indeed, this is not ‘piercing’. This same method should be understood for the Dhamma-rope as well.

Veṭhimaṃ nāma pupphadāmapupphahatthakesu daṭṭhabbaṃ. Keci hi matthakadāmaṃ karontā heṭṭhā ghaṭakākāraṃ dassetuṃ pupphehi veṭhenti, keci aṭṭha aṭṭha vā dasa dasa vā uppalapupphādīni suttena vā vākena vā daṇḍakesu bandhitvā uppalahatthake vā padumahatthake vā karonti, taṃ sabbaṃ purimanayeneva na vaṭṭati. Sāmaṇerehi uppāṭetvā thale ṭhapitauppalādīni kāsāvena bhaṇḍikampi bandhituṃ na vaṭṭati. Tesaṃyeva pana vākena vā daṇḍakena vā bandhituṃ aṃsabhaṇḍikaṃ vā kātuṃ vaṭṭati. Aṃsabhaṇḍikaṃ nāma khandhe ṭhapitakāsāvassa ubho ante āharitvā bhaṇḍikaṃ katvā tasmiṃ pasibbake viya pupphāni pakkhipanti, ayaṃ vuccati aṃsabhaṇḍikā, etaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭati. Daṇḍakehi paduminipaṇṇaṃ vijjhitvā uppalādīni paṇṇena veṭhetvā gaṇhanti, tatrāpi pupphānaṃ upari paduminipaṇṇameva bandhituṃ vaṭṭati, heṭṭhā daṇḍakaṃ pana bandhituṃ na vaṭṭati.

What is called ‘wrapping’ should be understood in relation to flower festoons and flower bouquets. Indeed, some, while making a festoon for the top, wrap flowers around the base to create a pot-like shape. Others tie blue lotuses and so on in eights or in tens with thread or bark-strips onto stalks, creating a blue lotus bouquet or a lotus bouquet. All of this is not permissible according to the preceding principle. It is not allowable for novices to pick blue lotuses and so on, place them on dry land, and then bind them into a bundle with a monastic robe. However, it is permissible to bind them with bark-strips or stalks, or to make a shoulder-bundle. A shoulder-bundle is made by taking both ends of a robe placed on the shoulder, making a bundle, and then inserting flowers into it as if into a pouch; this is called a shoulder-bundle, and it is permissible to make it. They may pierce a lotus leaf with lotus stalks, wrap blue lotuses and so on with the leaf, and hold them. Even in this case, it is only permissible to bind the lotus leaf over the flowers; however, binding the stalk below is not allowed.

Pūrimaṃ nāma mālāguṇe ca pupphapaṭe ca daṭṭhabbaṃ. Yo hi mālāguṇena cetiyaṃ vā bodhiṃ vā vedikaṃ vā parikkhipanto puna ānetvā purimaṭṭhānaṃ atikkāmeti, ettāvatā pūrimaṃ nāma hoti, ko pana vādo anekakkhattuṃ parikkhipantassa. Nāgadantakantarehi pavesetvā haranto olambakaṃ katvā puna nāgadantakaṃ parikkhipati, etampi pūrimaṃ nāma. Nāgadantake [M 0.0021] pana pupphavalayaṃ pavesetuṃ vaṭṭati. Mālāguṇehi pupphapaṭaṃ karonti, tatrāpi ekameva mālāguṇaṃ harituṃ vaṭṭati. Puna paccāharato pūrimameva hoti. Taṃ sabbaṃ purimanayeneva na vaṭṭati. Mālāguṇehi pana bahūhipi kataṃ pupphadāmaṃ labhitvā āsanamatthakādīsu bandhituṃ vaṭṭati. Atidīghaṃ pana mālāguṇaṃ ekavāraṃ haritvā parikkhipitvā puna itarassa bhikkhuno dātuṃ vaṭṭati, tenapi tatheva kātuṃ vaṭṭati.

The term ‘overlapping’ should be understood in the context of a flower garland and a flower cloth. For when a monk, while encircling a cetiya, a Bodhi tree, or a railing with a flower garland, brings it back again beyond its original position, by this much it is called ‘overlapping’. What then is to be said of one who encircles it many times? When one inserts a garland through the gaps between pegs, lets it hang down, and then again encircles a peg, this too is called ‘overlapping’. However, it is allowable to place a flower wreath on a peg. When making a flower cloth with flower garlands, it is allowable to carry only a single garland strand. If one brings it back again, it is indeed ‘overlapping’. All of this is not allowable according to the preceding principle. However, having obtained a flower festoon made with many garland strands, it is allowable to tie it on the top of a seat and so on. As for a very long flower garland, it is allowable to carry it once, encircle something with it, and then give it to another monk; it is also allowable for that monk to do likewise.

Vāyimaṃ [V 0.0022] nāma pupphajālapupphapaṭapuppharūpesu daṭṭhabbaṃ. Cetiye pupphajālaṃ karontassa ekamekamhi jālachiddake dukkaṭaṃ. Bhittichattabodhitthambhādīsupi eseva nayo. Pupphapaṭaṃ pana parehi pūritampi vāyituṃ na labbhati. Gopphimapuppheheva hatthiassādirūpakāni karonti, tānipi vāyimaṭṭhāne tiṭṭhanti. Purimanayeneva sabbaṃ na vaṭṭati. Aññehi kataparicchede pana pupphāni ṭhapentena hatthiassādirūpakampi kātuṃ vaṭṭati. Mahāpaccariyaṃ pana kaḷambakena aḍḍhacandakena ca saddhiṃ aṭṭha pupphavikatiyo vuttā.

The term ‘weaving’ should be understood in the context of flower-nets, flower-cloths, and flower-figures. For a monk who makes a flower-net at a cetiya, a dukkaṭa offense is incurred for each and every hole in the net. This very same principle applies to walls, umbrellas, Bodhi-tree pillars, and so on. Furthermore, it is not permitted to weave a flower-cloth, even one filled by others. When they make figures of elephants, horses, and so on with braided flowers, these also fall under the category of ‘weaving’. All of this is not allowable according to the preceding principle. However, within a framework made by others, it is allowable for a monk to make figures of elephants, horses, and so on by placing flowers. In the Mahāpaccariya, however, eight kinds of flower-work are mentioned, together with the ‘kaḷambaka’ and the ‘aḍḍhacandaka’.

32. Tattha kaḷambakoti aḍḍhacandakantare ghaṭikadāmaolambako vutto. Aḍḍhacandakoti aḍḍhacandākārena mālāguṇaparikkhepo. Tadubhayampi pūrimeyeva paviṭṭhaṃ. Kurundiyaṃ pana “dve tayo mālāguṇe ekato katvā pupphadāmakaraṇampi vāyimaṃyevā”ti vuttaṃ. Tampi idha pūrimaṭṭhāneyeva paviṭṭhaṃ. Na kevalañca pupphadāmameva, piṭṭhamayadāmampi geṇḍukapupphadāmampi kurundiyaṃ vuttaṃ. Kharapattadāmampi sikkhāpadassa sādhāraṇattā bhikkhūnampi bhikkhunīnampi neva kātuṃ, na kārāpetuṃ vaṭṭati, pūjānimittaṃ pana kappiyavacanaṃ sabbattha vattuṃ vaṭṭati. Pariyāyaobhāsanimittakammāni vaṭṭantiyeva.

32. Therein, a hanging garland shaped like a water-pot within a half-moon shaped garland is called a kaḷambaka. A garland encircled with strings of flowers in the shape of a half-moon is called an aḍḍhacandaka. Both of these are included in the former category. However, in the Kurundī it is said: 'Making a flower garland by combining two or three strings of flowers is also indeed woven work.' That too is included here only in the former category. And not only a flower garland, but also a garland made of flour and a flower garland shaped like a ball are mentioned in the Kurundī. As for a garland made of coarse grass leaves, because the training rule is common to both bhikkhus and bhikkhunīs, it is not allowable for them to make it, nor to have it made. However, for the purpose of veneration, it is allowable to make a permissible utterance everywhere. Indirect speech, hints, and signs are indeed allowable.

Yo haritvā vā harāpetvā vā pakkositvā vā pakkosāpetvā vā sayaṃ vā upagatānaṃ yaṃ kiñci attano santakaṃ pupphaṃ kulasaṅgahatthāya deti, tassa dukkaṭaṃ, parasantakaṃ deti, dukkaṭameva. Theyyacittena deti, bhaṇḍagghena kāretabbo. Esa nayo saṅghikepi. Ayaṃ pana viseso – senāsanatthāya niyamitaṃ issaravatāya dadato thullaccayanti.

For whatever bhikkhu—having brought a flower himself or having caused another to bring it, or having summoned a family himself or having caused another to summon them, or to a family that has approached on its own—gives any flower whatsoever belonging to himself for the purpose of ingratiating himself with families, for him there is a dukkaṭa offense. If he gives what belongs to another, it is a dukkaṭa indeed. If he gives with thievish intent, he should be dealt with according to the value of the article. This is the method also in the case of what belongs to the Saṅgha. However, this is the distinction: for one who, acting as the owner, gives what has been designated for the purpose of lodging, there is a thullaccaya offense.

33. Pupphaṃ nāma kassa dātuṃ vaṭṭati, kassa na vaṭṭatīti? Mātāpitūnaṃ tāva haritvāpi harāpetvāpi pakkositvāpi pakkosāpetvāpi dātuṃ vaṭṭati[M 0.0022], sesañātakānaṃ pakkosāpetvāva. Tañca kho vatthupūjanatthāya, maṇḍanatthāya pana sivaliṅgādipūjanatthāya vā kassacipi dātuṃ na vaṭṭati. Mātāpitūnañca harāpentena ñātisāmaṇereheva harāpetabbaṃ. Itare pana yadi sayameva icchanti, vaṭṭati. Sammatena pupphabhājakena pupphabhājanakāle sampattānaṃ sāmaṇerānaṃ upaḍḍhabhāgaṃ dātuṃ vaṭṭati. Kurundiyaṃ pana “sampattagihīnaṃ upaḍḍhabhāgaṃ”, mahāpaccariyaṃ “cūḷakaṃ dātuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti vuttaṃ. Asammatena apaloketvā dātabbaṃ. Ācariyupajjhāyesu sagāravā sāmaṇerā bahūni pupphāni āharitvā rāsiṃ katvā ṭhapenti, therā pātova sampattānaṃ saddhivihārikādīnaṃ upāsakādīnaṃ vā “tvaṃ idaṃ gaṇha, tvaṃ idaṃ gaṇhā”ti denti, pupphadānaṃ nāma na hoti. “Cetiyaṃ pūjessāmā”ti gahetvā gacchantāpi pūjaṃ karontāpi tattha tattha sampattānaṃ [V 0.0023] cetiyapūjanatthāya denti, etampi pupphadānaṃ nāma na hoti. Upāsake akkapupphādīhi pūjente disvā “vihāre kaṇikārapupphādīni atthi, upāsakā tāni gahetvā pūjethā”ti vattumpi vaṭṭati. Bhikkhū pupphapūjaṃ katvā divātaraṃ gāmaṃ paviṭṭhe “kiṃ, bhante, atidivā paviṭṭhatthā”ti pucchanti, “vihāre pupphāni bahūni, pūjaṃ akarimhā”ti vadanti. Manussā “bahūni kira vihāre pupphānī”ti punadivase pahūtaṃ khādanīyaṃ bhojanīyaṃ gahetvā vihāraṃ gantvā pupphapūjañca karonti dānañca denti, vaṭṭati.

33. As for flowers, to whom is it allowable to give, and to whom is it not allowable? First, it is allowable to give to one's parents—whether by taking them oneself, having them taken, inviting them, or having them invited. For other relatives, it is allowable to give only by having them invited. And that is allowable to give only for the purpose of venerating the Triple Gem; however, it is not allowable to give to anyone either for the purpose of adornment or for the purpose of worshiping Śiva liṅgas and the like. And when having flowers taken for one's parents, they should be had taken only by kinsman-novices. As for other novices, however, if they themselves wish to take them, it is allowable. By a flower-distributor appointed by the Saṅgha, it is allowable to give half a bhikkhu's portion to novices who have arrived at the time of flower distribution. In the Kurundī commentary, however, it is said: 'to laypeople who have arrived, half a novice's portion'; in the Mahāpaccariya commentary it is stated: 'It is allowable to give a small portion,' that is, a quarter of a bhikkhu's portion. By one not appointed, it should be given after announcing it. Novices who are respectful towards their teachers and preceptors bring many flowers, make a pile, and place them. The elders, in the morning, give them to their co-residents and others or to lay devotees and others who have arrived, saying, 'You take this, you take that'—this is not called a gift of flowers. Even those who, having taken flowers with the thought, 'We will worship the cetiya,' and while going or performing the worship, give them here and there to those who have arrived for the purpose of cetiya worship—this also is not called a gift of flowers. Having seen lay devotees worshiping with akka flowers and the like, it is also allowable to say: 'There are kaṇikāra flowers and others in the monastery; lay devotees, take those and worship.' When bhikkhus, after performing flower worship, enter the village rather late in the day, people ask: 'Venerable sirs, why have you entered so late?' They reply: 'There were many flowers in the monastery; we performed worship.' People, knowing, 'It seems there are many flowers in the monastery,' on the next day, take abundant soft and hard foods, go to the monastery, perform flower worship, and also give alms—this is allowable.

34. Manussā “mayaṃ, bhante, asukadivasaṃ nāma pūjessāmā”ti pupphavāraṃ yācitvā anuññātadivase āgacchanti, sāmaṇerehi ca pageva pupphāni ocinitvā ṭhapitāni honti, te rukkhesu pupphāni apassantā “kuhiṃ, bhante, pupphānī”ti vadanti, sāmaṇerehi ocinitvā ṭhapitāni, tumhe pana pūjetvā gacchatha, saṅgho aññaṃ divasaṃ pūjessatīti. Te pūjetvā dānaṃ datvā gacchanti, vaṭṭati. Mahāpaccariyaṃ pana kurundiyañca “therā sāmaṇerehi dāpetuṃ na labhanti, sace sayameva tāni pupphāni tesaṃ denti, vaṭṭati. Therehi pana ‘sāmaṇerehi ocinitvā ṭhapitānī’ti ettakameva vattabba”nti vuttaṃ. Sace pana pupphavāraṃ yācitvā anocitesu pupphesu yāgubhattādīni ādāya āgantvā sāmaṇere “ocinitvā dethā”ti vadanti, ñābhisāmaṇerānaṃyeva ocinitvā dātuṃ vaṭṭati. Aññātake ukkhipitvā rukkhasākhāya ṭhapenti, na orohitvā palāyitabbaṃ, ocinitvā dātuṃ vaṭṭati[M 0.0023]. Sace pana koci dhammakathiko “bahūni upāsakā vihāre pupphāni, yāgubhattādīni ādāya gantvā pupphapūjaṃ karothā”ti vadati, tasseva na kappatīti mahāpaccariyañca kurundiyañca vuttaṃ. Mahāaṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana “etaṃ akappiyaṃ na vaṭṭatī”ti avisesena vuttaṃ.

34. People, having requested a turn for the flowers and saying, 'Venerable sir, we will make an offering on such-and-such a day,' come on the permitted day. And the novices have already picked the flowers and set them aside. Not seeing flowers on the trees, they say, 'Venerable sir, where are the flowers?' 'They have been picked and set aside by the novices. But you, having made your offering, may go. The Saṅgha will make an offering on another day.' They, having made their offering and given alms, depart; this is allowable. However, in the Mahāpaccariya and the Kurundī it is said: 'The elders are not permitted to have the novices give them; if they themselves give those flowers to them, it is allowable. But by the elders, only this much should be said: "They have been picked and set aside by the novices."' If, however, having requested a turn for the flowers when the flowers have not yet been picked, they arrive bringing rice-gruel, cooked rice, and so on, and say to the novices, 'Pick and give them,' it is allowable only for kinsman-novices to pick and give. As for non-kinsman novices, they may be lifted up and placed on a tree branch. The novice should not climb down and run away; it is allowable to pick and give. But if some Dhamma-preacher says, 'Lay devotees, there are many flowers in the monastery; take rice-gruel, cooked rice, and so on, go, and perform the flower-offering,' it is not allowable for him alone. So it is said in the Mahāpaccariya and the Kurundī. In the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā, however, it is stated without distinction: 'This is improper and not allowable.'

35. Phalampi attano santakaṃ vuttanayeneva mātāpitūnañca sesañātīnañca dātuṃ vaṭṭati. Kulasaṅgahatthāya pana dentassa vuttanayeneva attano santake parasantake saṅghike senāsanatthāya niyamite ca dukkaṭādīni veditabbāni. Attano santakaṃyeva gilānamanussānaṃ vā sampattaissarānaṃ vā khīṇaparibbayānaṃ vā dātuṃ vaṭṭati, phaladānaṃ na hoti. Phalabhājakenapi sammatena saṅghassa phalabhājanakāle sampattamanussānaṃ upaḍḍhabhāgaṃ dātuṃ vaṭṭati, asammatena apaloketvā dātabbaṃ. Saṅghārāmepi phalaparicchedena vā rukkhaparicchedena vā katikā kātabbā “tato gilānamanussānaṃ vā aññesaṃ vā phalaṃ yācantānaṃ yathāparicchedena cattāri pañca phalāni dātabbāni, rukkhā vā dassetabbā ‘ito gahetuṃ labbhatī’”ti. “Idha phalāni sundarāni, ito gaṇhathā”ti evaṃ pana na vattabbaṃ. Attano santakaṃ sirīsacuṇṇaṃ vā [V 0.0024] aññaṃ vā yaṃ kiñci kasāvaṃ kulasaṅgahatthāya deti, dukkaṭaṃ. Parasantakādīsupi vuttanayeneva vinicchayo veditabbo. Ayaṃ pana viseso – saṅghassa rakkhitagopitāpi rukkhachalli garubhaṇḍamevāti. Mattikadantakaṭṭhaveḷupaṇṇesupi garubhaṇḍūpagaṃ ñatvā cuṇṇe vuttanayeneva vinicchayo veditabbo.

35. Fruits, too, that are one's own property, may be given to parents and other relatives in the manner stated. However, for one who gives for the sake of gaining family favor, the offenses beginning with dukkaṭa should be understood in the manner stated, whether the property is one's own, belonging to another, or belonging to the Saṅgha and designated for lodgings. One's own property may be given to sick persons, to visiting dignitaries, or to those with exhausted provisions; this is not a gift of fruit. By a fruit distributor who has been appointed, it is allowable to give half a portion to people who have arrived at the time of the Saṅgha's fruit distribution. By one who has not been appointed, it should be given after informing the Saṅgha. In a monastery of the Saṅgha, an agreement should be made regarding the division of fruits, either by amount or by tree: "From there, to sick persons or others who request fruit, four or five fruits should be given according to the division, or trees should be pointed out, saying, 'It is permitted to take from here.'" However, one should not say: "Here the fruits are beautiful, take from here." If one gives one's own sirīsa powder or any other astringent for the sake of gaining family favor, it is a dukkaṭa. Also regarding what belongs to another etc., the judgment should be understood in the manner stated. This, however, is the distinction: even tree bark protected and guarded by the Saṅgha is indeed heavy goods. Also regarding clay, tooth-sticks, bamboo, and leaves, having understood what is classified as heavy goods, the judgment should be understood in the manner stated for powder.

36. Jaṅghapesaniyanti gihīnaṃ dūteyyaṃ sāsanaharaṇakammaṃ vuccati, taṃ na kātabbaṃ. Gihīnañhi sāsanaṃ gahetvā gacchantassa pade pade dukkaṭaṃ. Taṃ kammaṃ nissāya laddhabhojanaṃ bhuñjantassapi ajjhohāre ajjhohāre dukkaṭaṃ. Paṭhamaṃ sāsanaṃ aggahetvāpi pacchā “ayaṃ dāni so gāmo, handa naṃ sāsanaṃ ārocemī”ti maggā okkamantassapi pade pade dukkaṭaṃ. Sāsanaṃ ārocetvā laddhabhojanaṃ bhuñjato purimanayeneva dukkaṭaṃ. Sāsanaṃ aggahetvā āgatena pana “bhante, tasmiṃ gāme itthannāmassa kā pavattī”ti pucchiyamānena kathetuṃ vaṭṭati, pucchitapañhe doso natthi. Pañcannaṃ pana sahadhammikānaṃ mātāpitūnaṃ paṇḍupalāsassa attano veyyāvaccakarassa [M 0.0024] sāsanaṃ harituṃ vaṭṭati, gihīnañca kappiyasāsanaṃ, tasmā “mama vacanena bhagavato pāde vandathā”ti vā “cetiyaṃ paṭimaṃ bodhiṃ saṅghattheraṃ vandathā”ti vā “cetiye gandhapūjaṃ karothā”ti vā “pupphapūjaṃ karothā”ti vā “bhikkhū sannipātetha, dānaṃ dassāma, dhammaṃ desāpayissāmā”ti vā īdisesu sāsanesu kukkuccaṃ na kātabbaṃ. Kappiyasāsanāni hi etāni, na gihīnaṃ gihikammapaṭisaṃyuttānīti. Imehi pana aṭṭhahi kuladūsakakammehi uppannapaccayā pañcannampi sahadhammikānaṃ na kappanti. Abhūtārocanarūpiyasaṃvohārehi uppannapaccayasadisāva honti.

36. The work of a messenger for laypeople, the act of carrying a message, is called jaṅghapesaniya; that should not be done. Indeed, for a bhikkhu who takes a message from laypeople and goes, there is a dukkaṭa offense at every step. Even for one who eats food obtained by means of that act, there is a dukkaṭa offense at every mouthful. Even if one at first does not take the message, but later, thinking, 'This is now that village; come, let me deliver the message to him,' turns off the path, there is a dukkaṭa offense at every step. For one who, having delivered the message, eats food obtained thereby, there is a dukkaṭa offense in the same manner as before. However, for one who has arrived without taking a message, if asked, 'Venerable sir, what is the news of so-and-so in that village?', it is allowable to speak; there is no fault in answering a question that is asked. However, it is allowable to carry a message for the five kinds of co-religionists, for one's mother and father, for a sick person, and for one's own attendant; and it is allowable to carry an allowable message for laypeople. Therefore, one should not have any scruple regarding messages such as: 'At my word, pay homage to the Blessed One’s feet,' or 'Pay homage to the cetiya, the image, the Bodhi tree, or the Saṅgha elder,' or 'Make an offering of incense at the cetiya,' or 'Make an offering of flowers,' or 'Gather the bhikkhus; we will give alms; we will have the Dhamma taught.' For these are allowable messages, not connected with the household affairs of laypeople. However, requisites obtained through these eight actions that corrupt families are not allowable even for the five kinds of co-religionists. They are indeed similar to requisites obtained through false reporting and dealings in gold and silver.

Pabbājanīyakammakato pana yasmiṃ gāme vā nigame vā kuladūsakakammaṃ kataṃ, yasmiñca vihāre vasati, neva tasmiṃ gāme vā nigame vā carituṃ labhati, na vihāre vasituṃ. Paṭippassaddhakammenapi ca tena yesu kulesu pubbe kuladūsakakammaṃ kataṃ, tato uppannapaccayā na gahetabbā, āsavakkhayapattenapi na gahetabbā, akappiyāva honti. “Kasmā na gaṇhathā”ti pucchitena “pubbe evaṃ katattā”ti vutte sace vadanti “na mayaṃ tena kāraṇena dema, idāni sīlavantatāya demā”ti, gahetabbā. Pakatiyā dānaṭṭhāneyeva kuladūsakakammaṃ kataṃ hoti, tato pakatidānameva gahetuṃ vaṭṭati. Yaṃ vaḍḍhetvā denti, taṃ na vaṭṭati. Yasmā ca pucchitapañhe doso natthi, tasmā aññampi bhikkhuṃ pubbaṇhe vā sāyanhe vā antaragharaṃ paviṭṭhaṃ koci puccheyya “kasmā, bhante, carathā”ti. Yenatthena carati, taṃ ācikkhitvā “laddhaṃ na laddha”nti vutte sace na laddhaṃ, “na laddha”nti vatvā yaṃ so deti, taṃ gahetuṃ vaṭṭati.

However, a bhikkhu who has been subjected to the act of banishment, in whatever village or town the act of corrupting families was committed, and in whatever monastery he resides, is not allowed to wander in that village or town, nor to dwell in that monastery. And even after the act has been revoked, requisites that have arisen from those families where the act of corrupting families was previously committed should not be accepted by him; they should not be accepted even upon attaining the destruction of the taints—they are indeed unallowable. If asked, 'Why do you not accept?' and having replied, 'Because it was done so before,' if they then say, 'We do not give for that reason; we give now because of your virtuous conduct,' they should be accepted. If the act of corrupting families was committed specifically at a place of ordinary giving, from there it is allowable to accept only the ordinary offering. Whatever they give after increasing it is not allowable. And since there is no fault in answering a question, if some lay supporter should ask a bhikkhu who has entered a house in the morning or evening, 'Venerable sir, for what reason do you wander?', it is allowable for that bhikkhu, after explaining the purpose for which he wanders, and upon being asked, 'Have you received it or not received it?', if he has not received it, to say, 'Not received,' and to accept what that person gives.

37. “Na [V 0.0025] ca, bhikkhave, paṇidhāya araññe vatthabbaṃ, yo vaseyya, āpatti dukkaṭassa. Na ca, bhikkhave, paṇidhāya piṇḍāya caritabbaṃ…pe… na ca, bhikkhave, paṇidhāya caṅkamitabbaṃ…pe… na ca, bhikkhave, paṇidhāya ṭhātabbaṃ…pe… na ca, bhikkhave, paṇidhāya nisīditabbaṃ…pe… na ca, bhikkhave, paṇidhāya seyyā kappetabbā, yo kappeyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (pārā. 223 ādayo) vuttattā “evaṃ (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.223) araññe vasantaṃ maṃ jano arahatte vā sekkhabhūmiyaṃ vā sambhāvessati, tato lokassa sakkato bhavissāmi garukato mānito pūjito”ti evaṃ patthanaṃ katvā araññe na vasitabbaṃ. Evaṃ paṇidhāya “araññe vasissāmī”ti gacchantassa [M 0.0025] padavāre padavāre dukkaṭaṃ, tathā araññe kuṭikaraṇacaṅkamananisīdananivāsanapārupanādīsu sabbakiccesu payoge payoge dukkaṭaṃ, tasmā evaṃ araññe na vasitabbaṃ. Evaṃ vasanto hi sambhāvanaṃ labhatu vā mā vā, dukkaṭaṃ āpajjati. Yo pana samādinnadhutaṅgo “dhutaṅgaṃ rakkhissāmī”ti vā “gāmante me vasato cittaṃ vikkhipati, araññaṃ sappāya”nti cintetvā vā “addhā araññe tiṇṇaṃ vivekānaṃ aññataraṃ pāpuṇissāmī”ti vā “araññaṃ pavisitvā arahattaṃ apāpuṇitvā na nikkhamissāmī”ti vā “araññavāso nāma bhagavatā pasattho, mayi ca araññe vasante bahū sabrahmacārī gāmantaṃ hitvā āraññakā bhavissantī”ti vā evaṃ anavajjavāsaṃ vasitukāmo hoti, teneva vasitabbaṃ. Piṇḍāya carantassapi “abhikkantādīni saṇṭhapetvā piṇḍāya carissāmī”ti nivāsanapārupanakiccato pabhuti yāva bhojanapariyosānaṃ, tāva payoge payoge dukkaṭaṃ, sambhāvanaṃ labhatu vā mā vā, dukkaṭameva. Khandhakavattasekhiyavattaparipūraṇatthaṃ pana sabrahmacārīnaṃ diṭṭhānugatiāpajjanatthaṃ vā pāsādikehi abhikkamapaṭikkamādīhi piṇḍāya pavisanto anupavajjo viññūnaṃ. Caṅkamanādīsupi eseva nayo.

37. “Monks, one should not dwell in the forest with a preconceived intention; whoever should so dwell incurs an offense of wrong-doing. Monks, one should not go for alms with a preconceived intention… one should not walk back and forth with a preconceived intention… one should not stand with a preconceived intention… one should not sit with a preconceived intention… one should not prepare a bed with a preconceived intention; whoever should do so incurs an offense of wrong-doing.” Because it is said: “If I dwell thus in the forest, people will esteem me as an Arahant or as one on the trainee’s path. Then I will be honored, respected, revered, and venerated by the world.” One should not dwell in the forest after making such an aspiration. For one going to the forest with the preconceived intention, ‘I will dwell there,’ there is an offense of wrong-doing at every step. Similarly, in the forest, in all activities such as building a hut, walking, sitting, putting on the lower and upper robes, and so on, there is an offense of wrong-doing with each effort. Therefore, one should not dwell in the forest in this way. For one dwelling thus, whether or not one gains esteem, one incurs an offense of wrong-doing. However, as for one who has undertaken an ascetic practice (dhutaṅga) and thinks, ‘I will maintain the ascetic practice,’ or reflects, ‘For me, living near a village distracts my mind; the forest is suitable,’ or thinks, ‘Surely, in the forest I will attain one of the three kinds of seclusion,’ or resolves, ‘Having entered the forest, I will not leave until I attain Arahantship,’ or considers, ‘Dwelling in the forest is praised by the Blessed One, and if I dwell in the forest, many companions in the holy life will abandon the vicinity of a village and become forest-dwellers’—such a one, desiring to dwell blamelessly, should indeed dwell there. For one who goes for alms with the thought, ‘I will go for alms after establishing my deportment, such as advancing and retreating,’ from the initial act of putting on the lower and upper robes until the end of the meal, there is an offense of wrong-doing with each effort—whether or not one gains esteem, it is still an offense of wrong-doing. However, for the purpose of fulfilling the duties of the Khandhakas and Sekhiyas, or for the purpose of setting an example to be followed by companions in the holy life, one who enters for alms with inspiring deportment—such as advancing and retreating—is blameless to the wise. This same principle applies to walking and other such activities.

Iti pāḷimuttakavinayavinicchayasaṅgahe

In the Pāḷimuttakavinayavinicchayasaṅgaha.

Kulasaṅgahavinicchayakathā samattā.

The Discourse on the Decision Concerning the Support of Lay Devotees is completed.

6. Macchamaṃsavinicchayakathā

6. The Discourse on the Decision Concerning Fish and Meat

38. Macchamaṃsesu [V 0.0026] pana macchaggahaṇena sabbampi jalajaṃ vuttaṃ. Tattha akappiyaṃ nāma natthi. Maṃsesu pana manussahatthiassasunakhaahisīhabyagghadīpiacchataracchānaṃ vasena dasa maṃsāni akappiyāni. Tattha manussamaṃse thullaccayaṃ, sesesu dukkaṭaṃ. Iti imesaṃ manussādīnaṃ dasannaṃ maṃsampi aṭṭhipi lohitampi cammampi lomampi sabbaṃ na vaṭṭati. Vasāsu pana ekā manussavasāva na vaṭṭati. Khīrādīsu akappiyaṃ nāma natthi. Imesu pana akappiyamaṃsesu aṭṭhiādīsu vā yaṃ kiñci ñatvā vā añatvā vā khādantassa āpattiyeva. Yadā jānāti, tadā desetabbā. “Apucchitvāva khādissāmī”ti gaṇhato paṭiggahaṇepi dukkaṭaṃ, “pucchitvā khādissāmī”ti gaṇhato [M 0.0026] anāpatti. Uddissakataṃ pana jānitvā khādantasseva āpatti, pacchā jānanto āpattiyā na kāretabbo (mahāva. aṭṭha. 281).

38. Now, regarding fish and meat: by the term 'fish,' all aquatic creatures are meant. Among them, there is nothing called 'unallowable.' However, regarding meats, ten kinds of meat are unallowable: that of humans, elephants, horses, dogs, snakes, lions, tigers, leopards, bears, and hyenas. Among these, for human flesh, there is a grave offense (thullaccaya); for the remaining ones, an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). Thus, of these ten beginning with humans, all their meat, bones, blood, skin, and hair are not allowable. However, regarding fats, only human fat is not allowable. In milk and so forth, there is nothing called 'unallowable.' However, regarding these unallowable meats or their bones and so forth, for one who eats any of it, whether knowingly or unknowingly, there is indeed an offense. When one becomes aware, it should be confessed. For one who takes it thinking, 'I will eat without asking,' there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) even upon receiving it. For one who takes it thinking, 'I will ask and then eat,' there is no offense. However, regarding meat from an animal killed specifically for a monk, there is an offense only for one who eats it knowingly. One who finds out afterwards should not be charged with an offense.

Tattha (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.410) uddissakataṃ nāma bhikkhūnaṃ atthāya vadhitvā sampāditaṃ macchamaṃsaṃ. Ubhayampi hi uddissakataṃ na vaṭṭati. Tampi adiṭṭhaṃ asutaṃ aparisaṅkitaṃ vaṭṭati. Tikoṭiparisuddhañhi macchamaṃsaṃ bhagavatā anuññātaṃ adiṭṭhaṃ asutaṃ aparisaṅkitaṃ. Tattha adiṭṭhaṃ nāma bhikkhūnaṃ atthāya migamacche vadhitvā gayhamānaṃ adiṭṭhaṃ. Asutaṃ nāma bhikkhūnaṃ atthāya migamacche vadhitvā gahitanti asutaṃ. Aparisaṅkitaṃ pana diṭṭhaparisaṅkitaṃ sutaparisaṅkitaṃ tadubhayavinimuttaparisaṅkitañca ñatvā tabbipakkhato jānitabbaṃ. Kathaṃ? Idha bhikkhū passanti manusse jālavāgurādihatthe gāmato vā nikkhamante araññe vā vicarante. Dutiyadivase ca nesaṃ taṃ gāmaṃ piṇḍāya paviṭṭhānaṃ samacchamaṃsaṃ piṇḍapātaṃ abhiharanti. Te tena diṭṭhena parisaṅkanti “bhikkhūnaṃ nu kho atthāya kata”nti, idaṃ diṭṭhaparisaṅkitaṃ, etaṃ gahetuṃ na vaṭṭati. Yaṃ evaṃ aparisaṅkitaṃ, taṃ vaṭṭati. Sace pana te manussā “kasmā, bhante, na gaṇhathā”ti pucchitvā tamatthaṃ sutvā “nayidaṃ, bhante, bhikkhūnaṃ atthāya kataṃ, amhehi attano atthāya vā rājayuttādīnaṃ vā atthāya kata”nti vadanti, kappati.

Therein, what is called 'specifically prepared' is fish or meat prepared by killing for the sake of monks. Indeed, both fish and meat that are specifically prepared are not allowable. That which is unseen, unheard, and unsuspected, however, is allowable. For fish and meat that is pure in three aspects—unseen, unheard, and unsuspected—has been permitted by the Blessed One. Therein, 'unseen' means not having seen animals or fish being killed and taken for the sake of monks. 'Unheard' means not having heard that animals or fish were killed and taken for the sake of monks. 'Unsuspected,' however, should be understood by way of its opposite, after having known suspicion due to seeing, suspicion due to hearing, and suspicion free from both of these. How? Here, monks see people with nets, traps, and so on in hand, either leaving a village or wandering in the forest. And on the next day, when those monks have entered that village for alms, people offer them almsfood containing fish or meat. Because of what they have seen, they suspect, 'Was this indeed prepared for the sake of the monks?' This is 'suspicion due to seeing'; it is not allowable to accept this. What is thus unsuspected is allowable. If, however, those people, after asking, 'Venerable sirs, why do you not accept it?' and hearing the reason, say, 'Venerable sirs, this was not prepared for the sake of the monks; we prepared it for our own sake or for the sake of royal officials and so on,' it is permissible.

Na heva kho bhikkhū passanti, apica kho suṇanti “manussā kira jālavāgurādihatthā gāmato vā nikkhamanti, araññe vā vicarantī”ti. Dutiyadivase ca tesaṃ taṃ gāmaṃ piṇḍāya paviṭṭhānaṃ samacchamaṃsaṃ piṇḍapātaṃ abhiharanti. Te tena sutena parisaṅkanti “bhikkhūnaṃ nu [V 0.0027] kho atthāya kata”nti, idaṃ sutaparisaṅkitaṃ nāma, etaṃ gahetuṃ na vaṭṭati. Yaṃ evaṃ aparisaṅkitaṃ, taṃ vaṭṭati. Sace pana te manussā “kasmā, bhante, na gaṇhathā”ti pucchitvā tamatthaṃ sutvā “nayidaṃ, bhante, bhikkhūnaṃ atthāya kataṃ, amhehi attano atthāya vā rājayuttādīnaṃ vā atthāya kata”nti vadanti, kappati.

Indeed, bhikkhus do not see, but they hear: “It is said that people, with nets, traps, and so forth in hand, are going out from the village or are wandering in the forest.” And on the second day, when those bhikkhus have entered that village for alms-food, people bring them alms-food with fish and meat. Because of what was heard, they suspect, “Was this prepared for the sake of the bhikkhus?” This is called ‘suspected on account of hearing’; it is not allowable to accept this. Whatever is thus unsuspected is allowable. But if those people, having asked, “Venerable sirs, why do you not accept it?” and having heard the reason, say, “Venerable sirs, this was not prepared for the sake of the bhikkhus; it was prepared by us for our own sake or for the sake of royal officials and so forth,” it is allowable.

Na heva kho pana bhikkhū passanti na suṇanti, apica kho tesaṃ taṃ gāmaṃ piṇḍāya paviṭṭhānaṃ pattaṃ gahetvā samacchamaṃsaṃ piṇḍapātaṃ abhisaṅkharitvā abhiharanti. Te parisaṅkanti “bhikkhūnaṃ nu kho atthāya kata”nti, idaṃ tadubhayavinimuttaparisaṅkitaṃ nāma, etampi gahetuṃ na vaṭṭati. Yaṃ evaṃ aparisaṅkitaṃ, taṃ vaṭṭati. Sace pana te manussā “kasmā, bhante, na gaṇhathā”ti pucchitvā [M 0.0027] tamatthaṃ sutvā “nayidaṃ, bhante, bhikkhūnaṃ atthāya kataṃ, amhehi attano atthāya vā rājayuttādīnaṃ vā atthāya kataṃ, pavattamaṃsaṃ vā kappiyameva labhitvā bhikkhūnaṃ atthāya sampādita”nti vadanti, kappati. Matānaṃ petakiccatthāya maṅgalādīnaṃ vā atthāya katepi eseva nayo. Yaṃ yañhi bhikkhūnaṃyeva atthāya akataṃ, yattha ca nibbematiko hoti, taṃ sabbaṃ kappati.

Furthermore, bhikkhus indeed neither see nor hear, but when they have entered that village for alms-food, people, having taken their bowls and having specially prepared alms-food with fish and meat, bring it to them. They suspect, “Was this prepared for the sake of the bhikkhus?” This is called ‘suspected while being free from both of those’; this also is not allowable to accept. Whatever is thus unsuspected is allowable. But if those people, having asked, “Venerable sirs, why do you not accept it?” and having heard the reason, say, “Venerable sirs, this was not prepared for the sake of the bhikkhus; it was prepared by us for our own sake or for the sake of royal officials and so forth, or, having obtained existing meat that is indeed allowable, it was prepared for the sake of the bhikkhus,” it is allowable. Even when it is prepared for the sake of funeral rites for the dead or for the sake of auspicious ceremonies and so forth, this is the very same principle. For whatever is not prepared for the sake of the bhikkhus alone, and in regard to which one is without doubt, all that is allowable.

39. Sace pana ekasmiṃ vihāre bhikkhūnaṃ uddissakataṃ hoti, te ca attano atthāya katabhāvaṃ na jānanti, aññe jānanti. Ye jānanti, tesaṃ na vaṭṭati, itaresaṃ pana vaṭṭati. Aññe na jānanti, teyeva jānanti, tesaṃyeva na vaṭṭati, aññesaṃ vaṭṭati. Tepi “amhākaṃ atthāya kata”nti jānanti, aññepi “etesaṃ atthāya kata”nti jānanti, sabbesampi na vaṭṭati. Sabbe na jānanti, sabbesampi vaṭṭati. Pañcasu hi sahadhammikesu yassa vā tassa vā atthāya uddissakataṃ sabbesaṃ na kappati.

39. Now, if in a certain monastery, meat or fish has been prepared specifically for the bhikkhus, and those specified bhikkhus do not know that it was prepared for their sake, but other bhikkhus know, it is not allowable for those who know, but it is allowable for the others. If the other bhikkhus do not know, and only those specified bhikkhus know, it is not allowable for them alone, but it is allowable for the others. If those specified bhikkhus know, 'It was prepared for our sake,' and the other bhikkhus also know, 'It was prepared for their sake,' it is not allowable for any of them. If none of them know, it is allowable for all of them. Indeed, among five co-religionists, meat or fish prepared specifically for the sake of this one or that one is not allowable for all of them.

Sace pana koci ekaṃ bhikkhuṃ uddissa pāṇaṃ vadhitvā tassa pattaṃ pūretvā deti, so ca attano atthāya katabhāvaṃ jānaṃyeva gahetvā aññassa bhikkhuno deti, so taṃ tassa saddhāya paribhuñjati, kassa āpattīti? Dvinnampi anāpatti. Yañhi uddissa kataṃ, tassa abhuttatāya anāpatti, itarassa ajānanatāya. Kappiyamaṃsassa hi paṭiggahaṇe āpatti natthi, uddissakatañca ajānitvā bhuttassa pacchā ñatvā āpattidesanākiccaṃ nāma natthi. Akappiyamaṃsaṃ pana ajānitvā bhuttena pacchā ñatvāpi āpatti desetabbā. Uddissakatañhi ñatvā bhuñjatova āpatti, akappiyamaṃsaṃ ajānitvā bhuñjantassapi āpattiyeva, tasmā āpattibhīrukena rūpaṃ sallakkhentenapi pucchitvāva maṃsaṃ paṭiggahetabbaṃ. Paribhogakāle “pucchitvā [V 0.0028] paribhuñjissāmī”ti vā gahetvā pucchitvāva paribhuñjitabbaṃ. Kasmā? Duviññeyyattā. Acchamaṃsampi hi sūkaramaṃsasadisaṃ hoti, dīpimaṃsādīni ca migamaṃsādisadisāni, tasmā pucchitvā gahaṇameva vattanti vadanti.

Now, if a certain person, having specified a bhikkhu, kills a living being, fills that bhikkhu's bowl, and gives it to him; and that bhikkhu, knowing that it was prepared for his sake, accepts it and gives it to another bhikkhu; and that other bhikkhu consumes it with faith in the first bhikkhu—for whom is there an offense? For both, there is no offense. Indeed, for the one for whom it was specifically prepared, there is no offense due to not having eaten it; for the other, there is no offense due to not knowing. Indeed, in the receiving of allowable meat, there is no offense. And for one who has eaten without knowing it was specifically prepared, upon knowing it afterwards, there is no duty called 'confession of an offense'. However, by one who has eaten unallowable meat without knowing, upon knowing it afterwards, the offense should be confessed. Indeed, an offense occurs only for one who eats knowing it was specifically prepared. For one who eats unallowable meat without knowing, there is indeed an offense. Therefore, a bhikkhu who is fearful of offenses should accept meat only after asking, even while observing its appearance. At the time of consumption, having accepted it with the thought, 'I will ask and then consume,' it should be consumed only after asking. Why? Because of the difficulty in distinguishing. Indeed, even bear meat is similar to pork, and leopard meat and so on are similar to deer meat and so on. Therefore, they say that the proper practice is only to accept after asking.

Iti pāḷimuttakavinayavinicchayasaṅgahe

Thus, in the Compendium of Vinaya Decisions Independent of the Pāḷi Canon,

Macchamaṃsavinicchayakathā samattā.

The Discourse on the Decision Regarding Fish and Meat is concluded.

7. Anāmāsavinicchayakathā

7. The Discourse on the Determination of What is Not to Be Touched

40. Anāmāsanti [M 0.0028][V 0.0029] na parāmasitabbaṃ. Tatrāyaṃ vinicchayo (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.281) – yasmā mātā vā hotu dhītā vā bhaginī vā, itthī nāma sabbāpi brahmacariyassa pāribanthikāva anāmāsā ca, tasmā “ayaṃ me mātā, ayaṃ me dhītā, ayaṃ me bhaginī”ti gehassitapemena āmasatopi dukkaṭameva vuttaṃ. Imaṃ pana bhagavato āṇaṃ anussarantena sacepi nadīsotena vuyhamānaṃ mātaraṃ passati, neva hatthena parāmasitabbā, paṇḍitena pana bhikkhunā nāvā vā phalakaṃ vā kadalikkhandho vā dārukkhandho vā upasaṃharitabbo. Tasmiṃ asati kāsāvampi upasaṃharitvā purato ṭhapetabbaṃ, “ettha gaṇhāhī”ti pana na vattabbā. Gahite “parikkhāraṃ kaḍḍhāmī”ti kaḍḍhantena gantabbaṃ. Sace pana bhāyati, purato purato gantvā “mā bhāyī”ti samassāsetabbā. Sace bhāyamānā puttassa sahasā khandhe vā abhiruhati, hatthe vā gaṇhāti, na “apehi mahallike”ti niddhunitabbā, thalaṃ pāpetabbā. Kaddame laggāyapi kūpe patitāyapi eseva nayo. Tatrāpi hi yottaṃ vā vatthaṃ vā pakkhipitvā hatthena gahitabhāvaṃ ñatvā uddharitabbā, na tveva āmasitabbā.

40. 'Not to be touched' means it should not be handled. Herein is the determination: Since whether it be a mother, a daughter, or a sister, any woman whatsoever is an obstacle to the holy life and is not to be touched, therefore, even touching with household-based affection, thinking, "This is my mother, this is my daughter, this is my sister," has been declared an offense of wrong-doing. Remembering this instruction of the Blessed One, even if one sees one's mother being swept away by a river current, one should not touch her with one's hand. Instead, a wise bhikkhu should offer her a boat, a plank, a banana trunk, or a piece of wood. If none of these are available, even his robe should be offered, placing it in front of her, but he should not say, "Take hold of this." If she takes hold of it, he should pull while thinking, "I am pulling a requisite," and proceed. If she is afraid, he should go ahead and reassure her, saying, "Do not be afraid." If, being afraid, she suddenly climbs onto his shoulder or grabs his hand, he should not shake her off, saying, "Go away, old woman," but should help her reach dry land. The same applies if she is stuck in mud or has fallen into a well. In such cases, after throwing in a rope or cloth and knowing that she has grasped it, he should pull her out—but he should not touch her directly.

Na kevalañca mātugāmassa sarīrameva anāmāsaṃ, nivāsanapārupanampi ābharaṇabhaṇḍampi antamaso tiṇaṇḍupakaṃ vā tālapaṇṇamuddikaṃ vā upādāya anāmāsameva. Tañca kho nivāsanapāvuraṇaṃ piḷandhanatthāya ṭhapitameva. Sace pana nivāsanaṃ vā pārupanaṃ vā parivattetvā cīvaratthāya pādamūle ṭhapeti, vaṭṭati. Ābharaṇabhaṇḍesu pana sīsapasādhanadantasūciādikappiyabhaṇḍaṃ “imaṃ, bhante, tumhākaṃ dema, gaṇhathā”ti dīyamānaṃ sipāṭikāsūciādiupakaraṇatthāya gahetabbaṃ. Suvaṇṇarajatamuttādimayaṃ pana anāmāsameva, dīyamānampi na gahetabbaṃ. Na kevalañca etāsaṃ sarīrūpagameva anāmāsaṃ, itthisaṇṭhānena kataṃ kaṭṭharūpampi dantarūpampi ayarūpampi loharūpampi tipurūpampi potthakarūpampi sabbaratanarūpampi antamaso piṭṭhamayarūpampi anāmāsameva. Paribhogatthāya pana “idaṃ tumhākaṃ hotū”ti labhitvā ṭhapetvā sabbaratanamayaṃ avasesaṃ bhinditvā upakaraṇārahaṃ upakaraṇe, paribhogārahaṃ paribhoge upanetuṃ vaṭṭati.

And it is not only the body of a woman that is not to be touched; her lower and upper garments, and her ornaments—even down to a grass head-ring or a palm-leaf ring—are also certainly not to be touched. And indeed, that lower garment and upper garment are not to be touched only when they are kept for the purpose of being worn. If, however, having exchanged a lower garment or an upper garment, it is placed at the feet for the purpose of a robe, it is allowable. As for ornaments, allowable items such as head ornaments, tooth-cleaners, and so forth, when offered with the words, 'Venerable sirs, we give this to you, please accept it,' should be accepted for the purpose of requisites such as a razor case, needles, and so forth. But items made of gold, silver, pearls, and so forth are certainly not to be touched; even when offered, they should not be accepted. And it is not only things connected to the bodies of these women that are not to be touched; a figure made in the shape of a woman—whether a wooden figure, an ivory figure, an iron figure, a bronze figure, a lead/tin figure, a stucco figure, a figure of any gem, or even down to a figure made of flour—is also certainly not to be touched. However, for the purpose of use, having received such a figure with the words, 'Let this be for you,' then setting aside the one made of any gem, it is allowable to break the remaining figures, destroying the female form, and to apply what is suitable for a requisite to requisites, and what is suitable for use to use.

41. Yathā [M 0.0029] ca itthirūpakaṃ, evaṃ sattavidhaṃ dhaññampi anāmāsameva. Tasmā khettamajjhena gacchantena tatthajātakampi dhaññaphalaṃ na āmasantena gantabbaṃ. Sace gharadvāre vā antarāmagge vā [V 0.0030] dhaññaṃ pasāritaṃ hoti, passena ca maggo atthi, na maddantena gantabbaṃ. Gamanamagge asati maggaṃ adhiṭṭhāya gantabbaṃ. Antaraghare dhaññassa upari āsanaṃ paññapetvā denti, nisīdituṃ vaṭṭati. Keci āsanasālāya dhaññaṃ ākiranti, sace sakkā hoti harāpetuṃ, harāpetabbaṃ. No ce, ekamantaṃ dhaññaṃ amaddantena pīṭhakaṃ paññapetvā nisīditabbaṃ. Sace okāso na hoti, manussā dhaññamajjheyeva paññapetvā denti, nisīditabbaṃ. Tatthajātakāni muggamāsādīni aparaṇṇānipi tālapanasādīni vā phalāni kīḷantena na āmasitabbāni. Manussehi rāsikatesupi eseva nayo. Araññe pana rukkhato patitāni phalāni “anupasampannānaṃ dassāmī”ti gaṇhituṃ vaṭṭati.

41. Just as a figure of a woman is not to be touched, so too the seven kinds of grain are not to be touched. Therefore, when walking through a field, one should not touch the fruit of the grain growing there. If grain is spread out at a house door or on a path, and there is a path by the side, one should not tread on it. If there is no path for going, one should go having determined the grain-covered area as a path. Inside a house, if they prepare and offer a seat on top of grain, it is allowable to sit. Some scatter grain in a sitting hall; if it can be removed, it should be removed. If not, one should set a stool to one side without treading on the grain and sit there. If there is no space, and people prepare and offer a seat right in the middle of the grain, one should sit. Pulses such as mung beans and black gram growing in their place, or fruits such as palmyra and jackfruit, should not be touched playfully. This same rule applies when they have been piled up by people. However, in the forest, it is allowable to take fruits that have fallen from a tree with the thought, 'I will give them to those who are not fully ordained.'

42. Muttā maṇi veḷuriyo saṅkho silā pavāḷaṃ rajataṃ jātarūpaṃ lohitaṅko masāragallanti imesu dasasu ratanesu muttā adhotā aviddhā yathājātāva āmasituṃ vaṭṭati, sesā anāmāsāti vadanti, taṃ na gahetabbaṃ. Mahāpaccariyaṃ pana “muttā dhotāpi adhotāpi anāmāsā, bhaṇḍamūlatthāya ca sampaṭicchituṃ na vaṭṭati, kuṭṭharogassa bhesajjatthāya pana vaṭṭatī”ti vuttaṃ, taṃ yuttaṃ. Antamaso jātiphalikaṃ upādāya sabbopi nīlapītādivaṇṇabhedo maṇi dhotaviddhavaṭṭito anāmāso, yathājāto pana ākaramutto pattādibhaṇḍamūlatthaṃ sampaṭicchituṃ vaṭṭatīti vuttaṃ, tampi mahāpaccariyaṃ paṭikkhittaṃ. Pacitvā kato kācamaṇiyeveko vaṭṭatīti vuttaṃ. Veḷuriyepi maṇisadisova vinicchayo.

42. Among these ten precious things—pearls, gems, lapis lazuli, conch shells, crystal, coral, silver, gold, red gems, and variegated gems—a pearl that is unwashed, undrilled, and just as it is by nature, is allowable to be touched. As for the rest, some teachers say they are not to be touched; that statement should not be accepted. However, in the Mahāpaccarī it is said: 'A pearl, whether washed or unwashed, is not to be touched, and it is not allowable to accept it for the value of goods; however, it is allowable to accept it for the purpose of medicine for leprosy.' That is correct. It is said that any gem with color variations such as blue or yellow, beginning with at least a nutmeg-colored one, if it has been washed, drilled, and rounded, is not to be touched. However, it is also said that if it is in its natural state, as it comes from the mine, it is allowable to accept it for the value of goods such as a bowl. That too is rejected in the Mahāpaccarī. It is said that only a single glass gem made by baking is allowable. For lapis lazuli also, the decision is the same as for a gem.

Saṅkho dhamanasaṅkho ca dhotaviddho ca ratanamisso anāmāso, pānīyasaṅkho dhotopi adhotopi āmāsova. Sesañca añjanādibhesajjatthāyapi bhaṇḍamūlatthāyapi sampaṭicchituṃ vaṭṭati. Silā dhotaviddhā ratanasaṃyuttā muggavaṇṇāva anāmāsā, sesā satthakanighaṃsanādiatthāya gaṇhituṃ vaṭṭati. Ettha ca ratanasaṃyuttāti suvaṇṇena saddhiṃ yojetvā pacitvā katāti vadanti. Pavāḷaṃ dhotaviddhaṃ anāmāsaṃ, sesaṃ āmāsañca bhaṇḍamūlatthañca sampaṭicchituṃ vaṭṭatīti vadanti, taṃ na gahetabbaṃ[M 0.0030]. Mahāpaccariyaṃ pana “dhotampi adhotampi sabbaṃ anāmāsañca na ca sampaṭicchituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti vuttaṃ, taṃ yuttaṃ.

A conch shell, that is, a blowing conch, even if polished and drilled or mixed with gems, is not to be touched; a water-drinking conch shell, whether polished or unpolished, is indeed to be touched. As for other conch shells, it is allowable to accept them for the purpose of medicine such as eye-ointment, and for the purpose of the value of goods. A crystal is not to be touched only if it is polished, drilled, conjoined with gems, and has a color like a mung bean; other crystals, it is allowable to take for the purpose of sharpening small knives and so on. Herein, 'conjoined with gems' means made by combining and smelting with gold, so they say. Coral, if polished and drilled, is not to be touched; other coral is to be touched, and it is allowable to accept it for the value of goods, so they say. That statement should not be accepted. However, in the Mahāpaccariya it is said: 'All coral whatsoever, whether polished or unpolished, is not to be touched, and it is not allowable to accept it.' That statement is correct.

Rajatañca jātarūpañca katabhaṇḍampi akatabhaṇḍampi sabbena sabbaṃ bījato paṭṭhāya anāmāsañca asampaṭicchanīyañca. Uttararājaputto kira suvaṇṇacetiyaṃ kārāpetvā mahāpadumattherassa pesesi. Thero “na kappatī”ti paṭikkhipi. Cetiyaghare suvaṇṇapadumasuvaṇṇabubbuḷakādīni honti, etānipi anāmāsāni. Cetiyagharagopakā pana rūpiyachaḍḍakaṭṭhāne ṭhitā[V 0.0031], tasmā tesaṃ keḷāpayituṃ vaṭṭatīti vuttaṃ. Kurundhiyaṃ pana tampi paṭikkhittaṃ, suvaṇṇacetiye kacavarameva harituṃ vaṭṭatīti ettakameva anuññātaṃ. Ārakūṭalohampi jātarūpagatikameva anāmāsanti sabbaṭṭhakathāsu vuttaṃ. Senāsanaparibhoge pana sabbopi kappiyo, tasmā jātarūparajatamayā sabbepi senāsanaparikkhārā āmāsā, bhikkhūnaṃ dhammavinayavaṇṇanaṭṭhāne ratanamaṇḍape karonti phalikatthambhe ratanadāmapaṭimaṇḍite, tattha sabbūpakaraṇāni bhikkhūnaṃ paṭijaggituṃ vaṭṭanti. Lohitaṅkamasāragallā dhotaviddhā anāmāsā, itare āmāsā, bhaṇḍamūlatthāya ca sampaṭicchituṃ vaṭṭatīti vuttaṃ. Mahāpaccariyaṃ pana “dhotāpi adhotāpi sabbaso anāmāsā, na ca sampaṭicchituṃ vaṭṭantī”ti paṭikkhittaṃ.

Silver and gold, whether as a finished article or an unfinished article, in every way, beginning from its seed-form, is not to be touched and is not to be received. It is said that Prince Uttara had a golden cetiya made and sent it to the Elder Mahāpaduma. The Elder rejected it, saying, 'It is not allowable.' In a cetiya-house, there are such things as golden lotuses and golden stars; these too are not to be touched. However, the guardians of the cetiya-house stand in the position of one who disposes of money; therefore, it is said that it is allowable for them to handle them by moving them from place to place. But in the Kurundī commentary, even that is rejected; only removing refuse from a golden cetiya is allowable—this much is permitted. Brass, being of the same nature as gold, is not to be touched, as is stated in all the aṭṭhakathās. Regarding the use of dwellings, however, all is allowable; therefore, all dwelling requisites made of gold and silver are to be touched. For the monks, in a place for explaining the Dhamma and Vinaya, they make jeweled pavilions adorned with crystal pillars and garlands of gems; there, it is allowable for the monks to attend to all the furnishings. Rubies and cat's-eye gems, when polished and drilled, are not to be touched; the others are to be touched. And it is said that it is allowable to receive them for the purpose of their value as goods. In the Mahāpaccariya, however, this is rejected, stating: 'Whether polished or unpolished, they are in every way not to be touched, nor is it allowable to receive them.'

43. Sabbaṃ āvudhabhaṇḍaṃ anāmāsaṃ, bhaṇḍamūlatthāya dīyamānampi na sampaṭicchitabbaṃ. Satthavaṇijjā nāma na vaṭṭati. Suddhadhanudaṇḍopi dhanujiyāpi patodopi tomaropi aṅkusopi antamaso vāsipharasuādīnipi āvudhasaṅkhepena katāni anāmāsāni. Sace kenaci vihāre satti vā tomaro vā ṭhapito hoti, vihāraṃ jaggantena “harantū”ti sāmikānaṃ pesetabbaṃ. Sace na haranti, taṃ acālentena vihāro paṭijaggitabbo. Yuddhabhūmiyaṃ pana patitaṃ asiṃ vā sattiṃ vā tomaraṃ vā disvā pāsāṇena vā kenaci vā asiṃ bhinditvā satthakatthāya gahetuṃ vaṭṭati. Itarānipi viyojetvā kiñci satthakatthāya, kiñci kattaradaṇḍādiatthāya gahetuṃ vaṭṭati. “Idaṃ gaṇhathā”ti dīyamānaṃ pana vināsetvā “kappiyabhaṇḍaṃ karissāmī”ti sabbampi sampaṭicchituṃ vaṭṭati.

43. All weapon-articles are not to be handled. Even if given for the sake of their value as goods, they should not be accepted. Trading in weapons is not allowable. Even a mere bow-staff, a bowstring, a goad, a lance, a hook, or even down to adzes, axes, and the like made in the manner of a weapon, are not to be handled. If a spear or a lance has been left in a monastery by someone, the one looking after the monastery should send a message to the owners, saying, “Please take it away.” If they do not take it away, the monastery should be maintained without moving the item. However, upon seeing a sword, a spear, or a lance that has fallen on a battlefield, it is allowable to break the sword with a stone or some other object and take it for the purpose of a small knife. It is also allowable to take the other items after dismantling them—some for the purpose of a small knife, and some for the purpose of a walking stick and the like. Furthermore, when such an item is being given with the words, “Take this,” it is allowable to accept it all after having destroyed it, with the thought, “I will make it an allowable requisite.”

Macchajālapakkhijālādīnipi [M 0.0031] phalakajālikādīnipi saraparittāṇānipi sabbāni anāmāsāni, paribhogatthāya labbhamānesu pana jālaṃ tāva “āsanassa vā cetiyassa vā upari bandhissāmi, chattaṃ vā veṭhessāmī”ti gahetuṃ vaṭṭati. Saraparittāṇaṃ sabbampi bhaṇḍamūlatthāya sampaṭicchituṃ vaṭṭati. Parūparodhanivāraṇañhi etaṃ, na uparodhakaranti. Phalakaṃ “dantakaṭṭhabhājanaṃ karissāmī”ti gahetuṃ vaṭṭati.

Fish-nets, bird-nets, and the like, shield-nets and the like, and all arrow-protections—all these are not to be handled. However, when such things are obtained for personal use, it is allowable to take a net, thinking, “I will tie it above a seat or a cetiya, or I will wrap an umbrella with it.” Any arrow-protection may be accepted in its entirety for the sake of its value as goods, for it serves to prevent assault from others; it does not cause assault. It is allowable to take a shield, thinking, “I will make it into a tooth-stick container.”

Cammavinaddhāni vīṇābheriādīni anāmāsāni. Kurundiyaṃ pana “bherisaṅghāṭopi vīṇāsaṅghāṭopi tucchapokkharampi mukhavaṭṭiyaṃ āropitacammampi vīṇādaṇḍakopi sabbaṃ anāmāsa”nti vuttaṃ. Onahituṃ vā onahāpetuṃ vā vādetuṃ vā vādāpetuṃ vā na labbhatiyeva. Cetiyaṅgaṇe pūjaṃ katvā manussehi chaḍḍitaṃ disvāpi acāletvāva antarantare sammajjitabbaṃ, kacavarachaḍḍanakāle pana kacavaraniyāmeneva haritvā ekamantaṃ nikkhipituṃ vaṭṭatīti [V 0.0032] mahāpaccariyaṃ vuttaṃ. Bhaṇḍamūlatthāya sampaṭicchitumpi vaṭṭati, paribhogatthāya labbhamānesu pana vīṇādoṇikañca bheripokkharañca dantakaṭṭhabhājanaṃ karissāma, cammaṃ satthakakosakanti evaṃ tassa tassa parikkhārassa upakaraṇatthāya gahetvā tathā tathā kātuṃ vaṭṭati.

Instruments such as lutes and great drums that are stretched with leather are not to be touched. However, in the Kurundī it is said: 'A drum stretched with leather, a lute stretched with leather, an empty drum-head or lute-head, leather placed on the rim, and the neck of a lute—all are not to be touched.' It is not permissible to stretch the leather onto an instrument oneself, to have another stretch it, to play it oneself, or to have another play it. Even if one sees such things discarded by people after making an offering in a cetiya courtyard, one should sweep in between them without moving them. However, at the time of discarding rubbish, it is proper to carry them away in the same manner as rubbish and place them to one side; so it is said in the Mahāpaccarī. It is also proper to accept them for the value of requisites. But when they are received for the purpose of use, it is proper to take the lute-bowl or the drum-head, thinking, 'We will make a tooth-stick container,' or the leather, thinking, 'We will make a sheath for a small knife.' Thus, having taken it for the purpose of making it a component of this or that requisite, it is proper to fashion it accordingly.

Iti pāḷimuttakavinayavinicchayasaṅgahe

Thus in the Collection of Vinaya Decisions Independent of the Canon,

Anāmāsavinicchayakathā samattā.

The Discourse on the Determination of What is Not to Be Touched is concluded.

8. Adhiṭṭhānavikappanavinicchayakathā

8. The Discourse on the Determination of Adhiṭṭhāna and Vikappana

44. Adhiṭṭhānavikappanesu [V 0.0033] pana – anujānāmi, bhikkhave, ticīvaraṃ adhiṭṭhātuṃ na vikappetuṃ, vassikasāṭikaṃ vassānaṃ cātumāsaṃ adhiṭṭhātuṃ tato paraṃ vikappetuṃ, nisīdanaṃ adhiṭṭhātuṃ na vikappetuṃ, paccattharaṇaṃ adhiṭṭhātuṃ na vikappetuṃ, kaṇḍuppaṭicchādiṃ yāva ābādhā adhiṭṭhātuṃ tato paraṃ vikappetuṃ, mukhapuñchanacoḷaṃ adhiṭṭhātuṃ na vikappetuṃ, parikkhāracoḷaṃ adhiṭṭhātuṃ na vikappetu”nti (mahāva. 358) vacanato ticīvarādiniyāmeneva adhiṭṭhahitvā paribhuñjitukaāmena “imaṃ saṅghāṭiṃ adhiṭṭhāmī”tiādinā nāmaṃ vatvā adhiṭṭhātabbaṃ. Vikappentena pana nāmaṃ aggahetvāva “imaṃ cīvaraṃ tuyhaṃ vikappemī”ti [M 0.0032] vatvā vikappetabbaṃ. Tattha (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.469) ticīvaraṃ adhiṭṭhahantena rajitvā kappabinduṃ datvā pamāṇayuttameva adhiṭṭhātabbaṃ. Assa pamāṇaṃ ukkaṭṭhaparicchedena sugatacīvarato ūnakaṃ vaṭṭati, lāmakaparicchedena saṅghāṭiyā uttarāsaṅgassa ca dīghato muṭṭhipañcakaṃ, tiriyaṃ muṭṭhittikaṃ pamāṇaṃ vaṭṭati. Antaravāsako dīghaso muṭṭhipañcako, tiriyaṃ dvihatthopi vaṭṭati. Pārupanenapi hi sakkā nābhiṃ paṭicchādetunti. Vuttappamāṇato pana atirekañca ūnakañca “parikkhāracoḷaka”nti adhiṭṭhātabbaṃ.

44. Now, regarding adhiṭṭhāna and vikappana: “I allow, O bhikkhus, the three robes to be determined but not to be shared; the rains-bathing cloth to be determined for the four months of the rains and thereafter to be shared; the sitting cloth to be determined but not to be shared; the ground-sheet to be determined but not to be shared; the itch-covering cloth to be determined as long as one is ill and thereafter to be shared; the face-wiping cloth to be determined but not to be shared; the requisite cloth to be determined but not to be shared.”

Tattha yasmā “dve cīvarassa adhiṭṭhānā kāyena vā adhiṭṭheti, vācāya vā adhiṭṭhetī”ti (pari. 322) vuttaṃ, tasmā purāṇasaṅghāṭiṃ “imaṃ saṅghāṭiṃ paccuddharāmī”ti paccuddharitvā navaṃ saṅghāṭiṃ hatthena gahetvā “imaṃ saṅghāṭiṃ adhiṭṭhāmī”ti cittena ābhogaṃ katvā kāyavikāraṃ karontena kāyena adhiṭṭhātabbā. Idaṃ kāyena adhiṭṭhānaṃ, taṃ yena kenaci sarīrāvayavena aphusantassa na vaṭṭati. Vācāya adhiṭṭhāne pana vacībhedaṃ katvā vācāya adhiṭṭhātabbā. Tatra duvidhaṃ adhiṭṭhānaṃ – sace hatthapāse hoti, “imaṃ saṅghāṭiṃ adhiṭṭhāmī”ti vācā bhinditabbā. Atha antogabbhe vā uparipāsāde vā sāmantavihāre vā hoti, ṭhapitaṭṭhānaṃ sallakkhetvā “etaṃ saṅghāṭiṃ adhiṭṭhāmī”ti vācā bhinditabbā. Esa nayo uttarāsaṅge antaravāsake ca. Nāmamattameva hi viseso, tasmā sabbāni saṅghāṭiṃ uttarāsaṅgaṃ antaravāsakanti evaṃ attano nāmeneva adhiṭṭhātabbāni. Sace adhiṭṭhahitvā ṭhapitavatthehi saṅghāṭiādīni karoti, niṭṭhite rajane ca kappe ca “imaṃ paccuddharāmī”ti paccuddharitvā puna adhiṭṭhātabbāni. Adhiṭṭhitena pana [V 0.0034] saddhiṃ mahantatarameva dutiyapaṭṭaṃ vā khaṇḍaṃ vā sibbantena puna adhiṭṭhātabbaṃ. Same vā khuddake vā adhiṭṭhānakiccaṃ natthi.

In this regard, because it is said, “There are two kinds of determination for a robe: one determines it by body, or one determines it by speech” (Pari. 322), therefore, having revoked the determination of the old outer robe (saṅghāṭi) by saying, “I revoke the determination of this outer robe,” one should take the new outer robe in hand and determine it by body, by making a mental resolution and performing a corresponding bodily gesture, saying, “I determine this outer robe.” This is determination by body; it is not valid for one who does not touch it with some part of the body. For determination by speech, however, one should determine it by making a verbal utterance. In this case, the determination is twofold: if the robe is within arm’s reach, the words, “I determine this outer robe,” should be uttered. If it is inside an inner chamber, on an upper floor, or in a nearby monastery, then having noted the place where it is kept, the words, “I determine that outer robe,” should be uttered. This is the method for the upper robe (uttarāsaṅga) and the inner robe (antaravāsaka) as well. Indeed, the only difference is the name; therefore, all robes should be determined by their own names, thus: ‘outer robe,’ ‘upper robe,’ and ‘inner robe.’ If one makes an outer robe or the like from cloth that has been determined and set aside, then when the dyeing and cutting are completed, one should revoke the previous determination by saying, “I revoke this,” and then determine them anew. Furthermore, when sewing a significantly larger second layer or a patch together with a determined robe, it must be determined anew. If the piece is of the same size or smaller, there is no need for determination.

Ticīvaraṃ pana parikkhāracoḷaṃ adhiṭṭhātuṃ vaṭṭati, na vaṭṭatīti? Mahāpadumatthero kirāha “ticīvaraṃ ticīvarameva adhiṭṭhātabbaṃ, sace parikkhāracoḷādhiṭṭhānaṃ labheyya, udositasikkhāpade parihāro niratthako bhaveyyā”ti. Evaṃ vutte kira avasesā bhikkhū āhaṃsu “parikkhāracoḷampi bhagavatāva ‘adhiṭṭhātabba’nti vuttaṃ, tasmā vaṭṭatī”ti. Mahāpaccariyampi vuttaṃ “parikkhāracoḷaṃ nāma pāṭekkaṃ nidhānamukhametaṃ. Ticīvaraṃ ‘parikkhāracoḷa’nti adhiṭṭhahitvā paribhuñjituṃ vaṭṭati, udositasikkhāpade (pārā. 471 ādayo) pana ticīvaraṃ adhiṭṭhahitvā pariharantassa [M 0.0033] parihāro vutto”ti. Ubhatovibhaṅgabhāṇako puṇṇavālikavāsī mahātissattheropi kirāha “mayaṃ pubbe mahātherānaṃ assumhā ‘araññavāsino bhikkhū rukkhasusirādīsu cīvaraṃ ṭhapetvā padhānaṃ padahanatthāya gacchanti, sāmantavihāre dhammassavanatthāya gatānañca tesaṃ sūriye uṭṭhite sāmaṇerā vā daharabhikkhū vā pattacīvaraṃ gahetvā gacchanti, tasmā sukhaparibhogatthaṃ ticīvaraṃ parikkhāracoḷaṃ adhiṭṭhātuṃ vaṭṭatī’”ti. Mahāpaccariyampi vuttaṃ “pubbe āraññikā bhikkhū abaddhasīmāya dupparihāranti ticīvaraṃ parikkhāracoḷameva adhiṭṭhahitvā paribhuñjiṃsū”ti.

Now, is it allowable to determine the three robes as an 'accessory cloth' (parikkhāracoḷa), or is it not? The Elder Mahāpaduma is said to have stated: “The three robes should be determined only as the three robes. If determination as an 'accessory cloth' were permitted, the safeguard in the Udosita training rule would become meaningless.” When this was said, the remaining bhikkhus are said to have replied: “The Blessed One himself has said that an 'accessory cloth' also ‘should be determined,’ therefore it is allowable.” In the Mahāpaccarī it is also said: “This which is called an 'accessory cloth' is a separate ground for storage. It is allowable to use the three robes after having determined them as an ‘accessory cloth.’ In the Udosita training rule, however, the safeguard is stated for one who looks after the three robes after having determined them as such.” The Elder Mahātissa, a resident of Puṇṇavālika and a reciter of both Vibhaṅgas, is also said to have remarked: “We formerly heard from the great elders that: ‘Forest-dwelling bhikkhus, having placed their robes in tree hollows and so forth, go for the purpose of striving in meditation; and when they have gone to a nearby monastery to hear the Dhamma, novices or young bhikkhus take their bowl and robes and follow them after the sun has risen. Therefore, for the sake of convenient use, it is allowable to determine the three robes as an 'accessory cloth.’” In the Mahāpaccarī it is also said: “Formerly, forest-dwelling bhikkhus, thinking, ‘It is difficult to look after them in an unconsecrated boundary,’ used the three robes only after having determined them as an 'accessory cloth.’”

45. Vassikasāṭikā anatirittappamāṇā nāmaṃ gahetvā vuttanayeneva cattāro vassike māse adhiṭṭhātabbā, tato paraṃ paccuddharitvā vikappetabbā. Vaṇṇabhedamattarattāpi cesā vaṭṭati, dve pana na vaṭṭanti. Nisīdanaṃ vuttanayena adhiṭṭhātabbameva, tañca kho pamāṇayuttaṃ ekameva, dve na vaṭṭanti. Paccattharaṇampi adhiṭṭhātabbameva, taṃ pana mahantampi vaṭṭati, ekampi vaṭṭati, bahūnipi vaṭṭanti, nīlampi pītakampi sadasampi pupphadasampīti sabbappakāraṃ vaṭṭati. Kaṇḍuppaṭicchādi yāva ābādho atthi, tāva pamāṇikā adhiṭṭhātabbā. Ābādhe vūpasante paccuddharitvā vikappetabbā, ekāva vaṭṭati. Mukhapuñchanacoḷaṃ adhiṭṭhātabbameva, yāva ekaṃ dhovīyati, tāva aññaṃ paribhogatthāya icchitabbanti dvepi vaṭṭanti. Apare pana therā “nidhānamukhametaṃ, bahūnipi vaṭṭantī”ti vadanti. Parikkhāracoḷe gaṇanā natthi, yattakaṃ icchati, tattakaṃ adhiṭṭhātabbameva. Thavikāpi parissāvanampi vikappanūpagapacchimacīvarappamāṇaṃ “parikkhāracoḷa”nti adhiṭṭhātabbameva. Tassa pamāṇaṃ dīghato dve vidatthiyo tiriyaṃ vidatthi, taṃ pana dīghato vaḍḍhakīhatthappamāṇaṃ, vitthārato tato upaḍḍhappamāṇaṃ hoti. Tatrāyaṃ pāḷi “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, āyāmena aṭṭhaṅgulaṃ sugataṅgulena caturaṅgulavitthataṃ pacchimaṃ cīvaraṃ vikappetu”nti [V 0.0035] (mahāva. 358). Bahūnipi ekato katvā “imāni cīvarāni parikkhāracoḷāni adhiṭṭhāmī”ti adhiṭṭhātumpi vaṭṭatiyeva. Bhesajjanavakammamātāpituādīnaṃ atthāya ṭhapentena anadhiṭṭhitepi natthi āpatti. Mañcabhisi pīṭhabhisi bimbohanaṃ pāvāro kojavoti etesu pana senāsanaparikkhāratthāya dinnapaccattharaṇe ca adhiṭṭhānakiccaṃ natthiyeva.

45. The rains-bathing cloth (vassikasāṭikā), provided it does not exceed the prescribed measurement, should be determined for the four months of the rains by stating its name, in accordance with the method described. After that period, its determination should be revoked and it should be placed under shared ownership (vikappana). It is allowable even if it is dyed merely to a different color, but two such cloths are not allowable. The sitting cloth (nisīdana) should be determined in the manner described; and indeed, only one of proper size is allowable—two are not. The ground-sheet (paccattharaṇa) should also be determined. However, a large one is allowable, a single one is allowable, and many are also allowable. All types are allowable, whether blue, yellow, with a fringe, or with a flower-patterned fringe. The itch-scratching cloth (kaṇḍuppaṭicchādi), of the prescribed size, should be determined for as long as the ailment persists. When the ailment has subsided, its determination should be revoked and it should be placed under shared ownership; only one is allowable. The face-wiping cloth (mukhapuñchanacoḷa) must be determined. Since another may be desired for use while one is being washed, two are allowable. Some elders, however, say, “This is a ground for storage; many are permissible.” For an 'accessory cloth' (parikkhāracoḷa), there is no numerical limit; as many as one desires may be determined. A bag (thavikā) and a water strainer (parissāvana), if they are at least the size of the smallest robe suitable for shared ownership, should be determined as an 'accessory cloth.' The measurement of that smallest robe is stated in the Pāli: “I allow, bhikkhus, the smallest robe, eight fingers in length by four fingers in width according to the Sugata-finger, to be placed under shared ownership” (Mahāvagga 358). As for the water strainer, its measurement is two spans in length and one span across; or, it is a carpenter's cubit in length and half of that in width. It is also allowable to bundle many cloths together and determine them by saying, “I determine these cloths as accessory cloths.” There is no offense for a bhikkhu who sets aside cloth for the sake of medicine, new construction work, his parents, and so on, even if it is not determined. However, for these items—a bed-covering (mañcabhisi), a chair-covering (pīṭhabhisi), a bolster (bimbohana), a blanket (pāvāra), a woolen rug (kojava)—and for a ground-sheet given as a requisite for a lodging, there is no need for determination whatsoever.

Sace [M 0.0034] pana (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.636-38) ñātakapavāritaṭṭhānato suttaṃ labhitvā ñātakapavāriteneva tantavāyena aññena vā mūlaṃ datvā cīvaraṃ vāyāpeti, vāyāpanapaccayā anāpatti. Dasāhātikkamanapaccayā pana āpattiṃ rakkhantena vikappanupagappamāṇamatte vīte tante ṭhitaṃyeva adhiṭṭhātabbaṃ. Dasāhātikkamena niṭṭhāpiyamānañhi nissaggiyaṃ bhaveyyāti.
