Ñātakādīhi tantaṃ āropāpetvā “tumhākaṃ, bhante, idaṃ cīvaraṃ gaṇheyyāthā”ti niyyātitepi eseva nayo.

But if one obtains thread from the place of a relative or an invited person and, having given payment to that same weaver who is a relative or an invited person, or to another, has a robe woven, there is no offense on account of having it woven. However, one who wishes to guard against an offense on account of exceeding ten days should determine the robe while it is still on the loom, once a portion of a size sufficient for vikappanā has been woven. For a robe that is being completed by exceeding ten days would become subject to forfeiture. This is the same principle even when relatives and others, having had the thread set up on the loom, dedicate it, saying, 'Venerable sir, this robe is for you; please accept it.'

Sace tantavāyo evaṃ payojito vā sayaṃ dātukāmo vā hutvā “ahaṃ, bhante, tumhākaṃ cīvaraṃ asukadivase nāma vāyitvā ṭhapessāmī”ti vadati, bhikkhu ca tena paricchinnadivasato paṭṭhāya dasāhaṃ atikkāmeti, nissaggiyaṃ pācittiyaṃ. Sace pana tantavāyo “ahaṃ tumhākaṃ cīvaraṃ vāyitvā sāsanaṃ pesessāmī”ti vatvā tatheva karoti, tena pesitabhikkhu pana tassa bhikkhuno na āroceti, añño disvā vā sutvā vā “tumhākaṃ, bhante, cīvaraṃ niṭṭhita”nti āroceti, etassa ārocanaṃ na pamāṇaṃ. Yadā pana tena pesitoyeva āroceti, tassa vacanaṃ sutadivasato paṭṭhāya dasāhaṃ atikkāmayato nissaggiyaṃ pācittiyaṃ.

If a weaver, being thus commissioned or wishing to give of his own accord, says, “Venerable sir, I will weave a robe for you and set it aside on such-and-such a day,” and the bhikkhu, starting from that specified day, lets ten days pass, it is a nissaggiya pācittiya offense. However, if the weaver says, “I will weave a robe for you and send a message,” and does so, but the bhikkhu who was sent does not inform that bhikkhu, and another, having seen or heard, informs him, saying, “Venerable sir, your robe is finished,” this notification is not the standard. But when the very one who was sent informs him, for one who lets ten days pass starting from the day his words are heard, it is a nissaggiya pācittiya offense.

Sace tantavāyo “ahaṃ tumhākaṃ cīvaraṃ vāyitvā kassaci hatthe pahiṇissāmī”ti vatvā tatheva karoti, cīvaraṃ gahetvā gatabhikkhu pana attano pariveṇe ṭhapetvā tassa na āroceti, añño koci bhaṇati “api, bhante, adhunā ābhataṃ cīvaraṃ sundara”nti. Kuhiṃ, āvuso, cīvaranti. Itthannāmassa hatthe pesitanti. Etassapi vacanaṃ na pamāṇaṃ. Yadā pana so bhikkhu cīvaraṃ deti, laddhadivasato paṭṭhāya dasāhaṃ atikkāmayato nissaggiyaṃ pācittiyaṃ. Sace pana vāyāpanamūlaṃ adinnaṃ hoti, yāva kākaṇikamattampi avasiṭṭhaṃ, tāva rakkhati.

If a weaver says, “I will weave a robe for you and send it by the hand of someone,” and does so, but the bhikkhu who took the robe places it in his own monastic dwelling without informing that bhikkhu; and if another says, “Venerable sir, is the robe that has recently been brought beautiful?” and when asked, “Friend, where is the robe?” is told, “It was sent into the hands of so-and-so,” even this statement is not authoritative. However, when that bhikkhu gives the robe, for one who lets ten days pass starting from the day it is received, it is a nissaggiya pācittiya offense. But if the payment for weaving has not been given, as long as even the amount of a kākaṇika remains, it protects.

46. Adhiṭṭhitacīvaraṃ (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.469) pana paribhuñjato kathaṃ adhiṭṭhānaṃ vijahatīti[V 0.0036]? Aññassa dānena acchinditvā gahaṇena vissāsaggāhena hīnāyāvattanena sikkhāpaccakkhānena kālakiriyāya liṅgaparivattanena paccuddharaṇena chiddabhāvenāti imehi navahi kāraṇehi vijahati. Tattha purimehi aṭṭhahi [M 0.0035] sabbacīvarāni adhiṭṭhānaṃ vijahanti, chiddabhāvena pana ticīvarasseva sabbaṭṭhakathāsu adhiṭṭhānavijahanaṃ vuttaṃ, tañca nakhapiṭṭhippamāṇena chiddena. Tattha nakhapiṭṭhippamāṇaṃ kaniṭṭhaṅgulinakhavasena veditabbaṃ, chiddañca vinividdhachiddameva. Chiddassa hi abbhantare ekatantu cepi acchinno hoti, rakkhati. Tattha saṅghāṭiyā ca uttarāsaṅgassa ca dīghantato vidatthippamāṇassa, tiriyantato aṭṭhaṅgulappamāṇassa padesassa orato chiddaṃ adhiṭṭhānaṃ bhindati, antaravāsakassa pana dīghantato vidatthippamāṇasseva, tiriyantato caturaṅgulappamāṇassa padesassa orato chiddaṃ adhiṭṭhānaṃ bhindati, parato na bhindati, tasmā jāte chidde ticīvaraṃ atirekacīvaraṭṭhāne tiṭṭhati, sūcikammaṃ katvā puna adhiṭṭhātabbaṃ. Yo pana dubbalaṭṭhāne paṭhamaṃ aggaḷaṃ datvā pacchā dubbalaṭṭhānaṃ chinditvā apaneti, adhiṭṭhānaṃ na bhijjati. Maṇḍalaparivattanepi eseva nayo. Dupaṭṭassa ekasmiṃ paṭale chidde vā jāte gaḷite vā adhiṭṭhānaṃ na bhijjati, khuddakaṃ cīvaraṃ mahantaṃ karoti, mahantaṃ vā khuddakaṃ karoti, adhiṭṭhānaṃ na bhijjati. Ubho koṭiyo majjhe karonto sace paṭhamaṃ chinditvā pacchā ghaṭeti, adhiṭṭhānaṃ bhijjati. Atha ghaṭetvā chindati, na bhijjati. Rajakehi dhovāpetvā setaṃ kārāpentassapi adhiṭṭhānaṃ adhiṭṭhānamevāti. Ayaṃ tāva adhiṭṭhāne vinicchayo.

46. How does the formal determination (adhiṭṭhāna) for a determined robe (adhiṭṭhitacīvara) cease when one uses it? It ceases through these nine causes: by giving it to another, by seizing it, by taking it on trust, by reverting to a lower state, by disavowing the training, by death, by a change of sex (liṅgaparivattana), by relinquishing it (paccuddharaṇa), or by being torn (chiddabhāva). Among these, the first eight causes make the determination cease for all robes, but being torn is stated in all the commentaries to make the determination cease only for the three robes—and that too only if the tear is the size of a fingernail’s surface. Here, the size of a fingernail’s surface should be understood as that of the little finger’s nail, and the tear must be a penetrating tear. For if even a single thread remains unbroken inside the tear, it protects the determination. Therein, for the outer robe (saṅghāṭī) and the upper robe (uttarāsaṅga), a tear within the area measuring a span from the long edge and eight finger-widths from the transverse edge breaks the determination; beyond that, it does not break. For the lower robe (antaravāsaka), however, a tear within the area measuring a span from the long edge and four finger-widths from the transverse edge breaks the determination; beyond that, it does not break. Therefore, if such a tear occurs, that robe of the triple set stands in the category of an extra robe, and one must mend it with needlework and then redetermine it. But if one first places a patch on a weak spot and afterwards cuts away the weak spot, the determination is not broken. This same method also applies to replacing a panel (maṇḍalaparivattana). For a double-layered robe, if a tear occurs or it becomes worn out in one layer, the determination is not broken. If one makes a small robe large, or makes a large robe small, the determination is not broken. If one brings both ends to the middle, and if one first cuts and then joins, the determination is broken. But if one joins them first and then cuts, it does not break. Even for one who has the robe washed by launderers and made white, the determination remains as it was. This, for now, is the analysis regarding the determination.

47. Vikappane pana dve vikappanā sammukhāvikappanā parammukhāvikappanā ca. Kathaṃ sammukhāvikappanā hoti? Cīvarānaṃ ekabahubhāvaṃ sannihitāsannihitabhāvañca ñatvā “imaṃ cīvara”nti vā “imāni cīvarānī”ti vā “etaṃ cīvara”nti vā “etāni cīvarānī”ti vā vatvā “tuyhaṃ vikappemī”ti vattabbaṃ, ayamekā sammukhāvikappanā. Ettāvatā nidhetuṃ vaṭṭati, paribhuñjituṃ pana vissajjetuṃ vā adhiṭṭhātuṃ vā na vaṭṭati. “Mayhaṃ santakaṃ, mayhaṃ santakāni paribhuñja vā vissajjehi vā yathāpaccayaṃ vā karohī”ti evaṃ pana vutte paccuddhāro nāma hoti, tato pabhuti paribhogādayopi vaṭṭanti.

47. Now, regarding vikappanā, there are two types: vikappanā in person (sammukhāvikappanā) and vikappanā in absence (parammukhāvikappanā). How is vikappanā in person performed? Having ascertained whether the robes are singular or plural, and whether they are near or far, and having said, “this robe,” or “these robes,” or “that robe,” or “those robes,” one should then say, “I make [this/these] common with you.” This is vikappanā in person. By this much, it is allowable to store the robe(s), but it is not allowable to use, to give away, or to determine it. However, when it is said [by the recipient], “It is your property; you may use it, give it away, or do with it as is suitable,” this is called a revocation (paccuddhāra). From that point on, using and so forth also become allowable.

Aparo nayo – tatheva cīvarānaṃ ekabahubhāvaṃ sannihitāsannihitabhāvañca ñatvā tasseva bhikkhuno santike “imaṃ cīvara”nti vā “imāni cīvarānī”ti vā “etaṃ cīvara”nti vā “etāni cīvarānī”ti vā vatvā pañcasu sahadhammikesu aññatarassa attanā abhirucitassa yassa kassaci nāmaṃ gahetvā “tissassa bhikkhuno vikappemī”ti vā “tissāya bhikkhuniyā, tissāya sikkhamānāya, tissassa sāmaṇerassa, tissāya sāmaṇeriyā [M 0.0036] vikappemī”ti [V 0.0037] vā vattabbaṃ, ayaṃ aparāpi sammukhāvikappanā. Ettāvatā nidhetuṃ vaṭṭati, paribhogādīsu pana ekampi na vaṭṭati. Tena pana bhikkhunā “tissassa bhikkhuno santakaṃ…pe… tissāya sāmaṇeriyā santakaṃ paribhuñja vā vissajjehi vā yathāpaccayaṃ vā karohī”ti vutte paccuddhāro nāma hoti, tato pabhuti paribhogādayopi vaṭṭanti.

Another method: In the same way, having ascertained whether the robes are singular or plural, and whether they are present or not present, in the presence of that same bhikkhu, and having said, “this robe,” or “these robes,” or “that robe,” or “those robes,” one should then take the name of any one of the five fellow Dhamma-practitioners whom one prefers and say, “I formally assign this to the bhikkhu Tissa,” or “I formally assign this to the bhikkhunī Tissā, to the female probationer Tissā, to the male novice Tissa, or to the female novice Tissā.” This is also another direct formal assignment. By this much, it is allowable to store it, but regarding using and so forth, not even one such act is allowable. However, when it is said by that bhikkhu, “It is the property of the bhikkhu Tissa… (and so on) … it is the property of the female novice Tissā; you may use it, give it away, or do with it as is suitable,” this is called a revocation. From that point on, using and so forth also become allowable.

Kathaṃ parammukhāvikappanā hoti? Cīvarānaṃ tatheva ekabahubhāvaṃ sannihitāsannihitabhāvañca ñatvā “imaṃ cīvara”nti vā “imāni cīvarānī”ti vā “etaṃ cīvara”nti vā “etāni cīvarānī”ti vā vatvā “tuyhaṃ vikappanatthāya dammī”ti vattabbaṃ. Tena vattabbo “ko te mitto vā sandiṭṭho vā”ti. Tato itarena purimanayeneva “tisso bhikkhū”ti vā…pe… “tissā sāmaṇerī”ti vā vattabbaṃ. Puna tena bhikkhunā “ahaṃ tissassa bhikkhuno dammī”ti vā…pe… “tissāya sāmaṇeriyā dammī”ti vā vattabbaṃ, ayaṃ parammukhāvikappanā. Ettāvatā nidhetuṃ vaṭṭati, paribhogādīsu pana ekampi na vaṭṭati. Tena pana bhikkhunā dutiyasammukhāvikappanāyaṃ vuttanayeneva “itthannāmassa santakaṃ paribhuñja vā vissajjehi vā yathāpaccayaṃ vā karohī”ti vutte paccuddhāro nāma hoti, tato pabhuti paribhogādayopi vaṭṭanti.

How does indirect formal assignment occur? Regarding the robes, having ascertained in the same way whether they are singular or plural, and whether they are present or not present, and having said, “this robe,” or “these robes,” or “that robe,” or “those robes,” one should say, “I give this to you for the purpose of formal assignment.” That bhikkhu should ask, “Who is your friend or acquaintance?” Then the other, in the same way as before, should say, “The bhikkhu Tissa,” or… (and so on)… “the female novice Tissā.” Again, that bhikkhu should say, “I give this to the bhikkhu Tissa,” or… (and so on)… “I give this to the female novice Tissā.” This is indirect formal assignment. By this much, it is allowable to store it, but regarding using and so forth, not even one such act is allowable. But when that bhikkhu, in the same way as stated in the second direct formal assignment, has said, “Use, or give away, or do as is suitable with what belongs to so-and-so,” this is called a revocation. From that point on, using and so forth are also allowable.

Dvinnaṃ vikappanānaṃ kiṃ nānākaraṇaṃ? Sammukhāvikappanāyaṃ sayaṃ vikappetvā parena paccuddharāpeti, parammukhāvikappanāyaṃ pareneva vikappāpetvā pareneva paccuddharāpeti, idamettha nānākaraṇaṃ. Sace pana yassa vikappeti, so paññattikovido na hoti, na jānāti paccuddharituṃ, taṃ cīvaraṃ gahetvā aññassa byattassa santikaṃ gantvā puna vikappetvā parena paccuddharāpetabbaṃ. Vikappitavikappanā nāmesā vaṭṭati. Evaṃ tāva cīvare adhiṭṭhānavikappanānayo veditabbo.

What is the difference between the two formal assignments? In a direct formal assignment, one formally assigns it oneself and has it revoked by another. In an indirect formal assignment, one has another both formally assign it and revoke it; this is the difference herein. But if the one to whom one formally assigns it is not skilled in the regulations and does not know how to revoke it, that robe should be taken, and having gone to another who is competent, it should be formally assigned again and one should have it revoked by that other. This, called a re-assignment of what was assigned, is allowable. Thus, the method of determination and formal assignment regarding a robe should be understood.

48. Patte pana ayaṃ nayo – pattaṃ adhiṭṭhahantena ukkaṭṭhamajjhimomakānaṃ aññataro pamāṇayuttova adhiṭṭhātabbo. Tassa pamāṇaṃ “aḍḍhāḷhakodanaṃ gaṇhātī”tiādinā (pārā. 602) nayena pāḷiyaṃ vuttaṃ. Tatrāyaṃ vinicchayo (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.602 ādayo) – anupahatapurāṇasālitaṇḍulānaṃ sukoṭṭitaparisuddhānaṃ dve magadhanāḷiyo gahetvā tehi taṇḍulehi anuttaṇḍulamakilinnamapiṇḍitaṃ suvisadaṃ kundamakuḷarāsisadisaṃ avassāvitodanaṃ pacitvā niravasesaṃ [M 0.0037] patte pakkhipitvā tassa odanassa catutthabhāgappamāṇo nātighano nātitanuko hatthahāriyo sabbasambhārasaṅkhato muggasūpo pakkhipitabbo, tato ālopassa ālopassa anurūpaṃ yāvacarimālopappahonakaṃ [V 0.0038] macchamaṃsādibyañjanaṃ pakkhipitabbaṃ, sappitelatakkarasakañjikādīni pana gaṇanūpagāni na honti. Tāni hi odanagatikāni honti, neva hāpetuṃ, na vaḍḍhetuṃ sakkonti. Evametaṃ sabbampi pakkhittaṃ sace pattassa mukhavaṭṭiyā heṭṭhimarājisamaṃ tiṭṭhati, suttena vā hīrena vā chindantassa suttassa vā hīrassa vā heṭṭhimantaṃ phusati, ayaṃ ukkaṭṭho nāma patto. Sace taṃ rājiṃ atikkamma thūpīkataṃ tiṭṭhati, ayaṃ ukkaṭṭhomako nāma patto. Sace taṃ rājiṃ na sampāpuṇāti antogadhameva hoti, ayaṃ ukkaṭṭhukkaṭṭho nāma patto.

48. Furthermore, regarding the bowl, this is the method: One who is formally determining a bowl should determine one of the large, medium, or small sizes that is of the proper measure. Its measure is stated in the Pāḷi by the method beginning with, “it holds cooked rice from half an āḷhaka [of uncooked rice],” and so on. Herein is the detailed explanation: Take two Magadhan nāḷis of unbroken, three-year-old Sāli rice that is well-pounded and thoroughly pure. With that rice, cook rice that is not too hard, not too soft, without lumps, very distinct, like a heap of jasmine buds, and from which the water has been drained. Place all of it into the bowl without remainder. A mung bean soup—of a measure of one-fourth of that rice, neither too thick nor too thin, suitable to be carried by hand, and prepared with all its ingredients—should be placed therein. Then, a suitable amount of curry, such as fish or meat, sufficient for every morsel up to the last, should be placed in. However, items such as ghee, oil, buttermilk, and rice gruel are not subject to calculation. For they are absorbed by the rice; they can neither decrease nor increase the measure. Thus, when all this has been placed in, if it stands level with the line below the rim of the bowl, and when one levels it off with a thread or a fiber, the lower edge of the thread or fiber touches it, this is called the large bowl. If it goes beyond that line and stands heaped up, this is called the large-inferior bowl. If it does not reach that line and remains only within it, this is called the large-superior bowl.

Ukkaṭṭhato upaḍḍhappamāṇo majjhimo nāma patto. Majjhimato upaḍḍhappamāṇo omako. Tasmā sace magadhanāḷiyā nāḷikodanādisabbampi pakkhittaṃ vuttanayeneva heṭṭhimarājisamaṃ tiṭṭhati, ayaṃ majjhimo nāma patto. Sace taṃ rājiṃ atikkamma thūpīkataṃ tiṭṭhati, ayaṃ majjhimomako nāma patto. Sace taṃ rājiṃ na sampāpuṇāti antogadhameva hoti, ayaṃ majjhimukkaṭṭho nāma patto. Sace magadhanāḷiyā upaḍḍhanāḷikodanādisabbampi pakkhittaṃ heṭṭhimarājisamaṃ tiṭṭhati, ayaṃ omako nāma patto. Sace taṃ rājiṃ atikkamma thūpīkataṃ tiṭṭhati, ayaṃ omakomako nāma patto. Sace taṃ rājiṃ na sampāpuṇāti antogadhameva hoti, ayaṃ omakukkaṭṭho nāma patto. Evamete nava pattā. Tesu dve apattā ukkaṭṭhukkaṭṭho ca omakomako cāti. Tasmā ete bhājanaparibhogena paribhuñjitabbā, na adhiṭṭhānūpagā na vikappanūpagā. Itare pana satta adhiṭṭhahitvā vā vikappetvā vā paribhuñjitabbā.

A bowl of half the measure of the large is called the medium bowl. A bowl of half the measure of the medium is called the small bowl. Therefore, if all the rice from one Magadhan nāḷi and so forth, when placed in the bowl in the manner stated, stands level with the lower line, this is called the medium bowl. If it rises above that line in a mound, this is called the medium-inferior bowl. If it does not reach that line and remains within, this is called the medium-superior bowl. If all the rice from half a Magadhan nāḷi and so forth, when placed in the bowl, stands level with the lower line, this is called the small bowl. If it rises above that line in a mound, this is called the small-inferior bowl. If it does not reach that line and remains within, this is called the small-superior bowl. Thus, there are these nine bowls. Among them, two are not proper bowls: the large-superior and the small-inferior. Therefore, these should be used merely as utensils, not being fit for formal determination or formal assignment. But the other seven should be used after being formally determined or formally assigned.

Pamāṇayuttānampi etesaṃ adhiṭṭhānavikappanūpagattaṃ evaṃ veditabbaṃ – ayopatto pañcahi pākehi, mattikāpatto dvīhi pākehi pakko adhiṭṭhānūpago. Ubhopi yaṃ mūlaṃ dātabbaṃ, tasmiṃ dinneyeva. Sace ekopi pāko ūno hoti, kākaṇikamattampi vā mūlaṃ adinnaṃ, na adhiṭṭhānūpago. Sace pattasāmiko vadati “yadā tumhākaṃ mūlaṃ bhavissati, tadā dassatha adhiṭṭhahitvā paribhuñjathā”ti, neva adhiṭṭhānūpago hoti, pākassa hi ūnattā pattasaṅkhyaṃ na gacchati, mūlassa sakalassa vā ekadesassa [M 0.0038] vā adinnattā sakabhāvaṃ na upeti, aññasseva santako hoti, tasmā pāke ca mūle ca suniṭṭhiteyeva adhiṭṭhānūpago hoti. Yo adhiṭṭhānūpago, sveva vikappanūpago. So hatthaṃ āgatopi anāgatopi adhiṭṭhātabbo vikappetabbo vā. Yadi hi pattakārako mūlaṃ labhitvā sayaṃ vā dātukāmo hutvā “ahaṃ bhante tumhākaṃ pattaṃ katvā asukadivase nāma pacitvā ṭhapessāmī”ti vadati, bhikkhu ca tena paricchinnadivasato paṭṭhāya dasāhaṃ atikkāmeti, nissaggiyaṃ pācittiyaṃ. Sace pana pattakārako “ahaṃ tumhākaṃ pattaṃ katvā pacitvā sāsanaṃ pesessāmī”ti vatvā tatheva karoti, tena [V 0.0039] pesitabhikkhu pana tassa bhikkhuno na āroceti, añño disvā vā sutvā vā “tumhākaṃ, bhante, patto niṭṭhito”ti āroceti, etassa ārocanaṃ na pamāṇaṃ. Yadā pana tena pesitoyeva āroceti, tassa vacanaṃ sutadivasato paṭṭhāya dasāhaṃ atikkāmayato nissaggiyaṃ pācittiyaṃ. Sace pana pattakārako “ahaṃ tumhākaṃ pattaṃ katvā pacitvā kassaci hatthe pahiṇissāmī”ti vatvā tatheva karoti, pattaṃ gahetvā āgatabhikkhu pana attano pariveṇe ṭhapetvā tassa na āroceti, añño koci bhaṇati “api, bhante, adhunā ābhato patto sundaro”ti. “Kuhiṃ, āvuso, patto”ti? “Itthannāmassa hatthe pesito”ti. Etassapi vacanaṃ na pamāṇaṃ. Yadā pana so bhikkhu pattaṃ deti, laddhadivasato paṭṭhāya dasāhaṃ atikkāmayato nissaggiyaṃ pācittiyaṃ, tasmā dasāhaṃ anatikkāmetvāva adhiṭṭhātabbo vikappetabbo vā.

Regarding these bowls of proper measure, it should be understood that their being subject to determination and assignment is as follows: an iron bowl fired five times and a clay bowl fired twice become subject to determination. For both, this is only so when the price to be given has been paid. If even a single firing is deficient, or if even a kākaṇika's worth of the price remains unpaid, it is not subject to determination. If the bowl’s owner says, 'When you have the price, then give it; having determined it, use it,' it is still not subject to determination. For due to the deficiency of the firing, it does not attain the designation of 'bowl,' and because the price—whether in whole or in part—has not been given, it does not become one's own property but remains the property of another. Therefore, only when both the firing and the price are fully settled does it become subject to determination. Whatever is subject to determination is also subject to assignment. It must be determined or assigned whether it has come into one's hand or not. For if the bowl-maker, having received the price and wishing to give it himself, says, 'Venerable sir, I will make your bowl and, having fired it, will have it ready on such-and-such a day,' and the monk lets ten days pass from that specified day, it is an offense of forfeiture with expiation. But if the bowl-maker says, 'I will make your bowl, fire it, and send a message,' and does so, but the monk sent by him does not inform that monk—and another, having seen or heard, says, 'Venerable sir, your bowl is finished'—this one's notification is not valid. But when the very one sent by him informs him, for the monk who lets ten days pass from the day his word was heard, it is an offense of forfeiture with expiation. But if the bowl-maker says, 'I will make your bowl, fire it, and send it by the hand of someone,' and does so, but the monk who came bringing the bowl places it in his own monastic dwelling without informing him—and some other monk says, 'Venerable sir, is the bowl that was just brought beautiful?' and is asked, 'Friend, where is the bowl?' and he replies, 'It was sent into the hand of so-and-so'—even this one's word is not valid. But when that monk gives the bowl, for the one who lets ten days pass from the day of receiving it, it is an offense of forfeiture with expiation. Therefore, one must determine or assign it without exceeding ten days.

Tattha dve pattassa adhiṭṭhānā kāyena vā adhiṭṭhāti, vācāya vā adhiṭṭhāti. Tesaṃ vasena adhiṭṭhahantena “imaṃ pattaṃ paccuddharāmī”ti vā “etaṃ pattaṃ paccuddharāmī”ti vā vatvā evaṃ sammukhe vā parammukhe vā ṭhitaṃ purāṇapattaṃ paccuddharitvā aññassa vā datvā navaṃ pattaṃ yattha katthaci ṭhitaṃ hatthena parāmasitvā “idaṃ pattaṃ adhiṭṭhāmī”ti cittena ābhogaṃ katvā kāyavikāraṃ karontena kāyena vā adhiṭṭhātabbo. Vacībhedaṃ katvā vācāya vā adhiṭṭhābhabbo. Tatra duvidhaṃ adhiṭṭhānaṃ – sace hatthapāse hoti, “imaṃ pattaṃ adhiṭṭhāmī”ti [M 0.0039] vācā bhinditabbā, atha antogabbhe vā uparipāsāde vā sāmantavihāre vā hoti, ṭhapitaṭṭhānaṃ sallakkhetvā “etaṃ pattaṃ adhiṭṭhāmī”ti vācā bhinditabbā. Adhiṭṭhahantena pana ekakena adhiṭṭhātumpi vaṭṭati, aññassa santike adhiṭṭhātumpi vaṭṭati. Aññassa santike ayamānisaṃso – sacassa “adhiṭṭhito nu kho me, no”ti vimati uppajjati, itaro sāretvā vimatiṃ chindissatīti. Sace koci dasa patte labhitvā sabbe attanāva paribhuñjitukāmo hoti, na sabbe adhiṭṭhātabbā, ekaṃ pattaṃ adhiṭṭhāya punadivase taṃ paccuddharitvā añño adhiṭṭhātabbo. Eteneva upāyena vassasatampi pariharituṃ sakkā.

In this matter, there are two determinations of a bowl: one determines it by body, or one determines it by speech. By means of these, one who is determining, having said, “I rescind this bowl,” or “I rescind that bowl,” and having thus rescinded an old bowl that is placed either in one’s presence or absence, or having given it to another, should then touch a new bowl placed anywhere with the hand. Having made the mental resolve, “I determine this bowl,” and making a bodily gesture, it should be determined by the body. Or, having made a verbal utterance, it should be determined by speech. In that regard, the determination is twofold: if it is within hand’s reach, the words, “I determine this bowl,” should be uttered. But if it is inside a chamber, on an upper floor, or in a nearby monastery, having noted its location, the words, “I determine that bowl,” should be uttered. Furthermore, one who is determining may do so alone, or it is permissible to determine it in the presence of another. In the presence of another, this is the benefit: if a doubt should arise for him, “Has it been determined by me or not?” the other can remind him and dispel the doubt. If someone, having received ten bowls, wishes to use them all himself, they should not all be determined. Having determined one bowl, on the next day, having rescinded that one, another should be determined. By this very method, it is possible to maintain them for even a hundred years.

Evaṃ appamattassa siyā adhiṭṭhānavijahananti? Siyā. Sace hi sayaṃ pattaṃ aññassa deti, vibbhamati vā, sikkhaṃ vā paccakkhāti, kālaṃ vā karoti, liṅgaṃ vāssa parivattati, paccuddharati vā, patte vā chiddaṃ hoti, adhiṭṭhānaṃ vijahati. Vuttañcetaṃ –

Even so, for a heedful monk, could there be an abandonment of the determination? There could be. For if he himself gives the bowl to another, or returns to the lay state, or renounces the training, or dies, or his gender changes, or he rescinds it, or a hole appears in the bowl, the determination is abandoned. And this has been said:

“Dinnavibbhantapaccakkhā[V 0.0040], kālakiriyākatena ca;

Liṅgapaccuddharā ceva, chiddena bhavati sattama”nti. (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.608) –

“By giving, returning to the lay state, and renunciation, and by the act of dying; also by change of gender and by rescinding, and seventh, by a hole, it is abandoned.”

Coragahaṇavissāsaggāhehipi vijahatiyeva. Kittakena chiddena adhiṭṭhānaṃ bhijjati? Yena kaṅgusitthaṃ nikkhamati ceva pavisati ca. Idañhi sattannaṃ dhaññānaṃ lāmakadhaññasitthaṃ. Tasmiṃ chidde ayacuṇṇena vā āṇiyā vā paṭipākatike kate dasāhabbhantare puna adhiṭṭhātabbo. Ayaṃ tāvettha adhiṭṭhāne vinicchayo.

A determination is indeed abandoned also through seizure by thieves or taking through intimacy. By a hole of what size is the determination broken? By a hole through which a grain of millet rice can both exit and enter. For this is the grain of the inferior grain among the seven types of grain. When that hole has been made normal again with iron powder or with a peg, it should be determined again within ten days. This, first, is the legal decision concerning determination herein.

49. Vikappane pana dve vikappanā sammukhāvikappanā ceva parammukhāvikappanā ca. Kathaṃ sammukhāvikappanā hoti? Pattānaṃ ekabahubhāvaṃ sannihitāsannihitabhāvañca ñatvā “imaṃ patta”nti vā “ime patte”ti vā “etaṃ patta”nti vā “ete patte”ti vā vatvā “tuyhaṃ vikappemī”ti vattabbaṃ, ayamekā sammukhāvikappanā. Ettāvatā nidhetuṃ vaṭṭati, paribhuñjituṃ pana vissajjetuṃ vā adhiṭṭhātuṃ vā na vaṭṭati. “Mayhaṃ santakaṃ paribhuñja vā vissajjehi vā yathāpaccayaṃ vā karohī”ti evaṃ pana vutte paccuddhāro nāma hoti, tato pabhuti paribhogādayopi vaṭṭanti.

49. Now, regarding assignment, there are two kinds of assignment: assignment in one's presence and assignment in one's absence. How does assignment in one's presence occur? Having known the state of the bowls as being one or many, and their state as being present or not present, and having said, 'this bowl' or 'these bowls' or 'that bowl' or 'those bowls,' one should say, 'I assign this to you.' This is one kind of assignment in one's presence. By this much, it is allowable to store it; however, it is not allowable to use, give away, or determine it. But when it is said, 'Use my possession, or give it away, or do with it as is suitable,' this is called a withdrawal. From then on, using it and so forth are also allowable.

Aparo nayo – tatheva pattānaṃ ekabahubhāvaṃ sannihitāsannihitabhāvañca ñatvā tasseva bhikkhuno santike “imaṃ patta”nti vā “ime patte”ti vā “etaṃ patta”nti vā “ete patte”ti vā vatvā pañcasu sahadhammikesu [M 0.0040] aññatarassa attanā abhirucitassa yassa kassaci nāmaṃ gahetvā “tissassa bhikkhuno vikappemī”ti vā “tissāya bhikkhuniyā, sikkhamānāya, sāmaṇerassa, tissāya sāmaṇeriyā vikappemī”ti vā vattabbaṃ, ayaṃ aparāpi sammukhāvikappanā. Ettāvatā nidhetuṃ vaṭṭati. Paribhogādīsu pana ekampi na vaṭṭati. Tena pana bhikkhunā tissassa bhikkhuno santakaṃ…pe… tissāya sāmaṇeriyā santakaṃ paribhuñja vā vissajjehi vā yathāpaccayaṃ vā karohīti vutte paccuddhāro nāma hoti, tato pabhuti paribhogādayopi vaṭṭanti.

Another method: similarly, knowing whether the bowls are one or many and whether they are present or not present, one should say in the presence of that very same monk, 'this bowl' or 'these bowls' or 'that bowl' or 'those bowls,' and then, taking the name of any one of the five co-religionists whom one likes, one should say, 'I assign this to the monk Tissa,' or 'to the nun Tissā, to the female probationer Tissā, to the male novice Tissa, or to the female novice Tissā.' This is also another kind of assignment in one's presence. By this much, it is permissible to put it aside. However, regarding using it and so forth, not even one is permissible. But when that monk says, '[This is] the property of the monk Tissa... or the property of the female novice Tissā; you may use it, or give it away, or do with it as is proper,' this is called withdrawal. From that point onwards, using it and so forth are also permissible.

Kathaṃ parammukhāvikappanā hoti? Pattānaṃ tatheva ekabahubhāvaṃ sannihitāsannihitabhāvañca ñatvā “imaṃ patta”nti vā “ime patte”ti vā “etaṃ patta”nti vā “ete patte”ti vā vatvā “tuyhaṃ vikappanatthāya dammī”ti vattabbaṃ. Tena vattabbo “ko te mitto vā sandiṭṭho vā”ti[V 0.0041]. Tato itarena purimanayena “tisso bhikkhū”ti vā…pe… “tissā sāmaṇerī”ti vā vattabbaṃ. Puna tena bhikkhunā “ahaṃ tissassa bhikkhuno dammī”ti vā…pe… “tissāya sāmaṇeriyā dammī”ti vā vattabbaṃ, ayaṃ parammukhāvikappanā. Ettāvatā nidhetuṃ vaṭṭati, paribhogādīsu pana ekampi na vaṭṭati. Tena pana bhikkhunā dutiyasammukhāvikappanāyaṃ vuttanayeneva “itthannāmassa santakaṃ paribhuñja vā vissajjehi vā yathāpaccayaṃ vā karohī”ti vutte paccuddhāro nāma hoti, tato pabhuti paribhogādayopi vaṭṭanti. Ayaṃ vikappane nayo.

How is assignment in one's absence done? Just as before, having known whether the bowls are singular or plural and whether they are present or not present, and having said, 'this bowl' or 'these bowls' or 'that bowl' or 'those bowls,' one should then say, 'I give this for the purpose of your assignment.' He should be asked: 'Who is your friend or acquaintance?' Then, the other, according to the previous method, should say: 'The monk Tissa,' or… 'The female novice Tissā.' Again, that monk should say: 'I give this to the monk Tissa,' or… 'I give this to the female novice Tissā.' This is assignment in one's absence. By this much, it is allowable to put it down, but among using it and so forth, not even one is allowable. However, when that monk, according to the very method stated in the second kind of assignment in one's presence, says, 'This is the possession of so-and-so. Use it, or give it away, or do with it as is suitable,' this is called withdrawal. From then on, using it and so forth are also allowable. This is the method for assignment.

50. Evaṃ adhiṭṭhahitvā vikappetvā ca paribhuñjantena patte bhinne kiṃ kātabbanti? Yassa patte rājimukhavaṭṭito heṭṭhā dvaṅgulappamāṇā na hoti tena na kiñci kātabbaṃ. Yassa (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.612-3) pana tādisā ekāpi rāji hoti, tena tassā rājiyā heṭṭhimapariyante pattavedhakena vijjhitvā pacitvā suttarajjukamakacirajjukādīhi vā tipusuttakena vā bandhitvā taṃ bandhanaṃ āmisassa alagganatthaṃ tipupaṭṭena vā kenaci vā baddhasilesena paṭicchādetabbaṃ. So ca patto adhiṭṭhahitvā paribhuñjitabbo. Sukhumaṃ vā chiddaṃ katvā bandhitabbo. Suddhehi pana madhukasitthakalākhāsajjurasādīhi bandhituṃ na vaṭṭati, phāṇitaṃ jhāpetvā pāsāṇacuṇṇena bandhituṃ vaṭṭati. Mukhavaṭṭisamīpe pana pattavedhakena vijjhiyamāno kapālassa bahalattā [M 0.0041] bhijjati, tasmā heṭṭhā vijjhitabbo. Yassa pana dve rājiyo, ekāyeva vā caturaṅgulā, tassa dve bandhanāni dātabbāni. Yassa tisso, ekāyeva vā chaḷaṅgulā, tassa tīṇi. Yassa catasso, ekāyeva vā aṭṭhaṅgulā, tassa cattāri. Yassa pañca, ekāyeva vā dasaṅgulā, so baddhopi abaddhopi apattoyeva, añño viññāpetabbo. Esa tāva mattikāpatte vinicchayo.

50. Having determined and assigned it in this way, what should be done if the bowl breaks while one is using it? For one whose bowl has no crack extending two finger-breadths below the rim, nothing needs to be done. But for one whose bowl has even a single crack of that kind, one should pierce it with a bowl-awl at the lower edge of that crack, fire it, and bind it with thread-string, fiber-string, etc., or with tin thread; and that binding should be covered with a tin plate or some strong adhesive to prevent food from sticking. That bowl should then be determined and used. Alternatively, a small hole can be made and bound. However, it is not permissible to bind it with pure beeswax, lac, resin, etc. It is permissible to bind it with molasses that has been heated with stone powder. When piercing near the rim with a bowl-awl, it breaks due to the thickness of the bowl, so it should be pierced lower down. For a bowl that has two cracks, or a single crack four finger-breadths long, two bindings should be applied. For one with three cracks, or a single crack six finger-breadths long, three bindings. For one with four cracks, or a single crack eight finger-breadths long, four bindings. For one with five cracks, or a single crack ten finger-breadths long, whether bound or unbound, it is no longer a bowl; another should be requested. This, for now, is the ruling regarding clay bowls.

Ayopatte pana sacepi pañca vā atirekāni vā chiddāni honti, tāni ca ayacuṇṇena vā āṇiyā vā lohamaṇḍalakena vā baddhāni maṭṭhāni honti, sveva patto paribhuñjitabbo, añño na viññāpetabbo. Atha pana ekampi chiddaṃ mahantaṃ hoti, lohamaṇḍalakena baddhampi maṭṭhaṃ na hoti, patte āmisaṃ laggati, akappiyo hoti, ayaṃ apatto, añño viññāpetabbo. Viññāpentena ca saṅghavasena pavāritaṭṭhāne pañcabandhaneneva pattena aññaṃ pattaṃ viññāpetuṃ vaṭṭati, puggalavasena pana pavāritaṭṭhāne ūnapañcabandhanenāpi vaṭṭati. Pattaṃ labhitvā paribhuñjantena ca yāgurandhanarajanapacanādinā aparibhogena na paribhuñjitabbo, antarāmagge pana byādhimhi uppanne aññasmiṃ bhājane asati mattikāya limpetvā yāguṃ vā pacituṃ udakaṃ vā tāpetuṃ vaṭṭati. Mañcapīṭhachattanāgadantakādike adesepi na [V 0.0042] nikkhipitabbo. Pattassa hi nikkhipanadeso “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, pattādhāraka”ntiādinā (cūḷava. 254) nayena khandhake vuttoyeva.

In the case of an iron bowl, however, even if there are five or more holes, and they are bound with iron powder, a peg, or an iron disc and made smooth, that very bowl should be used; another should not be requested. But if even one hole is large and, though bound with an iron disc, is not smooth, and food sticks in the bowl, it becomes unsuitable. This is not a bowl, and another should be requested. When requesting, it is allowable to request another bowl at a place of invitation by way of the Saṅgha only with a bowl that has five bindings. But by way of an individual, at a place of invitation, it is allowable even with one that has fewer than five bindings. Having obtained a bowl, one should not use it for an improper purpose such as cooking gruel, boiling dye, and so on. But on a journey, if an illness arises and there is no other vessel, it is allowable to smear it with clay to cook gruel or to heat water. It should not be placed in an improper place such as on a bed, a chair, a parasol, an elephant-tusk peg, and so on. For the place for setting down the bowl has indeed been stated in the Khandhaka by the method beginning with, “I allow, O monks, a bowl-stand.”

Iti pāḷimuttakavinayavinicchayasaṅgahe

Thus, in the Compilation of Vinaya Judgments Separate from the Pāḷi.

Adhiṭṭhānavikappanavinicchayakathā samattā.

The Discourse on the Judgments of Determination and Assignment is concluded.

9. Cīvaravippavāsavinicchayakathā

9. The Discourse on the Judgment of Separation from the Robe

51. Cīvarenavināvāsoti [V 0.0043] ticīvarādhiṭṭhānena adhiṭṭhitānaṃ tiṇṇaṃ cīvarānaṃ aññatarena vippavāso. Evaṃ adhiṭṭhitesu hi tīsu cīvaresu ekenapi vinā vasituṃ na vaṭṭati, vasantassa saha aruṇuggamanā cīvaraṃ nissaggiyaṃ [M 0.0042] hoti, tasmā aruṇuggamanasamaye cīvaraṃ aḍḍhateyyaratanappamāṇe hatthapāse katvā vasitabbaṃ. Gāmanivesanaudositaaḍḍamāḷapāsādahammiyanāvāsatthakhettadhaññakaraṇaārāmavihārarukkhamūlaajjhokāsesu pana ayaṃ viseso (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.477-8) – sace ekassa rañño gāmabhojakassa vā santako gāmo hoti, yena kenaci pākārena vā vatiyā vā parikhāya vā parikkhitto ca, evarūpe gāme cīvaraṃ nikkhipitvā gāmabbhantare yattha katthaci yathārucitaṭṭhāne aruṇaṃ uṭṭhāpetuṃ vaṭṭati. Sace pana aparikkhitto hoti, evarūpe gāme yasmiṃ ghare cīvaraṃ nikkhittaṃ, tasmiṃ vatthabbaṃ, tassa vā gharassa hatthapāse samantā aḍḍhateyyaratanabbhantare vasitabbaṃ. Taṃ pamāṇaṃ atikkamitvā sacepi iddhimā bhikkhu ākāse aruṇaṃ uṭṭhāpeti, cīvaraṃ nissaggiyameva hoti.

51. The term 'dwelling without a robe' means separation from any one of the three robes that have been formally determined as the three robes. For when these three robes have been so determined, it is not permissible to dwell even without one of them. For a monk dwelling thus, the robe becomes subject to forfeiture at the rising of the dawn. Therefore, at the time of dawn's rising, the robe should be kept within arm's reach, a distance of two and a half cubits, and one should dwell accordingly. However, there is this distinction regarding villages, houses, storehouses, half-mansions, palaces, storied mansions, boats, carts, fields, threshing floors, monastery parks, monasteries, the foot of trees, and open spaces: If a village is the property of a single king or a village headman, and is enclosed by any kind of wall, fence, or moat, in such a village, after placing the robe, one may greet the dawn anywhere within the village wherever one prefers. But if the village is unenclosed, in such a village, one must dwell in the house where the robe has been placed, or within arm's reach, a distance of two and a half cubits all around that house. If one exceeds this limit, even if a monk with psychic powers greets the dawn in the sky, the robe indeed becomes subject to forfeiture.

Sace nānārājūnaṃ vā bhojakānaṃ vā gāmo hoti vesālīkusinārādisadiso parikkhitto ca, evarūpe gāme yasmiṃ ghare cīvaraṃ nikkhittaṃ, tattha vā vatthabbaṃ, tattha saddasaṅghaṭṭanena vā janasambādhena vā vasituṃ asakkontena sabhāye vā vatthabbaṃ nagaradvāramūle vā. Tatrāpi vasituṃ asakkontena yattha katthaci phāsukaṭṭhāne vasitvā antoaruṇe āgamma tesaṃyeva sabhāyanagaradvāramūlānaṃ hatthapāse vasitabbaṃ. Gharassa pana cīvarassa vā hatthapāse vattabbameva natthi.

If a village belongs to various kings or headmen, is similar to Vesālī or Kusinārā, and is enclosed, in such a village, one must dwell in the house where the robe is placed. Or, if unable to dwell there due to the clash of sounds or crowding by people, one must dwell in the assembly hall or at the foot of the city gate. If unable to dwell even there, having dwelt in any comfortable place whatsoever, one must return before dawn and dwell within arm's reach of those very assembly halls or city gates. However, there is no need to speak of dwelling within arm's reach of the house or the robe.

Sace ghare aṭṭhapetvā “sabhāye ṭhapessāmī”ti sabhāyaṃ gacchanto hatthaṃ pasāretvā “handimaṃ cīvaraṃ ṭhapehī”ti evaṃ nikkhepasukhe hatthapāsagate kismiñci āpaṇe cīvaraṃ nikkhipati, tena purimanayeneva sabhāye vā vatthabbaṃ, dvāramūle vā tesaṃ hatthapāse vā vasitabbaṃ.

If, not having placed it in the house, one goes to the assembly hall thinking, 'I will place it in the assembly hall,' and stretching out the hand, deposits the robe in some shop that is within arm's reach and convenient for depositing, saying, 'Here, place this robe,' then by the former method, one should stay either in the assembly hall, or at the base of the gate, or within arm's reach of them.

Sace nagarassa bahūnipi dvārāni honti bahūni ca sabhāyāni, sabbattha vasituṃ na vaṭṭati. Yassā pana vīthiyā cīvaraṃ ṭhapitaṃ, yaṃ tassā sammukhaṭṭhāne sabhāyañca dvārañca, tassa sabhāyassa ca dvārassa ca hatthapāse vasitabbaṃ. Evañhi sati sakkā cīvarassa pavattiṃ jānituṃ[V 0.0044]. Sabhāyaṃ pana gacchantena yassa āpaṇikassa hatthe nikkhittaṃ, sace so taṃ cīvaraṃ atiharitvā ghare nikkhipati, vīthihatthapāso na rakkhati, gharassa hatthapāse [M 0.0043] vatthabbaṃ. Sace mahantaṃ gharaṃ hoti dve vīthiyo pharitvā ṭhitaṃ, purato vā pacchato vā hatthapāseyeva aruṇaṃ uṭṭhāpetabbaṃ. Sabhāye nikkhipitvā pana sabhāye vā tassa sammukhe nagaradvāramūle vā tesaṃyeva hatthapāse vā aruṇaṃ uṭṭhāpetabbaṃ. Sace pana gāmo aparikkhitto hoti, yasmiṃ ghare cīvaraṃ nikkhittaṃ, tasmiṃ ghare tassa gharassa vā hatthapāse vatthabbaṃ.

If a city has many gates and also many assembly halls, it is not allowable to stay everywhere. However, in whichever street the robe has been placed, one should stay within arm's reach of the assembly hall and the gate that are in a position opposite that street. For, this being so, it is possible to know the state of the robe. Furthermore, by one going to the assembly hall, if the robe is placed in the hands of a shopkeeper, and if he carries that robe away and deposits it in his house, the arm's reach of the street does not protect; one must stay within arm's reach of the house. If it is a large house spanning two streets, one should let dawn arise either in front or behind, but within arm’s reach of the house. Furthermore, having deposited the robe in the assembly hall, one should let dawn arise either in the assembly hall, or at the base of the city gate opposite it, or within arm’s reach of them. If, however, the village is unenclosed, one should stay in the house where the robe was deposited, or within arm's reach of that house.

Sace (pārā. 480) ekakulassa santakaṃ nivesanaṃ hoti parikkhittañca nānāgabbhaṃ nānāovarakaṃ, antonivesane cīvaraṃ nikkhipitvā antonivesane vatthabbaṃ. Sace aparikkhittaṃ, yasmiṃ gabbhe cīvaraṃ nikkhittaṃ hoti, tasmiṃ gabbhe vatthabbaṃ gabbhassa hatthapāse vā. Sace nānākulassa nivesanaṃ hoti parikkhittañca nānāgabbhaṃ nānāovarakaṃ, yasmiṃ gabbhe cīvaraṃ nikkhittaṃ hoti, tasmiṃ gabbhe vatthabbaṃ, sabbesaṃ sādhāraṇe gharadvāramūle vā gabbhassa vā gharadvāramūlassa vā hatthapāse. Sace aparikkhittaṃ hoti, yasmiṃ gabbhe cīvaraṃ nikkhittaṃ, tasmiṃ gabbhe vatthabbaṃ gabbhassa vā hatthapāse. Udositaaḍḍamāḷapāsādahammiyesupi nivesane vuttanayeneva vinicchayo veditabbo.

If a dwelling belonging to a single family is enclosed and has various inner rooms and various chambers, having placed the robe inside the dwelling, one should dwell inside the dwelling. If it is unenclosed, one should dwell in the inner room where the robe is placed, or within arm's reach of the inner room. If a dwelling belonging to various families is enclosed and has various inner rooms and various chambers, one should dwell in the inner room where the robe is placed, or at the base of the house door common to all, or within arm's reach of the inner room, or within arm's reach of the base of the house door. If it is unenclosed, one should dwell in the inner room where the robe is placed, or within arm's reach of the inner room. Also for storehouses, half-mansions, palaces, and storied mansions, the judgment should be understood in the same way as stated for a dwelling.

Sace ekakulassa nāvā hoti, antonāvāyaṃ cīvaraṃ nikkhipitvā antonāvāyaṃ vatthabbaṃ. Sace nānākulassa nāvā hoti nānāgabbhā nānāovarakā, yasmiṃ ovarake cīvaraṃ nikkhittaṃ hoti, tasmiṃ ovarake vatthabbaṃ ovarakassa hatthapāse vā.

If a boat belongs to one family, having placed the robe inside the boat, one should dwell inside the boat. If a boat belonging to various families has various compartments and various cabins, one should dwell in the cabin where the robe is placed, or within arm's reach of the cabin.

Sace ekakulassa sattho hoti, tasmiṃ satthe cīvaraṃ nikkhipitvā purato vā pacchato vā sattabbhantarā na vijahitabbā, passato abbhantaraṃ na vijahitabbaṃ. Ekaṃ abbhantaraṃ aṭṭhavīsatihatthaṃ hoti. Sace nānākulassa sattho hoti, satthe cīvaraṃ nikkhipitvā cīvarassa hatthapāse vasitabbaṃ. Sace sattho gacchanto gāmaṃ vā nadiṃ vā pariyādiyitvā tiṭṭhati, antopaviṭṭhena saddhiṃ ekābaddho hutvā orañca pārañca pharitvā ṭhito hoti, satthaparihāro labbhati. Atha gāme vā nadiyā vā pariyāpanno hoti, gāmaparihāro ceva nadīparihāro ca labbhati. Sace vihārasīmaṃ atikkamitvā tiṭṭhati, antosīmāya ca cīvaraṃ hoti, vihāraṃ gantvā [M 0.0044] vasitabbaṃ. Sace bahisīmāya cīvaraṃ hoti, satthasamīpeyeva vasitabbaṃ. Sace gacchanto sattho sakaṭe vā bhagge goṇe vā naṭṭhe antarā chijjati, yasmiṃ koṭṭhāse cīvaraṃ nikkhittaṃ, tattha vasitabbaṃ.

If a caravan belongs to a single family, having placed the robe in that caravan, one should not abandon the seven abbhantaras in front or behind, nor the one abbhantara to the side. One abbhantara is twenty-eight cubits. If the caravan belongs to various families, having placed the robe in the caravan, one should dwell within arm's reach of the robe. If the traveling caravan stops after encompassing a village or a river, and it is united with those that have entered within, standing spread out across both this side and the far side, then the caravan's protection is obtained. If, however, it is included within the village or the river, the protection of the village and the protection of the river are obtained. If the caravan stops having crossed the monastery boundary, and the robe is within the boundary, one should go to the monastery and dwell. If the robe is outside the boundary, one should dwell in the vicinity of the caravan itself. If the traveling caravan is interrupted in the middle when a cart is broken or an ox is lost, one should dwell in that section where the robe was placed.

Sace [V 0.0045] ekakulassa khettaṃ hoti parikkhittañca, antokhette cīvaraṃ nikkhipitvā antokhette vatthabbaṃ. Sace aparikkhittaṃ hoti, cīvarassa hatthapāse vasitabbaṃ. Sace nānākulassa khettaṃ hoti parikkhittañca, antokhette cīvaraṃ nikkhipitvā dvāramūle vatthabbaṃ dvāramūlassa hatthapāse vā. Sace aparikkhittaṃ hoti, cīvarassa hatthapāse vasitabbaṃ.

If a field belongs to a single family and is enclosed, having placed the robe inside the field, one should dwell inside the field. If it is unenclosed, one should dwell within arm's reach of the robe. If a field belongs to various families and is enclosed, having placed the robe inside the field, one should dwell at the entrance or within arm's reach of the entrance. If it is unenclosed, one should dwell within arm's reach of the robe.

Sace ekakulassa dhaññakaraṇaṃ hoti parikkhittañca, antodhaññakaraṇe cīvaraṃ nikkhipitvā antodhaññakaraṇe vatthabbaṃ. Sace aparikkhittaṃ hoti, cīvarassa hatthapāse vasitabbaṃ. Sace nānākulassa dhaññakaraṇaṃ hoti parikkhittañca, antodhaññakaraṇe cīvaraṃ nikkhipitvā dvāramūle vā vatthabbaṃ dvāramūlassa vā hatthapāse. Sace aparikkhittaṃ hoti, cīvarassa hatthapāse vasitabbaṃ. Pupphārāmaphalārāmesupi khette vuttanayeneva vinicchayo veditabbo.

If a threshing floor belongs to a single family and is enclosed, having placed the robe inside the threshing floor, one should dwell inside the threshing floor. If it is unenclosed, one should dwell within arm's reach of the robe. If a threshing floor belongs to various families and is enclosed, having placed the robe inside the threshing floor, one should dwell either at the entrance or within arm's reach of the entrance. If it is unenclosed, one should dwell within arm's reach of the robe. In the case of flower parks and fruit parks as well, the ruling should be understood according to the method stated for a field.

Sace ekakulassa vihāro hoti parikkhitto ca, antovihāre cīvaraṃ nikkhipitvā antovihāre vatthabbaṃ. Sace aparikkhitto hoti, yasmiṃ vihāre cīvaraṃ nikkhittaṃ, tasmiṃ vatthabbaṃ tassa vihārassa vā hatthapāse.

If a monastery belongs to a single family and is enclosed, having placed the robe inside the monastery, one should dwell inside the monastery. If it is unenclosed, one should dwell in that monastery in which the robe was placed, or within arm's reach of that monastery.

Sace ekakulassa rukkhamūlaṃ hoti, yaṃ majjhanhike kāle samantā chāyā pharati, antochāyāya cīvaraṃ nikkhipitvā antochāyāya vatthabbaṃ. Viraḷasākhassa pana rukkhassa ātapena phuṭṭhokāse ṭhapitaṃ nissaggiyameva hoti, tasmā tādisassa rukkhassa sākhacchāyāya vā khandhacchāyāya vā ṭhapetabbaṃ. Sace sākhāya vā viṭape vā ṭhapeti, upari aññasākhacchāyāya phuṭṭhokāseyeva ṭhapetabbaṃ. Khujjarukkhassa chāyā dūraṃ gacchati, chāyāya gataṭṭhāne ṭhapetuṃ vaṭṭatiyeva. Sace nānākulassa rukkhamūlaṃ hoti, cīvarassa hatthapāse vasitabbaṃ.

If there is the vicinity of a tree belonging to a single family, one should place the robe inside the shade—that place which the shade covers all around at midday—and dwell inside the shade. However, for a tree with sparse branches, a robe placed in a spot touched by the sun's heat is indeed subject to forfeiture. Therefore, for such a tree, it should be placed either in the shade of a branch or in the shade of the trunk. If one places it on a branch or on a bough, it should be placed only in a spot above that is touched by the shade of another branch. The shade of a crooked tree goes far; it is indeed permissible to place the robe in the place where the shade has gone. If the vicinity of a tree belongs to various families, one should dwell within arm's reach of the robe.

Ajjhokāse pana agāmake araññe cīvaraṃ ṭhapetvā tassa samantā sattabbhantare vasitabbaṃ. Agāmakaṃ nāma araññaṃ viñjhāṭavīādīsu vā samuddamajjhe vā macchabandhānaṃ agamanapathe dīpakesu labbhati. Tādise araññe majjhe [M 0.0045] ṭhitassa samantā sattabbhantaraparicchedo, vinibbedhena cuddasa honti. Majjhe nisinno puratthimāya vā pacchimāya vā disāya pariyante ṭhapitacīvaraṃ rakkhati. Sace pana aruṇuggamanasamaye kesaggamattampi puratthimaṃ disaṃ gacchati, pacchimāya disāya cīvaraṃ nissaggiyaṃ hoti. Esa nayo itarasmiṃ. Nissaggiyaṃ pana cīvaraṃ anissajjitvā paribhuñjanto dukkaṭaṃ āpajjati.

Furthermore, in an open space, in a wilderness without a nearby village, having placed a robe, one should reside within seven abbhantaras all around it. A wilderness without a nearby village is found in great forests such as the Viñjhāṭavī, or in the middle of the ocean on islets on a path not frequented by fishermen. For one standing in the middle of such a wilderness, the boundary all around is seven abbhantaras; by diameter, they are fourteen. Sitting in the middle, one guards the robe placed at the boundary in the eastern or western direction. If, however, at the time of sunrise, one goes even a hair's tip towards the eastern direction, the robe in the western direction becomes subject to forfeiture. This is the method in the other case. Furthermore, one who uses a robe subject to forfeiture without having relinquished it incurs a dukkaṭa offense.

52. Sace [V 0.0046] padhāniko bhikkhu sabbarattiṃ padhānamanuyuñjitvā paccūsasamaye “nahāyissāmī”ti tīṇi cīvarāni tīre ṭhapetvā nadiṃ otarati, nahāyantasseva cassa aruṇaṃ uṭṭhahati, kiṃ kātabbaṃ? So hi yadi uttaritvā cīvaraṃ nivāseti, nissaggiyaṃ cīvaraṃ, anissajjitvā paribhuñjanapaccayā dukkaṭaṃ āpajjati. Atha naggo gacchati, evampi dukkaṭaṃ āpajjatīti? Nāpajjati. So hi yāva aññaṃ bhikkhuṃ disvā vinayakammaṃ na karoti, tāva tesaṃ cīvarānaṃ aparibhogārahattā naṭṭhacīvaraṭṭhāne ṭhito hoti, naṭṭhacīvarassa ca akappiyaṃ nāma natthi, tasmā ekaṃ nivāsetvā dve hatthena gahetvā vihāraṃ gantvā vinayakammaṃ kātabbaṃ. Sace dūre vihāro hoti, antarāmagge manussā sañcaranti, ekaṃ nivāsetvā ekaṃ pārupitvā ekaṃ aṃsakūṭe ṭhapetvā gantabbaṃ. Sace vihāre sabhāgaṃ bhikkhuṃ na passati, bhikkhācāraṃ gatā honti, saṅghāṭiṃ bahigāme ṭhapetvā santaruttarena āsanasālaṃ gantvā vinayakammaṃ kātabbaṃ. Sace bahigāme corabhayaṃ hoti, pārupitvā gantabbaṃ. Sace āsanasālā sambādhā hoti, janākiṇṇā na sakkā ekamante cīvaraṃ apanetvā vinayakammaṃ kātuṃ, ekaṃ bhikkhuṃ ādāya bahigāmaṃ gantvā vinayakammaṃ katvā cīvarāni paribhuñjitabbāni.

52. If a striving monk, having engaged in meditative exertion throughout the night, at dawn thinks, 'I will bathe,' places his three robes on the bank, and descends into the river, but dawn arises while he is bathing, what is to be done? For if he comes out of the water and wears a robe, he incurs a dukkaṭa offense on account of using a forfeitable robe without having forfeited it. Then, if he goes naked, does he also incur a dukkaṭa offense? He does not. For until he sees another monk and performs the Vinaya act, he stands in the position of one whose robes are lost, because those robes are unfit for use. And for one whose robes are lost, there is nothing that is unallowable. Therefore, he should wear one robe, take the other two in his hand, go to the monastery, and perform the Vinaya act. If the monastery is far and people are traveling on the path, he should go wearing one, draping one, and placing one on his shoulder-tip. If in the monastery he does not see a suitable monk because they have gone on the alms-round, he should place the outer robe outside the village, go to the dining hall with the lower and upper robes, and perform the Vinaya act. If there is danger from thieves outside the village, he should go while draping it. If the dining hall is constricted and crowded with people, such that it is not possible to set aside the robe in a secluded place to perform the Vinaya act, he should take one monk, go outside the village, perform the Vinaya act, and then the robes may be used.

Sace therā bhikkhū daharānaṃ hatthe pattacīvaraṃ datvā maggaṃ gacchantā pacchimayāme sayitukāmā honti, attano attano cīvaraṃ hatthapāse katvāva sayitabbaṃ. Sace gacchantānaṃyeva asampattesu daharesu aruṇaṃ uggacchati, cīvaraṃ nissaggiyaṃ hoti, nissayo pana na paṭippassambhati. Daharānampi purato gacchantānaṃ theresu asampattesu eseva nayo. Maggaṃ virajjhitvā araññe aññamaññaṃ apassantesupi eseva nayo. Sace pana daharā “mayaṃ, bhante, muhuttaṃ sayitvā asukasmiṃ nāma okāse tumhe sampāpuṇissāmā”ti vatvā yāva aruṇuggamanā sayanti, cīvarañca nissaggiyaṃ hoti, nissayo ca paṭippassambhati. Dahare uyyojetvā theresu sayantesupi eseva nayo. Dvedhāpathaṃ disvā therā “ayaṃ maggo”[M 0.0046], daharā “ayaṃ maggo”ti vatvā aññamaññassa vacanaṃ aggahetvā gatā, saha aruṇassa uggamanā cīvarāni ca nissaggiyāni honti, nissayo ca paṭippassambhati. Sace daharā maggato okkamma “antoaruṇeyeva nivattissāmā”ti bhesajjatthāya gāmaṃ pavisitvā āgacchanti, asampattānaṃyeva ca nesaṃ aruṇo uggacchati, cīvarāni nissaggiyāni honti, nissayo pana na paṭippassambhati. Sace pana dhenubhayena vā sunakhabhayena vā muhuttaṃ ṭhatvā “gamissāmā”ti ṭhatvā vā nisīditvā vā gacchanti, antarā aruṇe uggate cīvarāni ca nissaggiyāni honti, nissayo ca paṭippassambhati.

If elder monks, having given their bowl and robes to junior monks, wish to lie down in the last watch of the night while traveling, they should lie down only after placing their own robes within arm's reach. If, while they are still traveling, dawn breaks before the junior monks have rejoined them, the robes become forfeitable, but the dependence is not relinquished. The same rule applies to the junior monks walking ahead when the elders have not yet arrived. Even if they stray from the path and do not see each other in the wilderness, the same rule applies. But if the junior monks say, 'Venerable sirs, we will sleep for a moment and meet you at such-and-such a place,' and sleep until dawn, the robes become forfeitable, and the dependence is relinquished. The same rule applies when the elders dismiss the junior monks and then sleep. If, seeing a fork in the road, the elders say, 'This is the path,' and the junior monks say, 'This is the path,' and they go without heeding each other's words, with the rising of dawn, the robes become forfeitable, and the dependence is relinquished. If the junior monks leave the path, thinking, 'We will return before dawn,' and enter a village for medicine, and dawn breaks before they have rejoined the elders, the robes become forfeitable, but the dependence is not relinquished. But if, because of fear of a cow or a dog, they stop for a moment and then proceed, thinking 'We will go,' whether standing or sitting, and dawn breaks in between, the robes become forfeitable, and the dependence is relinquished.

Sace [V 0.0047] “antoaruṇeyeva āgamissāmā”ti antosīmāyaṃ gāmaṃ paviṭṭhānaṃ antarā aruṇo uggacchati, neva cīvarāni nissaggiyāni honti, na nissayo paṭippassambhati. Sace pana “vibhāyatu tāvā”ti nisīdanti, aruṇe uggate na cīvarāni nissaggiyāni honti, nissayo pana paṭippassambhati. Sace yepi “antoaruṇeyeva āgamissāmā”ti sāmantavihāraṃ dhammassavanatthāya saussāhā gacchanti, antarāmaggeyeva ca nesaṃ aruṇo uggacchati, cīvarāni nissaggiyāni honti, nissayo pana na paṭippassambhati. Sace dhammagāravena “yāvapariyosānaṃ sutvāva gamissāmā”ti nisīdanti, saha aruṇassa uggamanā cīvarānipi nissaggiyāni honti, nissayo ca paṭippassambhati. Therena daharaṃ cīvaradhovanatthāya gāmakaṃ pesentena attano cīvaraṃ paccuddharitvāva dātabbaṃ, daharassapi cīvaraṃ paccuddharāpetvāva ṭhapetabbaṃ. Sace asatiyā gacchati, attano cīvaraṃ paccuddharitvā daharassa cīvaraṃ vissāsena gahetvā ṭhapetabbaṃ. Sace thero na sarati, daharova sarati, daharena attano cīvaraṃ paccuddharitvā therassa cīvaraṃ vissāsena gahetvā gantvā vattabbaṃ “bhante, tumhākaṃ cīvaraṃ adhiṭṭhahitvā paribhuñjathā”ti. Attanopi cīvaraṃ adhiṭṭhātabbaṃ. Evaṃ ekassa satiyāpi āpattimokkho hoti.

If, for those who have entered a village within the boundary, thinking, 'We will come back before dawn,' dawn rises on the way, the robes do not become subject to forfeiture, nor is the dependence relinquished. But if they sit down, thinking, 'Let it become light first,' when dawn has risen, the robes do not become subject to forfeiture, but the dependence is relinquished. If those monks who go with effort to a nearby monastery to listen to the Dhamma, thinking, 'We will come back before dawn,' and for them dawn rises right on the path, the robes become subject to forfeiture, but the dependence is not relinquished. If, out of respect for the Dhamma, they sit down, thinking, 'We will go only after listening to the very end,' then together with the rising of the dawn, the robes also become subject to forfeiture, and the dependence is also relinquished. When an elder sends a junior monk to a small village for the purpose of washing a robe, he should give his own robe only after having formally removed its determination; the junior monk's robe should also be left only after having had its determination formally removed. If he goes due to unmindfulness, the elder should formally remove the determination of his own robe and, taking the junior's robe with trust, he should put it aside. If the elder does not remember, but the junior monk does, the junior monk should formally remove the determination of his own robe, and taking the elder's robe with trust, he should go and say: 'Venerable sir, please determine your robe and then use it.' He should also determine his own robe. Thus, even with the mindfulness of one, there is release from the offense.

Iti pāḷimuttakavinayavinicchayasaṅgahe

Thus in the Compendium of Decisions on the Vinaya Apart from the Pāḷi Canon:

Cīvaravippavāsavinicchayakathā samattā.

The Discourse on the Decision Concerning Separation from Robes is concluded.

10. Bhaṇḍapaṭisāmanavinicchayakathā

10. The Discourse on the Decision Concerning the Safeguarding of Requisites

53. Bhaṇḍassa [M 0.0047][V 0.0048] paṭisāmananti paresaṃ bhaṇḍassa gopanaṃ. Paresañhi (pāci. aṭṭha. 506) kappiyavatthu vā hotu akappiyavatthu vā, antamaso mātu kaṇṇapiḷandhanaṃ kālapaṇṇampi gihisantakaṃ bhaṇḍāgārikasīsena paṭisāmentassa pācittiyaṃ. Sace pana mātāpitūnaṃ santakaṃ avassaṃ paṭisāmetabbaṃ kappiyabhaṇḍaṃ hoti, attano atthāya gahetvā paṭisāmetabbaṃ. “Idaṃ paṭisāmetvā dehī”ti pana vutte “na vaṭṭatī”ti paṭikkhipitabbaṃ. Sace “paṭisāmehī”ti pātetvā gacchanti, palibodho nāma hoti, paṭisāmetuṃ vaṭṭati. Vihāre kammaṃ karontā vaḍḍhakīādayo vā rājavallabhā vā “attano upakaraṇabhaṇḍaṃ vā sayanabhaṇḍaṃ vā paṭisāmetvā dethā”ti vadanti, chandenapi bhayenapi na kātabbameva, guttaṭṭhānaṃ pana dassetuṃ vaṭṭati, balakkārena pātetvā gatesu ca paṭisāmetuṃ.

53. The meaning of 'safeguarding belongings' is the protection of others' belongings. Indeed, for others, whether it be an allowable item or an unallowable item—even to the extent of a mother's ear ornament or a palm-leaf—for a monk who safeguards a householder's belongings in the manner of a treasurer, there is a pācittiya offense. However, if it is an allowable item belonging to one's mother and father that must necessarily be safeguarded, it should be taken for one's own purpose and safeguarded. But when it is said, 'Having safeguarded this item, give it back,' it should be refused, saying, 'It is not allowable.' If they leave it behind and go, saying, 'Safeguard it!', it becomes what is called an encumbrance; it is allowable to safeguard it. If carpenters and so on, or royal favorites, who are doing work in the monastery say, 'Having safeguarded our tools or bedding, give them back,' it should not be done at all, either out of favor or out of fear. However, it is allowable to show them a secure place. And when they have left items by force and gone, it is allowable to safeguard them.

Sace (pārā. aṭṭha. 1.111) attano hatthe paṭisāmanatthāya ṭhapitaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ sāmikena “dehi me bhaṇḍa”nti yācito adātukāmo “nāhaṃ gaṇhāmī”ti bhaṇati, sampajānamusāvādepi adinnādānassa payogattā dukkaṭaṃ. “Kiṃ tumhe bhaṇatha, nevidaṃ mayhaṃ anurūpaṃ, na tumhāka”ntiādīni vadantassapi dukkaṭameva. “Raho mayā etassa hatthe ṭhapitaṃ, na añño koci jānāti, dassati nu kho me, no”ti sāmiko vimatiṃ uppādeti, bhikkhussa thullaccayaṃ. Tassa pharusādibhāvaṃ disvā sāmiko “na mayhaṃ dassatī”ti dhuraṃ nikkhipati, tatra sacāyaṃ bhikkhu “kilametvā naṃ dassāmī”ti dāne saussāho, rakkhati tāva. Sacepi so dāne nirussāho, bhaṇḍasāmiko pana gahaṇe saussāho, rakkhatiyeva. Yadi pana tasmiṃ dāne nirussāho bhaṇḍasāmiko “na mayhaṃ dassatī”ti dhuraṃ nikkhipati, evaṃ ubhinnaṃ dhuranikkhepena bhikkhuno pārājikaṃ. Yadipi mukhena “dassāmī”ti vadati, cittena pana adātukāmo, evampi sāmikassa dhuranikkhepe pārājikaṃ. Taṃ pana saṅgopanatthāya attano hatthe parehi ṭhapitaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ aguttadesato ṭhānā cāvetvā guttaṭṭhāne ṭhapanatthāya harato anāpatti. Theyyacittenapi ṭhānā cāventassa avahāro natthi. Kasmā? Attano hatthe nikkhittattā, bhaṇḍadeyyaṃ pana hoti. Theyyacittena paribhuñjatopi eseva nayo.

If a monk, regarding an item placed in his own hand for safekeeping, is asked by the owner, 'Give me my item,' and, being unwilling to give it, says, 'I did not take it,' then even in the case of a deliberate lie, because it is a preliminary act of taking what is not given, a dukkaṭa offense is incurred. For a monk who says such things as, 'What are you saying? This is not suitable for me, nor is it suitable for you,' it is also a dukkaṭa offense. If the owner gives rise to doubt, thinking, 'In private, it was placed by me in his hand; no one else knows. Will he give it to me, or will he not?' for the monk, a thullaccaya offense is incurred. If the owner, seeing that monk's harshness and so on, abandons the claim, thinking, 'He will not give it to me,' and in that case, if this monk is zealous in giving, thinking, 'Having first made him weary, I will give it to him,' then for the time being, it is guarded. And even if that monk is not zealous in giving, but the owner of the item is zealous in taking it, it is indeed guarded. But if that monk is not zealous in giving, and the owner of the item abandons the claim, thinking, 'He will not give it to me,' thus, through the abandoning of the claim by both, for the monk, a pārājika offense is incurred. Even if he says with his mouth, 'I will give it,' but with his mind is unwilling to give, even so, upon the owner's abandoning of the claim, a pārājika offense is incurred. However, for a monk who, for the sake of safeguarding, carries an item placed in his own hand by others from an insecure place, having moved it from its spot for the purpose of placing it in a secure place, there is no offense. Even for one who moves it from its place with a thievish mind, there is no carrying away. Why? Because it was placed in his own hand; however, the item is to be given. For one who uses it with a thievish mind, this is the same principle.

54. Pañcannaṃ [M 0.0048] sahadhammikānaṃ santakaṃ pana yaṃ kiñci parikkhāraṃ paṭisāmetuṃ vaṭṭati. Sace [V 0.0049] āgantuko bhikkhu āvāsikānaṃ cīvarakammaṃ karontānaṃ samīpe pattacīvaraṃ ṭhapetvā “ete saṅgopessantī”ti maññamāno nahāyituṃ vā aññatra vā gacchati, sace taṃ āvāsikā saṅgopenti, iccetaṃ kusalaṃ. No ce, naṭṭhe gīvā na hoti. Sacepi so “idaṃ, bhante, ṭhapethā”ti vatvā gacchati, itare ca kiccapasutattā na jānanti, eseva nayo. Athāpi te “idaṃ, bhante, ṭhapethā”ti vuttā “mayaṃ byāvaṭā”ti paṭikkhipanti, itaro ca “avassaṃ ṭhapessantī”ti anādiyitvā gacchati, eseva nayo. Sace pana te tena yācitā vā ayācitā vā “mayaṃ ṭhapessāma, tvaṃ gacchā”ti vadanti, taṃ saṅgopitabbaṃ. No ce saṅgopenti, naṭṭhe gīvā. Kasmā? Sampaṭicchitattā.

54. However, it is allowable to look after any requisite whatsoever belonging to the five fellow Dhamma-practitioners. If a visiting monk, while resident monks are engaged in robe-making, leaves his bowl and robe nearby thinking, 'They will look after these,' and goes off to bathe or elsewhere, and if the resident monks do safeguard them, then this is skillful. If not, there is no liability if they are lost. Even if he says, 'Venerables, please keep this,' and leaves, but the others, being preoccupied with their work, do not notice, the same principle applies. Furthermore, if they are told, 'Venerables, please keep this,' but refuse, saying, 'We are busy,' and he, disregarding this, thinking, 'They will surely keep it,' and leaves, the same principle applies. But if they, whether asked or not, say, 'We will keep it, you may go,' then it must be safeguarded. If they do not safeguard it, there is liability if it is lost. Why? Because it was accepted.

Yo bhikkhu bhaṇḍāgāriko hutvā paccūsasamaye eva bhikkhūnaṃ pattacīvarāni heṭṭhāpāsādaṃ oropetvā dvāraṃ apidahitvā tesampi anārocetvāva dūre bhikkhācāraṃ gacchati, tāni ce corā haranti, tasseva gīvā. Yo pana bhikkhu bhikkhūhi “oropetha, bhante, pattacīvarāni, kālo salākaggahaṇassā”ti vutto “samāgatātthā”ti pucchitvā “āma samāgatāmhā”ti vutte pattacīvarāni nīharitvā nikkhipitvā bhaṇḍāgāradvāraṃ bandhitvā “tumhe pattacīvarāni gahetvā heṭṭhāpāsādadvāraṃ paṭijaggitvā gaccheyyāthā”ti vatvā gacchati. Tatra ceko alasajātiko bhikkhu bhikkhūsu gatesu pacchā akkhīni puñchanto uṭṭhahitvā udakaṭṭhānaṃ mukhadhovanatthaṃ gacchati, taṃ khaṇaṃ disvā corā tassa pattacīvaraṃ haranti, suhaṭaṃ, bhaṇḍāgārikassa gīvā na hoti.

A monk who, being the storekeeper, at dawn lowers the monks' bowls and robes to the lower story, and without closing the door and without informing them, goes to a village far away for the alms-round—if thieves steal them, there is liability for that very storekeeper. But as for the monk who, when told by the other monks, 'Venerable Sir, please lower the bowls and robes, it is time to collect the lots,' asks, 'Have you all assembled?' and when they reply, 'Yes, we have assembled,' brings out the bowls and robes, places them down, secures the storeroom door, and says, 'You all, having taken your bowls and robes, should guard the door of the lower story and then go,' and then departs. If among them one lazy-natured monk, after the other monks have gone, gets up later wiping his eyes and goes to the place with water to wash his face, and seeing that opportunity, thieves steal his bowl and robe—the loss is rightful, and there is no liability for the storekeeper.

Sacepi koci bhaṇḍāgārikassa anārocetvāva bhaṇḍāgāre attano parikkhāraṃ ṭhapeti, tasmimpi naṭṭhe bhaṇḍāgārikassa gīvā na hoti. Sace pana bhaṇḍāgāriko taṃ disvā “aṭṭhāne ṭhapita”nti gahetvā ṭhapeti, naṭṭhe tasseva gīvā. Sacepi ṭhapitabhikkhunā “mayā, bhante, īdiso nāma parikkhāro ṭhapito, upadhāreyyāthā”ti vutto “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchati, dunnikkhittaṃ vā maññamāno aññasmiṃ ṭhāne ṭhapeti, naṭṭhe tasseva gīvā. “Nāhaṃ jānāmī”ti paṭikkhipantassa pana natthi gīvā. Yopi tassa passantasseva ṭhapeti, bhaṇḍāgārikañca na sampaṭicchāpeti, naṭṭhaṃ sunaṭṭhameva. Sace pana naṃ bhaṇḍāgāriko aññatra ṭhapeti, naṭṭhe gīvā[M 0.0049]. Sace bhaṇḍāgāraṃ suguttaṃ, sabbo saṅghassa cetiyassa ca parikkhāro tattheva ṭhapīyati, bhaṇḍāgāriko ca bālo abyatto dvāraṃ vivaritvā dhammakathaṃ vā sotuṃ aññaṃ vā kiñci kātuṃ katthaci gacchati, taṃ khaṇaṃ disvā yattakaṃ corā haranti, sabbaṃ tassa gīvā. Bhaṇḍāgārato nikkhamitvā bahi caṅkamantassa vā dvāraṃ vivaritvā sarīraṃ utuṃ gāhāpentassa vā tattheva [V 0.0050] samaṇadhammānuyogena nisinnassa vā tattheva nisīditvā kenaci kammena byāvaṭassa vā uccārapassāvapīḷitassapi sato tattheva upacāre vijjamāne bahi gacchato vā aññena vā kenaci ākārena pamattassa sato dvāraṃ vivaritvā vā vivaṭameva pavisitvā vā sandhiṃ chinditvā vā yattakaṃ tassa pamādapaccayā corā haranti, sabbaṃ tasseva gīvā. “Uṇhasamaye pana vātapānaṃ vivaritvā nipajjituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti vadanti. Uccārapīḷitassa pana tasmiṃ upacāre asati aññattha gacchantassa gilānapakkhe ṭhitattā avisayo, tasmā gīvā na hoti.

Even if a certain bhikkhu places his own requisites in the storehouse without informing the storekeeper, should those requisites be lost, the storekeeper has no responsibility. However, if the storekeeper sees them and, thinking, 'They have been placed in an unsuitable spot,' takes and stores them, should they be lost, the responsibility is his alone. Also, if the bhikkhu who placed the requisites says, 'Venerable Sir, I have placed such-and-such a requisite here; please take note of it,' and the storekeeper accepts by saying, 'Very well,' or, thinking it is poorly placed, stores it in another place, should it be lost, the responsibility is his alone. However, for one who refuses by saying, 'I do not know,' there is no responsibility. And also, for one who places an item while the storekeeper is watching but does not get his acknowledgement, should it be lost, it is well and truly lost. However, if the storekeeper places that item elsewhere, should it be lost, there is responsibility. If the storehouse is well-guarded, and all the requisites of the Saṅgha and the cetiya are stored right there, but the storekeeper—being foolish and incompetent—opens the door and goes somewhere to listen to a Dhamma talk or to do something else, and thieves, seeing that opportunity, steal any amount, all of it is his responsibility. If, on account of the storekeeper's negligence—such as having gone out from the storehouse and walking outside; or having opened the door and airing his body; or sitting right there engaged in the duties of a recluse; or sitting right there occupied with some work; or, though afflicted by the need for feces and urine, going outside even when a suitable vicinity is available right there; or being negligent in any other way—thieves steal any amount of requisites by opening the door, or by entering through an already open door, or by breaking through a wall, all of it is his responsibility alone. They say, 'During the hot season, it is permissible to open a window and lie down.' However, for one afflicted by the need for feces who goes elsewhere because there is no suitable vicinity, since he is considered to be in the category of the sick, it is not a matter for blame; therefore, there is no responsibility.

55. Yo pana anto uṇhapīḷito dvāraṃ suguttaṃ katvā bahi nikkhamati, corā taṃ gahetvā “dvāraṃ vivarā”ti vadanti, yāvatatiyaṃ na vivaritabbaṃ. Yadi pana te corā “sace na vivarasi, tañca māressāma, dvārañca bhinditvā parikkhāraṃ harissāmā”ti pharasuādīni ukkhipanti, “mayi ca mate saṅghassa ca senāsane vinaṭṭhe guṇo natthī”ti vivarituṃ vaṭṭati. Idhāpi “avisayattā gīvā natthī”ti vadanti. Sace koci āgantuko kuñcikaṃ vā deti, dvāraṃ vā vivarati, yattakaṃ corā haranti, sabbaṃ tassa gīvā. Saṅghena bhaṇḍāgāraṃ guttatthāya sūciyantakañca kuñcikamuddikā ca yojetvā dinnā hoti, bhaṇḍāgāriko ghaṭikamattaṃ datvā nipajjati, corā vivaritvā parikkhāraṃ haranti, tasseva gīvā. Sūciyantakañca kuñcikamuddikañca yojetvā nipannaṃ panetaṃ sace corā āgantvā “dvāraṃ vivarāhī”ti vadanti, tattha purimanayeneva paṭipajjitabbaṃ. Evaṃ suguttaṃ katvā nipanne pana sace bhittiṃ vā chadanaṃ vā bhinditvā umaṅgena vā pavisitvā haranti, na tassa gīvā.

55. If a storekeeper inside, oppressed by heat, secures the door well and goes outside, and thieves seize him and say, 'Open the door!'—he should not open it up to the third time. But if those thieves raise weapons like axes and say, 'If you do not open it, we will kill you and, breaking the door, will take the requisites,' then it is permissible to open it, thinking, 'There is no benefit in my being killed and the Saṅgha's dwelling being destroyed.' Here too, they say, 'There is no culpability because it is beyond his control.' If some visitor gives a key or opens the door, whatever the thieves take, all of it is his culpability. If the Saṅgha has provided a needle-lock and a key-seal to be fitted for the purpose of guarding the storeroom, and the storekeeper lies down having inserted only the bolt, and thieves open it and take the requisites, it is his culpability alone. But if, while he is lying down having fitted the needle-lock and the key-seal, thieves come and say, 'Open the door!'—in that case, he should proceed according to the previous method. However, if, while he is lying down having secured it well in this way, thieves take the requisites by breaking through the wall or the roof, or by entering through a tunnel, it is not his culpability.

Sace bhaṇḍāgāre aññepi therā vasanti, vivaṭe dvāre attano attano parikkhāraṃ gahetvā gacchanti, bhaṇḍāgāriko tesu gatesu dvāraṃ na jaggati, sace tattha kiñci avaharīyati, bhaṇḍāgārikassa issaravatāya bhaṇḍāgārikasseva gīvā, therehi pana sahāyehi bhavitabbaṃ. Ayañhi sāmīci. Yadi bhaṇḍāgāriko “tumhe bahi ṭhatvā tumhākaṃ parikkhāraṃ gaṇhatha[M 0.0050], mā pavisitthā”ti vadati, tesañca eko lolamahāthero sāmaṇerehi ceva upaṭṭhākehi ca saddhiṃ bhaṇḍāgāraṃ pavisitvā nisīdati ceva nipajjati ca, yattakaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ nassati, sabbaṃ tassa gīvā, bhaṇḍāgārikena pana avasesatherehi ca sahāyehi bhavitabbaṃ. Atha bhaṇḍāgārikova lolasāmaṇere ca upaṭṭhāke ca gahetvā bhaṇḍāgāre nisīdati ceva nipajjati ca, yattakaṃ nassati, sabbaṃ tasseva gīvā. Tasmā bhaṇḍāgārikeneva tattha vasitabbaṃ, avasesehi appeva rukkhamūle vasitabbaṃ, na ca bhaṇḍāgāreti.

If other senior monks are also staying in the storeroom, they take their own requisites and leave when the door is open. Once they have left, the storekeeper does not guard the door. If anything is stolen from there, the storekeeper alone is liable because of his authority; the senior monks, however, should be companions. This is proper conduct. If the storekeeper says, 'Wait outside and take your requisites; do not enter,' but one unrestrained senior monk enters the storeroom with his novices and attendants, and sits or lies down, whatever goods are lost, he is entirely liable. The storekeeper and the remaining senior monks, however, should be companions. But if the storekeeper himself, taking unrestrained novices and attendants, sits or lies down in the storeroom, whatever is lost, he alone is liable. Therefore, only the storekeeper should stay there, while the others should stay even at the foot of a tree, and not in the storeroom.

56. Ye [V 0.0051] pana attano attano sabhāgabhikkhūnaṃ vasanagabbhesu parikkhāraṃ ṭhapenti, parikkhāre naṭṭhe yehi ṭhapito, tesaṃyeva gīvā, itarehi pana sahāyehi bhavitabbaṃ. Yadi pana saṅgho bhaṇḍāgārikassa vihāreyeva yāgubhattaṃ dāpeti, so ca bhikkhācāratthāya gāmaṃ gacchati, naṭṭhaṃ tasseva gīvā. Bhikkhācāraṃ pavisantehi atirekacīvaraṃ rakkhaṇatthāya ṭhapitavihāravārikassapi yāgubhattaṃ vā nivāpaṃ vā labhamānasseva bhikkhācāraṃ gacchato yaṃ tattha nassati, sabbaṃ gīvā. Na kevalañca ettakameva, bhaṇḍāgārikassa viya yaṃ tassa pamādapaccayā nassati, sabbaṃ gīvā.

56. Furthermore, when monks place their requisites in the dwelling cells of their fellow monks, if the requisites are lost, the liability falls only on those with whom they were placed; the other monks, however, should be companions. But if the Saṅgha provides the storekeeper with rice gruel and meals in the monastery itself, and he goes to the village for the alms-round, whatever is lost is his liability alone. When monks entering the village for the alms-round appoint a monastery attendant to guard an extra robe, if that attendant, while receiving rice gruel or provisions, goes on the alms-round, whatever is lost there is entirely his liability. And not only this; just as with the storekeeper, whatever is lost through his negligence is entirely his liability.

Sace vihāro mahā hoti, aññaṃ padesaṃ rakkhituṃ gacchantassa aññasmiṃ padese nikkhittaṃ haranti, avisayattā gīvā na hoti. Īdise pana vihāre vemajjhe sabbesaṃ osaraṇaṭṭhāne parikkhāre ṭhapetvā nisīditabbaṃ, vihāravārikā vā dve tayo ṭhapetabbā. Sace tesampi appamattānaṃ ito cito ca rakkhataṃyeva kiñci nassati, gīvā na hoti. Vihāravārike bandhitvā haritabhaṇḍampi corānaṃ paṭipathaṃ gatesu aññena maggena haritabhaṇḍampi na tesaṃ gīvā. Sace vihāravārikānaṃ vihāre dātabbaṃ yāgubhattaṃ vā nivāpo vā na hoti, tehi pattabbalābhato atirekā dve tisso yāgusalākā tesaṃ pahonakabhattasalākā ca ṭhapetuṃ vaṭṭati, nibaddhaṃ katvā pana na ṭhapetabbā. Manussā hi vippaṭisārino honti “vihāravārikāyeva amhākaṃ bhattaṃ bhuñjantī”ti, tasmā parivattetvā parivattetvā ṭhapetabbā. Sace tesaṃ sabhāgā salākabhattādīni āharitvā denti, iccetaṃ kusalaṃ[M 0.0051]. No ce denti, vāraṃ gāhāpetvā nīharāpetabbāni. Sace vihāravāriko dve tisso yāgusalākā ca cattāri pañca salākabhattāni ca labhamāno bhikkhācāraṃ gacchati, bhaṇḍāgārikassa viya sabbaṃ naṭṭhaṃ gīvā hoti. Sace saṅghassa vihārapālānaṃ dātabbaṃ bhattaṃ vā nivāpo vā natthi, bhikkhū vihāravāraṃ gahetvā attano attano nissitake vihāraṃ jaggāpenti, sampattavāraṃ aggahetuṃ na labhati. Yathā aññe bhikkhū karonti, tatheva kātabbaṃ. Bhikkhūhi pana asahāyassa vā adutiyassa vā yassa sabhāgo bhikkhu bhattaṃ ānetvā dātā natthi, evarūpassa vāro na pāpetabbo.

If the monastery is large, and while one is going to guard one area, things left in another area are stolen, there is no liability because it is beyond one's sphere of control. In such a monastery, one should sit having placed one's requisites in the middle, in a place of assembly for all. Alternatively, two or three monastery attendants should be appointed. If, even while they are being diligent and guarding here and there, something is lost, there is no liability. If goods are stolen after the monastery attendants have been tied up, or if goods are stolen by another route while they have gone to intercept the thieves, it is not their liability. If there is no gruel-meal or provision to be given to the monastery attendants in the monastery, it is appropriate to set aside for them two or three gruel-tickets and sufficient meal-tickets, in excess of the gain to be received. However, they should not be set aside as a fixed arrangement. For people may become resentful, thinking, 'The monastery attendants are eating only our food.' Therefore, they should be set aside by rotation. If their fellow monks bring and give them ticket-meals and the like, this is good. If they do not give, a turn should be assigned and they (the provisions) should be provided. If a monastery attendant, while receiving two or three gruel-tickets and four or five meal-tickets, goes on alms-round, then like a storekeeper, everything that is lost becomes a liability.
