If the Saṅgha has no meal or provision to give to the monastery guards, the monks, taking turns, should have the monastery guarded by those dependent on them. One cannot refuse to take one's turn when it comes. It should be done just as the other monks do. However, the monks should not assign a turn to one who has no companion, no second, or no fellow monk to bring and give him food.

Yampi pākavaṭṭatthāya vihāre ṭhapenti, taṃ gahetvā upajīvantena ṭhātabbaṃ. Yo taṃ na upajīvati, so vāraṃ na gāhāpetabbo. Phalāphalatthāyapi vihāre bhikkhuṃ ṭhapenti, jaggitvā gopetvā phalavārena bhājetvā khādanti. Yo tāni khādati, tena ṭhātabbaṃ, anupajīvanto na gāhāpetabbo. Senāsanamañcapīṭhapaccattharaṇarakkhaṇatthāyapi ṭhapenti, āvāse vasantena ṭhātabbaṃ, abbhokāsiko pana rukkhamūliko vā na gāhāpetabbo. Eko navako hoti, bahussuto pana bahūnaṃ [V 0.0052] dhammaṃ vāceti, paripucchaṃ deti, pāḷiṃ vaṇṇeti, dhammakathaṃ katheti, saṅghassa bhāraṃ nittharati, ayaṃ lābhaṃ paribhuñjantopi āvāse vasantopi vāraṃ na gāhāpetabbo. “Purisaviseso nāma ñātabbo”ti vadanti. Uposathāgārapaṭimāgharajagganakassa pana diguṇaṃ yāgubhattaṃ, devasikaṃ taṇḍulanāḷi, saṃvacchare ticīvaraṃ dasavīsagghanakaṃ kappiyabhaṇḍañca dātabbaṃ. Sace pana tassa taṃ labhamānasseva pamādena tattha kiñci nassati, sabbaṃ gīvā. Bandhitvā balakkārena acchinnaṃ, na gīvā. Tattha cetiyassa vā saṅghassa vā santakena cetiyassa santakaṃ rakkhāpetuṃ vaṭṭati, cetiyassa santakena saṅghassa santakaṃ rakkhāpetuṃ na vaṭṭati. Yaṃ pana cetiyassa santakena saddhiṃ saṅghassa santakaṃ ṭhapitaṃ hoti, taṃ cetiyasantake rakkhāpite rakkhitameva hotīti evaṃ vaṭṭati. Pakkhavārena uposathāgārādīni rakkhatopi pamādavasena naṭṭhaṃ gīvāyevāti.

Whatever is placed in the monastery for the purpose of cooking, one who lives by taking it should remain stationed. Whoever does not make use of it should not be assigned a turn. For the sake of fruits, they also appoint a monk in the monastery; having guarded and protected them, they divide and eat them by turns of fruit. Whoever eats those should remain stationed; one who does not make use of them should not be assigned a turn. They also appoint someone to guard the lodgings, beds, chairs, and coverings. One who lives in the dwelling should remain stationed, but a monk who dwells in the open air or at the foot of a tree should not be assigned a turn. There is one who is a junior monk but is learned, who teaches the Dhamma to many, gives explanations after inquiries, expounds the Pāḷi, gives Dhamma talks, and bears the burden of the Saṅgha. Even if he enjoys gains or lives in the dwelling, he should not be assigned a turn. They say, 'He should be known as a distinguished person.' For the guardian of the Uposatha hall and the image house, a double portion of gruel and meal should be given, along with a daily nāḷi of rice, and annually three robes and allowable goods worth ten or twenty. But if, while receiving these, anything is lost there due to his negligence, he is liable for it all. If it is snatched by force after he has been bound, there is no liability. There, it is proper to have the shrine's property guarded by means of what belongs to the shrine or the Saṅgha, but it is not proper to have the Saṅgha's property guarded by means of what belongs to the shrine. However, whatever belonging to the Saṅgha is placed together with the shrine's property, when the shrine's property is guarded, that is considered guarded as well; thus this is proper. Even for one who guards the Uposatha hall and other places by fortnightly turn, what is lost through negligence is indeed a liability.

Iti pāḷimuttakavinayavinicchayasaṅgahe

Thus, in the Compendium of Vinaya Decisions Not Found in the Pāḷi Canon

Bhaṇḍapaṭisāmanavinicchayakathā samattā.

The discourse on the decision regarding the storing of goods is concluded.

11. Kayavikkayasamāpattivinicchayakathā

11. Discourse on the Determination of Engaging in Buying and Selling

57. Kayavikkayasamāpattīti [M 0.0052][V 0.0053] kayavikkayasamāpajjanaṃ. “Iminā imaṃ dehī”tiādinā (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.595) hi nayena parassa kappiyabhaṇḍaṃ gaṇhanto kayaṃ samāpajjati, attano kappiyabhaṇḍaṃ dento vikkayaṃ. Ayaṃ pana kayavikkayo ṭhapetvā pañca sahadhammike avasesehi gihipabbajitehi antamaso mātāpitūhipi saddhiṃ na vaṭṭati.

57. The term `kayavikkayasamāpatti` means the act of engaging in buying and selling. For, by the method beginning with, “With this, give this,” one who takes another’s allowable goods engages in buying, and one who gives one’s own allowable goods engages in selling. However, this buying and selling is not allowable with anyone other than the five fellow Dhamma-practitioners; it is not allowable with the remaining householders and renunciants, not even with one’s own mother and father.

Tatrāyaṃ vinicchayo – vatthena vā vatthaṃ hotu, bhattena vā bhattaṃ, yaṃ kiñci kappiyaṃ “iminā imaṃ dehī”ti vadati, dukkaṭaṃ. Evaṃ vatvā mātuyāpi attano bhaṇḍaṃ deti, dukkaṭaṃ, “iminā imaṃ dehī”ti vutto vā “imaṃ dehi, imaṃ te dassāmī”ti taṃ vatvā vā mātuyāpi bhaṇḍaṃ attanā gaṇhāti, dukkaṭaṃ, attano bhaṇḍe parahatthaṃ, parabhaṇḍe ca attano hatthaṃ sampatte nissaggiyaṃ pācittiyaṃ. Mātaraṃ vā pana pitaraṃ vā “imaṃ dehī”ti vadato viññatti na hoti, “imaṃ gaṇhāhī”ti dadato saddhādeyyavinipātanaṃ na hoti. Aññātakaṃ “imaṃ dehī”ti vadato viññatti, “imaṃ gaṇhāhī”ti dadato saddhādeyyavinipātanaṃ, “iminā imaṃ dehī”ti kayavikkayaṃ āpajjato nissaggiyaṃ. Tasmā kappiyabhaṇḍaṃ parivattantena mātāpitūhipi saddhiṃ kayavikkayaṃ, aññātakehi saddhiṃ tisso āpattiyo mocentena parivattetabbaṃ.

Herein is the determination: whether it be cloth for cloth, or food for food, or any allowable item, if one says, “With this, give this,” it is a `dukkaṭa` offense. Having said this, if one gives one’s own goods even to one’s mother, it is a `dukkaṭa` offense. If, having been told, “With this, give this,” or having said, “Give this, I will give you that,” one takes goods for oneself even from one’s mother, it is a `dukkaṭa` offense. When one’s own goods have reached another’s hand and another’s goods have reached one’s own hand, it is a `nissaggiya pācittiya` offense. However, for one who says to one’s mother or father, “Give this,” there is no offense of improper requesting. For one who gives, saying, “Take this,” there is no offense of destroying what is given in faith. For one who says to a non-relative, “Give this,” there is an offense of improper requesting. For one who gives, saying, “Take this,” there is an offense of destroying what is given in faith. For one who engages in buying and selling by saying, “With this, give this,” there is a `nissaggiya` offense. Therefore, when exchanging allowable goods, one should do so while avoiding buying and selling even with one’s parents, and while avoiding the three offenses with non-relatives.

Tatrāyaṃ parivattanavidhi – bhikkhussa pātheyyataṇḍulā honti, so antarāmagge bhattahatthaṃ purisaṃ disvā “amhākaṃ taṇḍulā atthi, na ca no imehi attho, bhattena pana attho”ti vadati, puriso taṇḍule gahetvā bhattaṃ deti, vaṭṭati. Tissopi āpattiyo na honti, antamaso nimittakammamattampi na hoti. Kasmā? Mūlassa atthitāya. Yo pana evaṃ akatvā “iminā imaṃ dehī”ti parivatteti, yathāvatthukameva. Vighāsādaṃ disvā “imaṃ odanaṃ bhuñjitvā rajanaṃ vā dārūni vā āharā”ti vadati, rajanachalligaṇanāya dārugaṇanāya ca nissaggiyāni honti. “Imaṃ odanaṃ bhuñjitvā imaṃ nāma karothā”ti dantakārādīhi sippikehi dhammakaraṇādīsu taṃ taṃ parikkhāraṃ kāreti, rajakehi vā vatthaṃ dhovāpeti, yathāvatthukameva. Nahāpitena kese chindāpeti[M 0.0053], kammakārehi navakammaṃ kāreti, yathāvatthukameva. Sace pana “idaṃ bhattaṃ bhuñjitvā idaṃ karothā”ti na vadati, “idaṃ bhattaṃ bhuñja, bhuttosi, bhuñjissasi, idaṃ nāma karohī”ti vadati, vaṭṭati. Ettha ca kiñcāpi vatthadhovane vā kesacchedane [V 0.0054] vā bhūmisodhanādinavakamme vā parabhaṇḍaṃ attano hatthagataṃ nissajjitabbaṃ nāma natthi, mahāaṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana daḷhaṃ katvā vuttattā na sakkā etaṃ paṭikkhipituṃ, tasmā yathā nissaggiyavatthumhi paribhutte vā naṭṭhe vā pācittiyaṃ deseti, evamidhāpi desetabbaṃ.

In that regard, this is the procedure for exchange: A monk has rice for provisions. On the way, having seen a man with food in his hand, he says, “We have rice, but we have no need for this; we need food instead.” If the man takes the rice and gives the food, it is allowable. The three offenses also do not arise; not even the mere act of making a hint occurs. Why? Because of the existence of the principal item. But whoever, not having done it in this way, exchanges by saying, “Give this for this,” it is in accordance with the object. Having seen one who eats leftovers, if he says, “Having eaten this cooked rice, bring dye or firewood,” then by the count of the dye-barks and by the count of the firewood, they become items to be forfeited. If, saying, “Having eaten this cooked rice, do such-and-such,” he has artisans such as ivory-workers make those various requisites among items such as a water-strainer, or has a robe washed by launderers, it is in accordance with the object. If he has his hair cut by a barber, or has new work done by laborers, it is in accordance with the object. But if he does not say, “Having eaten this food, do this,” but says, “Eat this food; you have eaten; you will eat; do such-and-such,” it is allowable. And here, although in the case of having a robe washed, or having hair cut, or new work such as clearing the ground, there are no goods of another that have come into one's own hand and ought to be forfeited, yet because it is stated firmly in the Great Commentary, it is not possible to reject this. Therefore, just as one confesses a pācittiya offense when an article to be forfeited has been used or is lost, so too here it should be confessed.

Yaṃ kiñci kappiyabhaṇḍaṃ gaṇhitukāmatāya agghaṃ pucchituṃ vaṭṭati, tasmā “ayaṃ tava patto kiṃ agghatī”ti pucchite “idaṃ nāmā”ti vadati, sace attano kappiyabhaṇḍaṃ mahagghaṃ hoti, evañca naṃ paṭivadati “upāsaka mama idaṃ vatthu mahagghaṃ, tava pattaṃ aññassa dehī”ti. Taṃ sutvā itaro “aññaṃ thālakampi dassāmī”ti vadati, gaṇhituṃ vaṭṭati. Sace so patto mahaggho, bhikkhuno vatthu appagghaṃ, pattasāmiko cassa appagghabhāvaṃ na jānāti, patto na gahetabbo, “mama vatthu appaggha”nti ācikkhitabbaṃ. Mahagghabhāvaṃ ñatvā vañcetvā gaṇhantopi hi bhaṇḍaṃ agghāpetvā kāretabbataṃ āpajjati. Sace pattasāmiko “hotu, bhante, sesaṃ mama puññaṃ bhavissatī”ti deti, vaṭṭati. Kappiyakārakassa pana “iminā imaṃ gahetvā dehī”ti ācikkhituṃ vaṭṭati, tasmā yassa hatthato bhaṇḍaṃ gaṇhāti, taṃ ṭhapetvā aññaṃ antamaso tassa puttabhātikampi kappiyakārakaṃ katvā “iminā imaṃ nāma gahetvā dehī”ti ācikkhati, so ce cheko hoti, punappunaṃ apanetvā vivaditvā gaṇhāti, tuṇhībhūtena ṭhātabbaṃ. No ce cheko hoti, na jānāti gahetuṃ, vāṇijako ca taṃ vañceti, “mā gaṇhāhī”ti vattabbo.

When one wishes to acquire any allowable item, it is proper to ask the price. Therefore, when asked, “What is this bowl of yours worth?” he says, “It is worth such-and-such.” If one’s own allowable item is of great value, one may reply to him thus: “Lay supporter, this item of mine is of great value; sell your bowl to another.” Upon hearing this, if the other says, “I will also give another dish,” it is permissible to accept it. If that bowl is of great value, while the monk’s item is of little value, and the owner of the bowl does not know its state of being of little value, the bowl should not be taken. It should be stated, “My item is of little value.” Indeed, even one who, knowing its great value, takes it deceitfully, incurs the obligation of having the item appraised and the transaction settled. If the owner of the bowl gives it, saying, “Let it be, Venerable Sir, the remainder will be my merit,” it is permissible. For an attendant, however, it is proper to instruct, “Take this and give that in exchange.” Therefore, setting aside the person from whose hand one wishes to acquire the goods, one may appoint another—even that person’s son or brother—as an attendant, instructing, “With this, take that particular item and give it.” If that attendant is clever, and acquires it after repeatedly rejecting and disputing, one should remain silent. If he is not clever and does not know how to acquire it, and the merchant deceives him, it should be said, “Do not take it.”

“Idaṃ paṭiggahitaṃ telaṃ vā sappi vā amhākaṃ atthi, amhākañca aññena appaṭiggahitakena attho”ti vutte pana sace so taṃ gahetvā aññaṃ deti, paṭhamaṃ attano telaṃ na mināpetabbaṃ. Kasmā? Nāḷiyañhi avasiṭṭhatelaṃ hoti, taṃ pacchā minantassa appaṭiggahitaṃ dūseyya. Ayañca kayavikkayo nāma kappiyabhaṇḍavasena vutto. Kappiyena hi kappiyaṃ parivattentassa kayavikkayasikkhāpadena nissaggiyaṃ vuttaṃ, akappiyena pana akappiyaṃ parivattentassa, kappiyena vā akappiyaṃ akappiyena vā kappiyaṃ parivattentassa [M 0.0054] rūpiyasaṃvohārasikkhāpadena nissaggiyaṃ, tasmā ubhosu vā ekasmiṃ vā akappiye sati rūpiyasaṃvohāro nāma hoti.

If, when it is said, 'We have this received oil or ghee, but we need another that has not been received,' he takes that and gives another, one's own oil should not be measured out first. Why? Because there is remaining oil in the measure, and that would spoil the unreceived oil of the one measuring later. And this, called 'buying and selling,' is spoken of by way of allowable goods. Indeed, for one exchanging an allowable item with an allowable item, it is said to be an item for forfeiture according to the training rule on buying and selling. But for one exchanging an unallowable item with an unallowable item, or an allowable item with an unallowable one, or an unallowable item with an allowable one, it is an item for forfeiture according to the training rule on transactions involving valuables. Therefore, when there is an unallowable item in both or in one, it is called a transaction involving valuables.

58. Rūpiyasaṃvohārassa ca garubhāvadīpanatthaṃ idaṃ pattacatukkaṃ veditabbaṃ. Yo hi rūpiyaṃ uggaṇhitvā tena ayabījaṃ samuṭṭhāpeti, taṃ koṭṭāpetvā tena lohena pattaṃ kāreti, ayaṃ patto mahāakappiyo nāma, na sakkā kenaci upāyena kappiyo kātuṃ. Sacepi taṃ vināsetvā [V 0.0055] thālakaṃ kāreti, tampi akappiyaṃ. Vāsiṃ kāreti, tāya chinnadantakaṭṭhampi akappiyaṃ. Baḷisaṃ kāreti, tena māritā macchāpi akappiyā. Vāsiṃ tāpetvā udakaṃ vā khīraṃ vā uṇhāpeti, tampi akappiyameva.

58. And for the purpose of illustrating the gravity of transactions involving valuables, this fourfold set of bowls should be understood. Indeed, a bhikkhu who, having accepted gold or silver, produces iron ore with it, has it pounded, and causes a bowl to be made from that iron—this bowl is called 'greatly unallowable.' It cannot be made allowable by any means. Even if, having destroyed it, one causes a small dish to be made, that too is unallowable. If one causes an adze to be made, even a tooth-stick cut with it is unallowable. If one causes a fishhook to be made, fish killed with it are also unallowable. If one heats the adze and causes water or milk to be warmed, that too is indeed unallowable.

Yo pana rūpiyaṃ uggaṇhitvā tena pattaṃ kiṇāti, ayampi patto akappiyo. “Pañcannampi sahadhammikānaṃ na kappatī”ti mahāpaccariyaṃ vuttaṃ. Sakkā pana kappiyo kātuṃ. So hi mūle mūlasāmikānaṃ, patte ca pattasāmikānaṃ dinne kappiyo hoti, kappiyabhaṇḍaṃ datvā gahetvā paribhuñjituṃ vaṭṭati.

Furthermore, a bhikkhu who, having accepted gold or silver, buys a bowl with it, this bowl too is unallowable. It is stated in the Mahāpaccariya: 'It is not allowable for the five companions in the Dhamma.' But it can be made allowable. Indeed, it becomes allowable when the price is given to the owners of the price and the bowl is given to the owners of the bowl. It is then proper to use it, having acquired it by giving an allowable item in exchange.

Yopi rūpiyaṃ uggaṇhāpetvā kappiyakārakena saddhiṃ kammārakulaṃ gantvā pattaṃ disvā “ayaṃ mayhaṃ ruccatī”ti vadati, kappiyakārako ca taṃ rūpiyaṃ datvā kammāraṃ saññāpeti, ayampi patto kappiyavohārena gahitopi dutiyapattasadisoyeva, mūlassa sampaṭicchitattā akappiyo. Kasmā sesānaṃ na kappatīti? Mūlassa anissaṭṭhattā.

And if a monk, having had money accepted on his behalf, goes with an attendant to a blacksmith's workshop, and upon seeing a bowl, says, 'This one pleases me,' and the attendant gives that money and informs the blacksmith; this bowl, although acquired through an allowable expression, is just like the second bowl. It is unallowable because the principal amount was accepted. Why is it not allowable for the others? Because the principal amount was not relinquished.

Yo pana rūpiyaṃ asampaṭicchitvā “therassa pattaṃ kiṇitvā dehī”ti pahitakappiyakārakena saddhiṃ kammārakulaṃ gantvā pattaṃ disvā “ime kahāpaṇe gahetvā imaṃ dehī”ti kahāpaṇe dāpetvā gahito, ayaṃ patto etasseva bhikkhuno na vaṭṭati dubbicāritattā, aññesaṃ pana vaṭṭati mūlassa asampaṭicchitattā. Mahāsumattherassa kira upajjhāyo anuruddhatthero nāma ahosi. So attano evarūpaṃ pattaṃ sappissa pūretvā saṅghassa nissajji. Tipiṭakacūḷanāgattherassa saddhivihārikānaṃ evarūpo patto ahosi. Taṃ theropi sappissa pūretvā saṅghassa nissajjāpesīti. Idaṃ akappiyapattacatukkaṃ.

Now, as for the bowl which, without accepting money oneself, is acquired by going with an attendant who was sent with the instruction, 'Buy a bowl for the Elder and give it,' to a blacksmith's workshop, and upon seeing a bowl, causing the kahāpanas to be given by saying, 'Take these kahāpanas and give this one'—this bowl is not allowable for that very monk due to being improperly managed. But it is allowable for others because the principal amount was not accepted. It is said that the preceptor of the Elder Mahāsumana was an elder named Anuruddha. He, having filled such a bowl of his with ghee, relinquished it to the Sangha. The co-residents of the Elder Tipiṭakacūḷanāga had such a bowl. That Elder also, having filled it with ghee, caused it to be relinquished to the Sangha. This is the tetrad of unallowable bowls.

Sace [M 0.0055] pana rūpiyaṃ asampaṭicchitvā “therassa pattaṃ kiṇitvā dehī”ti pahitakappiyakārakena saddhiṃ kammārakulaṃ gantvā pattaṃ disvā “ayaṃ mayhaṃ ruccatī”ti vā “imāhaṃ gahessāmī”ti vā vadati, kappiyakārako ca taṃ rūpiyaṃ datvā kammāraṃ saññāpeti, ayaṃ patto sabbakappiyo buddhānampi paribhogāraho. Imaṃ pana rūpiyasaṃvohāraṃ karontena “iminā imaṃ gahetvā dehī”ti kappiyakārakampi ācikkhituṃ na vaṭṭati.

But if, without accepting money oneself, one goes with an attendant who was sent with the instruction, 'Buy a bowl for the Elder and give it,' to a blacksmith's workshop, and upon seeing a bowl, says either, 'This one pleases me,' or, 'I will take this one,' and the attendant gives that money and informs the blacksmith, this bowl is completely allowable and worthy of being used even by the Buddhas. However, a monk engaging in this transaction with money is not allowed to instruct even the attendant by saying, 'With this, take this merchandise and give it.'

Iti pāḷimuttakavinayavinicchayasaṅgahe

Thus in the Compendium of Vinaya Decisions Independent of the Canon,

Kayavikkayasamāpattivinicchayakathā samattā.

The Discourse on the Determination Regarding Engaging in Buying and Selling is concluded.

12. Rūpiyādipaṭiggahaṇavinicchayakathā

12. The Discourse on the Decision Regarding the Acceptance of Money and So Forth

59. Rūpiyādipaṭiggahoti [V 0.0056] jātarūpādipaṭiggaṇhanaṃ. Tattha (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.583-4) jātarūpaṃ rajataṃ jātarūpamāsako rajatamāsakoti catubbidhaṃ nissaggiyavatthu. Tambalohādīhi kato lohamāsako. Sāradārunā vā veḷupesikāya vā antamaso tālapaṇṇenapi rūpaṃ chinditvā kato dārumāsako. Lākhāya vā niyyāsena vā rūpaṃ samuṭṭhāpetvā kato jatumāsako. Yo yo yattha yattha janapade yadā yadā vohāraṃ gacchati, antamaso aṭṭhimayopi cammamayopi rukkhaphalabījamayopi samuṭṭhāpitarūpopi asamuṭṭhāpitarūpopīti ayaṃ sabbopi rajatamāsakeneva saṅgahito. Muttā maṇi veḷuriyo saṅkho silā pavāḷaṃ lohitaṅko masāragallaṃ satta dhaññāni dāsidāsakhettavatthupupphārāmaphalārāmādayoti idaṃ dukkaṭavatthu. Tattha nissaggiyavatthuṃ attano vā saṅghagaṇapuggalacetiyānaṃ vā atthāya sampaṭicchituṃ na vaṭṭati. Attano atthāya sampaṭicchato nissaggiyaṃ pācittiyaṃ hoti, sesānaṃ atthāya dukkaṭaṃ. Dukkaṭavatthuṃ sabbesampi atthāya sampaṭicchato dukkaṭameva.

59. The acceptance of money and so forth refers to the acceptance of gold and so forth. Therein, gold, silver, gold coins, and silver coins are the four kinds of objects entailing relinquishment. A metal coin is one made of copper, bronze, and so forth. A wooden coin is one made by cutting a shape from heartwood or a strip of bamboo, or even from a palm leaf. A lac coin is one made by forming a shape from lac or resin. Whatever, wherever, in whatever country, whenever, comes into use as currency—even if made of bone, leather, or the seeds of tree-fruits, whether shaped or unshaped—all this is included under silver coins. Pearls, gems, beryl, conch, crystal, coral, rubies, cat’s-eye gems, the seven kinds of grain, male and female slaves, fields, land, flower gardens, fruit orchards, and so forth—these are objects entailing a wrongdoing. Therein, it is not allowable to accept an object entailing relinquishment for one’s own sake or for the sake of the Sangha, a group, an individual, or a cetiya. For one who accepts it for one’s own sake, there is an offense of relinquishment and confession; for the sake of others, it is a wrongdoing. An object entailing a wrongdoing, when accepted for the sake of anyone, is merely a wrongdoing.

Tatrāyaṃ vinicchayo (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.538-9) – sace koci jātarūparajataṃ āharitvā “idaṃ saṅghassa dammi, ārāmaṃ vā karotha cetiyaṃ vā bhojanasālādīnaṃ vā aññatara”nti vadati, idaṃ sampaṭicchituṃ na vaṭṭati. Sace pana “nayidaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ sampaṭicchituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti paṭikkhitte “vaḍḍhakīnaṃ vā kammakārānaṃ vā hatthe bhavissati[M 0.0056], kevalaṃ tumhe sukatadukkaṭaṃ jānāthā”ti vatvā tesaṃ hatthe datvā pakkamati, vaṭṭati. Athāpi “mama manussānaṃ hatthe bhavissati, mayhameva vā hatthe bhavissati, kevalaṃ tumhe yaṃ yassa dātabbaṃ, tadatthāya pesethā”ti vadati, evampi vaṭṭati. Sace pana saṃghaṃ vā gaṇaṃ vā puggalaṃ vā anāmasitvā “idaṃ hiraññasuvaṇṇaṃ cetiyassa dema, vihārassa dema, navakammassa demā”ti vadanti, paṭikkhipituṃ na vaṭṭati, “ime idaṃ bhaṇantī”ti kappiyakārakānaṃ ācikkhitabbaṃ. “Cetiyādīnaṃ atthāya tumhe gahetvā ṭhapetvā”ti vutte pana “amhākaṃ gahetuṃ na vaṭṭatī”ti paṭikkhipitabbaṃ.

Herein is the determination: If someone brings gold and silver and says, “I give this to the Sangha—build a monastery, or a shrine, or one among dining halls and so forth,” it is not permissible to accept it. However, if, when it is refused with the words, “It is not permissible for bhikkhus to accept this,” they say, “It will be in the hands of carpenters or workers; you only need to know what is well done and what is poorly done,” and then place it in their hands and depart, it is permissible. Alternatively, if they say, “It will be in the hands of my people, or in my own hands; you only send whatever is to be given to whom, for that purpose,” this too is permissible. But if, without addressing the Sangha, a group, or an individual, they say, “We give this gold and silver for the shrine, for the monastery, for renovations,” it should not be refused. One should inform the stewards, saying, “These people are saying this.” If, however, they say, “Take and set this aside for the shrine and so forth,” it should be refused by saying, “It is not permissible for us to take it.”

Sace pana koci bahuṃ hiraññasuvaṇṇaṃ ānetvā “idaṃ saṃghassa dammi, cattāro paccaye paribhuñjathā”ti vadati, tañce saṃgho sampaṭicchati, paṭiggahaṇepi paribhogepi āpatti. Tatra ceko [V 0.0057] bhikkhu “nayidaṃ kappatī”ti paṭikkhipati, upāsako ca “yadina kappati, mayhameva bhavissatī”ti taṃ ādāya gacchati. So bhikkhu “tayā saṃghassa lābhantarāyo kato”ti na kenaci kiñci vattabbo. Yo hi taṃ codeti, sveva sāpattiko hoti. Tena panekena bahū anāpattikā katā. Sace pana bhikkhūhi “na vaṭṭatī”ti paṭikkhitte “kappiyakārakānaṃ vā hatthe bhavissati, mama purisānaṃ vā mayhaṃ vā hatthe bhavissati, kevalaṃ tumhe paccaye paribhuñjathā”ti vadati, vaṭṭati.

Furthermore, if someone brings a large amount of gold and silver and says, “I give this to the Sangha; you may make use of the four requisites,” and the Sangha accepts it, there is an offense in both the receiving and the using thereof. Therein, if one bhikkhu objects, saying, “This is not allowable,” and the lay follower, saying, “If it is not allowable, it will be mine,” takes it and departs, that bhikkhu should not be told anything by anyone, such as, “You have caused an obstruction to the Sangha’s gain.” For whoever accuses him, that very person incurs an offense. On the contrary, by that one bhikkhu, many have been made free from offense. However, if, when it is refused by the bhikkhus saying, “It is not permissible,” he says, “It will be in the hands of the stewards, or in the hands of my men, or in my own hands; you should simply make use of the requisites,” then it is permissible.

Catupaccayatthāya ca dinnaṃ yena yena paccayena attho hoti, taṃ tadatthaṃ upanetabbaṃ. Civaratthāya dinnaṃ cīvareyeva upanetabbaṃ. Sace cīvarena tādiso attho natthi, piṇḍapātādīhi saṃgho kilamati, saṃghasuṭṭhutāya apaloketvā tadatthāyapi upanetabbaṃ. Esa nayo piṇḍapātagilānapaccayatthāya dinnepi. Senāsanatthāya dinnaṃ pana senāsanassa garubhaṇḍattā senāsaneyeva upanetabbaṃ. Sace pana bhikkhūsu senāsanaṃ chaḍḍetvā gatesu senāsanaṃ vinassati, īdise kāle senāsanaṃ vissajjetvāpi bhikkhūnaṃ paribhogo anuññāto, tasmā senāsanajagganatthaṃ mūlacchejjaṃ akatvā yāpanamattaṃ paribhuñjitabbaṃ.

And what is given for the sake of the four requisites should be applied for the purpose of whichever requisite is needed. What is given for robes should be applied only to robes. If there is no such need for robes, and the Sangha is in hardship concerning almsfood and other requisites, then, having announced it to the Sangha for its well-being, it may be applied for that purpose as well. This same principle should be understood for what is given for the sake of almsfood and medicine. However, what is given for lodging, due to lodging being a heavy article, should be applied only to lodging. But if, when the bhikkhus have departed, having abandoned the lodging, the lodging is perishing, at such a time, use by the bhikkhus is permitted even after having disposed of the lodging. Therefore, for the sake of maintaining the lodging, without exhausting the principal, it should be used only to the extent of sustenance.

60. Sace koci “mayhaṃ tisassasampādanakaṃ mahātaḷākaṃ atthi, taṃ saṃghassa dammī”ti vadati, tañce saṃgho sampaṭicchati, paṭiggahaṇepi paribhogepi āpattiyeva. Yo pana taṃ paṭikkhipati, so purimanayeneva na kenaci kiñci vattabbo. Yo hi taṃ codeti, sveva sāpattiko hoti[M 0.0057]. Tena panekena bahū anāpattikā katā. Yo pana “tādisaṃyeva taḷākaṃ dammī”ti vatvā bhikkhūhi “na vaṭṭatī”ti paṭikkhitto vadati “asukañca asukañca saṅghassa taḷākaṃ atthi, taṃ kathaṃ vaṭṭatī”ti. So vattabbo “kappiyaṃ katvā dinnaṃ bhavissatī”ti. Kathaṃ dinnaṃ kappiyaṃ hotīti. “Cattāro paccaye paribhuñjathā”ti vatvā dinnanti. So sace “sādhu, bhante cattāro paccaye paribhuñjathā”ti deti, vaṭṭati. Athāpi “taḷākaṃ gaṇhathā”ti vatvā “na vaṭṭatī”ti paṭikkhitto “kappiyakārako atthī”ti pucchitvā “natthī”ti vutte “idaṃ asuko nāma vicāressati, asukassa vā hatthe mayhaṃ vā hatthe bhavissati, saṅgho kappiyabhaṇḍaṃ paribhuñjatū”ti vadati, vaṭṭati. Sacepi “na vaṭṭatī”ti paṭikkhitto “udakaṃ paribhuñjissati, bhaṇḍakaṃ dhovissati, migapakkhino pivissantī”ti vadati, evampi vaṭṭati. Athāpi “na vaṭṭatī”ti paṭikkhitto vadati “kappiyasīsena gaṇhathā”ti. “Sādhu upāsaka, saṅgho pānīyaṃ pivissati, bhaṇḍakaṃ dhovissati, migapakkhino pivissantī”ti vatvā paribhuñjituṃ vaṭṭati. Athāpi “mama taḷākaṃ vā pokkharaṇiṃ vā saṅghassa [V 0.0058] dammī”ti vutte “sādhu upāsaka, saṅgho pānīyaṃ pivissatī”tiādīni vatvā paribhuñjituṃ vaṭṭatiyeva.

60. If someone says, “I have a great reservoir that yields three crops, and I give it to the Sangha,” and the Sangha accepts it, there is an offense in both the receiving and the using. But whoever rejects it should not be told anything by anyone, in accordance with the previous method. Indeed, whoever reproaches him is himself the one with an offense. By that one bhikkhu, many have been made free from offense. But if someone, after saying, “I give just such a reservoir,” is rejected by the bhikkhus with, “It is not allowable,” and then says, “The Sangha has such-and-such a reservoir and such-and-such a reservoir; how is that allowable?” he should be told, “It must have been given after having been made allowable.” How, when given, is it allowable? It is given after saying, “You may use the four requisites.” If he says, “Very well, venerable sirs, you may use the four requisites,” and gives it, it is allowable. Furthermore, if, after saying, “Take the reservoir,” and being rejected with, “It is not allowable,” he asks, “Is there a steward?” and when it is said, “There is not,” he then says, “So-and-so will manage this, or it will be in the hands of so-and-so, or in my hands; let the Sangha use the allowable goods,” it is allowable. Even if, having been rejected with, “It is not allowable,” he says, “The Sangha will use the water, wash their robes, and animals and birds will drink,” this too is allowable. Furthermore, if, having been rejected with, “It is not allowable,” he says, “Take it with an allowable basis,” it is allowable to use it after replying, “Very well, lay follower, the Sangha will drink the water, wash their robes, and animals and birds will drink.” Furthermore, when it is said, “I give my reservoir or pond to the Sangha,” it is indeed allowable to use it after replying, “Very well, lay follower, the Sangha will drink the water,” and so forth.

Yadi pana bhikkhūhi hatthakammaṃ yācitvā sahatthena ca kappiyapathaviṃ khaṇitvā udakaparibhogatthāya taḷākaṃ kāritaṃ hoti, tañce nissāya sassaṃ nipphādetvā manussā vihāre kappiyabhaṇḍaṃ denti, vaṭṭati. Atha manussā eva saṅghassa upakāratthāya saṅghikabhūmiṃ khaṇitvā taṃ nissāya nipphannasassato kappiyabhaṇḍaṃ denti, etampi vaṭṭati. “Amhākaṃ ekaṃ kappiyakārakaṃ ṭhapethā”ti vutte ca ṭhapetumpi labbhati. Atha te manussā rājabalinā upaddutā pakkamanti, aññe paṭipajjanti, na ca bhikkhūnaṃ kiñci denti, udakaṃ vāretuṃ labbhati, tañca kho kasikammakāleyeva, na sassakāle. Sace te vadanti “nanu, bhante, pubbepi manussā imaṃ nissāya sassaṃ akaṃsū”ti, tato vattabbā “te saṅghassa imañca imañca upakāraṃ akaṃsu, idañcidañca kappiyabhaṇḍakaṃ adaṃsū”ti. Sace te vadanti “mayampi dassāmā”ti, evampi vaṭṭati.

If, however, bhikkhus, having requested manual labor and having dug with their own hands on allowable land, have a pond made for the purpose of using water, and if people, relying on it, produce a crop and give allowable goods in the monastery, it is allowable. Furthermore, if people themselves, for the benefit of the Sangha, dig on Sangha-owned land and give allowable goods from the crop produced by relying on it, this too is allowable. And when it is said, “Appoint a steward for us,” it is also allowable to appoint one. If those people, oppressed by royal taxes, depart and others take over, and they give nothing to the bhikkhus, it is allowable to stop the water—and that only at the time of cultivation, not when the crop is growing. If they say, “Venerable sirs, did not people previously also produce crops relying on this?” they should be told, “Those people performed such and such services for the Sangha and gave such and such allowable goods.” If they say, “We too will give,” in that case also it is allowable.

Sace pana koci abyatto akappiyavohārena taḷākaṃ paṭiggaṇhāti vā kāreti vā, taṃ bhikkhūhi na paribhuñjitabbaṃ, taṃ nissāya laddhakappiyabhaṇḍampi akappiyameva[M 0.0058]. Sace bhikkhūhi pariccattabhāvaṃ ñatvā sāmiko vā tassa puttadhītaro vā añño vā koci vaṃse uppanno puna kappiyavohārena deti, vaṭṭati. Pacchinne kulavaṃse yo tassa janapadassa sāmiko, so acchinditvā kappiyavohārena puna deti cittalapabbate bhikkhunā nīhaṭaudakavāhakaṃ aḷanāgarājamahesī viya, evampi vaṭṭati. Kappiyavohārepi udakavasena paṭiggahitataḷāke suddhacittānaṃ mattikuddharaṇapāḷibandhanādīni ca kātuṃ vaṭṭati. Taṃ nissāya pana sassaṃ karonte disvā kappiyakārakaṃ ṭhapetuṃ na vaṭṭati. Yadi te sayameva kappiyabhaṇḍaṃ denti, gahetabbaṃ. No ce denti, na codetabbaṃ. Paccayavasena paṭiggahitataḷāke kappiyakārakaṃ ṭhapetuṃ vaṭṭati, mattikuddharaṇapāḷibandhanādīni kāretuṃ na vaṭṭati. Sace kappiyakārakā sayameva karonti, vaṭṭati. Abyattena pana lajjibhikkhunā kārāpitesu kiñcāpi paṭiggahaṇaṃ kappiyaṃ, bhikkhussa pana payogapaccayā uppannena missattā visagatapiṇḍapāto viya akappiyamaṃsarasamissabhojanaṃ viya ca dubbinibhogaṃ hoti, sabbesaṃ akappiyameva.

If, however, some unskilled bhikkhu accepts or causes to be made a reservoir with an unallowable expression, it should not be used by bhikkhus; even allowable goods obtained in dependence on it are indeed unallowable. If, having known the state of its relinquishment by the bhikkhus, the owner, or his sons and daughters, or some other person arisen in his lineage gives it again with an allowable expression, it is allowable. When the family lineage is cut off, if the ruler of that district, having rescinded its former status, gives it again with an allowable expression—just as the chief queen of King Aḷanāga rescinded the status of the water channel constructed by a bhikkhu on Cittalapabbata and gave it again—even so, it is allowable. Even with an allowable expression, in the case of a reservoir accepted for the purpose of water, it is allowable for those with a pure mind to do such things as removing soil and building an embankment. However, having seen people cultivating crops in dependence on it, it is not allowable to appoint a steward. If they give allowable goods of their own accord, it should be accepted. If they do not give, they should not be prompted. In the case of a reservoir accepted for the purpose of requisites, it is allowable to appoint a steward, but it is not allowable to have such things as removing soil and building an embankment done. If the stewards do so of their own accord, it is allowable. However, in the case of things caused to be made by an unskilled but conscientious bhikkhu, although the acceptance is allowable, because it is mixed with what has arisen from that bhikkhu's effort, it becomes difficult to apportion for use—like almsfood mixed with poison or a meal mixed with the broth of unallowable meat—and is indeed unallowable for all.

61. Sace pana udakassa okāso atthi, taḷākassa pāḷi thirā, “yathā bahuṃ udakaṃ gaṇhāti, evaṃ karohi, tīrasamīpe udakaṃ karohī”ti evaṃ udakameva vicāreti, vaṭṭati. Uddhane [V 0.0059] aggiṃ na pātenti, “udakakammaṃ labbhatu upāsakā”ti vattuṃ vaṭṭati, “sassaṃ katvā āharathā”ti vattuṃ pana na vaṭṭati. Sace pana taḷāke atibahuṃ udakaṃ disvā passato vā piṭṭhito vā mātikaṃ nīharāpeti, vanaṃ chindāpetvā kedāre kārāpeti, porāṇakedāresu vā pakatibhāgaṃ aggahetvā atirekaṃ gaṇhāti, navasasse vā aparicchinnabhāge “ettake kahāpaṇe dethā”ti kahāpaṇe uṭṭhāpeti, sabbesaṃ akappiyaṃ.

61. If, however, there is a place for water and the embankment of the pond is firm, it is allowable to manage only the water thus: 'Do it in such a way that it holds much water; make water near the bank.' If they do not place fire on the stove, it is allowable to say, 'O lay followers, let the water-work be obtained,' but it is not allowable to say, 'Cultivate the crop and bring it.' If, however, having seen too much water in the pond, one has a channel led out from the side or from the back, has the forest cleared to make fields, takes more than the customary share in old fields, or demands kahāpaṇas from an undivided portion of the new crop, saying, 'Give this many kahāpaṇas'—it is unallowable for all.

Yo pana “kasatha vapathā”ti avatvā “ettakāya bhūmiyā ettako nāma bhāgo”ti evaṃ bhūmiṃ vā patiṭṭhāpeti, “ettake bhūmibhāge amhehi sassaṃ kataṃ, ettakaṃ nāma bhāgaṃ gaṇhathā”ti vadantesu kassakesu bhūmippamāṇagahaṇatthaṃ rajjuyā vā daṇḍena vā mināti, khale vā ṭhatvā rakkhati, khalato vā nīharāpeti, koṭṭhāgāre vā paṭisāmeti, tasseva taṃ akappiyaṃ. Sace kassakā kahāpaṇe āharitvā “ime saṅghassa āhaṭā”ti vadanti, aññataro ca bhikkhu “na saṅgho kahāpaṇe khādatī”ti saññāya “ettakehi kahāpaṇehi sāṭake āharatha[M 0.0059], ettakehi yāguādīni sampādethā”ti vadati, yaṃ te āharanti, taṃ sabbesaṃ akappiyaṃ. Kasmā? Kahāpaṇānaṃ vicāritattā. Sace dhaññaṃ āharitvā “idaṃ saṅghassa āhaṭa”nti vadanti, aññataro ca bhikkhu purimanayeneva “ettakehi vīhīhi idañcidañca āharathā”ti vadati, yaṃ te āharanti, taṃ tasseva akappiyaṃ. Kasmā? Dhaññassa vicāritattā. Sace taṇḍulaṃ vā aparaṇṇaṃ vā āharitvā “idaṃ saṅghassa āhaṭa”nti vadanti, aññataro ca bhikkhu purimanayeneva “ettakehi taṇḍulehi idañcidañca āharathā”ti vadati, yaṃ te āharanti, taṃ sabbesaṃ kappiyaṃ. Kasmā? Kappiyānaṃ taṇḍulādīnaṃ vicāritattā. Kayavikkayepi anāpatti kappiyakārakassa ācikkhitattā.

Now, whatever bhikkhu, without saying, 'Plow, sow,' establishes the land by saying, 'For this much land, this is the share'; or, when the farmers say, 'We have cultivated the crop in this much portion of land; take this much of a share,' he measures for the purpose of taking the measure of the land with a rope or a measuring rod; or, standing on the threshing floor, he guards it; or has it brought out from the threshing floor; or has it stored in a granary—that grain is unallowable for that very bhikkhu. If farmers bring kahāpaṇas and say, 'These have been brought for the Sangha,' and a certain bhikkhu, with the perception that 'the Sangha does not use kahāpaṇas,' says, 'With this many kahāpaṇas, bring robes; with this many, prepare gruel and so on,' whatever they bring is unallowable for all. Why? Because the kahāpaṇas have been managed. If they bring grain and say, 'This has been brought for the Sangha,' and a certain bhikkhu, in the same way as before, says, 'With this much paddy, bring this and that,' whatever they bring is unallowable for that very bhikkhu. Why? Because the grain has been managed. If they bring husked rice or other grains and say, 'This has been brought for the Sangha,' and a certain bhikkhu, in the same way as before, says, 'With this much husked rice, bring this and that,' whatever they bring is allowable for all. Why? Because allowable things such as husked rice and so on have been managed. In buying and selling also, there is no offense, because the kappiyakāraka has been informed.

62. Pubbe pana cittalapabbate eko bhikkhu catusāladvāre “aho vata sve saṅghassa ettakappamāṇe pūve paceyyu”nti ārāmikānaṃ saññājananatthaṃ bhūmiyaṃ maṇḍalaṃ akāsi. Taṃ disvā cheko ārāmiko tatheva katvā dutiyadivase bheriyā ākoṭitāya sannipatite saṅghe pūvaṃ gahetvā saṅghattheraṃ āha – “bhante, amhehi ito pubbe neva pitūnaṃ, na pitāmahānaṃ evarūpaṃ sutapubbaṃ, ekena ayyena catusāladvāre pūvatthāya saññā katā, ito dāni pabhuti ayyā attano attano cittānurūpaṃ vadantu, amhākampi phāsuvihāro bhavissatī”ti. Mahāthero tatova nivatti, ekabhikkhunāpi pūvo na gahito. Evaṃ pubbe tatruppādaṃ na paribhuñjiṃsu. Tasmā –

62. Formerly, on Cittalapabbata, a certain bhikkhu at the hall with four entrances, for the purpose of giving a signal to the monastery attendants, drew a circle on the ground, thinking, 'Oh, if only tomorrow they would cook cakes of this quantity for the Sangha!' Seeing this, a clever monastery attendant made them accordingly, and on the next day, when the great drum was beaten and the Sangha had assembled, he took the cakes and said to the Elder of the Sangha, 'Venerable Sir, before this, we have never heard of such a thing from our fathers, nor from our grandfathers—that a noble one at the hall with four entrances made a signal for cakes. From this day forward, let the noble ones speak according to their own minds; it will be an ease for us too.' The Great Elder turned back from that very place, and not even by a single bhikkhu was a cake taken. Thus, in the past, they did not make use of what arose on that occasion. Therefore:

Sallekhaṃ [V 0.0060] accajantena, appamattena bhikkhunā;

Kappiyepi na kātabbā, āmisatthāya lolatāti. (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.538-9);

By a bhikkhu not abandoning the practice of effacement, by one who is diligent, greed for the sake of material gain should not be practiced, even in regard to allowable things.

Yo cāyaṃ taḷāke vutto, pokkharaṇīudakavāhakamātikādīsupi eseva nayo.

And this principle which was stated for a reservoir—this very same principle should also be understood for lotus ponds, small water channels, main canals, and so on.

63. Pubbaṇṇāparaṇṇaucchuphalāphalādīnaṃ viruhanaṭṭhānaṃ yaṃ kiñci khettaṃ vā vatthuṃ vā “dammī”ti vuttepi “na vaṭṭatī”ti paṭikkhipitvā taḷāke vuttanayeneva yadā kappiyavohārena “catupaccayaparibhogatthāya dammī”ti vadati, tadā sampaṭicchitabbaṃ, “vanaṃ dammi araññaṃ dammī”ti vutte pana vaṭṭati. Sace manussā bhikkhūhi anāṇattāyeva tattha rukkhe chinditvā aparaṇṇādīni sampādetvā [M 0.0060] bhikkhūnaṃ bhāgaṃ denti, vaṭṭati, adentā na codetabbā. Sace kenacideva antarāyena tesu pakkantesu aññe karonti, na ca bhikkhūnaṃ kiñci denti, te vāretabbā. Sace vadanti “nanu, bhante, pubbe manussā idha sassāni akaṃsū”ti, tato vattabbā “te saṅghassa idañcidañca kappiyabhaṇḍaṃ adaṃsū”ti. Sace vadanti “mayampi dassāmā”ti, evaṃ vaṭṭati.

63. Any field or plot of land for the growing of early and late crops, sugarcane, fruits, and so on—even if someone says, 'I give it,' it should be refused, saying, 'It is not allowable.' Only when, in the manner stated concerning the pond, one says with allowable usage, 'I give it for the purpose of using the four requisites,' should it be accepted. However, if someone says, 'I give a grove, I give a forest,' it is allowable. If people, without being instructed by the bhikkhus, cut down trees there, prepare late crops and so on, and give a share to the bhikkhus, it is allowable; if they do not give, they should not be urged. If, due to some obstacle, those people depart and others cultivate it but give nothing to the bhikkhus, they should be prevented. If they say, 'Venerable sirs, did not people previously cultivate crops here?' then it should be said, 'Those people gave such and such allowable requisites to the Sangha.' If they say, 'We too will give,' then it is allowable.

Kiñci sassuṭṭhānakaṃ bhūmippadesaṃ sandhāya “sīmaṃ demā”ti vadanti, vaṭṭati. Sīmaparicchedanatthaṃ pana thambhā vā pāsāṇā vā sayaṃ na ṭhapetabbā, bhūmi nāma anagghā, appakenapi pārājiko bhaveyya. Ārāmikānaṃ pana vattabbaṃ “iminā ṭhānena amhākaṃ sīmā gatā”ti. Sacepi hi te adhikaṃ gaṇhanti, pariyāyena kathitattā anāpatti. Yadi pana rājarājamahāmattādayo sayameva thambhe ṭhapāpetvā “cattāro paccaye paribhuñjathā”ti denti, vaṭṭatiyeva.

If, referring to some piece of ground where crops grow, people say, 'We give a boundary,' it is allowable. For the purpose of demarcating the boundary, however, one should not personally set up posts or stones, for land is invaluable; even with a small piece, a pārājika offense could be incurred. The monastery attendants, however, should be told, 'Our boundary extends to this place.' For even if they take more, since it was spoken indirectly, there is no offense. However, if kings, royal ministers, and so on, of their own accord have posts set up and give, saying, 'Make use of the four requisites,' it is indeed allowable.

Sace [V 0.0061] koci antosīmāyaṃ taḷākaṃ vā khaṇati, vihāramajjhena vā mātikaṃ neti, cetiyaṅgaṇabodhiyaṅgaṇādīni dussanti, vāretabbo. Sace saṅgho kiñci labhitvā āmisagarukatāya na vāreti, eko bhikkhu vāreti, sova bhikkhu issaro. Sace eko bhikkhu na vāreti “netha tumhe”ti, tesaṃyeva pakkho hoti. Saṅgho vāreti, saṅghova issaro. Saṅghikesu hi kammesu yo dhammakammaṃ karoti, sova issaro. Sace vāriyamānopi karoti, heṭṭhā gahitaṃ paṃsuṃ heṭṭhā pakkhipitvā, upari gahitaṃ paṃsuṃ upari pakkhipitvā pūretabbā.

If someone digs a pond within the sīmā, or leads a water channel through the middle of the monastery, and the cetiya-courtyard, Bodhi-courtyard, and so on are damaged thereby, he should be prevented. If the Saṅgha, having received something, does not prevent it due to esteem for material gain, and a single bhikkhu prevents it, that very bhikkhu is the master. If a single bhikkhu does not prevent it, saying, “You may proceed,” he is of their faction. If the Saṅgha prevents it, the Saṅgha is the master. For in matters belonging to the Saṅgha, whoever performs a lawful act, that very one is the master. If, even while being prevented, he does it, the place should be filled by putting the soil taken from below back below, and putting the soil taken from above back above.

Sace koci yathājātameva ucchuṃ vā aparaṇṇaṃ vā alābukumbhaṇḍādikaṃ vā valliphalaṃ dātukāmo “etaṃ sabbaṃ ucchukhettaṃ aparaṇṇavatthuṃ valliphalāvāṭaṃ dammī”ti vadati, saha vatthunā parāmaṭṭhattā na vaṭṭatīti mahāsumatthero āha. Mahāpadumatthero pana “abhilāpamattametaṃ, sāmikānaṃyeva hi so bhūmibhāgo, tasmā vaṭṭatī”ti āha. “Dāsaṃ dammī”ti vadati, na vaṭṭati. “Ārāmikaṃ dammi, veyyāvaccakaraṃ dammi, kappiyakārakaṃ dammī”ti vutte vaṭṭati. Sace ārāmiko purebhattampi pacchābhattampi saṅghasseva kammaṃ karoti, sāmaṇerassa viya sabbaṃ bhesajjaṃ paṭijagganampi tassa kātabbaṃ. Sace purebhattameva saṅghassa kammaṃ karoti, pacchābhattaṃ attano karoti, sāyaṃ nivāpo na dātabbo. Yepi pañcadivasavārena [M 0.0061] vā pakkhavārena vā saṅghassa kammaṃ katvā sesakāle attano kammaṃ karonti, tesampi karaṇakāleyeva bhattañca nivāpo ca dātabbo. Sace saṅghassa kammaṃ natthi, attanoyeva kammaṃ katvā jīvanti, te ce hatthakammamūlaṃ ānetvā denti, gahetabbaṃ. No ce denti, na kiñci vattabbā. Yaṃ kiñci rajakadāsampi pesakāradāsampi ārāmikanāmena sampaṭicchituṃ vaṭṭati.

If someone, wishing to give sugarcane or pulses, or gourds, pumpkins, and so on, or vine fruits as they naturally grow, says, “I give all this sugarcane field,” or “this pulse field,” or “this vine fruit enclosure,” it is unallowable because it is considered together with the land—so said the Elder Mahāsuma. However, the Elder Mahāpaduma said, “This is merely a verbal expression, for that portion of land belongs only to the owners; therefore, it is allowable.” If one says, “I give a slave,” it is unallowable. When it is said, “I give a monastery attendant,” “I give a service provider,” or “I give a provisioner,” it is allowable. If a monastery attendant performs work for the Saṅgha both before and after the meal, all medical care must be provided for him, just as for a novice. If he works for the Saṅgha only before the meal and works for himself after the meal, the evening provision should not be given. For those, too, who work for the Saṅgha by a five-day or a fortnightly turn and work for themselves in the remaining time, both food and provision should be given only at the time of their work. If there is no work for the Saṅgha and they make a living by doing their own work, should they bring the wages of their handiwork and give it, it should be accepted. If they do not give it, nothing should be said. It is allowable to accept any whatsoever, even a laundry-slave or a weaver-slave, under the name of 'monastery attendant'.

Sace “gāvo demā”ti vadanti, “na vaṭṭatī”ti paṭikkhipitabbā. Imā gāvo kutoti. Paṇḍitehi pañcagorasaparibhogatthāya dinnāti. “Mayampi pañcagorasaparibhogatthāya demā”ti vutte vaṭṭanti. Ajikādīsupi eseva nayo. “Hatthiṃ dema, assaṃ, mahiṃsaṃ, kukkuṭaṃ, sūkaraṃ demā”ti vadanti, sampaṭicchituṃ na vaṭṭati. Sace keci manussā “appossukkā, bhante, tumhe hotha, mayaṃ ime gahetvā tumhākaṃ kappiyabhaṇḍaṃ dassāmā”ti gaṇhanti, vaṭṭati. Kukkuṭasūkare “sukhaṃ jīvantū”ti araññe vissajjāpetuṃ vaṭṭati. “Imaṃ taḷākaṃ, imaṃ khettaṃ, imaṃ vatthuṃ vihārassa demā”ti vutte paṭikkhipituṃ na labbhati.

If they say, “We give cows,” they should be refused, saying, “It is not allowable.” If it is asked why they are not allowable, and the reply is, “They were given by the wise for the purpose of using the five products of the cow,” and the donors then say, “We too give for the purpose of using the five products of the cow,” they are allowable. This same principle is to be understood for goats and so on. If they say, “We give an elephant, a horse, a buffalo, a chicken, a pig,” it is not allowable to accept. If some people say, “Venerable sirs, be free from concern; we will take these and give you allowable requisites,” and they take them, it is allowable. It is allowable to have chickens and pigs released into the forest with the thought, “May they live happily.” If it is said, “We give this pond, this field, this land to the monastery,” it is not proper to refuse.

64. Sace koci bhikkhuṃ uddissa dūtena hiraññasuvaṇṇādicīvaracetāpannaṃ pahiṇeyya “iminā cīvaracetāpannena cīvaraṃ cetāpetvā itthannāmaṃ bhikkhuṃ cīvarena acchādehī”ti, so ce dūto taṃ bhikkhuṃ upasaṅkamitvā evaṃ vadeyya “idaṃ kho, bhante, āyasmantaṃ uddissa cīvaracetāpannaṃ ābhataṃ, paṭiggaṇhatu āyasmā cīvaracetāpanna”nti, tena bhikkhunā so dūto evamassa vacanīyo “na kho mayaṃ, āvuso, cīvaracetāpannaṃ paṭiggaṇhāma, cīvarañca kho mayaṃ paṭiggaṇhāma kālena kappiya”nti. So ce dūto taṃ bhikkhuṃ evaṃ vadeyya “atthi panāyasmato koci veyyāvaccakaro”ti, cīvaratthikena bhikkhunā veyyāvaccakaro niddisitabbo ārāmiko vā upāsako vā “eso kho, āvuso, bhikkhūnaṃ veyyāvaccakaro”ti. Na vattabbo “tassa dehī”ti vā “so vā nikkhipissati, so vā parivattessati, so vā cetāpessatī”ti[V 0.0062]. So ce dūto taṃ veyyāvaccakaraṃ saññāpetvā taṃ bhikkhuṃ upasaṅkamitvā evaṃ vadeyya “yaṃ kho, bhante, āyasmā veyyāvaccakaraṃ niddisi, āṇatto so mayā, upasaṅkamatu āyasmā kālena, cīvarena taṃ acchādessatī”ti. Cīvaratthikena bhikkhunā veyyāvaccakaro upasaṅkamitvā dvattikkhattuṃ codetabbo sāretabbo [M 0.0062] “attho me, āvuso, cīvarenā”ti. Na vattabbo “dehi me cīvaraṃ, āhara me cīvaraṃ, parivattehi me cīvaraṃ, cetāpehi me cīvara”nti. Sace dvattikkhattuṃ codayamāno sārayamāno taṃ cīvaraṃ abhinipphādeti, iccetaṃ kusalaṃ. No ce abhinipphādeti, tattha gantvā catukkhattuṃ pañcakkhattuṃ chakkhattuparamaṃ tuṇhībhūtena uddissa ṭhātabbaṃ, na āsane nisīditabbaṃ, na āmisaṃ paṭiggahetabbaṃ, na dhammo bhāsitabbo. “Kiṃ kāraṇā āgatosī”ti pucchiyamānena “jānāhi, āvuso”ti ettakameva vattabbaṃ.

64. If someone, intending it for a bhikkhu, were to send a messenger with the price for a robe, such as gold or silver, saying, 'With this price for a robe, have a robe bought or exchanged and clothe the bhikkhu of such-and-such a name with the robe,' and if that messenger were to approach the bhikkhu and say, 'Venerable Sir, this price for a robe has been brought for the venerable one; may the venerable one accept the price for a robe,' the bhikkhu should reply to the messenger thus: 'Friend, we do not accept the price for a robe, but we do accept a robe at the proper time, if it is allowable.' If the messenger were to say to the bhikkhu, 'Does the venerable one have a steward?' then the bhikkhu in need of a robe may point out a steward—a monastery attendant or a lay follower—saying, 'Friend, this is the steward for the bhikkhus.' He should not say, 'Give it to him,' or 'He will keep it,' or 'He will exchange it,' or 'He will have it bought.' If the messenger, having instructed that steward, approaches the bhikkhu and says, 'Venerable Sir, the steward you pointed out has been instructed by me. Let the venerable one approach him at the proper time; he will clothe you with a robe,' then the bhikkhu in need of a robe should approach the steward and should urge and remind him two or three times, saying, 'Friend, I need a robe.' He should not say, 'Give me a robe,' 'Bring me a robe,' 'Exchange a robe for me,' or 'Have a robe bought for me.' If, after being urged and reminded two or three times, the attendant produces the robe, that is good. If he does not produce it, the bhikkhu should go there and stand silently, indicating his purpose, up to four, five, or six times at most. He should not sit down, accept material gain, or speak the Dhamma. If asked, 'Why have you come?' he should only say, 'Know, friend.'

Sace āsane vā nisīdati, āmisaṃ vā paṭiggaṇhāti, dhammaṃ vā bhāsati, ṭhānaṃ bhañjati. Sace catukkhattuṃ codeti, catukkhattuṃ ṭhātabbaṃ. Pañcakkhattuṃ codeti, dvikkhattuṃ ṭhātabbaṃ. Chakkhattuṃ codeti, na ṭhātabbaṃ. Ekāya hi codanāya ṭhānadvayaṃ bhañjati. Yathā chakkhattuṃ codetvā na ṭhātabbaṃ, evaṃ dvādasakkhattuṃ ṭhatvā na codetabbaṃ. Tasmā sace codetiyeva na tiṭṭhati, cha codanā labbhanti. Sace tiṭṭhatiyeva na codeti, dvādasa ṭhānāni labbhanti. Sace codetipi tiṭṭhatipi, ekāya codanāya dve ṭhānāni hāpetabbāni. Tattha yo ekadivasameva punappunaṃ gantvā chakkhattuṃ codeti, sakiṃyeva vā gantvā “attho me, āvuso, cīvarenā”ti chakkhattuṃ vadati, tattha ekadivasameva punappunaṃ gantvā dvādasakkhattuṃ tiṭṭhati, sakimeva vā gantvā tatra tatra ṭhāne tiṭṭhati, sopi sabbacodanāyo sabbaṭṭhānāni ca bhañjati, ko pana vādo nānādivasesu. Tato ce uttari vāyamamāno taṃ cīvaraṃ abhinipphādeti, payoge dukkaṭaṃ, paṭilābhena nissaggiyaṃ hoti. No ce sakkoti taṃ abhinipphādetuṃ, yato rājato rājamahāmattato vā assa bhikkhuno taṃ cīvaracetāpannaṃ ānītaṃ, tassa santikaṃ sāmaṃ vā gantabbaṃ, dūto vā pāhetabbo “yaṃ kho tumhe āyasmanto bhikkhuṃ uddissa cīvaracetāpannaṃ pahiṇittha, na taṃ tassa bhikkhuno kiñci atthaṃ anubhoti, yuñjantāyasmanto sakaṃ, mā tumhākaṃ santakaṃ vinassatū”ti. Ayaṃ tattha sāmīci. Yo pana neva sāmaṃ gacchati, na dūtaṃ pāheti, vattabhede dukkaṭaṃ āpajjati.

If he sits on a seat, or accepts a material thing, or speaks the Dhamma, he breaks the standing. If he requests four times, it is allowable to stand four times. If he requests five times, it is allowable to stand twice. If he requests six times, it is not allowable to stand. Indeed, by one request, he breaks a pair of standings. Just as having requested six times it is not allowable to stand, so also having stood twelve times it is not allowable to request. Therefore, if he only requests and does not stand, six requests are obtained. If he only stands and does not request, twelve standings are obtained. If he both requests and stands, by one request two standings are to be diminished. In this case, a bhikkhu who on a single day, going again and again, requests six times; or going only once, says, ‘Friend, I have need of a robe,’ six times; or on a single day, going again and again, stands twelve times; or going only once, stands in this or that place—he also breaks all requests and all standings. What then is to be said of one who does so on different days? If, striving further than that, he accomplishes that robe, there is an offense of wrong conduct in the effort, and upon its acquisition, it becomes subject to forfeiture. If he is not able to accomplish it, he should either go himself to the king or royal minister from whom that robe-fund for the bhikkhu was brought, or a messenger should be sent, saying: ‘Venerable sirs, the robe-fund that you sent with a certain bhikkhu in mind does not accomplish any purpose for that bhikkhu. Venerable sirs, make use of your own property; let not what is yours be lost.’ This is the proper conduct in that case. But the bhikkhu who neither goes himself nor sends a messenger incurs an offense of wrong conduct for the breach of duty.

65. Kiṃ pana (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.538-9) sabbakappiyakārakesu evaṃ paṭipajjitabbanti? Na paṭipajjitabbaṃ. Ayañhi kappiyakārako nāma saṅkhepato duvidho niddiṭṭho [V 0.0063] aniddiṭṭho ca. Tattha niddiṭṭho duvidho bhikkhunā niddiṭṭho dūtena niddiṭṭhoti. Aniddiṭṭhopi duvidho [M 0.0063] mukhavevaṭikakappiyakārako parammukhakappiyakārakoti. Tesu bhikkhunā niddiṭṭho sammukhāsammukhavasena catubbidho hoti, tathā dūtena niddiṭṭhopi. Kathaṃ? Idhekacco bhikkhussa cīvaratthāya dūtena akappiyavatthuṃ pahiṇati, dūto taṃ bhikkhuṃ upasaṅkamitvā “idaṃ, bhante, itthannāmena tumhākaṃ cīvaratthāya pahitaṃ, gaṇhatha na”nti vadati, bhikkhu “nayidaṃ kappatī”ti paṭikkhipati, dūto “atthi pana te, bhante, veyyāvaccakaro”ti pucchati, puññatthikehi ca upāsakehi “bhikkhūnaṃ veyyāvaccaṃ karothā”ti āṇattā vā, bhikkhūnaṃ vā sandiṭṭhasambhattā keci veyyāvaccakarā honti, tesaṃ aññataro tasmiṃ khaṇe bhikkhussa santike nisinno hoti, bhikkhu taṃ niddisati “ayaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ veyyāvaccakaro”ti, dūto tassa hatthe akappiyavatthuṃ datvā “therassa cīvaraṃ kiṇitvā dehī”ti gacchati, ayaṃ bhikkhunā sammukhāniddiṭṭho.

65. But should one proceed in this way with all stewards? No, one should not proceed thus. For this 'steward,' in brief, is of two kinds: designated and undesignated. Among them, the designated is of two kinds: designated by a bhikkhu and designated by a messenger. The undesignated is also of two kinds: the steward who is present and has given verbal agreement, and the steward who is absent. Among these, the one designated by a bhikkhu is fourfold, by way of being in his presence or not in his presence; likewise, the one designated by a messenger. How? Here, a certain person sends an unallowable item to a bhikkhu for a robe through a messenger. The messenger approaches that bhikkhu and says, 'Venerable sir, this has been sent by so-and-so for your robe. Accept it.' The bhikkhu refuses, saying, 'This is not allowable.' The messenger asks, 'But, venerable sir, do you have a steward?' Now, some stewards are those who have been instructed by merit-seeking lay devotees to 'Perform service for the bhikkhus,' while others are acquaintances and associates of the bhikkhus. One of them is sitting near the bhikkhu at that moment. The bhikkhu designates him, saying, 'This is a steward of the bhikkhus.' The messenger, having given the unallowable item into his hand, says, 'Having bought a robe for the Elder, give it to him,' and departs. This is one designated by a bhikkhu in his presence.

No ce bhikkhussa santike nisinno hoti, apica kho bhikkhu niddisati “asukasmiṃ nāma gāme itthannāmo bhikkhūnaṃ veyyāvaccakaro”ti, so gantvā tassa hatthe akappiyavatthuṃ datvā “therassa cīvaraṃ kiṇitvā dadeyyāsī”ti āgantvā bhikkhussa ārocetvā gacchati, ayameko bhikkhunā asammukhāniddiṭṭho.

If he is not sitting near the bhikkhu, the bhikkhu nevertheless designates him, saying, 'In such-and-such a village, so-and-so is a steward of the bhikkhus.' The messenger goes, and having given the unallowable item into the steward's hand, says, 'You should buy a robe for the Elder and give it to him.' Then, having returned and informed the bhikkhu, he departs. This is one designated by a bhikkhu not in his presence.

Na heva kho so dūto attanā āgantvā āroceti, apica kho aññaṃ pahiṇati “dinnaṃ mayā, bhante, tassa hatthe cīvaracetāpannaṃ, tumhe cīvaraṃ gaṇheyyāthā”ti, ayaṃ dutiyo bhikkhunā asammukhāniddiṭṭho.

Nor does that messenger himself come and inform the bhikkhu, but he sends another, saying, “Venerable sir, I have given the robe-fund into the hands of that person; you should receive the robe.” This is the second designated by a bhikkhu not in his presence.

Na heva kho aññaṃ pahiṇati, apica gacchantova bhikkhuṃ vadati “ahaṃ tassa hatthe cīvaracetāpannaṃ dassāmi, tumhe cīvaraṃ gaṇheyyāthā”ti, ayaṃ tatiyo bhikkhunā asammukhāniddiṭṭhoti evaṃ eko sammukhāniddiṭṭho tayo asammukhāniddiṭṭhāti ime cattāro bhikkhunā niddiṭṭhaveyyāvaccakarā nāma. Etesu idha vuttanayeneva paṭipajjitabbaṃ.

Nor does he send another, but while going, he tells the bhikkhu, “I will give the robe-fund into his hand; you should take the robe.” This is the third designated by a bhikkhu not in his presence. Thus, one is designated in his presence, and three are designated not in his presence—these are the four types of stewards designated by a bhikkhu. Among these, one should proceed in the manner stated herein.

Aparo bhikkhu purimanayeneva dūtena pucchito natthitāya vā avicāretukāmatāya vā “natthamhākaṃ kappiyakārako”ti vadati, tasmiṃ khaṇe koci manusso āgacchati, dūto tassa hatthe akappiyavatthuṃ datvā “imassa hatthato cīvaraṃ gaṇheyyāthā”ti vatvā gacchati, ayaṃ dūtena sammukhāniddiṭṭhoti evaṃ eko sammukhāniddiṭṭho.

Another bhikkhu, when questioned by a messenger in the same manner as before, either because there is no steward or because of an unwillingness to consider, says, “We have no steward.” At that moment, a person arrives. The messenger places the unallowable item in that person’s hand and, having said, “You should receive the robe from this person’s hand,” departs. This is the one designated by a messenger in his presence. Thus, there is one designated in his presence.

Aparo [M 0.0064][V 0.0064] dūto gāmaṃ pavisitvā attanā abhirucitassa kassaci hatthe akappiyavatthuṃ datvā purimanayeneva āgantvā vā āroceti, aññaṃ vā pahiṇati “ahaṃ asukassa nāma hatthe cīvaracetāpannaṃ dassāmi, tumhe cīvaraṃ gaṇheyyāthā”ti vatvā vā gacchati, ayaṃ tatiyo dūtena asammukhāniddiṭṭhoti evaṃ eko sammukhāniddiṭṭho tayo asammukhāniddiṭṭhāti ime cattāro dūtena niddiṭṭhaveyyāvaccakarā nāma. Etesu meṇḍakasikkhāpade vuttanayeneva paṭipajjitabbaṃ. Vuttañhetaṃ –

Another messenger enters a village, places the unallowable item in the hand of someone he approves of, and then either returns and informs the monk in the same way as before, or sends another, or departs after saying, “I will give the robe-fund into the hand of so-and-so by name; you should take the robe.” This is the third designated by a messenger not in the monk's presence. Thus, one is designated in his presence and three are designated not in his presence—these four are called stewards designated by a messenger. Among these, one should proceed as stated in the Meṇḍaka training rule. For it has been said:

“Santi, bhikkhave, manussā saddhā pasannā, te kappiyakārakānaṃ hatthe hiraññaṃ upanikkhipanti ‘iminā yaṃ ayyassa kappiyaṃ, taṃ dethā’ti. Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, yaṃ tato kappiyaṃ, taṃ sādituṃ, na tvevāhaṃ, bhikkhave, ‘kenaci pariyāyena jātarūparajataṃ sāditabbaṃ pariyesitabba’nti vadāmī”ti (mahāva. 299).

“O monks, there are faithful and devoted people who place money in the hands of stewards, saying, ‘With this, give whatever is allowable for the venerable one.’ I allow, O monks, that you may consent to what is allowable from that. But I do not say, O monks, that by any means whatsoever gold and silver should be consented to or sought.”

Ettha codanāya parimāṇaṃ natthi, mūlaṃ asādiyantena sahassakkhattumpi codanāya vā ṭhānena vā kappiyabhaṇḍaṃ sādituṃ vaṭṭati. No ce deti, aññaṃ kappiyakārakaṃ ṭhapetvāpi āharāpetabbaṃ. Sace icchati, mūlasāmikānampi kathetabbaṃ. No ce icchati, na kathetabbaṃ.

Here, there is no limit to the requesting. Without consenting to the principal, it is permissible to obtain allowable goods even a thousand times through requesting or by standing. If the steward does not give, another steward should be appointed to have it brought. If one wishes, the original owners may also be told. If one does not wish, they should not be told.

Aparo bhikkhu purimanayeneva dūtena pucchito “natthamhākaṃ kappiyakārako”ti vadati, tadañño samīpe ṭhito sutvā “āhara bho, ahaṃ ayyassa cīvaraṃ cetāpetvā dassāmī”ti vadati. Dūto “handa bho dadeyyāsī”ti tassa hatthe datvā bhikkhussa anārocetvāva gacchati, ayaṃ mukhavevaṭikakappiyakārako. Aparo bhikkhuno upaṭṭhākassa vā aññassa vā hatthe akappiyavatthuṃ datvā “therassa cīvaraṃ dadeyyāsī”ti ettova pakkamati, ayaṃ parammukhākappiyakārakoti ime dve aniddiṭṭhakappiyakārakā nāma. Etesu aññātakaappavāritesu viya paṭipajjitabbaṃ. Sace sayameva cīvaraṃ ānetvā dadanti, gahetabbaṃ. No ce, na kiñci vattabbā. Yathā ca dūtassa hatthe cīvaratthāya akappiyavatthumhi pesite vinicchayo vutto, evaṃ piṇḍapātādīnampi atthāya pesite sayaṃ āgantvā dīyamāne ca vinicchayo veditabbo.

Another monk, when asked by a messenger in the same way as before, says, “We have no steward.” Then another person standing nearby, hearing this, says, “Bring it, sir, I will have a robe procured for the venerable one and give it.” The messenger, saying, “Here, sir, please give it,” gives the item into that person's hand and departs without informing the monk. This is called the steward-by-word-of-mouth. Another messenger, having given an unallowable item into the hand of the monk's attendant or someone else, says, “Please give a robe to the elder,” and then departs from that very spot. This is called the steward-in-absence. These two are called undesignated stewards. In their case, one should act as one would towards an unknown, uninvited person. If they bring the robe of their own accord and give it, it may be accepted. If not, nothing should be said. Just as the ruling was given regarding an unallowable item sent by a messenger for the purpose of a robe, so too should the ruling be understood when an item is sent for the purpose of almsfood and other requisites, and also when items are brought and given of one's own accord.

66. Upanikkhittasādiyane [M 0.0065] pana ayaṃ vinicchayo (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.583-4) – kiñci akappiyavatthuṃ pādamūle ṭhapetvā “idaṃ ayyassa hotū”ti vutte sacepi cittena sādiyati, gaṇhitukāmo hoti, kāyena vā vācāya vā “nayidaṃ kappatī”ti paṭikkhipati, anāpatti[V 0.0065]. Kāyavācāhi vā appaṭikkhipitvāpi suddhacitto hutvā “nayidaṃ amhākaṃ kappatī”ti na sādiyati, anāpattiyeva. Tīsu dvāresu hi yena kenaci paṭikkhittaṃ paṭikkhittameva hoti. Sace pana kāyavācāhi appaṭikkhipitvā cittena adhivāseti, kāyavācāhi kattabbassa paṭikkhepassa akaraṇato akiriyasamuṭṭhānaṃ kāyadvāre ca vacīdvāre ca āpattiṃ āpajjati, manodvāre pana āpatti nāma natthi.

66. Regarding consenting to what is deposited, this is the decision: If someone places an unallowable item at one’s feet and says, “May this be for the venerable sir,” even if one consents to it with the mind and desires to take it, but rejects it by body or by speech, saying, “This is not allowable,” there is no offense. Or, even without rejecting it by body and speech, if, being pure in mind, one does not consent to it, thinking, “This is not allowable for us,” there is indeed no offense. For, among the three doors, what is rejected by any one of them is indeed rejected. However, if, without rejecting it by body and speech, one consents to it with the mind, then due to the non-performance of the rejection that should be done by body and speech, one commits an offense originating from inaction at the body-door and at the speech-door. But at the mind-door, there is no such thing as an offense.

Eko sataṃ vā sahassaṃ vā pādamūle ṭhapeti “tuyhidaṃ hotū”ti, bhikkhu “nayidaṃ kappatī”ti paṭikkhipati, upāsako “pariccattaṃ mayā tumhāka”nti gato, añño tattha āgantvā pucchati “kiṃ, bhante, ida”nti, yaṃ tena ca attanā ca vuttaṃ, taṃ ācikkhitabbaṃ. So ce vadati “gopayissāmahaṃ, bhante, guttaṭṭhānaṃ dassethā”ti, sattabhūmikampi pāsādaṃ abhiruhitvā “idaṃ guttaṭṭhāna”nti ācikkhitabbaṃ, “idha nikkhipāhī”ti na vattabbaṃ. Ettāvatā kappiyañca akappiyañca nissāya ṭhitaṃ hoti, dvāraṃ pidahitvā rakkhantena vasitabbaṃ. Sace kiñci vikkāyikabhaṇḍaṃ pattaṃ vā cīvaraṃ vā gahetvā āgacchati, “idaṃ gahessatha, bhante”ti vutte “upāsaka, atthi amhākaṃ iminā attho, vatthu ca evarūpaṃ nāma saṃvijjati, kappiyakārako natthī”ti vattabbaṃ. Sace so vadati “ahaṃ kappiyakārako bhavissāmi, dvāraṃ vivaritvā dethā”ti, dvāraṃ vivaritvā “imasmiṃ okāse ṭhapita”nti vattabbaṃ, “idaṃ gaṇhā”ti na vattabbaṃ. Evampi kappiyañca akappiyañca nissāya ṭhitameva hoti. So ce taṃ gahetvā tassa kappiyabhaṇḍaṃ deti, vaṭṭati. Sace adhikaṃ gaṇhāti, “na mayaṃ tava bhaṇḍaṃ gaṇhāma, nikkhamāhī”ti vattabbo.

A certain lay supporter places a hundred or a thousand at the monk's feet, saying, 'Let this be for you.' The monk refuses, saying, 'This is not allowable.' The lay follower departs, saying, 'I have relinquished it for you.' Another lay supporter arrives there and asks, 'What is this, venerable sir?' Whatever was said by both that person and oneself should be explained. If he says, 'I will guard it, venerable sir, show me a secure place,' then even ascending a seven-storied building, it should be pointed out, saying, 'This is a secure place.' However, one should not say, 'Place it here.' At this point, it remains situated relying on both what is allowable and what is unallowable. The door should be closed, and one should dwell guarding it. If someone arrives carrying some merchandise for sale, such as a bowl or a robe, and says, 'Venerable sir, will you take this?' one should reply, 'Lay follower, we have a need for this, and an item of such a kind is available, but there is no steward.' If he says, 'I will be the steward. Open the door and give it,' the door should be opened, and it should be said, 'It is placed in this spot.' One should not say, 'Take this.' Even in this way, it indeed remains situated, relying on both what is allowable and what is unallowable. If he takes that and gives allowable goods to the monk, it is permissible. But if he takes more, he should be told, 'We are not taking your goods. Leave.'

67. Yena pana jātarūpādicatubbidhaṃ nissaggiyavatthu paṭiggahitaṃ, tena kiṃ kātabbanti? Saṅghamajjhe nissajjitabbaṃ. Kathaṃ? Tena bhikkhunā (pārā. 584) saṅghaṃ upasaṅkamitvā ekaṃsaṃ uttarāsaṅgaṃ karitvā vuḍḍhānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ pāde vanditvā ukkuṭikaṃ nisīditvā añjaliṃ paggahetvā evamassa vacanīyo “ahaṃ, bhante, rūpiyaṃ [M 0.0066] paṭiggahesiṃ, idaṃ me nissaggiyaṃ, imāhaṃ nissajjāmī”ti nissajjitvā āpatti desetabbā. Byattena bhikkhunā paṭibalena āpatti paṭiggahetabbā. Sace tattha āgacchati ārāmiko vā upāsako vā, so vattabbo “āvuso, idaṃ jānāhī”ti. Sace so bhaṇati “iminā kiṃ āharissāmī”ti, na vattabbo “imaṃ vā imaṃ vā āharā”ti, kappiyaṃ ācikkhitabbaṃ sappiṃ vā telaṃ vā madhuṃ vā phāṇitaṃ vā. Ācikkhantena ca “iminā sappiṃ vā telaṃ vā madhuṃ vā phāṇitaṃ vā āharā”ti na vattabbaṃ, “idañcidañca saṅghassa kappiya”nti ettakameva vattabbaṃ. Sace so tena [V 0.0066] parivattetvā kappiyaṃ āharati, rūpiyapaṭiggāhakaṃ ṭhapetvā sabbeheva bhājetvā paribhuñjitabbaṃ, rūpiyapaṭiggāhakena bhāgo na gahetabbo.

67. Now, as to a monk by whom a fourfold object for forfeiture, beginning with gold, has been received—what is to be done by him? It should be relinquished in the midst of the Sangha. How? That monk should approach the Sangha, arrange his upper robe over one shoulder, pay respect at the feet of the senior monks, sit in a squatting position, raise his joined palms, and speak thus: 'Venerable sirs, I have received gold or silver. This of mine is to be forfeited. I relinquish this.' Having thus relinquished it, the offense should be confessed. The offense should be received by a competent, capable monk. If a monastery attendant or a lay follower arrives there, he should be told, 'Friend, know this.' If he says, 'With this, what shall I bring?', he should not be told, 'Bring this or that.' What is allowable should be indicated: ghee, oil, honey, or molasses. And when indicating, it should not be said, 'With this, bring ghee, oil, honey, or molasses.' Only this much should be said: 'This and that is allowable for the Sangha.' If that person exchanges it and brings what is allowable, it should be distributed and used by all, except for the receiver of the gold or silver. The receiver of the gold or silver should not take a share.

Aññesaṃ (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.583-4) bhikkhūnaṃ vā ārāmikānaṃ vā pattabhāgampi labhitvā paribhuñjituṃ na vaṭṭati, antamaso makkaṭādīhi tato haritvā araññe ṭhapitaṃ vā tesaṃ hatthato gaḷitaṃ vā tiracchānapaṭiggahitampi paṃsukūlampi na vaṭṭatiyeva. Tato āhaṭena phāṇitena senāsanadhūpanampi na vaṭṭati. Sappinā vā telena vā padīpaṃ katvā dīpāloke nipajjituṃ, kasiṇaparikammaṃ kātuṃ, potthakampi vācetuṃ na vaṭṭati. Telamadhuphāṇitehi pana sarīre vaṇaṃ makkhetuṃ na vaṭṭatiyeva. Tena vatthunā mañcapīṭhādīni vā gaṇhanti, uposathāgāraṃ vā bhojanasālaṃ vā karonti, paribhuñjituṃ na vaṭṭati. Chāyāpi gehaparicchedena ṭhitāva na vaṭṭati, paricchedātikkantā āgantukattā vaṭṭati. Taṃ vatthuṃ vissajjetvā katena maggenapi setunāpi nāvāyapi uḷumpenāpi gantuṃ na vaṭṭati. Tena vatthunā khaṇāpitāya pokkharaṇiyā ubbhidodakaṃ pātuṃ vā paribhuñjituṃ vā na vaṭṭati. Anto udake pana asati aññaṃ āgantukaṃ udakaṃ vā vassodakaṃ vā paviṭṭhaṃ vaṭṭati. Kītāya yena saddhiṃ kītā, taṃ āgantukampi na vaṭṭati. Taṃ vatthuṃ upanikkhepaṃ ṭhapetvā saṅgho paccaye paribhuñjati, tepi paccayā tassa na vaṭṭanti. Ārāmo gahito hoti, sopi paribhuñjituṃ na vaṭṭati. Yadi bhūmipi bījampi akappiyaṃ, neva bhūmiṃ, na phalaṃ paribhuñjituṃ vaṭṭati. Sace bhūmiṃyeva kiṇitvā aññāni bījāni ropitāni, phalaṃ vaṭṭati. Atha bījāni kiṇitvā kappiyabhūmiyaṃ ropitāni, phalaṃ na vaṭṭati, bhūmiyaṃ nisīdituṃ vā nipajjituṃ vā vaṭṭati.

It is not allowable for that monk to use it, even if he obtains a share that has come to other monks or monastery attendants. Even if it is carried away from there by monkeys or other animals and left in the forest, or if it falls from their hands, or even if it is an item taken possession of by an animal, or a dust-heap rag, it is certainly not allowable. It is not allowable to fumigate a lodging with molasses brought from there. Having made a lamp with ghee or oil, it is not allowable to lie down in its light, to do the preliminary work for a kasiṇa, or to read a book. Furthermore, it is certainly not allowable to anoint a wound on the body with oil, honey, or molasses. If, with that item, they acquire beds, chairs, and so on, or build an Uposatha hall or a dining hall, it is not allowable to use them. Even the shadow is not allowable as long as it remains within the boundary of the building; once it has gone beyond the boundary, it is allowable on account of being a 'guest' shadow. It is not allowable to travel by a path, a bridge, a boat, or a raft made with that relinquished item. It is not allowable to drink or use the spring water from a pond that was caused to be dug with that item. However, if there is no spring water inside, other incoming water or rainwater that has entered is allowable. If a pond is bought, the water with which it was bought is not allowable, even if it is incoming water. If the Sangha, having placed that item as a deposit, uses the requisites obtained from it, those requisites are not allowable for that monk. If a monastery is acquired, it is also not allowable to use it. If both the land and the seed are unallowable, it is not allowable to use either the land or the fruit. If only the land is bought and other seeds are planted, the fruit is allowable. Now, if seeds are bought and planted on allowable land, the fruit is not allowable; however, it is allowable to sit or lie down on the land.

Sace [M 0.0067] pana tattha āgato kappiyakārako taṃ parivattetvā saṅghassa kappiyaṃ sappitelādiṃ āharituṃ na jānāti, so vattabbo “āvuso, imaṃ chaḍḍehī”ti. Sace so chaḍḍeti, iccetaṃ kusalaṃ. No ce chaḍḍeti, pañcahaṅgehi samannāgato bhikkhu rūpiyachaḍḍako sammannitabbo yo na chandāgatiṃ gaccheyya, na dosāgatiṃ gaccheyya, na mohāgatiṃ gaccheyya, na bhayāgatiṃ gaccheyya, chaḍḍitāchaḍḍitañca jāneyya. Evañca pana sammannitabbo, paṭhamaṃ bhikkhu yācitabbo, yācitvā byattena bhikkhunā paṭibalena saṅgho ñāpetabbo –

If, however, the attendant who comes there does not know how to exchange it for what is allowable for the Sangha, such as ghee or oil, he should be told, 'Friend, discard this.' If he discards it, that is good. If he does not discard it, a monk possessing five qualities should be designated as a discarder of money: one who would not go to a wrong course through desire, would not go to a wrong course through aversion, would not go to a wrong course through delusion, would not go to a wrong course through fear, and who knows what has been discarded and what has not been discarded. And he should be designated thus: first, a monk should be requested. Having made the request, a competent and capable monk should inform the Sangha—

“Suṇātu me, bhante, saṅgho, yadi saṅghassa pattakallaṃ, saṅgho itthannāmaṃ bhikkhuṃ rūpiyachaḍḍakaṃ sammanneyya, esā ñatti. Suṇātu me, bhante, saṅgho, saṅgho itthannāmaṃ bhikkhuṃ rūpiyachaḍḍakaṃ sammannati, yassāyasmato khamati itthannāmassa bhikkhuno rūpiyachaḍḍakassa sammuti[V 0.0067], so tuṇhassa. Yassa nakkhamati, so bhāseyya. Sammato saṅghena itthannāmo bhikkhu rūpiyachaḍḍako, khamati saṅghassa, tasmā tuṇhī, evametaṃ dhārayāmī”ti (pārā. 585).

“Venerable sirs, may the Sangha hear me. If it is the proper time for the Sangha, the Sangha should designate the monk named so-and-so as a discarder of money. This is the motion. Venerable sirs, may the Sangha hear me. The Sangha designates the monk named so-and-so as a discarder of money. Whichever venerable one approves of the designation of the monk named so-and-so as a discarder of money, let him be silent. Whoever does not approve, let him speak. The monk named so-and-so has been designated by the Sangha as a discarder of money. It is agreeable to the Sangha, therefore it is silent. Thus do I hold this.”

68. Tena sammatena (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.585) bhikkhunā nimittaṃ akatvā akkhīni nimīletvā nadiyā vā papāte vā vanagahane vā gūthaṃ viya anapekkhena patitokāsaṃ asamannārahantena chaḍḍetabbaṃ. Sace nimittaṃ katvā pāteti, dukkaṭaṃ āpajjati. Evaṃ jigucchitabbepi rūpiye bhagavā pariyāyena bhikkhūnaṃ paribhogaṃ ācikkhi. Rūpiyapaṭiggāhakassa pana kenaci pariyāyena tato uppannapaccayaparibhogo na vaṭṭati. Yathā cāyaṃ etassa na vaṭṭati, evaṃ asantasambhāvanāya vā kuladūsakakammena vā kuhanādīhi vāuppannapaccayā neva tassa, na aññassa vaṭṭanti, dhammena samena uppannāpi apaccavekkhitvā paribhuñjituṃ na vaṭṭanti. Cattāro hi paribhogā – theyyaparibhogo iṇaparibhogo dāyajjaparibhogo sāmiparibhogoti. Tattha saṅghamajjhepi nisīditvā paribhuñjantassa dussīlassa paribhogo theyyaparibhogo nāma. Sīlavato apaccavekkhitaparibhogo iṇaparibhogo nāma. Tasmā cīvaraṃ paribhoge paribhoge paccavekkhitabbaṃ, piṇḍapāto ālope ālope[M 0.0068], tathā asakkontena purebhattapacchābhattapurimayāmamajjhimayāmapacchimayāmesu. Sacassa apaccavekkhato aruṇo uggacchati, iṇaparibhogaṭṭhāne tiṭṭhati. Senāsanampi paribhoge paribhoge paccavekkhitabbaṃ. Bhesajjassa paṭiggahaṇepi paribhogepi satipaccayatā vaṭṭati, evaṃ santepi paṭiggahaṇe satiṃ katvā paribhoge akarontasseva āpatti, paṭiggahaṇe pana satiṃ akatvā paribhoge karontassa anāpatti. Catubbidhā hi suddhi – desanāsuddhi saṃvarasuddhi pariyeṭṭhisuddhi paccavekkhaṇasuddhīti.

68. That appointed monk should discard it without making a sign, closing his eyes, as if it were excrement, into a river, a precipice, or a dense forest, without concern, not paying attention to the place where it has fallen. If he makes a sign and discards it, he commits an offense of wrong-doing. Even though gold and silver are to be regarded with such disgust, the Blessed One, by way of an expedient, taught the use of things derived from them for monks. However, for a monk who accepts gold and silver, the use of requisites arisen from that is not permissible by any expedient. And just as this is not permissible for him, so too, requisites obtained by means of displaying a non-existent superior human state, or by an act that corrupts families, or by deceit and so on, are not permissible for him, nor are they permissible for another. Even requisites obtained righteously and justly are not to be used without reflection. For there are four kinds of use: stolen use, debt use, inheritance use, and ownership use. Among these, the use by an immoral person, even one sitting and partaking in the midst of the Sangha, is called stolen use. For a virtuous person, use without reflection is called debt use. Therefore, a robe should be reflected upon at each use, and almsfood at each mouthful. One who is unable to do so should reflect before the meal, after the meal, in the first, middle, and last watches of the night. If dawn breaks while one has not reflected, it remains as debt use. Lodgings, too, should be reflected upon at each use. For medicine, mindfulness is required both at receiving and at use. Even so, if one receives with mindfulness but uses without it, there is an offense. However, if one receives without mindfulness but uses with mindfulness, there is no offense. For there are four kinds of purification: purification by confession, purification by restraint, purification by seeking, and purification by reflection.
