Tattha desanāsuddhi nāma pātimokkhasaṃvarasīlaṃ. Tañhi desanāya sujjhanato “desanāsuddhī”ti vuccati. Saṃvarasuddhi nāma indriyasaṃvarasīlaṃ. Tañhi “na punevaṃ karissāmī”ti cittādhiṭṭhānasaṃvareneva sujjhanato “saṃvarasuddhī”ti vuccati. Pariyeṭṭhisuddhi nāma ājīvapārisuddhisīlaṃ. Tañhi anesanaṃ pahāya dhammena samena paccaye uppādentassa pariyesanāya suddhattā “pariyeṭṭhisuddhī”ti vuccati. Paccavekkhaṇasuddhi nāma paccayaparibhogasannissitasīlaṃ. Tañhi “paṭisaṅkhā yoniso cīvaraṃ paṭisevāmī”tiādinā (ma. ni. 1.23; a. ni. 6.58) nayena vuttena paccavekkhaṇena sujjhanato “paccavekkhaṇasuddhī”ti [V 0.0068] vuccati, tena vuttaṃ “paṭiggahaṇe pana satiṃ akatvā paribhoge karontassa anāpattī”ti.

Among these, purity by confession is the virtue of Pātimokkha-restraint. Indeed, it is called 'purity by confession' because it is purified by confession. Purity by restraint is the virtue of sense-faculty restraint. Indeed, it is called 'purity by restraint' because it is purified only by the restraint that is the mind's resolution, 'I will not do so again.' Purity by seeking is the virtue of purification of livelihood. Indeed, it is called 'purity by seeking' because it is purified by the seeking of one who, having abandoned improper seeking, produces requisites righteously and justly. Purity by reflection is the virtue dependent on the use of requisites. Indeed, it is called 'purity by reflection' because it is purified by reflection spoken of in the manner beginning, 'Wisely reflecting, I use the robe...' Therefore, it was said: 'However, for one who, not having applied mindfulness at the time of receiving, does so at the time of use, there is no offense.'

Sattannaṃ sekkhānaṃ paccayaparibhogo dāyajjaparibhogo nāma. Te hi bhagavato puttā, tasmā pitusantakānaṃ paccayānaṃ dāyādā hutvā te paccaye paribhuñjanti. Kiṃ pana te bhagavato paccaye paribhuñjanti, gihīnaṃ paccaye paribhuñjantīti? Gihīhi dinnāpi bhagavatā anuññātattā bhagavato santakā honti, tasmā bhagavato paccaye paribhuñjantīti veditabbaṃ. Dhammadāyādasutta (ma. ni. 1.29 ādayo) ñcettha sādhakaṃ. Khīṇāsavānaṃ paribhogo sāmiparibhogo nāma. Te hi taṇhāya dāsabyaṃ atītattā sāmino hutvā paribhuñjanti. Iti imesu paribhogesu sāmiparibhogo ca dāyajjaparibhogo ca sabbesampi vaṭṭati, iṇaparibhogo na vaṭṭati, theyyaparibhoge kathāyeva natthi.

The use of requisites by the seven trainees is named use as an heir. Indeed, they are the sons of the Blessed One; therefore, having become heirs to the requisites belonging to their father, they use those requisites. Do they, however, use the requisites of the Blessed One, or do they use the requisites of householders? Even though given by householders, because they are permitted by the Blessed One, they become the property of the Blessed One. Therefore, it should be understood that they use the requisites of the Blessed One. And the Dhammadāyāda Sutta is the authority in this matter. The use by the canker-free ones is named use as an owner. Indeed, having transcended servitude to craving, they use them as owners. Thus, among these uses, both use as an owner and use as an heir are permissible for all. Use as a debt is not permissible; in the case of use as a theft, there is nothing at all to be said.

Aparepi cattāro paribhogā – lajjiparibhogo alajjiparibhogo dhammiyaparibhogo adhammiyaparibhogoti. Tattha alajjino lajjinā saddhiṃ [M 0.0069] paribhogo vaṭṭati, āpattiyā na kāretabbo. Lajjino alajjinā saddhiṃ yāva na jānāti, tāva vaṭṭati. Ādito paṭṭhāya hi alajjī nāma natthi, tasmā yadāssa alajjibhāvaṃ jānāti, tadā vattabbo “tumhe kāyadvāre vacīdvāre ca vītikkamaṃ karotha, taṃ appatirūpaṃ, mā evamakatthā”ti. Sace anādiyitvā karotiyeva, yadi tena saddhiṃ paribhogaṃ karoti, sopi alajjīyeva hoti. Yopi attano bhārabhūtena alajjinā saddhiṃ paribhogaṃ karoti, sopi nivāretabbo. Sace na oramati, ayampi alajjīyeva hoti. Evaṃ eko alajjī alajjisatampi karoti. Alajjino pana alajjināva saddhiṃ paribhoge āpatti nāma natthi. Lajjino lajjinā saddhiṃ paribhogo dvinnaṃ khattiyakumārānaṃ suvaṇṇapātiyaṃ bhojanasadiso. Dhammiyādhammiyaparibhogo paccayavaseneva veditabbo. Tattha sace puggalopi alajjī, piṇḍapātopi adhammiyo, ubho jegucchā. Puggalo alajjī, piṇḍapāto dhammiyo, puggalaṃ jigucchitvā piṇḍapāto na gahetabbo. Mahāpaccariyaṃ pana “dussīlo saṅghato uddesabhattādīni labhitvā saṅghasseva deti, etāni yathādānameva gahitattā vaṭṭantī”ti vuttaṃ. Puggalo lajjī, piṇḍapāto adhammiyo, piṇḍapāto jeguccho na gahetabbo. Puggalo lajjī, piṇḍapātopi dhammiyo, vaṭṭati.

There are also four other kinds of consumption: consumption with a scrupulous person, consumption with an unscrupulous person, consumption in conformity with the Dhamma, and consumption not in conformity with the Dhamma. Among these, the consumption of an unscrupulous person with a scrupulous person is allowable; the unscrupulous person should not be made to incur an offense. For a scrupulous person, consumption with an unscrupulous person is allowable for as long as one does not know of their unscrupulousness. Indeed, from the beginning of monkhood, there is no one called 'unscrupulous'; therefore, when one knows of that person's state of being unscrupulous, they should be told: 'You commit transgressions through the door of the body and the door of speech; that is unsuitable. Do not act in such a way.' If, not taking this to heart, they continue to do so, and if one engages in consumption with them, that person also becomes unscrupulous. Whoever engages in consumption with an unscrupulous person who is a burden to them should also be prevented. If they do not desist, this person also becomes unscrupulous. Thus, one unscrupulous person makes even a hundred unscrupulous. However, there is no offense when unscrupulous persons consume with each other. Consumption of scrupulous persons with each other is like two young nobles eating from a golden bowl. Consumption in conformity with the Dhamma and not in conformity with the Dhamma should be understood by way of the requisites. In this regard, if the person is unscrupulous and the almsfood is not in conformity with the Dhamma, both are reprehensible. If the person is unscrupulous but the almsfood is in conformity with the Dhamma, having found the person reprehensible, the almsfood should not be accepted. However, in the Mahāpaccarī it is said: 'If a person of bad conduct, having obtained designated meals and so on from the Saṅgha, gives them to the Saṅgha itself, these are allowable, since they are accepted just as they were given.' If the person is scrupulous but the almsfood is not in conformity with the Dhamma, the almsfood is reprehensible and should not be accepted. If the person is scrupulous and the almsfood is also in conformity with the Dhamma, it is allowable.

Apare dve paggahā dve ca paribhogā – lajjipaggaho alajjipaggaho, dhammaparibhogo āmisaparibhogoti. Tattha alajjino lajjiṃ paggahetuṃ vaṭṭati, na so āpattiyā kāretabbo[V 0.0069]. Sace pana lajjī alajjiṃ paggaṇhāti, anumodanāya ajjhesati, dhammakathāya ajjhesati, kulesu upatthambheti, itaropi “amhākaṃ ācariyo īdiso ca īdiso cā”ti tassa parisati vaṇṇaṃ bhāsati, ayaṃ sāsanaṃ osakkāpeti antaradhāpetīti veditabbo. Dhammaparibhogaāmisaparibhogesu pana yattha āmisaparibhogo vaṭṭati, dhammaparibhogopi tattha vaṭṭati. Yo pana koṭiyaṃ ṭhito, gantho tassa puggalassa accayena nassissati, taṃ dhammānuggahena uggaṇhituṃ vaṭṭatīti vuttaṃ. Tatridaṃ vatthu – mahābhaye kira ekasseva bhikkhuno mahāniddeso paguṇo ahosi. Atha catunikāyikatissattherassa upajjhāyo mahātipiṭakatthero nāma [M 0.0070] mahārakkhitattheraṃ āha “āvuso mahārakkhita, etassa santike mahāniddesaṃ gaṇhāhī”ti. “Pāpo kirāyaṃ, bhante, na gaṇhāmī”ti. “Gaṇhāvuso, ahaṃ te santike nisīdissāmī”ti. “Sādhu, bhante, tumhesu nisinnesu gaṇhissāmī”ti paṭṭhapetvā rattindivaṃ nirantaraṃ pariyāpuṇanto osānadivase heṭṭhāmañce itthiṃ disvā “bhante, sutaṃyeva me pubbe, sacāhaṃ evaṃ jāneyyaṃ, na īdisassa santike dhammaṃ pariyāpuṇeyya”nti āha. Tassa pana santike bahū mahātherā uggaṇhitvā mahāniddesaṃ patiṭṭhāpesunti.

Furthermore, there are two kinds of support and two kinds of consumption: support of the scrupulous and support of the unscrupulous, and consumption of the Dhamma and consumption of material things. In this regard, it is allowable for an unscrupulous person to support a scrupulous person; he should not be made to incur an offense. But if a scrupulous person supports an unscrupulous person, requests him for an appreciation, requests him for a Dhamma talk, supports him among families, and if the other also speaks praise of him in an assembly, saying, 'Our teacher is of such and such qualities,' he should be known as one who causes the Dispensation to decline and to disappear. As for the consumption of the Dhamma and the consumption of material things, wherever the consumption of material things is allowable, the consumption of the Dhamma is also allowable there. But regarding a text that is on the verge of extinction and will be lost with the passing of that person, it is said: 'It is allowable to learn it for the sake of supporting the Dhamma.' On this, there is this story: During the great danger, it is said that only one bhikkhu was well-versed in the Mahāniddesa. Then, the preceptor of Tissatthera, master of the four Nikāyas, an elder named Mahātipiṭakatthera, said to Mahārakkhitatthera: 'Friend Mahārakkhita, learn the Mahāniddesa from him.' 'Venerable sir, this one is reportedly evil; I will not learn from him.' 'Learn, friend, I will sit near you.' 'Good, venerable sir, I will learn while you are seated near.' Having begun, he studied continuously day and night. On the final day, seeing a woman beneath the couch, he said: 'Venerable sir, I had only heard of this before; if I had truly known this, I would not have studied the Dhamma from such a one.' Yet, many great elders learned from him and established the Mahāniddesa.

Iti pāḷimuttakavinayavinicchayasaṅgahe

Thus, in the Compilation of Vinaya Adjudications Independent of the Pāḷi Canon,

Rūpiyādipaṭiggahaṇavinicchayakathā samattā.

The Discussion on the Adjudication Regarding the Acceptance of Silver and so forth is Concluded.

13. Dānalakkhaṇādivinicchayakathā

13. The Discourse on the Adjudication of the Characteristics of Giving and so forth

69. Dānavissāsaggāhehi [V 0.0070] lābhassa pariṇāmananti ettha tāva dānanti attano santakassa cīvarādiparikkhārassa saddhivihārikādīsu yassa kassaci dānaṃ. Tatridaṃ dānalakkhaṇaṃ – “idaṃ tuyhaṃ demi dadāmi dajjāmi oṇojemi pariccajāmi vissajjāmī”ti vā “itthannāmassa demi…pe… vissajjāmī”ti vā vadati, sammukhāpi parammukhāpi dinnaṃyeva hoti. “Tuyhaṃ gaṇhāhī”ti vutte “mayhaṃ gaṇhāmī”ti vadati, sudinnaṃ suggahitañca. “Tava santakaṃ karohi, tava santakaṃ hotu, tava santakaṃ hotī”ti vutte “mama santakaṃ karomi, mama santakaṃ hotu, mama santakaṃ karissāmī”ti vadati, dudinnaṃ duggahitañca. Neva dātā dātuṃ jānāti, na itaro gahetuṃ, sace pana “tava santakaṃ karohī”ti vutte “sādhu, bhante, mayhaṃ gaṇhāmī”ti gaṇhāti, suggahitaṃ. Sace pana eko “idaṃ cīvaraṃ gaṇhāhī”ti vadati, itaro “na gaṇhāmī”ti vadati, puna so “dinnaṃ mayā tuyhaṃ, gaṇhāhī”ti vadati, itaropi “na mayhaṃ iminā attho”ti vadati, tato purimopi “mayā dinna”nti dasāhaṃ atikkāmeti, pacchimopi “mayā paṭikkhitta”nti, kassa āpattīti? Na kassaci. Yassa pana ruccati, tena adhiṭṭhahitvā paribhuñjitabbaṃ. “Itthannāmassa dehī”ti dinnaṃ yāva parassa hatthaṃ na pāpuṇāti, tāva yo pahiṇati, tasseva santakaṃ, “itthannāmassa dammī”ti dinnaṃ pana yassa pahīyati, tassa santakaṃ. Tasmā bhikkhu bhikkhussa hatthe cīvaraṃ pahiṇati “idaṃ [M 0.0071] cīvaraṃ itthannāmassa dehī”ti. So antarāmagge yo pahiṇati, tassa vissāsā gaṇhāti, suggahitaṃ. Yassa pahīyati, tassa vissāsā gaṇhāti, duggahitaṃ.

69. In the heading ‘the diversion of a gain through giving and taking with trust,’ firstly, ‘giving’ is the giving of one’s own requisites, such as robes, to any recipient among co-residents and others. Herein, this is the characteristic of giving: one says, “I give this to you, I offer, I present, I relinquish, I abandon, I renounce,” or one says, “I give to so-and-so… I renounce,” and whether in one’s presence or absence, it is indeed given. When it is said, “Take this for yourself,” and one says, “I take it for myself,” it is well-given and well-received. When it is said, “Make it your property, let it be your property, it is your property,” and one says, “I make it my property, let it be my property, I will make it my property,” it is badly given and badly received. The giver does not know how to give, nor does the other know how to receive. If, however, when it is said, “Make it your property,” one takes it, saying, “Very well, venerable sir, I take it for myself,” it is well-received. Furthermore, if one monk says, “Take this robe,” and the other says, “I will not take it,” and that monk says again, “It is given by me to you, take it,” and the other also says, “I have no need for this,” and then the first lets ten days pass thinking, “It was given by me,” and the latter also lets ten days pass thinking, “It was rejected by me,” to whom is there an offense? To no one. However, the one who desires it should use it after having determined it for himself. Something given with the words, “Give this to so-and-so,” remains the property of the one who sends it as long as it does not reach the other’s hand. But something given with the words, “I give to so-and-so,” becomes the property of the one to whom it is sent. Therefore, a monk sends a robe in the hand of another monk, saying, “Give this robe to so-and-so.” If that intermediary, on the way, takes it with trust in the one who sends it, it is well-received. If he takes it with trust in the one to whom it is sent, it is badly received.

Bhikkhu (mahāva. 378-379) bhikkhussa hatthe cīvaraṃ pahiṇati “imaṃ cīvaraṃ itthannāmassa dehī”ti. So antarāmagge suṇāti “yo pahiṇati, so kālakato”ti, tassa matakacīvaraṃ adhiṭṭhāti, svādhiṭṭhitaṃ. Yassa pahīyati, tassa vissāsā gaṇhāti, duggahitaṃ. Bhikkhu bhikkhussa hatthe cīvaraṃ pahiṇati “imaṃ cīvaraṃ itthannāmassa dehī”ti. So antarāmagge suṇāti “yassa pahīyati, so kālakato”ti, tassa matakacīvaraṃ adhiṭṭhāti, dvādhiṭṭhitaṃ. Yo pahiṇati, tassa vissāsā gaṇhāti, suggahitaṃ. Bhikkhu bhikkhussa hatthe cīvaraṃ pahiṇati “imaṃ cīvaraṃ itthannāmassa dehī”ti. So antarāmagge suṇāti “ubho kālakatā”ti, yo pahiṇati, tassa matakacīvaraṃ adhiṭṭhāti, svādhiṭṭhitaṃ. Yassa pahīyati, tassa matakacīvaraṃ adhiṭṭhāti, dvādhiṭṭhitaṃ. Bhikkhu bhikkhussa hatthe cīvaraṃ pahiṇati “imaṃ cīvaraṃ itthannāmassa dammī”ti. So antarāmagge yo pahiṇati, tassa vissāsā gaṇhāti, duggahitaṃ. Yassa pahīyati, tassa vissāsā gaṇhāti, suggahitaṃ. Bhikkhu bhikkhussa hatthe cīvaraṃ pahiṇati “imaṃ cīvaraṃ itthannāmassa dammī”ti. So antarāmagge suṇāti “yo pahiṇati, so kālakato”ti, tassa [V 0.0071] matakacīvaraṃ adhiṭṭhāti, dvādhiṭṭhitaṃ. Yassa pahīyati, tassa vissāsā gaṇhāti, suggahitaṃ. Bhikkhu bhikkhussa hatthe cīvaraṃ pahiṇati “imaṃ cīvaraṃ itthannāmassa dammī”ti. So antarāmagge suṇāti “yassa pahīyati, so kālakato”ti, tassa matakacīvaraṃ adhiṭṭhāti, svādhiṭṭhitaṃ. Yo pahiṇati, tassa vissāsā gaṇhāti, duggahitaṃ. Bhikkhu bhikkhussa hatthe cīvaraṃ pahiṇati “imaṃ cīvaraṃ itthannāmassa dammī”ti. So antarāmagge suṇāti “ubho kālakatā”ti. Yo pahiṇati, tassa matakacīvaraṃ adhiṭṭhāti, dvādhiṭṭhitaṃ. Yassa pahīyati, tassa matakacīvaraṃ adhiṭṭhāti, svādhiṭṭhitaṃ.

A monk sends a robe by the hand of a monk, saying, 'Give this robe to so-and-so.' That monk, on the way, hears, 'The one who sent it has died.' He determines it as the robe of the deceased; it is well-determined. If he takes it through trust in the one for whom it was sent, it is wrongly taken. A monk sends a robe by the hand of a monk, saying, 'Give this robe to so-and-so.' That monk, on the way, hears, 'The one for whom it was sent has died.' He determines it as the robe of the deceased; it is wrongly determined. If he takes it through trust in the one who sent it, it is well-taken. A monk sends a robe by the hand of a monk, saying, 'Give this robe to so-and-so.' That monk, on the way, hears, 'Both have died.' Regarding the one who sent it, he determines it as the robe of the deceased; it is well-determined. Regarding the one for whom it was sent, he determines it as the robe of the deceased; it is wrongly determined. A monk sends a robe by the hand of a monk, saying, 'I give this robe to so-and-so.' That monk, on the way, if he takes it through trust in the one who sent it, it is wrongly taken. If he takes it through trust in the one for whom it was sent, it is well-taken. A monk sends a robe by the hand of a monk, saying, 'I give this robe to so-and-so.' That monk, on the way, hears, 'The one who sent it has died.' He determines it as the robe of the deceased; it is wrongly determined. If he takes it through trust in the one for whom it was sent, it is well-taken. A monk sends a robe by the hand of a monk, saying, 'I give this robe to so-and-so.' That monk, on the way, hears, 'The one for whom it was sent has died.' He determines it as the robe of the deceased; it is well-determined. If he takes it through trust in the one who sent it, it is wrongly taken. A monk sends a robe by the hand of a monk, saying, 'I give this robe to so-and-so.' That monk, on the way, hears, 'Both have died.' Regarding the one who sent it, he determines it as the robe of the deceased; it is wrongly determined. Regarding the one for whom it was sent, he determines it as the robe of the deceased; it is well-determined.

Pariccajitvā dinnaṃ puna kenaci kāraṇena kupito āharāpetuṃ na labhati. Attanā dinnampi hi cīvaraṃ sakasaññāya acchindato nissaggiyaṃ, aññaṃ parikkhāraṃ antamaso sūcimpi acchindato dukkaṭaṃ. Sace pana “bhante, tumhākaṃ [M 0.0072] idaṃ sāruppa”nti sayameva deti, gahetuṃ vaṭṭati. Atha pana “āvuso, mayaṃ tuyhaṃ ‘vattapaṭivattaṃ karissati, amhākaṃ santike upajjhaṃ gaṇhissati, dhammaṃ pariyāpuṇissatī’ti cīvaraṃ adamhā, so dāni tvaṃ na vattaṃ karosi, na upajjhaṃ gaṇhāsi, na dhammaṃ pariyāpuṇāsī”ti evamādīni vutto “bhante, cīvaratthāya maññe bhaṇatha, idaṃ vo cīvara”nti deti, evampi vaṭṭati. Disāpakkamantaṃ vā pana daharaṃ “nivattetha na”nti bhaṇati, so na nivattati, cīvare gahetvā nirundhathāti, evañce nivattati, sādhu. Sace “pattacīvaratthāya maññe tumhe bhaṇatha, gaṇhatha na”nti deti, evampi vaṭṭati. Vibbhamantaṃ vā disvā “mayaṃ tuyhaṃ ‘vattaṃ karissatī’ti pattacīvaraṃ adamhā, so dāni tvaṃ vibbhamitvā carasī”ti vadati, itaro “gaṇhatha tumhākaṃ pattacīvara”nti deti, evampi vaṭṭati. “Mama santike upajjhaṃ gaṇhantasseva demi, aññattha gaṇhantassa na demi, vattaṃ karontasseva demi, akarontassa na demi, dhammaṃ pariyāpuṇantasseva demi, apariyāpuṇantassa na demi, avibbhamantasseva demi, vibbhamantassa na demī”ti evaṃ pana dātuṃ na vaṭṭati, dadato dukkaṭaṃ, āharāpetuṃ pana vaṭṭati, vissajjetvā dinnaṃ acchinditvā gaṇhanto bhaṇḍagghena kāretabbo. Ayaṃ tāva dāne vinicchayo.

Having given something away, if one becomes angry for some reason, one does not get to have it brought back again. Indeed, for a bhikkhu who snatches back even a robe given by himself with the perception that it is his own, it entails forfeiture; for one who snatches back another requisite, even down to a needle, it is a dukkaṭa offense. But if one gives of one's own accord, saying, 'Venerable sir, this is suitable for you,' it is allowable to take it. Or else, if one says, 'Friend, we gave you a robe thinking, "He will perform the major and minor duties, he will take a preceptor from us, he will master the Dhamma." But now you do not perform the duties, you do not take a preceptor, you do not master the Dhamma,' and having been told such things, the other gives it back, saying, 'Venerable sirs, I suppose you speak for the sake of the robe; this is your robe,' even so, it is allowable. Or else, regarding a young bhikkhu who is departing for another region, one says, 'Turn him back!' but he does not turn back, one says, 'Having taken his robes, restrain him!' If he turns back in this way, it is good. If he gives them back, saying, 'I suppose you speak for the sake of the bowl and robes; take them!' even so, it is allowable. Or, having seen a young bhikkhu who is disrobing and saying, 'We gave you a bowl and robes thinking, "He will perform the duties," but now you are going about having disrobed,' and the other gives them back, saying, 'Take your bowl and robes,' even so, it is allowable. However, it is not allowable to give thus: 'I give only to one who takes a preceptor from me, not to one who takes one elsewhere; I give only to one who performs the duties, not to one who does not; I give only to one who masters the Dhamma, not to one who does not; I give only to one who does not disrobe, not to one who disrobes.' For the one who gives thus, it is a dukkaṭa offense. But it is allowable to have it brought back. One who takes back by snatching what was given after having been relinquished should be dealt with according to the value of the goods. This, for now, is the legal decision on giving.

70. Vissāsaggāhalakkhaṇaṃ pana iminā suttena jānitabbaṃ –

70. Now, the characteristic of taking through trust is to be understood through this discourse:

“Anujānāmi[V 0.0072], bhikkhave, pañcahaṅgehi samannāgatassa vissāsaṃ gahetuṃ sandiṭṭho ca hoti, sambhatto ca, ālapito ca, jīvati ca, gahite ca attamano hotī”ti (mahāva. 356).

“O monks, I allow taking on trust from one endowed with five factors: he is a friend who has been seen, he is a companion with whom one has shared meals, he is one who has said, 'Take whatever you desire,' he is alive, and he is pleased when something is taken.”

Tattha (pārā. aṭṭha. 1.131) sandiṭṭhoti diṭṭhamattakamitto. Sambhattoti daḷhamitto. Ālapitoti “mama santakaṃ yaṃ icchasi, taṃ gaṇheyyāsi, āpucchitvā gahaṇe kāraṇaṃ natthī”ti vutto. Jīvatīti anuṭṭhānaseyyāya sayitopi yāvajīvitindriyupacchedaṃ na pāpuṇāti. Gahite ca attamanoti gahite tuṭṭhacitto hoti. “Evarūpassa santakaṃ gahite me attamano bhavissatī”ti jānantena gahetuṃ vaṭṭati. Anavasesapariyādānavasena cetāni pañcaṅgāni vuttāni, vissāsaggāho pana tīhi aṅgehi ruhati sandiṭṭho, jīvati, gahite attamano, sambhatto, jīvati, gahite attamano, ālapito, jīvati, gahite attamanoti. Yo pana na jīvati, na ca [M 0.0073] gahite attamano hoti, tassa santakaṃ vissāsaggāhena gahitampi puna dātabbaṃ. Dadamānena ca matakadhanaṃ tāva ye tassa dhane issarā gahaṭṭhā vā pabbajitā vā, tesaṃ dātabbaṃ. Anattamanassa santakaṃ tasseva dātabbaṃ, yo pana paṭhamaṃyeva “suṭṭhu kataṃ tayā mama santakaṃ gaṇhantenā”ti vacībhedena vā cittuppādamattena vā anumoditvā pacchā kenaci kāraṇena kupito, paccāharāpetuṃ na labhati, yopi adātukāmo, cittena pana adhivāseti, na kiñci vadati, sopi puna paccāharāpetuṃ na labhati. Yo pana “mayā tumhākaṃ santakaṃ gahitaṃ vā paribhuttaṃ vā”ti vutte “gahitaṃ vā hotu paribhuttaṃ vā, mayā pana taṃ kenacideva karaṇīyena ṭhapitaṃ, taṃ pākatikaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti vadati, ayaṃ paccāharāpetuṃ labhati. Ayaṃ vissāsaggāhe vinicchayo.

Here, an 'acquaintance' is a friend merely by sight. A 'steadfast friend' is a firm friend. An 'individual who has given permission' is one who has been told, 'Whatever of mine you wish, you may take; there is no need to ask permission when taking.' 'He is living' means that even if one is lying down in a state from which one cannot rise, as long as one has not reached the severance of the life faculty, one is considered to be living. 'And is pleased when it is taken' means one has a pleased mind when it is taken. It is permissible for one to take, knowing: 'If the belonging of such a person is taken, he will be pleased.' These five factors are stated in terms of complete and unreserved taking. However, taking based on trust is established by three factors: the owner is an acquaintance, is living, and is pleased when it is taken; or is a steadfast friend, is living, and is pleased when it is taken; or is one who has given permission, is living, and is pleased when it is taken. But as for one who is living, yet is not pleased when it is taken, even if their belongings were taken based on trust, they must be returned. When giving, the wealth of the deceased should first be given to those—whether laypeople or monastics—who have authority over that wealth. The belonging of one who is displeased should be returned to that very person. If someone initially approves, either by a verbal expression, saying, 'You have done well in taking my belongings,' or merely by a mental arising of approval, but later becomes angry for some reason, they cannot have it brought back. Also, one who is unwilling to give but endures it in his mind without saying anything, he too cannot have it brought back. However, if, when it is said, 'I have taken or used your belongings,' the other replies, 'Let it be taken or used, but I had set it aside for some purpose; it should be restored to its original condition,' then this person can have it brought back. This is the legal decision concerning taking based on trust.

71. Lābhassa pariṇāmananti idaṃ pana aññesaṃ atthāya pariṇatalābhassa attano aññassa vā pariṇāmanaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Tatrāyaṃ vinicchayo (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.659-660) – saṅghassa pariṇataṃ sahadhammikānaṃ vā gihīnaṃ vā antamaso mātusantakampi “idaṃ mayhaṃ dehī”ti saṅghassa pariṇatabhāvaṃ ñatvā attano pariṇāmetvā gaṇhantassa nissaggiyaṃ pācittiyaṃ, “imassa bhikkhuno dehī”ti evaṃ aññassa pariṇāmentassa suddhikapācittiyaṃ. Tasmā yopi vassikasāṭikasamaye mātugharepi saṅghassa pariṇataṃ vassikasāṭikaṃ ñatvā attano pariṇāmeti, nissaggiyaṃ pācittiyaṃ, parassa pariṇāmeti, suddhikapācittiyaṃ. Manussā “saṅghabhattaṃ karissāmā”ti sappitelādīni āharanti, gilāno cepi bhikkhusaṅghassa pariṇatabhāvaṃ ñatvā kiñci yācati, nissaggiyaṃ pācittiyameva. Sace pana so “tumhākaṃ sappiādīni [V 0.0073] ābhatāni atthī”ti pucchitvā “āma, atthī”ti vutte “mayhampi dethā”ti vadati, vaṭṭati. Athāpi naṃ kukkuccāyantaṃ upāsakā vadanti “saṅghopi amhehi dinnameva labhati, gaṇhatha, bhante”ti, evampi vaṭṭati.

71. This, however, is said with reference to the diverting, for oneself or for another, of a gain that has already been diverted for the sake of others. Herein, this is the decision: Regarding something diverted to the Sangha—whether it belongs to co-religionists, or to householders, or even to one's own mother—for a monk who, knowing the fact of its having been diverted to the Sangha, says, 'Give this to me,' and takes it after having diverted it to himself, it is an offense requiring forfeiture and confession. If one diverts it to another by saying, 'Give this to such-and-such monk,' it is a pure offense of confession. Therefore, whatever monk, during the rains-cloth season, even in his mother’s house, knowing that a rains-cloth has been diverted to the Sangha, diverts it to himself, it is an offense requiring forfeiture and confession; if he diverts it to another, it is a pure offense of confession. People, intending, 'We will prepare a meal for the Sangha,' bring ghee, oil, and so on. Even if a sick monk, knowing the fact that these have been diverted to the Sangha, asks for something, it is indeed an offense requiring forfeiture and confession. However, if that monk asks, 'Do you have ghee, oil, and so on that has been brought?' and when they reply, 'Yes, we do,' he then says, 'Give some to me also,' it is allowable. Furthermore, if the lay devotees say to him, who is scrupulous, 'Venerable sir, the Sangha, too, receives only what is given by us. Please accept,' even so it is allowable.

Ekasmiṃ vihāre saṅghassa pariṇataṃ aññavihāraṃ uddisitvā “asukasmiṃ nāma vihāre saṅghassa dethā”ti pariṇāmeti, “kiṃ saṅghassa dānena, cetiyassa pūjaṃ karothā”ti evaṃ cetiyassa vā pariṇāmeti, dukkaṭaṃ. Cetiyassa pariṇataṃ aññacetiyassa vā saṅghassa vā gaṇassa vā puggalassa vā pariṇāmeti, dukkaṭameva. Niyametvā aññacetiyassa atthāya [M 0.0074] ropitamālāvacchato aññacetiyamhi pupphampi āropetuṃ na vaṭṭati, ekassa cetiyassa pana chattaṃ vā paṭākaṃ vā āropetvā ṭhitaṃ disvā sesaṃ aññacetiyassa dāpetuṃ vaṭṭati. Antamaso sunakhassapi pariṇataṃ “imassa sunakhassa mā dehi, etassa dehī”ti evaṃ aññapuggalassa pariṇāmeti, dukkaṭaṃ. Sace pana dāyakā “mayaṃ saṅghabhattaṃ kātukāmā, cetiyapūjaṃ kātukāmā, ekassa bhikkhuno parikkhāraṃ dātukāmā, tumhākaṃ ruciyā dassāma, bhaṇatha kattha demā”ti vadanti, evaṃ vutte tena bhikkhunā “yattha icchatha, tattha dethā”ti vattabbā. Sace pana kevalaṃ “kattha demā”ti pucchanti, “yattha tumhākaṃ deyyadhammo paribhogaṃ vā labheyya, paṭisaṅkhāraṃ vā labheyya, ciraṭṭhitiko vā assa, yattha vā pana tumhākaṃ cittaṃ pasīdati, tattha dethā”ti vattuṃ vaṭṭati.

In a monastery, if one diverts something intended for the Sangha, directing it to another monastery, saying, “Give this to the Sangha in such-and-such a monastery,” or if one diverts it to a shrine, saying, “Why give to the Sangha? Make an offering to the shrine,” it is a dukkaṭa offense. If one diverts something intended for a shrine to another shrine, or to the Sangha, or to a group, or to an individual, it is likewise a dukkaṭa offense. If flowers have been specifically planted for the purpose of one shrine, it is not permissible to place even a single flower from that planting on another shrine. However, if one sees an umbrella or banner already placed on one shrine, it is permissible to have the remainder given to another shrine. Even if something was intended for a dog, saying, “Do not give this to this dog, give it to that one,” and thus diverting it to another being, is a dukkaṭa offense. But if donors say, “We wish to prepare a meal for the Sangha, or to make an offering to a shrine, or to give requisites to a single monk—we will give according to your preference, tell us where we should give?” then, when spoken to in this way, the monk should say, “Give where you wish.” If they simply ask, “Where should we give?” it is permissible to say, “Give where your donation would be of use, or where it would be maintained, or where it would last long, or where your mind is pleased.”

Iti pāḷimuttakavinayavinicchayasaṅgahe

Thus in the Pāḷimuttakavinayavinicchayasaṅgaha.

Dānalakkhaṇādivinicchayakathā samattā.

The Discourse on the Analysis of the Characteristics of Giving and so forth is concluded.

14. Pathavīkhaṇanavinicchayakathā

14. The Discourse on the Analysis of Digging the Earth

72. Pathavīti [V 0.0074] dve pathavī jātā ca pathavī ajātā ca pathavīti. Tattha jātā nāma pathavī suddhapaṃsukā suddhamattikā appapāsāṇā appasakkharā appakaṭhalā appamarumbā appavālukā yebhuyyenapaṃsukā yebhuyyenamattikā, adaḍḍhāpi vuccati “jātā pathavī”ti. Yopi paṃsupuñjo vā mattikāpuñjo vā atirekacātumāsaṃ ovaṭṭho, sopi vuccati “jātā pathavī”ti. Ajātā nāma pathavī suddhapāsāṇā suddhasakkharā suddhakaṭhalā suddhamarumbā suddhavālukā appapaṃsukā appamattikā yebhuyyenapāsāṇā yebhuyyenasakkharā yebhuyyenakaṭhalā yebhuyyenamarumbā yebhuyyenavālukā, daḍḍhāpi vuccati “ajātā pathavī”ti. Yopi paṃsupuñjo vā mattikāpuñjo vā omakacātumāsaṃ ovaṭṭho, sopi vuccati “ajātā pathavī”ti (pāci. 84-86).

72. Earth: There are two kinds of earth: born earth and unborn earth. Herein, born earth is that which is pure dust, pure clay, with few stones, few pebbles, few potsherds, little rubble, or little sand—mostly dust or mostly clay. Even unburnt earth is called 'born earth.' Also, whatever heap of dust or heap of clay has been rained on for more than four months, that too is called 'born earth.' Unborn earth is that which is pure stones, pure pebbles, pure potsherds, pure rubble, pure sand, with little dust or little clay—mostly stones, mostly pebbles, mostly potsherds, mostly rubble, or mostly sand. Even burnt earth is called 'unborn earth.' Also, whatever heap of dust or heap of clay has been rained on for less than four months, that too is called 'unborn earth.'

Tattha jātapathaviṃ khaṇantassa khaṇāpentassa vā pācittiyaṃ. Tatrāyaṃ vinicchayo (pāci. aṭṭha. 86) – sace sayaṃ khaṇati, pahāre pahāre pācittiyaṃ. Sace [M 0.0075] aññaṃ āṇāpeti, sakiṃ āṇatto sacepi sakaladivasaṃ khaṇati, āṇāpakassa ekameva pācittiyaṃ. Sace pana kusīto hoti, punappunaṃ āṇāpetabbo, taṃ āṇāpetvā khaṇāpentassa vācāya vācāya pācittiyaṃ. Sace “pokkharaṇiṃ khaṇāhī”ti vadati, vaṭṭati. Khatāyeva hi pokkharaṇī nāma hoti. Tasmā ayaṃ kappiyavohāro. Esa nayo “vāpiṃ taḷākaṃ āvāṭaṃ khaṇā”tiādīsupi. “Imaṃ okāsaṃ khaṇa, imasmiṃ okāse pokkharaṇiṃ khaṇā”ti vattuṃ pana na vaṭṭati. “Kandaṃ khaṇa, mūlaṃ khaṇā”ti aniyametvā vattuṃ vaṭṭati, “imaṃ valliṃ khaṇa, imasmiṃ okāse kandaṃ vā mūlaṃ vā khaṇā”ti vattuṃ na vaṭṭati.

Therein, for one who digs or causes to be dug born earth, there is a pācittiya offense. Herein is the decision: If one digs oneself, a pācittiya offense is to be known for every strike. If one orders another, and if the one ordered, having been ordered once, digs for the entire day, for the one who gave the order there is only one pācittiya offense. But if he is lazy, he is to be ordered again and again; for the one who, having ordered him, causes him to dig, there is a pācittiya offense for every word of command. If one says, 'Dig a pond,' it is allowable. For it is only after being dug that it is called a pond. Therefore, this is allowable speech. This is the method also in such cases as 'Dig a reservoir, a tank, a pit.' But it is not allowable to say, 'Dig this place,' or 'In this place, dig a pond.' It is allowable to say without specifying, 'Dig a tuber, dig a root,' but it is not allowable to say, 'Dig this vine,' or 'In this place, dig a tuber or a root.'

73. Pokkharaṇiṃ sodhentehi yo kuṭehi ussiñcituṃ sakkā hoti tanukakaddamo, taṃ apanetuṃ vaṭṭati, bahalo na vaṭṭati. Ātapena sukkhakaddamo phalati, tatra yo heṭṭhā pathaviyā asambandho, tameva apanetuṃ vaṭṭati. Udakena gataṭṭhāne udakapappaṭako nāma hoti, vātapahārena calati, taṃ apanetuṃ vaṭṭati. Pokkharaṇīādīnaṃ taṭaṃ bhijjitvā udakasāmantā patati. Sace omakacātumāsaṃ ovaṭṭhaṃ, chindituṃ bhindituṃ vā vaṭṭati, cātumāsato uddhaṃ na vaṭṭati. Sace pana [V 0.0075] udakeyeva patati, devena atirekacātumāsaṃ ovaṭṭhepi udakeyeva udakassa patitattā vaṭṭati.

73. When cleaning a pond, it is allowable to remove thin mud that can be scooped out with pots; thick mud is not allowable. Dry mud flakes off due to the sun's heat; it is allowable to remove only that which is not connected to the earth below. In a place where water has gone, there is what is called a water-scum; if it moves when struck by the wind, it is allowable to remove it. The bank of a pond or the like may break and fall near the water. If it has been rained on for less than four months, it is allowable to cut or break it; if for more than four months, it is not allowable. But if it falls into the water itself, even if it has been rained on for more than four months, it is allowable, because the rain falls upon the water itself.

Pāsāṇapiṭṭhiyaṃ soṇḍiṃ khaṇanti, sace tattha paṭhamameva sukhumarajaṃ patati, taṃ devena ovaṭṭhaṃ hoti, cātumāsaccayena akappiyapathavīsaṅkhyaṃ gacchati. Udake pariyādinne soṇḍiṃ sodhentehi vikopetuṃ na vaṭṭati. Sace paṭhamameva udakena pūrati, pacchā rajaṃ patati, taṃ vikopetuṃ vaṭṭati. Tattha hi deve vassantepi udakeyeva udakaṃ patati. Piṭṭhipāsāṇe sukhumarajaṃ hoti, deve phusāyante allīyati, tampi cātumāsaccayena vikopetuṃ na vaṭṭati. Akatapabbhāre vammiko uṭṭhito hoti, yathāsukhaṃ vikopetuṃ vaṭṭati. Sace abbhokāse uṭṭhahati, omakacātumāsaṃ ovaṭṭhoyeva vaṭṭati. Rukkhādīsu āruḷhaupacikamattikāyampi eseva nayo. Gaṇḍuppādagūthamūsikukkaragokaṇṭakādīsupi eseva nayo. Gokaṇṭako nāma gāvīnaṃ khuracchinnakaddamo vuccati. Sace pana heṭṭhimatalena bhūmisambandho hoti, ekadivasampi na vaṭṭati. Kasitaṭṭhāne naṅgalacchinnamattikāpiṇḍaṃ gaṇhantassa eseva nayo.

They dig a cistern on a stone slab; if fine dust falls there first and is then rained upon, after four months it is counted as unallowable earth. When the water has been used up, it is not allowable for those cleaning the cistern to disturb it. If it fills with water first and dust falls afterward, it is allowable to disturb it, for there, even when it rains, the rain falls only upon the water. On a flat stone there is fine dust; when sprinkled by rain, it adheres. It is not allowable to disturb that either, after the passing of four months. If a termite mound has arisen in an unused mountain hollow, it is allowable to disturb it as one pleases. If it arises in an open space, it is allowable only if it has been rained on for less than four months. The same principle applies to earth brought up by termites onto trees and so forth. The same principle also applies to earthworm castings, mouse-leavings, earth disturbed by dogs, and earth from cow-hoof marks, and so forth. ‘Gokaṇṭaka’ refers to mud cut by the hooves of cows. But if it is connected to the ground by its lower surface, it is not allowable even if it has been rained on for only a single day. For one who takes a clod of earth cut by a plowshare in a plowed place, the same principle applies.

Purāṇasenāsanaṃ [M 0.0076] hoti acchadanaṃ vā vinaṭṭhacchadanaṃ vā atirekacātumāsaṃ ovaṭṭhaṃ jātapathavīsaṅkhyameva gacchati, tato avasesaṃ chadaniṭṭhakaṃ vā gopānasīādikaṃ upakaraṇaṃ vā “iṭṭhakaṃ gaṇhāmi, gopānasiṃ bhittipādaṃ padarattharaṇaṃ pāsādatthambhaṃ gaṇhāmī”ti saññāya gaṇhituṃ vaṭṭati, tena saddhiṃ mattikā patati, anāpatti, bhittimattikaṃ gaṇhantassa pana āpatti. Sace yā yā atintā, taṃ taṃ gaṇhāti, anāpatti. Antogehe mattikāpuñjo hoti, tasmiṃ ekadivasaṃ ovaṭṭhe gehaṃ chādenti. Sace sabbo tinto, cātumāsaccayena jātapathavīyeva. Athassa uparibhāgoyeva tinto, anto atinto, yattakaṃ tintaṃ, taṃ kappiyakārakehi kappiyavohārena apanāmetvā sesaṃ yathāsukhaṃ vaḷañjetuṃ vaṭṭati udakena temitattā. Ekābaddhāyeva hi jātapathavī hoti, na itarāti. Abbhokāse mattikāpākāro hoti, atirekacātumāsaṃ ovaṭṭho jātapathavīsaṅkhyaṃ gacchati, tattha laggapaṃsuṃ pana allahatthena chupitvā gahetuṃ vaṭṭati. Sace iṭṭhakapākāro hoti, yebhuyyenakaṭhalaṭṭhāne tiṭṭhati, yathāsukhaṃ vikopetuṃ vaṭṭati. Abbhokāse ṭhitamaṇḍapatthambhaṃ ito cito ca sañcāletvā pathaviṃ vikopentena gahetuṃ na vaṭṭati, ujukameva uddharituṃ vaṭṭati. Aññampi sukkharukkhaṃ sukkhakhāṇukaṃ vā gaṇhantassa eseva nayo.

An old lodging, whether unroofed or with a ruined roof, if it has been rained upon for more than four months, is counted as 'born earth'. From that, it is allowable to take the remaining roofing bricks or building materials such as rafters, with the perception, 'I take a brick, I take a rafter, the plank laid at the foot of the wall, a stone pillar.' If earth falls along with it, there is no offense. But for one who takes earth from the wall, there is an offense. If one takes whichever wall is not wet, there is no offense. Inside a building, there may be a pile of earth. When that pile has been rained on for one day, they roof the building. If the whole pile is wet, with the passing of four months it is indeed 'born earth'. But if only its upper part is wet and the inside is not wet, then having had the wet portion removed by stewards using an allowable expression, it is allowable to use the remainder as one wishes; this is because it is merely moistened by water. For only when it is a single connected mass is it 'born earth'; the other part is not. If there is an earth wall in an open space and it has been rained on for more than four months, it is counted as 'born earth'. But it is allowable to take the dust clinging to it after touching it with a wet hand. If it is a brick wall, and it stands on ground that is mostly potsherds, it is allowable to dismantle it as one wishes. It is not allowable to take a pavilion pillar standing in an open space by shaking it to and fro, thereby breaking up the earth; it is allowable to pull it straight up. This is the same method for one who takes another dry tree or a dry stump.

74. Navakammatthaṃ thambhaṃ vā pāsāṇaṃ vā rukkhaṃ vā daṇḍakehi uccāletvā pavaṭṭentā gacchanti[V 0.0076], tattha jātapathavī bhijjati, sace suddhacittā pavaṭṭenti, anāpatti. Atha pana tena apadesena pathaviṃ bhinditukāmāyeva honti, āpatti. Sākhādīni kaḍḍhantānampi pathaviyaṃ dārūni phālentānampi eseva nayo. Pathaviyaṃ aṭṭhisūcikaṇṭakādīsupi yaṃ kiñci ākoṭetuṃ vā pavesetuṃ vā na vaṭṭati, “passāvadhārāya vegena pathaviṃ bhindissāmī”ti evaṃ passāvampi kātuṃ na vaṭṭati. Karontassa bhijjati, āpatti, “visamabhūmiṃ samaṃ karissāmī”ti sammajjaniyā ghaṃsitumpi na vaṭṭati. Vattasīseneva hi sammajjitabbaṃ. Keci kattarayaṭṭhiyā bhūmiṃ koṭṭenti, pādaṅguṭṭhakena vilikhanti, “caṅkamitaṭṭhānaṃ dassessāmā”ti punappunaṃ bhūmiṃ bhindantā caṅkamanti, sabbaṃ na vaṭṭati, vīriyasampaggahatthaṃ pana samaṇadhammaṃ karontena suddhacittena caṅkamituṃ [M 0.0077] vaṭṭati. “Hatthaṃ khovissāmā”ti pathaviyaṃ ghaṃsanti, na vaṭṭati, aghaṃsantena pana allahatthaṃ pathaviyaṃ ṭhapetvā rajaṃ gahetuṃ vaṭṭati.

74. When they go along causing a post, a stone, or a tree to roll for new construction, having lifted it with poles, the natural earth is broken there. If they cause it to roll with a pure mind, there is no offense. But if they intend to break the earth by that pretext, there is an offense. The same rule applies to those pulling branches and so forth, or splitting wood on the earth. It is not allowable to drive out or to drive in anything whatsoever in the earth, such as bone-needles, thorns, and so forth. Even thinking, 'I will break the earth with the force of my stream of urine,' it is not permissible to urinate with such intent. If the earth breaks while one is doing so, there is an offense. With the intention, 'I will level the uneven ground,' one should not even scrape it with a broom. Indeed, it should be swept only as a matter of duty. Some strike the ground with a walking stick or scratch it with their big toe. Thinking, 'We will mark the walking meditation path,' they walk up and down, repeatedly breaking the ground; all of this is not permissible. However, it is permissible to walk up and down with a pure mind while undertaking the ascetic's practice for the sake of exerting energy. Thinking, 'We will wash our hands,' they rub them on the earth; this is not permissible. However, without rubbing, it is allowable to place a damp hand on the earth to take up dust.

Keci kaṇḍukacchuādīhi ābādhikā chinnataṭādīsu aṅgapaccaṅgāni ghaṃsanti, na vaṭṭati. Jātapathaviṃ dahati vā dahāpeti vā, pācittiyaṃ, antamaso pattampi pacanto yattakesu ṭhānesu aggiṃ deti vā dāpeti vā, tattakāni pācittiyāni, tasmā pattaṃ pacantenapi pubbe pakkaṭṭhāneyeva pacitabbo. Adaḍḍhāya pathaviyā aggiṃ ṭhapetuṃ na vaṭṭati, pattapacanakapālassa pana upari aggiṃ ṭhapetuṃ vaṭṭati. Dārūnaṃ upari ṭhapeti, so aggi tāni dahanto gantvā pathaviṃ dahati, na vaṭṭati. Iṭṭhakakapālādīsupi eseva nayo. Tatrāpi hi iṭṭhakādīnaṃyeva upari ṭhapetuṃ vaṭṭati. Kasmā? Tesaṃ anupādānattā. Na hi tāni aggissa upādānasaṅkhyaṃ gacchanti, sukkhakhāṇusukkharukkhādīsupi aggiṃ dātuṃ na vaṭṭati. Sace pana “pathaviṃ appattameva nibbāpetvā gamissāmī”ti deti, vaṭṭati. Pacchā nibbāpetuṃ na sakkoti, avisayattā anāpatti. Tiṇukkaṃ gahetvā gacchanto hatthe ḍayhamāne bhūmiyaṃ pāteti, anāpatti. Patitaṭṭhāneyeva upādānaṃ datvā aggiṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭati. Daḍḍhapathaviyā ca yattakaṃ ṭhānaṃ usumāya anugataṃ, sabbaṃ vikopetuṃ vaṭṭati.

Some, afflicted with itching sores, scabies, and so forth, rub their limbs on broken riverbanks and the like; this is not permissible. One who burns or causes to be burned earth where things have grown commits a pācittiya offense. Even when firing an alms-bowl, for however many places one sets fire or causes fire to be set, that many pācittiya offenses are incurred. Therefore, even one who is firing an alms-bowl must fire it only in a place previously fired. It is not permissible to place fire on unburnt earth. However, it is permissible to place fire on top of a potsherd for firing a bowl. If one places fire on firewood, and that fire, burning it, spreads and burns the earth, it is not permissible. The same principle applies to bricks, potsherds, and the like. In that case, it is indeed permissible to place fire only on top of the bricks and so forth. Why? Because they are not fuel. Indeed, they are not counted as fuel for the fire. It is also not permissible to set fire to dry stumps, dry trees, and the like. However, if one sets fire thinking, “I will extinguish it before it reaches the earth,” it is permissible. If one is later unable to extinguish it, there is no offense because it is beyond one’s control. If a monk holding a grass torch while walking drops it on the ground when his hand is being burned, there is no offense. It is permissible to make a fire by placing fuel only on the spot where it fell. And on burnt earth, it is permissible to disturb the entire area that has been pervaded by heat.

Yo pana ajānanako bhikkhu araṇisahitena aggiṃ nibbattetvā hatthena ukkhipitvā “kiṃ karomī”ti vadati, “jālehī”ti vattabbo. “Hattho ḍayhatī”ti vadati, “yathā na ḍayhati, tathā karohī”ti vattabbo. “Bhūmiyaṃ pātehī”ti pana na vattabbo. Sace hatthe ḍayhamāne pāteti, “pathaviṃ dahissāmī”ti apātitattā anāpatti, patitaṭṭhāne pana aggiṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭati. “Imassa thambhassa āvāṭaṃ jāna, mahāmattikaṃ jāna, thusamattikaṃ jāna, mahāmattikaṃ dehi, thusamattikaṃ dehi, mattikaṃ āhara, paṃsuṃ āhara, mattikāya attho, paṃsunā attho[V 0.0077], imassa thambhassa āvāṭaṃ kappiyaṃ karohi, imaṃ mattikaṃ kappiyaṃ karohi, imaṃ paṃsuṃ kappiyaṃ karohī”ti evaṃ kappiyavohārena yaṃ kiñci kārāpetuṃ vaṭṭati. Aññavihito kenaci saddhiṃ kiñci kathento pādaṅguṭṭhakena kattarayaṭṭhiyā vā pathaviṃ vilikhanto tiṭṭhati, evaṃ asatiyā vilikhantassa bhindantassa vā anāpatti.

Any monk who, being ignorant of the training rule, having produced fire with a fire-drill, lifts it with his hand and says, "What shall I do?" should be told, "Kindle it." If he says, "My hand is burning," he should be told, "Act in such a way that it does not burn." However, he should not be told, "Drop it on the ground." If, while his hand is burning, he drops it, because it was not dropped with the thought, "I will burn the earth," there is no offense. However, it is allowable to make a fire in the place where it has fallen. It is allowable to have anything whatsoever done using such allowable expressions as: "Know the hole for this post," "Know the large clay," "Know the chaff-mixed clay," "Give the large clay," "Give the chaff-mixed clay," "Bring clay," "Bring dust," "There is a need for clay," "There is a need for dust," "Make the hole for this post allowable," "Make this clay allowable," "Make this dust allowable." If, while speaking about something with someone, one stands scratching the ground with the big toe or a walking stick, being distracted, thus for one who is scratching or breaking the ground through mindlessness, there is no offense.

Iti pāḷimuttakavinayavinicchayasaṅgahe

Thus, in the Compilation of Vinaya Decisions outside the Pāḷi Canon,

Pathavīkhaṇanavinicchayakathā samattā.

The Discourse on the Decision concerning Earth-Digging is concluded.

15. Bhūtagāmavinicchayakathā

15. 15. The Discourse on the Decision concerning Plant Life

75. Bhūtagāmoti [M 0.0078][V 0.0078] pañcahi bījehi jātānaṃ rukkhalatādīnametaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Tatrimāni pañca bījāni – mūlabījaṃ khandhabījaṃ phaḷubījaṃ aggabījaṃ bījabījanti. Tattha mūlabījaṃ nāma haliddi siṅgiveraṃ vacā vacattaṃ ativisaṃ kaṭukarohiṇī usīraṃ bhaddamuttakaṃ, yāni vā panaññānipi atthi mūle jāyanti mūle sañjāyanti, etaṃ mūlabījaṃ nāma. Khandhabījaṃ nāma assattho nigrodho pilakkho udumbaro kacchako kapitthano, yāni vā panaññānipi atthi khandhe jāyanti khandhe sañjāyanti, etaṃ khandhabījaṃ nāma. Phaḷubījaṃ nāma ucchu veḷu naḷo, yāni vā panaññānipi atthi pabbe jāyanti pabbe sañjāyanti, etaṃ phaḷubījaṃ nāma. Aggabījaṃ nāma ajjukaṃ phaṇijjakaṃ hiriveraṃ, yāni vā panaññānipi atthi agge jāyanti agge sañjāyanti, etaṃ aggabījaṃ nāma. Bījabījaṃ nāma pubbaṇṇaṃ aparaṇṇaṃ, yāni vā panaññānipi atthi bīje jāyanti bīje sañjāyanti, etaṃ bījabījaṃ nāma (pāci. 91). Tattha bhūtagāme bhūtagāmasaññī chindati vā chindāpeti vā bhindati vā bhindāpeti vā pacati vā pacāpeti vā, pācittiyaṃ. Bhūtagāmañhi vikopentassa pācittiyaṃ, bhūtagāmaparimocitaṃ pañcavidhampi bījagāmaṃ vikopentassa dukkaṭaṃ.

75. The term 'bhūtagāma' refers to plants born from five kinds of seeds—trees, creepers, and so on. Herein, these are the five kinds of seeds: root-seed, stem-seed, joint-seed, tip-seed, and seed-seed. Among these, root-seed refers to turmeric, ginger, sweet flag, vacattaṃ, ativisaṃ, kaṭukarohiṇī, usīraṃ, bhaddamuttakaṃ, or any other plants that grow or sprout from roots—this is called root-seed. Stem-seed refers to the sacred fig, banyan, pilakkha, udumbara, kacchako, kapitthana, or any other plants that grow or sprout from stems—this is called stem-seed. Joint-seed refers to sugarcane, bamboo, reeds, or any other plants that grow or sprout from joints—this is called joint-seed. Tip-seed refers to ajjuka, phaṇijjaka, hirivera, or any other plants that grow or sprout from tips—this is called tip-seed. Seed-seed refers to grain and pulse, or any other plants that grow or sprout from seeds—this is called seed-seed. Therein, if one who perceives a plant as a plant cuts, causes to cut, breaks, causes to break, cooks, or causes to cook it, it is a pācittiya offense. For one who damages a plant, it is a pācittiya offense. For one who damages any of the five kinds of seed-groups, freed from the plant state, it is a dukkaṭa offense.

76. Bījagāmabhūtagāmo (pāci. aṭṭha. 922) nāmesa atthi udakaṭṭho, atthi thalaṭṭho. Tattha udakaṭṭho sāsapamattikatilabījakādibhedā sapaṇṇikā ca apaṇṇikā ca sabbā sevālajāti, antamaso udakapappaṭakaṃ upādāya “bhūtagāmo”ti veditabbo. Udakapappaṭako nāma upari thaddho pharusavaṇṇo heṭṭhā mudu nīlavaṇṇo hoti. Tattha yassa sevālassa mūlaṃ oruhitvā pathaviyaṃ patiṭṭhitaṃ, tassa pathavī ṭhānaṃ. Yo udake sañcarati, tassa udakaṃ. Pathaviyaṃ patiṭṭhitaṃ yattha katthaci vikopentassa, uddharitvā vā ṭhānantaraṃ saṅkāmentassa pācittiyaṃ, udake sañcarantaṃ vikopentasseva pācittiyaṃ. Hatthehi pana ito cito caviyūhitvā nahāyituṃ vaṭṭati. Sakalañhi udakaṃ tassa ṭhānaṃ, tasmā na so ettāvatā ṭhānantaraṃ saṅkāmito hoti. Udakato pana udakena vinā sañcicca ukkhipituṃ na vaṭṭati, udakena saddhiṃ ukkhipitvā puna udake pakkhipituṃ vaṭṭati. Uppalinipaduminiādīni jalajavallitiṇāni udakato uddharantassa vā tattheva vikopentassa vā pācittiyaṃ, parehi uppāṭitāni vikopentassa dukkaṭaṃ. Tāni hi bījagāme saṅgahaṃ [M 0.0079] gacchanti, tilabījakasāsapamattikasevālopi [V 0.0079] udakato uddhaṭo amilāto aggabījasaṅgahaṃ gacchati. Mahāpaccariyādīsu “anantakatilabījakaudakapappaṭakādīni dukkaṭavatthūnī”ti vuttaṃ, tattha kāraṇaṃ na dissati. Andhakaṭṭhakathāyaṃ “sampuṇṇabhūtagāmaṃ na hoti, tasmā dukkaṭa”nti vuttaṃ, tampi na sameti. Bhūtagāme hi pācittiyaṃ bījagāme dukkaṭaṃ vuttaṃ. Asampuṇṇabhūtagāmo nāma tatiyo koṭṭhāso neva pāḷiyaṃ, na aṭṭhakathāsu āgato, athetaṃ bījagāmasaṅgahaṃ gamissatīti, tampi na yuttaṃ abhūtagāmamūlattā tādisassa bījagāmassāti. Apica “garukalahukesu garuke ṭhātabba”nti etaṃ vinayalakkhaṇaṃ.

76. This is what is called the seed-group and the plant-group: there is that which is established in water, and there is that which is established on land. Among these, the water-established plant-group should be understood as all types of moss—such as the varieties of small moss the size of a mustard seed and small moss with sesame-like seeds, both with leaves and without leaves—up to and including water-moss. Water-moss is firm and rough in appearance on top, and soft and green in color underneath. Among these, for any moss whose root, having descended, is established in the earth, the earth is its place. For that which moves about in the water, the water is its place. For one who destroys in any place whatsoever that which is established in the earth, or who, having uprooted it, moves it to another place, there is a pācittiya offense. For destroying that which moves about in the water, there is a pācittiya offense for the act of destroying alone. However, it is allowable to push it aside from here and there with one's hands in order to bathe. For the entire water is its place; therefore, by just that much, it is not considered to have been moved to another place. But it is not allowable to intentionally lift it from the water without water; it is allowable to lift it up together with water and then put it back into the water. For one who pulls out from the water water-born creepers and grasses such as blue water lilies and lotuses, or destroys them right there in the water, there is a pācittiya offense. For one who destroys those that have been uprooted by others, there is a dukkaṭa offense. For those are included in the seed-group. Also, small moss with sesame-like seeds and moss the size of a mustard seed, when taken out of the water and not yet withered, are included in the category of seeds propagated from cuttings (aggabīja). In the Mahāpaccarī and other commentaries, it is said: 'A kind of grass called anantaka, small moss with sesame-like seeds, water-moss, etc., are occasions for a dukkaṭa offense,' but the reason for this is not apparent. In the Andhakaṭṭhakathā it is said, 'It is not a complete plant-group, therefore it is a dukkaṭa,' but that also does not agree. For in the case of a plant-group, a pācittiya is stated, and in the case of a seed-group, a dukkaṭa is stated. A third category called 'incomplete plant-group' has come neither in the Pāḷi nor in the commentaries. If one were to say, 'Then this will be included in the seed-group,' that also is not correct, because such a seed-group is not the origin of a plant-group. Furthermore, 'Between a grave and a light offense, one should adhere to the graver offense'—this is a characteristic of the Vinaya.

Thalaṭṭhe chinnarukkhānaṃ avasiṭṭho haritakhāṇu nāma hoti, tattha kakudhakarañjapiyaṅgupanasādīnaṃ khāṇu uddhaṃ vaḍḍhati, so bhūtagāmena saṅgahito. Tālanāḷikerādīnaṃ khāṇu uddhaṃ na vaḍḍhati, so bījagāmena saṅgahito. Kadaliyā pana aphalitāya khāṇu bhūtagāmena saṅgahito, phalitāya bījagāmena. Kadalī pana phalitā yāva nīlapaṇṇā, tāva bhūtagāmeneva saṅgahitā, tathā phalito veḷu. Yadā pana aggato paṭṭhāya sussati, tadā bījagāmena saṅgahaṃ gacchati. Katarabījagāmena? Phaḷubījagāmena. Kiṃ tato nibbattati? Na kiñci. Yadi hi nibbatteyya, bhūtagāmena saṅgahaṃ gaccheyya. Indasālādirukkhe chinditvā rāsiṃ karonti, kiñcāpi rāsikatadaṇḍakehi ratanappamāṇāpi sākhā nikkhamanti, bījagāmeneva pana saṅgahaṃ gacchanti. Maṇḍapatthāya vā vatiatthāya vā valliāropanatthāya vā bhūmiyaṃ nikhaṇanti, mūlesu ceva paṇṇesu ca niggatesu puna bhūtagāmasaṅkhyaṃ gacchanti, mūlamattesu pana paṇṇamattesu vā niggatesupi bījagāmena saṅgahitā eva.

On dry land, the remaining stump of a felled tree is called a green stump. There, the stumps of trees like kakudha, karañja, piyaṅgu, and panasa grow upward and are classified under the plant group. The stumps of trees like the palmyra palm and coconut do not grow upward and are classified under the seed group. As for the banana plant, if it is fruitless, its stump is classified under the plant group, but if it has borne fruit, it is classified under the seed group. A banana plant that has borne fruit is considered under the plant group as long as its leaves remain green; similarly with a bamboo that bears fruit. However, when it begins to dry from the top, it then falls under the seed group. Under which seed group? By the joint-seed group. What arises from it? Nothing. For if anything were to arise, it would be classified under the plant group. When trees like indasāla are cut and piled up, even if branches a cubit in length sprout from the stacked logs, they are still classified under the seed group. If they are planted in the ground for the purpose of making a pavilion, a fence, or for supporting vines, and if both roots and leaves emerge, they then return to the plant group classification. But if only roots or only leaves emerge, they remain classified under the seed group.

Yāni kānici bījāni pathaviyaṃ vā udakena siñcitvā ṭhapitāni, kapālādīsu vā allapaṃsuṃ pakkhipitvā nikkhittāni honti, sabbāni mūlamatte vā paṇṇamatte vā niggatepi bījāniyeva. Sacepi mūlāni ca upari aṅkuro ca niggacchati, yāva aṅkuro harito na hoti, tāva bījāniyeva. Muggādīnaṃ pana paṇṇesu uṭṭhitesu, vīhiādīnaṃ vā aṅkure harite nīlavaṇṇe jāte bhūtagāmasaṅgahaṃ gacchanti. Tālaṭṭhīnaṃ paṭhamaṃ sūkaradāṭhā viya mūlaṃ niggacchati, niggatepi yāva upari pattavaṭṭi na niggacchati, tāva bījagāmo nāmayeva. Nāḷikerassa tacaṃ bhinditvā dantasūci viya aṅkuro niggacchati, yāva migasiṅgasadisā [M 0.0080] nīlapattavaṭṭi na hoti, tāva bījagāmoyeva. Mūle aniggatepi tādisāya pattavaṭṭiyā jātāya amūlakabhūtagāme saṅgahaṃ gacchati.

Whatever seeds are placed in the earth and sprinkled with water, or are placed in moist soil in potsherds and the like, all of them, even when only a root or only a leaf has emerged, are just seed-kind. Even if roots and a sprout emerge above, as long as the sprout is not green, they are just seed-kind. However, for mung beans and the like, when the leaves have arisen, or for rice and the like, when the sprout has become green and dark green in color, they are included in the category of vegetation. For palm seeds, first a root emerges like a boar's tusk; even when it has emerged, as long as a leaf-shoot does not emerge above, it is named just seed-kind. For the coconut, a sprout like an ivory point emerges, having broken through the husk; as long as a dark green leaf-shoot similar to a deer's horn has not appeared, it is just seed-kind. Even when the root has not emerged, when such a leaf-shoot has arisen, it is included in the category of rootless vegetation.

Ambaṭṭhiādīni [V 0.0080] vīhiādīhi vinicchinitabbāni. Vandākā vā aññā vā yā kāci rukkhe jāyitvā rukkhaṃ ottharati, rukkhova tassā ṭhānaṃ, taṃ vikopentassa vā tato uddharantassa vā pācittiyaṃ. Ekā amūlikā latā hoti, aṅguliveṭhako viya vanappagumbadaṇḍake veṭheti, tassāpi ayameva vinicchayo. Gehapamukhapākāravedikā cetiyādīsu nīlavaṇṇo sevālo hoti, yāva dve tīṇi pattāni na sañjāyanti, tāva aggabījasaṅgahaṃ gacchati. Pattesu jātesu pācittiyavatthu, tasmā tādisesu ṭhānesu sudhālepampi dātuṃ na vaṭṭati, anupasampannena littassa upari sinehalepo dātuṃ vaṭṭati. Sace nidāghasamaye sukkhasevālo tiṭṭhati, taṃ sammuñjanīādīhi ghaṃsitvā apanetuṃ vaṭṭati. Pānīyaghaṭādīnaṃ bahi sevālo dukkaṭavatthu, anto abbohāriko, dantakaṭṭhapūvādīsu kaṇṇakampi abbohārikameva. Vuttañhetaṃ “sace gerukaparikammakatā bhitti kaṇṇakitā hoti, coḷakaṃ temetvā pīḷetvā pamajjitabbā”ti (mahāva. 66).

Mango seeds and so on should be determined by the standard of paddy and so on. If a parasitic plant (vandākā) or any other vine grows on a tree and covers it, the tree itself is its base. For a monk who damages that tree which is its base, or uproots the plant from it, there is a Pācittiya offense. There is a certain rootless vine that, like a finger-ring, entwines a forest shrub's stalk; for this also, the ruling is the very same. On the fronts of dwellings, on walls, railings, cetiyas, and so on, blue-colored moss grows. As long as two or three leaves have not yet sprouted, it is classified as a shoot-seed. When leaves have sprouted, it is an occasion for a Pācittiya offense. Therefore, in such places, it is not allowable even to apply plaster. It is allowable to apply a smoothing plaster on top of a surface that has been plastered by a non-ordained person. If, in the hot season, dry moss remains, it is allowable to remove it by scrubbing it with a broom or the like. Moss on the outside of a drinking water pot or the like is an occasion for a Dukkaṭa offense; inside, it is not a matter for an offense. On tooth-sticks, cakes, and so on, even fungus is not a matter for an offense. For it has been said: “If a wall prepared with red ochre becomes moldy, a piece of cloth should be moistened, squeezed, and used to wipe it clean” (Mahāvagga 66).

77. Pāsāṇajāti pāsāṇadaddusevālaseleyyakādīni aharitavaṇṇāni apattakāni ca dukkaṭavatthukāni. Ahicchattakaṃ yāva makuṭaṃ hoti, tāva dukkaṭavatthu, pupphitakālato paṭṭhāya abbohārikaṃ, allarukkhato pana ahicchattakaṃ gaṇhanto rukkhatacaṃ vikopeti, tasmā tattha pācittiyaṃ. Rukkhapapaṭikāyapi eseva nayo. Yā pana indasālakakudhādīnaṃ papaṭikā rukkhato muccitvā tiṭṭhati, taṃ gaṇhantassa anāpatti. Niyyāsampi rukkhato muccitvā ṭhitaṃ sukkharukkhe vā laggaṃ gaṇhituṃ vaṭṭati, allarukkhato na vaṭṭati. Lākhāyapi eseva nayo. Rukkhaṃ cāletvā paṇḍupalāsaṃ vā pariṇatakaṇikārādipupphaṃ vā pātentassa pācittiyameva. Hatthakukkuccena mudukesu indasālanuhīkhandhādīsu vā tatthajātakatālapaṇṇādīsu vā akkharaṃ chindantassapi eseva nayo. Sāmaṇerānaṃ pupphaṃ ocinantānaṃ sākhaṃ onāmetvā dātuṃ vaṭṭati. Tehi pana pupphehi pānīyaṃ na vāsetabbaṃ, pānīyavāsatthikena sāmaṇeraṃ ukkhipitvā ocināpetabbāni. Phalasākhāpi attanā [M 0.0081] khāditukāmena na onāmetabbā, sāmaṇeraṃ ukkhipitvā phalaṃ gāhāpetabbaṃ. Kiñci gacchaṃ vālataṃ vā uppāṭentehi sāmaṇerehi saddhiṃ gahetvā ākaḍḍhituṃ na vaṭṭati, tesaṃ pana ussāhajananatthaṃ anākaḍḍhantena kaḍḍhanākāraṃ dassentena viya agge gahetuṃ vaṭṭati. Yesaṃ rukkhānaṃ sākhā ruhati, tesaṃ sākhaṃ makkhikabījanādīnaṃ atthāya kappiyaṃ akārāpetvā gahitaṃ, tace vā patte vā antamaso nakhenapi vilekhantassa dukkaṭaṃ. Allasiṅgiverādīsupi eseva nayo. Sace pana kappiyaṃ kārāpetvā sītale padese ṭhapitassa mūlaṃ sañjāyati, uparibhāge chindituṃ vaṭṭati. Sace aṅkuro jāyati, heṭṭhābhāge chindituṃ vaṭṭati, mūle ca aṅkure ca jāte na vaṭṭati.

77. Stone-born things such as stone fungus, stone lichen, moss, alum, and so forth, which are not of a green color and are without leaves, are objects of a dukkaṭa offense. As long as a mushroom is a bud, it is an object of a dukkaṭa offense; from the time it blossoms, it is not an object of an offense. However, one who takes a mushroom from a living tree damages the tree's bark; therefore, in that case, there is a pācittiya offense. This is also the rule for tree bark. But as for the bark of Indasāla, Kudha, and other such trees that has been released from the tree and remains so, for one who takes it, there is no offense. It is also allowable to take resin that has been released from a tree and remains so, or that is stuck to a dry tree; but from a living tree, it is not allowable. This is also the rule for lac. For one who shakes a tree and causes a withered leaf or a mature Kaṇikāra flower and so on to fall, there is a pācittiya offense indeed. Due to mischievousness of hand, for one who carves a letter on soft things like the stems of Indasāla or Snuhī, or on palm leaves and so on growing there, this is also the rule. It is allowable to bend down a branch and give it to novices who are picking flowers. But with those flowers, drinking water should not be scented. By a monk who wishes to scent drinking water, a novice should be lifted up and the flowers should be caused to be picked. A fruit-bearing branch should also not be bent down by one who wishes to eat from it himself; a novice should be lifted up and the fruit should be caused to be taken. It is not allowable to hold and pull any shrub or creeper together with novices who are uprooting it. But for the purpose of encouraging them, it is allowable to hold it at the tip as if showing the manner of pulling, while not actually pulling. Regarding those trees whose branches can propagate, if a branch is taken for the purpose of a fly-whisk and so on without having it made allowable, for one who scratches its bark or a leaf, even with just a fingernail, there is a dukkaṭa offense. This is also the rule for fresh ginger and so on. But if, for something that has been made allowable and placed in a cool place, a root grows, it is allowable to cut the upper part. If a sprout grows, it is allowable to cut the lower part. When both a root and a sprout have grown, it is not allowable.

“Sammuñjanīsalākāyapi [V 0.0081] tiṇāni chindissāmī”ti bhūmiyaṃ sammajjanto sayaṃ vā chindati, aññena vā chedāpeti, na vaṭṭati. Caṅkamantopi “chijjanakaṃ chijjatu, bhijjanakaṃ bhijjatu, caṅkamitaṭṭhānaṃ dassessāmī”ti sañcicca pādehi akkamanto tiṇavalliādīni sayaṃ vā chindati, aññena vā chedāpeti, na vaṭṭati. Sacepi hi tiṇaṃ vā lataṃ vā ganthiṃ karontassa bhijjati, ganthimpi kātuṃ na vaṭṭati. Tālarukkhādīsu pana corānaṃ anāruhaṇatthāya dārumakkaṭakaṃ ākoṭenti, kaṇṭake bandhanti, bhikkhussa evaṃ kātuṃ na vaṭṭati. Sace dārumakkaṭako rukkhe allīnamattova hoti, rukkhaṃ na pīḷeti, vaṭṭati. “Rukkhaṃ chinda, lataṃ chinda, kandaṃ vā mūlaṃ vā uppāṭehī”ti vattuṃ vaṭṭati aniyamitattā. Niyametvā pana “imaṃ rukkhaṃ chindā”tiādi vattuṃ na vaṭṭati. Nāmaṃ gahetvāpi “ambarukkhaṃ caturaṃsavalliṃ āluvakandaṃ muñjatiṇaṃ asukarukkhacchalliṃ chinda bhinda uppāṭehī”tiādivacanampi aniyamitameva hoti. “Imaṃ ambarukkha”ntiādivacanameva hi niyamitaṃ nāma, taṃ na vaṭṭati. Pattampi pacitukāmo tiṇādīnaṃ upari sañcicca aggiṃ karonto sayaṃ vā pacati, aññena vā pacāpeti, na vaṭṭati. Aniyametvā pana “mugge paca, māse pacā”tiādi vattuṃ vaṭṭati, “ime mugge pacā”ti evaṃ vattuṃ na vaṭṭati. “Imaṃ mūlabhesajjaṃ jāna, imaṃ mūlaṃ vā paṇṇaṃ vā dehi, imaṃ rukkhaṃ vā lataṃ vā āhara, iminā pupphena phalena vā attho, imaṃ rukkhaṃ vā lataṃ vā phalaṃ vā kappiyaṃ karohī”ti evaṃ pana vattuṃ vaṭṭati. Ettāvatā bhūtagāmaparimocitaṃ kataṃ hoti.

If one, thinking, 'I will cut the grass even with a broom,' while sweeping the ground, either cuts it oneself or has another cut it, it is not allowable. Also, while walking on a path, if one intentionally steps with the thought, 'Let what is fit to be cut be cut, let what is fit to be broken be broken, I will make the walking place clear,' and either cuts grass, vines, and the like oneself or has another cut them, it is not allowable. Indeed, if grass or a vine would break while one is tying a knot with it, it is not allowable even to tie the knot. However, on palm trees and the like, people may hammer in wooden devices or tie thorns to prevent thieves from climbing; for a bhikkhu to do so is not allowable. If a wooden device is merely leaning against a tree without harming it, it is allowable. To say, 'Cut a tree, cut a vine, uproot a bulb or a root,' is allowable because it is not specified. But to specify by saying, 'Cut this tree,' or similar, is not allowable. Even if one uses a name, saying, 'Cut a mango tree, a four-angled vine, an āluva bulb, muñja grass, the bark of such-and-such a tree; break it; uproot it,' such speech is still considered unspecified. Only speech such as, 'This mango tree,' is considered specified, and that is not allowable. If one who wishes to cook a leaf intentionally makes a fire on top of grass and the like, and either cooks it oneself or has another cook it, it is not allowable. But without specifying, it is allowable to say, 'Cook mung beans, cook black gram beans,' and so on. To say, 'Cook these mung beans,' is not allowable. However, it is allowable to say, 'Know this root-medicine,' 'Give this root or leaf,' 'Bring this tree or vine,' 'There is a need for this flower or fruit,' or 'Make this tree, vine, or fruit allowable.' By this much, it is made to be freed from the category of living vegetation.

78. Paribhuñjantena [M 0.0082] pana bījagāmaparimocanatthaṃ puna kappiyaṃ kārāpetabbaṃ. Kappiyakaraṇañcettha iminā suttānusārena veditabbaṃ –

78. However, by one who is consuming, it should be made allowable again for the purpose of freeing it from the category of seed-life. And the making allowable in this matter should be understood according to this discourse:

“Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, pañcahi samaṇakappehi phalaṃ paribhuñjituṃ aggiparijitaṃ satthaparijitaṃ nakhaparijitaṃ abījaṃ nibbaṭṭabījaññeva pañcama”nti (cūḷava. 250).

I allow, O monks, to consume fruit by five methods of making it allowable for ascetics: that which is made allowable by fire, that which is made allowable by a knife, that which is made allowable by a nail, that which has immature seeds, and fifthly, that from which the seed has been removed.

Tattha aggiparijitanti agginā parijitaṃ adhibhūtaṃ daḍḍhaṃ phuṭṭhanti attho. Satthaparijitanti satthena parijitaṃ adhibhūtaṃ chinnaṃ viddhaṃ vāti attho. Esa nayo nakhaparijite. Abījanibbaṭṭabījāni sayameva kappiyāni. Agginā kappiyaṃ karontena kaṭṭhaggigomayaggiādīsu yena kenaci antamaso lohakhaṇḍenapi ādittena kappiyaṃ kātabbaṃ, tañca kho ekadese phusantena “kappiya”nti vatvāva kātabbaṃ. Satthena karontena yassa kassaci lohamayasatthassa antamaso sūcinakhacchedanānampi tuṇḍena vā dhārāya vā chedaṃ vā vedhaṃ [V 0.0082] vā dassentena “kappiya”nti vatvāva kātabbaṃ. Nakhena kappiyaṃ karontena pūtinakhena na kātabbaṃ, manussānaṃ pana sīhabyagghadīpimakkaṭānaṃ sakuntānañca nakhā tikhiṇā honti, tehi kātabbaṃ. Assamahiṃsasūkaramigagorūpādīnaṃ khurā atikhiṇā, tehi na kātabbaṃ, katampi akataṃ hoti. Hatthinakhā pana khurā na honti, tehi ca vaṭṭati. Yehi pana kātuṃ vaṭṭati, tehi tatthajātakehipi uddharitvā gahitakepi chedaṃ vā vedhaṃ vā dassentena “kappiya”nti vatvāva kātabbaṃ.

Herein, 'made allowable by fire' means made allowable, overcome, scorched, or touched by fire. 'Made allowable by a knife' means made allowable, overcome, cut, or pierced by it. This same method applies to 'made allowable by a nail'. Fruits with immature seeds and those with seeds removed are allowable in themselves. When making something allowable by fire, it should be done with any kind of fire—such as a wood fire or a cow-dung fire—or at the very least, even with a heated piece of iron; and this should be done only by touching a part of it and saying, 'It is allowable.' When making it allowable with a knife, it should be done with any kind of iron knife, or at the very least, with the point or edge of a needle or nail-cutter, by showing a cut or a piercing and saying, 'It is allowable.' When making something allowable with a nail, it should not be done with a rotten nail. The nails of humans, lions, tigers, leopards, monkeys, and birds, however, are sharp; it should be done with these. The hooves of horses, buffaloes, pigs, deer, cattle, and so on are not sharp; it should not be done with these. Even if done, it is as if not done. Elephants' nails, however, are not hooves, and it is permissible with them. With whichever nails it is permissible to do it, with those—whether still attached or cut off and taken—it should be done by showing a cut or a piercing and saying, 'It is allowable.'

Tattha sacepi bījānaṃ pabbatamatto rāsi, rukkhasahassaṃ vā chinditvā ekābaddhaṃ katvā ucchūnaṃ vā mahābhāro bandhitvā ṭhapito hoti, ekasmiṃ bīje vā rukkhasākhāya vā ucchumhi vā kappiye kate sabbaṃ kataṃ hoti. Ucchū ca dārūni ca ekato baddhāni honti, “ucchuṃ kappiyaṃ karissāmī”ti dāruṃ vijjhati, vaṭṭatiyeva. Sace pana yāya rajjuyā vā valliyā vā baddhāni, taṃ vijjhati, na vaṭṭati. Ucchukhaṇḍānaṃ pacchiṃ pūretvā āharanti, ekasmiṃ khaṇḍe kappiye kate sabbaṃ katameva. Marīcapakkādīhi ca missetvā bhattaṃ āharanti, “kappiyaṃ karohī”ti vutte sacepi bhattasitthe vijjhati, vaṭṭatiyeva. Tilataṇḍulādīsupi eseva nayo. Yāguyā pakkhittāni pana ekābaddhāni [M 0.0083] hutvā na santiṭṭhanti, tattha ekamekaṃ vijjhitvā kappiyaṃ kātabbameva. Kapitthaphalādīnaṃ anto miñjaṃ kaṭāhaṃ muñcitvā sañcarati, bhindāpetvā kappiyaṃ kārāpetabbaṃ, ekābaddhaṃ hoti, kaṭāhepi kātuṃ vaṭṭati.

In that context, even if there is a heap of seeds the size of a mountain, or a thousand trees are cut down and made into one bundle, or a great load of sugarcane is tied up and placed aside, if what is allowable is done to one seed, or to one of the trees, or to one stalk of sugarcane, all of it is considered to have been made allowable. If sugarcane and firewood are bound together, and one, intending 'I will make the sugarcane allowable,' pierces the firewood, it is indeed permissible. But if one pierces the rope or vine by which they are bound, it is not permissible. If they bring sugarcane pieces filling a basket, when what is allowable is done to one piece, all of it is indeed considered to have been made allowable. If they bring food mixed with ripe peppers and so on, and when told, 'Make it allowable,' even if one pierces a lump of cooked rice, it is indeed permissible. This same method applies to sesame mixed with rice and so on. However, as for things put into porridge, they do not remain well-established as a single mass; in that case, each one must be pierced individually to make it allowable. In the case of fruits like the wood-apple and so on, if the kernel inside moves about, having detached from the shell, one should have it broken open and have what is allowable made. If it is attached as one piece to the shell, it is permissible to make it allowable on the shell as well.

Iti pāḷimuttakavinayavinicchayasaṅgahe

Thus, in the Compilation of Vinaya Decisions Independent of the Pāḷi Canon,

Bhūtagāmavinicchayakathā samattā.

The discourse on the determination of plant life is concluded.

16. Sahaseyyavinicchayakathā

16. The Discourse on the Determination of Lying Down Together

79. Duvidhaṃ [V 0.0083] sahaseyyakanti “yo pana bhikkhu anupasampannena uttaridirattatirattaṃ sahaseyyaṃ kappeyya, pācittiyaṃ (pāci. 49). Yo pana bhikkhu mātugāmena sahaseyyaṃ kappeyya, pācittiya”nti (pāci. 56) evaṃ vuttaṃ sahaseyyasikkhāpadadvayaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Tatrāyaṃ vinicchayo (pāci. aṭṭha. 50-51) – anupasampannena saddhiṃ tiṇṇaṃ rattīnaṃ upari catutthadivase atthaṅgate sūriye sabbacchannasabbaparicchanne yebhuyyacchannayebhuyyaparicchanne vā senāsane pubbāpariyena vā ekakkhaṇe vā nipajjantassa pācittiyaṃ. Tattha chadanaṃ anāhacca diyaḍḍhahatthubbedhena pākārādinā yena kenaci paricchannampi sabbaparicchannamicceva veditabbaṃ. Yaṃ senāsanaṃ upari pañcahi chadanehi aññena vā kenaci sabbameva paricchannaṃ, idaṃ sabbacchannaṃ nāma senāsanaṃ. Aṭṭhakathāsu pana pākaṭavohāraṃ gahetvā vācuggatavasena “sabbacchannaṃ nāma pañcahi chadanehi channa”nti vuttaṃ. Kiñcāpi vuttaṃ, atha kho dussakuṭiyaṃ sayantassapi na sakkā anāpatti kātuṃ, tasmā yaṃ kiñci paṭicchādanasamatthaṃ idha chadanañca paricchannañca veditabbaṃ. Pañcavidhacchadaneyeva hi gayhamāne padaracchannepi sahaseyyā na bhaveyya, tasmā yaṃ senāsanaṃ bhūmito paṭṭhāya yāvachadanaṃ āhacca pākārena vā aññena vā kenaci antamaso vatthenapi parikkhittaṃ, idaṃ sabbaparicchannaṃ nāma senāsanaṃ. Chadanaṃ anāhacca sabbantimena pariyāyena diyaḍḍhahatthubbedhena pākārādinā parikkhittampi sabbaparicchannameva. Yassa pana upari bahutaraṃ ṭhānaṃ channaṃ, appaṃ acchannaṃ, samantato vā bahutaraṃ parikkhittaṃ, appaṃ aparikkhittaṃ, idaṃ yebhuyyenachannaṃ yebhuyyenaparicchannaṃ nāma.

79. The meaning of the phrase 'co-habitation is of two kinds' should be understood thus: it was said with reference to the pair of training rules on co-habitation spoken as follows: “Whatever bhikkhu should arrange to lie down together with an unordained person for more than two or three nights, there is a pācittiya offense. Furthermore, whatever bhikkhu should arrange to lie down together with a woman, there is a pācittiya offense.” Herein, this is the legal decision to be understood: For a bhikkhu who lies down with an unordained person beyond three nights, on the fourth day after the sun has set, in a lodging that is completely roofed and completely enclosed, or mostly roofed and mostly enclosed, whether before or after the other, or at the same moment, there is a pācittiya offense. Therein, even a lodging enclosed by a wall or the like, or by anything whatsoever, with a height of one and a half cubits that does not reach the roof, should be understood as 'completely enclosed'. A lodging that is completely covered above by the five kinds of roofing or by anything else whatsoever is called a 'completely roofed' lodging. However, in the Commentaries, taking the common expression, it is said by way of a recited phrase: “'Completely roofed' means roofed by the five kinds of roofing.” Although it is so said, nevertheless, it is not possible to make it a non-offense even for one sleeping in a cloth tent. Therefore, here, whatever is capable of covering should be understood as both a roof and an enclosure. For if only the five kinds of roofing were to be taken, the offense of co-habitation would not occur even in a lodging roofed with planks. Therefore, a lodging that is enclosed from the ground up to the roof by a wall, or by anything else, even by a cloth, is called a 'completely enclosed' lodging. Even a lodging enclosed by a wall or the like with a height of one and a half cubits, which does not reach the roof—this being the minimum requirement—is indeed 'completely enclosed'. But a lodging of which the greater part above is roofed and a small part is unroofed, or of which the greater part all around is enclosed and a small part is unenclosed, is called 'mostly roofed' and 'mostly enclosed'.

Iminā [M 0.0084] lakkhaṇena samannāgato sacepi sattabhūmiko pāsādo ekūpacāro hoti, satagabbhaṃ vā catusālaṃ, ekaṃ senāsanamicceva saṅkhaṃ gacchati. Evarūpe senāsane anupasampannena saddhiṃ catutthadivase atthaṅgate sūriye nipajjantassa pācittiyaṃ vuttaṃ. Sace pana sambahulā sāmaṇerā, eko bhikkhu, sāmaṇeragaṇanāya pācittiyā. Te ce uṭṭhāyuṭṭhāya nipajjanti, tesaṃ payoge payoge bhikkhussa āpatti, bhikkhussa uṭṭhāyuṭṭhāya nipajjane pana bhikkhusseva payogena bhikkhussa āpatti. Sace sambahulā bhikkhū, eko sāmaṇero, ekopi sabbesaṃ āpattiṃ karoti. Tassa uṭṭhāyuṭṭhāya nipajjanenapi bhikkhūnaṃ āpattiyeva. Ubhayesaṃ sambahulabhāvepi eseva nayo.

A lodging endowed with this characteristic—even if it is a seven-storied mansion with a single surrounding area, or a hundred-chambered building with four halls—is counted as a single lodging. In such a lodging, for one who lies down together with an unordained person on the fourth day after the sun has set, a Pācittiya offense is stated. However, if there are many novices and one bhikkhu, there are Pācittiya offenses according to the number of novices. If those novices get up and lie down again and again, for each of their actions, an offense occurs for the bhikkhu. But in the case of the bhikkhu getting up and lying down again and again, an offense occurs for the bhikkhu by the bhikkhu's own action. If there are many bhikkhus and one novice, even that one novice causes an offense for all the bhikkhus. Also by that novice getting up and lying down again and again, an offense indeed occurs for the bhikkhus. Even when both parties are numerous, this is the same method.

80. Apicettha [V 0.0084] ekāvāsādikampi catukkaṃ veditabbaṃ. Yo hi ekasmiṃ āvāse ekeneva anupasampannena saddhiṃ tirattaṃ sahaseyyaṃ kappeti, tassa catutthadivasato paṭṭhāya devasikā āpatti. Yopi ekasmiṃyeva āvāse nānāanupasampannehi saddhiṃ tirattaṃ sahaseyyaṃ kappeti, tassapi. Yopi nānāāvāsesu ekeneva anupasampannena saddhiṃ tirattaṃ sahaseyyaṃ kappeti, tassapi. Yopi nānāāvāsesu nānāanupasampannehi saddhiṃ yojanasatampi gantvā sahaseyyaṃ kappeti, tassapi catutthadivasato paṭṭhāya devasikā āpatti.

80. Moreover, in this training rule, the tetrad beginning with 'a single residence' should also be understood. For whatever bhikkhu arranges to lie down together for three nights with only one unordained person in a single residence, for him a daily offense occurs, starting from the fourth day. The same applies to one who arranges to lie down together for three nights with various unordained persons in that same single residence. The same applies to one who arranges to lie down together for three nights with only one unordained person in various residences. And for one who, having gone even a hundred yojanas, arranges to lie down together in various residences with various unordained persons, for him also a daily offense occurs, starting from the fourth day.

Ayañca sahaseyyāpatti nāma “bhikkhuṃ ṭhapetvā avaseso anupasampanno nāmā”ti vacanato antamaso pārājikavatthubhūtena tiracchānagatenapi saddhiṃ hoti, tasmā sacepi godhābiḷālamaṅgusādīsu koci pavisitvā bhikkhuno vasanasenāsane ekūpacāraṭṭhāne sayati, sahaseyyāva hoti. Yadi pana thambhānaṃ upari katapāsādassa uparimatalena saddhiṃ asambaddhabhittikassa bhittiyā upariṭhitasusiratulāsīsassa susirena pavisitvā tulāya abbhantare sayitvā teneva susirena nikkhamitvā gacchati, heṭṭhāpāsāde sayitabhikkhussa anāpatti.
