Sace chadane chiddaṃ hoti, tena pavisitvā antochadane vasitvā teneva pakkamati, nānūpacāre uparimatale chadanabbhantare sayitassa āpatti, heṭṭhimatale sayitassa anāpatti. Sace antopāsādeneva ārohitvā sabbatalāni paribhuñjanti, ekūpacārāni honti, tesu yattha katthaci [M 0.0085] sayitassa āpatti, sabhāsaṅkhepena kate aḍḍhakuṭṭake senāsane sayitassa tulāvāḷasaghāṭādīsu kapotādayo sayanti, āpattiyeva. Parikkhepassa bahigate nibbakosabbhantare sayanti, anāpatti. Parimaṇḍalaṃ vā caturassaṃ vā ekacchadanāya gabbhamālāya satagabbhaṃ cepi senāsanaṃ hoti, tatra ce ekena sādhāraṇadvārena pavisitvā visuṃ pākārena aparicchinnagabbhūpacāre sabbagabbhepi pavisanti, ekagabbhepi anupasampanne nipanne sabbagabbhesu nipannānaṃ āpatti. Sace sapamukhā gabbhā honti, pamukhañca upari acchannaṃ, pamukhe sayito gabbhe sayitānaṃ āpattiṃ na karoti. Sace pana gabbhacchadaneneva saddhiṃ sambandhachadanaṃ, tatra sayito sabbesaṃ āpattiṃ karoti. Kasmā? Sabbacchannattā ca sabbaparicchannattā ca. Gabbhaparikkhepoyeva hissa parikkhepo.

This offense of lying down together is so called because, according to the statement, 'Leaving aside a bhikkhu, the remainder is called unordained,' it occurs at the very least even with an animal that is the basis for a pārājika offense. Therefore, if any creature such as an iguana, cat, or mongoose enters and lies down in a bhikkhu's dwelling within a single perimeter, it is indeed an offense of lying down together. However, if, in a mansion built on pillars whose walls are not connected with the upper floor, an animal enters through the hollow of a beam-end placed upon a wall, sleeps inside the beam, and departs through that same hollow, there is no offense for the bhikkhu sleeping in the lower mansion. If there is a hole in the roof, and an animal enters through it, stays inside the roof space, and then departs the same way, for one sleeping on the upper floor, which has a separate perimeter, there is an offense; for one sleeping on the lower floor, there is no offense. If they ascend from within the mansion and use all the floors, these are considered to have a single perimeter; for one sleeping anywhere among them, there is an offense. If, for a bhikkhu sleeping in a half-walled dwelling made in the manner of an assembly hall, pigeons and other such creatures enter and sleep on the beams, rafters, and so on, it is indeed an offense. If they sleep outside the enclosure, within an unroofed space, there is no offense. If a dwelling, whether circular or square, is a row of cells under a single roof, even if it has a hundred cells, and if they enter through a single common door into cells whose perimeters are not divided by separate walls, and they can enter all the cells, then if an unordained person lies down in even one cell, it is an offense for those lying in all the cells. If the cells have porches, and a porch is unroofed above, one sleeping on the porch does not cause an offense for those sleeping in the cell. But if the porch has a roof connected with the roof of the cell, one sleeping there causes an offense for all. Why? Because of being completely covered and completely enclosed. Indeed, the enclosure of the cell is the enclosure of the porch.

81. Yepi ekasāladvisālatisālacatusālasannivesā mahāpāsādā ekasmiṃ okāse pāde dhovitvā paviṭṭhena sakkā honti sabbattha anuparigantuṃ, tesupi sahaseyyāpattiyā na muccati. Sace tasmiṃ tasmiṃ ṭhāne upacāraṃ paricchinditvā katā honti, ekūpacāraṭṭhāneyeva āpatti. Dvīhi dvārehi yuttassa sudhāchadanamaṇḍapassa majjhe pākāraṃ karonti, ekena dvārena pavisitvā [V 0.0085] ekasmiṃ paricchede anupasampanno sayati, ekasmiṃ bhikkhu, anāpatti. Pākāre godhādīnaṃ pavisanamattaṃ chiddaṃ hoti, ekasmiñca paricchede godhā sayanti, anāpattiyeva. Na hi chiddena gehaṃ ekūpacāraṃ nāma hoti. Sace pākāramajjhe chinditvā dvāraṃ yojenti, ekūpacāratāya āpatti. Taṃ dvāraṃ kavāṭena pidahitvā sayanti, āpattiyeva. Na hi dvārapidahanena gehaṃ nānūpacāraṃ nāma hoti, dvāraṃ vā advāraṃ. Kavāṭañhi saṃvaraṇavivaraṇehi yathāsukhaṃ vaḷañjanatthāya kataṃ, na vaḷañjupacchedanatthāya. Sace taṃ dvāraṃ puna iṭṭhakāhi pidahanti, advāraṃ hoti, purime nānūpacārabhāveyeva tiṭṭhati. Dīghapamukhaṃ cetiyagharaṃ hoti, ekaṃ kavāṭaṃ anto, ekaṃ bahi, dvinnaṃ kavāṭānaṃ antare anupasampanno antocetiyaghare sayantassa āpattiṃ karoti ekūpacārattā.

81. Even in great mansions with one, two, three, or four halls, where one can wash their feet in one spot and, having entered, can move around everywhere—even in those, one is not released from the offense of lying down together. If in each of those places, perimeters have been demarcated, the offense occurs only in the place of a single perimeter. In a pavilion with a plastered roof and two doors, if a wall is built in the middle, and one enters through one door and an unordained person sleeps in one section while a bhikkhu sleeps in the other, there is no offense. If there is a hole in the wall just large enough for an iguana or other such creature to enter, and in one section iguanas lie down, there is no offense indeed. For a dwelling is not, on account of a hole, called one of a single perimeter. If a door is installed by cutting through the middle of the wall, there is an offense on account of it being of a single perimeter. If they sleep with that door closed by a door-leaf, there is an offense indeed. For by the mere closing of a door, a dwelling is not called one of separate perimeters, nor does a door become a non-door. For a door-leaf is made for the purpose of convenient use by closing and opening, not for the purpose of cutting off use. If they again block that door with bricks, it becomes a non-door, and it remains in its former state of having separate perimeters. In a shrine-house with a long entrance hall, where one door is inside and one is outside, if an unordained person sleeps in the space between the two doors, it causes an offense for one sleeping inside the shrine-house, on account of it being of a single perimeter.

Ayañhettha saṅkhepo – senāsanaṃ khuddakaṃ vā hotu mahantaṃ vā, aññena saddhiṃ sambandhaṃ vā asambandhaṃ vā, dīghaṃ vā vaṭṭaṃ vā caturassaṃ vā, ekabhūmikaṃ [M 0.0086] vā anekabhūmikaṃ vā, yaṃ yaṃ ekūpacāraṃ, sabbattha sahaseyyāpatti hotīti. Ettha ca yena kenaci paṭicchadanena sabbacchanne sabbaparicchanne pācittiyaṃ, yebhuyyenachanne yebhuyyenaparicchanne pācittiyaṃ, sabbacchanne yebhuyyenaparicchanne pācittiyaṃ, sabbacchanne upaḍḍhaparicchanne pācittiyaṃ, yebhuyyenachanne upaḍḍhaparicchanne pācittiyaṃ, sabbaparicchanne yebhuyyenachanne pācittiyaṃ, sabbaparicchanne upaḍḍhacchanne pācittiyaṃ, yebhuyyenaparicchanne upaḍḍhacchanne pācittiyanti aṭṭha pācittiyāni. Upaḍḍhacchanne upaḍḍhaparicchanne dukkaṭaṃ, sabbacchanne cūḷakaparicchanne dukkaṭaṃ, yebhuyyenachanne cūḷakaparicchanne dukkaṭaṃ, sabbaparicchanne cūḷakacchanne dukkaṭaṃ, yebhuyyenaparicchanne cūḷakacchanne dukkaṭanti pañca dukkaṭāni veditabbāni. Sabbacchanne sabbaaparicchanne, sabbaparicchanne sabbaacchanne, yebhuyyenaacchanne yebhuyyenaaparicchanne, upaḍḍhacchanne cūḷakaparicchanne, upaḍḍhaparicchanne cūḷakacchanne cūḷakaparicchanne ca anāpatti. Mātugāmena saha nipajjantassapi ayameva vinicchayo. Ayañhettha viseso – anupasampannena saddhiṃ nipajjantassa catutthadivase āpatti, mātugāmena saddhiṃ paṭhamadivaseti. Yakkhipetīhi pana dissamānakarūpāhi tiracchānagatitthiyā ca methunadhammavatthubhūtāya eva dukkaṭaṃ, sesāhi anāpatti.

Indeed, this is the summary herein: whether a lodging be small or large, whether connected with another or unconnected, whether long, round, or square, whether single-storied or multi-storied—whatever lodging has a common surrounding area, in all such cases the offense of lying down together occurs. And herein, in a lodging that is completely roofed and completely enclosed by any kind of covering, there is a Pācittiya offense. In one that is mostly roofed and mostly enclosed, there is a Pācittiya offense. In one that is completely roofed and mostly enclosed, there is a Pācittiya offense. In one that is completely roofed and half-enclosed, there is a Pācittiya offense. In one that is mostly roofed and half-enclosed, there is a Pācittiya offense. In one that is completely enclosed and mostly roofed, there is a Pācittiya offense. In one that is completely enclosed and half-roofed, there is a Pācittiya offense. In one that is mostly enclosed and half-roofed, there is a Pācittiya offense. Thus, eight Pācittiya offenses should be known. In a lodging that is half-roofed and half-enclosed, there is a Dukkaṭa offense. In one that is completely roofed and minimally enclosed, there is a Dukkaṭa offense. In one that is mostly roofed and minimally enclosed, there is a Dukkaṭa offense. In one that is completely enclosed and minimally roofed, there is a Dukkaṭa offense. In one that is mostly enclosed and minimally roofed, there is a Dukkaṭa offense. Thus, five Dukkaṭa offenses should be known. There is no offense in a lodging that is completely roofed but completely unenclosed; completely enclosed but completely unroofed; mostly unroofed and mostly unenclosed; half-roofed and minimally enclosed; half-enclosed and minimally roofed; and minimally enclosed. For one lying down together with a woman, this is the very same ruling. Herein, this is the distinction: for one lying down with an unordained person, the offense occurs on the fourth day; with a woman, it occurs on the first day. However, with female yakkhas and petīs of visible form, and with a female animal, there is a Dukkaṭa offense only if she is a potential object for the act of sexual intercourse; with the others, there is no offense.

Iti pāḷimuttakavinayavinicchayasaṅgahe

Thus in the Compendium of Vinaya Determinations External to the Canon:

Sahaseyyavinicchayakathā samattā.

The Discourse on the Ruling of Lying Down Together is concluded.

17. Mañcapīṭhādisaṅghikasenāsanesu paṭipajjitabbavinicchayakathā

17. The Discourse on the Ruling Concerning Conduct in Communal Lodgings with Beds, Chairs, and so forth

82. Vihāre [V 0.0086] saṅghike seyyaṃ, santharitvāna pakkamoti saṅghike vihāre seyyaṃ santharitvāna aññattha vasitukāmatāya vihārato pakkamanaṃ. Tatrāyaṃ vinicchayo –

82. Regarding the summary passage, “Having spread bedding in a communal dwelling, one departs,” the meaning is: departing from the dwelling with the desire to live elsewhere, after having spread bedding in a communal dwelling. Therein, this is the ruling:

“Yo pana bhikkhu saṅghike vihāre seyyaṃ santharitvā vā santharāpetvā vā taṃ pakkamanto neva uddhareyya na uddharāpeyya anāpucchaṃ vā gaccheyya, pācittiya”nti (pāci. 115) –

“Whatever bhikkhu, having spread out bedding himself or having had it spread out in a communal dwelling, then departing, should neither put it away himself nor have it put away, or should go without asking leave, there is a pācittiya offense.”

Vacanato [M 0.0087] saṅghike vihāre seyyaṃ sayaṃ santharitvā aññena vā santharāpetvā uddharaṇādīni akatvā parikkhittassa ārāmassa parikkhepaṃ, aparikkhittassa upacāraṃ atikkamantassa pācittiyaṃ.

According to that statement, for a bhikkhu who, in a communal dwelling, having spread bedding himself or having had it spread by another, crosses the enclosure of an enclosed monastery or the vicinity of an unenclosed one without performing the acts of putting it away and so forth, there is a pācittiya offense.

Tattha seyyā nāma bhisi cimilikā uttarattharaṇaṃ bhūmattharaṇaṃ taṭṭikā cammakhaṇḍo nisīdanaṃ paccattharaṇaṃ tiṇasanthāro paṇṇasanthāroti dasavidhā. Tattha bhisīti mañcakabhisi vā pīṭhakabhisi vā. Cimilikā nāma sudhādiparikammakatāya bhūmiyā vaṇṇānurakkhaṇatthaṃ katā, taṃ heṭṭhā pattharitvā upari kaṭasārakaṃ pattharanti. Uttarattharaṇaṃ nāma mañcapīṭhānaṃ upari attharitabbakapaccattharaṇaṃ. Bhūmattharaṇaṃ nāma bhūmiyaṃ attharitabbā kaṭasārakādivikati. Taṭṭikā nāma tālapaṇṇehi vā vākehi vā katataṭṭikā. Cammakhaṇḍo nāma sīhabyagghadīpitaracchacammādīsupi yaṃ kiñci cammaṃ. Aṭṭhakathāsu hi senāsanaparibhoge paṭikkhittacammaṃ na dissati, tasmā sīhabyagghacammādīnaṃ pariharaṇeyeva paṭikkhepo veditabbo. Nisīdananti sadasaṃ veditabbaṃ. Paccattharaṇanti pāvāro kojavoti ettakameva vuttaṃ. Tiṇasanthāroti yesaṃ kesañci tiṇānaṃ santhāro. Esa nayo paṇṇasanthārepi. Evaṃ pana imaṃ dasavidhaṃ seyyaṃ saṅghike vihāre santharitvā vā santharāpetvā vā pakkamantena āpucchitvā pakkamitabbaṃ, āpucchantena ca bhikkhumhi sati bhikkhu āpucchitabbo, tasmiṃ asati sāmaṇero, tasmiṃ asati ārāmiko, tasmiṃ asati yena vihāro kārito, so vihārasāmiko, tassa vā kule yo koci āpucchitabbo, tasmimpi asati catūsu pāsāṇesu mañcaṃ ṭhapetvā mañce avasesamañcapīṭhāni [V 0.0087] āropetvā upari bhisiādikaṃ dasavidhampi seyyaṃ rāsiṃ katvā dārubhaṇḍaṃ mattikābhaṇḍaṃ paṭisāmetvā dvāravātapānāni pidahitvā gamiyavattaṃ pūretvā gantabbaṃ.

Herein, bedding is of ten kinds: a mattress, a coarse cloth floor-covering, an upper cover, a ground cover, a plaited mat, a piece of hide, a sitting mat, a bed-covering, a grass covering, and a leaf covering. Among these, a “mattress” refers to either a bed mattress or a seat mattress. A “coarse cloth floor-covering” is made to preserve the color of a floor finished with plaster, etc.; it is spread underneath, and a woven mat is spread over it. An “upper cover” refers to a spread that should be laid over a bed or a seat. A “ground cover” refers to a decorated covering such as a reed mat, to be spread on the ground. A `taṭṭikā` is a mat made of palm leaves or bark fibers. A “piece of hide” refers to any hide, even among those of lions, tigers, leopards, hyenas, and so on. Indeed, in the commentaries, a prohibited hide is not seen in the context of using lodgings; therefore, the prohibition regarding the hides of lions, tigers, and so on, should be understood as applying only to carrying them about. A “sitting mat” is to be understood as having a fringe. A “bed-covering” is mentioned only as a woolen cloak or a quilt. A “grass covering” refers to a covering made of any kind of grass. The same applies to a “leaf covering.” Furthermore, having spread or had spread these ten kinds of bedding in a communal monastery, one who is departing should ask leave and then depart. And when asking leave, if a bhikkhu is present, a bhikkhu should be asked. If he is not present, a novice should be asked. If he is not present, a monastery attendant should be asked. If he is not present, the person by whom the monastery was built—the monastery donor—or anyone in his family should be asked. If even they are not present, after placing the bed on four stones, placing the remaining beds and seats on the bed, gathering all ten kinds of bedding—such as the mattress, etc.—into a pile on top, putting away the wooden and earthenware items, closing the doors and windows, and fulfilling the duties of departure, one should go.

Sace pana senāsanaṃ ovassati, chadanatthañca tiṇaṃ vā iṭṭhakā vā ānītā honti, sace ussahati, chādetabbaṃ. No ce sakkoti, yo okāso anovassako, tattha mañcapīṭhādīni nikkhipitvā gantabbaṃ. Sace sabbampi ovassati, ussahantena antogāme upāsakānaṃ ghare ṭhapetabbaṃ. Sace tepi “saṅghikaṃ nāma, bhante, bhāriyaṃ, aggidāhādīnaṃ bhāyāmā”ti na sampaṭicchanti, abbhokāsepi pāsāṇānaṃ upari mañcaṃ ṭhapetvā sesaṃ pubbe vuttanayeneva nikkhipitvā tiṇehi ca paṇṇehi ca paṭicchādetvā gantuṃ vaṭṭati. Yañhi tattha aṅgamattampi avasissati, taṃ aññesaṃ tattha [M 0.0088] āgatabhikkhūnaṃ upakāraṃ bhavissatīti. Uddharitvā gacchantena pana mañcapīṭhakavāṭaṃ sabbaṃ apanetvā saṃharitvā cīvaravaṃse laggetvāva gantabbaṃ. Pacchā āgantvā vasanakabhikkhunāpi puna mañcapīṭhaṃ ṭhapayitvā gacchantena tatheva kātabbaṃ. Antokuṭṭato seyyaṃ bahikuṭṭe paññapetvā vasantena gamanakāle puna gahitaṭṭhāneyeva paṭisāmetabbaṃ. Uparipāsādato oropetvā heṭṭhāpāsāde vasantassapi eseva nayo. Rattiṭṭhānadivāṭṭhānesu mañcapīṭhaṃ paññapetvā bahigamanakāle puna gahitaṭṭhāneyeva ṭhapetabbaṃ.

If, however, the lodging is leaking, and grass or tiles have been brought for roofing, if one is able, it should be roofed. If one is not able, the beds, chairs, and so forth, should be placed in a non-leaking spot, and one should depart. If the entire lodging is leaking, if one is able, they should be stored in the houses of lay devotees within the village. If they do not accept, saying, “Venerable sir, property belonging to the Saṅgha is a heavy responsibility; we fear fire and such dangers,” then it is allowable to depart after placing the bed on top of stones in an open space, arranging the rest in the manner previously stated, and covering them with grass and leaves. For whatever small part remains there will be of use to other bhikkhus who arrive there later. However, when departing and taking things away, one should remove the entire bed, chair, and door-leaf, gather them up, hang them on the robe-line, and then depart. Later, a bhikkhu who returns to stay should also set up the bed and chair again, and when departing, should do likewise. A bhikkhu who takes bedding from inside a chamber and arranges it outside to dwell, at the time of departure, should put it back in the place from which it was taken. The same rule applies to one who has brought items down from an upper storey to stay on a lower storey. In places for use at night and during the day, after setting up a bed and chair, when going outside, they should be placed back in the place from which they were taken.

83. Senāsanesu pana ayaṃ āpucchitabbānāpucchitabbavinicchayo – yā tāva bhūmiyaṃ dīghasālā vā paṇṇasālā vā hoti, yaṃ vā rukkhatthambhesu katagehaṃ upacikānaṃ uṭṭhānaṭṭhānaṃ hoti, tato pakkamantena tāva āpucchitvāva pakkamitabbaṃ. Tasmiñhi katipayāni divasāni ajaggiyamāne vammikāva santiṭṭhanti. Yaṃ pana pāsāṇapiṭṭhiyaṃ vā pāsāṇatthambhesu vā katasenāsanaṃ siluccayaleṇaṃ vā sudhālittasenāsanaṃ vā, yattha yattha upacikāsaṅkā natthi, tato pakkamantassa āpucchitvāpi anāpucchitvāpi gantuṃ vaṭṭati, āpucchanaṃ pana vattaṃ. Sace tādisepi senāsane ekena passena upacikā ārohanti, āpucchitvāva gantabbaṃ. Yo pana āgantuko bhikkhu saṅghikasenāsanaṃ gahetvāva santaṃ bhikkhuṃ anuvattanto attano senāsanaṃ aggahetvā vasati, yāva so na gaṇhāti, tāva taṃ senāsanaṃ purimabhikkhusseva palibodho. Yadā pana so senāsanaṃ gahetvā attano issariyena vasati, tato paṭṭhāya āgantukasseva palibodho. Sace ubhopi vibhajitvā gaṇhanti, ubhinnampi palibodho.

83. Regarding lodgings, this is the determination of when one must and need not ask for leave. First, if there is a long hall or a leaf hut on the ground, or a dwelling built on wooden pillars that is a place for termites to arise, one who is departing from there must first ask for leave before leaving. For if it is left untended for only a few days, termite mounds will become established. However, if the lodging is built on a stone slab or on stone pillars, or is a cave in a rocky mountain, or is a plastered dwelling—wherever there is no suspicion of termites—one who is departing may leave either with or without asking for leave, though asking for leave is a duty. If even in such a lodging termites climb up on one side, one must ask for leave before leaving. Furthermore, if a visiting bhikkhu attends upon a resident bhikkhu who has taken a communal lodging, and the visitor himself dwells there without taking his own lodging, that lodging remains an encumbrance for the first bhikkhu as long as the visitor does not take it. But when the visitor has taken the lodging and dwells with his own authority, from then on the lodging becomes an encumbrance for the visitor only. If both divide and take it, it becomes an encumbrance for both.

Mahāpaccariyaṃ pana vuttaṃ – sace dve tayo ekato hutvā paññapenti, gamanakāle sabbehi āpucchitabbaṃ. Tesu ce paṭhamaṃ gacchanto “pacchimo jaggissatī”ti ābhogaṃ katvā gacchati, vaṭṭati[V 0.0088], pacchimassa ābhogena mutti natthi. Bahū ekaṃ pesetvā santharāpenti, gamanakāle sabbehi vā āpucchitabbaṃ, ekaṃ vā pesetvā āpucchitabbaṃ. Aññato mañcapīṭhādīni ānetvā aññatra vasitvā gamanakāle tattheva netabbāni. Sace aññato ānetvā vasamānassa añño vuḍḍhataro āgacchati, na paṭibāhitabbo[M 0.0089], “mayā, bhante, aññāvāsato ānītaṃ, pākatikaṃ kareyyāthā”ti vattabbaṃ. Tena “evaṃ karissāmī”ti sampaṭicchite itarassa gantuṃ vaṭṭati. Evaṃ aññattha haritvāpi saṅghikaparibhogena paribhuñjantassa hi naṭṭhaṃ vā jiṇṇaṃ vā corehi vā haṭaṃ gīvā neva hoti, puggalikaparibhogena paribhuñjantassa pana gīvā hoti. Aññassa mañcapīṭhaṃ pana saṅghikaparibhogena vā puggalikaparibhogena vā paribhuñjantassa naṭṭhaṃ gīvāyeva. Antovihāre seyyaṃ santharitvā “ajjeva āgantvā paṭijaggissāmī”ti evaṃ sāpekkho nadīpāraṃ gāmantaraṃ vā gantvā yatthassa gamanacittaṃ uppannaṃ, tattheva ṭhito kañci pesetvā āpucchati, nadīpūrarājacorādīsu vā kenaci palibodho hoti upadduto, na sakkoti paccāgantuṃ, evaṃbhūtassa anāpatti.

However, it is stated in the Mahāpaccariya: If two or three bhikkhus together arrange bedding, at the time of departure, all should ask for leave. If among them the first one to depart leaves, having reflected, “The last one will take care of it,” it is allowable; but there is no release from the offense for the last one by that reflection. If many bhikkhus send one to have bedding spread, at the time of departure, either all should ask for leave, or one should be sent to ask for leave. Beds, chairs, and so forth, brought from another place should be taken back to that same place at the time of departure, after one has dwelt elsewhere. If, while one is dwelling having brought them from another place, another, more senior bhikkhu arrives, he should not be prevented. One should say, “Venerable sir, I brought this from another dwelling; please restore it to its original state.” When he has agreed, saying, “I will do so,” it is allowable for the other to depart. Indeed, for one who uses an item as communal property, even if taken elsewhere, there is no liability if it is lost, worn out, or taken by thieves; but for one who uses it as personal property, there is liability. Regarding another’s bed or chair, for one using it either as communal property or as personal property, if it is lost, there is indeed liability. Having spread bedding within the monastery with the expectation, “I will return this very day and take care of it,” one might go to the other side of a river or to another village. In whatever place the thought to travel further arises, standing right there, one should send someone to ask for leave. Or, if one is obstructed and afflicted by some danger among dangers such as a flooding river, the king, or thieves, and is unable to return, for one in such a situation, there is no offense.

Vihārassa upacāre pana upaṭṭhānasālāya vā maṇḍape vā rukkhamūle vā seyyaṃ santharitvā vā santharāpetvā vā taṃ pakkamanto neva uddharati na uddharāpeti anāpucchaṃ vā gacchati, dukkaṭaṃ. Vuttappakārañhi dasavidhaṃ seyyaṃ antogabbhādimhi guttaṭṭhāne paññapetvā gacchantassa yasmā seyyāpi senāsanampi upacikāhi palujjati, vammikarāsiyeva hoti, tasmā pācittiyaṃ vuttaṃ. Bahi pana upaṭṭhānasālādīsu paññapetvā gacchantassa seyyāmattameva nasseyya ṭhānassa aguttatāya, na senāsanaṃ, tasmā ettha dukkaṭaṃ vuttaṃ. Mañcapīṭhaṃ pana yasmā na sakkā sahasā upacikāhi khāyituṃ, tasmā taṃ vihārepi santharitvā gacchantassa dukkaṭaṃ. Vihārassūpacāre upaṭṭhānasālāyaṃ maṇḍape rukkhamūlepi santharitvā pakkamantassa dukkaṭameva.

However, in the vicinity of a monastery—in an assembly hall, a pavilion, or at the foot of a tree—if one, having spread or having caused to be spread bedding, departs without putting it away, without having it put away, or without asking leave, there is an offense of wrong-doing. For, when one departs after having arranged the tenfold bedding of the type described in a guarded place such as an inner chamber, since both the bedding and the lodging are destroyed by termites and become just an anthill, a pācittiya offense is stated. But when one departs after having arranged it outside in an assembly hall and so forth, only the bedding would be lost due to the place being unguarded, not the lodging; therefore, in this case, an offense of wrong-doing is stated. As for a bed or a bench, however, since it cannot be quickly eaten by termites, for one who departs after having spread it even in a monastery, an offense of wrong-doing is stated. For one who departs after having spread it in the vicinity of a monastery, in an assembly hall, in a pavilion, or at the foot of a tree, it is an offense of wrong-doing indeed.

84. “Yo pana bhikkhu saṅghikaṃ mañcaṃ vā pīṭhaṃ vā bhisiṃ vā kocchaṃ vā ajjhokāse santharitvā vā santharāpetvā vā taṃ pakkamanto neva uddhareyya na uddharāpeyya anāpucchaṃ vā gaccheyya, pācittiya”nti (pāci. 109) vacanato saṅghikāni pana mañcapīṭhādīni cattāri ajjhokāse santharitvā vā santharāpetvā vā uddharaṇādīni akatvā “ajjeva āgamissāmī”ti gacchantassapi thāmamajjhimassa purisassa leḍḍupātātikkame pācittiyaṃ. Ettha kocchaṃ nāma vākamayaṃ vā usīramayaṃ vā muñjamayaṃ vā pabbajamayaṃ vā heṭṭhā ca upari ca vitthataṃ majjhe saṃkhittaṃ paṇavasaṇṭhānaṃ katvā baddhaṃ. Taṃ kira majjhe sīhabyagghacammaparikkhittampi [V 0.0089] karonti, akappiyacammaṃ nāmettha natthi. Senāsanañhi sovaṇṇamayampi vaṭṭati, tasmā taṃ mahagghaṃ hoti.

84. “Whatever bhikkhu, having spread out or having caused to be spread out a bed, a bench, a mattress, or a woven mat belonging to the Sangha in the open air, then departing, should neither put it away himself nor have it put away, or should depart without asking leave, it is a pācittiya.” According to this, as for the four items belonging to the Sangha, such as a bed and a bench, if one, having spread or having caused them to be spread in the open air, departs without performing the act of putting them away and so forth, even thinking, “I will return today itself,” there is a pācittiya offense upon transgressing the distance of a clod’s throw by a man of medium strength. Herein, what is called a koccha is a mat made of bark-fibre, or of vetiver grass, or of muñja grass, or of babbaja grass, which is wide below and above, narrowed in the middle, and made and bound into the shape of a paṇava drum. It is said that they also make it covered in the middle with the skins of lions and tigers; herein, there is no such thing as an unallowable hide. For a lodging, even one made of gold is allowable; therefore, it is of great value.

“Anujānāmi, [M 0.0090] bhikkhave, aṭṭha māse avassikasaṅkete maṇḍape vā rukkhamūle vā yattha kākā vā kulalā vā na ūhadanti, tattha senāsanaṃ nikkhipitu”nti (pāci. 110) vacanato pana vassikavassānamāsāti evaṃ apaññāte cattāro hemantike, cattāro gimhiketi aṭṭha māse sākhāmaṇḍape vā padaramaṇḍape vā rukkhamūle vā nikkhipituṃ vaṭṭati. Yasmiṃ pana kākā vā kulalā vā aññe vā sakuntā dhuvanivāsena kulāvake katvā vasanti, tassa rukkhassa mūle na nikkhipitabbaṃ. “Aṭṭha māse”ti vacanato yesu janapadesu vassakāle na vassati, tesu cattāro māse nikkhipituṃ na vaṭṭatiyeva. “Avassikasaṅkete”ti vacanato yattha hemante devo vassati, tattha hemantepi ajjhokāse nikkhipituṃ na vaṭṭati. Gimhe pana sabbattha vigatavalāhakaṃ visuddhaṃ nataṃ hoti, evarūpe kāle kenacideva karaṇīyena ajjhokāse mañcapīṭhaṃ nikkhipituṃ vaṭṭati.

“Bhikkhus, I allow you to place a lodging for eight months in a place designated as not rainy, such as in a pavilion or at the root of a tree, where crows or hawks do not defecate.” Because of this, for eight months—four months of winter and four months of summer, thus not designated as the months of the rainy season—it is allowable to place lodgings in a branch-roofed pavilion, a plank-roofed pavilion, or at the root of a tree. However, at the root of a tree where crows, hawks, or other birds live permanently, having made nests, it should not be placed. From the statement “for eight months,” in those regions where it does not rain during the rainy season, it is not at all allowable to place lodgings during those four months. From the statement “in a place designated as not rainy,” where it rains during the winter, it is not allowable to place lodgings in the open air even during the winter. But in the summer, when the sky is everywhere free of clouds and clear, at such a time, it is allowable to place a bed or a bench in the open air for some particular reason.

85. Abbhokāsikenapi vattaṃ jānitabbaṃ. Tassa hi sace puggalikamañcako atthi, tattheva sayitabbaṃ. Saṅghikaṃ gaṇhantena vettena vā vākena vā vītamañcako gahetabbo, tasmiṃ asati purāṇamañcako gahetabbo, tasmiṃ asati navavāyimo vā onaddhako vā gahetabbo. Gahetvā pana “ahaṃ ukkaṭṭharukkhamūliko ukkaṭṭhaabbhokāsiko”ti cīvarakuṭimpi akatvā asamaye ajjhokāse vā rukkhamūle vā paññapetvā nipajjituṃ na vaṭṭati. Sace pana catugguṇenapi cīvarena katā kuṭi atementaṃ rakkhituṃ na sakkoti, sattāhavaddalikādīni bhavanti, bhikkhuno kāyānugatikattā vaṭṭati. Araññe paṇṇakuṭīsu vasantānaṃ sīlasampadāya pasannacittā manussā navaṃ mañcapīṭhaṃ denti “saṅghikaparibhogena paribhuñjathā”ti, vasitvā gacchantehi sāmantavihāre sabhāgabhikkhūnaṃ pesetvā gantabbaṃ, sabhāgānaṃ abhāvena anovassake nikkhipitvā gantabbaṃ, anovassake asati rukkhe laggetvā gantabbaṃ. Cetiyaṅgaṇe sammajjaniṃ gahetvā bhojanasālaṅgaṇaṃ vā uposathāgāraṅgaṇaṃ vā pariveṇadivāṭṭhānaaggisālādīsu vā aññataraṃ sammajjitvā dhovitvā puna sammajjanimāḷakeyeva ṭhapetabbā. Uposathāgārādīsu aññatarasmiṃ gahetvā avasesāni sammajjantassapi eseva nayo.

85. The duty for an open-air dweller should also be known. If he has a personal bed, he should sleep right there. When taking a communal one, a bedstead woven with cane or bark-string should be taken; if that is unavailable, an old bedstead should be taken; if that too is unavailable, a newly woven one or one bound with leather straps should be taken. However, having taken one, it is not proper to prepare a spot and lie down in the open or at the root of a tree at an improper time, without even making a robe-hut, thinking, ‘I am a strict tree-root dweller, a strict open-air dweller.’ But if even a hut made with a four-fold robe cannot protect him from getting wet, and there are continuous rains for seven days and so on, it is allowable as it is for the well-being of the monk's body. People with devoted minds, due to the accomplishment in virtue of those dwelling in leaf-huts in the forest, may give a new bed and chair, saying, ‘Use this as a communal requisite.’ When leaving after having stayed there, they should send them to monks of a similar kind in a nearby monastery before going. In the absence of such monks, they should place them in a place sheltered from rain before going. If there is no such place, they should hang them on a tree before going. Having taken a broom in the cetiya courtyard, one should sweep and wash the dining hall courtyard, or the Uposatha hall courtyard, or another place such as the monastic cells, day-quarters, or fire-halls, and then the broom should be placed back on the broom-rack. This same method applies also for one who takes a broom from the Uposatha hall or a similar place and sweeps the remaining areas.

Yo [M 0.0091] pana bhikkhācāramaggaṃ sammajjanto gantukāmo hoti, tena sammajjitvā sace antarāmagge sālā atthi, tattha ṭhapetabbā. Sace natthi, valāhakānaṃ anuṭṭhitabhāvaṃ sallakkhetvā “yāvāhaṃ [V 0.0090] gāmato nikkhamāmi, tāva na vassissatī”ti jānantena yattha katthaci nikkhipitvā puna paccāgacchantena pākatikaṭṭhāne ṭhapetabbā. “Sace vassissatīti jānanto ajjhokāse ṭhapeti, dukkaṭa”nti mahāpaccariyaṃ vuttaṃ. Sace pana tatra tatreva sammajjanatthāya sammajjanī nikkhittā hoti, taṃ taṃ ṭhānaṃ sammajjitvā tatra tatreva nikkhipituṃ vaṭṭati, āsanasālaṃ sammajjantena vattaṃ jānitabbaṃ. Tatridaṃ vattaṃ – majjhato paṭṭhāya pādaṭṭhānābhimukhā vālikā haritabbā, kacavaraṃ hatthehi gahetvā bahi chaḍḍetabbaṃ.

Now, should a monk wish to sweep the alms-round path before going, he should sweep it. If there is a hall on the path, the broom should be placed there. If there is not, he should observe the absence of clouds and, knowing, ‘It will not rain before I depart from the village,’ he may place it anywhere. Upon returning, it should be put back in its usual place. It is stated in the Mahāpaccariya: ‘If, knowing it will rain, one places it in an open space, there is an offense of wrong-doing.’ However, if a broom has been placed in various places for the purpose of sweeping, it is allowable to leave it in that same place after sweeping that place. When sweeping the seating hall, the proper procedure should be known. Herein is the procedure: starting from the middle, the sand should be swept towards the place for the feet, and rubbish should be taken by hand and discarded outside.

86. Sace vuttappakāraṃ catubbidhampi saṅghikaṃ senāsanaṃ ajjhokāse vā rukkhamūle vā maṇḍape vā anupasampannena santharāpeti, yena santharāpitaṃ, tassa palibodho. Sace pana upasampannena santharāpeti, yena santhataṃ, tassa palibodho. Tatrāyaṃ vinicchayo (pāci. aṭṭha. 111) – thero bhojanasālāyaṃ bhattakiccaṃ katvā daharaṃ āṇāpeti “gaccha divāṭṭhāne mañcapīṭhaṃ paññapehī”ti. So tathā katvā nisinno, thero yathāruci vicaritvā tattha gantvā thavikaṃ vā uttarāsaṅgaṃ vā ṭhapeti, tato paṭṭhāya therassa palibodho. Nisīditvā sayaṃ gacchanto neva uddharati na uddharāpeti, leḍḍupātātikkame pācittiyaṃ. Sace pana thero tattha thavikaṃ vā uttarāsaṅgaṃ vā aṭṭhapetvā caṅkamantova daharaṃ “gaccha tva”nti bhaṇati, tena “idaṃ, bhante, mañcapīṭha”nti ācikkhitabbaṃ. Sace thero vattaṃ jānāti, “tvaṃ gaccha, ahaṃ pākatikaṃ karissāmī”ti vattabbaṃ. Sace bālo hoti anuggahitavatto, “gaccha, mā idha tiṭṭha, neva nisīdituṃ na nipajjituṃ demī”ti daharaṃ tajjetiyeva. Daharena “bhante, sukhaṃ sayathā”ti kappaṃ labhitvā vanditvā gantabbaṃ. Tasmiṃ gate therasseva palibodho, purimanayeneva cassa āpatti veditabbā.

86. If one has the fourfold Saṅgha lodging of the kind previously described—whether in the open air, at the root of a tree, or in a pavilion—spread by one not fully ordained, the encumbrance belongs to the one who had it spread. But if one has it spread by an ordained person, the encumbrance belongs to the one who spread it. Herein is the decision: An elder, having finished his meal duty in the dining hall, commands a junior, 'Go and prepare a bed and seat in the day-quarters.' That junior, having done so, sits down. The elder, having wandered according to his wish, goes there and places a bag or an upper robe. From then on, the encumbrance is the elder's. Having sat down, if he himself, when leaving, neither removes it nor has it removed, upon exceeding the distance of a clod-throw, there is a Pācittiya offense. But if the elder, without placing a bag or an upper robe there, while walking to and fro, tells the junior, 'You go,' the junior should inform him, 'Venerable sir, this bed and seat has been prepared.' If the elder knows the proper conduct, he should say, 'You go, I will restore it to its normal state.' If he is a fool and untrained in the proper conduct, he should just threaten the junior, saying, 'Go, do not stand here. I give no permission to sit or to lie down.' The junior, having obtained leave, should say, 'Venerable sir, may you lie down comfortably,' pay respects, and go. When he has gone, the encumbrance is the elder's alone, and the offense for him should be known in the same way as before.

Atha pana āṇattikkhaṇeyeva daharo “mayhaṃ bhaṇḍe bhaṇḍadhovanādi kiñci karaṇīyaṃ atthī”ti vadati, thero pana taṃ “paññapetvā gacchāhī”ti vatvā bhojanasālato nikkhamitvā aññattha gacchati, pāduddhārena kāretabbo[M 0.0092]. Sace tattheva gantvā nisīdati, purimanayeneva cassa leḍḍupātātikkame āpatti. Sace pana thero sāmaṇeraṃ āṇāpeti, sāmaṇere tattha mañcapīṭhaṃ paññapetvā nisinnepi bhojanasālato aññattha gacchanto pāduddhārena kāretabbo. Gantvā nisinno puna gamanakāle leḍḍupātātikkame āpattiyā kāretabbo. Sace pana āṇāpento “mañcapīṭhaṃ paññapetvā tattheva nisīdā”ti āṇāpeti, yatricchati, tatra gantvā āgantuṃ labhati. Sayaṃ pana pākatikaṃ akatvā gacchantassa leḍḍupātātikkame pācittiyaṃ. Antarasannipāte [V 0.0091] mañcapīṭhādīni paññapetvā nisinnehi gamanakāle ārāmikānaṃ “idaṃ paṭisāmethā”ti vattabbaṃ, avatvā gacchantānaṃ leḍḍupātātikkame āpatti.

Alternatively, at the very moment of the command, if the junior says, 'I have some duty concerning my requisites, such as washing robes,' and the elder, having said to him, 'Having arranged it, you may go,' departs from the dining hall and goes elsewhere, he should be made to incur an offense with each step. If he goes to that very place and sits down, for him there is an offense upon exceeding a clod's throw, in the same way as before. But if the elder commands a novice, even when the novice, having arranged a bed or a bench in that place, is seated, the elder who is going from the dining hall to another place should be made to incur an offense with each step. Having gone and sat down, when he departs again, he should be made to incur an offense upon exceeding a clod's throw. But if the one commanding gives the command, 'Having arranged a bed or a bench, you should sit in that very place,' he is permitted to go wherever he wishes and to return. However, for one who goes without having restored it to its original state himself, there is a Pācittiya offense upon exceeding a clod's throw. In a chance assembly, those who have arranged and are seated on beds, benches, and so forth, should say to the monastery attendants at the time of departure, 'Please put these away.' For those who go without having said so, there is an offense upon exceeding a clod's throw.

87. Mahādhammassavanaṃ nāma hoti, tattha uposathāgāratopi bhojanasālatopi āharitvā mañcapīṭhāni paññapenti, āvāsikānaṃyeva palibodho. Sace āgantukā “idaṃ amhākaṃ upajjhāyassa, idaṃ ācariyassā”ti gaṇhanti, tato paṭṭhāya tesaṃ palibodho. Gamanakāle pākatikaṃ akatvā leḍḍupātaṃ atikkamantānaṃ āpatti. Mahāpaccariyaṃ pana vuttaṃ “yāva aññe na nisīdanti, tāva yehi paññattaṃ, tesaṃ bhāro, aññesu āgantvā nisinnesu nisinnakānaṃ bhāro. Sace te anuddharitvā vā anuddharāpetvā vā gacchanti, dukkaṭaṃ. Kasmā? Anāṇattiyā paññapitattā”ti. Dhammāsane paññatte yāva ussārako vā dhammakathiko vā nāgacchati, tāva paññāpakānaṃ palibodho. Tasmiṃ āgantvā nisinne tassa palibodho. Sakalaṃ ahorattaṃ dhammassavanaṃ hoti, añño ussārako vā dhammakathiko vā uṭṭhāti, añño nisīdati, yo yo āgantvā nisīdati, tassa tasseva bhāro. Uṭṭhahantena pana “idamāsanaṃ tumhākaṃ bhāro”ti vatvā gantabbaṃ. Sacepi itarasmiṃ anāgate paṭhamaṃ nisinno uṭṭhāya gacchati, tasmiñca antoupacāraṭṭheyeva itaro āgantvā nisīdati, uṭṭhāya gato āpattiyā na kāretabbo. Sace pana itarasmiṃ anāgateyeva paṭhamaṃ nisinno uṭṭhāyāsanā leḍḍupātaṃ atikkamati, āpattiyā kāretabbo. “Sabbattha leḍḍupātātikkame paṭhamapāde dukkaṭaṃ, dutiyapāde pācittiya”nti ayaṃ nayo mahāpaccariyaṃ vuttoti.

87. There is what is called a great occasion of listening to the Dhamma. There, they bring beds and chairs from the Uposatha hall and from the dining hall and arrange them; this is the responsibility of the resident monks only. If visiting monks take them, saying, 'This is for our preceptor, this is for our teacher,' then from that point on, it is their responsibility. At the time of departure, for those who cross beyond a clod's throw without restoring them to their original state, there is a Pācittiya offense. However, in the Mahāpaccarī it is said: 'As long as other monks have not sat down, the burden is on those by whom they were arranged. When other monks have come and are seated, the burden is on those who are seated. If they leave without putting them away or having them put away, it is a Dukkaṭa offense. Why? Because they were arranged without being instructed.' Regarding what is arranged on the Dhamma-seat, as long as the reciter or the Dhamma-speaker does not arrive, the responsibility belongs to those who arranged it. When he has come and is seated, the responsibility is his. Suppose the listening to the Dhamma goes on for the entire day and night; one reciter or Dhamma-speaker gets up, and another sits down. For each one who comes and sits down, the burden is his alone. But the one who is getting up should say, 'This seat is your burden,' and then go. And if, before the other arrives, the one first seated gets up and goes, and while he is still within the inner precinct, the other comes and sits down, the one who got up and went should not be made to incur an offense. But if, before the other arrives, the one first seated gets up from the seat and crosses beyond a clod's throw, he should be made to incur an offense. 'In all cases of crossing a clod's throw, with the first step, it is a Dukkaṭa offense; with the second step, it is a Pācittiya offense.' This principle is stated in the Mahāpaccarī.

88. Sace [M 0.0093] pana vuttappakārasenāsanato aññaṃ saṅghikaṃ cimilikaṃ vā uttarattharaṇaṃ vā bhūmattharaṇaṃ vā taṭṭikaṃ vā cammakhaṇḍaṃ vā pādapuñchaniṃ vā phalakapīṭhaṃ vā ajjhokāse santharitvā vā santharāpetvā vā taṃ pakkamanto neva uddharati na uddharāpeti anāpucchaṃ vā gacchati, dukkaṭaṃ. Ādhārakaṃ pattapidhānakaṃ pādakaṭhalikaṃ tālavaṇṭaṃ bījanipattakaṃ yaṃ kiñci dārubhaṇḍaṃ antamaso pānīyauḷuṅkaṃ pānīyasaṅkhaṃ ajjhokāse nikkhipitvā gacchantassapi dukkaṭaṃ. Ajjhokāse rajanaṃ pacitvā rajanabhājanaṃ rajanauḷuṅko rajanadoṇikāti sabbaṃ aggisālāya paṭisāmetabbaṃ. Sace aggisālā natthi, anovassake pabbhāre nikkhipitabbaṃ. Tasmimpi asati yattha olokentā bhikkhū passanti, tādise ṭhāne ṭhapetvā gantuṃ vaṭṭati. Aññapuggalike pana mañcapīṭhādisenāsanepi dukkaṭameva. Ettha pana “yasmiṃ vissāsaggāho na ruhati, tassa santake dukkaṭaṃ. Yasmiṃ pana vissāsaggāho ruhati, tassa santakaṃ attano puggalikameva hotī”ti mahāpaccariyādīsu vuttaṃ. Attano puggalike pana anāpattiyeva. Yo bhikkhu [V 0.0092] vā sāmaṇero vā ārāmiko vā lajjī hoti, attano palibodhaṃ viya maññati, tathārūpaṃ anāpucchitvā gacchantassapi anāpatti. Yo pana ātape otāpento “āgantvā uddharissāmī”ti gacchati, tassapi anāpatti.

88. If, after spreading out or having someone spread out in the open air any communal item other than the types of lodgings already mentioned—such as a cimilika mat, an upper cover, a ground cover, a rug, a piece of leather, a foot-wiping cloth, or a foot-washing board—a departing monk neither removes it nor has it removed, or leaves without asking permission, he commits a dukkaṭa offense. It is also a dukkaṭa offense for one who leaves after placing in the open air any wooden article, such as a bowl stand, a bowl cover, a foot-rubbing potsherd, a palm-leaf fan, a four-cornered fan, or even down to a water ladle or a water-drinking conch shell. After boiling dye in the open air, all items—the dye-boiling pot, the dye ladle, and the dye trough—must be put away in the fire-hall. If there is no fire-hall, they should be placed in a cave not reached by rain. If that is also not available, it is permissible to place them in a location where monks looking around may see them and then depart. In the case of lodgings such as a bed or bench belonging to another person, it is indeed a dukkaṭa offense. Here, in the Mahāpaccariya and other commentaries it is said: 'Where taking with trust is not established, a dukkaṭa offense is incurred regarding that person's property. But where taking with trust is established, that person's property is considered as one's own personal property.' Regarding one's own personal belongings, however, there is no offense. If a monk, a novice, or a monastery attendant is conscientious and considers it as his own responsibility, there is no offense for one who leaves without informing such a person. Also, if one is drying an item in the sun and leaves with the thought, 'I will come back and put it away,' for him too there is no offense.

Iti pāḷimuttakavinayavinicchayasaṅgahe

Thus, in the Compilation of Extra-Canonical Vinaya Judgments,

Mañcapīṭhādisaṅghikasenāsanesu

Regarding communal lodgings such as beds and benches,

Paṭipajjitabbavinicchayakathā samattā.

The Discourse on the Determination of What Should Be Practiced is completed.

18. Kālikavinicchayakathā

18. The Discourse on the Determination of Time-Bound Requisites

89. Kālikānipi [V 0.0093] cattārīti ettha (pāci. aṭṭha. 255-256) yāvakālikaṃ yāmakālikaṃ sattāhakālikaṃ yāvajīvikanti imāni cattāri kālikāni veditabbāni. Tattha purebhattaṃ paṭiggahetvā paribhuñjitabbaṃ yaṃ kiñci khādanīyabhojanīyaṃ yāva majjhanhikasaṅkhato kālo, tāva paribhuñjitabbato yāvakālikaṃ. Saddhiṃ anulomapānehi aṭṭhavidhaṃ pānaṃ yāva rattiyā pacchimayāmasaṅkhāto [M 0.0094] yāmo, tāva paribhuñjitabbato yāmo kālo assāti yāmakālikaṃ. Sappiādi pañcavidhaṃ bhesajjaṃ paṭiggahetvā sattāhaṃ nidhetabbato sattāho kālo assāti sattāhakālikaṃ. Ṭhapetvā udakaṃ avasesaṃ sabbampi paṭiggahitaṃ yāvajīvaṃ pariharitvā sati paccaye paribhuñjitabbato yāvajīvikanti vuccati.

89. In this mātikā-item, 'the four kālikas,' these four kālikas should be known as: yāvakālika, yāmakālika, sattāhakālika, and yāvajīvika. Therein, whatever hard or soft food is received before noon and is to be consumed until the time designated as midday, is called yāvakālika because it is to be consumed for that period. The eight kinds of drinks, together with suitable drinks, are to be consumed until the watch designated as the last watch of the night; it is called yāmakālika because a watch is its time. The five kinds of medicine, such as ghee, having been received, are to be stored for seven days; it is called sattāhakālika because seven days is its time. Excluding water, all other received items, because they are to be kept for life and consumed when a need arises, are called yāvajīvika.

90. Tattha yāvakālikesu bhojanīyaṃ nāma odano kummāso sattu maccho maṃsanti. Pañca bhojanāni yāmakālikaṃ sattāhakālikaṃ yāvajīvikañca ṭhapetvā avasesaṃ khādanīyaṃ nāma. Ettha (pāci. aṭṭha. 248-9) pana yaṃ tāva sakkhalimodakādi pubbaṇṇāparaṇṇamayaṃ khādanīyaṃ, tattha vattabbameva natthi. Yampi vanamūlādippabhedaṃ āmisagatikaṃ hoti. Seyyathidaṃ – mūlakhādanīyaṃ kandakhādanīyaṃ muḷālakhādanīyaṃ matthakakhādanīyaṃ khandhakhādanīyaṃ tacakhādanīyaṃ pattakhādanīyaṃ pupphakhādanīyaṃ phalakhādanīyaṃ aṭṭhikhādanīyaṃ piṭṭhakhādanīyaṃ niyyāsakhādanīyanti, idampi khādanīyasaṅkhyameva gacchati.

90. Therein, among the yāvakālika items, that which is called bhojanīya is: rice, barley-meal, roasted flour, fish, and meat. Excluding these five bhojanīyas, and the yāmakālika, sattāhakālika, and yāvajīvika items, the remainder is called khādanīya. Here, as for whatever khādanīya is made from grains, such as sakkhalī and modaka, there is nothing more to be said. And whatever varieties, such as forest roots, are meal-like—namely: root edibles, tuber edibles, lotus-stalk edibles, shoot edibles, stem edibles, bark edibles, leaf edibles, flower edibles, fruit edibles, seed edibles, flour edibles, and sap edibles—all this is also counted as khādanīya.

Tattha pana āmisagatikasallakkhaṇatthaṃ idaṃ mukhamattanidassanaṃ – mūlakhādanīye tāva mūlakamūlaṃ khārakamūlaṃ caccumūlaṃ tambakamūlaṃ taṇḍuleyyakamūlaṃ vatthuleyyakamūlaṃ vajakalimūlaṃ jajjharimūlanti evamādīni sūpeyyapaṇṇamūlāni āmisagatikāni. Ettha ca vajakalimūle jaraṭṭhaṃ chinditvā chaḍḍenti, taṃ yāvajīvikaṃ hoti. Aññampi evarūpaṃ eteneva nayena veditabbaṃ. Mūlakakhārakajajjharimūlānaṃ pana jaraṭṭhānipi āmisagatikānevāti vuttaṃ. Yāni pana pāḷiyaṃ –

Now, in this matter, for the purpose of noting the characteristic of being in the category of food, this mere indication should be understood: First, among edible roots, the roots of plants with leaves suitable for curry, such as radish root, khāraka root, caccu root, tambaka root, taṇḍuleyyaka root, vatthuleyyaka root, vajakali root, and jajjhari root, are in the category of food. And among these, in the case of the vajakali root, they cut off and discard the mature part; that part is a lifetime requisite. Any other such mature root should be understood by this same method. However, it is said that even the mature parts of radish, khāraka, and jajjhari roots are indeed in the category of food. And those which are in the Pāḷi—

“Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, mūlāni bhesajjāni haliddiṃ siṅgiveraṃ vacaṃ vacattaṃ ativisaṃ kaṭukarohiṇiṃ usīraṃ bhaddamuttakaṃ, yāni vā panaññānipi atthi mūlāni bhesajjāni [V 0.0094] neva khādanīye khādanīyatthaṃ pharanti, na bhojanīye bhojanīyatthaṃ pharantī”ti (mahāva. 263) –

“Monks, I allow medicinal roots: turmeric, ginger, vaca, vacatta, ativisa, kaṭukarohiṇī, usīra, and bhaddamuttaka; and whatever other medicinal roots there may be that do not fulfill the function of hard food in the category of hard food, nor fulfill the function of soft food in the category of soft food.”

Vuttāni, tāni yāvajīvikāni. Tesaṃ cūḷapañcamūlaṃ mahāpañcamūlantiādinā nayena gaṇiyamānānaṃ gaṇanāya anto natthi, khādanīyatthañca bhojanīyatthañca apharaṇabhāvoyeva panetesaṃ lakkhaṇaṃ. Tasmā yaṃ kiñci mūlaṃ tesu tesu janapadesu pakatiāhāravasena manussānaṃ khādanīyatthaṃ bhojanīyatthañca pharati, taṃ yāvakālikaṃ, itaraṃ yāvajīvikanti veditabbaṃ[M 0.0095]. Subahuṃ vatvāpi hi imasmiṃyeva lakkhaṇe ṭhātabbaṃ. Nāmasaññāsu pana vuccamānāsu taṃ taṃ nāmaṃ ajānantānaṃ sammohoyeva hoti, tasmā nāmasaññāya ādaraṃ akatvā lakkhaṇameva dassitaṃ. Yathā ca mūle, evaṃ kandādīsupi lakkhaṇaṃ dassayissāma, tasseva vasena vinicchayo veditabbo. Yañca taṃ pāḷiyaṃ haliddādi aṭṭhavidhaṃ vuttaṃ, tassa khandhatacapupphaphalādi sabbaṃ yāvajīvikanti vuttaṃ.

Those that were mentioned are lifetime requisites. When enumerating them by the method of ‘the five minor roots,’ ‘the five major roots,’ and so on, there is no end to the count. However, their characteristic is indeed the state of not fulfilling the function of hard food and soft food. Therefore, whatever root in various regions fulfills the function of hard food and soft food for people by way of being their staple food, that is a time-limited requisite; the other is a lifetime requisite—thus it should be known. For even after saying a great deal, one must stand firm on this very characteristic. But when names are mentioned, for those who do not know those particular names, there is only confusion. Therefore, without giving importance to the names, only the characteristic has been shown. And just as for roots, so too for tubers and so on we will show the characteristic; the decision should be understood by means of that very characteristic. And as for the eight kinds beginning with turmeric that were mentioned in the Pāḷi, it is said that all of their parts—trunk, bark, flower, fruit, and so on—are lifetime requisites.

Kandakhādanīye duvidho kando dīgho ca bhisakiṃsukakandādi, vaṭṭo ca uppalakaserukakandādi, yaṃ gaṇṭhītipi vadanti. Tattha sabbesaṃ kandānaṃ jiṇṇajaraṭṭhaṭṭhānañca challi ca sukhumamūlāni ca yāvajīvikāni, taruṇo pana sukhakhādanīyo sālakalyāṇipotakakando kiṃsukapotakakando ambāṭakakando ketakakando māluvakando bhisasaṅkhāto padumapuṇḍarīkakando piṇḍālumasāluādayo ca khīravallikando āluvakando siggukando tālakando nīluppalarattuppalakumudasogandhikānaṃ kandā kadalikando veḷukando kaserukakandoti evamādayo tesu tesu janapadesu pakatiāhāravasena manussānaṃ khādanīyatthañca bhojanīyatthañca pharaṇakakandā yāvakālikā. Khīravallikando adhoto yāvajīviko, dhoto yāvakāliko. Khīrakākolijīvikausabhakalasuṇādikandā pana yāvajīvikā. Te pāḷiyaṃ “yāni vā panaññānipi atthi mūlāni bhesajjānī”ti evaṃ (mahāva. 263) mūlabhesajjasaṅgaheneva saṅgahitā.

Regarding edible tubers: there are two kinds of tubers: long ones, such as the bhisa and kiṃsuka tubers, and round ones, such as the uppala and kaseruka tubers, which are also called gaṇṭhi (knotted roots). Among all these tubers, the old and withered parts, the outer bark, and the fine rootlets are lifetime allowances. However, the tender part, which is pleasant to eat—such as the sālakalyāṇipotaka tuber, the kiṃsukapotaka tuber, the ambāṭaka tuber, the ketaka tuber, the māluvaka tuber; the tuber of the paduma and puṇḍarīka lotuses, known as bhisa; piṇḍālu, masālu, and others; the khīravallika tuber, the āluvaka tuber, the sigguka tuber, the tālaka tuber; the tubers of the blue lotus, red lotus, kumuda, and sogandhika; the banana tuber, the bamboo tuber, and the kaseruka tuber—these and others which, in various regions, serve as staple food for people, fulfilling the purpose of both hard and soft food, are short-term allowances. The khīravallika tuber, if unwashed, is a lifetime allowance; if washed, it is a short-term allowance. The tubers of khīrakākoli, jīvika, usabhaka, lasuṇa (garlic), and so on, are lifetime allowances. In the Pāli Canon, these are included only under the category of medicinal roots with the phrase, 'Or whatever other roots there are that are medicinal.'

Muḷālakhādanīye padumamuḷālaṃ puṇḍarīkamuḷālaṃ mūlasadisaṃyeva. Erakamuḷālaṃ kandulamuḷālanti evamādi tesu tesu janapadesu pakatiāhāravasena manussānaṃ khādanīyatthaṃ bhojanīyatthañca pharaṇakamuḷālaṃ yāvakālikaṃ, haliddisiṅgiveramakacicaturassavalliketakatālahintālakuntālanāḷikerapūgarukkhādimuḷālaṃ pana yāvajīvikaṃ. Taṃ sabbampi pāḷiyaṃ “yāni vā panaññānipi atthi mūlāni bhesajjānī”ti evaṃ mūlabhesajjasaṅgaheneva saṅgahitaṃ.

Regarding edible stalks: the stalk of the paduma lotus and the stalk of the puṇḍarīka lotus are just like roots. The eraka (reed) stalk, the kandula (Butea monosperma) stalk, and so on—such stalks that in various regions serve as staple food for people, fulfilling the purpose of both hard and soft food, are short-term allowances. However, the stalks of turmeric, ginger, makaci, caturassavallī, ketaka (screwpine), tāla (palmyra), hintāla (date palm), kuntāla, nāḷikera (coconut), and pūga (areca) trees, and so on, are lifetime allowances. All of these are included in the Pāli Canon only under the category of medicinal roots with the phrase, 'Or whatever other roots there are that are medicinal.'

Matthakakhādanīye [V 0.0095] tālahintālakuntālaketakanāḷikerapūgarukkhakhajjūrivettaerakakadalīnaṃ kaḷīrasaṅkhātā matthakā, veṇukaḷīro naḷakaḷīro ucchukaḷīro [M 0.0096] mūlakakaḷīro sāsapakaḷīro satāvarikaḷīro sattannaṃ dhaññānaṃ kaḷīrāti evamādi tesu tesu janapadesu pakatiāhāravasena manussānaṃ khādanīyatthaṃ bhojanīyatthañca pharaṇako rukkhavalliādīnaṃ matthako yāvakāliko, haliddisiṅgiveravacamakacilasuṇānaṃ kaḷīrā, tālahintālakuntālanāḷikerakaḷīrānañca chinditvā pātito jaraṭṭhabundo yāvajīviko.

Regarding edible shoots: the tops—called shoots (kaḷīra)—of palmyra, hintāla, kuntāla, screwpine, coconut, areca, date palm, rattan, eraka grass, and banana; and bamboo shoots, reed shoots, sugarcane shoots, radish shoots, mustard shoots, asparagus shoots, the shoots of the seven kinds of grain, and so on—the tops of such trees, vines, and the like, which in various regions serve as staple food for people, fulfilling the purpose of both hard and soft food, are short-term allowances. The shoots of turmeric, ginger, acorus calamus, makaci, and garlic, as well as the old, hardened base of palmyra, hintāla, kuntāla, and coconut shoots that has fallen after being cut, are lifetime allowances.

Khandhakhādanīye antopathavīgato sālakalyāṇīkhandho ucchukhandho nīluppalarattuppalakumudasogandhikānaṃ daṇḍakakhandhāti evamādi tesu tesu janapadesu pakatiāhāravasena manussānaṃ khādanīyatthaṃ bhojanīyatthañca pharaṇako khandho yāvakāliko, uppalajātīnaṃ paṇṇadaṇḍako padumajātīnaṃ sabbopi daṇḍako karavindadaṇḍādayo ca avasesasabbakhandhā yāvajīvikā.

Regarding edible stems: the underground stem of the sālakalyāṇī plant, the stem of sugarcane, the stalks of the blue lotus, red lotus, kumuda, and sogandhika, and so on—such stems that in various regions serve as staple food for people, fulfilling the purpose of both hard and soft food, are short-term allowances. The leaf-stalks of water lily varieties, all stalks of lotus varieties, karavinda stalks, and so on, and all other remaining stems, are lifetime allowances.

Tacakhādanīye ucchutacova eko yāvakāliko, sopi saraso, seso sabbo yāvajīviko. Tesaṃ pana matthakakhandhatacānaṃ tiṇṇampi pāḷiyaṃ kasāvabhesajjena saṅgaho veditabbo. Vuttañhetaṃ –

Regarding edible barks: only sugarcane bark is a short-term allowance, and that too, only when it is juicy. All other bark is a lifetime allowance. However, it should be understood that these three—shoots, stems, and barks—are included in the Pāli Canon under the category of astringent medicines. For it has been said:

“Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, kasāvāni bhesajjāni nimbakasāvaṃ kuṭajakasāvaṃ paṭolakasāvaṃ phaggavakasāvaṃ nattamālakasāvaṃ, yāni vā panaññānipi atthi kasāvāni bhesajjāni neva khādanīye khādanīyatthaṃ pharanti, na bhojanīye bhojanīyatthaṃ pharantī”ti (mahāva. 263).

‘Monks, I allow astringent medicines: neem astringent, kutaja astringent, patola astringent, phaggava astringent, nattamāla astringent, or whatever other astringent medicines there may be that do not serve the purpose of a hard food (khādanīya) nor the purpose of a soft food (bhojanīya).’ (Mahāva. 263)

Ettha hi etesampi saṅgaho sijjhati. Vuttakasāvāni ca sabbakappiyānīti veditabbāni.

For in this statement, the inclusion of these items is also accomplished. And it should be known that the aforementioned astringents are all allowable.

Pattakhādanīye mūlakaṃ khārako caccu tambako taṇḍuleyyako papunnāgo vatthuleyyako vajakali jajjhari sellu siggu kāsamaddako ummācīnamuggo māso rājamāso ṭhapetvā mahānipphāvaṃ avasesanipphāvo aggimantho sunisannako setavaraṇo nāḷikā bhūmiyaṃ jātaloṇīti etesaṃ pattāni, aññāni ca evarūpāni tesu tesu janapadesu pakatiāhāravasena manussānaṃ khādanīyatthañca bhojanīyatthañca pharaṇakāni pattāni ekaṃsena yāvakālikāni[V 0.0096], yā panaññā [M 0.0097] mahānakhapiṭṭhimattapaṇṇā loṇirukkhe ca gacche ca ārohati, tassā pattaṃ yāvajīvikaṃ. Brahmipattañca yāvakālikanti dīpavāsino vadanti. Ambapallavaṃ yāvakālikaṃ, asokapallavaṃ pana yāvajīvikaṃ. Yāni caññāni pāḷiyaṃ –

Regarding edible leaves: the leaves of radish, khāraka, caccu, tambaka, taṇḍuleyyaka, papunnāga, vatthuleyyaka, vajakali, jajjhari, sellu, siggu, kāsamaddaka, ummā, cīna, mugga, māsa, and rājamāsa; and, setting aside the mahānipphāva bean, the leaves of all remaining nipphāva beans, aggimantha, sunisannaka, setavaraṇa, nāḷikā, and the salt-herb that grows on the ground—the leaves of these plants, and other such leaves that in various regions serve as staple food for people, fulfilling the purpose of both hard and soft food, are definitely short-term allowances. But as for another salt-herb with leaves the size of a large fingernail, which climbs on trees and bushes, its leaf is a lifetime allowance. The leaf of the brahmi plant is also a short-term allowance—so say the dwellers of the island of Sri Lanka. The mango shoot is a short-term allowance, but the ashoka shoot is a lifetime allowance. And whatever other leaves are mentioned in the Pāli Canon—

“Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, paṇṇāni bhesajjāni nimbapaṇṇaṃ kuṭajapaṇṇaṃ paṭolapaṇṇaṃ sulasipaṇṇaṃ kappāsapaṇṇaṃ, yāni vā panaññānipi atthi paṇṇāni bhesajjāni neva khādanīye khādanīyatthaṃ pharanti, na bhojanīye bhojanīyatthaṃ pharantī”ti (mahāva. 263) –

‘I allow, monks, leaves as medicine: neem leaves, kutaja leaves, patola leaves, sulasi leaves, cotton leaves, and whatever other leaves there are that are medicinal, which do not serve the purpose of a hard food (khādanīya) nor the purpose of a soft food (bhojanīya).’ (Mahāva. 263)

Vuttāni, tāni yāvajīvikāni. Na kevalañca paṇṇāni, tesaṃ pupphaphalānipi. Yāvajīvikapaṇṇānaṃ pana phaggavapaṇṇaṃ ajjukapaṇṇaṃ phaṇijjakapaṇṇaṃ tambūlapaṇṇaṃ paduminipaṇṇanti evaṃ gaṇanavasena anto natthi.

Those leaves that have been mentioned are lifetime allowances. And not only the leaves, but their flowers and fruits are also lifetime allowances. However, among the leaves that are lifetime allowances, there is no end to the enumeration of such leaves as the phaggava leaf, the ajjuka leaf, the phaṇijjaka leaf, the tambūla leaf, and the paduminī leaf.

Pupphakhādanīye mūlakapupphaṃ khārakapupphaṃ caccupupphaṃ tambakapupphaṃ vajakalipupphaṃ jajjharipupphaṃ cūḷanipphāvapupphaṃ mahānipphāvapupphaṃ kaserukapupphaṃ nāḷikeratālaketakānaṃ taruṇapupphāni setavaraṇapupphaṃ siggupupphaṃ uppalapadumajātikānaṃ pupphānaṃ kaṇṇikāmattaṃ agandhipupphaṃ karīrapupphaṃ jīvantī pupphanti evamādi tesu tesu janapadesu pakatiāhāravasena manussānaṃ khādanīyatthaṃ bhojanīyatthañca pharaṇapupphaṃ yāvakālikaṃ, asokabakulakuyyakapunnāgacampakajātikaravīrakaṇikārakundanavamālikamallikādīnaṃ pana pupphaṃ yāvajīvikaṃ, tassa gaṇanāya anto natthi. Pāḷiyaṃ panassa kasāvabhesajjena saṅgaho veditabbo.

Regarding edible flowers: the flowers of radish, khāraka, caccu, tambaka, vajakali, jajjhari, cūḷanipphāva, mahānipphāva, kaseruka; the tender flowers of coconut, palmyra, and ketaka; setavaraṇa flowers; siggu flowers; only the pericarp of flowers of the water-lily and lotus varieties; scentless flowers; karīra flowers; jīvantī flowers—and so on. In various regions, such flowers that serve as 'khādanīya' and 'bhojanīya' for people as their natural food are allowable until midday. However, flowers such as asoka, bakula, kuyyaka, punnāga, campaka, jātī, karavīra, kaṇikāra, kunda, navamālikā, mallikā, and others are allowable for life. There is no end to their enumeration. In the Pāḷi, however, their inclusion should be understood by way of astringent medicine.

Phalakhādanīye panasalabujatālanāḷikeraambajambuambāṭakatintiṇikamātuluṅgakapitthalābukumbhaṇḍapussaphalatimbarūsakatipusavātiṅgaṇacocamocamadhukādīnaṃ phalāni, yāni loke tesu tesu janapadesu pakatiāhāravasena manussānaṃ khādanīyatthaṃ bhojanīyatthañca pharanti, sabbāni tāni yāvakālikāni, nāmagaṇanavasena tesaṃ na sakkā pariyantaṃ dassetuṃ. Yāni pana pāḷiyaṃ –

Regarding edible fruits: the fruits of jackfruit, breadfruit, palmyra, coconut, mango, rose apple, hog plum, tamarind, citron, wood apple, gourd, ash gourd, muskmelon, cluster fig, cucumber, eggplant, seeded banana, seedless banana, madhuca, and others. All those fruits that, in various regions, serve as 'khādanīya' and 'bhojanīya' for people as their natural food are allowable until midday. It is not possible to provide a complete list by name and number. However, those in the Pāḷi—

“Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, phalāni bhesajjāni bilaṅgaṃ pippaliṃ marīcaṃ harītakaṃ vibhītakaṃ āmalakaṃ goṭṭhaphalaṃ, yāni vā panaññānipi [M 0.0098] atthi phalāni bhesajjāni neva khādanīye khādanīyatthaṃ pharanti, na bhojanīye bhojanīyatthaṃ pharantī”ti (mahāva. 263) –

“Monks, I allow fruits that are medicinal: bilaṅga, pippali, marīca, harītaka, vibhītaka, āmalaka, goṭṭhaphala, and whatever other fruits there are that are medicinal, which do not serve as an edible food nor as a staple food.”

Vuttāni[V 0.0097], tāni yāvajīvikāni. Tesampi aparipakkāni acchivabimbavaraṇaketakakāsmarīādīnaṃ phalāni jātiphalaṃ kaṭukaphalaṃ eḷā takkolanti evaṃ nāmavasena na sakkā pariyantaṃ dassetuṃ.

Those fruits that have been mentioned are allowable for life. Also, of these, the unripe fruits of such plants as acchiva, bimba, varaṇa, ketaka, kāsmarī, and others; as well as jātiphala, kaṭukaphala, eḷā, and takkola—thus it is not possible to provide a complete list by name.

Aṭṭhikhādanīye labujaṭṭhi panasaṭṭhi ambāṭakaṭṭhi sālaṭṭhi khajjūrīketakatimbarūsakānaṃ taruṇaphalaṭṭhi tintiṇikaṭṭhi bimbaphalaṭṭhi uppalapadumajātīnaṃ pokkharaṭṭhīti evamādīni tesu tesu janapadesu manussānaṃ pakatiāhāravasena khādanīyatthaṃ bhojanīyatthañca pharaṇakāni aṭṭhīni yāvakālikāni, madhukaṭṭhi punnāgaṭṭhi harītakādīnaṃ aṭṭhīni siddhatthakaṭṭhi rājikaṭṭhīti evamādīni aṭṭhīni yāvajīvikāni. Tesaṃ pāḷiyaṃ phalabhesajjeneva saṅgaho veditabbo.

Regarding edible seeds: the seeds of breadfruit, jackfruit, hog plum, and sal; the young fruit seeds of date palm, ketaka, and cluster fig; tamarind seeds, bimba fruit seeds, and the seeds of lotus varieties such as uppala and paduma—these and similar seeds that people in various regions consume as natural food, fulfilling the purpose of both hard and soft food, are allowable until midday. The seeds of madhuca, punnāga, harītaka and so on, red mustard seeds, and white mustard seeds—these and similar seeds are allowable for life. In the Pāḷi, their inclusion should be understood only under the category of medicinal fruit.

Piṭṭhakhādanīye sattannaṃ tāva dhaññānaṃ dhaññānulomānaṃ aparaṇṇānañca piṭṭhaṃ panasapiṭṭhaṃ labujapiṭṭhaṃ ambāṭakapiṭṭhaṃ sālapiṭṭhaṃ dhotakatālapiṭṭhaṃ khīravallipiṭṭhañcāti evamādīni tesu tesu janapadesu pakatiāhāravasena manussānaṃ khādanīyatthaṃ bhojanīyatthañca pharaṇakāni piṭṭhāni yāvakālikāni, adhotakaṃ tālapiṭṭhaṃ khīravallipiṭṭhaṃ assagandhādipiṭṭhāni ca yāvajīvikāni. Tesaṃ pāḷiyaṃ kasāvehi mūlaphalehi ca saṅgaho veditabbo.

Regarding edible flours: firstly, the flour of the seven grains, of that which conforms to the grains, and of pulses; jackfruit flour, breadfruit flour, hog plum flour, sal fruit flour, washed palmyra flour, and khīravalli flour—these and similar flours that people in various regions consume as natural food, fulfilling the purpose of both hard and soft food, are allowable until midday. Unwashed palmyra flour, khīravalli flour, assagandhā flour, and so on, are allowable for life. In the Pāḷi, their inclusion should be understood under the categories of astringents, and roots and fruits.

Niyyāsakhādanīye – eko ucchuniyyāsova sattāhakāliko, sesā –

Regarding edible saps: only sugarcane sap is allowable for seven days; the rest—

“Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, jatūni bhesajjāni hiṅguṃ hiṅgujatuṃ hiṅgusipāṭikaṃ takaṃ takapattiṃ takapaṇṇiṃ sajjulasaṃ, yāni vā panaññānipi atthi jatūni bhesajjānī”ti (mahāva. 263) –

“Monks, I allow resins that are medicines: hiṅgu, hiṅgujatu, hiṅgusipāṭikaṃ, taka, takapattiṃ, takapaṇṇiṃ, sajjulasaṃ; and whatever other resins there are that are medicines.”

Evaṃ pāḷiyaṃ vuttā niyyāsā yāvajīvikā. Tattha yevāpanakavasena saṅgahitānaṃ ambaniyyāso kaṇikāraniyyāsoti evaṃ nāmavasena na sakkā pariyantaṃ dassetuṃ. Evaṃ imesu mūlakhādanīyādīsu yaṃ kiñci yāvakālikaṃ, sabbampi imasmiṃ atthe avasesaṃ khādanīyaṃ nāmāti saṅgahitaṃ.

Thus, the saps mentioned in the Pāḷi are allowable for life. Among these, those included by way of the general clause ‘yevāpanaka’—such as mango sap and kaṇikāra sap—cannot be exhaustively listed by name. Thus, among these edible roots and so on, whatever is allowable until midday is all included in this context under the term ‘remaining edible’.

91. Yāmakālikesu [M 0.0099] pana aṭṭha pānāni nāma ambapānaṃ jambupānaṃ cocapānaṃ mocapānaṃ madhukapānaṃ muddikapānaṃ sālūkapānaṃ phārusakapānanti imāni aṭṭha pānāni. Tattha (mahāva. aṭṭha. 300) ambapānanti āmehi vā pakkehi vā ambehi katapānaṃ. Tattha āmehi karontena [V 0.0098] ambataruṇāni bhinditvā udake pakkhipitvā ātape ādiccapākena pacitvā parissāvetvā tadahupaṭiggahitakehi madhusakkārakappūrādīhi yojetvā kātabbaṃ, evaṃ kataṃ purebhattameva kappati. Anupasampannehi kataṃ labhitvā pana purebhattaṃ paṭiggahitaṃ purebhattaṃ sāmisaparibhogenapi vaṭṭati, pacchābhattaṃ nirāmisaparibhogena yāva aruṇuggamanā vaṭṭati. Esa nayo sabbapānesu. Jambupānanti jambuphalehi katapānaṃ. Cocapānanti aṭṭhikakadaliphalehi katapānaṃ. Mocapānanti anaṭṭhikehi kadaliphalehi katapānaṃ. Madhukapānanti madhukānaṃ jātirasena katapānaṃ. Taṃ pana udakasambhinnaṃ vaṭṭati, suddhaṃ na vaṭṭati. Muddikapānanti muddikā udake madditvā ambapānaṃ viya katapānaṃ. Sālūkapānanti rattuppalanīluppalādīnaṃ sālūke madditvā katapānaṃ. Phārusakapānanti phārusakaphalehi ambapānaṃ viya katapānaṃ. Imāni aṭṭha pānāni sītānipi ādiccapākānipi vaṭṭanti, aggipākāni na vaṭṭanti.

91. Now, among the drinks allowable for a watch of the night, there are eight kinds of drinks: mango drink, jambu drink, seeded banana drink, seedless banana drink, madhuka drink, grape drink, lotus-root drink, and phārusaka drink. Here, 'mango drink' means a drink made with raw or ripe mangoes. When made with raw mangoes, young mangoes should be crushed, placed in water, cooked by the heat of the sun, strained, and then mixed with honey, sugar, camphor, and so forth, received that same day. Prepared thus, it is allowable only before the midday meal. However, having received a drink made by the non-ordained: if it is received before the meal, it is allowable before the meal even when consumed with food; after the meal, it is allowable until the rising of the dawn only when consumed without food. This is the rule for all drinks. 'Jambu drink' is a drink made with jambu fruits. 'Seeded banana drink' is a drink made with seeded banana fruits. 'Seedless banana drink' is a drink made with seedless banana fruits. 'Madhuka drink' is a drink made with the natural juice of madhuka fruits. However, it is allowable when mixed with water; pure, it is not allowable. 'Grape drink' is a drink made by crushing grapes in water, similar to mango drink. 'Lotus-root drink' is a drink made by crushing the roots of red lotuses, blue lotuses, and so forth. 'Phārusaka drink' is a drink made with phārusaka fruits, similar to mango drink. These eight drinks are allowable whether cooled or heated by the sun, but they are not allowable if cooked over a fire.

Avasesāni vettatintiṇikamātuluṅgakapitthakosambakaramandādikhuddakaphalapānāni aṭṭhapānagaakāneva. Tāni kiñcāpi pāḷiyaṃ na vuttāni, atha kho kappiyaṃ anulomenti, tasmā kappanti. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, sabbaṃ phalarasaṃ ṭhapetvā dhaññaphalarasa”nti (mahāva. aṭṭha. 300) vuttattā ṭhapetvā sānulomadhaññaphalarasaṃ aññaṃ phalapānaṃ nāma akappiyaṃ natthi, sabbaṃ yāmakālikameva. Tattha sānulomadhaññaphalaraso nāma sattannañceva dhaññānaṃ tālanāḷikerapanasalabujaalābukumbhaṇḍapussaphalatipusaeḷālukāti navannañca mahāphalānaṃ sabbesañca pubbaṇṇāparaṇṇānaṃ anulomadhaññānaṃ raso yāvakāliko, tasmā pacchābhattaṃ na vaṭṭati. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, sabbaṃ pattarasaṃ ṭhapetvā ḍākarasa”nti (mahāva. 300) vuttattā pakkaḍākarasaṃ ṭhapetvā yāvakālikapattānampi sītodakena madditvā kataraso vā ādiccapāko vā vaṭṭati. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, sabbaṃ puppharasaṃ ṭhapetvā madhukapuppharasa”nti vuttattā madhukapuppharasaṃ ṭhapetvā sabbopi puppharaso vaṭṭati.

The remaining minor fruit drinks—such as those of vetta, tintiṇika, citron, wood apple, kosamba, karamanda, and so forth—are of the same category as the eight drinks. Although these are not explicitly mentioned in the Pāḷi, they are allowable because they conform to what is permissible. Therefore, they are allowable. Since it is stated, 'Bhikkhus, I allow all fruit juices except for the juice of grain-fruit,' it follows that, apart from the juice of grain-fruit and that which is analogous to it, there is no other fruit drink that is impermissible; all are allowable from after midday until the next dawn. Here, 'the juice of grain-fruit and that which is analogous to it' refers to the juice of the seven types of grain, the nine great fruits—namely palmyra, coconut, jackfruit, breadfruit, gourd, ash gourd, muskmelon, cucumber, and eḷāluka—and all early and late crops which are analogous to grain. Their juice is allowable only until midday; therefore, it is not permitted after the midday meal. Since it is stated, 'Bhikkhus, I allow all leaf-juices except for the juice of cooked leaves,' it follows that, apart from the juice of cooked leaves, the juice of even leaves that are allowable only until midday, made by crushing them with cold water or prepared by the heat of the sun, is allowable. Since it is stated, 'Bhikkhus, I allow all flower-juices except for the juice of the madhuka flower,' it follows that, apart from the juice of the madhuka flower, all other flower-juices are allowable.

92. Sattāhakālikaṃ [M 0.0100] nāma sappi navanītaṃ telaṃ madhu phāṇitanti imāni pañca bhesajjāni. Tattha sappi nāma gosappi vā ajikāsappi vā mahiṃsasappi vā yesaṃ maṃsaṃ kappati, tesaṃ sappi. Navanītaṃ nāma tesaṃyeva navanītaṃ. Telaṃ nāma tilatelaṃ sāsapatelaṃ madhukatelaṃ eraṇḍatelaṃ vasātelaṃ. Madhu nāma makkhikāmadhu. Phāṇitaṃ nāma ucchumhā nibbattaṃ (paci. 260). Yāvajīvikaṃ pana heṭṭhā yāvakālike mūlakhādanīyādīsu vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ.

92. That which is allowable for seven days refers to these five medicines: ghee, fresh butter, oil, honey, and molasses. Herein, ghee means cow's ghee, goat's ghee, or buffalo's ghee; that is, the ghee of those animals whose flesh is permissible. Fresh butter means the fresh butter from those same animals. Oil means sesame oil, mustard oil, madhuca oil, castor oil, and tallow. Honey means the honey of bees. Molasses means that which is produced from sugarcane. As for that which is allowable for life, it should be understood according to the method stated previously in the section on items allowable until midday, concerning root-foods and so on.

93. Tattha [V 0.0099] (pāci. aṭṭha. 256) aruṇodaye paṭiggahitaṃ yāvakālikaṃ satakkhattumpi nidahitvā yāva kālo nātikkamati, tāva paribhuñjituṃ vaṭṭati, yāmakālikaṃ ekaṃ ahorattaṃ, sattāhakālikaṃ sattarattaṃ, itaraṃ sati paccaye yāvajīvampi paribhuñjituṃ vaṭṭati. Paṭiggahetvā ekarattaṃ vītināmitaṃ pana yaṃ kiñci yāvakālikaṃ vā yāmakālikaṃ vā ajjhoharitukāmatāya gaṇhantassa paṭiggahaṇe tāva dukkaṭaṃ, ajjhoharato pana ekamekasmiṃ ajjhohāre sannidhipaccayā pācittiyaṃ. Sacepi patto duddhoto hoti, yaṃ aṅguliyā ghaṃsantassa lekhā paññāyati, gaṇṭhikapattassa vā gaṇṭhikantare sneho paviṭṭho hoti, so uṇhe otāpentassa paggharati, uṇhayāguyā vā gahitāya sandissati, tādise pattepi punadivase bhuñjantassa pācittiyaṃ, tasmā pattaṃ dhovitvā puna tattha acchodakaṃ vā āsiñcitvā aṅguliyā vā ghaṃsitvā nisnehabhāvo jānitabbo. Sace hi udake vā snehabhāvo, patte vā aṅgulilekhā paññāyati, duddhoto hoti, telavaṇṇapatte pana aṅgulilekhā paññāyati, sā abbohārikā. Yampi bhikkhū nirapekkhā sāmaṇerānaṃ pariccajanti, tañce sāmaṇerā nidahitvā denti, sabbaṃ vaṭṭati. Sayaṃ paṭiggahetvā apariccattameva hi dutiyadivase na vaṭṭati. Tato hi ekasitthampi ajjhoharato pācittiyameva. Akappiyamaṃsesu manussamaṃse thullaccayena saddhiṃ pācittiyaṃ, avasesesu dukkaṭena saddhiṃ.

93. There, among these, food allowable until midday (yāvakālika), received at dawn, can be consumed as long as midday has not passed, even if stored a hundred times. Food allowable for a watch (yāmakālika) is for one day and night; food allowable for seven days (sattāhakālika) is for seven days; and the other kind (yāvajīvika), if there is a cause, such as illness, can be consumed for life. However, if any item, whether allowable until midday or for a watch, is received and kept overnight, then for one who takes it with the intention of consuming it, a dukkaṭa offense is incurred at the time of taking. For one who then consumes it, a pācittiya offense is incurred for each mouthful due to storing. Even if the bowl is badly washed, so that when rubbed with a finger, a streak is visible, or if grease has seeped into the crevices of a mended bowl and drips when warmed, or if it is noticeable when hot gruel is received—consuming from such a bowl the next day incurs a pācittiya offense. Therefore, having washed the bowl, one should ascertain that it is free from grease by pouring clear water into it or by rubbing it with a finger. For if a state of greasiness appears in the water, or a finger-streak appears on the bowl, it is considered badly washed. However, in a bowl the color of oil, a finger-streak may appear, but it is not a factor for an offense. Whatever food monks, being unconcerned, relinquish to novices, if those novices store it and then give it, all of it is allowable. For it is only that which one has received oneself and not relinquished to laypeople or novices that is not allowable on the second day. From that, consuming even a single lump of rice is a pācittiya offense. Among the unallowable meats, for human flesh, there is a pācittiya offense together with a thullaccaya offense; for the remaining kinds, a pācittiya offense together with a dukkaṭa offense.

Yāmakālikaṃ sati paccaye ajjhoharato pācittiyaṃ, āhāratthāya ajjhoharato dukkaṭena saddhiṃ pācittiyaṃ. Sace pavārito hutvā anatirittakataṃ ajjhoharati, pakatiāmise dve pācittiyāni, manussamaṃse thullaccayena saddhiṃ dve, sesaakappiyamaṃse dukkaṭena saddhiṃ. Yāmakālikaṃ sati [M 0.0101] paccaye sāmisena mukhena ajjhoharato dve, nirāmisena ekameva. Āhāratthāya ajjhoharato vikappadvayepi dukkaṭaṃ vaḍḍhati. Sace vikāle ajjhoharati, pakatibhojane sannidhipaccayā ca vikālabhojanapaccayā ca dve pācittiyāni, akappiyamaṃse thullaccayaṃ dukkaṭañca vaḍḍhati. Yāmakālike vikālapaccayā anāpatti. Anatirittapaccayā pana vikāle sabbavikappesu anāpatti.

For one who consumes a yāmakālika item when there is a reason, there is a pācittiya offense. For one who consumes it for the sake of nourishment, there is a pācittiya offense together with a dukkaṭa offense. If, having been satisfied, one consumes what has not been made surplus: for ordinary alms-food, there are two pācittiya offenses; for human flesh, two pācittiya offenses together with a thullaccaya offense; for the remaining unallowable flesh, two pācittiya offenses together with a dukkaṭa offense. For one who consumes a yāmakālika item when there is a reason with a mouth containing alms-food, there are two pācittiya offenses; with a mouth without alms-food, there is only one pācittiya offense. For one who consumes it for the sake of nourishment, a dukkaṭa offense is added in both alternatives. If one consumes at the wrong time: for ordinary food, there are two pācittiya offenses, one due to the factor of storing and one due to the factor of eating at the wrong time; for unallowable flesh, a thullaccaya offense and a dukkaṭa offense are added. For a yāmakālika item, there is no offense due to the factor of the wrong time. However, due to the factor of not making it surplus, there is no offense in all alternatives at the wrong time.

Sattāhakālikaṃ pana yāvajīvikañca āhāratthāya paṭiggaṇhato paṭiggaṇhanapaccayā tāva dukkaṭaṃ, ajjhoharato pana sace nirāmisaṃ hoti, ajjhohāre dukkaṭaṃ. Atha āmisasaṃsaṭṭhaṃ paṭiggahetvā ṭhapitaṃ hoti, yathāvatthukaṃ pācittiyameva.

Now, regarding a sattāhakālika item and a yāvajīvika item: for one who receives it for the sake of nourishment, there is first a dukkaṭa offense due to the factor of receiving. But for one who consumes it, if it is unmixed with alms-food, there is a dukkaṭa offense for every swallow. Now, if what is mixed with alms-food has been received and stored, there is only a pācittiya offense, according to the item.

94. Sattāhakālikesu pana sappiādīsu ayaṃ vinicchayo (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.622) – sappi [V 0.0100] tāva purebhattaṃ paṭiggahitaṃ tadahupurebhattaṃ sāmisampi nirāmisampi paribhuñjituṃ vaṭṭati, pacchābhattato paṭṭhāya sattāhaṃ nirāmisaṃ paribhuñjitabbaṃ. Sattāhātikkame sace ekabhājane ṭhapitaṃ, ekaṃ nissaggiyaṃ. Sace bahūsu, vatthugaṇanāya nissaggiyāni. Pacchābhattaṃ paṭiggahitaṃ nirāmisameva vaṭṭati, purebhattaṃ vā pacchābhattaṃ vā uggahitakaṃ katvā nikkhittaṃ ajjhoharituṃ na vaṭṭati, abbhañjanādīsu upanetabbaṃ. Sattāhātikkamepi anāpatti anajjhoharaṇīyataṃ āpannattā. Sace anupasampanno purebhattaṃ paṭiggahitanavanītena sappiṃ katvā deti, purebhattaṃ sāmisampi vaṭṭati, sace sayaṃ karoti, sattāhampi nirāmisameva vaṭṭati. Pacchābhattaṃ paṭiggahitanavanītena yena kenaci katasappi sattāhampi nirāmisameva vaṭṭati, uggahitakena kate pubbe vuttasuddhasappinayeneva vinicchayo veditabbo. Purebhattaṃ paṭiggahitakhīrena vā dadhinā vā katasappi anupasampannena kataṃ sāmisampi tadahupurebhattaṃ vaṭṭati, sayaṃkataṃ nirāmisameva vaṭṭati.

94. Concerning ghee and other items allowed for seven days, this is the ruling: As for ghee, if received before noon, it is allowable to consume it on that day before noon either with or without staple food. Starting from after noon, it should be consumed without staple food for seven days. If the seven days are exceeded, and if it was placed in a single container, it is one item for forfeiture. If in many containers, there are items for forfeiture according to the number of containers. Ghee received after noon is allowable only without staple food. If, having been received either before or after noon, it is set aside, thus invalidating the reception, it is not allowable to consume; it should be used for anointing and so forth. Even when the seven days are exceeded, there is no offense because it has reached a state of being inconsumable.
