If an unordained person makes ghee with fresh butter that was received before noon and gives it, it is allowable with staple food before noon. If one makes it oneself, it is allowable only without staple food for the seven days. Ghee made with fresh butter received after noon, no matter by whom it is made, is allowable only without staple food for the seven days. If it is made from butter for which the reception was invalidated, the ruling should be understood according to the previously stated method for pure ghee. Ghee made from milk or curd received before noon, if made by an unordained person, is allowable with staple food on that day before noon; if made by oneself, it is allowable only without staple food.

95. Navanītaṃ tāpentassa hi sāmaṃpāko na hoti, sāmaṃpakkena pana tena saddhiṃ āmisaṃ na vaṭṭati, pacchābhattato paṭṭhāya ca na vaṭṭatiyeva. Sattāhātikkamepi anāpatti savatthukassa paṭiggahitattā. Pacchābhattaṃ paṭiggahitakehi kataṃ pana abbhañjanādīsu upanetabbaṃ. Purebhattampi ca uggahitakehi kataṃ, ubhayesampi sattāhātikkame anāpatti. Esa [M 0.0102] nayo akappiyamaṃsasappimhi. Ayaṃ pana viseso – yattha pāḷiyaṃ āgatasappinā nissaggiyaṃ, tattha iminā dukkaṭaṃ. Andhakaṭṭhakathāyaṃ kāraṇapatirūpakaṃ vatvā manussasappi ca navanītañca paṭikkhittaṃ, taṃ duppaṭikkhittaṃ sabbaaṭṭhakathāsu anuññātattā. Parato cassa vinicchayopi āgacchissati. Pāḷiyaṃ āgatanavanītampi purebhattaṃ paṭiggahitaṃ tadahupurebhattaṃ sāmisampi vaṭṭati, pacchābhattato paṭṭhāya nirāmisameva. Sattāhātikkame nānābhājanesu ṭhapite bhājanagaṇanāya, ekabhājanepi amissetvā piṇḍapiṇḍavasena ṭhapite piṇḍagaṇanāya nissaggiyāni. Pacchābhattaṃ paṭiggahitaṃ sappinayena veditabbaṃ. Ettha pana dadhiguḷikāyopi takkabindūnipi honti, tasmā dhotaṃ vaṭṭatīti upaḍḍhattherā āhaṃsu. Mahāsivatthero pana “bhagavatā anuññātakālato paṭṭhāya takkato uddhaṭamattameva khādiṃsū”ti āha. Tasmā navanītaṃ paribhuñjantena dhovitvā dadhitakkamakkhikākipillikādīni apanetvā paribhuñjitabbaṃ. Pacitvā sappiṃ katvā paribhuñjitukāmena adhotampi paribhuñjituṃ vaṭṭati. Yaṃ tattha dadhigataṃ vā takkagataṃ vā, taṃ khayaṃ gamissati. Ettāvatā hi savatthukapaṭiggahitaṃ nāma na hotīti ayamettha adhippāyo. Āmisena saddhiṃ pakkattā pana tasmimpi kukkuccāyanti kukkuccakā. Idāni uggahetvā ṭhapitanavanīte ca purebhattaṃ khīradadhīni paṭiggahetvā katanavanīte [V 0.0101] ca pacchābhattaṃ tāni paṭiggahetvā katanavanīte ca uggahitakehi katanavanīte ca akappiyamaṃsanavanīte ca sabbo āpattānāpattiparibhogāparibhoganayo sappimhi vuttakkameneva gahetabbo. Telabhikkhāya paviṭṭhānaṃ pana bhikkhūnaṃ tattheva sappimpi navanītampi pakkatelampi apakkatelampi ākiranti. Tattha takkadadhibindūnipi bhattasitthānipi taṇḍulakaṇāpi makkhikādayopi honti, ādiccapākaṃ katvā parissāvetvā gahitaṃ sattāhakālikaṃ hoti. Paṭiggahetvā ca ṭhapitabhesajjehi saddhiṃ pacitvā natthupānampi kātuṃ vaṭṭati. Sace vaddalisamaye lajjī sāmaṇero yathā tattha patitataṇḍulakaṇādayo na paccanti, evaṃ aggimhi vilīyāpetvā parissāvetvā puna pacitvā deti, purimanayeneva sattāhaṃ vaṭṭati.

95. For a monk who heats fresh butter, it does not become 'self-cooked'. However, with that which has become 'self-cooked', staple food is not allowable. And from after noon onward, it is not allowable at all. Even if seven days pass, there is no offense, because it was accepted together with its basis. However, what is prepared from items accepted after noon should be used for purposes such as anointing. And also in the case of what is prepared from items whose acceptance was broken, even if in the forenoon—in both cases, there is no offense even if seven days pass. This is the method for ghee from non-permissible flesh. However, this is the distinction: where, according to the Pāḷi, it is an offense of forfeiture with the ghee mentioned therein, with this ghee it is a dukkaṭa offense. In the Andhakaṭṭhakathā, having stated a plausible reason, human ghee and fresh butter are rejected. That rejection is a poor one, because they are permitted in all the commentaries. And a decision on this will come later. Regarding fresh butter mentioned in the Pāḷi, if accepted in the forenoon, it is allowable even with staple food during the forenoon of that day. From the afternoon onward, it is allowable only without staple food. If seven days are exceeded, when it is kept in various containers, the items are to be forfeited according to the number of containers. Even in a single container, if kept as lumps without being mixed, they are to be forfeited according to the number of lumps. What is accepted in the afternoon should be understood according to the method for ghee. Herein, there can also be small lumps of curd and drops of buttermilk; therefore, 'it is allowable when washed,' said the Upaḍḍha Theras. The Elder Mahāsiva, however, said: 'From the time it was permitted by the Blessed One, they ate only that which was just skimmed from the buttermilk.' Therefore, one consuming fresh butter should wash it, remove curd, buttermilk, flies, ants, and so on, and then consume it. For one who wishes to cook it into ghee and consume it, it is allowable to use it even unwashed. Whatever curd or buttermilk is in it will be destroyed. For merely by this, it does not become what is called 'accepted with its basis'—this is the intention here. However, because it was cooked together with edible matter, scrupulous people feel scrupulous even about that. Now, in the case of fresh butter that has been set aside after its acceptance was broken; and fresh butter made from milk and curd accepted in the forenoon; and fresh butter made from those items accepted in the afternoon; and fresh butter made from items whose acceptance was broken; and fresh butter from non-permissible flesh—the entire method concerning offense and no-offense, use and non-use, should be understood in the very same way as was stated for ghee. Moreover, for monks who have entered for an oil-almsround, people may pour into their very bowls ghee, fresh butter, cooked oil, and uncooked oil. Therein, there may be drops of buttermilk and curd, grains of cooked rice, particles of raw rice, flies, and so on. Having been heated by the sun, strained, and taken, it becomes a seven-day allowable. And having accepted it, it is allowable to cook it together with stored medicines and to make it into a nasal treatment or a drink. If, during a time of scarcity, a scrupulous novice, in such a way that the particles of raw rice and so on that have fallen in do not get cooked, melts it over a fire, strains it, cooks it again, and gives it, it is allowable for seven days according to the previous method.

96. Telesu tilatelaṃ tāva purebhattaṃ paṭiggahitaṃ purebhattaṃ sāmisampi vaṭṭati, pacchābhattato paṭṭhāya nirāmisameva vaṭṭati. Sattāhātikkame [M 0.0103] tassa bhājanagaṇanāya nissaggiyabhāvo veditabbo. Pacchābhattaṃ paṭiggahitaṃ sattāhaṃ nirāmisameva vaṭṭati, uggahitakaṃ katvā nikkhittaṃ ajjhoharituṃ na vaṭṭati, sīsamakkhanādīsu upanetabbaṃ, sattāhātikkamepi anāpatti. Purebhattaṃ tile paṭiggahetvā katatelaṃ purebhattaṃ sāmisampi vaṭṭati, pacchābhattato paṭṭhāya anajjhoharaṇīyaṃ hoti, sīsamakkhanādīsu upanetabbaṃ, sattāhātikkamepi anāpatti. Pacchābhattaṃ tile paṭiggahetvā katatelaṃ anajjhoharaṇīyameva savatthukapaṭiggahitattā. Sattāhātikkamepi anāpatti, sīsamakkhanādīsu upanetabbaṃ. Purebhattaṃ vā pacchābhattaṃ vā uggahitakatilehi katatelepi eseva nayo. Purebhattaṃ paṭiggahitatile bhajjitvā vā tilapiṭṭhaṃ vā sedetvā uṇhodakena vā temetvā katatelaṃ sace anupasampannena kataṃ, purebhattaṃ sāmisampi vaṭṭati, attanā kataṃ nibbaṭṭitattā purebhattaṃ nirāmisaṃ vaṭṭati, sāmaṃpakkattā sāmisaṃ na vaṭṭati. Savatthukapaṭiggahitattā pana pacchābhattato paṭṭhāya ubhayampi anajjhoharaṇīyaṃ, sīsamakkhanādīsu upanetabbaṃ, sattāhātikkamepi anāpatti. Yadi pana appaṃ uṇhodakaṃ hoti abbhukkiraṇamattaṃ, abbohārikaṃ hoti sāmaṃpākagaṇanaṃ na gacchati. Sāsapatelādīsupi avatthukapaṭiggahitesu avatthukatilatele vuttasadisova vinicchayo.

96. Regarding oils: Sesame oil received before noon is allowable before noon, even with staple food. From after noon onward, it is allowable only without staple food. If seven days pass, its forfeitable nature should be understood by counting the containers. Sesame oil received after noon is allowable for seven days only without staple food. Once taken up and put aside, it is not allowable to consume but may be used for anointing the head, etc. Even if seven days pass, there is no offense. Sesame oil made from sesame seeds received before noon is allowable before noon, even with staple food. From after noon onward, it becomes unfit for consumption but may be used for anointing the head, etc. Even if seven days pass, there is no offense. Sesame oil made from sesame seeds received after noon is entirely unfit for consumption because it was received with its basis. Even if seven days pass, there is no offense, and it may be used for anointing the head, etc. The same rule applies to sesame oil made from sesame seeds whose offering has lapsed, whether received before noon or after noon. If sesame oil is made from sesame seeds received before noon—whether by roasting the sesame seeds, steaming sesame flour, or soaking them in hot water—and if it is prepared by an unordained person, it is allowable before noon even with staple food. If prepared by oneself, because it has been extracted, it is allowable before noon without staple food; because it is 'self-cooked', it is not allowable with staple food. However, because it was received with its basis, from after noon onward, both types are unfit for consumption but may be used for anointing the head, etc. Even if seven days pass, there is no offense. If, however, only a small amount of hot water is used—just enough for sprinkling—it is considered insignificant and does not count as 'self-cooking'. For mustard oil and other such oils received without a basis, the ruling is the same as that stated for sesame oil received without a basis.

Sace pana purebhattaṃ paṭiggahitānaṃ sāsapādīnaṃ cuṇṇehi ādiccapākena sakkā telaṃ kātuṃ, taṃ purebhattaṃ sāmisampi vaṭṭati, pacchābhattato paṭṭhāya nirāmisameva vaṭṭati, sattāhātikkame nissaggiyaṃ. Yasmā pana sāsapamadhukacuṇṇāni sedetvā eraṇḍakaṭṭhīni ca bhajjitvā eva telaṃ karonti, tasmā etesaṃ telaṃ anupasampannehi kataṃ purebhattaṃ sāmisampi vaṭṭati, vatthūnaṃ yāvajīvikattā pana savatthukapaṭiggahaṇe doso natthi. Attanā kataṃ sattāhaṃ nirāmisaparibhogeneva [V 0.0102] paribhuñjitabbaṃ. Uggahitakehi kataṃ anajjhoharaṇīyaṃ, bāhiraparibhoge vaṭṭati, sattāhātikkamepi anāpatti. Telakaraṇatthāya sāsapamadhukaeraṇḍakaṭṭhīni paṭiggahetvā katatelaṃ sattāhakālikaṃ, dutiyadivase kataṃ chāhaṃ vaṭṭati, tatiyadivase kataṃ pañcāhaṃ vaṭṭati, catuttha, pañcama, chaṭṭha, sattamadivase kataṃ tadaheva vaṭṭati. Sace yāva aruṇassa uggamanā tiṭṭhati, nissaggiyaṃ, aṭṭhamadivase kataṃ anajjhoharaṇīyaṃ, anissaggiyattā pana bāhiraparibhoge [M 0.0104] vaṭṭati. Sacepi na karoti, telatthāya gahitasāsapādīnaṃ sattāhātikkame dukkaṭameva. Pāḷiyaṃ pana anāgatāni aññānipi nāḷikeranimbakosambakaramandādīnaṃ telāni atthi, tāni paṭiggahetvā sattāhaṃ atikkāmayato dukkaṭaṃ hoti. Ayametesu viseso – sesaṃ yāvakālikavatthuṃ yāvajīvikavatthuñca sallakkhetvā sāmaṃpākasavatthukapurebhattapacchābhattapaṭiggahitauggahitavatthuvidhānaṃ sabbaṃ vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ.

If, however, oil can be made from the powders of mustard seeds and so forth, received before noon, by heating in the sun, that oil is allowable even with a relish before noon. From after noon onwards, it is allowable only without a relish. On exceeding seven days, it is to be forfeited. However, since they make oil by steaming the powders of mustard and madhuka seeds, and by roasting castor beans, the oil from these, when made by the unordained, is allowable even with a relish before noon. Furthermore, as the base substances are for life-long use, there is no fault in receiving the oil together with its substance. Oil made by oneself should be consumed for seven days only without a relish. Oil made from items taken up without a formal offering is not to be swallowed; it is allowable for external use, and there is no offense even on exceeding seven days. Having received mustard seeds, madhuka seeds, and castor beans for the purpose of making oil, the oil made from them is a seven-day item. If made on the second day, it is allowable for six days; if made on the third day, for five days; if on the fourth day, for four days; if on the fifth day, for three days; if on the sixth day, for two days; and if made on the seventh day, it is allowable only on that very day. If it remains until the rising of the dawn, it is to be forfeited. Oil made on the eighth day is not to be swallowed; however, as it is not subject to forfeiture, it is allowable for external use. Even if one does not make the oil, for the mustard seeds and so forth that were received for the purpose of oil, on exceeding seven days, there is a dukkaṭa offense. Furthermore, in the Pāḷi, there are also other oils not mentioned, such as those from coconut, neem, kosamba, karamanda, and so forth. For one who receives these and allows them to exceed seven days, there is a dukkaṭa offense. This is the distinction among these. The remainder should be understood in the very manner already stated, having considered temporary items and life-long items, and all the procedures regarding self-cooked items, items received with their substance, items received before noon, items received after noon, and items taken up without a formal offering.

Vasātelaṃ nāma “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, pañca vasāni acchavasaṃ macchavasaṃ susukāvasaṃ sūkaravasaṃ gadrabhavasa”nti (mahāva. 262) evaṃ anuññātavasānaṃ telaṃ. Ettha ca “acchavasa”nti vacanena ṭhapetvā manussavasaṃ sabbesaṃ akappiyamaṃsānaṃ vasā anuññātā. Macchaggahaṇena ca susukāpi gahitā honti, vāḷamacchattā pana visuṃ vuttaṃ. Macchādiggahaṇena cettha sabbesampi kappiyamaṃsānaṃ vasā anuññātā. Maṃsesu hi dasa manussahatthiassasunakhaahisīhabyagghadīpiacchataracchānaṃ maṃsāni akappiyāni, vasāsu ekā manussavasā. Khīrādīsu akappiyaṃ nāma natthi. Anupasampannehi kataṃ nibbaṭṭitaṃ vasātelaṃ purebhattaṃ paṭiggahitaṃ purebhattaṃ sāmisampi vaṭṭati, pacchābhattato paṭṭhāya sattāhaṃ nirāmisameva vaṭṭati. Yaṃ pana tattha sukhumarajasadisaṃ maṃsaṃ vā nhāru vā aṭṭhi vā lohitaṃ vā hoti, taṃ abbohārikaṃ. Sace pana vasaṃ paṭiggahetvā sayaṃ karoti, purebhattaṃ paṭiggahetvā pacitvā parissāvetvā sattāhaṃ nirāmisaparibhogena paribhuñjitabbaṃ. Nirāmisaparibhogañhi sandhāya idaṃ vuttaṃ “kāle paṭiggahitaṃ kāle nippakkaṃ kāle saṃsaṭṭhaṃ telaparibhogena paribhuñjitu”nti (mahāva. 262). Tatrāpi abbohārikaṃ abbohārikameva, pacchābhattaṃ pana paṭiggahetuṃ vā kātuṃ vā na vaṭṭatiyeva. Vuttañhetaṃ –

Fat-oil is the oil from fats permitted thus: 'I allow, O monks, five fats: bear fat, fish fat, crocodile fat, pig fat, and donkey fat' (Mahāvagga 262). Herein, by the word 'bear fat', the fat of all animals with unallowable meat is permitted, with the exception of human fat. And by the inclusion of 'fish', crocodiles are also included; however, because they are fierce fish, this is stated separately. And herein, by the inclusion of 'fish' and so on, the fats of all animals with allowable meat are also permitted. For among meats, the meats of ten beings—humans, elephants, horses, dogs, snakes, lions, tigers, leopards, bears, and hyenas—are unallowable; among fats, only human fat is unallowable. In milk and similar products, there is nothing unallowable. Fat-oil prepared by non-ordained persons, extracted and received before noon, may be used with relish before noon. From after noon onward, it may be used only without relish for seven days. However, any fine particles resembling dust—whether flesh, sinew, bone, or blood—are unusable. If one receives the fat and prepares it oneself, it should be received before noon, cooked, strained, and consumed without relish for seven days. For it was with reference to consumption without relish that this was said: 'Received at the proper time, cooked at the proper time, mixed at the proper time, it may be consumed with the use of oil' (Mahāvagga 262). Even in that case, what is unusable remains unusable. However, it is not at all permissible to receive or prepare it after noon. For this was said—

“Vikāle ce, bhikkhave, paṭiggahitaṃ vikāle nippakkaṃ vikāle saṃsaṭṭhaṃ, taṃ ce paribhuñjeyya, āpatti tiṇṇaṃ dukkaṭānaṃ. Kāle ce, bhikkhave, paṭiggahitaṃ vikāle nippakkaṃ vikāle saṃsaṭṭhaṃ, taṃ ce paribhuñjeyya, āpatti dvinnaṃ dukkaṭānaṃ. Kāle ce, bhikkhave, paṭiggahitaṃ kāle nippakkaṃ vikāle saṃsaṭṭhaṃ, taṃ ce paribhuñjeyya, āpatti dukkaṭassa[V 0.0103]. Kāle ce, bhikkhave, paṭiggahitaṃ kāle nippakkaṃ kāle saṃsaṭṭhaṃ, taṃ ce paribhuñjeyya, anāpattī”ti (mahāva. 262).

“Bhikkhus, if it is received at the wrong time, cooked at the wrong time, and mixed at the wrong time, should one consume it, one incurs an offense of three dukkaṭas. Bhikkhus, if it is received at the right time, cooked at the wrong time, and mixed at the wrong time, should one consume it, one incurs an offense of two dukkaṭas. Bhikkhus, if it is received at the right time, cooked at the right time, but mixed at the wrong time, should one consume it, one incurs an offense of a dukkaṭa. Bhikkhus, if it is received at the right time, cooked at the right time, and mixed at the right time, should one consume it, there is no offense.”

Upatissattheraṃ [M 0.0105] pana antevāsikā pucchiṃsu “bhante, sappinavanītavasāni ekato pacitvā nibbaṭṭitāni vaṭṭanti, na vaṭṭantī”ti? “Na vaṭṭanti, āvuso”ti. Thero kirettha pakkatelakasaṭe viya kukkuccāyati. Tato naṃ uttari pucchiṃsu “bhante, navanīte dadhiguḷikā vā takkabindu vā hoti, etaṃ vaṭṭatī”ti? “Etampi, āvuso, na vaṭṭatī”ti. Tato naṃ āhaṃsu “bhante, ekato pacitvā ekato saṃsaṭṭhāni tejavantāni honti, rogaṃ niggaṇhantī”ti. “Sādhāvuso”ti thero sampaṭicchi. Mahāsumatthero panāha “kappiyamaṃsavasāva sāmisaparibhoge vaṭṭati, itarā nirāmisaparibhoge vaṭṭatī”ti. Mahāpadumatthero pana “idaṃ ki”nti paṭikkhipitvā “nanu vātābādhikā bhikkhū pañcamūlakasāvayāguyaṃ acchasūkaratelādīni pakkhipitvā yāguṃ pivanti, sā tejussadattā rogaṃ niggaṇhātī”ti vatvā “vaṭṭatī”ti āha.

The disciples then asked the Elder Upatissa, ‘Venerable sir, when ghee, fresh butter, and tallow are cooked together and extracted, are they allowable, or not?’ ‘They are not allowable, friends,’ he replied. The elder, it is said, felt scruple in this matter as if at burnt oil-dregs. Then they further asked him, ‘Venerable sir, if there is a lump of curd or a drop of buttermilk in the fresh butter, is that allowable?’ ‘This too, friends, is not allowable,’ he replied. Then they said to him, ‘Venerable sir, when cooked together and mixed together, they become potent and suppress illness.’ ‘Good, friends,’ the elder agreed. But the Elder Mahāsumana said, ‘Tallow from allowable meat is allowable only for consumption with relish; the other is allowable for consumption without relish.’ The Elder Mahāpaduma, however, rejected this, saying, ‘What is this?’ and then added, ‘Surely, bhikkhus afflicted with wind-illness drink gruel, having added bear fat, pig oil, and the like to a decoction-gruel of the five roots. Due to its potency, it suppresses the illness.’ Having said this, he declared, ‘It is allowable.’

97. Madhu nāma madhukarīhi madhumakkhikāhi khuddakamakkhikāhi bhamaramakkhikāhi ca kataṃ madhu. Taṃ purebhattaṃ paṭiggahitaṃ purebhattaṃ sāmisaparibhogampi vaṭṭati, pacchābhattato paṭṭhāya sattāhaṃ nirāmisaparibhogameva vaṭṭati, sattāhātikkame nissaggiyaṃ. Sace silesasadisaṃ mahāmadhuṃ khaṇḍaṃ katvā ṭhapitaṃ, itaraṃ vā nānābhājanesu, vatthugaṇanāya nissaggiyāni. Sace ekameva khaṇḍaṃ, ekabhājane vā itaraṃ, ekameva nissaggiyaṃ. Uggahitakaṃ vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ, arumakkhanādīsu upanetabbaṃ. Madhupaṭalaṃ vā madhusitthakaṃ vā sace madhunā amakkhitaṃ parisuddhaṃ, yāvajīvikaṃ, madhumakkhitaṃ pana madhugatikameva. Cīrikā nāma sapakkhā dīghamakkhikā tumbaḷanāmikā ca aṭṭhipakkhikā kāḷamahābhamarā honti, tesaṃ āsayesu niyyāsasadisaṃ madhu hoti, taṃ yāvajīvikaṃ.

97. Honey is that which is made by honey-making bees, honey-flies, small bees, and bumblebees. That honey, if received before noon, is allowable for consumption with staple food before noon; from after noon onward, it is allowable only for consumption without staple food for seven days. Upon exceeding seven days, it is to be forfeited. If a large, gum-like honey is made into pieces and stored, or the other kind is stored in various containers, they are to be forfeited according to the number of items. If it is only one piece, or the other kind is in one container, it is only one item to be forfeited. An invalidated offering should be understood in the manner previously stated; it may be used for anointing wounds and so forth. Honeycomb or beeswax, if pure and not smeared with honey, is allowable for life. But if smeared with honey, it follows the same rule as honey. There are winged bees called Cīrikā, long-winged bees called Tumbaḷa, and large black bumblebees with bone-like wings. In their habitats, there is a honey similar to resin, and that is allowable for life.

98. Phāṇitaṃ nāma ucchurasaṃ upādāya apakkā vā avatthukapakkā vā sabbāpi avatthukā ucchuvikati. Taṃ phāṇitaṃ purebhattaṃ paṭiggahitaṃ purebhattaṃ sāmisampi vaṭṭati, pacchābhattato paṭṭhāya sattāhaṃ nirāmisameva vaṭṭati, sattāhātikkame vatthugaṇanāya nissaggiyaṃ. Bahū piṇḍā cuṇṇe katvā ekabhājane pakkhittā honti ghanasannivesā, ekameva nissaggiyaṃ. Uggahitakaṃ vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ, gharadhūpanādīsu upanetabbaṃ. Purebhattaṃ [M 0.0106] paṭiggahitena aparissāvitaucchurasena kataphāṇitaṃ sace anupasampannena kataṃ, sāmisampi vaṭṭati, sayaṃkataṃ nirāmisameva [V 0.0104] vaṭṭati, pacchābhattato paṭṭhāya pana savatthukapaṭiggahitattā anajjhoharaṇīyaṃ, sattāhātikkamepi anāpatti. Pacchābhattaṃ aparissāvitapaṭiggahitena katampi anajjhoharaṇīyameva, sattāhātikkamepi anāpatti. Esa nayo ucchuṃ paṭiggahetvā kataphāṇitepi. Purebhattaṃ pana parissāvitapaṭiggahitena kataṃ sace anupasampannena kataṃ, purebhattaṃ sāmisampi vaṭṭati, pacchābhattato paṭṭhāya sattāhaṃ nirāmisameva. Sayaṃkataṃ purebhattampi nirāmisameva, pacchābhattaṃ parissāvitapaṭiggahitena kataṃ pana nirāmisameva sattāhaṃ vaṭṭati. Uggahitakataṃ vuttanayameva. “Jhāmaucchuphāṇitaṃ vā koṭṭitaucchuphāṇitaṃ vā purebhattameva vaṭṭatī”ti mahāaṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttaṃ. Mahāpaccariyaṃ pana “etaṃ savatthukapakkaṃ vaṭṭati, no vaṭṭatī”ti pucchaṃ katvā “ucchuphāṇitaṃ pacchābhattaṃ no vaṭṭanakaṃ nāma natthī”ti vuttaṃ, taṃ yuttaṃ. Sītodakena kataṃ madhukapupphaphāṇitaṃ purebhattaṃ sāmisampi vaṭṭati, pacchābhattato paṭṭhāya sattāhaṃ nirāmisameva vaṭṭati, sattāhātikkame vatthugaṇanāya dukkaṭaṃ, khīraṃ pakkhipitvā kataṃ madhukaphāṇitaṃ yāvakālikaṃ. Khaṇḍasakkharaṃ pana khīrajallikaṃ apanetvā sodhenti, tasmā vaṭṭati.

98. Phāṇita is defined as any special product derived from sugarcane juice, whether it is uncooked, or cooked without the substance [of bagasse], or any special product of sugarcane without the substance [of bagasse]. If such phāṇita is received before midday, it is permissible even with food before midday. From after midday, it is permissible only without food for seven days. Beyond seven days, it is subject to forfeiture according to the number of items. Even if many lumps are ground into powder and placed in a single vessel, forming a solid mass, it is a single forfeiture. An invalidated offering should be understood in the manner already stated; it may be used for such things as fumigating a dwelling. If phāṇita is made from unstrained sugarcane juice received before midday, and if it is made by a non-ordained person, it is permissible even with food. If made by oneself, it is permissible only without food. However, from after midday, because it was received with the substance [of bagasse], it is not to be consumed; even beyond seven days, there is no offense. Phāṇita made with unstrained [juice] received after midday is also not to be consumed; even beyond seven days, there is no offense. This same principle applies to phāṇita made after receiving the sugarcane stalk itself. However, if phāṇita is made from strained [juice] received before midday, and if it is made by a non-ordained person, it is permissible even with food before midday. From after midday, it is permissible only without food for seven days. If made by oneself, even before midday, it is permissible only without food. However, phāṇita made from strained [juice] received after midday is permissible only without food for seven days. If made from an invalidated offering, it is as already stated. The Mahā-aṭṭhakathā states: ‘Phāṇita from burnt sugarcane or phāṇita from crushed sugarcane is permissible only before midday.’ However, the Mahāpaccariya, having raised the question ‘Is this permissible or not when cooked with the substance [of the stalk]?’ states: ‘There is no such thing as sugarcane phāṇita that is not permissible after midday.’ That is reasonable. Phāṇita made from madhuka flowers with cold water is permissible even with food before midday. From after midday, it is permissible only without food for seven days. Beyond seven days, there is an offense of wrong conduct according to the number of items. If milk is added to madhuka phāṇita, it is permissible only until midday. Lump sugar, however, is purified by removing the milky scum; therefore, it is permissible.

99. Madhukapupphaṃ pana purebhattampi allaṃ vaṭṭati. Bhajjitampi vaṭṭati, bhajjitvā tilādīhi missaṃ vā amissaṃ vā katvā koṭṭitaṃ vaṭṭati. Yadi pana taṃ gahetvā merayatthāya yojenti, yojitaṃ bījato paṭṭhāya na vaṭṭati. Kadalīkhajjūrīambalabujapanasaciñcādīnaṃ sabbesaṃ yāvakālikaphalānaṃ phāṇitaṃ yāvakālikameva. Maricapakkehi phāṇitaṃ karonti, taṃ yāvajīvikaṃ. Evaṃ yathāvuttāni sattāhakālikāni sappiādīni pañca “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, pañca bhesajjānī”ti (mahāva. 260) bhesajjanāmena anuññātattā bhesajjakiccaṃ karontu vā mā vā, āhāratthaṃ pharituṃ samatthānipi paṭiggahetvā tadahupurebhattaṃ yathāsukhaṃ, pacchābhattato paṭṭhāya sati paccaye vuttanayena sattāhaṃ paribhuñjitabbāni, sattāhātikkame pana bhesajjasikkhāpadena nissaggiyaṃ pācittiyaṃ. Sacepi sāsapamattaṃ hoti, sakiṃ vā aṅguliyā gahetvā jivhāya sāyanamattaṃ, nissajjitabbameva pācittiyañca desetabbaṃ. Nissaṭṭhaṃ paṭilabhitvā na ajjhoharitabbaṃ, na kāyikena paribhogena paribhuñjitabbaṃ[M 0.0107], kāyo vā kāye aru vā na makkhetabbaṃ. Tehi makkhitāni kāsāvakattarayaṭṭhiupāhanapādakaṭhalikamañcapīṭhādīnipi aparibhogāni. “Dvāravātapānakavāṭesupi hatthena gahaṇaṭṭhānaṃ na makkhetabba”nti mahāpaccariyaṃ vuttaṃ. “Kasāve pana pakkhipitvā dvāravātapānakavāṭāni makkhetabbānī”ti mahāaṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttaṃ. Padīpe vā kāḷavaṇṇe vā upanetuṃ vaṭṭati. Aññena pana bhikkhunā kāyikena paribhogena paribhuñjitabbaṃ, na ajjhoharitabbaṃ. “Anāpatti antosattāhaṃ adhiṭṭhetī”ti (pārā. 625) vacanato [V 0.0105] pana sattāhabbhantare sappiñca telañca vasañca muddhani telaṃ vā abbhañjanaṃ vā madhuṃ arumakkhanaṃ phāṇitaṃ gharadhūpanaṃ adhiṭṭheti anāpatti, neva nissaggiyaṃ hoti. Sace adhiṭṭhitatelaṃ anadhiṭṭhitatelabhājane ākiritukāmo hoti, bhājane ce sukhumaṃ chiddaṃ, paviṭṭhaṃ paviṭṭhaṃ telaṃ purāṇatelena ajjhottharīyati, puna adhiṭṭhātabbaṃ. Atha mahāmukhaṃ hoti, sahasāva bahu telaṃ pavisitvā purāṇatelaṃ ajjhottharati, puna adhiṭṭhānakiccaṃ natthi. Adhiṭṭhitagatikameva hi taṃ hoti. Etena nayena adhiṭṭhitatelabhājane anadhiṭṭhitatelaākiraṇampi veditabbaṃ.

99. The madhuka flower, however, is allowable even when fresh before the meal. It is allowable even when fried; having fried it, whether mixed with sesame and so forth or unmixed, and then pounded, it is allowable. However, if it is taken and used for the purpose of liquor, once it has been so used, it is not allowable from the adding of the yeast onward. For all fruits allowable for a limited time, such as bananas, dates, mangoes, breadfruit, jackfruit, and tamarind, their phāṇita is also allowable for a limited time. They make phāṇita with ripe peppers; that is allowable for life. Thus, the five seven-day allowances—ghee and so forth—as stated, 'Monks, I allow five medicines' (Mahāvagga 260), being permitted under the name of medicine, whether they serve a medicinal purpose or not, even if they are capable of fulfilling the purpose of food, should be accepted and consumed at will in the forenoon of that same day. From after the meal onward, if there is a reason, they may be used for seven days in the manner described. However, exceeding seven days incurs a Nissaggiya Pācittiya offense under the training rule concerning medicines. Even if it is just a mustard seed’s worth, or just the amount taken once on a fingertip to be tasted with the tongue, it must be forfeited, and the Pācittiya offense must be confessed. Having received back what has been forfeited, it should not be swallowed, nor used by way of bodily application; neither the body nor a wound on the body should be smeared with it. Items smeared with these—such as robes, staffs, sandals, foot-rubbers, beds, or chairs—also become unusable. The Mahāpaccarī states: 'Even on doors, windows, and shutters, the place grasped by the hand should not be smeared.' However, the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā states: 'But having put it in dye, doors, windows, and shutters may be smeared.' It is allowable to use it for a lamp or for a black color. However, it may be used by another bhikkhu by way of bodily application, but it should not be swallowed. However, according to the text, 'There is no offense if one determines it within seven days' (Pārā. 625), if within seven days one determines ghee, oil, or fat as oil for the head or as an unguent, honey as a salve for wounds, or phāṇita as fumigation for a dwelling, there is no offense, and it does not become subject to forfeiture. If one wishes to pour determined oil into a container of undetermined oil, and if the container has a fine hole, the oil, as it enters, is covered over by the old oil, and it must be determined again. But if the opening is large, and much oil enters at once and covers over the old oil, there is no need for a new determination, for that old oil comes to be of the nature of the determined. By this same method, the pouring of undetermined oil into a container of determined oil should also be understood.

Sace pana sattāhātikkantaṃ anupasampannassa pariccajitvā deti, puna tena attano santakaṃ katvā dinnaṃ paribhuñjituṃ vaṭṭati. Sace hi so abhisaṅkharitvā vā anabhisaṅkharitvā vā tassa bhikkhuno natthukammatthaṃ dadeyya, gahetvā natthukammaṃ kātabbaṃ. Sace bālo hoti, dātuṃ na jānāti, aññena bhikkhunā vattabbo “atthi te sāmaṇera tela”nti? “Āma, bhante, atthī”ti. Āhara therassa bhesajjaṃ karissāmāti. Evampi vaṭṭati. Sace dvinnaṃ santakaṃ ekena paṭiggahitaṃ avibhattaṃ hoti, sattāhātikkame dvinnampi anāpatti, paribhuñjituṃ pana na vaṭṭati. Sace yena paṭiggahitaṃ, so itaraṃ bhaṇati “āvuso, imaṃ telaṃ sattāhamattaṃ paribhuñjituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti, so ca paribhogaṃ na karoti, kassa āpatti? Na kassaci. Kasmā? Yena paṭiggahitaṃ, tena vissajjitattā, itarassa appaṭiggahitattā.

However, if one gives what has passed seven days to a non-ordained person, having relinquished it, it is allowable to again use what was given by that person after he has made it his own property. Indeed, if he—whether having prepared it or not having prepared it—should give it to that bhikkhu for the purpose of nose treatment, having taken it, the nose treatment should be performed. If he is ignorant and does not know how to give, he should be told by another bhikkhu, 'Novice, do you have oil?' 'Yes, venerable sir, I have.' 'Bring it; we will prepare medicine for the elder.' Even this is allowable. If the property of two is received by one and is undivided, when seven days have passed, there is no offense for both, but it is not allowable to use it. If the one by whom it was received tells the other, 'Friend, it is allowable to use this oil for just seven days,' and that one does not make use of it, whose is the offense? No one's. Why? For the one by whom it was received, because of its having been relinquished; for the other, because of its not having been received.

100. Imesu (mahāva. aṭṭha. 305) pana catūsu kālikesu yāvakālikaṃ yāmakālikanti idameva dvayaṃ antovutthakañceva sannidhikārakañca hoti, sattāhakālikañca yāvajīvikañca akappiyakuṭiyaṃ nikkhipitumpi vaṭṭati, sannidhimpi na [M 0.0108] janeti. Yāvakālikaṃ pana attanā saddhiṃ sambhinnarasāni tīṇipi yāmakālikādīni attano sabhāvaṃ upaneti. Yāmakālikaṃ dvepi sattāhakālikādīni attano sabhāvaṃ upaneti, sattāhakālikampi attanā saddhiṃ saṃsaṭṭhaṃ yāvajīvikaṃ attano sabhāvaññeva upaneti, tasmā yāvakālikena tadahupaṭiggahitena saddhiṃ saṃsaṭṭhaṃ sambhinnarasaṃ sesakālikattayaṃ tadahupurebhattameva vaṭṭati. Yāmakālikena saṃsaṭṭhaṃ pana itaradvayaṃ tadahupaṭiggahitaṃ yāva aruṇuggamanā vaṭṭati. Sattāhakālikena pana tadahupaṭiggahitena saddhiṃ saṃsaṭṭhaṃ tadahupaṭiggahitaṃ vā purepaṭiggahitaṃ vā yāvajīvikaṃ sattāhaṃ kappati. Dvīhapaṭiggahitena chāhaṃ. Tīhapaṭiggahitena pañcāhaṃ…pe… sattāhapaṭiggahitena tadaheva kappatīti veditabbaṃ. Kālayāmasattāhātikkamesu cettha vikālabhojanasannidhibhesajjasikkhāpadānaṃ vasena āpattiyo veditabbā.

100. Among these four kālikas (Mahāva. Aṭṭha. 305), only this pair, the yāvakālika and the yāmakālika, both causes the antovuttha offense and causes accumulation. The sattāhakālika and the yāvajīvika may be deposited even in an unsuitable dwelling, and they do not generate accumulation. However, the yāvakālika imparts its own nature to the three other items beginning with yāmakālika when they are mixed with it and have a similar taste. The yāmakālika imparts its own nature to the other two items, the sattāhakālika and the yāvajīvika. Even the sattāhakālika imparts only its own nature to a yāvajīvika mixed with it. Therefore, the remaining group of three kālikas, when mixed with a yāvakālika received on that day and having a similar taste, is permissible only in the forenoon of that day. However, the other pair, when received on that day and mixed with a yāmakālika, is permissible until the rising of dawn. However, a yāvajīvika—whether received on that day or received before—when mixed with a sattāhakālika received on that day, is allowable for seven days. If the sattāhakālika was received two days before, it is allowable for six days. If three days before, for five days… and if received seven days before, it is allowable only on that day—this should be understood. Here, in exceeding the time limit, the watch limit, and the seven-day limit, offenses should be understood by way of the training rules concerning untimely eating, accumulation, and medicine.

Sace [V 0.0106] pana ekato paṭiggahitānipi cattāri kālikāni sambhinnarasāni na honti, tassa tasseva kālassa vasena paribhuñjituṃ vaṭṭanti. Sace hi challimpi anapanetvā sakaleneva nāḷikeraphalena saddhiṃ ambapānādipānakaṃ paṭiggahitaṃ hoti, nāḷikeraṃ apanetvā taṃ vikālepi kappati. Upari sappipiṇḍaṃ ṭhapetvā sītalapāyāsaṃ denti, yaṃ pāyāsena asaṃsaṭṭhaṃ sappi, taṃ apanetvā sattāhaṃ paribhuñjituṃ vaṭṭati. Thaddhamadhuphāṇitādīsupi eseva nayo. Takkolajātiphalādīhi alaṅkaritvā piṇḍapātaṃ denti, tāni uddharitvā dhovitvā yāvajīvaṃ paribhuñjitabbāni. Yāguyaṃ pakkhipitvā dinnasiṅgiverādīsupi telādīsu pakkhipitvā dinnalaṭṭhimadhukādīsupi eseva nayo. Evaṃ yaṃ yaṃ asambhinnarasaṃ hoti, taṃ taṃ ekato paṭiggahitampi yathā suddhaṃ hoti, tathā dhovitvā tacchetvā vā tassa tassa kālassa vasena paribhuñjituṃ vaṭṭati. Sace sambhinnarasaṃ hoti saṃsaṭṭhaṃ, na vaṭṭati.

However, if the four kālikas, even though received together, are not of blended flavor, it is permissible to consume them according to their respective times. For if a drink such as mango juice is received together with a whole coconut, without having removed even the husk, then having removed the coconut, that drink is permissible even at an improper time. If they offer cold milk-rice with a lump of ghee placed on top, the ghee that is not mixed with the milk-rice may be removed and consumed for seven days. This same method also applies to hardened honey, molasses, and so forth. If they offer alms-food adorned with cubebs, nutmeg, and so forth, these should be removed, washed, and may be consumed for life. This same method also applies to ginger and so forth given after being put into rice-gruel, and to licorice and so forth given after being put into oil and so forth. Thus, whatever is not of blended flavor, even though received together, it is permissible to consume it according to its respective time, having washed or peeled it so that it becomes pure. If it is of blended flavor and is mixed, it is not permissible.

Iti pāḷimuttakavinayavinicchayasaṅgahe

Thus, in the Compendium of Determinations on the Vinaya External to the Pāḷi Canon,

Kālikavinicchayakathā samattā.

The Discourse on the Determination of Time-Specific Requisites is concluded.

19. Kappiyabhūmivinicchayakathā

19. The Discourse on the Determination of Permissible Ground

101. Kappiyācatubhūmiyoti [M 0.0109][V 0.0107] ettha “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, catasso kappiyabhūmiyo ussāvanantikaṃ gonisādikaṃ gahapatiṃ sammuti”nti (mahāva. 295) vacanato ussāvanantikā gonisādikā gahapati sammutīti imā catasso kappiyabhūmiyo veditabbā. Tattha (mahāva. aṭṭha. 295) ussāvanantikā tāva evaṃ kātabbā – yo thambhānaṃ vā upari bhittipāde vā nikhanitvā vihāro karīyati, tassa heṭṭhā thambhapaṭicchakā pāsāṇā bhūmigatikā eva. Paṭhamatthambhaṃ pana paṭhamabhittipādaṃ vā patiṭṭhāpentehi bahūhi samparivāretvā “kappiyakuṭiṃ karoma, kappiyakuṭiṃ karomā”ti vācaṃ nicchārentehi manussesu ukkhipitvā patiṭṭhāpentesu āmasitvā vā sayaṃ ukkhipitvā vā thambho vā bhittipādo vā patiṭṭhāpetabbo. Kurundimahāpaccarīsu pana “kappiyakuṭi kappiyakuṭīti vatvā patiṭṭhāpetabba”nti vuttaṃ. Andhakaṭṭhakathāyaṃ “saṅghassa kappiyakuṭiṃ adhiṭṭhāmī”ti vuttaṃ, taṃ pana avatvāpi aṭṭhakathāsu vuttanayena vutte doso natthi. Idaṃ panettha sādhāraṇalakkhaṇaṃ “thambhapatiṭṭhāpanañca vacanapariyosānañca samakālaṃ vaṭṭatī”ti. Sace hi aniṭṭhite vacane thambho patiṭṭhāti, appatiṭṭhite vā tasmiṃ vacanaṃ niṭṭhāti, akatā hoti kappiyakuṭi. Teneva mahāpaccariyaṃ vuttaṃ “bahūhi samparivāretvā vattabbaṃ, avassañhi ettha ekassapi vacananiṭṭhānañca thambhapatiṭṭhānañca ekato bhavissatī”ti. Iṭṭhakāsilāmattikākuṭṭakāsu pana kuṭīsu heṭṭhā cayaṃ bandhitvā vā abandhitvā vā karontu, yato paṭṭhāya bhittiṃ uṭṭhāpetukāmā honti, taṃ sabbapaṭhamaṃ iṭṭhakaṃ vā silaṃ vā mattikāpiṇḍaṃ vā gahetvā vuttanayeneva kappiyakuṭi kātabbā, iṭṭhakādayo bhittiyaṃ paṭhamiṭṭhakādīnaṃ heṭṭhā na vaṭṭanti, thambhā pana upari uggacchanti, tasmā vaṭṭanti. Andhakaṭṭhakathāyaṃ “thambhehi kariyamāne catūsu koṇesu cattāro thambhā, iṭṭhakādikuṭṭe catūsu koṇesu dve tisso iṭṭhakā adhiṭṭhātabbā”ti vuttaṃ. Tathā pana akatāyapi doso natthi, aṭṭhakathāsu hi vuttameva pamāṇaṃ.

101. Regarding 'the four permissible grounds' here, based on the statement, 'I allow, O monks, four permissible grounds: the ussāvanantika, the gonisādika, the gahapati, and the sammuti' (Mahāvagga 295), these four—ussāvanantikā, gonisādikā, gahapati, and sammuti—should be known as the permissible grounds. Therein (Mahāvagga Aṭṭhakathā 295), firstly, the ussāvanantikā should be made thus: for a vihāra that is made either upon posts or by digging in wall-foundations, the stones underneath that support the posts are just like the ground. However, when establishing the first post or the first wall-foundation, many bhikkhus should surround it and, while laypeople are lifting and establishing it, the post or wall-foundation should be established by the bhikkhus either by touching it or by lifting it themselves, while uttering the words, 'We are making a permissible hut, we are making a permissible hut.' But in the Kurundī and Mahāpaccarī, it is said: 'It should be established while saying, "A permissible hut, a permissible hut."' In the Andhakaṭṭhakathā, it is said: 'I determine this permissible hut for the Saṅgha.' However, even without saying this, there is no fault if it is done according to the method stated in the commentaries. Herein, this is the general characteristic: 'The establishing of the post and the conclusion of the utterance are allowable at the same time.' For if the post is established before the utterance is finished, or if the utterance is finished before the post is established, the permissible hut is not made. For that very reason, it is said in the Mahāpaccarī: 'It should be said by many having surrounded it, for surely, herein, for at least one person, the conclusion of the utterance and the establishing of the post will occur together.' But in huts with walls of brick, stone, or clay, let them make it either having bound a foundation below or without having bound one; from where they desire to raise the wall, having taken that very first brick, or that stone, or that lump of clay, the permissible hut should be made in the very manner stated. Bricks and so forth are not allowable below the first bricks and so forth of the wall, but posts go upwards; therefore, they are allowable. In the Andhakaṭṭhakathā, it is said: 'When it is being made with posts, four posts should be made at the four corners; in a hut with walls of brick and so forth, two or three bricks should be determined at the four corners.' However, even if it is not made in that way, there is no fault, for what is stated in the commentaries is indeed the authority.

Gonisādikā duvidhā ārāmagonisādikā vihāragonisādikāti. Tāsu yattha neva ārāmo, na senāsanāni parikkhittāni honti, ayaṃ ārāmagonisādikā nāma. Yattha senāsanāni sabbāni [M 0.0110] vā ekaccāni vā parikkhittāni, ārāmo aparikkhitto, ayaṃ vihāragonisādikā nāma. Iti ubhayatrāpi ārāmassa aparikkhittabhāvoyeva pamāṇaṃ. “Ārāmo [V 0.0108] pana upaḍḍhaparikkhittopi bahutaraṃ parikkhittopi parikkhittoyeva nāmā”ti kurundimahāpaccarīsu vuttaṃ, ettha kappiyakuṭiṃ laddhuṃ vaṭṭati.

A cattle-ground (gonisādikā) is of two kinds: a monastery cattle-ground (ārāmagonisādikā) and a dwelling cattle-ground (vihāragonisādikā). Among these, where neither the monastery grounds nor the lodgings are enclosed, this is called the monastery cattle-ground. Where all or some of the lodgings are enclosed, but the monastery grounds are unenclosed, this is called the dwelling cattle-ground. Thus, in both cases, the unenclosed state of the monastery grounds is indeed the standard. It is stated in the Kurundī and Mahāpaccarī: 'However, monastery grounds, even if half-enclosed or mostly enclosed, are still called enclosed.' Here, it is permissible to obtain a permissible hut.

Gahapatīti manussā āvāsaṃ katvā “kappiyakuṭiṃ dema, paribhuñjathā”ti vadanti, esā gahapati nāma, “kappiyakuṭiṃ kātuṃ demā”ti vuttepi vaṭṭatiyeva. Andhakaṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana “yasmā bhikkhuṃ ṭhapetvā sesasahadhammikānaṃ sabbesañca devamanussānaṃ hatthato paṭiggaho ca sannidhi ca antovutthañca tesaṃ santakaṃ bhikkhussa vaṭṭati, tasmā tesaṃ gehāni vā tehi dinnakappiyakuṭi vā gahapatīti vuccatī”ti vuttaṃ, punapi vuttaṃ “bhikkhusaṅghassa vihāraṃ ṭhapetvā bhikkhunupassayo vā ārāmikānaṃ vā titthiyānaṃ vā devatānaṃ vā nāgānaṃ vā api brahmānaṃ vimānaṃ kappiyakuṭi hotī”ti, taṃ suvuttaṃ. Saṅghasantakameva hi bhikkhusantakaṃ vā gehaṃ gahapatikuṭikā na hoti.

A 'householder's hut' (gahapati) is when people, having built a residence, say, 'We give a permissible hut, make use of it.' This is called a 'householder's hut'. Even if they say, 'We give [materials] to build a permissible hut,' it is indeed permissible. However, in the Andhakaṭṭhakathā, it is stated: 'Because, excluding a monk, acceptance from the hand, storage, and what is kept inside, belonging to the remaining co-religionists and all devas and humans, is permissible for a monk, therefore their houses or a permissible hut given by them are called a "householder's hut."' It is further stated: 'Excluding a monastery of the Sangha of monks, a nun's residence, or a house of monastery attendants, or of heretics, or of deities, or of nāgas, or even a mansion of a brahmā can be a permissible hut.' That statement is well said. For indeed, a house belonging to the Sangha or belonging to a monk is not a householder's hut.

Sammuti nāma ñattidutiyakammavācāya sāvetvā sammatā. Evañca pana, bhikkhave, sammannitabbā, byattena bhikkhunā paṭibalena saṅgho ñāpetabbo –

A hut by designation (sammuti) is one designated after being announced by means of a motion and a second proclamation. And thus, O monks, it should be designated. A competent and capable monk should inform the Sangha:

“Suṇātu me, bhante, saṅgho. Yadi saṅghassa pattakallaṃ saṅgho itthannāmaṃ vihāraṃ kappiyabhūmiṃ sammanneyya, esā ñatti.

“Venerable sirs, may the Saṅgha hear me. If the time is suitable for the Saṅgha, the Saṅgha should designate such-and-such a dwelling as permissible ground. This is the motion.”

“Suṇātu me, bhante, saṅgho. Saṅgho itthannāmaṃ vihāraṃ kappiyabhūmiṃ sammannati. Yassāyasmato khamati itthannāmassa vihārassa kappiyabhūmiyā sammuti, so tuṇhassa. Yassa nakkhamati, so bhāseyya.

“Venerable sirs, may the Saṅgha hear me. The Saṅgha designates the dwelling named so-and-so as permissible ground. To whichever venerable one the designation of the dwelling named so-and-so as permissible ground is agreeable, he should be silent. To whom it is not agreeable, he should speak.”

“Sammato saṅghena itthannāmo vihāro kappiyabhūmi khamati saṅghassa, tasmā tuṇhī, evametaṃ dhārayāmī”ti (mahāva. 295).

“The dwelling named so-and-so has been designated by the Saṅgha as permissible ground. It is agreeable to the Saṅgha; therefore, it is silent. Thus do I understand this.”

Kammavācaṃ avatvā apalokanakammavasena sāvetvā katāpi sammatā eva.

Even a hut that is designated by having it announced through an act of announcement, without reciting the formal procedure, is indeed a validly designated one.

102. Yaṃ [M 0.0111] (mahāva. aṭṭha. 295) imāsu catūsu kappiyabhūmīsu vuttaṃ āmisaṃ, taṃ sabbaṃ antovutthasaṅkhyaṃ na gacchati. Bhikkhūnañca bhikkhunīnañca antovutthaantopakkamocanatthañhi kappiyakuṭiyo anuññātā. Yaṃ pana akappiyabhūmiyaṃ sahaseyyappahonake gehe vuttaṃ [V 0.0109] saṅghikaṃ vā puggalikaṃ vā bhikkhussa bhikkhuniyā vā santakaṃ ekarattampi ṭhapitaṃ, taṃ antovutthaṃ, tattha pakkañca antopakkaṃ nāma hoti, etaṃ na kappati. Sattāhakālikaṃ pana yāvajīvikañca vaṭṭati.

102. Whatever edible requisite is stored in these four permissible grounds, all of that does not fall under the category of ‘stored within.’ Indeed, for monks and for nuns, permissible huts are allowed for the purpose of being free from ‘stored within’ and ‘cooked within.’ However, whatever possession—whether belonging to the Saṅgha or an individual, of a monk or of a nun—is kept for even one night in an impermissible ground, in a dwelling suitable for co-residence, that is ‘stored within.’ There, what is cooked is also called ‘cooked within’; this is not permissible. However, seven-day items and lifetime items are permissible.

Tatrāyaṃ vinicchayo – sāmaṇero bhikkhussa taṇḍulādikaṃ āmisaṃ āharitvā kappiyakuṭiyaṃ nikkhipitvā punadivase pacitvā deti, antovutthaṃ na hoti. Tattha akappiyakuṭiyaṃ nikkhittasappiādīsu kiñci pakkhipitvā deti. Mukhasannidhi nāma hoti. Mahāpaccariyaṃ pana “antovutthaṃ hotī”ti vuttaṃ. Tattha nāmamattameva nānākaraṇaṃ, bhikkhu akappiyakuṭiyaṃ ṭhapitasappiñca yāvajīvikapaṇṇañca ekato pacitvā paribhuñjati, sattāhaṃ nirāmisaṃ vaṭṭati. Sace āmisasaṃsaṭṭhaṃ katvā paribhuñjati, antovutthañceva sāmaṃpakkañca hoti. Etenupāyena sabbasaṃsaggā veditabbā. Yaṃ kiñci āmisaṃ bhikkhuno pacituṃ na vaṭṭati. Sacepissa uṇhayāguyā sulasipaṇṇāni vā siṅgiveraṃ vā loṇaṃ vā pakkhipanti, tampi cāletuṃ na vaṭṭati, “yāguṃ nibbāpemī”ti pana cāletuṃ vaṭṭati. Uttaṇḍulabhattaṃ labhitvā pidahituṃ na vaṭṭati. Sace pana manussā pidahitvā denti, vaṭṭati. “Bhattaṃ mā nibbāyatū”ti pidahituṃ vaṭṭati, khīratakkādīsu pana sakiṃ kuthitesu aggiṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭati punapākassa anuññātattā.

Herein is the determination: If a novice brings rice or other edibles for a monk, places it in an allowable hut, and on the next day cooks and gives it, it is not considered ‘stored within.’ If, to that food, he adds something like ghee that was placed in an unallowable hut and then gives it, this is called ‘storing in proximity to the mouth.’ In the Mahāpaccarī, however, it is said that this is ‘stored within.’ Therein, the distinction is only a matter of name. If a monk cooks ghee that was stored in an unallowable place together with lifetime-allowable leaves and consumes them, it is allowable for seven days when unmixed with staple food. If he consumes it mixed with staple food, it becomes both ‘stored within’ and ‘cooked by oneself.’ By this method, all such mixtures are to be understood. It is not allowable for a monk to cook any kind of edible. If people add holy basil leaves, ginger, or salt to his hot gruel, it is not allowable for him to stir it; however, it is allowable to stir it with the thought, ‘I am cooling the gruel.’ Having received undercooked rice, it is not allowable to cover it. But if people cover it and give it, it is allowable. It is allowable to cover it with the thought, ‘May the rice not get cold.’ But in the case of milk, buttermilk, and so on, once they have been boiled, it is allowable to place them on a fire, as reheating is permitted.

Imā pana kappiyakuṭiyo kadā jahitavatthukā honti? Ussāvanantikā tāva yā thambhānaṃ upari bhittipāde vā nikhanitvā katā, sā sabbesu thambhesu ca bhittipādesu ca apanītesu jahitavatthukā hoti. Sace pana thambhe vā bhittipāde vā parivattenti, yo yo ṭhito, tattha tattha patiṭṭhāti, sabbesupi parivattitesu ajahitavatthukāva hoti. Iṭṭhakādīhi katā cayassa upari bhittiatthāya ṭhapitaṃ iṭṭhakaṃ vā silaṃ vā mattikāpiṇḍaṃ vā ādiṃ katvā vināsitakāle jahitavatthukāva hoti. Yehi pana iṭṭhakādīhi adhiṭṭhitā, tesu apanītesupi tadaññesu patiṭṭhātīti ajahitavatthukāva hoti. Gonisādikā [M 0.0112] pākārādīhi parikkhepe kate jahitavatthukāva hoti. Puna tasmiṃ ārāme kappiyakuṭiṃ laddhuṃ vaṭṭati. Sace pana punapi pākārādayo tattha tattha khaṇḍā honti, tato tato gāvo pavisanti, puna kappiyakuṭi hoti. Itarā pana dve gopānasīmattaṃ ṭhapetvā sabbasmiṃ chadane vinaṭṭhe jahitavatthukāva honti. Sace gopānasīnaṃ upari ekampi pakkhapāsakamaṇḍalaṃ atthi, rakkhati.

Now, when do these allowable huts become abandoned as to their site? First, a hut with projecting eaves, which is made on top of pillars or by embedding posts into wall foundations, becomes abandoned as to its site when all the pillars and wall foundations are removed. But if they replace the pillars or the wall foundations, it remains established on whichever one is left standing; even if all are replaced, it is still not abandoned as to its site. A hut made of bricks and so forth becomes abandoned as to its site when it is destroyed, starting from the first brick, stone, or lump of clay placed on the mound for the wall. However, if it was established with certain bricks and so forth, even when those are removed, as long as it remains established on others, it is not considered abandoned as to its site. A cattle-pen hut becomes abandoned as to its site when an enclosure by walls and so forth is made. Then, it is allowable to obtain another allowable hut in that monastery. But if the walls and so forth are again broken here and there, and cattle enter from those places, it again becomes an allowable hut. The other two types of huts, however, become abandoned as to their site when the entire roofing is destroyed, leaving only the ridgepole. But if even a single rafter-end remains above the ridgepole, it preserves its status.

103. Yatra [V 0.0110] panimā catassopi kappiyabhūmiyo natthi, tattha kiṃ kātabbanti? Anupasampannassa datvā tassa santakaṃ katvā paribhuñjitabbaṃ. Tatridaṃ vatthu – karavikatissatthero kira vinayadharapāmokkho mahāsīvattherassa santikaṃ agamāsi. So dīpālokena sappikumbhaṃ passitvā “bhante, kimeta”nti pucchi. Thero “āvuso, gāmato sappikumbho ābhato lūkhadivase sappinā bhuñjanatthāyā”ti āha. Tato naṃ tissatthero “na vaṭṭati, bhante”ti āha. Thero punadivase pamukhe nikkhipāpesi. Tissatthero puna ekadivasaṃ āgato taṃ disvā tatheva pucchitvā “bhante, sahaseyyappahonakaṭṭhāne ṭhapetuṃ na vaṭṭatī”ti āha. Thero punadivase bahi nīharāpetvā nikkhipāpesi, taṃ corā hariṃsu. So puna ekadivasaṃ āgataṃ tissattheramāha “āvuso, tayā ‘na vaṭṭatī’ti vutte so kumbho bahi nikkhitto corehi haṭo”ti. Tato naṃ tissatthero āha “nanu, bhante, anupasampannassa dātabbo assa, anupasampannassa hi datvā tassa santakaṃ katvā paribhuñjituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti.

103. In a monastery where these four allowable grounds do not exist, what is to be done? It should be given to an unordained person, made his property, and then used. Herein is the story: The Elder Karavikatissa, it is said, a foremost Vinaya-holder, went to the Elder Mahāsīva. Seeing a pot of ghee by the light of a lamp, he asked, “Venerable sir, what is this?” The Elder replied, “Friend, a pot of ghee was brought from the village for the purpose of eating with ghee on a day of coarse food.” Then the Elder Tissa said to him, “Venerable sir, it is not allowable.” The next day, the Elder had it placed at the front. When the Elder Tissa came again one day and saw it, he asked as before and said, “Venerable sir, it is not allowable to place it in a location suitable for co-residence.” The following day, the Elder had it taken outside and placed there; thieves took it. When the Elder Tissa came again one day, the Elder Mahāsīva said, “Friend, because you said ‘it is not allowable,’ that pot was placed outside and was taken by thieves.” Then the Elder Tissa said to him, “Venerable sir, should it not have been given to an unordained person? For it is allowable to give it to an unordained person, make it his property, and then use it.”

Iti pāḷimuttakavinayavinicchayasaṅgahe

Thus, in the Compendium of Vinaya Determinations Apart from the Pāḷi,

Kappiyabhūmivinicchayakathā samattā.

The Discourse on the Determination of Allowable Grounds is concluded.

20. Paṭiggahaṇavinicchayakathā

20. Discourse on the Determination of Receiving

104. Khādanīyādipaṭiggāhoti [V 0.0111] ajjhoharitabbassa yassa kassaci khādanīyassa vā bhojanīyassa vā paṭiggahaṇaṃ. Tatrāyaṃ vinicchayo – pañcahi aṅgehi paṭiggahaṇaṃ ruhati, thāmamajjhimassa purisassa uccāraṇamattaṃ hoti, hatthapāso paññāyati, abhihāro paññāyati, devo vā manusso [M 0.0113] vā tiracchānagato vā kāyena kāyapaṭibaddhena nissaggiyena vā deti, tañce bhikkhu kāyena vā kāyapaṭibaddhena vā paṭiggaṇhāti. Evaṃ pañcahaṅgehi paṭiggahaṇaṃ ruhati.

104. The receiving of edible food and so forth is the acceptance of any kind of edible food or staple food that is to be swallowed. Herein, this is the determination: receiving becomes valid with five factors. (1) It is of a size that can be lifted by a person of medium strength. (2) It is within hand's reach. (3) The bringing forward of the offering is apparent. (4) A deva, a human, or an animal gives it with the body, with what is attached to the body, or by means of relinquishment. (5) The bhikkhu receives that which is given with the body or with what is attached to the body. Thus, with these five factors, receiving becomes valid.

Tattha ṭhitanisinnanipannānaṃ vasena evaṃ hatthapāso veditabbo – sace bhikkhu nisinno hoti, āsanassa pacchimantato paṭṭhāya, sace ṭhito, paṇhiantato paṭṭhāya, sace nipanno, yena passena nipanno, tassa pārimantato paṭṭhāya, dāyakassa nisinnassa vā ṭhitassa vā nipannassa vā ṭhapetvā pasāritahatthaṃ yaṃ āsannataraṃ aṅgaṃ, tassa orimantena paricchinditvā aḍḍhateyyahattho hatthapāso nāma.

Therein, the hand-reach should be understood thus, according to those who are standing, sitting, or lying down. For the bhikkhu: if sitting, it is reckoned from the back edge of the seat; if standing, from the edge of the heel; if lying down, from the farthest edge of the side on which he is lying. For the donor, whether sitting, standing, or lying down, excluding the outstretched hand, it is reckoned from the near-side edge of whichever limb is nearest. The space thus demarcated, measuring two and a half cubits, is called the hand-reach.

Sace pana dāyakapaṭiggāhakesu eko ākāse hoti, eko bhūmiyaṃ, bhūmaṭṭhassa ca sīsena, ākāsaṭṭhassa ca ṭhapetvā dātuṃ vā gahetuṃ vā pasāritahatthaṃ yaṃ āsannataraṃ aṅgaṃ, tassa orimantena hatthapāsapamāṇaṃ paricchinditabbaṃ. Sacepi eko kūpe hoti, eko kūpataṭe, eko vā pana rukkhe, eko pathaviyaṃ, vuttanayeneva hatthapāsapamāṇaṃ paricchinditabbaṃ. Evarūpe hatthapāse ṭhatvā sacepi pakkhī mukhatuṇḍakena vā hatthī vā soṇḍāya gahetvā pupphaṃ vā phalaṃ vā deti, paṭiggahaṇaṃ ruhati. Sace pana aḍḍhaṭṭhamaratanassapi hatthino khandhe nisinno tena soṇḍāya dīyamānaṃ gaṇhāti, vaṭṭatiyeva. Hatthādīsu yena kenaci sarīrāvayavena antamaso pādaṅguliyāpi dīyamānaṃ kāyena dinnaṃ nāma hoti. Paṭiggahaṇepi eseva nayo. Yena kenaci hi sarīrāvayavena gahitaṃ kāyena gahitameva hoti. Sacepi natthukaraṇiyaṃ dīyamānaṃ nāsāpuṭena akallako vā mukhena paṭiggaṇhāti, ābhogameva hettha pamāṇaṃ.

If, however, among the donor and receiver, one is in the air and one is on the ground, the measure of the hand-reach should be determined from the head for the one on the ground, and for the one in the air, from the near-side edge of the nearest limb, excluding the outstretched hand for giving or receiving. If one is in a well and one is on the well’s edge, or if one is in a tree and one is on the ground, the measure of the hand-reach should be determined in the manner stated. Standing within such a hand-reach, if a bird with its beak or an elephant with its trunk takes and gives a flower or a fruit, the receiving is valid. If, however, one sitting on the back of an elephant that is seven and a half cubits tall receives what is given by its trunk, it is indeed permissible. Regarding elephants and so on, anything given by any part of the body whatsoever—at the least, even by a toe—is called 'given by the body.' In receiving also, this is the same method. Indeed, anything taken by any part of the body whatsoever is taken by the body. If what is given for nasal application is received with the nostril, or if an infirm person receives with the mouth, herein intention alone is the measure.

105. Kaṭacchuādīsu pana yena kenaci upakaraṇena dinnaṃ kāyapaṭibaddhena dinnaṃ nāma hoti. Paṭiggahaṇepi eseva nayo. Yena kenaci hi sarīrasambaddhena pattathālakādinā gahitaṃ kāyapaṭibaddhena [V 0.0112] gahitameva hoti. Kāyato pana kāyapaṭibaddhato ca mocetvā hatthapāse ṭhitassa kāye vā kāyapaṭibaddhe vā pātiyamānampi nissaggiyena payogena dinnaṃ nāma hoti. Eko bahūni bhattabyañjanabhājanāni sīse katvā [M 0.0114] bhikkhussa santikaṃ āgantvā ṭhitakova “gaṇhathā”ti vadati, na tāva abhihāro paññāyati, tasmā na gahetabbaṃ. Sace pana īsakampi onamati, bhikkhunā hatthaṃ pasāretvā heṭṭhimabhājanaṃ ekadesenapi sampaṭicchitabbaṃ. Ettāvatā sabbabhājanāni paṭiggahitāni honti. Tato paṭṭhāya oropetvā ugghāṭetvā vā yaṃ icchati, taṃ gahetuṃ vaṭṭati. Bhattapacchiādimhi pana ekabhājane vattabbameva natthi.

105. Regarding items such as ladles, whatever is given by any implement is considered given by that which is connected to the body. The same method applies to receiving. For indeed, whatever is received by anything connected to the body—such as a bowl or a plate—is considered received by that which is connected to the body. Furthermore, having released it from the body or from something connected to the body, even when it is being dropped onto the body or onto something connected to the body of one standing within hand-reach, it is considered given by an act of relinquishment. If one person, having placed many containers of food and curry on their head, comes near a bhikkhu and, while still standing, says, 'Take this,' the presentation is not yet apparent; therefore, it should not be accepted. But if they bend even slightly, the bhikkhu should extend his hand and accept at least a part of the lowest container. By this much, all the containers are considered received. From that point on, having had them taken down or opened, it is allowable to take whatever is desired. However, in the case of a single container such as a food basket, there is nothing further to be said.

Kājena bhattaṃ harantopi sace kājaṃ onametvā deti, vaṭṭati. Tiṃsahattho veṇu hoti, ekasmiṃ ante guḷakumbho baddho, ekasmiṃ sappikumbho, tañce paṭiggaṇhāti, sabbaṃ paṭiggahitameva. Ucchuyantadoṇito paggharantameva “rasaṃ gaṇhathā”ti vadati, abhihāro na paññāyatīti na gahetabbo. Sace pana kasaṭaṃ chaḍḍetvā hatthena ussiñcitvā deti, vaṭṭati. Bahū pattā mañce vā pīṭhe vā kaṭasāre vā doṇiyaṃ vā phalake vā ṭhapitā honti, yattha ṭhitassa dāyako hatthapāse hoti, tattha ṭhatvā paṭiggahaṇasaññāya mañcādīni aṅguliyāpi phusitvā ṭhitena vā nisinnena vā nipannena vā yaṃ tesu pattesu dīyati, taṃ sabbaṃ paṭiggahitaṃ hoti. Sacepi “paṭiggahessāmī”ti mañcādīni abhiruhitvā nisīdati, vaṭṭatiyeva.

Even if one carrying food on a carrying pole offers it by lowering the pole, it is allowable. If a bamboo pole thirty cubits long has a pot of molasses tied at one end and a pot of ghee at the other, and if one accepts the pot of ghee, everything is considered accepted. If one says, 'Take the juice' as it is dripping from the trough of a sugarcane press, it should not be taken, as the presentation is not apparent. But if, having discarded the dregs, one scoops it up with the hand and gives it, it is allowable. Many bowls may be placed on a bed, a bench, a large mat, a trough, or a board. Suppose a donor is within hand's reach of a bhikkhu standing in a certain place. If that bhikkhu, standing there with the perception of receiving, touches the bed or other item even with a fingertip—whether he himself is standing, sitting, or lying down—then whatever is given into those bowls is all considered received. Even if one climbs onto the bed or other such item thinking, 'I will receive,' and then sits down, it is indeed allowable.

Pathaviyaṃ pana sacepi kucchiyā kucchiṃ āhacca ṭhitā honti, yaṃ yaṃ aṅguliyā vā sūciyā vā phusitvā nisinno hoti, tattha tattha dīyamānameva paṭiggahitaṃ hoti. Yattha katthaci mahākaṭasārahatthattharaṇādīsu ṭhapitapatte paṭiggahaṇaṃ na ruhatīti vuttaṃ, taṃ hatthapāsātikkamaṃ sandhāya vuttanti veditabbaṃ, hatthapāse pana sati yattha katthaci vaṭṭati aññatra tatthajātakā. Tatthajātake pana paduminipaṇṇe vā kiṃsukapaṇṇādimhi vā na vaṭṭati. Na hi taṃ kāyapaṭibaddhasaṅkhyaṃ gacchati. Yathā ca tatthajātake, evaṃ khāṇuke bandhitvā ṭhapitamañcādimhi asaṃhārime phalake vā pāsāṇe vā na ruhatiyeva. Tepi hi tatthajātakasaṅkhyupagā honti. Bhūmiyaṃ atthatesu sukhumesu tintiṇikādipaṇṇesu paṭiggahaṇaṃ na ruhati. Na hi tāni sandhāretuṃ samatthānīti. Mahantesu pana paduminipaṇṇādīsu ruhati. Sace hatthapāsaṃ atikkammaṭhito dīghadaṇḍakena uḷuṅkena deti, “āgantvā dehī”ti vattabbo. Vacanaṃ asutvā vā anādiyitvā vā patte ākiratiyeva, puna paṭiggahetabbaṃ. Dūre ṭhatvā bhattapiṇḍaṃ khipantepi eseva nayo.

However, on the ground, even if they are standing touching belly to belly, it is considered validly received only when given into the very bowl that one, while sitting, has touched with a finger or a needle. As for the statement that receiving is not valid in a bowl placed on a large mat, elephant saddle, etc., it should be understood that this was said with reference to being beyond hand's reach. However, when within hand's reach, it is valid anywhere except for that which is grown in that place. As for that which is grown in that place, such as a lotus leaf or a kiṃsuka leaf, etc., it is not valid, for it does not come into the category of something connected to the body. And just as with that which is grown in that place, so too receiving is certainly not valid on a bed, etc., tied to a stump, or on an immovable plank or stone slab, for these too are included in the category of that which is grown in that place. Receiving is not valid on delicate leaves, such as those of the tamarind, etc., spread on the ground, for they are not capable of supporting it. However, on large lotus leaves and the like, it is valid. If someone standing beyond hand's reach gives with a long-handled ladle, they should be told, 'Come and give.' If they pour it into the bowl anyway, either not having heard or not heeding the instruction, it must be received again. The same rule applies when someone stands at a distance and throws a lump of food.

106. Sace [M 0.0115][V 0.0113] pattathavikato nīhariyamāne patte rajanacuṇṇāni honti, sati udake dhovitabbo, asati rajanacuṇṇaṃ puñchitvā paṭiggahetvā vā piṇḍāya caritabbaṃ. Sace piṇḍāya carantassa patte rajaṃ patati, paṭiggahetvā bhikkhā gaṇhitabbā, appaṭiggahetvā gaṇhato vinayadukkaṭaṃ, taṃ pana puna paṭiggahetvā bhuñjato anāpatti. Sace pana “paṭiggahetvā dethā”ti vutte vacanaṃ asutvā vā anādiyitvā vā bhikkhaṃ dentiyeva, vinayadukkaṭaṃ natthi, puna paṭiggahetvā aññā bhikkhā gahetabbā. Sace mahāvāto tato tato rajaṃ pāteti, na sakkā hoti bhikkhaṃ gahetuṃ, “anupasampannassa dassāmī”ti suddhacittena ābhogaṃ katvā gaṇhituṃ vaṭṭati. Evaṃ piṇḍāya caritvā vihāraṃ vā āsanasālaṃ vā gantvā taṃ anupasampannassa datvā puna tena dinnaṃ vā tassa vissāsena vā paṭiggahetvā bhuñjituṃ vaṭṭati. Sace bhikkhācāre sarajaṃ pattaṃ bhikkhussa deti, so vattabbo “imaṃ paṭiggahetvā bhikkhaṃ vā gaṇheyyāsi paribhuñjeyyāsi vā”ti, tena tathā kātabbaṃ. Sace rajaṃ upari uppilavati, kañjikaṃ pavāhetvā sesaṃ bhuñjitabbaṃ. Sace antopaviṭṭhaṃ hoti, paṭiggahetabbaṃ. Anupasampanne asati hatthato amocenteneva yattha anupasampanno atthi, tattha netvā paṭiggahetabbaṃ. Sukkhabhatte patitarajaṃ apanetvā bhuñjituṃ vaṭṭati. Sace atisukhumaṃ hoti, upari bhattena saddhiṃ apanetabbaṃ, paṭiggahetvā vā bhuñjitabbaṃ. Yāguṃ vā sūpaṃ vā purato ṭhapetvā āluḷentānaṃ bhājanato phusitāni uggantvā patte patanti, patto paṭiggahetabbo.

106. If, while taking the bowl out from its bag, there are dye powders on the bowl, it should be washed if there is water. If there is no water, the dye powder should be wiped off, and having had the bowl formally received, one should go for alms. If dust falls into the bowl while going for alms, the almsfood should be accepted after the bowl has been formally received. If one accepts the alms without it having been formally received, it is a Vinaya offense of wrong-doing. However, for one who eats after having it formally received again, there is no offense. But if, when one has said, “Please give after having it formally received,” they give the almsfood anyway, not having heard or not having paid attention, there is no Vinaya offense of wrong-doing; one should have the bowl formally received again and accept other almsfood. If a strong wind scatters dust from all sides, making it impossible to receive alms, one may accept it after making a reflection with a pure mind, “I will give this to an unordained person.” After going for alms in this way, one may return to the monastery or a sitting hall, give the almsfood to an unordained person, and then it is allowable to eat it after having it formally received back from that person or with their trust. If, during the almsround, one gives a dusty bowl to a bhikkhu, he should be told, “Having had this bowl formally received, you should then accept almsfood or consume it.” He should act accordingly. If dust floats on top, it should be made to flow away with gruel, and the remainder should be eaten. If the dust has mixed in, it should be formally received. If there is no unordained person present, one should take it to where an unordained person is, without letting it go from the hand, and have it formally received there. In the case of dry food, it is allowable to eat after removing the fallen dust. If the dust is very fine, it should be removed together with the food on top, or it should be eaten after having the bowl formally received. If, while porridge or soup is being stirred in front, drops splash up from the vessel and fall into the bowl, the bowl should be formally received.

107. Uḷuṅkena āharitvā dentānaṃ paṭhamataraṃ uḷuṅkato thevā patte patanti, supatitā, abhihaṭattā doso natthi. Sacepi carukena bhatte ākiriyamāne carukato masi vā chārikā vā patati, abhihaṭattā nevatthi doso. Anantarassa bhikkhuno dīyamānaṃ pattato uppatitvā itarassa patte patati, supatitaṃ. Paṭiggahitameva hi taṃ hoti. Sace jajjharisākhādiṃ phāletvā ekassa bhikkhuno dentānaṃ sākhato phusitāni aññassa patte patanti, patto paṭiggahetabbo, yassa pattassa upari phālenti, tassa patte patitesu dātukāmatāya abhihaṭattā doso natthi. Pāyāsassa pūretvā pattaṃ denti, uṇhattā heṭṭhā gahetuṃ na sakkoti, mukhavaṭṭiyāpi gahetuṃ vaṭṭati. Sace [M 0.0116] tathāpi na sakkoti, ādhārakena gahetabbo. Āsanasālāya pattaṃ gahetvā nisinno bhikkhu niddaṃ okkanto hoti, neva āhariyamānaṃ, na dīyamānaṃ jānāti, appaṭiggahitaṃ hoti. Sace pana ābhogaṃ katvā nisinno hoti, vaṭṭati. Sacepi so hatthena ādhārakaṃ muñcitvā pādena pelletvā niddāyati, vaṭṭatiyeva. Pādena ādhārakaṃ akkamitvā paṭiggaṇhantassa pana jāgarantassapi anādarapaṭiggahaṇaṃ hoti, tasmā na kattabbaṃ. Keci “evaṃ ādhārakena paṭiggahaṇaṃ kāyapaṭibaddhapaṭibaddhena paṭiggahaṇaṃ nāma hoti[V 0.0114], tasmā na vaṭṭatī”ti vadanti, taṃ vacanamattameva, atthato pana sabbampetaṃ kāyapaṭibaddhameva hoti. Kāyasaṃsaggepi cesa nayo dassito. Yampi bhikkhussa dīyamānaṃ patati, tampi sāmaṃ gahetvā paribhuñjituṃ vaṭṭati.

107. When donors bring food with a ladle to give, if drops from the ladle fall into the bowl first, they are well-fallen; because it was brought to be given, there is no fault. Even if, while food is being served with a small pot, soot or ash falls from the pot, because it was brought to be given, there is no fault at all. If something being given to an adjacent bhikkhu jumps from his bowl and falls into the bowl of another, it is well-fallen. Indeed, it is considered as having been received. If, while breaking a branch of jajjhari or the like and giving it to one bhikkhu, droplets from the branch fall into another's bowl, that bowl should be formally received. If they break it above a bhikkhu's bowl and droplets fall into his bowl, because it was brought with the desire to give, there is no fault. If they give a bowl filled with milk-rice, and due to the heat, he is not able to hold it from below, it is permissible to hold it even by the rim. If he is still not able to do so, it should be taken with a support. If a bhikkhu, having taken his bowl and sat down in the dining hall, falls asleep, and knows neither that food is being brought nor that it is being given, it is considered not properly received. But if he is seated having paid attention, it is permissible. Even if he, having released the support with his hand, secures it with his foot and falls asleep, it is indeed permissible. But for one who receives the bowl while stepping on the support with his foot, even if he is awake, it is a disrespectful receiving; therefore, it should not be done. Some say, 'Thus, receiving with a support is called 'receiving with something connected to that which is connected to the body'; therefore, it is not permissible.' That is merely their statement. But in essence, all of this is indeed connected to the body. And this principle has been shown in the case of bodily contact as well. Whatever is being given to a bhikkhu and falls, it is permissible for him to take it himself and consume it.

Tatridaṃ suttaṃ –

Herein, this is the Sutta:

“Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, yaṃ dīyamānaṃ patati, taṃ sāmaṃ gahetvā paribhuñjituṃ, pariccattaṃ taṃ, bhikkhave, dāyakehī”ti (cūḷava. 273).

“Bhikkhus, I allow you to take for yourselves and consume whatever falls while being given. Bhikkhus, that has been relinquished by the donors.”

Idañca pana suttaṃ neyyatthaṃ, tasmā evamettha adhippāyo veditabbo – yaṃ dīyamānaṃ dāyakassa hatthato parigaḷitvā suddhāya vā bhūmiyā paduminipaṇṇe vā vatthakaṭasārakādīsu vā patati, taṃ sāmaṃ gahetvā paribhuñjituṃ vaṭṭati. Yaṃ pana sarajāya bhūmiyaṃ patati, taṃ rajaṃ puñchitvā vā dhovitvā vā paṭiggahetvā vā paribhuñjitabbaṃ. Sace pavaṭṭantaṃ aññassa bhikkhuno santikaṃ gacchati, tena āharāpetumpi vaṭṭati. Sace taṃ bhikkhuṃ vadati “tvaṃyeva khādā”ti, tassapi khādituṃ vaṭṭati, anāṇattena pana tena na gahetabbaṃ. “Anāṇattenapi itarassa dassāmīti gahetuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti kurundiyaṃ vuttaṃ. Kasmā panetaṃ itarassa bhikkhuno gahetuṃ na vaṭṭatīti? Bhagavatā ananuññātattā. Bhagavatā hi “sāmaṃ gahetvā paribhuñjitu”nti vadantena yasseva taṃ dīyamānaṃ patati, tassa appaṭiggahitakampi taṃ gahetvā paribhogo anuññāto. “Pariccattaṃ taṃ, bhikkhave, dāyakehī”ti vacanena panettha parasantakabhāvo dīpito, tasmā aññassa sāmaṃ gahetvā paribhuñjituṃ na vaṭṭati, tassa pana āṇattiyā vaṭṭatīti ayaṃ kirettha adhippāyo. Yasmā ca etaṃ appaṭiggahitakattā [M 0.0117] anuññātaṃ, tasmā yathāṭhitaṃyeva anāmasitvā kenaci pidahitvā ṭhapitaṃ dutiyadivasepi paribhuñjituṃ vaṭṭati, sannidhipaccayā anāpatti, paṭiggahetvā pana paribhuñjitabbaṃ. Taṃ divasaṃyeva hi tassa sāmaṃ gahetvā paribhogo anuññāto, na tato paranti ayampi kirettha adhippāyo.

This Sutta, however, is one requiring interpretation; therefore, its intention here should be understood thus: Whatever falls from the donor’s hand while being given, onto clean ground, a lotus leaf, a piece of cloth, a mat, or the like, may be picked up by oneself and consumed. However, what falls on dusty ground should be consumed after wiping off the dust, washing it, or having it formally offered. If it rolls towards another bhikkhu, it is permissible to have him bring it. If he tells that bhikkhu, 'You yourself may eat it,' then that bhikkhu may also eat it, but it should not be taken by him without being instructed. In the Kurundi Commentary, it is stated: 'It is permissible to take it even without being instructed, with the intention of giving it to the other.' Why, then, is it not permissible for the other bhikkhu to take it? Because it has not been permitted by the Blessed One. For the Blessed One, in saying, 'Pick it up yourself and consume it,' permitted the consumption of what falls, even if unaccepted, by the very one to whom it was being given. By the statement, 'Monks, that has been relinquished by the donors,' the state of being another's property is indicated here. Therefore, it is not permissible for another to pick it up and consume it himself, but it is permissible by the instruction of that bhikkhu—this is indeed the intention here. And since this is permitted on account of its unaccepted state, it is permissible to consume it even on the second day, left as it is, untouched and covered by something, without incurring an offense due to storing. However, it should be consumed after having it formally offered. For consumption by taking it oneself is permitted only on that same day, not thereafter—this too is indeed the intention here.

108. Idāni abbohārikanayo vuccati. Bhuñjantānañhi dantā khīyanti, nakhā khīyanti, pattassa vaṇṇo khīyati, sabbaṃ abbohārikaṃ. Satthakena ucchuādīsu phālitesu malaṃ paññāyati, etaṃ navasamuṭṭhitaṃ nāma, paṭiggahetvā paribhuñjitabbaṃ. Satthakaṃ dhovitvā phālitesu malaṃ na paññāyati, lohagandhamattaṃ hoti, taṃ abbohārikaṃ. Yampi satthakaṃ gahetvā pariharanti[V 0.0115], tena phālitepi eseva nayo. Na hi taṃ paribhogatthāya pariharantīti. Mūlabhesajjādīni pisantānaṃ vā koṭṭentānaṃ vā nisadanisadapotakaudukkhalamusalādīni khīyanti, pariharaṇakavāsiṃ tāpetvā bhesajjatthāya takke vā khīre vā pakkhipanti, tattha nīlikā paññāyati, satthake vuttasadisova vinicchayo. Āmakatakkādīsu pana sayaṃ na pakkhipitabbā, pakkhipati ce, sāmaṃpākato na muccati. Deve vassante piṇḍāya carantassa sarīrato vā cīvarato vā kiliṭṭhaudakaṃ patte patati, paṭiggahetabbaṃ. Rukkhamūlādīsu bhuñjantassa patitepi eseva nayo. Sace pana sattāhaṃ vassante deve suddhaṃ udakaṃ hoti, abbhokāsato vā patati, vaṭṭati.

108. Now the method of what is not to be reckoned is explained. For of those who are eating, teeth wear down, nails wear down, and the color of the bowl fades; all this is not to be reckoned. When sugarcane and so forth are split with a small knife, should rust appear, this is called 'newly arisen'; it should be consumed after having it formally offered. When the small knife is washed and they are split, rust does not appear and there is only the smell of metal; that is not to be reckoned. And as for the small knife which they take and carry about, even when something is split with it, this is the very same principle, for indeed, they do not carry it for the sake of consumption. For those grinding or pounding root-medicines and so forth, the grinding slab, the small grinding stone, the mortar, the pestle, and so forth wear down. If a heated portable adze is placed in buttermilk or milk for medicinal purposes, and a bluish color appears therein, the decision is to be understood as just like that stated for the small knife. However, into uncooked buttermilk and so forth, it should not be placed by oneself; if one does place it, one is not free from the offense of cooking for oneself. When it is raining, if soiled water from the body or robe of a bhikkhu wandering for alms-food falls into his bowl, it should be formally received. The same principle applies if something falls in while one is eating at the foot of a tree and so forth. But if, when it has been raining for seven days, the water is pure, or if it falls from the open sky, it is allowable.

109. Sāmaṇerassa odanaṃ dentena tassa pattagataṃ acchupanteneva dātabbo, patto vāssa paṭiggahetabbo. Appaṭiggahite odanaṃ chupitvā puna attano patte odanaṃ gaṇhantassa uggahitako hoti. Sace pana dātukāmo hutvā “āhara, sāmaṇera, pattaṃ, odanaṃ gaṇhāhī”ti vadati, itaro “alaṃ mayha”nti paṭikkhipati, puna “tavetaṃ mayā pariccatta”nti ca vutte “na mayhaṃ etenattho”ti vadati, satakkhattumpi pariccajatu, yāva attano hatthagataṃ, tāva paṭiggahitameva hoti. Sace pana ādhārake ṭhitaṃ nirapekkho “gaṇhāhī”ti vadati, puna paṭiggahetabbaṃ. Sāpekkho ādhārake pattaṃ ṭhapetvā “etto pūvaṃ vā bhattaṃ vā gaṇhāhī”ti sāmaṇeraṃ vadati, sāmaṇero hatthaṃ dhovitvā sacepi satakkhattuṃ gahetvā attano pattagataṃ aphusantova attano patte [M 0.0118] pakkhipati, puna paṭiggahaṇakiccaṃ natthi. Yadi pana attano pattagataṃ phusitvā tato gaṇhāti, sāmaṇerasantakena saṃsaṭṭhaṃ hoti, puna paṭiggahetabbaṃ. Keci pana “sacepi gayhamānaṃ chijjitvā tattha patati, puna paṭiggahetabba”nti vadanti. Taṃ “ekaṃ bhattapiṇḍaṃ gaṇha, ekaṃ pūvaṃ gaṇha, imassa guḷapiṇḍassa ettakaṃ padesaṃ gaṇhā”ti evaṃ paricchinditvā vutte veditabbaṃ, idha pana paricchedo natthi, tasmā yaṃ sāmaṇerassa patte patati, tadeva paṭiggahaṇaṃ vijahati, hatthagataṃ pana yāva sāmaṇero vā “ala”nti na oramati, bhikkhu vā na vāreti, tāva bhikkhusseva santakaṃ, tasmā paṭiggahaṇaṃ na vijahati. Sace attano vā bhikkhūnaṃ vā yāgupacanakabhājane kesañci atthāya bhattaṃ pakkhipati, “sāmaṇera, bhājanassa upari hatthaṃ karohī”ti vatvā tassa hatthe pakkhipitabbaṃ. Tassa hatthato bhājane patitañhi dutiyadivase bhājanassa akappiyabhāvaṃ na karoti pariccattattā. Sace evaṃ akatvā pakkhipati, pattamiva bhājanaṃ nirāmisaṃ katvā paribhuñjitabbaṃ.

109. When a bhikkhu gives rice to a novice, it should be given without touching the food that is in the novice's bowl, or the novice's bowl should be formally received. For a bhikkhu who, having touched the rice in an unreceived bowl, then takes rice into his own bowl, the formal acceptance of his own food is broken. If, however, wishing to give, he says, 'Novice, bring your bowl and take this rice,' and the other refuses, saying, 'Enough for me,' and when it is said again, 'This has been relinquished to you by me,' he says, 'I have no need for this,' then even if he relinquishes it a hundred times, as long as the food is in his own hand, it remains formally received. If, however, having placed the food on a stand, he says without attachment, 'Take it,' it must be formally received again. If, with attachment, having placed the bowl on a stand, he says to the novice, 'Take a cake or rice from here,' and the novice, after washing his hands, even if he takes it a hundred times and places it in his own bowl without touching the food already in his bowl, there is no need for formal reception again.
