If, however, having touched the food in his own bowl, he then takes from that bhikkhu's bowl, it becomes mixed with what belongs to the novice and must be formally received again. Some teachers, however, say: 'Even if what is being taken breaks off and falls back, it must be formally received again.' That should be understood to apply in a case where it is specified, such as, 'Take one lump of rice,' 'Take one cake,' or 'Take this much of this lump of jaggery.' But here, there is no specification; therefore, whatever falls into the novice's bowl, only that gives up its status as formally received. However, what remains with the bhikkhu, as long as the novice does not consent, saying, 'Enough,' or the bhikkhu does not prevent him, so long it is the property of the bhikkhu alone; therefore, it does not give up its status as formally received. If one puts rice into a pot for cooking gruel for oneself or for other bhikkhus, intending some for another person, one should say, 'Novice, place your hand over the pot,' and then place it into his hand. For what has fallen from his hand into the pot does not make the pot improper for use on the second day, because it has been relinquished. If one puts it in without doing so, the pot, like a bowl, should be used only after having been made free of provisions.

110. Dāyakā [V 0.0116] yāgukuṭaṃ ṭhapetvā gatā, taṃ daharasāmaṇero paṭiggaṇhāpetuṃ na sakkoti, bhikkhu pattaṃ upanāmeti, sāmaṇero kuṭassa gīvaṃ pattassa mukhavaṭṭiyaṃ ṭhapetvā āvajjeti, pattagatā yāgu paṭiggahitāva hoti. Atha vā bhikkhu bhūmiyaṃ hatthaṃ ṭhapeti, sāmaṇero pavaṭṭetvā hatthaṃ āropeti, vaṭṭati. Pūvapacchibhattapacchiucchubhārādīsupi eseva nayo. Sace paṭiggahaṇūpagaṃ bhāraṃ dve tayo sāmaṇerā denti, ekena vā balavatā ukkhittaṃ dve tayo bhikkhū gaṇhanti, vaṭṭati. Mañcassa vā pīṭhassa vā pāde telaghaṭaṃ vā phāṇitaghaṭaṃ vā laggenti, bhikkhussa mañcepi pīṭhepi nisīdituṃ vaṭṭati, uggahitakaṃ nāma na hoti.

110. Donors have placed a gruel pot and departed, but a young novice is unable to have it formally offered. A bhikkhu brings his bowl near; the novice, placing the neck of the pot on the rim of the bowl, pours. The gruel that has entered the bowl is thereby formally received. Alternatively, a bhikkhu places his hand on the ground; the novice, having tipped the item, places it onto his hand; this is allowable. This same method applies to baskets of cakes, baskets of rice, heavy bundles of sugarcane, and so forth. If a load suitable for formal receiving is given by two or three novices, or if what is lifted by one strong novice is received by two or three bhikkhus, it is allowable. If they attach an oil pot or a molasses pot to the leg of a bed or a stool, it is allowable for a bhikkhu to sit on the bed or stool; it is not considered to have been 'taken up'.

Nāgadantake vā aṅkusake vā dve telaghaṭā laggitā honti upari paṭiggahitako, heṭṭhā appaṭiggahitako. Uparimaṃ gahetuṃ vaṭṭati, heṭṭhā paṭiggahitako, upari appaṭiggahitako, uparimaṃ gahetvā itaraṃ gaṇhato uparimo uggahitako hoti. Heṭṭhāmañce appaṭiggahitakaṃ telathālakaṃ hoti, tañce sammajjanto sammuñjaniyā ghaṭṭeti, uggahitakaṃ na hoti, “paṭiggahitakaṃ gaṇhissāmī”ti appaṭiggahitakaṃ gahetvā ñatvā puna ṭhapeti, uggahitakaṃ na hoti, bahi nīharitvā sañjānāti, bahi aṭṭhapetvā haritvā tattheva ṭhapetabbaṃ, natthi doso. Sace [M 0.0119] pana pubbe vivaritvā ṭhapitaṃ, na pidahitabbaṃ. Yathā pubbe ṭhitaṃ, tatheva ṭhapetabbaṃ. Sace bahi ṭhapeti, puna na chupitabbaṃ.

If two oil pots are hung on a peg or a hook, the upper one having been formally received and the lower one not, it is allowable to take the upper one. If the lower one has been formally received and the upper one has not, for one who, while holding the upper one, takes the other, the upper one becomes 'taken up'. If there is an unreceived oil bowl under a bed, and one who is sweeping touches it with a broom, it does not become 'taken up'. If, thinking, 'I will take a formally received item,' one takes an unreceived item and, upon realizing, puts it back, it does not become 'taken up'. If one takes it outside and then recognizes it, one should not place it outside but should bring it back and place it in the very same spot; there is no fault. However, if it was previously placed open, it should not be closed. It should be placed just as it was situated before. If one does place it outside, it should not be touched again.

111. Paṭiggahitake telādimhi kaṇṇikā uṭṭheti, siṅgiverādimhi ghanacuṇṇaṃ, taṃsamuṭṭhānameva nāma taṃ, puna paṭiggahaṇakiccaṃ natthi. Tālaṃ vā nāḷikeraṃ vā āruḷho yottena phalapiṇḍiṃ otāretvā upari ṭhitova “gaṇhathā”ti vadati, na gahetabbaṃ. Sace añño bhūmiyaṃ ṭhito yottapāsake gahetvā ukkhipitvā deti, vaṭṭati. Saphalaṃ mahāsākhaṃ kappiyaṃ kāretvā paṭiggaṇhāti, phalāni paṭiggahitāneva honti, yathāsukhaṃ paribhuñjituṃ vaṭṭati. Antovatiyaṃ ṭhatvā vatiṃ chinditvā ucchuṃ vā timbarūsakaṃ vā denti, hatthapāse sati vaṭṭati. Daṇḍakesu apaharitvā niggataṃ gaṇhantassa vaṭṭati, paharitvā niggate aṭṭhakathāsu doso na dassito. Mayaṃ pana “yaṃ ṭhānaṃ pahaṭaṃ, tato sayaṃpatitamiva hotī”ti takkayāma, tampi ṭhatvā gacchante yujjati suṅkaghātato pavaṭṭetvā bahipatitabhaṇḍaṃ viya. Vatiṃ vā pākāraṃ vā laṅghāpetvā denti, sace pana aputhulo pākāro, antopākāre bahipākāre ca ṭhitassa hatthapāso pahoti, hatthasatampi uddhaṃ gantvā sampattaṃ gahetuṃ vaṭṭati.

111. In formally received oil or the like, fungus arises; in ginger or the like, a solid powder forms. This is called 'that which has arisen from it'; there is no need for it to be formally received again. If one who has climbed a palm or coconut tree lowers a cluster of fruit with a rope and, while remaining above, says, 'Take it,' it should not be taken. If another person standing on the ground takes hold of the loop of the rope, lifts it up, and gives it, it is allowable. If one formally receives a large branch together with its fruit, having had it made allowable, the fruits are considered to have been formally received; it is allowable to consume them as one pleases. If people standing inside a fence, having cut through the fence, give sugarcane or timbarūsaka fruit, it is allowable if it is within arm's reach. It is allowable for one to take that which has come out from the fence-posts without being struck. In the case of it coming out after being struck, no fault is shown in the commentaries. We, however, reason thus: 'From whatever place was struck, it is as if it fell by itself.' In that case also, it is proper for one standing there to take it when it arrives, like goods that, having been knocked from a customs post, have fallen outside. If they give something, causing it to pass over a fence or a wall, and if the wall is not thick, and it is within the arm's reach of one standing either inside or outside the wall, it is allowable to take that which has arrived, even if it has gone upwards a hundred cubits.

Bhikkhu gilānaṃ sāmaṇeraṃ khandhena vahati, so phalāphalaṃ disvā gahetvā khandhe nisinnova deti[V 0.0117], vaṭṭati. Aparo bhikkhuṃ vahanto khandhe nisinnassa bhikkhuno deti, vaṭṭatiyeva. Bhikkhu phaliniṃ sākhaṃ chāyatthāya gahetvā gacchati, phalāni khādituṃ citte uppanne paṭiggahāpetvā khādituṃ vaṭṭati. Macchikavāraṇatthaṃ kappiyaṃ kāretvā paṭiggaṇhāti, khāditukāmo ce hoti, mūlapaṭiggahaṇameva vaṭṭati, khādantassa natthi doso. Bhikkhu paṭiggahaṇārahaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ manussānaṃ yāne ṭhapetvā maggaṃ gacchati, yānaṃ kaddame laggati, daharo cakkaṃ gahetvā ukkhipati, vaṭṭati, uggahitakaṃ nāma na hoti. Nāvāya ṭhapetvā nāvaṃ arittena vā pājeti, hatthena vā kaḍḍhati, vaṭṭati. Uḷumpepi eseva nayo. Cāṭiyaṃ vā kuṇḍake vā ṭhapetvāpi taṃ anupasampannena gāhāpetvā anupasampannaṃ bāhāyaṃ gahetvā tarituṃ vaṭṭati. Tasmimpi asati anupasampannaṃ gāhāpetvā taṃ bāhāyaṃ gahetvā tarituṃ vaṭṭati.

A bhikkhu carries a sick novice on his shoulder. That novice, seeing fruit and taking it, gives it while still seated on the bhikkhu's shoulder; it is allowable. Another person carrying a bhikkhu gives something to the bhikkhu seated on his shoulder; this is indeed allowable. A bhikkhu, having taken a fruit-bearing branch for the sake of shade, goes along. When the thought to eat the fruits arises, having had them formally received, it is allowable to eat them. For the purpose of a fly-whisk, having had a suitable item made, one formally receives it. If one becomes desirous of eating it, the initial formal receiving itself is sufficient; for one who eats it, there is no fault. A bhikkhu, having placed goods suitable for formal receiving in a vehicle belonging to laypeople, goes along a road. If the vehicle gets stuck in the mud and a young person takes and lifts the wheel, it is allowable; it is not considered to have been 'taken up'. Having placed the goods in a boat, if one propels the boat with an oar or pulls it by hand, it is allowable. For a raft also, this is the same method. Having placed the goods in a pot or a pail, and having had an unordained person hold it, it is allowable to cross over by taking that unordained person by the arm. When such a container is not present, having had an unordained person hold the goods, it is allowable to cross over by taking that unordained person by the arm.

Upāsakā [M 0.0120] gamikabhikkhūnaṃ pātheyyataṇḍule denti, sāmaṇerā bhikkhūnaṃ taṇḍule gahetvā attano taṇḍule gahetuṃ na sakkonti, bhikkhū tesaṃ taṇḍule gaṇhanti, sāmaṇerā attanā gahitataṇḍulesu khīṇesu itarehi taṇḍulehi yāguṃ pacitvā sabbesaṃ pattāni paṭipāṭiyā ṭhapetvā yāguṃ ākiranti, paṇḍito sāmaṇero attano pattaṃ gahetvā therassa deti, therassa pattaṃ dutiyattherassāti evaṃ sabbānipi parivatteti, sabbehi sāmaṇerassa santakaṃ bhuttaṃ hoti, vaṭṭati. Sacepi sāmaṇero apaṇḍito hoti, attano patte yāguṃ sayameva pātuṃ ārabhati, “āvuso, tuyhaṃ yāguṃ mayhaṃ dehī”ti therehi paṭipāṭiyā yācitvāpi pivituṃ vaṭṭati, sabbehi sāmaṇerassa santakameva bhuttaṃ hoti, neva uggahitapaccayā, na sannidhipaccayā vajjaṃ phusanti. Ettha pana mātāpitūnaṃ telādīni, chāyādīnaṃ atthāya sākhādīni ca harantānaṃ imesañca viseso na dissati, tasmā kāraṇaṃ upaparikkhitabbaṃ.

Lay followers give travelling bhikkhus rice for provisions. Novices take the bhikkhus' rice, and being unable to take their own rice, the bhikkhus take the novices' rice. When the rice carried by the novices is exhausted, they cook gruel with the other rice. Having arranged all the bowls in order, they pour the gruel. A wise novice takes his own bowl and gives it to the elder; he gives the elder's bowl to the second elder, and in this way, he exchanges all the bowls. Thus, what is eaten by all is the possession of the novice, and it is allowable. Even if the novice is unwise and begins to drink the gruel in his own bowl himself, it is also allowable to drink after the elders have requested it in turn, saying, 'Friend, give me your gruel.' What is eaten by all is still only the possession of the novice. They incur no fault, neither on account of it having been 'taken up' nor on account of storing. Here, however, no distinction is seen between this case and that of those who carry oil and so forth for their parents, or branches and so forth for the sake of shade and other purposes. Therefore, the reason should be investigated.

112. Sāmaṇero bhattaṃ pacitukāmo taṇḍule dhovitvā niccāletuṃ na sakkoti, bhikkhunā taṇḍule ca bhājanañca paṭiggahetvā taṇḍule dhovitvā niccāletvā bhājanaṃ uddhanaṃ āropetabbaṃ, aggi na kātabbo, pakkakāle vivaritvā pakkabhāvo jānitabbo. Sace duppakkaṃ hoti, pākatthāya pidahituṃ na vaṭṭati, rajassa vā chārikāya vā apatanatthāya vaṭṭati, pakkakāle oropituṃ bhuñjitumpi vaṭṭati, puna paṭiggahaṇakiccaṃ natthi. Sāmaṇero paṭibalo pacituṃ, khaṇo panassa natthi katthaci gantukāmo, bhikkhunā sataṇḍulodakaṃ bhājanaṃ paṭiggahetvā uddhanaṃ āropetvā “aggiṃ jāletvā gacchā”ti vattabbo. Tato paraṃ purimanayeneva sabbaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭati. Bhikkhu yāguatthāya suddhabhājanaṃ āropetvā udakaṃ tāpeti, vaṭṭati. Tatte udake sāmaṇero taṇḍule pakkhipati, tato paṭṭhāya bhikkhunā aggi na [V 0.0118] kātabbo, pakkayāguṃ paṭiggahetvā pātuṃ vaṭṭati. Sāmaṇero yāguṃ pacati, hatthakukkuccako bhikkhu kīḷanto bhājanaṃ āmasati, pidhānaṃ āmasati, uggataṃ pheṇaṃ chinditvā paharati, tasseva pātuṃ na vaṭṭati, durupaciṇṇaṃ nāma hoti. Sace pana dabbiṃ vā uḷuṅkaṃ vā gahetvā anukkhipanto [M 0.0121] āloḷeti, sabbesaṃ na vaṭṭati, sāmaṃpākañceva hoti durupaciṇṇañca. Sace ukkhipati, uggahitakampi hoti.

112. A novice, wishing to cook rice, having washed the rice grains, is not able to drain them; a bhikkhu, having formally received both the rice grains and the pot, having washed the rice grains and drained them, should place the pot on the stove. Fire should not be made. When it is cooked, having opened it, the state of being cooked should be known. If it is undercooked, it is not allowable to cover it for the purpose of cooking; it is allowable to cover it for the purpose of preventing dust or ashes from falling in. When it is cooked, it is allowable to take it down and to eat it; there is no further duty of formal reception. A novice is capable of cooking, but he has no time, wishing to go somewhere; a bhikkhu, having formally received the pot with rice and water and having placed it on the stove, should say, 'Having lit the fire, go.' Beyond that, it is allowable to do everything by the former method. A bhikkhu, for the purpose of gruel, having placed a clean pot on the stove, heats water; this is allowable. When the water is hot, the novice adds the rice grains. Starting from that point, fire should not be made by the bhikkhu. Having formally received the cooked gruel, it is allowable to drink it. A novice cooks gruel. A bhikkhu of restless hands, playing, touches the pot, touches the lid, or having cut the risen foam, removes it; it is not allowable for him alone to drink it; this is called 'improperly handled'. But if, having taken a ladle or a dipper, he stirs without lifting, it is not allowable for any of them. It is both cooked by oneself and improperly handled. If he lifts it, it is also 'taken up'.

113. Bhikkhunā piṇḍāya caritvā ādhārake patto ṭhapito hoti. Tatra ce añño lolabhikkhu kīḷanto pattaṃ āmasati, pattapidhānaṃ āmasati, tasseva tato laddhabhattaṃ na vaṭṭati. Sace na pattaṃ ukkhipitvā ṭhapeti, sabbesaṃ na vaṭṭati. Tatthajātakaphalinisākhāya vā valliyā vā gahetvā cāleti, tasseva tato laddhaphalaṃ na vaṭṭati, durupaciṇṇadukkaṭañca āpajjati. “Phalarukkhaṃ pana apassayituṃ vā tattha kaṇṭakaṃ vā bandhituṃ vaṭṭati, durupaciṇṇaṃ na hotī”ti mahāpaccariyaṃ vuttaṃ. Araññe patitaṃ pana ambaphalādiṃ disvā “sāmaṇerassa dassāmī”ti āharitvā dātuṃ vaṭṭati. Sīhavighāsādiṃ disvāpi “sāmaṇerassa dassāmī”ti paṭiggahetvā vā appaṭiggahetvā vā āharitvā dātuṃ vaṭṭati. Sace pana sakkoti vitakkaṃ sodhetuṃ, tato laddhaṃ khāditumpi vaṭṭati, neva āmakamaṃsapaṭiggahaṇapaccayā, na uggahitakapaccayā vajjaṃ phusati. Mātāpitūnaṃ atthāya telādīni gahetvā gacchato antarāmagge byādhi uppajjati, tato yaṃ icchati, taṃ paṭiggahetvā paribhuñjituṃ vaṭṭati. Sace pana mūlepi paṭiggahitaṃ hoti, puna paṭiggahaṇakiccaṃ natthi. Mātāpitūnaṃ taṇḍule āharitvā deti, te tatoyeva yāguādīni sampādetvā tassa denti, vaṭṭati, sannidhipaccayā uggahitapaccayā vā doso natthi.

113. A bhikkhu, having gone for alms, has placed his bowl on a stand. If, in that place, another frivolous bhikkhu, while playing, touches the bowl or the bowl-lid, the food obtained from that bowl is not allowable for him alone. If, having lifted the bowl, he does not place it back, it is not allowable for any of them. If, having grabbed a branch or a vine of a fruit-bearing tree that has grown there, he shakes it, the fruit obtained from that is not allowable for him alone, and he incurs a dukkaṭa offense for improper handling. It is said in the Mahāpaccarī: 'However, it is allowable to lean against a fruit tree or to tie a thorn on it; it is not improper handling.' However, having seen a fallen mango or other fruit in the forest, it is allowable to bring it and give it, thinking, 'I will give this to a novice.' Also, having seen leftover food such as a lion's leavings, it is allowable to bring it and give it, thinking, 'I will give this to a novice,' whether having formally received it or not. But if he is able to purify his thought, it is also allowable to eat what is obtained from that; he does not incur a fault on account of formally receiving raw meat, nor on account of its being taken up. If a bhikkhu, having taken oil or other items for his parents' sake, falls ill along the way, it is allowable to formally receive and consume whatever item he desires from that. But if it was formally received from the outset, there is no need for formal reception again. If he brings rice and gives it to his parents, and they prepare gruel or other dishes from that very rice and give it to him, it is allowable; there is no fault on account of storing or on account of its being taken up.

114. Bhikkhu pidahitvā udakaṃ tāpeti, yāva parikkhayā paribhuñjituṃ vaṭṭati. Sace panettha chārikā patati, paṭiggahetabbaṃ. Dīghasaṇḍāsena thālakaṃ gahetvā telaṃ pacantassa chārikā patati, hatthena amuñcanteneva pacitvā otāretvā paṭiggahetabbaṃ. Sace aṅgārāpi dārūnipi paṭiggahetvā ṭhapitāni, mūlapaṭiggahaṇameva vaṭṭati. Bhikkhu ucchuṃ khādati, sāmaṇero “mayhampi dethā”ti vadati, “ito chinditvā gaṇhā”ti vutto gaṇhāti, avasese puna paṭiggahaṇakiccaṃ natthi. Guḷapiṇḍaṃ khādantassapi eseva nayo. Vuttokāsato chinditvā gahitāvasesañhi ajahitapaṭiggahaṇameva hoti. Bhikkhu guḷaṃ bhājento paṭiggahetvā koṭṭhāse karoti, bhikkhūpi sāmaṇerāpi āgantvā ekaggahaṇeneva ekamekaṃ koṭṭhāsaṃ gaṇhanti, gahitāvasesaṃ [V 0.0119] paṭiggahitameva hoti. Sace lolasāmaṇero [M 0.0122] gaṇhitvā gaṇhitvā puna ṭhapeti, tassa gahitāvasesaṃ appaṭiggahitakameva hoti.

114. A bhikkhu heats water in a covered vessel; it is allowable to consume it until it is exhausted without it being formally re-offered. If ashes fall into it, it must be formally received. If, while a bhikkhu is cooking oil, holding a small pot with long tongs, ashes fall in, he should, without letting go with his hand, finish cooking, take it down, and then have it formally received. If embers have been formally received and set aside, the initial formal reception itself is valid. A bhikkhu eats sugarcane, and a novice says, "Give me some too." Being told, "Cut off a piece from here and take it," he takes it; there is no need for further formal reception of the remainder. The same principle applies to one eating a lump of jaggery. For the remainder, after a piece is cut and taken from the indicated place, is indeed that for which the formal reception has not been abandoned. If a bhikkhu, having formally received jaggery, divides it and makes portions, and other bhikkhus or novices come and each takes a portion with a single act of taking, the remaining portion is considered as having been formally received. If a frivolous novice takes portions repeatedly and places them back, the remainder that he handled is considered as not having been formally received.

Bhikkhu dhūmavaṭṭiṃ paṭiggahetvā dhūmaṃ pivati, mukhañca kaṇṭho ca manosilāya litto viya hoti, yāvakālikaṃ bhuñjituṃ vaṭṭati, yāvakālikena yāvajīvikasaṃsagge doso natthi. Pattaṃ vā rajanaṃ vā pacantassa kaṇṇanāsacchiddehi dhūmo pavisati, byādhipaccayā pupphaṃ vā phalaṃ vā upasiṅghati, abbohārikattā vaṭṭati. Bhattuggāro tāluṃ āhacca antoyeva pavisati, avisayattā vaṭṭati, mukhaṃ paviṭṭhaṃ pana ajjhoharato vikāle āpatti. Dantantare laggassa āmisassa raso pavisati, āpattiyeva. Sace sukhumaṃ āmisaṃ hoti, raso na paññāyati, abbohārikapakkhaṃ bhajati. Upakaṭṭhe kāle nirudakaṭṭhāne bhattaṃ bhuñjitvā kakkhāretvā dve tayo kheḷapiṇḍe pātetvā udakaṭṭhānaṃ gantvā mukhaṃ vikkhāletabbaṃ. Paṭiggahetvā ṭhapitasiṅgiverādīnaṃ aṅkurā nikkhamanti, puna paṭiggahaṇakiccaṃ natthi. Loṇe asati samuddodakena loṇakiccaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭati, paṭiggahetvā ṭhapitaloṇodakaṃ loṇaṃ hoti, loṇaṃ vā udakaṃ hoti, raso vā phāṇitaṃ hoti, phāṇitaṃ vā raso hoti, mūlapaṭiggahaṇameva vaṭṭati.

If a monk, having received a medicinal roll, inhales the smoke, and his mouth and throat become as if smeared with realgar, it is allowable to consume it as a temporary provision. There is no fault in the mixing of a temporary provision with a lifelong provision. For a monk who is firing a bowl or boiling dye, if smoke enters through the orifices of the ears and nose, or if, on account of illness, one smells a flower or a fruit, it is allowable because it is not considered consumption. If a belch of food, having touched the palate, enters back inside, it is allowable as it is not within the scope of an offense. However, for one who swallows that which has reached the mouth, there is an offense if it is at the wrong time. If the juice of food stuck between the teeth enters, it is indeed an offense. If the food is very fine and its taste is not discernible, it falls into the category of the non-consumable. When it is close to noon, having eaten in a place without water, one should clear the throat, spit out two or three lumps of phlegm, then go to a place with water and rinse the mouth. If sprouts emerge from ginger or other such items that were received and stored, there is no need for a subsequent receiving. In the absence of salt, it is allowable to use seawater for the purpose of salting. If saltwater that was received and stored becomes salt, or salt becomes water, or juice becomes molasses, or molasses becomes juice, the original receiving itself is allowable.

Himakarakā udakagatikā eva. Pārihārikena katakaṭṭhinā udakaṃ pasādenti, taṃ abbohārikaṃ, āmisena saddhiṃ vaṭṭati. Āmisagatikehi kapitthaphalādīhi pasāditaṃ purebhattameva vaṭṭati. Pokkharaṇīādīsu udakaṃ bahalaṃ hoti, vaṭṭati. Sace pana mukhe hatthe ca laggati, na vaṭṭati, paṭiggahetvā paribhuñjitabbaṃ. Khettesu kasitaṭṭhāne bahalaṃ udakaṃ hoti, paṭiggahetabbaṃ. Sace sanditvā kandarādīni pavisitvā nadiṃ pūreti, vaṭṭati. Kakudhasobbhādayo honti rukkhato patitehi pupphehi sañchannodakā. Sace puppharaso na paññāyati, paṭiggahaṇakiccaṃ natthi. Parittaṃ udakaṃ hoti, raso paññāyati, paṭiggahetabbaṃ. Pabbatakandarādīsu kāḷavaṇṇapaṇṇacchannaudakepi eseva nayo.

Hailstones are indeed in the category of water. When they clarify water with a portable clearing nut, that water is not considered a consumable; it is allowable together with food. Water clarified with items in the category of food, such as wood-apple fruits and so on, is allowable only before the meal. In lotus ponds and so on, if the water is thick, it is allowable. But if it sticks to the mouth and hands, it is not allowable; it should be received and then consumed. In fields, in a plowed place, if the water is thick, it should be received. If it flows, enters ravines and so on, and fills a river, it is allowable. In the case of Kakudha trees, pools, and so on, the water may be covered with flowers fallen from trees. If the essence of the flowers is not discernible, there is no need for receiving. If the water is scant and the essence is discernible, it should be received. In mountain ravines and so on, and also for water covered with dark-colored leaves, this same principle applies.

Pānīyaghaṭe sareṇukāni vā savaṇṭakhīrāni vā pupphāni pakkhittāni honti, paṭiggahetabbaṃ, pupphāni vā paṭiggahetvā pakkhipitabbāni. Pāṭalimallikā pakkhittā honti, vāsamattaṃ tiṭṭhati, taṃ abbohārikaṃ. Dubhiyadivasepi [M 0.0123] āmisena saddhiṃ vaṭṭati. Bhikkhunā ṭhapitapupphavāsitakapānīyato sāmaṇero pānīyaṃ gahetvā pītāvasesakaṃ tattheva ākirati, paṭiggahetabbaṃ. Padumasarādīsu udakaṃ santharitvā ṭhitaṃ pupphareṇuṃ ghaṭena vikkhambhetvā udakaṃ gahetuṃ vaṭṭati. Kappiyaṃ kārāpetvā paṭiggahetvā ṭhapitaṃ dantakaṭṭhaṃ hoti, sace tassa rasaṃ pivitukāmo[V 0.0120], mūlapaṭiggahaṇameva vaṭṭati, appaṭiggahetvā ṭhapitaṃ paṭiggahetabbaṃ. Ajānantassa rase paviṭṭhepi āpattiyeva. Acittakañhi idaṃ sikkhāpadaṃ.

In a drinking water pot, if flowers with pollen or flowers with milky-sapped stalks are put in, it should be received; or, the flowers should be received and then put in. If Pāṭali and Mallikā flowers have been put in and only the fragrance remains, that water is not considered a consumable. Even on the second day, it is allowable together with food. If a novice takes water from a drinking pot scented with flowers and set aside by a monk, and after drinking, pours the remainder back into that same pot, it should be received. In lotus lakes and so on, it is allowable to take water by pushing aside with a pot the flower pollen that has spread over the surface. If a tooth-stick has been made allowable, received, and set aside, and if one wishes to drink its juice, the original receiving itself is sufficient. A tooth-stick that was set aside without being received should be received. For one who does not know, even when the juice has been ingested, there is indeed an offense, for this training rule is non-intentional.

115. Mahābhūtesu kiṃ vaṭṭati, kiṃ na vaṭṭatīti? Khīraṃ tāva vaṭṭati, kappiyamaṃsakhīraṃ vā hotu akappiyamaṃsakhīraṃ vā, pivantassa anāpatti. Assu kheḷo siṅghāṇikā muttaṃ karīsaṃ semhaṃ dantamalaṃ akkhigūthako kaṇṇagūthako sarīre uṭṭhitaloṇanti idaṃ sabbaṃ vaṭṭati. Yaṃ panettha ṭhānato cavitvā patte vā hatthe vā patati, taṃ paṭiggahetabbaṃ, aṅgalaggaṃ paṭiggahitakameva. Uṇhapāyāsaṃ bhuñjantassa sedo aṅgulianusārena ekābaddhova hutvā pāyāse santiṭṭhati, piṇḍāya vā carantassa hatthato pattassa mukhavaṭṭito vā pattatalaṃ orohati, ettha paṭiggahaṇakiccaṃ natthi, jhāmamahābhūte idaṃ nāma na vaṭṭatīti natthi, dujjhāpitaṃ pana na vaṭṭati. Sujjhāpitaṃ pana manussaṭṭhimpi cuṇṇaṃ katvā lehe upanetuṃ vaṭṭati. Cattāri mahāvikaṭāni asati kappiyakārake sāmaṃ gahetvā paribhuñjituṃ vaṭṭanti. Ettha ca dubbacopi asamatthopi kappiyakārako asantapakkheyeva tiṭṭhati. Chārikāya asati sukkhadāruṃ jhāpetvā chārikā gahetabbā. Sukkhadārumhi asati alladāruṃ rukkhato chinditvāpi kātuṃ vaṭṭati. Idaṃ pana catubbidhampi mahāvikaṭaṃ kālodissaṃ nāma, sappadaṭṭhakkhaṇeyeva vaṭṭati.

115. Regarding bodily substances, what is allowable, and what is not allowable? First, milk is allowable—whether it be the milk of an animal whose flesh is allowable or the milk of an animal whose flesh is not allowable, there is no offense for one who drinks it. Tears, saliva, mucus, urine, feces, phlegm, tooth plaque, eye discharge, earwax, and salt that has formed on the body—all this is allowable. If any of these, having shifted from its place, falls into a bowl or onto the hand, it should be received. What is stuck to a limb is considered as having been received. For one eating hot porridge, if sweat flows down the fingers as a single continuous stream and settles in the porridge, or for one walking for alms-food, if it descends from the hand or from the rim of the bowl into the bottom of the bowl, in such cases, there is no need for receiving. Regarding burnt substances, there is nothing that is not allowable; however, what is poorly burnt is not allowable. But what is well-burnt is allowable—even a human bone, having been ground into a powder, is allowable to be applied as a paste. The four great medicines, when there is no suitable attendant to make them allowable, are allowable to be taken and consumed by oneself. And herein, a suitable attendant who is difficult to instruct or is incapable is considered as being in the category of 'not present'. When there is no ash, dry wood should be burnt to obtain ash. When there is no dry wood, it is allowable to make it even by cutting green wood from a tree. However, these four kinds of great medicines are designated as 'timely'; they are allowable only at the moment of being bitten by a snake.

Iti pāḷimuttakavinayavinicchayasaṅgahe

In the Compendium of Vinaya Decisions outside the Canon,

Paṭiggahaṇavinicchayakathā samattā.

The Discussion on the Analysis of Receiving is concluded.

21. Pavāraṇāvinicchayakathā

21. Discussion on the Determination of Pavāraṇā

116. Paṭikkhepapavāraṇāti [V 0.0121] pañcannaṃ bhojanānaṃ aññataraṃ bhuñjamānena yassa kassaci abhihaṭabhojanassa paṭikkhepasaṅkhātā pavāraṇā. Sā ca na kevalaṃ paṭikkhepamattena hoti, atha kho pañcaṅgavasena. Tatrimāni [M 0.0124] pañcaṅgāni – asanaṃ, bhojanaṃ, dāyakassa hatthapāse ṭhānaṃ, abhihāro, abhihaṭassa paṭikkhepoti. Tattha asananti vippakatabhojanaṃ, bhuñjamāno cesa puggalo hotīti attho. Bhojananti pavāraṇappahonakaṃ bhojanaṃ, odanādīnañca aññataraṃ paṭikkhipitabbaṃ bhojanaṃ hotīti attho. Dāyakassa hatthapāse ṭhānanti pavāraṇappahonakaṃ bhojanaṃ gaṇhitvā dāyakassa aḍḍhateyyahatthappamāṇe okāse avaṭṭhānaṃ. Abhihāroti hatthapāse ṭhitassa dāyakassa kāyena abhihāro. Abhihaṭassa paṭikkhepoti evaṃ abhihaṭassa kāyena vā vācāya vā paṭikkhepo. Iti imesaṃ pañcannaṃ aṅgānaṃ vasena pavāraṇā hoti. Vuttampi cetaṃ –

116. Refusal-Pavāraṇā: For one who is eating one of the five kinds of food, it is the prohibition called 'refusal' concerning food brought forward by any donor whatsoever. And this does not occur merely by refusal, but rather it occurs by way of five factors. These five factors are: eating, the food, the donor's standing within arm's reach, the offering, and the refusal of what is offered. Herein, 'eating' means the food is unfinished; the meaning is that this person is in the act of eating. 'The food' means food suitable for pavāraṇā; the meaning is that it is food to be refused, being one of rice, etc. 'The donor's standing within arm's reach' means the donor standing in a place within the measure of two and a half cubits, having taken food suitable for pavāraṇā. 'The offering' means the offering by body of the donor who is standing within arm's reach. 'The refusal of what is offered' means the refusal of what is thus offered, either by body or by speech. Thus, pavāraṇā occurs by way of these five factors. And this has been said:

“Pañcahi, upāli, ākārehi pavāraṇā paññāyati, asanaṃ paññāyati, bhojanaṃ paññāyati, hatthapāse ṭhito, abhiharati, paṭikkhepo paññāyatī”ti (pari. 428).

“Upāli, pavāraṇā is discerned by five aspects: eating is discerned, the food is discerned, one stands within arm's reach, one offers, and the refusal is discerned.”

117. Tatrāyaṃ vinicchayo (pāci. aṭṭha. 238-9) – “asana”ntiādīsu tāva yaṃ asnāti, yañca bhojanaṃ hatthapāse ṭhitena abhihaṭaṃ paṭikkhipati, taṃ odano kummāso sattu maccho maṃsanti imesaṃ aññatarameva veditabbaṃ. Tattha odano nāma sāli vīhi yavo godhumo kaṅgu varako kudrūsakoti sattannaṃ dhaññānaṃ taṇḍulehi nibbatto. Tatra sālīti antamaso nīvāraṃ upādāya sabbāpi sālijāti. Vīhīti sabbāpi vīhijāti. Yavagodhumesu bhedo natthi. Kaṅgūti setarattakāḷabhedā sabbāpi kaṅgujāti. Varakoti antamaso varakacorakaṃ upādāya sabbāpi setavaṇṇā varakajāti. Kudrūsakoti kāḷakudrūsako ceva sāmākādibhedā ca sabbāpi tiṇadhaññajāti. Nīvāravarakacorakā cettha dhaññānulomāti vadanti, dhaññāni hontu dhaññānulomāni vā, etesaṃ vuttappabhedānaṃ sattannaṃ dhaññānaṃ taṇḍule gahetvā “bhattaṃ pacissāmā”ti vā “yāguṃ pacissāmā”ti vā “ambilapāyāsādīsu aññataraṃ pacissāmā”ti vā yaṃ kiñci sandhāya pacantu, sace uṇhaṃ sītalaṃ vā bhuñjantānaṃ bhojanakāle gahitagahitaṭṭhāne odhi paññāyati, odanasaṅgahameva gacchati, pavāraṇaṃ janeti. Sace odhi na paññāyati, yāgusaṅgahaṃ gacchati, pavāraṇaṃ na janeti.

117. Herein, this is the determination: First, in the case of “eating,” etc., whatever is eaten, and whatever food brought forward by one standing within arm’s reach is refused, should be understood as any one of these five: cooked rice, barley-meal, flour-cakes, fish, or meat. Therein, “cooked rice” refers to what is produced from the husked grains of seven kinds of grain: sāli, vīhi, yava, godhuma, kaṅgu, varaka, and kudrūsaka. Among these, “sāli” includes all varieties of sāli, even down to nīvāra. “Vīhi” includes all varieties of vīhi. There is no distinction between yava and godhuma. “Kaṅgu” includes all varieties, whether white, red, or black. “Varaka” includes all white-colored varieties, even down to varaka-coraka. “Kudrūsaka” includes black kudrūsaka as well as varieties such as sāmāka and all other grass-grains. Here, they say that nīvāra, varaka, and coraka are analogous to grain. Whether they be grains or analogous to grain, let them take the husked grains of these seven aforementioned types and cook them with any intention, whether “we will cook rice,” or “we will cook gruel,” or “we will cook one among sour gruel, milk-rice, etc.” If, for those eating it whether hot or cold, a boundary is discerned at the place where each portion is taken at the time of eating, it is included only in the category of cooked rice and generates the pavāraṇā. If a boundary is not discerned, it is included in the category of gruel and does not generate the pavāraṇā.

Yopi [M 0.0125][V 0.0122] pāyāso vā paṇṇaphalakaḷīramissakā ambilayāgu vā uddhanato otāritamattā abbhuṇhā hoti āvajjitvā pivituṃ sakkā, hatthena gahitokāsepi odhiṃ na dasseti, pavāraṇaṃ na janeti. Sace pana usumāya vigatāya sītalabhūtā ghanabhāvaṃ gacchati, odhiṃ dasseti, puna pavāraṇaṃ janeti, pubbe tanubhāvo na rakkhati. Sacepi dadhitakkādīni āropetvā bahū paṇṇaphalakaḷīre pakkhipitvā muṭṭhimattāpi taṇḍulā pakkhittā honti, bhojanakāle ce odhi paññāyati, pavāraṇaṃ janeti. Ayāguke nimantane “yāguṃ dassāmā”ti bhatte udakakañjikakhīrādīni ākiritvā “yāguṃ gaṇhathā”ti denti. Kiñcāpi tanuko hoti, pavāraṇaṃ janetiyeva. Sace pana pakkuthitesu udakādīsu pakkhipitvā pacitvā denti, yāgusaṅgahameva gacchati. Yāgusaṅgahaṃ gatepi tasmiṃ vā aññasmiṃ vā yattha macchamaṃsaṃ pakkhipanti, sace sāsapamattampi macchamaṃsakhaṇḍaṃ vā nhāru vā paññāyati, pavāraṇaṃ janeti, suddharasako pana rasakayāgu vā na janeti. Ṭhapetvā vuttadhaññataṇḍule aññehi veṇutaṇḍulādīhi vā kaṇḍamūlaphalehi vā yehi kehici kataṃ bhattampi pavāraṇaṃ na janeti, pageva ghanayāgu. Sace panettha macchamaṃsaṃ pakkhipanti, janeti. Mahāpaccariyaṃ “pupphiatthāya bhattampi pavāraṇaṃ janetī”ti vuttaṃ. Pupphiatthāya bhattaṃ nāma pupphikhajjakatthāya kuthitudake pakkhipitvā seditataṇḍulā vuccanti. Sace pana te taṇḍule sukkhāpetvā khādanti, vaṭṭati, neva sattusaṅkhyaṃ, na bhattasaṅkhyaṃ gacchanti. Puna tehi katabhattaṃ pavāretiyeva. Te taṇḍule sappitelādīsu vā pacanti, pūvaṃ vā karonti, na pavārenti. Puthukā vā tāhi katasattubhattādīni vā na pavārenti.

Also that milk-rice, or sour gruel mixed with leaves, fruits, and shoots, which, just taken down from the stove, is freshly hot and can be drunk by tilting, and even in the place where it is taken with the hand does not show a boundary, does not occasion refusal. But if, when the steam has departed and it has become cool, it reaches a state of thickness, it shows a boundary and again occasions refusal; its previous state of being thin does not protect it. Even if, having added curds, buttermilk, and so on, and having put in many leaves, fruits, and shoots, even a handful of rice grains are put in, and if at mealtime a boundary is discerned, it occasions refusal. At an invitation without gruel, when they say, “We will give gruel,” and having poured water, rice-scum, milk, and so on into the food, they give it, saying, “Take the gruel.” Although it is thin, it certainly occasions refusal. But if, having put it into boiling water and so on and having cooked it, they give it, it indeed goes into the category of gruel. Even when it has gone into the category of gruel, in that or in another liquid where they put fish or meat, if even a piece of fish or meat the size of a mustard seed, or a tendon, is discerned, it occasions refusal. But pure broth or broth-gruel does not occasion it. Setting aside the aforementioned grains and rice, even food made with other things, such as bamboo-rice, or with tubers, roots, and fruits, or with whatsoever else, does not occasion refusal—how much more so thick gruel. But if they put fish or meat in this, it occasions it. In the Mahāpaccarī it is said: “Even food for the sake of parched grain occasions refusal.” ‘Food for the sake of parched grain’ is the name for rice grains that have been put in boiling water and steamed for the sake of parched-grain-food. But if, having dried those rice grains, they eat them, it is allowable; they go neither into the category of roasted grain flour nor into the category of cooked rice. Furthermore, food made with those rice grains certainly occasions refusal. If they cook those rice grains in ghee, oil, and so on, or make cakes, they do not occasion refusal. Flattened rice, or roasted grain flour, cooked rice, and so on made with those grains, do not occasion refusal.

Kummāso nāma yavehi katakummāso. Aññehi pana muggādīhi katakummāso pavāraṇaṃ na janeti.

The term kummāsa refers to kummāsa made from barley. However, kummāsa made from other grains such as mung beans does not generate the pavāraṇā.

Sattu nāma sālivīhiyavehi katasattu. Kaṅguvarakakudrūsakasīsānipi bhajjitvā īsakaṃ koṭṭetvā thuse palāpetvā puna daḷhaṃ koṭṭetvā cuṇṇaṃ karonti. Sacepi taṃ allattā ekabaddhaṃ hoti, sattusaṅgahameva gacchati. Kharapākabhajjitānaṃ vīhīnaṃ taṇḍule koṭṭetvā denti, tampi cuṇṇaṃ sattusaṅgahameva gacchati. Samapākabhajjitānaṃ pana vīhīnaṃ vā vīhipalāsānaṃ vā taṇḍulā bhajjitataṇḍulā eva vā na pavārenti. Tesaṃ [M 0.0126] pana taṇḍulānaṃ cuṇṇaṃ pavāreti, kharapākabhajjitānaṃ vīhīnaṃ kuṇḍakampi pavāreti. Samapākabhajjitānaṃ pana ātapasukkhānaṃ vā kuṇḍakaṃ na pavāreti. Lājā vā tehi katabhattasattuādīni vā na pavārenti, bhajjitapiṭṭhaṃ vā [V 0.0123] yaṃ kiñci suddhakhajjakaṃ vā na pavāreti. Macchamaṃsapūritakhajjakaṃ pana sattumodako vā pavāreti. Maccho maṃsañca pākaṭameva.

The term sattu refers to sattu made from sāli rice, vīhi rice, or barley. They also roast kaṅgu, varaka, kudrūsaka, and sīsa, pound them slightly, winnow away the husks, then pound them again firmly to make a powder. Even if it becomes one mass due to moisture, it is still included under sattu. When they pound and give the rice grains of paddy that has been roasted hard, that powder is also included under sattu. However, the rice grains of paddy or paddy chaff that are roasted just until crisp, or even roasted rice grains themselves, do not complete the pavāraṇā. But the powder of those rice grains does complete the pavāraṇā; even the broken rice of paddy that has been roasted hard completes the pavāraṇā. However, the broken rice of paddy that is evenly roasted or sun-dried does not complete the pavāraṇā. Popped rice, or cooked rice, sattu, and other such things made from it, or roasted flour, or any kind of pure solid food, do not complete the pavāraṇā. But solid food filled with fish or meat, or a sattu sweet-ball, does complete the pavāraṇā. Fish and meat are obvious.

Ayaṃ pana viseso – sace yāguṃ pivantassa yāgusitthamattāneva dve macchakhaṇḍāni vā maṃsakhaṇḍāni vā ekabhājane vā nānābhājane vā denti, tāni ce akhādanto aññaṃ yaṃ kiñci pavāraṇappahonakaṃ paṭikkhipati, na pavāreti. Tato ekaṃ khāditaṃ, ekaṃ hatthe vā patte vā hoti, so ce aññaṃ paṭikkhipati, pavāreti. Dvepi khāditāni honti, mukhe sāsapamattampi avasiṭṭhaṃ natthi, sacepi aññaṃ paṭikkhipati, na pavāreti. Kappiyamaṃsaṃ khādanto kappiyamaṃsaṃ paṭikkhipati, pavāreti. Kappiyamaṃsaṃ khādanto akappiyamaṃsaṃ paṭikkhipati, na pavāreti. Kasmā? Avatthutāya. Yañhi bhikkhuno khādituṃ vaṭṭati, taṃyeva paṭikkhipato pavāraṇā hoti. Idaṃ pana jānanto akappiyattā paṭikkhipati, ajānantopi paṭikkhipitabbaṭṭhāne ṭhitameva paṭikkhipati nāma, tasmā na pavāreti. Sace pana akappiyamaṃsaṃ khādanto kappiyamaṃsaṃ paṭikkhipati, pavāreti. Kasmā? Vatthutāya. Yañhi tena paṭikkhittaṃ, taṃ pavāraṇāya vatthu, yaṃ pana khādati, taṃ kiñcāpi paṭikkhipitabbaṭṭhāne ṭhitaṃ, khādiyamānaṃ pana maṃsabhāvaṃ na jahati, tasmā pavāreti. Akappiyamaṃsaṃ vā khādanto akappiyamaṃsaṃ paṭikkhipati, purimanayeneva na pavāreti. Kappiyamaṃsaṃ vā akappiyamaṃsaṃ vā khādanto pañcannaṃ bhojanānaṃ yaṃ kiñci kappiyabhojanaṃ paṭikkhipati, pavāreti. Kuladūsakavejjakammauttarimanussadhammārocanasāditarūpiyādīhi nibbattaṃ buddhapaṭikuṭṭhaṃ anesanāya uppannaṃ akappiyabhojanaṃ paṭikkhipati, na pavāreti. Kappiyabhojanaṃ vā akappiyabhojanaṃ paṭikkhipati, na pavāreti. Kappiyabhojanaṃ vā akappiyabhojanaṃ vā bhuñjantopi kappiyabhojanaṃ paṭikkhipati, pavāreti. Akappiyabhojanaṃ paṭikkhipati, na pavāretīti sabbattha vuttanayeneva kāraṇaṃ veditabbaṃ.

This, however, is the distinction: If, to a bhikkhu drinking gruel, they give just two pieces of fish or meat, equivalent in amount to the rice grains in the gruel, whether in a single bowl or in different bowls, and if, without eating them, he refuses any other food that is sufficient to constitute a pavāraṇā, he does not complete the pavāraṇā. If one of them is eaten, and one is in his hand or in his bowl, and if he then refuses other food, he completes the pavāraṇā. If both pieces have been eaten, and not even the amount of a mustard seed remains in his mouth, even if he refuses other food, he does not complete the pavāraṇā. While eating allowable meat, if he refuses allowable meat, he completes the pavāraṇā. While eating allowable meat, if he refuses unallowable meat, he does not complete the pavāraṇā. Why? Because it is not a valid basis. For a pavāraṇā occurs for one who refuses only that food which is proper for a bhikkhu to eat. But this unallowable meat, he refuses knowing it is unallowable. Even if he does not know, he is said to be refusing something that stands in the category of what ought to be refused; therefore, he does not complete the pavāraṇā. But if, while eating unallowable meat, he refuses allowable meat, he completes the pavāraṇā. Why? Because it is a valid basis. For that which is refused by him is the basis for the pavāraṇā. As for what he is eating, although it stands in the category of what ought to be refused, while being eaten it does not abandon its nature as meat; therefore, he completes the pavāraṇā. While eating unallowable meat, if he refuses unallowable meat, he does not complete the pavāraṇā, by the same method as before. While eating either allowable meat or unallowable meat, if he refuses any allowable food among the five kinds of food, he completes the pavāraṇā. If he refuses unallowable food that has arisen from improper search, is censured by the Buddha, and is produced by such means as acts of a family-defiler, the practice of medicine, proclaiming superior human states, or accepting gold and silver and the like, he does not complete the pavāraṇā. Even while eating either allowable food or unallowable food, if he refuses allowable food, he completes the pavāraṇā. If he refuses unallowable food, he does not complete the pavāraṇā. Thus, in all cases, the reason should be understood according to the method already stated.

118. Evaṃ “asana”ntiādīsu yañca asnāti, yañca bhojanaṃ hatthapāse ṭhitena abhihaṭaṃ paṭikkhipanto pavāraṇaṃ āpajjati, taṃ utvā idāni yathā āpajjati, tassa jānanatthaṃ ayaṃ vinicchayo – asanaṃ bhojananti ettha tāva yena ekasitthampi ajjhohaṭaṃ hoti so [M 0.0127] sace pattamukhahatthānaṃ yattha katthaci pañcasu bhojanesu ekasmimpi sati aññaṃ pañcasu bhojanesu ekampi paṭikkhipati, pavāreti. Katthaci bhojanaṃ natthi, āmisagandhamattaṃ paññāyati, na pavāreti. Mukhe ca hatthe ca bhojanaṃ natthi, patte atthi, tasmiṃ pana āsane abhuñjitukāmo, vihāraṃ vā pavisitvā bhuñjitukāmo, aññassa vā dātukāmo tasmiṃ ce antare [V 0.0124] bhojanaṃ paṭikkhipati, na pavāreti. Kasmā? Vippakatabhojanabhāvassa upacchinnattā. “Yopi aññatra gantvā bhuñjitukāmo mukhe bhattaṃ gilitvā sesaṃ ādāya gacchanto antarāmagge aññaṃ bhojanaṃ paṭikkhipati, tassapi pavāraṇā na hotī”ti mahāpaccariyaṃ vuttaṃ. Yathā ca patte, evaṃ hatthepi. Mukhepi vā vijjamānaṃ bhojanaṃ sace anajjhoharitukāmo hoti, tasmiñca khaṇe aññaṃ paṭikkhipati, na pavāreti. Ekasmiñhi pade vuttaṃ lakkhaṇaṃ sabbattha veditabbaṃ hoti. Apica kurundiyaṃ esa nayo dassitoyeva. Vuttañhi tattha “mukhe bhattaṃ gilitaṃ, hatthe bhattaṃ vighāsādassa dātukāmo, patte bhattaṃ bhikkhussa dātukāmo, sace tasmiṃ khaṇe paṭikkhipati, na pavāretī”ti.

118. Thus, in the passages beginning with 'asana,' a bhikkhu completes the pavāraṇā when he refuses either the food he is eating or the food brought by one standing within arm's reach. Having understood this, for the purpose of knowing the manner in which one completes it, this is the analysis: Herein, regarding 'eating food,' firstly, if a bhikkhu who has swallowed even a single mouthful refuses another of the five kinds of food while one of the five kinds of food is present anywhere in his bowl, mouth, or hand, he completes the pavāraṇā. If there is no food anywhere, but only the smell of food is perceived, he does not complete the pavāraṇā. If there is no food in the mouth or hand, but there is in the bowl, and he does not wish to eat it in that seat—wishing either to enter the monastery to eat, or to give it to another—if in that interval he refuses food, he does not complete the pavāraṇā. Why? Because the state of being in the middle of eating has been interrupted. It is said in the Mahāpaccarī: 'If a bhikkhu, intending to eat elsewhere, swallows the food in his mouth and, taking the remainder, is going along, and on the way refuses other food, that bhikkhu also does not complete the pavāraṇā.' And as with the bowl, so too should it be understood with the hand. Or, if food is present in the mouth but he does not wish to swallow it, and at that moment he refuses other food, he does not complete the pavāraṇā. For the characteristic stated in one instance should be understood everywhere. Moreover, this method is indeed shown in the Kurundī. For it is stated there: 'When food in the mouth has been swallowed, or when one wishes to give food in the hand to one who eats scraps, or when one wishes to give food in the bowl to a fellow bhikkhu—if one refuses other food at that moment, he does not complete the pavāraṇā.'

Hatthapāse ṭhitoti ettha pana sace bhikkhu nisinno hoti, āsanassa pacchimantato paṭṭhāya, sace ṭhito, paṇhiantato paṭṭhāya, sace nipanno, yena passena nipanno, tassa pārimantato paṭṭhāya, dāyakassa nisinnassa vā ṭhitassa vā nipannassa vā ṭhapetvā pasāritahatthaṃ yaṃ āsannataraṃ aṅgaṃ, tassa orimantena paricchinditvā aḍḍhateyyahattho “hatthapāso”ti veditabbo. Tasmiṃ ṭhatvā abhihaṭaṃ paṭikkhipantasseva pavāraṇā hoti, na tato paraṃ.

Here, regarding the phrase 'standing within arm's reach': if a bhikkhu is sitting, it is to be measured starting from the back edge of the seat; if standing, starting from the end of the heel; if lying down, starting from the far edge of the side on which he is lying. Furthermore, 'arm's reach' is to be understood as two and a half cubits, a space delimited by the near edge of the nearest limb of the donor—whether the donor is sitting, standing, or lying down—excluding his outstretched hand. The pavāraṇā occurs only for one who refuses what is brought forward while standing within that arm's reach; it does not occur beyond that.

Abhiharatīti hatthapāsabbhantare ṭhito gahaṇatthaṃ upanāmeti. Sace pana anantaranisinnopi bhikkhu hatthe vā ūrūsu vā ādhārake vā ṭhitaṃ pattaṃ anabhiharitvā “bhattaṃ gaṇhāhī”ti vadati, taṃ paṭikkhipato pavāraṇā natthi. Bhattapacchiṃ ānetvā purato bhūmiyaṃ ṭhapetvā “gaṇhāhī”ti vuttepi eseva nayo. Īsakaṃ pana uddharitvā vā apanāmetvā vā “gaṇhathā”ti vutte paṭikkhipato pavāraṇā hoti. Therāsane nisinno thero dūre nisinnassa daharabhikkhussa pattaṃ pesetvā “ito odanaṃ gaṇhāhī”ti vadati, gaṇhitvā pana gato tuṇhī tiṭṭhati, daharo “alaṃ mayha”nti paṭikkhipati, na pavāreti. Kasmā? Therassa dūrabhāvato dūtassa [M 0.0128] ca anabhiharaṇato. Sace pana gahetvā āgato bhikkhu “idaṃ bhattaṃ gaṇhā”ti vadati, taṃ paṭikkhipato pavāraṇā hoti. Parivesanāyaeko ekena hatthena odanapacchiṃ, ekena kaṭacchuṃ gahetvā bhikkhuṃ parivisati, tatra ce añño āgantvā “ahaṃ pacchiṃ dhāressāmi, tvaṃ odanaṃ dehī”ti vatvā gahitamattameva karoti, parivesako eva pana taṃ dhāreti, tasmā sā abhihaṭāva hoti, tato dātukāmatāya gaṇhantaṃ paṭikkhipantassa pavāraṇā hoti. Sace pana parivesakena phuṭṭhamattāva hoti, itarova naṃ dhāreti, tato dātukāmatāya gaṇhantaṃ paṭikkhipantassa pavāraṇā na hoti, kaṭacchunā uddhaṭabhatte pana hoti. Kaṭacchunā abhihāroyeva hi tassa abhihāro. “Dvinnaṃ samabhārepi paṭikkhipanto pavāretiyevā”ti mahāpaccariyaṃ [V 0.0125] vuttaṃ. Anantarassa bhikkhuno bhatte dīyamāne itaro pattaṃ hatthena pidahati, pavāraṇā natthi. Kasmā? Aññassa abhihaṭe paṭikkhittattā.

‘He brings it forward’ means: a donor standing within arm’s reach offers it for the purpose of it being taken. But if, without lifting or tilting the bowl placed on the hand, thighs, or a stand of a monk sitting nearby, one says, ‘Take the food,’ for the one who refuses that food, there is no pavāraṇā. Even if a food basket is brought and placed on the ground in front, and it is said, ‘Take it,’ this same principle applies. However, if it is slightly lifted or tilted, and it is said, ‘Take,’ for the one who refuses, a pavāraṇā occurs. An elder monk sitting in the elder’s seat, having sent a bowl to a junior monk sitting far away, says, ‘Take rice from this.’ But the messenger who went, having taken it, stands silently. The junior monk refuses, saying, ‘Enough for me.’ This does not constitute a pavāraṇā. Why? Because of the elder’s distance and because the messenger does not bring it forward. But if the monk who came, having taken it, says, ‘Take this food,’ for the one who refuses that food, a pavāraṇā occurs. For serving, one person serves a monk, holding a rice basket with one hand and a ladle with the other. And if another person comes there and says, ‘I will hold the basket, you give the rice,’ and merely takes hold of it, while the server himself continues to hold it, it is therefore indeed considered brought forward by him. For the monk who refuses the food being taken from that basket with the desire to give, a pavāraṇā occurs. But if it is merely touched by the server, and the other person holds it, for the one who refuses the food being taken from that basket with the desire to give, a pavāraṇā does not occur. However, for food scooped with a ladle, it does occur, for the bringing forward by the ladle is indeed his (the server’s) act of bringing forward. It is said in the Mahāpaccarī: ‘Even in the case of an equal load shared by two people, one who refuses indeed completes the pavāraṇā.’ While food is being given to the monk nearby, if another monk covers his bowl with his hand, there is no pavāraṇā. Why? Because it was refused when it was being brought forward for another.

Paṭikkhepo paññāyatīti ettha vācāya abhihaṭaṃ paṭikkhipato pavāraṇā natthi, kāyena abhihaṭaṃ pana yena kenaci ākārena kāyena vā vācāya vā paṭikkhipantassa pavāraṇā hotīti veditabbo. Tatra kāyena paṭikkhepo nāma aṅguliṃ vā hatthaṃ vā makkhikābījaniṃ vā cīvarakaṇṇaṃ vā cāleti, bhamukāya vā ākāraṃ karoti, kuddho vā oloketi. Vācāya paṭikkhepo nāma “ala”nti vā “na gaṇhāmī”ti vā “mā ākirā”ti vā “apagacchā”ti vā vadati. Evaṃ yena kenaci ākārena kāyena vā vācāya vā paṭikkhitte pavāraṇā hoti.

Herein, regarding ‘a refusal is understood’: for one who refuses what is brought forward by word only, there is no pavāraṇā. But for what is brought forward physically, it should be understood that for one who refuses it in any manner whatsoever, whether by body or by speech, a pavāraṇā occurs. Therein, refusal by body means: one moves a finger, or a hand, or a fly-whisk; or one makes a gesture with the eyebrows; or one looks angrily. Refusal by speech means: one says, ‘Enough,’ or ‘I do not accept,’ or ‘Do not pour it in,’ or ‘Go away.’ Thus, when a refusal is made in any manner whatsoever, whether by body or by speech, a pavāraṇā occurs.

119. Eko abhihaṭe bhatte pavāraṇāya bhīto hatthe apanetvā punappunaṃ patte odanaṃ ākirantaṃ “ākira ākira, koṭṭetvā koṭṭetvā pūrehī”ti vadati, ettha kathanti? Mahāsumatthero tāva “anākiraṇatthāya vuttattā pavāraṇā hotī”ti āha. Mahāpadumatthero pana “ākira pūrehīti vadantassa nāma kassaci pavāraṇā atthī”ti vatvā “na pavāretī”ti āha.

119. When food was brought forward, a certain bhikkhu, fearing to make a pavāraṇā, removed his hands and said to one who was repeatedly pouring rice into his bowl, 'Pour, pour! Packing it down, packing it down, fill it up!' What is the case here? The Elder Mahāsumata, for his part, said: 'Because it was said for the purpose of not having more poured in, it constitutes a pavāraṇā.' The Elder Mahāpaduma, however, said: 'For someone who is actually saying, "Pour, fill it up!", could there ever be a pavāraṇā?' and having so said, he stated: 'It is not a pavāraṇā.'

Aparo bhattaṃ abhiharantaṃ bhikkhuṃ sallakkhetvā “kiṃ, āvuso, itopi kiñci gaṇhissasi, dammi te kiñcī”ti āha, tatrāpi “evaṃ nāgamissatīti vuttattā pavāraṇā hotī”ti mahāsumatthero āha. Mahāpadumatthero [M 0.0129] pana “gaṇhissasīti vadantassa nāma kassaci pavāraṇā atthī”ti vatvā “na pavāretī”ti āha.

Another bhikkhu, noticing a bhikkhu bringing food, said: 'Friend, will you take something from this as well? I will give you something.' In this case too, the Elder Mahāsumata said: 'Because it was said with the thought, "Thus he will not approach," it constitutes a pavāraṇā.' The Elder Mahāpaduma, however, said: 'For someone who is actually saying, "Will you take?", could there ever be a pavāraṇā?' and having so said, he stated: 'It is not a pavāraṇā.'

Eko samaṃsakaṃ rasaṃ abhiharitvā “rasaṃ gaṇhathā”ti vadati, taṃ sutvā paṭikkhipato pavāraṇā natthi. “Macchamaṃsarasa”nti vutte paṭikkhipato pavāraṇā hoti, “idaṃ gaṇhathā”ti vuttepi hotiyeva. Maṃsaṃ visuṃ katvā “maṃsarasaṃ gaṇhathā”ti vadati, “tattha ce sāsapamattampi maṃsakhaṇḍaṃ atthi, taṃ paṭikkhipato pavāraṇā hoti. Sace pana parissāvito hoti, vaṭṭatī”ti abhayatthero āha.

If someone brings a sauce containing meat and says, ‘Take the sauce,’ for one who declines upon hearing this, there is no pavāraṇā. But if it is said, ‘Fish-and-meat sauce,’ for one who declines, a pavāraṇā occurs. Even if it is said, ‘Take this,’ it still occurs. If the meat is separated and one says, ‘Take the meat sauce,’ and if there is even a mustard-seed-sized piece of meat in it, for one who declines it, a pavāraṇā occurs. ‘But if it has been strained, it is permissible,’ said the Elder Abhaya.

Maṃsarasena āpucchantaṃ mahāthero “muhuttaṃ āgamehī”ti vatvā “thālakaṃ, āvuso, āharā”ti āha, ettha kathanti? Mahāsumatthero tāva “abhihārakassa gamanaṃ upacchinnaṃ, tasmā [V 0.0126] pavāretī”ti āha. Mahāpadumatthero pana “ayaṃ kuhiṃ gacchati, kīdisaṃ etassa gamanaṃ, gaṇhantassapi nāma kassaci pavāraṇā atthī”ti vatvā “na pavāretī”ti āha.

To one offering meat sauce, the great elder said, ‘Wait a moment,’ and then said, ‘Friend, bring a bowl.’ What is the case here? The Elder Mahāsumata, for his part, said: ‘The server’s departure is interrupted; therefore, it constitutes a pavāraṇā.’ The Elder Mahāpaduma, however, said: ‘Where is this person going? What sort of departure is this? Can there be a pavāraṇā for one who is still receiving?’ and declared: ‘It is not a pavāraṇā.’”

Kaḷīrapanasādīhi missetvā maṃsaṃ pacanti, taṃ gahetvā “kaḷīrasūpaṃ gaṇhatha, panasabyañjanaṃ gaṇhathā”ti vadanti, evampi na pavāreti. Kasmā? Apavāraṇārahassa nāmena vuttattā. Sace pana “macchasūpaṃ maṃsasūpa”nti vā “idaṃ gaṇhathā”ti vā vadanti, pavāreti, maṃsakarambako nāma hoti. Taṃ dātukāmopi “karambakaṃ gaṇhathā”ti vadati, vaṭṭati, na pavāreti, “maṃsakarambaka”nti vā “ida”nti vā vutte pana pavāreti. Esa nayo sabbesu macchamaṃsamissakesu.

They cook meat mixed with ingredients like bamboo shoots and jackfruit. Taking it, they say, 'Take the bamboo shoot soup; take the jackfruit curry.' Even so, this does not constitute a formal refusal. Why? Because it is called by a name that is not grounds for a formal refusal. But if they say, 'Fish soup, meat soup,' or 'Take this,' it does constitute a formal refusal. There is what is called a 'mixed meat dish'. Even one who wishes to give this may say, 'Take the mixed dish'; this is allowable and does not constitute a formal refusal. But when it is called 'mixed meat dish' or 'this,' it does constitute a formal refusal. This is the principle in all cases involving mixed fish and meat dishes.

120. “Yo pana nimantane bhuñjamāno maṃsaṃ abhihaṭaṃ ‘uddissakata’nti maññamāno paṭikkhipati, pavāritova hotī”ti mahāpaccariyaṃ vuttaṃ. Missakakathā pana kurundiyaṃ suṭṭhu vuttā. Evañhi tattha vuttaṃ – piṇḍacāriko bhikkhu bhattamissakaṃ yāguṃ āharitvā “yāguṃ gaṇhathā”ti vadati, na pavāreti, “bhattaṃ gaṇhathā”ti vutte pavāreti. Kasmā? Yenāpucchito, tassa atthitāya. Ayamettha adhippāyo – “yāgumissakaṃ gaṇhathā”ti vadati, tatra ce yāgu bahutarā vā hoti samasamā vā, na pavāreti. Yāgu mandā, bhattaṃ bahutaraṃ, pavāreti. Idañca sabbaaṭṭhakathāsu vuttattā na sakkā paṭikkhipituṃ, kāraṇaṃ panettha duddasaṃ. “Bhattamissakaṃ gaṇhathā”ti vadati, bhattaṃ bahutaraṃ vā samaṃ vā appataraṃ vā hoti, pavāretiyeva[M 0.0130]. Bhattaṃ vā yāguṃ vā anāmasitvā “missakaṃ gaṇhathā”ti vadati, tatra ce bhattaṃ bahutaraṃ vā samakaṃ vā hoti, pavāreti, appataraṃ na pavāreti, idañca karambakena na samānetabbaṃ. Karambako hi maṃsamissakopi hoti amaṃsamissakopi, tasmā karambakanti vutte pavāraṇā natthi, idaṃ pana bhattamissakameva. Ettha vuttanayeneva pavāraṇā hoti. Bahurase bhatte rasaṃ, bahukhīre khīraṃ, bahusappimhi ca pāyāse sappiṃ gaṇhathāti visuṃ katvā deti, taṃ paṭikkhipato pavāraṇā natthi.

120. “Whatever monk, while eating at an invitation, refuses meat that has been brought, thinking, ‘It was prepared specifically,’ is considered to have formally refused.” This is stated in the Mahāpaccariya. However, the discussion on mixed offerings is well explained in the Kurundiya. Indeed, there it is stated thus: A monk on almsround brings gruel mixed with rice and says, “Take the gruel”; this does not constitute a formal refusal. If it is said, “Take the rice,” it constitutes a formal refusal. Why? Because of the presence of that with which he was invited. This is the meaning here: if he says, “Take the gruel-mixture,” and if in that mixture the gruel is more or equal in quantity, this does not constitute a formal refusal. If the gruel is less and the rice is more, it constitutes a formal refusal. And this, being stated in all the commentaries, cannot be rejected, but the reason here is difficult to see. If he says, “Take the rice-mixture,” whether the rice is more, equal, or less, it indeed constitutes a formal refusal. Without specifying either the rice or the gruel, if he says, “Take the mixture,” and if in that mixture the rice is more or equal, it constitutes a formal refusal; if it is less, it does not constitute a formal refusal. And this ruling should not be equated with a mixed dish. For a mixed dish can be mixed with meat and can be without meat; therefore, when ‘mixed dish’ is said, there is no formal refusal. But this refers to a rice-mixture, and a formal refusal occurs only by the method stated herein. If, in the case of rice with much liquid, one offers it separately, saying, 'Take the liquid'; in the case of rice with much milk, 'Take the milk'; and in the case of rice-porridge with much ghee, 'Take the ghee'—for one who refuses that, there is no formal refusal.

Yo pana gacchanto pavāreti, so gacchantova bhuñjituṃ labhati. Kaddamaṃ vā udakaṃ vā patvā ṭhitena atirittaṃ kāretabbaṃ. Sace antarā nadī pūrā hoti, nadītīre gumbaṃ anupariyāyantena bhuñjitabbaṃ. Atha nāvā vā setu vā atthi, taṃ abhiruhitvāpi caṅkamanteneva bhuñjitabbaṃ, gamanaṃ na upacchinditabbaṃ. Yāne vā hatthiassapiṭṭhe vā candamaṇḍale vā sūriyamaṇḍale vā nisīditvā pavāritena yāva majjhanhikaṃ, tāva tesu gacchantesupi nisinneneva [V 0.0127] bhuñjitabbaṃ. Yo ṭhito pavāreti, ṭhiteneva, yo nisinno pavāreti, nisinneneva paribhuñjitabbaṃ, taṃ taṃ iriyāpathaṃ vikopentena atirittaṃ kāretabbaṃ. Yo ukkuṭiko nisīditvā pavāreti, tena ukkuṭikeneva bhuñjitabbaṃ. Tassa pana heṭṭhā palālapīṭhaṃ vā kiñci vā nisīdanakaṃ dātabbaṃ. Pīṭhake nisīditvā pavāritena āsanaṃ acāletvāva catasso disā parivattantena bhuñjituṃ labbhati. Mañce nisīditvā pavāritena ito vā etto vā sañcarituṃ na labbhati. Sace pana naṃ saha mañcena ukkhipitvā aññatra nenti, vaṭṭati. Nipajjitvā pavāritena nipanneneva paribhuñjitabbaṃ. Parivattantena yena passena nipanno, tassa ṭhānaṃ nātikkametabbaṃ.

A bhikkhu who has formally refused while walking may eat while continuing to walk. If, having reached mud or water, he stands, he must have the food made allowable as ‘extra’. If a river is full along the way, he should eat while circling a thicket on the riverbank. If there is a boat or a bridge, he may board it and eat while pacing back and forth; the journey should not be interrupted. For one who has formally refused while seated in a vehicle, on the back of an elephant or a horse, on the moon’s disc, or on the sun’s disc, he should eat while remaining seated as long as it is before midday, even if those conveyances are moving. One who formally refuses while standing should eat while standing; one who formally refuses while sitting should eat while sitting. If he changes his posture, he must have the food made allowable as ‘extra’. One who formally refuses while sitting in a squatting position should eat while remaining in a squatting position. However, a seat of straw or some other sitting mat should be given to be placed beneath him. For one who has formally refused while sitting on a stool, it is allowable to eat while turning to the four directions without moving the seat. For one who has formally refused while sitting on a bed, it is not allowable to move from here to there. But if they lift him along with the bed and take him elsewhere, it is permissible. One who has formally refused while lying down should eat while remaining lying down. While turning over, he should not go beyond the place of the side on which he was lying.

121. Pavāritena pana kiṃkātabbanti? Yena iriyāpathena pavārito hoti, taṃ vikopetvā aññena iriyāpathena ce bhuñjati, atirittaṃ kārāpetvā bhuñjitabbaṃ. Anatirittaṃ pana yaṃ kiñci yāvakālikasaṅgahitaṃ khādanīyaṃ vā bhojanīyaṃ vā khādati vā bhuñjati vā, ajjhohāre ajjhohāre pācittiyaṃ.

121. But what is to be done by one who has formally refused? If one eats in a posture different from the one in which one has formally refused, one must have the food made allowable as ‘extra’ before eating. But if one chews or eats any hard or soft food included in the yāvakālika category that has not been made allowable as ‘extra’, there is a pācittiya offense for every mouthful.

Tattha anatirittaṃ nāma nātirittaṃ, na adhikanti attho. Taṃ pana yasmā kappiyakatādīhi sattahi vinayakammākārehi akataṃ vā gilānassa anadhikaṃ vā hoti, tasmā padabhājane vuttaṃ –

Herein, 'not a leftover' means not a leftover, that is, not in excess. And since this is either not done by the seven kinds of Vinaya procedures beginning with making something allowable, or it is not a leftover for a sick person, therefore it is said in the analysis of the terms:

“Anatirittaṃ [M 0.0131] nāma akappiyakataṃ hoti, appaṭiggahitakataṃ hoti, anuccāritakataṃ hoti, ahatthapāse kataṃ hoti, abhuttāvinā kataṃ hoti, bhuttāvinā ca pavāritena āsanā vuṭṭhitena kataṃ hoti, ‘alametaṃ sabba’nti avuttaṃ hoti, na gilānātirittaṃ hoti, etaṃ anatirittaṃ nāmā”ti (pāci. 239).

“‘Not a leftover’ means: it is done without being made allowable; it is done without having been accepted; it is done while not within hand's reach; it is done by one who has not eaten; it is done by one who, having eaten and formally refused, has risen from his seat; it is not said, 'This is all sufficient'; it is not a leftover from a sick person. This is called 'not a leftover’.”

Tattha akappiyakatanti yaṃ tattha phalaṃ vā kandamūlādiṃ vā pañcahi samaṇakappehi kappiyaṃ akataṃ, yañca akappiyamaṃsaṃ vā akappiyabhojanaṃ vā, etaṃ akappiyaṃ nāma. Taṃ akappiyaṃ “alametaṃ sabba”nti evaṃ atirittaṃ katampi “akappiyakata”nti veditabbaṃ. Appaṭiggahitakatanti bhikkhunā appaṭiggahitaṃyeva purimanayena atirittaṃ kataṃ. Anuccāritakatanti kappiyaṃ kāretuṃ āgatena bhikkhunā īsakampi anukkhittaṃ vā anapanāmitaṃ vā kataṃ. Ahatthapāse katanti kappiyaṃ kāretuṃ āgatassa hatthapāsato bahi ṭhitena kataṃ. Abhuttāvinā katanti yo “alametaṃ sabba”nti atirittaṃ karoti, tena pavāraṇappahonakabhojanaṃ [V 0.0128] abhuttena kataṃ. Bhuttāvinā pavāritena āsanā vuṭṭhitena katanti idaṃ uttānameva. “Alametaṃ sabba”nti avuttanti vacībhedaṃ katvā evaṃ avuttaṃ hoti. Iti imehi sattahi vinayakammākārehi yaṃ atirittaṃ kappiyaṃ akataṃ, yañca na gilānātirittaṃ, tadubhayampi “anatiritta”nti veditabbaṃ.

Herein, 'done without being made allowable' refers to any fruit or root, etc., that has not been made allowable by the five ways of making things allowable for a monk, and also unallowable meat or unallowable food; this is called 'unallowable'. Even when that unallowable food is made a leftover by saying, 'This is all sufficient,' it should be understood as 'done without being made allowable'. 'Done without having been accepted' means that it is made a leftover by a monk without his having accepted it, in the aforementioned manner. 'Done without being raised' means that it is done by a monk who has come to make it allowable without even slightly lifting up or moving aside (the bowl). 'Done while not within hand's reach' means that it is done by one standing outside the hand's reach of the monk who has come to make it allowable. 'Done by one who has not eaten' means that whoever makes something a leftover by saying, 'This is all sufficient,' does so without having eaten the food that is the basis for formal satisfaction. The phrase 'done by one who, having eaten and been formally satisfied, has risen from his seat' is self-evident. 'Not said, "This is all sufficient"' means that this phrase is not uttered. Thus, both the food for which the procedure for making it a leftover has not been done according to these seven kinds of Vinaya procedures, and that which is not a leftover from a sick person, should be understood as 'not left over'.

122. Atirittaṃ pana tasseva paṭipakkhanayena veditabbaṃ. Teneva vuttaṃ padabhājane –

122. As for 'left over', however, it should be understood by way of the opposite of that very 'not left over'. For that reason, it is said in the analysis of the terms:

“Atirittaṃ nāma kappiyakataṃ hoti, paṭiggahitakataṃ hoti, uccāritakataṃ hoti, hatthapāse kataṃ hoti, bhuttāvinā kataṃ hoti, bhuttāvinā pavāritena āsanā avuṭṭhitena kataṃ hoti, ‘alametaṃ sabba’nti vuttaṃ hoti, gilānātirittaṃ hoti, etaṃ atirittaṃ nāmā”ti (pāci. 239).

What is called 'surplus' is that which has been made allowable, that which has been made received, that which has been made lifted, that which has been made within arm's reach, that which has been made by one who has eaten, that which has been made by one who has eaten, has indicated satisfaction, and has not risen from his seat, that which has been declared as 'This is all enough,' and that which is a surplus for the sick—this is what is called 'surplus.'

Apicettha bhuttāvinā kataṃ hotīti anantaranisinnassa sabhāgassa bhikkhuno pattato ekampi sitthaṃ vā maṃsahīraṃ vā khāditvā katampi “bhuttāvināva kataṃ hotī”ti veditabbaṃ. Āsanā avuṭṭhitenāti ettha pana asammohatthaṃ [M 0.0132] ayaṃ vinicchayo – dve bhikkhū pātoyeva bhuñjamānā pavāritā honti, ekena tattheva nisīditabbaṃ, itarena niccabhattaṃ vā salākabhattaṃ vā ānetvā upaḍḍhaṃ tassa bhikkhuno patte ākiritvā hatthaṃ dhovitvā sesaṃ tena bhikkhunā kappiyaṃ kārāpetvā bhuñjitabbaṃ. Kasmā? Yañhi tassa hatthe laggaṃ, taṃ akappiyaṃ hoti. Sace pana paṭhamaṃ nisinno bhikkhu sayameva tassa pattato hatthena gaṇhāti, hatthadhovanakiccaṃ natthi. Sace pana evaṃ ‘kappiyaṃ kāretvā bhuñjantassa puna kiñci byañjanaṃ vā khādanīyaṃ vā patte ākira’nti yena paṭhamaṃ kappiyaṃ kataṃ hoti, so puna kātuṃ na labhati. Yena akataṃ, tena kātabbaṃ, yañca akataṃ, taṃ kātabbaṃ. Yena akatanti aññena bhikkhunā yena paṭhamaṃ na kataṃ, tena kātabbaṃ. Yañca akatanti yena paṭhamaṃ kappiyaṃ kataṃ, tenapi yaṃ akataṃ, taṃ kātabbaṃ. Paṭhamabhājane pana kātuṃ na labbhati. Tattha hi kariyamāne paṭhamaṃ katena saddhiṃ kataṃ hoti, tasmā aññasmiṃ bhājane kātuṃ vaṭṭatīti adhippāyo. Evaṃ kataṃ pana tena bhikkhunā paṭhamaṃ katena saddhiṃ bhuñjituṃ vaṭṭati.

Moreover, here, 'is made by one who has eaten' means that even if one eats a single grain of rice or a strip of meat from the bowl of a fellow monk sitting immediately next, when the act is performed it should be understood as 'is made by one who has eaten.' Regarding 'by one who has not risen from his seat,' this ruling is for the sake of avoiding confusion: If two monks eating in the morning have indicated satisfaction, one should remain seated right there. The other, having brought either regular almsfood or ticket-food, should pour half into that monk's bowl, wash his hand, and have the remaining portion made allowable by that monk before eating it. Why? Because whatever adheres to his hand becomes unallowable. However, if the monk who was seated first himself takes from that monk's bowl with his hand, there is no need to wash the hand. But if, after having it made allowable and while eating, some further curry or edible food is poured into the bowl, the one who first made it allowable cannot do so again. It must be done by one who has not yet done so, and that which has not been made allowable must be made allowable. 'By one who has not yet done so' means it must be done by another monk who did not do it the first time. 'And that which has not been made allowable' means that food should be made allowable by a monk who has not already done so. However, it is not permissible to make it allowable in the first bowl, for if it were made allowable there, it would be considered made allowable along with what was first made allowable. Therefore, it is permissible to make it allowable in another bowl—this is the intention. When it has been made allowable in this way, however, it is permissible for that monk to eat it together with the monk who first made it allowable.

Kappiyaṃ karontena ca na kevalaṃ patteyeva, kuṇḍepi pacchiyampi yattha katthaci purato ṭhapetvā onāmitabhājane kātabbaṃ. Taṃ sace bhikkhusataṃ pavāritaṃ hoti, sabbesaṃ bhuñjituṃ vaṭṭati, appavāritānampi vaṭṭati. Yena pana kappiyaṃ kataṃ, tassa na vaṭṭati. Sacepi pavāretvā [V 0.0129] piṇḍāya paviṭṭhaṃ bhikkhuṃ pattaṃ gahetvā avassaṃ bhuñjanake maṅgalanimantane nisīdāpenti, atirittaṃ kārāpetvāva bhuñjitabbaṃ. Sace tattha añño bhikkhu natthi, āsanasālaṃ vā vihāraṃ vā pattaṃ pesetvā kāretabbaṃ, kappiyaṃ karontena pana anupasampannassa hatthe ṭhitaṃ na kātabbaṃ. Sace āsanasālāyaṃ abyatto bhikkhu hoti, sayaṃ gantvā kappiyaṃ kārāpetvā ānetvā bhuñjitabbaṃ.

And when making food allowable, it should not be done only in the bowl, but it should be done in a pot, a basket, or in any vessel whatsoever that is placed in front and tilted. If a hundred monks have been satisfied with a meal, it is allowable for all of them to eat that surplus food; it is also allowable for those who have not been satisfied. However, for the monk by whom it was made allowable, it is not allowable for him to eat it. Even if, after a monk has been satisfied and has entered a village for alms, they take his bowl and make him sit at an auspicious invitation where he must certainly eat, he should eat only after having it made surplus. If there is no other monk there, the bowl should be sent to a rest house or a monastery to have it made allowable. However, a monk who is making it allowable should not do so to food that is in the hand of an unordained person. If in the rest house there is a monk who is unskilled in this Vinaya procedure, one should go oneself, have it made allowable, bring it back, and then eat.

Gilānātirittanti ettha na kevalaṃ yaṃ gilānassa bhuttāvasesaṃ hoti, taṃ gilānātirittaṃ, atha kho yaṃ kiñci gilānaṃ uddissa “ajja vā yadā vā icchati, tadā khādissatī”ti āhaṭaṃ, taṃ sabbaṃ gilānātirittanti veditabbaṃ. Yāmakālikaṃ pana sattāhakālikaṃ yāvajīvikaṃ vā yaṃ [M 0.0133] kiñci anatirittaṃ āhāratthāya paribhuñjantassa ajjhohāre ajjhohāre dukkaṭaṃ. Sace pana yāmakālikādīni āmisasaṃsaṭṭhāni honti, āhāratthāyapi anāhāratthāyapi paṭiggahetvā ajjhoharantassa pācittiyameva, asaṃsaṭṭhāni pana sati paccaye bhuñjantassa anāpatti.

Herein, regarding the term 'surplus for the sick,' it is not only that which is the leftover from a sick person's meal that is 'surplus for the sick'; but rather, whatever food is brought with reference to a sick person, thinking, 'He will eat today or whenever he wishes,' all of that should be known as 'surplus for the sick.' Furthermore, for one who consumes for the purpose of nourishment any time-limited item for a watch, for seven days, or for life that is not surplus, there is a dukkaṭa offense with every mouthful. But if time-limited items for a watch and so on are mixed with staple food, for one who accepts and consumes them, whether for the purpose of nourishment or not for the purpose of nourishment, there is a pācittiya offense indeed. However, for one who eats unmixed items when there is a reason, there is no offense.

Iti pāḷimuttakavinayavinicchayasaṅgahe

Thus, in the Compendium of Vinaya Decisions Outside the Pāḷi Canon,

Pavāraṇāvinicchayakathā samattā.

The Discussion on the Decision Regarding Pavāraṇā is concluded.

22. Pabbajjāvinicchayakathā

22. The Discussion on the Determination of Going Forth

123. Pabbajjāti [V 0.0130] ettha pana pabbajjāpekkhaṃ kulaputtaṃ pabbājentena ye pāḷiyaṃ “na bhikkhave pañcahi ābādhehi phuṭṭho pabbājetabbo”tiādinā (mahāva. 89) paṭikkhittā puggalā, te vajjetvā pabbajjādosavirahito puggalo pabbājetabbo. Tatrāyaṃ vinicchayo (mahāva. aṭṭha. 88) – kuṭṭhaṃ gaṇḍo kilāso soso apamāroti imehi pañcahi ābādhehi phuṭṭho na pabbājetabbo, pabbājento pana dukkaṭaṃ āpajjati “yo pabbājeyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti vuttattā. Tattha kuṭṭhanti rattakuṭṭhaṃ vā hotu kāḷakuṭṭhaṃ vā, yaṃ kiñci kiṭibhadaddaukacchuādippabhedampi sabbaṃ kuṭṭhamevāti vuttaṃ. Tañce nakhapiṭṭhippamāṇampi vaḍḍhanakapakkhe ṭhitaṃ hoti, na pabbājetabbo. Sace pana nivāsanapāvuraṇehi pakatipaṭicchannaṭṭhāne nakhapiṭṭhippamāṇaṃ avaḍḍhanakapakkhe ṭhitaṃ hoti, vaṭṭati. “Mukhe pana hatthapādapiṭṭhīsu vā sacepi avaḍḍhanakapakkhe ṭhitaṃ, nakhapiṭṭhito ca khuddakatarampi na vaṭṭatiyevā”ti kurundiyaṃ vuttaṃ. Tikicchāpetvā pabbājentenapi pakativaṇṇe jāteyeva pabbājetabbo, godhāpiṭṭhisadisacuṇṇaokiraṇasarīrampi pabbājetuṃ na vaṭṭati.

123. Regarding the going forth, when a son of good family seeking the going forth is to be given it, those individuals rejected in the Pāḷi by the text beginning, “Monks, one afflicted with five diseases should not be given the going forth,” should be avoided. A person free from the faults that are an obstacle to the going forth should be given the going forth. Herein, this is the analysis: one afflicted with these five diseases—leprosy, boils, a skin disease (kilāsa), consumption, or epilepsy—should not be given the going forth. If one gives the going forth to such a person, one commits an offense of dukkaṭa, as it is said, “Whoever should give the going forth, commits an offense of dukkaṭa.” Therein, “leprosy” means either red leprosy or black leprosy; it is said that whatever kind, including varieties such as skin eruptions, ringworm, and scabies, all is considered leprosy. If that leprosy, even if only the size of a fingernail, is in a state of spreading, he should not be given the going forth. But if it is the size of a fingernail and is in a non-spreading state, located in a place normally concealed by the lower and upper robes, it is allowable. However, it is stated in the Kurundī: “But if it is on the face, or on the backs of the hands or feet, even if it is in a non-spreading state and is even smaller than a fingernail, it is not allowable at all.” Even when giving the going forth after having it treated, one should only give the going forth when the natural skin color has been restored. It is also not allowable to give the going forth to one whose body is sprinkled with powder resembling the back of a monitor lizard.

Gaṇḍoti medagaṇḍo vā hotu añño vā, yo koci kolaṭṭhimattakopi ce vaḍḍhanakapakkhe ṭhito gaṇḍo hoti, na pabbājetabbo. Paṭicchannaṭṭhāne pana kolaṭṭhimatte avaḍḍhanakapakkhe ṭhite vaṭṭati, mukhādike appaṭicchannaṭṭhāne avaḍḍhanakapakkhe ṭhitepi na vaṭṭati. Tikicchāpetvā pabbājentenapi sarīraṃ sacchaviṃ kārāpetvā pabbājetabbo. Uṇṇigaṇḍā nāma [M 0.0134] honti gothanakā viya aṅgulikā viya ca tattha tattha lambanti, etepi gaṇḍāyeva, tesu sati pabbājetuṃ na vaṭṭati. Daharakāle khīrapīḷakā yobbannakāle ca mukhe kharapīḷakā nāma honti, mahallakakāle nassanti, na tā gaṇḍasaṅkhyaṃ gacchanti, tāsu sati pabbājetuṃ vaṭṭati. Aññā pana sarīre kharapīḷakā nāma, aparā padumakaṇṇikā nāma honti, aññā sāsapabījakā nāma sāsapamattāyeva sakalasarīraṃ pharanti, sabbā kuṭṭhajātikāva, tāsu sati na pabbājetabbo.

A tumor: whether it be a fleshy tumor or another kind, if there is any tumor, even one the size of a jujube seed, that is in a growing phase, he should not be given the going forth. However, in a concealed place, if it is the size of a jujube seed and in a non-growing phase, it is allowable. In an unconcealed place, such as the face, even if it is in a non-growing phase, it is not allowable. Even when giving the going forth after having it treated, he should be given the going forth only after the body has been restored to its natural skin. There are what are called hanging tumors; like a cow's teat or like a fingertip, they hang down on various parts of the body. These too are indeed tumors; if they are present, it is not allowable to give him the going forth. In childhood, there are what are called milk pimples, and in youth, on the face, there are what are called rough pimples; in old age, they disappear. These are not counted as tumors; if they are present, it is allowable to give him the going forth. Furthermore, there are on the body what are called warts. Others are called lotus-pod blotches. Still others are called mustard-seed spots; being just the size of a mustard seed, they spread over the entire body. All are of a leprous nature. If these are present, he should not be given the going forth.

Kilāsoti na bhijjanakaṃ na paggharaṇakaṃ padumapuṇḍarīkapattavaṇṇaṃ kuṭṭhaṃ. Yena gunnaṃ viya sabalaṃ sarīraṃ hoti, tasmiṃ kuṭṭhe vuttanayeneva vinicchayo veditabbo. Sosoti sosabyādhi. Tasmiṃ [V 0.0131] sati na pabbājetabbo. Apamāroti pittummādo vā yakkhummādo vā. Tattha pubbaverikena amanussena gahito duttikiccho hoti, appamattakepi pana apamāre sati na pabbājetabbo.

Kilāsa is a leprous condition that does not break open and does not ooze, having the color of a lotus or white lotus petal. By this, the body becomes speckled like that of cattle; concerning this leprous condition, the decision should be understood in the manner already stated. Sosa is the wasting disease. If this is present, he should not be given the going forth. Apamāra is epilepsy, which may be madness due to bile or madness due to a yakkha. Among these, one who is seized by a non-human being who was a former enemy is difficult to cure; however, even if the epilepsy is slight, he should not be given the going forth.

124. “Na, bhikkhave, rājabhaṭo pabbājetabbo, yo pabbājeyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (mahāva. 90) vacanato rājabhaṭopi na pabbājetabbo. Ettha ca amacco vā hotu mahāmatto vā sevako vā kiñci ṭhānantaraṃ patto vā appatto vā, yo koci rañño bhattavetanabhaṭo, sabbo rājabhaṭoti saṅkhyaṃ gacchati, so na pabbājetabbo. Tassa pana puttanattabhātukā ye rājato bhattavetanaṃ na gaṇhanti, te pabbājetuṃ vaṭṭati. Yo pana rājato laddhaṃ nibaddhabhogaṃ vā māsasaṃvaccharaparibbayaṃ vā raññoyeva niyyādeti, puttabhātuke vā taṃ ṭhānaṃ sampaṭicchāpetvā rājānaṃ “na dānāhaṃ devassa bhaṭo”ti āpucchati, yena vā yaṃkāraṇā vetanaṃ gahitaṃ, taṃ kammaṃ kataṃ hoti, yo vā “pabbajassū”ti raññā anuññāto hoti, tampi pabbājetuṃ vaṭṭati.

124. “Monks, a royal servant should not be given the going forth. Whoever should give one the going forth, there is an offense of dukkaṭa.” According to this statement, a royal servant should not be given the going forth.
