And here, whether he is a minister, a great minister, a servant, or has attained some position or has not, whoever is a servant of the king living on food and wages, all are counted as a royal servant; he should not be given the going forth. However, his sons, grandsons, and brothers who do not receive food and wages from the king, it is allowable to give them the going forth. But whoever returns to the king himself a fixed income or a monthly or annual allowance received from the king, or having made his sons or brothers accept that position, asks leave of the king, saying, “Now I am not Your Majesty’s servant,” or for whom the work for which the wages were taken has been completed, or who has been permitted by the king with the words, “Go forth,” it is also allowable to give him the going forth.

125. Coropi dhajabandho na pabbājetabbo “na, bhikkhave, dhajabandho coro pabbājetabbo, yo pabbājeyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (mahāva. 91) vuttattā. Tattha dhajaṃ bandhitvā viya vicaratīti dhajabandho, mūladevādayo viya loke pākaṭoti vuttaṃ hoti. Tasmā yo gāmaghātaṃ vā panthaduhanaṃ vā nagare sandhicchedādikammaṃ vā karonto vicarati, paññāyati [M 0.0135] ca “asuko nāma idaṃ idaṃ karotī”ti, so na pabbājetabbo. Yo pana rājaputto rajjaṃ patthento gāmaghātādīni karoti, so pabbājetabbo. Rājāno hi tasmiṃ pabbajite tussanti, sace pana na tussanti, na pabbājetabbo. Pubbe mahājane pākaṭo coro pacchā corakammaṃ pahāya pañca sīlāni samādiyati, tañce manussā evaṃ jānanti, pabbājetabbo. Ye pana ambalabujādicorakā sandhicchedādicorā eva vā adissamānā theyyaṃ karonti, pacchāpi “iminā nāma idaṃ kata”nti na paññāyanti, tepi pabbājetuṃ vaṭṭati.

125. A flag-bearing robber should also not be given the going forth, because it is said: “Monks, a flag-bearing robber should not be given the going forth. Whoever should give him the going forth, there is an offense of dukkaṭa.” Herein, one who moves about as though bearing a flag is called a 'flag-bearer' (dhajabandha); this means he is notorious in the world, like Mūladeva and others. Therefore, one who roams committing village raids, highway robberies, or acts like breaking into houses in cities—and is known as “so-and-so does such things”—should not be given the going forth. However, if a prince aspiring to the throne commits village raids and the like, he may be given the going forth, for kings are pleased when such a one has gone forth. But if they are displeased, he should not be given the going forth. If a robber who was previously notorious among the public later abandons his criminal acts and undertakes the five precepts, and people know him to be such, he may be given the going forth. But those who, like thieves of mangoes and jackfruit or housebreakers, commit theft unseen, and are not later known as “this was done by so-and-so,” it is also allowable to give them the going forth.

126. Kārabhedako pana coro na pabbājetabbo “na, bhikkhave, kārabhedako coro pabbājetabbo, yo pabbājeyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (mahāva. 92) vuttattā. Tattha kāro vuccati bandhanāgāraṃ. Idha pana andubandhanaṃ vā hotu saṅkhalikabandhanaṃ vā rajjubandhanaṃ vā gāmabandhanaṃ vā nigamabandhanaṃ vā nagarabandhanaṃ vā purisagutti vā janapadabandhanaṃ vā dīpabandhanaṃ vā, yo etesu yaṃ kiñci bandhanaṃ bhinditvā vā chinditvā vā muñcitvā vā vivaritvā vā [V 0.0132] apassamānānaṃ vā palāyati, so kārabhedakoti saṅkhyaṃ gacchati. Tasmā īdiso kārabhedako coro dīpabandhanaṃ bhinditvā dīpantaraṃ gatopi na pabbājetabbo. Yo pana na coro, kevalaṃ hatthakammaṃ akaronto “evaṃ no apalāyanto karissatī”ti rājayuttādīhi baddho, so kāraṃ bhinditvā palātopi pabbājetabbo. Yo pana gāmanigamapaṭṭanādīni keṇiyā gahetvā taṃ asampādento bandhanāgāraṃ pavesito hoti, sopi palāyitvā āgato na pabbājetabbo. Yopi kasikammādīhi dhanaṃ sampādetvā jīvanto “nidhānaṃ iminā laddha”nti pesuññaṃ upasaṃharitvā kenaci bandhāpito hoti, taṃ tattheva pabbājetuṃ na vaṭṭati, palāyitvā gataṃ pana gataṭṭhāne pabbājetuṃ vaṭṭati.

126. A thief who is a prison-breaker, however, should not be ordained, as it has been stated: “Bhikkhus, a thief who is a prison-breaker should not be ordained. Whoever should ordain him commits an offense of wrongdoing.” Therein, `kāra` is called a prison. Here, however, whether it be confinement by stocks, confinement by iron fetters, confinement by rope, confinement to a village, confinement to a market town, confinement to a city, being under the guard of men, confinement to a country, or confinement to an island—whoever, having broken, cut, untied, or opened any such confinement, or escapes unseen, is reckoned as a prison-breaker. Therefore, such a thief who is a prison-breaker, even one who, having broken confinement to an island, has gone to another island, should not be ordained. But one who is not a thief, who is bound by royal officials or the like merely for not performing his service—they thinking, “Thus bound, he will not run away and will work for us”—may be ordained even if he breaks confinement and escapes. But one who, having taken a village, market town, port, or the like on lease, fails to provide that revenue and is put into prison, he too, having escaped and come, should not be ordained. And one who, while making a living by acquiring wealth through agriculture and so on, is caused to be bound by someone bringing forward the slander, “A hidden treasure has been found by this one”—it is not proper to ordain him right there. But for one who has escaped and gone away, it is proper to ordain him in the place he has gone to.

127. “Na, bhikkhave, likhitako coro pabbājetabbo, yo pabbājeyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (mahāva. 93) vacanato pana likhitako coro na pabbājetabbo. Tattha likhitako nāma yo koci corikaṃ vā aññaṃ vā garuṃ rājāparādhaṃ katvā palāto, rājā ca naṃ [M 0.0136] paṇṇe vā potthake vā “itthannāmo yattha dissati, tattha gahetvā māretabbo”ti vā “hatthapādādīni assa chinditabbānī”ti vā “ettakaṃ nāma daṇḍaṃ āharāpetabbo”ti vā likhāpeti, ayaṃ likhitako nāma, so na pabbājetabbo.

127. “Bhikkhus, a proscribed thief should not be ordained; whoever should ordain him commits an offense of wrongdoing.” Therefore, a proscribed thief is not to be ordained. Herein, a ‘proscribed one’ is so called: someone who, having committed theft or another serious offense against the king, has fled, and the king has it inscribed on a leaf or in a book, “Wherever so-and-so is seen, there he is to be seized and killed,” or “His hands, feet, and so on are to be cut off,” or “Such-and-such a fine is to be exacted from him.” This is called a ‘proscribed one,’ and he is not to be ordained.

128. Kasāhato katadaṇḍakammopi na pabbājetabbo “na, bhikkhave, kasāhato katadaṇḍakammo pabbājetabbo, yo pabbājeyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (mahāva. 94) vacanato. Ettha pana yo vacanapesanādīni akaronto haññati, na so katadaṇḍakammo. Yo pana keṇiyā vā aññathā vā kiñci gahetvā khāditvā puna dātuṃ asakkonto “ayameva te daṇḍo hotū”ti kasāhi haññati, ayameva kasāhato katadaṇḍakammo. So ca kasāhi vā hato hotu aḍḍhadaṇḍakādīnaṃ vā aññatarena, yāva allavaṇo hoti, na tāva pabbājetabbo, vaṇe pana pākatike katvā pabbājetabbo. Sace pana jāṇūhi vā kapparehi vā nāḷikerapāsāṇādīhi vā ghātetvā mutto hoti, sarīre cassa gaṇṭhiyo paññāyanti, na pabbājetabbo, phāsukaṃ katvā eva gaṇṭhīsu sannisinnāsu pabbājetabbo.

128. One who has been struck with a whip and has undergone punishment is also not to be ordained, in accordance with the saying: “Bhikkhus, one who has been struck with a whip and has undergone punishment is not to be ordained; whoever should ordain him commits an offense of wrongdoing.” Herein, however, one who is beaten for not carrying out verbal orders, errands, and so on, is not one who has undergone punishment. But one who, having taken and consumed something by means of a toll or in some other way, is unable to return it and is beaten with whips, it being said, “Let this itself be your punishment”—this very one is ‘one struck with a whip who has undergone punishment.’ And whether he has been struck with whips or with another of the instruments such as a half-staff, as long as he has a fresh wound, he is not to be ordained. But when the wounds have become normal, he may be ordained. If, however, he has been released after being struck with knees, elbows, or with things like coconuts or stones, and swellings are visible on his body, he is not to be ordained. Only after he has been made well and the swellings have subsided may he be ordained.

129. Lakkhaṇāhato pana katadaṇḍakammo na pabbājetabbo “na, bhikkhave, lakkhaṇahato katadaṇḍakammo pabbājetabbo, yo pabbājeyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (mahāva. 95) vacanato. Etthapi katadaṇḍakammabhāvo purimanayeneva veditabbo. Yassa pana nalāṭe vā ūruādīsu vā tattena lohena lakkhaṇaṃ āhataṃ hoti, so sace bhujisso, yāva allavaṇo hoti[V 0.0133], tāva na pabbājetabbo. Sacepissa vaṇā ruḷhā honti chaviyā samaparicchedā, lakkhaṇaṃ na paññāyati, timaṇḍalaṃ nivatthassa uttarāsaṅge kate paṭicchannokāse ce hoti, pabbājetuṃ vaṭṭati, appaṭicchannokāse ce, na vaṭṭati.

129. However, one who has been branded and has undergone punishment should not be ordained, according to the saying: “Bhikkhus, one who has been branded and has undergone punishment should not be ordained. Whoever should ordain him commits an offense of wrongdoing.” Here too, the state of having undergone punishment should be understood in the same way as before. But for one who has been branded with a hot iron on the forehead or on the thighs and so on, if he is a rebel, he should not be ordained as long as the wound is raw. And if his wounds have healed, are of the same complexion as the skin, and the brand is not discernible, he is fit to be ordained if it is in a place covered when the upper robe is put on over the lower robe; but if it is in an uncovered place, he is not fit.

130. “Na, bhikkhave, iṇāyiko pabbājetabbo, yo pabbājeyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (mahāva. 96) vacanato iṇāyikopi na pabbājetabbo. Tattha iṇāyiko nāma yassa pitipitāmahehi vā iṇaṃ gahitaṃ hoti[M 0.0137], sayaṃ vā iṇaṃ gahitaṃ hoti, yaṃ vā āṭhapetvā mātāpitūhi kiñci gahitaṃ hoti, so taṃ iṇaṃ paresaṃ dhāretīti iṇāyiko. Yaṃ pana aññe ñātakā āṭhapetvā kiñci gaṇhanti, so na iṇāyiko. Na hi te taṃ āṭhapetuṃ issarā, tasmā taṃ pabbājetuṃ vaṭṭati, itaraṃ na vaṭṭati. Sace panassa ñātisālohitā “mayaṃ dassāma, pabbājetha na”nti iṇaṃ attano bhāraṃ karonti, añño vā koci tassa ācārasampattiṃ disvā “pabbājetha naṃ, ahaṃ iṇaṃ dassāmī”ti vadati, pabbājetuṃ vaṭṭati. Tesu asati bhikkhunā tathārūpassa upaṭṭhākassapi ārocetabbaṃ “sahetuko satto iṇapalibodhena na pabbajatī”ti. Sace so paṭipajjati, pabbājetabbo. Sacepi attano kappiyabhaṇḍaṃ atthi, “etaṃ dassāmī”ti pabbājetabbo. Sace pana neva ñātakādayo paṭipajjanti, na attano dhanaṃ atthi, “pabbājetvā bhikkhāya caritvā mocessāmī”ti pabbājetuṃ na vaṭṭati. Sace pabbājeti, dukkaṭaṃ. Palātopi ānetvā dātabbo. No ce deti, sabbaṃ iṇaṃ gīvā hoti. Ajānitvā pabbājayato anāpatti, passantena pana ānetvā iṇasāmikānaṃ dassetabbo, apassantassa gīvā na hoti.

130. “Bhikkhus, a debtor should not be ordained. Whoever should ordain him commits an offense of wrongdoing.” Therefore, a debtor should not be ordained. Herein, ‘a debtor’ is one whose parents or grandparents have taken a debt, or who has taken a debt himself, or one whom his parents have pledged to take something; such a person bears that debt for others and is thus called a debtor. However, if other relatives pledge him and take something, he is not a debtor, for they are not authorized to pledge him. Therefore, it is allowable to ordain him; the other case is not allowable. But if his blood relatives take the debt upon themselves as their own burden, saying, “We will pay; ordain him,” or if some other person, seeing his good conduct, says, “Ordain him; I will pay the debt,” it is allowable to ordain him. In their absence, the monk should inform even a supporter of such a person, saying, “A person with potential cannot be ordained due to the obstacle of debt.” If that supporter undertakes to settle it, he should be ordained. Also, if he has his own allowable goods, he should be ordained with the understanding, “I will give this.” But if relatives and others do not undertake to settle it, and he has no wealth of his own, it is not allowable to ordain him with the thought, “Having ordained him, I will have him go on alms-round and get him released from the debt.” If one ordains him, one commits an offense of wrongdoing. Even one who has fled should be brought and handed over. If one does not hand him over, the entire debt becomes one's own responsibility. For one who ordains him unknowingly, there is no offense. But one who sees him should bring him and point him out to the creditors. For one who does not see him, the debt does not become his responsibility.

Sace iṇāyiko aññaṃ desaṃ gantvā pucchiyamānopi “nāhaṃ kassaci kiñci dhāremī”ti vatvā pabbajati, iṇasāmiko ca taṃ pariyesanto tattha gacchati, daharo taṃ disvā palāyati, so theraṃ upasaṅkamitvā “ayaṃ, bhante, kena pabbājito, mama ettakaṃ nāma dhanaṃ gahetvā palāto”ti vadati, therena vattabbaṃ “mayā, upāsaka, ‘aṇaṇo aha’nti vadanto pabbājito, kiṃ dāni karomi, passa me pattacīvara”nti. Ayaṃ tattha sāmīci. Palāte pana gīvā na hoti. Sace pana naṃ therassa sammukhāva disvā “ayaṃ mama iṇāyiko”ti vadati, “tava iṇāyikaṃ tvameva jānāhī”ti vattabbo, evampi gīvā na hoti. Sacepi so “pabbajito ayaṃ dāni kuhiṃ gamissatī”ti vadati, therena “tvaṃyeva jānāhī”ti vattabbo. Evampissa palāte gīvā na hoti. Sace pana thero “kuhiṃ dāni ayaṃ gamissati, idheva acchatū”ti vadati, so ce palāyati, gīvā hoti. Sace so sahetuko satto hoti vattasampanno[M 0.0138][V 0.0134], therena “īdiso aya”nti vattabbaṃ. Iṇasāmiko ce “sādhū”ti vissajjeti, iccetaṃ kusalaṃ, “upaḍḍhupaḍḍhaṃ dethā”ti vadati, dātabbaṃ. Aparena samayena atiārādhako hoti, “sabbaṃ dethā”ti vuttepi dātabbameva. Sace pana uddesaparipucchādīsu kusalo hoti bahūpakāro bhikkhūnaṃ, bhikkhācāravattena pariyesitvāpi iṇaṃ dātabbameva.

If a debtor goes to another region and, when questioned, says, “I do not owe anything to anyone,” and then goes forth, and the creditor, searching for him, arrives there, and the young monk, seeing him, flees—if the creditor approaches the elder and says, “Venerable sir, by whom was this one given the going-forth? He took such-and-such wealth from me and fled,” the elder should say, “Lay follower, he was given the going-forth by me because he said, ‘I am free from debt.’ What can I do now? See my bowl and robe.” This is the proper conduct in that case. If he flees, the responsibility does not fall on the preceptor. But if, upon seeing him in the elder’s presence, the creditor says, “This is my debtor,” the elder should reply, “You yourself know your debtor.” Even so, the responsibility does not fall on the preceptor. And if the creditor says, “Now that he has gone forth, where will he go?” the elder should reply, “You yourself know.” Even in this case, if the young monk flees, the responsibility does not fall on the preceptor. But if the elder says, “Where will he go now? Let him stay right here,” and he then flees, the responsibility falls on the preceptor. If the young monk is a person with the right conditions, endowed with good conduct, the elder should say, “He is such a person.” If the creditor responds, “Good,” and releases him from the debt, that is skillful. If he says, “Give half,” it should be given. If, at a later time, the young monk becomes one who greatly pleases his teacher, then even when it is said, “Give all of it,” it must be given. And if he is skilled in such things as recitation and questioning and is of great service to the monks, the debt must be paid, even by seeking the funds through the alms-round.

131. Dāsopi na pabbājetabbo “na, bhikkhave, dāso pabbājetabbo, yo pabbājeyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (mahāva. 97) vacanato. Tattha cattāro dāsā antojāto dhanakkīto karamarānīto sāmaṃ dāsabyaṃ upagatoti. Tattha antojāto nāma jātiyā dāso gharadāsiyā putto. Dhanakkīto nāma mātāpitūnaṃ santikā putto vā sāmikānaṃ santikā dāso vā dhanaṃ datvā dāsacārittaṃ āropetvā kīto. Ete dvepi na pabbājetabbā. Pabbājentena tattha tattha cārittavasena adāse katvā pabbājetabbā. Karamarānīto nāma tiroraṭṭhaṃ vilopaṃ vā katvā upalāpetvā vā tiroraṭṭhato bhujissamānusakāni āharanti, antoraṭṭheyeva vā katāparādhaṃ kiñci gāmaṃ rājā “vilumpathā”ti ca āṇāpeti, tato mānusakānipi āharanti, tattha sabbe purisā dāsā, itthiyo dāsiyo. Evarūpo karamarānīto dāso yehi ānīto, tesaṃ santike vasanto vā bandhanāgāre baddho vā purisehi rakkhiyamāno vā na pabbājetabbo, palāyitvā pana gato gataṭṭhāne pabbājetabbo. Raññā tuṭṭhena “karamarānītake muñcathā”ti vatvā vā sabbasādhāraṇena vā nayena bandhanamokkhe kate pabbājetabbova.

131. A slave also should not be given the going-forth. “Monks, a slave should not be given the going-forth. Whoever should give the going-forth to one, commits an offense of wrong-doing.” In that context, there are four types of slaves: one born in the house, one bought with wealth, one brought as a captive of war, and one who has voluntarily entered into slavery. Among them, ‘one born in the house’ is the name for a slave by birth, the son of a female slave born in the house. ‘One bought with wealth’ is the name for one who is bought—either a son from his parents or a slave from his masters—by giving wealth and having been established in the conduct of a slave. These two also should not be given the going-forth. One giving them the going-forth should make them non-slaves according to the custom in each respective place before giving them the going-forth. ‘One brought as a captive of war’ refers to when they bring free persons from another country, having either plundered or enticed them from that other country; or, even within the country, a king commands, “Plunder a certain village that has committed an offense,” and from there they also bring people. In that case, all the men are slaves, and the women are female slaves. A slave brought as a captive of war of this kind should not be given the going-forth if he is living in the presence of those by whom he was brought, or is bound in a prison, or is being guarded by men. But if, having escaped, he has gone elsewhere, he should be given the going-forth in the place he has gone to. When a release from bondage is made, either by a pleased king saying, “Release those brought as captives of war,” or by a general amnesty, he should indeed be given the going-forth.

Sāmaṃ dāsabyaṃ upagato nāma jīvitahetu vā ārakkhahetu vā “ahaṃ te dāso”ti sayameva dāsabhāvaṃ upagato rājūnaṃ hatthiassagomahiṃsagopakādayo viya. Tādiso dāso na pabbājetabbo. Rañño vaṇṇadāsīnaṃ puttā honti amaccaputtasadisā, tepi na pabbājetabbā. Bhujissitthiyo asaññatā vaṇṇadāsīhi saddhiṃ vicaranti, tāsaṃ putte pabbājetuṃ vaṭṭati. Sace sayameva paṇṇaṃ āropenti, na vaṭṭati. Bhaṭiputtagaṇādīnaṃ dāsāpi tehi adinnā na pabbājetabbā. Vihāresu [M 0.0139] rājūhi ārāmikadāsā nāma dinnā honti, tepi pabbājetuṃ na vaṭṭati, bhujisse katvā pana pabbājetuṃ vaṭṭati. Mahāpaccariyaṃ “antojātadhanakkītake ānetvā bhikkhusaṅghassa ‘ārāmike demā’ti denti, takkaṃ sīse āsittakasadisāva honti, te pabbājetuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti vuttaṃ. Kurundiyaṃ pana “ārāmikaṃ demāti kappiyavohārena denti, yena kenaci vohārena dinno hotu, neva pabbājetabbo”ti vuttaṃ. Duggatamanussā “saṅghaṃ nissāya jīvissāmā”ti vihāre kappiyakārakā honti, ete pabbājetuṃ vaṭṭati. Yassa mātāpitaro dāsā[V 0.0135], mātā eva vā dāsī, pitā adāso, taṃ pabbājetuṃ na vaṭṭati. Yassa pana mātā adāsī, pitā dāso, taṃ pabbājetuṃ vaṭṭati. Bhikkhussa ñātakā vā upaṭṭhākā vā dāsaṃ denti “imaṃ pabbājetha, tumhākaṃ veyyāvaccaṃ karissatī”ti, attano vāssa dāso atthi, bhujisso katova pabbājetabbo. Sāmikā dāsaṃ denti “imaṃ pabbājetha, sace abhiramissati, adāso. Vibbhamissati ce, amhākaṃ dāsova bhavissatī”ti, ayaṃ tāvakāliko nāma, taṃ pabbājetuṃ na vaṭṭatīti kurundiyaṃ vuttaṃ. Nissāmikadāso hoti, sopi bhujisso katova pabbājetabbo. Ajānanto pabbājetvā upasampādetvā vā pacchā jānanti, bhujissaṃ kātumeva vaṭṭati.

A person who has voluntarily entered into servitude is one who, whether for the sake of livelihood or protection, has of his own accord entered the state of servitude by declaring, “I am your slave,” like the kings’ elephant-keepers, horse-keepers, cowherds, and buffalo-herds. Such a slave should not be given the going-forth. The sons of the king’s concubines are like the sons of ministers; they too should not be given the going-forth. Free women who are unrestrained associate with concubines; it is permissible to give the going-forth to their sons. If they themselves present a leaf of submission, it is not permissible. The slaves of groups such as mercenary soldiers, if not given by their owners, should not be given the going-forth. In monasteries, those given by kings as monastery slaves should not be given the going-forth; however, after they have been made free, it is permissible to give them the going-forth. In the Mahāpaccariya, it is said: “If they bring those born in the household or purchased with wealth and give them to the community of monks, saying, ‘We give these as monastery attendants,’ they are like buttermilk poured on the head; it is permissible to give them the going-forth.” But in the Kurundī, it is said: “If they are given as monastery attendants using allowable terminology, by whatever expression they are given, they should never be given the going-forth.” Impoverished people who become monastery workers in a monastery, thinking, “We will live depending on the Saṅgha,”—it is permissible to give them the going-forth. If a person’s parents are slaves, or if only the mother is a slave and the father is not, it is not permissible to give that person the going-forth. But if the mother is not a slave and the father is, it is permissible to give that person the going-forth. If a monk’s relatives or supporters give a slave, saying, “Give this one the going-forth; he will perform services for you,” or if the monk has his own slave, he should be given the going-forth only after being made a freeman. If owners give a slave, saying, “Give this one the going-forth. If he delights in the life, he is no longer a slave. But if he disrobes, he will be our slave again,”—this is called a temporary freedman. It is not permissible to give him the going-forth, so it is said in the Kurundī. If there is a slave without an owner, he too should be given the going-forth only after being made a freeman. If one, not knowing, gives the going-forth or the higher ordination and finds out later, it is proper only to make that person free.

Imassa ca atthassa pakāsanatthaṃ idaṃ vatthuṃ vadanti – ekā kira kuladāsī ekena saddhiṃ anurādhapurā palāyitvā rohaṇe vasamānā puttaṃ paṭilabhi, so pabbajitvā upasampannakāle lajjī kukkuccako ahosi. Athekadivasaṃ mātaraṃ pucchi “kiṃ upāsike tumhākaṃ bhātā vā bhaginī vā natthi, na kiñci ñātakaṃ passāmī”ti. Tāta, ahaṃ anurādhapure kuladāsī, tava pitarā saddhiṃ palāyitvā idha vasāmīti. Sīlavā bhikkhu “asuddhā kira me pabbajjā”ti saṃvegaṃ labhitvā mātaraṃ tassa kulassa nāmagottaṃ pucchitvā anurādhapuraṃ āgamma tassa kulassa gharadvāre aṭṭhāsi, “aticchatha, bhante”ti vuttepi nātikkami. Te āgantvā “kiṃ, bhante”ti pucchiṃsu. “Tumhākaṃ itthannāmā dāsī palātā atthī”ti? “Atthi, bhante”. Ahaṃ tassā putto, sace maṃ tumhe anujānātha, pabbajjaṃ labhāmi, tumhe mayhaṃ sāmikāti. Te haṭṭhatuṭṭhā hutvā “suddhā, bhante, tumhākaṃ pabbajjā”ti taṃ bhujissaṃ katvā mahāvihāre [M 0.0140] vasāpesuṃ catūhi paccayehi paṭijaggantā. Thero taṃ kulaṃ nissāya vasamānoyeva arahattaṃ pāpuṇīti.

To illustrate this point, they tell the following story: It is said that a household slave girl fled from Anurādhapura with a man and, while living in Rohaṇa, gave birth to a son. Having gone forth and received higher ordination, he became conscientious and scrupulous. Then one day, he asked his mother, “Laywoman, do you not have a brother or a sister? I do not see any relatives.” “Dear son, I was a household slave girl in Anurādhapura. Having fled with your father, I now live here.” The virtuous monk, thinking, “It seems my going forth is impure,” was struck with a sense of spiritual urgency. He asked his mother for the name and clan of that household, then went to Anurādhapura and stood at the door of that family’s house. Even when told, “Please enter, venerable sir,” he did not go in. They came and asked, “What is it, venerable sir?” He asked, “Do you have a slave girl named so-and-so who ran away?” “Yes, venerable sir.” “I am her son. If you permit me, I may receive the going forth; you are my masters.” Delighted and overjoyed, they said, “Your going forth is pure, venerable sir.” They made him a free man and, while providing for him with the four requisites, had him stay at the Great Monastery. The elder, while living in dependence on that family, attained arahantship.

132. “Na, bhikkhave, hatthacchinno pabbājetabbo. Na pādacchinno, na hatthapādacchinno, na kaṇṇacchinno, na kaṇṇanāsacchinno, na aṅgulicchinno, na aḷacchinno, na kaṇḍaracchinno, na phaṇahatthako, na khujjo, na vāmano na galagaṇḍī, na lakkhaṇāhato, na kasāhato, na likhitako, na sīpadī, na pāparogī, na parisadūsako, na kāṇo, na kuṇī, na khañjo, na pakkhahato, na chinniriyāpatho, na jarādubbalo, na andho, na mūgo, na badhiro, na andhamūgo, na andhabadhiro, na mūgabadhiro, na andhamūgabadhiro pabbājetabbo, yo pabbājeyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (mahāva. 119) vacanato pana hatthacchinnādayopi na pabbājetabbā.

132. “Monks, one whose hand is cut off should not be given the going forth. One whose foot is cut off should not be given the going forth. One whose hand and foot are cut off should not be given the going forth. One whose ear is cut off should not be given the going forth. One whose ear and nose are cut off should not be given the going forth. One whose finger is cut off should not be given the going forth. One whose thumb or big toe is cut off should not be given the going forth. One whose tendon is cut off should not be given the going forth. One who has webbed hands should not be given the going forth. One who is hunchbacked should not be given the going forth. A dwarf should not be given the going forth. One who has a goiter should not be given the going forth. One who is branded should not be given the going forth. One who is whipped should not be given the going forth. One who is proscribed should not be given the going forth. One who has elephantiasis should not be given the going forth. One who is afflicted with a foul disease should not be given the going forth. One who corrupts the assembly should not be given the going forth. One who is one-eyed should not be given the going forth. One with a crooked limb should not be given the going forth. One who is lame should not be given the going forth. One who is paralyzed on one side should not be given the going forth. One whose posture is broken should not be given the going forth. One who is weak with old age should not be given the going forth. One who is blind should not be given the going forth. One who is mute should not be given the going forth. One who is deaf should not be given the going forth. One who is blind and mute should not be given the going forth. One who is blind and deaf should not be given the going forth. One who is mute and deaf should not be given the going forth. One who is blind, mute, and deaf should not be given the going forth. Whoever gives the going forth to such a person commits an offense of wrongdoing.” Therefore, those whose hands are cut off, and so on, should also not be given the going forth.

Tattha [V 0.0136] hatthacchinnoti yassa hatthatale vā maṇibandhe vā kappare vā yattha katthaci eko vā dve vā hatthā chinnā honti. Pādacchinnoti yassa aggapāde vā gopphakesu vā jaṅghāya vā yattha katthaci eko vā dve vā pādā chinnā honti. Hatthapādacchinnoti yassa vuttappakāreneva catūsu hatthapādesu dve vā tayo vā sabbe vā hatthapādā chinnā honti. Kaṇṇacchinnoti yassa kaṇṇamūle vā kaṇṇasakkhalikāya vā eko vā dve vā kaṇṇā chinnā honti. Yassa pana kaṇṇāvaṭṭe chijjanti, sakkā ca hoti saṅghāṭetuṃ, so kaṇṇaṃ saṅghāṭetvā pabbājetabbo. Nāsacchinnoti yassa ajapadake vā agge vā ekapuṭe vā yattha katthaci nāsā chinnā hoti. Yassa pana nāsikā sakkā hoti sandhetuṃ, so taṃ phāsukaṃ katvā pabbājetabbo. Kaṇṇanāsacchinno ubhayavasena veditabbo. Aṅgulicchinnoti yassa nakhasesaṃ adassetvā ekā vā bahū vā aṅguliyo chinnā honti. Yassa pana suttatantumattampi nakhasesaṃ paññāyati, taṃ pabbājetuṃ vaṭṭati. Aḷacchinnoti yassa catūsu aṅguṭṭhakesu aṅguliyaṃ vuttanayeneva eko vā bahū vā aṅguṭṭhakā chinnā honti. Kaṇḍaracchinnoti yassa kaṇḍaranāmakā mahānhārū purato vā pacchato vā chinnā honti, yesu ekassapi chinnattā aggapādena vā caṅkamati, mūlena vā caṅkamati, na pādaṃ patiṭṭhāpetuṃ sakkoti.

Herein, 'one whose hand is cut off' is one for whom one or both hands are cut off at any place on the palm, the wrist, or the elbow. 'One whose foot is cut off' is one for whom one or both feet are cut off at any place on the front of the foot, the ankles, or the shin. 'One whose hands and feet are cut off' is one for whom, in the manner already stated, two, three, or all of the four hands and feet are cut off. 'One whose ear is cut off' is one for whom one or both ears are cut off at the base of the ear or the earlobe. But for one whose ear-rim is cut, and it is possible to reattach it, he should be given the going forth after having reattached the ear. 'One whose nose is cut off' is one for whom the nose is cut off at any place on the root, the tip, or one nostril. But for one whose nose it is possible to join, he should be given the going forth after having made it secure. 'One whose ears and nose are cut off' should be understood by way of both cases. 'One whose finger is cut off' is one for whom one or many fingers are cut off without leaving a remnant of the nail. But for one for whom even a thread-like remnant of the nail is apparent, it is proper to give him the going forth. 'One whose thumb or big toe is cut off' is one for whom, among the two thumbs and two big toes, one or many are cut off in the same way as stated for the fingers. 'One whose tendons are cut off' is one for whom the great sinews named 'kaṇḍara' are cut from the front or from the back, due to even one of which being cut, one walks on the front of the foot or on the heel, and is not able to place the foot firmly.

Phaṇahatthakoti [M 0.0141] yassa vaggulipakkhakā viya aṅguliyo sambaddhā honti, etaṃ pabbājetukāmena aṅgulantarikāyo phāletvā sabbaṃ antaracammaṃ apanetvā phāsukaṃ katvā pabbājetabbo. Yassapi cha aṅguliyo honti, taṃ pabbājetukāmena adhikaṃ aṅguliṃ chinditvā phāsukaṃ katvā pabbājetabbo. Khujjoti yo urassa vā piṭṭhiyā vā passassa vā nikkhantattā khujjasarīro. Yassa pana kiñci kiñci aṅgapaccaṅgaṃ īsakaṃ vaṅkaṃ, taṃ pabbājetuṃ vaṭṭati. Mahāpuriso eva hi brahmujugatto, avaseso satto akhujjo nāma natthi. Vāmanoti jaṅghavāmano vā kaṭivāmano vā ubhayavāmano vā. Jaṅghavāmanassa kaṭito paṭṭhāya heṭṭhimakāyo rasso hoti, uparimakāyo paripuṇṇo. Kaṭivāmanassa kaṭito paṭṭhāya uparimakāyo rasso hoti, heṭṭhimakāyo paripuṇṇo. Ubhayavāmanassa ubhopi kāyā rassā honti, yesaṃ rassattā bhūtānaṃ viya parivaṭumo mahākucchighaṭasadiso attabhāvo hoti, taṃ tividhampi pabbājetuṃ na vaṭṭati.

‘One with a webbed hand’ is he whose fingers are joined together like a bat's wing; if one wishes to give the going forth to such a person, the spaces between the fingers should be split, all the skin in between removed, and after making it comfortable, he should be given the going forth. For one who has six fingers, if one wishes to give him the going forth, the extra finger should be cut off, and after making it comfortable, he should be given the going forth. ‘A hunchback’ is one whose body is hunched due to the protrusion of the chest, the back, or the side. However, for one whose major or minor limbs are slightly bent, it is allowable to give him the going forth. Indeed, only the Great Man has a body as straight as a Brahmā's; among other beings, there is none who can be called 'not hunched'. ‘A dwarf’ is one with short shanks, one with a short waist, or one short in both respects. For one with short shanks, the lower part of the body from the waist downwards is short, while the upper part of the body is complete. For one with a short waist, the upper part of the body from the waist upwards is short, while the lower part of the body is complete. For one short in both respects, both parts of the body are short. For those whose bodily form, due to shortness, is rounded like that of goblins and similar to a large-bellied pot, it is not allowable to give the going forth to any of these three types.

Galagaṇḍīti yassa kumbhaṇḍaṃ viya gale gaṇḍo hoti. Desanāmattameva cetaṃ, yasmiṃ kismiñci pana padese gaṇḍe sati na pabbājetabbo. Tattha vinicchayo “na, bhikkhave, pañcahi ābādhehi phuṭṭho pabbājetabbo”ti (mahāva. 89) ettha vuttanayeneva veditabbo. Lakkhaṇāhatakasāhatalikhitakesu [V 0.0137] yaṃ vattabbaṃ, taṃ heṭṭhā vuttameva. Sīpadīti bhārapādo vuccati. Yassa pādo thūlo hoti sañjātapīḷako kharo, so na pabbājetabbo. Yassa pana na tāva kharabhāvaṃ gaṇhāti, sakkā hoti upanāhaṃ bandhitvā udakaāvāṭe pavesetvā udakavālikāya pūretvā yathā sirā paññāyanti, jaṅghā ca telanāḷikā viya hoti, evaṃ milāpetuṃ, tassa pādaṃ īdisaṃ katvā taṃ pabbājetuṃ vaṭṭati. Sace puna vaḍḍhati, upasampādentenapi tathā katvāva upasampādetabbo. Pāparogīti arisabhagandarapittasemhakāsasosādīsu yena kenaci rogena niccāturo atekiccharogo jeguccho amanāpo, ayaṃ na pabbājetabbo.

Galagaṇḍī refers to one who has a goiter on the neck like a gourd. This is merely a designation; however, one with a lump in any part of the body should not be given the going forth. The ruling here should be understood according to the method stated in the Pāḷi: 'Monks, one afflicted with five kinds of diseases should not be given the going forth.' Regarding those who have been branded, beaten with a cane, or inscribed, what is to be said has already been stated below. Sīpadī refers to what is called 'one with a heavy foot.' One whose foot is swollen, has developed sores, and is rough should not be given the going forth. However, for one whose foot has not yet become rough, it is possible to reduce it by binding it with a poultice, inserting it into a small pit of water, and filling it with hot water and hot sand so that the veins appear and the shin becomes like an oil-tube. Having made the foot like this, it is proper to give him the going forth. If it grows again, the one conferring the higher ordination must also treat it in the same way before conferring the higher ordination. Pāparogī refers to one who, with any of the diseases such as hemorrhoids, fistula, diseases of the bile, diseases of phlegm, cough, consumption, and so on, is constantly ill, has an incurable disease, is repulsive, and is unpleasant. Such a person should not be given the going forth.

133. Parisadūsakoti yo attano virūpatāya parisaṃ dūseti, atidīgho vā hoti aññesaṃ sīsappamāṇanābhippadeso, atirasso vā ubhayavāmanabhūtarūpaṃ viya, atikāḷo vā jhāpitakkhette khāṇuko [M 0.0142] viya, accodāto vā dadhitakkādīhi pamajjitatambalohavaṇṇo, atikiso vā mandamaṃsalohito aṭṭhisirācammasarīro viya, atithūlo vā bhāriyamaṃso mahodaro mahābhūtasadiso, abhimahantasīso vā pacchiṃ sīse katvā ṭhito viya, atikhuddakasīso vā sarīrassa ananurūpena atikhuddakena sīsena samannāgato, kūṭakūṭasīso vā tālaphalapiṇḍisadisena sīsena samannāgato, sikharasīso vā uddhaṃ anupubbatanukena sīsena samannāgato, nāḷisīso vā mahāveṇupabbasadisena sīsena samannāgato, kappasīso vā pabbhārasīso vā catūsu passesu yena kenaci passena onatena sīsena samannāgato, vaṇasīso vā pūtisīso vā kaṇṇikakeso vā pāṇakehi khāyitakedāre sassasadisehi tahiṃ tahiṃ uṭṭhitehi kesehi samannāgato, nillomasīso vā thūlathaddhakeso vā tālahīrasadisehi kesehi samannāgato, jātipalitehi paṇḍarakeso vā pakatitambakeso vā ādittehi viya kesehi samannāgato, āvaṭṭasīso vā gunnaṃ sarīre āvaṭṭasadisehi uddhaggehi kesāvaṭṭehi samannāgato, sīsalomehi saddhiṃ ekābaddhabhamukalomo vā jālabaddhena viya nalāṭena samannāgato.

133. An 'Assembly-defiler' is one who, due to his own deformed appearance, defiles the assembly: being excessively tall, whose navel is at the level of others' heads; or excessively short, like a goblin-figure dwarfed in both upper and lower parts; or excessively dark, like a stump in a burnt field; or excessively white; or having a complexion like copper polished with curd, buttermilk, and so on; or excessively thin, with little flesh and blood, like a body of only skin, bones, and sinews; or excessively fat, with heavy flesh and a large belly, like a great goblin; or having an excessively large head, as if standing with a basket placed on his head; or having an excessively small head that is disproportionate to his body; or having a lumpy head like a cluster of palm fruits; or having a peaked head that gradually tapers upwards; or having a tube-like head like a large bamboo joint; or having a head like an elephant; or having a depressed head that is sloped on any one of its four sides; or having a head full of sores; or having a putrid head; or having hair in patches, like crops in a field eaten by insects; or being bald-headed; or having thick, stiff hair like palm fibers; or having hair that is white from birth; or having naturally red hair, as if on fire; or having a head with hair whorls with upturned tips, like the whorls on the body of cattle; or having eyebrows joined as one with the hair of the head, or having a forehead as if bound by a net.

Sambaddhabhamuko vā nillomabhamuko vā makkaṭabhamuko vā atimahantakkhi vā atikhuddakakkhi vā mahiṃsacamme vāsikoṇena paharitvā katachiddasadisehi akkhīhi samannāgato, visamakkhi vā ekena mahantena, ekena khuddakena akkhinā samannāgato, visamacakkalo vā ekena uddhaṃ, ekena adhoti evaṃ visamajātehi akkhicakkehi samannāgato, kekaro vā gambhīrakkhi vā yassa gambhīre udapāne udakatārakā viya akkhitārakā paññāyanti, nikkhantakkhi vā yassa kakkaṭasseva akkhitārakā nikkhantā honti, hatthikaṇṇo vā mahantāhi kaṇṇasakkhalīhi samannāgato, mūsikakaṇṇo vā jatukakaṇṇo [V 0.0138] vā khuddakāhi kaṇṇasakkhalīhi samannāgato, chiddamattakaṇṇo vā yassa vinā kaṇṇasakkhalīhi kaṇṇacchiddamattameva hoti, aviddhakaṇṇo vā, yonakajātiko pana parisadūsako na hoti, sabhāvoyeva hi so tassa. Kaṇṇabhagandariko vā niccapūtinā kaṇṇena samannāgato, gaṇḍakaṇṇo [M 0.0143] vā sadā paggharitapubbena kaṇṇena samannāgato, ṭaṅkitakaṇṇo vā gobhattanāḷikāya aggasadisehi kaṇṇehi samannāgato, atipiṅgalakkhi vā, madhupiṅgalaṃ pana pabbājetuṃ vaṭṭati. Nippakhumakkhi vā assupaggharaṇakkhi vā pupphitakkhi vā akkhipākena samannāgatakkhi vā.

Or one with joined eyebrows, or hairless eyebrows, or monkey-like eyebrows; or who has excessively large eyes; or excessively small eyes, like holes made by striking a buffalo hide with the corner of an adze; or who has uneven eyes, one large and one small; or whose eye-sockets are uneven, one higher and one lower; or who has a squint; or deep-set eyes, where the pupils appear like water-bubbles in a deep well; or bulging eyes, where the pupils protrude like a crab’s; or one with elephant-like ears, endowed with large ear-flaps; or one with mouse-like ears or bat-like ears, endowed with small ear-flaps; or one whose ears are merely holes without ear-flaps; or one whose ears are not pierced—but one of the Yona race is not a defiler of the assembly, for that is his natural state. Or one who has a fistula in the ear, endowed with a constantly putrid ear; or one with a boil on the ear, endowed with an ear that always oozes pus; or one with pointed ears like the tip of a cow-feeding tube; or one with very tawny eyes—though one with honey-tawny eyes is permissible for the going forth; or one with eyes that lack eyelashes; or eyes that constantly water; or eyes with a film over them; or eyes afflicted with inflammation.

Atimahantanāsiko vā atikhuddakanāsiko vā cipiṭanāsiko vā majjhe appatiṭṭhahitvā ekapasse ṭhitavaṅkanāsiko vā dīghanāsiko vā sukatuṇḍasadisāya jivhāya lehituṃ sakkuṇeyyāya nāsikāya samannāgato, niccaṃ paggharitasiṅghāṇikanāso vā, mahāmukho vā yassa paṭaṅgamaṇḍūkasseva mukhanimittaṃyeva mahantaṃ hoti, mukhaṃ pana lābusadisaṃ atikhuddakaṃ, bhinnamukho vā vaṅkamukho vā mahāoṭṭho vā ukkhalimukhavaṭṭisadisehi oṭṭhehi samannāgato, tanukaoṭṭho vā bhericammasadisehi dante pidahituṃ asamatthehi oṭṭhehi samannāgato, mahādharoṭṭho vā tanukauttaroṭṭho vā tanukaadharoṭṭho vā mahāuttaroṭṭho vā oṭṭhachinnako vā eḷamukho vā uppakkamukho vā saṅkhatuṇḍako vā bahi setehi anto atirattehi oṭṭhehi samannāgato, duggandhakuṇapamukho vā, mahādanto vā aṭṭhakadantasadisehi dantehi samannāgato, asuradanto vā heṭṭhā vā upari vā bahi nikkhantadanto, yassa pana sakkā hoti oṭṭhehi pidahituṃ, kathentasseva paññāyati, no akathentassa, taṃ pabbājetuṃ vaṭṭati. Pūtidanto vā niddanto vā atikhuddakadanto vā yassa pana dantantare kalandakadanto viya sukhumadanto hoti, taṃ pabbājetuṃ vaṭṭati.

Or one with an excessively large nose, or an excessively small nose, or a flattened nose, or a nose that is not set straight in the middle but is crooked to one side; or one with a long nose, that is, one endowed with a nose like a parrot's beak that can be licked with the tongue; or one who constantly has a runny nose; or one with a large mouth, that is, one whose mouth's appearance is large like that of a large-mouthed frog, but the mouth opening itself is very small like a gourd; or one with a split mouth or a crooked mouth; or one with thick lips resembling the rim of a pot; or one with thin lips, unable to cover the teeth, resembling the hide of a drum; or one with a large lower lip, or a thin upper lip, or a thin lower lip, or a large upper lip; or one with a split lip; or one with a slobbering mouth; or one with an inflamed mouth; or one with lips like a conch, that is, one endowed with lips that are white on the outside and very red on the inside; or one whose mouth smells like a rotting corpse; or one with large teeth resembling the teeth of a harrow; or one with fang-like teeth protruding either below, above, or outward. However, for one whose teeth can be covered by the lips, and are visible only when speaking but not when silent, it is permissible to ordain him. One with rotten teeth, or one with no teeth, or one with excessively small teeth. However, for one who has a fine tooth like a squirrel's tooth in the space between the teeth, it is permissible to ordain him.

Mahāhanuko vā gohanusadisena hanunā samannāgato, dīghahanuko vā cipiṭahanuko vā antopaviṭṭhena viya atirassena hanukena samannāgato, bhinnahanuko vā vaṅkahanuko vā nimmassudāṭhiko vā bhikkhunīsadisamukho, dīghagalo vā bakagalasadisena galena samannāgato, rassagalo vā antopaviṭṭhena viya galena samannāgato, bhinnagalo vā bhaṭṭhaaṃsakūṭo vā ahattho vā ekahattho vā atirassahattho vā atidīghahattho vā bhinnauro vā bhinnapiṭṭhi vā kacchugatto vā kaṇḍugatto vā daddugatto vā godhāgatto vā yassa godhāya viya gattato cuṇṇāni patanti. Sabbañcetaṃ virūpakaraṇaṃ sandhāya vitthāritavasena [M 0.0144] vuttaṃ, vinicchayo panettha pañcābādhesu vuttanayena veditabbo.

Or one with a large jaw, possessing a jaw like a cow's; or one with a long jaw; or one with a flat jaw, possessing an excessively short jaw as if it were sunken inwards; or one with a broken jaw; or one with a crooked jaw; or one without a beard or mustache, having a face like a bhikkhunī's; or one with a long neck, possessing a neck like a heron's; or one with a short neck, possessing a neck as if it were sunken inwards; or one with a broken neck; or one with a broken shoulder-tip; or one without hands; or one with only one hand; or one with excessively short arms; or one with excessively long arms; or one with a broken chest; or one with a broken back; or one whose body is afflicted with scabies; or one whose body is afflicted with itching; or one whose body is afflicted with ringworm; or one with a body like an iguana's, from whose body powders fall as from an iguana. All this has been stated in detail with reference to what causes disfigurement; the decision here, however, should be understood according to the method stated in the context of the five diseases.

Bhaṭṭhakaṭiko [V 0.0139] vā mahāānisado vā uddhanakūṭasadisehi ānisadamaṃsehi accuggatehi samannāgato, mahāūruko vā vātaṇḍiko vā mahājāṇuko vā saṅghaṭṭanajāṇuko vā dīghajaṅgho vā yaṭṭhisadisajaṅgho, vikaṭo vā saṅghaṭṭo vā ubbaddhapiṇḍiko vā, so duvidho heṭṭhā oruḷhāhi vā upari āruḷhāhi vā mahatīhi jaṅghapiṇḍikāhi samannāgato, mahājaṅgho vā thūlajaṅghapiṇḍiko vā mahāpādo vā mahāpaṇhi vā piṭṭhikapādo vā pādavemajjhato uṭṭhitajaṅgho, vaṅkapādo vā, so duvidho anto vā bahi vā parivattapādo, gaṇṭhikaṅguli vā siṅgiveraphaṇasadisāhi aṅgulīhi samannāgato, andhanakho vā kāḷavaṇṇehi pūtinakhehi samannāgato, sabbopi esa parisadūsako. Evarūpo parisadūsako na pabbājetabbo.

Or one with a broken hip; or one with large buttocks, possessing excessively prominent buttock-flesh like a tripod stove; or one with large thighs; or one with a large scrotum; or one with large knees; or one who is knock-kneed; or one with long shanks; or one with shanks like a staff; or one who walks askew; or one who is knock-kneed; or one with pendulous calves—this person is of two kinds, possessing large calf-muscles that either hang down below or rise up above; or one with large shanks; or one with thick calf-muscles; or one with large feet; or one with large heels; or one with a foot where the shank rises from the middle of the sole; or one with crooked feet—this person is of two kinds, having feet that turn either inwards or outwards; or one with gnarled fingers, possessing fingers like ginger rhizomes; or one with ruined nails, possessing black, putrid nails. Every such person is a defiler of the assembly. Such a defiler of the assembly is not to be given the going forth.

134. Kāṇoti pasannandho vā hotu pupphādīhi vā upahatapasādo, dvīhi vā ekena vā akkhinā na passati, so na pabbājetabbo. Mahāpaccariyaṃ pana ekakkhikāṇo “kāṇo”ti vutto, dviakkhikāṇo andhena saṅgahito. Mahāaṭṭhakathāyaṃ jaccandho “andho”ti vutto. Tasmā ubhayampi pariyāyena yujjati. Kuṇīti hatthakuṇī vā pādakuṇī vā aṅgulikuṇī vā, yassa etesu hatthādīsu yaṃ kiñci vaṅkaṃ paññāyati. Khañjoti natajāṇuko vā bhinnajaṅgho vā majjhe saṃkuṭitapādattā kuṇṭhapādako vā piṭṭhipādamajjhena caṅkamanto, agge saṃkuṭitapādattā kuṇṭhapādako vā piṭṭhipādaggena caṅkamanto, aggapādeneva caṅkamanakhañjo vā paṇhikāya caṅkamanakhañjo vā pādassa bāhirantena caṅkamanakhañjo vā pādassa abbhantarena caṅkamanakhañjo vā gopphakānaṃ upari bhaggattā sakalena piṭṭhipādena caṅkamanakhañjo vā. Sabbopesa khañjoyeva, na pabbājetabbo.

134. A `kāṇa` is one who is blind due to the destruction of the clear element, or whose clear element is afflicted by cataracts and so forth, who does not see with both eyes or with one eye; such a person should not be given the going forth. However, in the Mahāpaccarī, one who is blind in one eye is called a `kāṇa`, while one who is blind in both eyes is included under `andha`. In the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā, one who is born blind is called `andha`. Therefore, both are applicable by way of alternative meaning. A `kuṇī` is one with a crooked hand, a crooked foot, or a crooked finger—in whom any crookedness in these limbs is apparent. A `khañja` is one with a bent knee, or a broken shin; or one with a foot deformed due to contraction in the middle, who walks on the middle of the instep; or one with a foot deformed due to contraction at the front, who walks on the tip of the instep; or one who is lame from walking only on the forefoot; or one who is lame from walking on the heel; or one who is lame from walking on the outer edge of the foot; or one who is lame from walking on the inner edge of the foot; or one who is lame from walking on the entire instep due to a fracture above the ankles. All of these are indeed `khañja`; they should not be given the going forth.

Pakkhahatoti yassa eko hattho vā pādo vā addhasarīraṃ vā sukhaṃ na vahati. Chinniriyāpathoti pīṭhasappī vuccati. Jarādubbaloti jiṇṇabhāvena [M 0.0145] dubbalo attano cīvararajanādikammampi kātuṃ asamattho. Yo pana mahallakopi balavā hoti, attānaṃ paṭijaggituṃ sakkoti, so pabbājetabbo. Andhoti jaccandho vuccati. Mūgoti yassa vacībhedo na pavattati, yassapi pavattati, saraṇagamanaṃ pana paripuṇṇaṃ bhāsituṃ na sakkoti, tādisaṃ mammanampi pabbājetuṃ na vaṭṭati. Yo pana saraṇagamanamattaṃ paripuṇṇaṃ bhāsituṃ sakkoti, taṃ pabbājetuṃ vaṭṭati. Badhiroti yo sabbena sabbaṃ na suṇāti. Yo pana mahāsaddaṃ suṇāti, taṃ pabbājetuṃ vaṭṭati. Andhamūgādayo ubhayadosavasena vuttā. Yesañca pabbajjā paṭikkhittā, upasampadāpi tesaṃ paṭikkhittāva. Sace pana ne saṅgho upasampādeti, sabbepi sūpasampannā, kārakasaṅgho pana ācariyupajjhāyā ca āpattito na muccanti.

One who is paralyzed (pakkhahata) is one whose hand, foot, or half of the body cannot function with ease. One whose movements are impaired is called a 'stool-crawler' (pīṭhasappī). One who is weak due to old age (jarādubbala) is one who is frail due to being worn out and unable to perform even his own tasks such as dyeing robes. However, if one is old but still strong and capable of looking after oneself, he may be given the going forth. One who is blind (andha) is one who is blind from birth. A mute person (mūga) is one whose speech does not come forth; or even if it does, but he cannot fully pronounce the going for refuge—it is not proper to give the going forth to such a mumbling person. But if one can fully pronounce just the going for refuge, it is proper to give him the going forth. A deaf person (badhira) is one who cannot hear at all. However, if one can hear a loud sound, it is proper to give him the going forth. The blind-and-mute and others are mentioned on account of having a double fault. And for those whose going forth is prohibited, their higher ordination is also prohibited. But if the Saṅgha should confer higher ordination on them, all are well-ordained; however, the acting Saṅgha, as well as the preceptor and teacher, are not free from an offense.

135. Paṇḍako [V 0.0140] ubhatobyañjanako theyyasaṃvāsako titthiyapakkantako tiracchānagato mātughātako pitughātako arahantaghātako lohituppādako saṅghabhedako bhikkhunīdūsakoti ime pana ekādasa puggalā “paṇḍako, bhikkhave, anupasampanno na upasampādetabbo, upasampanno nāsetabbo”ti (mahāva. 109) ādivacanato abhabbā, neva nesaṃ pabbajjā, na upasampadā ca ruhati, tasmā na pabbājetabbā na upasampādetabbā, jānitvā pabbājento upasampādento ca dukkaṭaṃ āpajjati. Ajānitvāpi pabbājitā upasampāditā ca jānitvā liṅganāsanāya nāsetabbā.

135. A eunuch (paṇḍaka), a hermaphrodite (ubhatobyañjanaka), one who lives in communion as a thief (theyyasaṃvāsaka), one who has gone over to another sect (titthiyapakkantaka), an animal (tiracchānagata), a matricide (mātughātaka), a patricide (pitughātaka), a murderer of an arahant (arahantaghātaka), one who sheds the blood of a Buddha (lohituppādaka), a schismatic (saṅghabhedaka), and one who violates a bhikkhunī (bhikkhunīdūsaka)—these eleven persons are incapable. On account of the saying beginning, "A eunuch, bhikkhus, who is unordained should not be ordained; if ordained, he should be expelled," they are incapable. For them, neither the going forth nor the higher ordination takes root. Therefore, they should not be given the going forth nor the higher ordination. One who knowingly gives the going forth or the higher ordination incurs a dukkaṭa offense. Even if they were given the going forth or ordained unknowingly, upon knowing, they should be expelled by the destruction of their sign.

Tattha paṇḍakoti āsittapaṇḍako usūyapaṇḍako opakkamikapaṇḍako pakkhapaṇḍako napuṃsakapaṇḍakoti pañca paṇḍakā. Tesu yassa paresaṃ aṅgajātaṃ mukhena gahetvā asucinā āsittassa pariḷāho vūpasammati, ayaṃ āsittapaṇḍako. Yassa paresaṃ ajjhācāraṃ passato usūyāya uppannāya pariḷāho vūpasammati, ayaṃ usūyapaṇḍako. Yassa upakkamena bījāni apanītāni, ayaṃ opakkamikapaṇḍako. Ekacco pana akusalavipākānubhāvena kāḷapakkhe paṇḍako hoti, juṇhapakkhe panassa pariḷāho vūpasammati, ayaṃ pakkhapaṇḍako. Yo pana paṭisandhiyaṃyeva abhāvako uppanno, ayaṃ na puṃsakapaṇḍako. Tesu āsittapaṇḍakassa [M 0.0146] ca usūyapaṇḍakassa ca pabbajjā na vāritā, itaresaṃ tiṇṇaṃ vāritā. “Tesupi pakkhapaṇḍakassa yasmiṃ pakkhe paṇḍako hoti, tasmiṃyevassa pakkhe pabbajjā vāritā”ti kurundiyaṃ vuttaṃ.

Herein, as to the paṇḍaka, there are five types: the āsittapaṇḍaka, the usūyapaṇḍaka, the opakkamikapaṇḍaka, the pakkhapaṇḍaka, and the napuṃsakapaṇḍaka. Among these, the āsittapaṇḍaka is one for whom the burning of passion subsides when, having taken another's genitals into the mouth, he is sprinkled with impurity. The usūyapaṇḍaka is one for whom the burning of passion subsides by means of envy that has arisen upon seeing the misconduct of others. The opakkamikapaṇḍaka is one whose testicles have been removed by a procedure. A certain one, by the power of the result of unwholesome kamma, is a paṇḍaka in the dark fortnight, but in the bright fortnight his burning of passion subsides; this is the pakkhapaṇḍaka. One who is born without sexual characteristics from the very moment of conception, this is the napuṃsakapaṇḍaka. Among them, the going forth is not forbidden for the āsittapaṇḍaka and the usūyapaṇḍaka; it is forbidden for the other three. It is said in the Kurundī: "Even among those, for the pakkhapaṇḍaka, the going forth is forbidden only in that fortnight in which he is a paṇḍaka."

136. Ubhatobyañjanakoti (mahāva. aṭṭha. 116) itthinimittuppādanakammato ca purisanimittuppādanakammato ca ubhatobyañjanamassa atthīti ubhatobyañjanako. So duvidho hoti itthiubhatobyañjanako purisaubhatobyañjanakoti. Tattha itthiubhatobyañjanakassa itthinimittaṃ pākaṭaṃ hoti, purisanimittaṃ paṭicchannaṃ. Purisaubhatobyañjanakassa purisanimittaṃ pākaṭaṃ, itthinimittaṃ paṭicchannaṃ. Itthiubhatobyañjanakassa itthīsu purisattaṃ karontassa itthinimittaṃ paṭicchannaṃ hoti, purisanimittaṃ pākaṭaṃ. Purisaubhatobyañjanakassa purisānaṃ itthibhāvaṃ upagacchantassa purisanimittaṃ paṭicchannaṃ hoti, itthinimittaṃ pākaṭaṃ hoti. Itthiubhatobyañjanako sayañca gabbhaṃ gaṇhāti, parañca gaṇhāpeti, purisaubhatobyañjanako pana sayaṃ na gaṇhāti, paraṃ pana gaṇhāpetīti idametesaṃ nānākaraṇaṃ. Imassa pana duvidhassapi ubhatobyañjanakassa neva pabbajjā atthi, na upasampadā.

136. An ubhatobyañjanaka is so called because for this person there exist the characteristics of both sexes, due to the kamma that produces female characteristics and the kamma that produces male characteristics. This person is of two types: the female ubhatobyañjanaka and the male ubhatobyañjanaka. For the female ubhatobyañjanaka, the female characteristics are manifest, while the male characteristics are concealed. For the male ubhatobyañjanaka, the male characteristics are manifest, while the female characteristics are concealed. When a female ubhatobyañjanaka acts as a male among females, her female characteristics become concealed, and her male characteristics become manifest. When a male ubhatobyañjanaka assumes a female nature among males, his male characteristics become concealed, and his female characteristics become manifest. A female ubhatobyañjanaka both conceives herself and causes another to conceive, whereas a male ubhatobyañjanaka does not himself conceive but causes another to conceive—this is the distinction between them. For both types of this ubhatobyañjanaka, however, there is neither the going forth nor the higher ordination.

137. Theyyasaṃvāsakoti tayo theyyasaṃvāsakā liṅgatthenako saṃvāsatthenako ubhayatthenakoti[V 0.0141]. Tattha yo sayaṃ pabbajitvā vihāraṃ gantvā na bhikkhuvassāni gaṇeti, na yathāvuḍḍhaṃ vandanaṃ sādiyati, na āsanena paṭibāhati, na uposathapavāraṇādīsu sandissati, ayaṃ liṅgamattasseva thenitattā liṅgatthenako nāma. Yo pana bhikkhūhi pabbājito sāmaṇero samāno videsaṃ gantvā “ahaṃ dasavasso vā vīsativasso vā”ti musā vatvā bhikkhuvassāni gaṇeti, yathāvuḍḍhaṃ vandanaṃ sādiyati, āsanena paṭibāhati, uposathapavaāraṇādīsu sandissati, ayaṃ saṃvāsamattasseva thenitattā saṃvāsatthenako nāma. Bhikkhuvassagaṇanādiko hi sabbopi kiriyabhedo imasmiṃ atthe “saṃvāso”ti veditabbo. Sikkhaṃ paccakkhāya “na maṃ koci jānātī”ti puna evaṃ paṭipajjantepi eseva nayo. Yo pana sayaṃ pabbajitvā vihāraṃ gantvā bhikkhuvassāni gaṇeti, yathāvuḍḍhaṃ vandanaṃ sādiyati, āsanena paṭibāhati, uposathapavāraṇādīsu sandissati, ayaṃ liṅgassa ceva [M 0.0147] saṃvāsassa ca thenitattā ubhayatthenako nāma. Ayaṃ tividhopi theyyasaṃvāsako anupasampanno na upasampādetabbo, upasampanno nāsetabbo, puna pabbajjaṃ yācantopi na pabbājetabbo.

137. As to one in clandestine communion (`theyyasaṃvāsaka`), there are three kinds of those in clandestine communion: one who is a thief of the sign (`liṅgatthenaka`), one who is a thief of communion (`saṃvāsatthenaka`), and one who is a thief of both (`ubhayatthenaka`). Among them, one who, having gone forth by himself and gone to a monastery, does not count the years as a bhikkhu, does not consent to veneration according to seniority, does not prevent others by means of a seat, and does not appear at the Uposatha, Pavāraṇā, and so forth—this one, because of stealing only the sign, is called a `liṅgatthenaka`. But one who, having been given the going forth by bhikkhus, while being a novice, goes to another region and, speaking falsely, says, “I have ten rains or twenty rains,” and then counts the years as a bhikkhu, consents to veneration according to seniority, prevents others by means of a seat, and appears at the Uposatha, Pavāraṇā, and so forth—this one, because of stealing only communion, is called a `saṃvāsatthenaka`. Indeed, in this context, every kind of action, beginning with the counting of the years as a bhikkhu, should be understood as `saṃvāsa` (communion). Even for one who, having renounced the training, thinking, “No one knows me,” practices thus again, this is the same principle. But one who, having gone forth by himself and gone to a monastery, counts the years as a bhikkhu, consents to veneration according to seniority, prevents others by means of a seat, and appears at the Uposatha, Pavāraṇā, and so forth—this one, because of stealing both the sign and communion, is called an `ubhayatthenaka`. Any of these three kinds of those in clandestine communion, if he has not received the higher ordination, should not be given the higher ordination. If he has received the higher ordination, he should be expelled. Even if he requests the going forth again, he should not be given the going forth.

138. Ettha ca asammohatthaṃ idaṃ pakiṇṇakaṃ veditabbaṃ –

138. And here, for the sake of non-bewilderment, this miscellaneous ruling should be known:

“Rājadubbhikkhakantāra, rogaveribhayena vā;

Cīvarāharaṇatthaṃ vā, liṅgaṃ ādiyatīdha yo.

Whoever here in this Dispensation takes up the sign due to fear of a king, or of famine, or of the wilderness, or of disease, or of an enemy, or for the sake of carrying robes,

“Saṃvāsaṃ nādhivāseti, yāva so suddhamānaso;

Theyyasaṃvāsako nāma, tāva esa na vuccatī”ti. (mahāva. aṭṭha. 110);

as long as he is of pure mind, he does not consent to communion; for that long, he is not called a `theyyasaṃvāsaka`.

Tatrāyaṃ vitthāranayo – idhekaccassa rājā kuddho hoti, so “evaṃ me sotthi bhavissatī”ti sayameva liṅgaṃ gahetvā palāyati. Taṃ disvā rañño ārocenti, rājā “sace pabbajito, na taṃ labbhā kiñci kātu”nti tasmiṃ kodhaṃ paṭivineti. So “vūpasantaṃ me rājabhaya”nti saṅghamajjhaṃ anosaritvāva gihiliṅgaṃ gahetvā āgato pabbājetabbo. Athāpi “sāsanaṃ nissāya mayā jīvitaṃ laddhaṃ, handa dāni ahaṃ pabbajāmī”ti uppannasaṃvego teneva liṅgena āgantvā āgantukavattaṃ na sādiyati, bhikkhūhi puṭṭho vā apuṭṭho vā yathābhūtamattānaṃ āvikatvā pabbajjaṃ yācati, liṅgaṃ apanetvā pabbājetabbo. Sace pana so vattaṃ sādiyati, pabbajitālayaṃ [V 0.0142] dasseti, sabbaṃ pubbe vuttaṃ vassagaṇanādibhedaṃ vidhiṃ paṭipajjati, ayaṃ na pabbājetabbo.

Herein is the detailed explanation: In this world, a king is angry with a certain person. That person, thinking, 'Thus there will be safety for me,' himself takes the sign and flees. Seeing him, they inform the king. The king, thinking, 'If he has gone forth, it is not possible to do anything to him,' dispels his anger towards that person. That person, thinking, 'The fear of the king has subsided for me,' comes, having taken the sign of a householder without having approached the midst of the Sangha; he should be given the going forth. Or if, with a sense of spiritual urgency having arisen, he thinks, 'Relying on the Dispensation, my life was saved. Well now, I will go forth,' and having come with that very sign, he does not consent to the duties of a newcomer; whether asked by the bhikkhus or not, having revealed himself as he truly is, he requests the going forth; having removed the sign, he should be given the going forth. But if he consents to the duties, shows the disposition of one who has gone forth, and undertakes all the previously mentioned procedures, such as the distinction of counting the years, this person should not be given the going forth.

Idha panekacco dubbhikkhe jīvituṃ asakkonto sayameva liṅgaṃ gahetvā sabbapāsaṇḍiyabhattāni bhuñjanto dubbhikkhe vītivatte saṅghamajjhaṃ anosaritvāva gihiliṅgaṃ gahetvā āgatoti sabbaṃ purimasadisameva.

But here, a certain person, being unable to live during a famine, himself takes the sign and eats food offered to all sectarians. When the famine has passed, he comes, having taken the sign of a householder without having approached the midst of the Sangha; all is just like the previous case.

Aparo mahākantāraṃ nittharitukāmo hoti, satthavāho ca pabbajite gahetvā gacchati. So “evaṃ maṃ satthavāho gahetvā gamissatī”ti sayameva liṅgaṃ gahetvā satthavāhena saddhiṃ kantāraṃ nittharitvā khemantaṃ patvā saṅghamajjhaṃ anosaritvāva gihiliṅgaṃ gahetvā āgatoti sabbaṃ purimasadisameva.

Another person wishes to cross a great wilderness, and a caravan leader takes with him those who have gone forth. That person, thinking, 'Thus the caravan leader will take me,' himself takes the sign and, together with the caravan leader, crosses the wilderness. Having reached a safe place, he comes, having taken the sign of a householder without having approached the midst of the Sangha; all is just like the previous case.

Aparo [M 0.0148] rogabhaye uppanne jīvituṃ asakkonto sayameva liṅgaṃ gahetvā sabbapāsaṇḍiyabhattāni bhuñjanto rogabhaye vūpasante saṅghamajjhaṃ anosaritvāva gihiliṅgaṃ gahetvā āgatoti sabbaṃ purimasadisameva.

Another person, when danger from disease has arisen, being unable to live, himself takes the sign and eats food offered to all sectarians. When the danger from disease has subsided, he comes, having taken the sign of a householder without having approached the midst of the Sangha; all is just like the previous case.

Aparassa eko veriko kuddho hoti, ghātetukāmo naṃ vicarati. So “evaṃ me sotthi bhavissatī”ti sayameva liṅgaṃ gahetvā palāyati. Veriko “kuhiṃ so”ti pariyesanto “pabbajitvā palāto”ti sutvā “sace pabbajito, na taṃ labbhā kiñci kātu”nti tasmiṃ kodhaṃ paṭivineti. So “vūpasantaṃ me veribhaya”nti saṅghamajjhaṃ anosaritvāva gihiliṅgaṃ gahetvā āgatoti sabbaṃ purimasadisameva.

For another person, an enemy is angry and goes about wanting to kill him. Thinking, 'Thus I will be safe,' he himself takes the sign and flees. The enemy, searching 'Where is he?' and hearing 'He has gone forth and fled,' thinks, 'If he has gone forth, it is not possible to do anything to him,' and dispels his anger towards him. That person, thinking, 'The fear of the enemy has subsided for me,' comes, having taken the sign of a householder without having approached the midst of the Sangha; all is just like the previous case.

Aparo ñātikulaṃ gantvā sikkhaṃ paccakkhāya gihī hutvā “imāni cīvarāni idha nassissanti, sacepi imāni gahetvā vihāraṃ gamissāmi, antarāmagge maṃ ‘coro’ti gahessanti, yaṃnūnāhaṃ kāyaparihāriyāni katvā gaccheyya”nti cīvarāharaṇatthaṃ nivāsetvā ca pārupitvā ca vihāraṃ gacchati. Taṃ dūratova āgacchantaṃ disvā sāmaṇerā ca daharā ca abbhuggacchanti, vattaṃ dassenti. So na sādiyati, yathābhūtamattānaṃ āvikaroti. Sace bhikkhū “na dāni mayaṃ taṃ muñcissāmā”ti balakkārena pabbājetukāmā honti, kāsāyāni apanetvā puna pabbājetabbo. Sace pana “nayime maṃ hīnāyāvattabhāvaṃ jānantī”ti taṃyeva bhikkhubhāvaṃ [V 0.0143] paṭijānitvā sabbaṃ pubbe vuttaṃ vassagaṇanādibhedaṃ vidhiṃ paṭipajjati, ayaṃ na pabbājetabbo.

Another goes to his relatives' family, renounces the training, and becomes a householder, thinking: 'These robes will be ruined here. If I take them and go to the monastery, they might seize me on the way, calling me a thief. What if I were to make them wearable on my person and go?' Thus, for the sake of carrying the robes, he wears the lower robe and drapes the upper robe, and goes to the monastery. Seeing him coming from afar, the novices and young bhikkhus go forward to greet him and perform their duties. He does not consent and reveals himself as he truly is. If the bhikkhus, thinking, 'We will not release him now,' wish to give him the going forth by force, the ochre robes must be removed and he must be given the going forth again. But if, thinking, 'These bhikkhus do not know that I have returned to the lower state,' he claims that very status of a bhikkhu and follows the entire procedure previously mentioned, with its details such as the counting of years, this one should not be given the going forth.

Aparo mahāsāmaṇero ñātikulaṃ gantvā uppabbajitvā kammantānuṭṭhānena ubbāḷho puna “dāni ahaṃ sāmaṇero bhavissāmi, theropi me uppabbajitabhāvaṃ na jānātī”ti tadeva pattacīvaraṃ ādāya vihāraṃ gacchati, tamatthaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ na āroceti, sāmaṇerabhāvaṃ paṭijānāti, ayaṃ theyyasaṃvāsakoyeva, pabbajjaṃ na labhati. Sacepissa liṅgaggahaṇakāle evaṃ hoti “nāhaṃ kassaci ārocessāmī”ti, vihārañca gato āroceti, gahaṇeneva theyyasaṃvāsako. Athāpissa gahaṇakāle “ācikkhissāmī”ti cittaṃ uppannaṃ hoti, vihārañca gantvā “kuhiṃ tvaṃ, āvuso, gato”ti vutto “na dāni maṃ ime jānantī”ti vañcetvā [M 0.0149] nācikkhati, “nācikkhissāmī”ti saha dhuranikkhepena ayampi theyyasaṃvāsakova. Sace panassa gahaṇakālepi “ācikkhissāmī”ti hoti, vihāraṃ gantvāpi ācikkhati, ayaṃ puna pabbajjaṃ labhati.

Another senior novice goes to his relatives' family, disrobes, and becomes oppressed by the exertion of worldly affairs. Again, thinking, 'Now I will become a novice; the elder also does not know that I have disrobed,' he takes that same bowl and robes and goes to the monastery. He does not inform the monks of this matter and professes to be a novice. This one is indeed one who lives in communion by theft; he does not receive the going-forth. If, at the time of taking the outward sign, he has the thought, 'I will not inform anyone,' but upon reaching the monastery he does inform them, he is one who lives in communion by theft from the very moment of taking. Or if, at the time of taking, the thought arises, 'I will inform,' but upon reaching the monastery, when asked, 'Where have you been, friend?' he deceives them, thinking, 'These monks do not know me now,' and does not inform—this one too, upon abandoning his resolve, is one who lives in communion by theft. But if at the time of taking he has the thought, 'I will inform,' and upon reaching the monastery he does inform, this one again receives the going-forth.

Aparo daharasāmaṇero mahanto vā pana abyatto. So purimanayeneva uppabbajitvā ghare vacchakagorakkhaṇādīni kammāni kātuṃ na icchati. Tamenaṃ ñātakā tāniyeva kāsāyāni acchādetvā thālakaṃ vā pattaṃ vā hatthe datvā “gaccha, samaṇova hohī”ti gharā nīharanti. So vihāraṃ gacchati, neva naṃ bhikkhū jānanti “ayaṃ uppabbajitvā puna sayameva pabbajito”ti, nāpi sayaṃ jānāti “yo evaṃ pabbajati, so theyyasaṃvāsako nāma hotī”ti. Sace pana taṃ paripuṇṇavassaṃ upasampādenti, sūpasampanno. Sace pana anupasampannakāleyeva vinayavinicchaye vattamāne suṇāti “yo evaṃ pabbajati, so theyyasaṃvāsako nāma hotī”ti, tena “mayā evaṃ kata”nti bhikkhūnaṃ ācikkhitabbaṃ. Evaṃ puna pabbajjaṃ labhati. Sace pana “dāni na maṃ koci jānātī”ti nāroceti, dhuraṃ nikkhittamatteyeva theyyasaṃvāsako.

Another, whether a young novice or a senior one, is unlearned. Having disrobed in the same way as before, he does not wish to do work at home such as tending calves and cattle. His relatives then dress him in those very saffron robes, place a small bowl or an alms-bowl in his hand, and saying, 'Go, be a recluse,' they send him out of the house. He goes to the monastery, and the monks do not know, 'This one, having disrobed, has gone forth again by himself,' nor does he himself know, 'One who goes forth in this way is called one who lives in communion by theft.' If, however, they give him higher ordination when he has completed twenty years of age, he is validly ordained. But if, while still not having received higher ordination, during a Vinaya ruling he hears, 'One who goes forth in this way is called one who lives in communion by theft,' he should inform the monks, saying, 'I have acted in this way.' Thus, he receives the going-forth again. If, however, thinking, 'Now no one knows me,' he does not inform them, he becomes one who lives in communion by theft at the very moment of laying down the burden.

Bhikkhu sikkhaṃ paccakkhāya liṅgaṃ anapanetvā dussīlakammaṃ katvā vā akatvā vā puna sabbaṃ pubbe vuttaṃ vassagaṇanādibhedaṃ vidhiṃ paṭipajjati, theyyasaṃvāsako hoti. Sikkhaṃ appaccakkhāya saliṅge ṭhito methunaṃ paṭisevitvā vassagaṇanādibhedaṃ vidhiṃ āpajjanto theyyasaṃvāsako na hoti, pabbajjāmattaṃ labhati. Andhakaṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana “eso theyyasaṃvāsako”ti vuttaṃ, taṃ na gahetabbaṃ.

A monk who, having renounced the training without removing the outward sign, whether he has committed an immoral act or not, again follows the entire previously stated procedure with its distinctions such as the counting of years, becomes one who lives in communion by theft. One who, without renouncing the training, while remaining in his own outward sign, engages in sexual intercourse and then undertakes the procedure with its distinctions such as the counting of years, does not become one who lives in communion by theft; he receives only the going-forth. However, in the Andhaka commentary it is said, 'This person is one who lives in communion by theft,' but that should not be accepted.

Eko [V 0.0144] bhikkhu kāsāye saussāhova odātaṃ nivāsetvā methunaṃ paṭisevitvā puna kāsāyāni nivāsetvā vassagaṇanādibhedaṃ vidhiṃ āpajjati, ayampi theyyasaṃvāsako na hoti, pabbajjāmattaṃ labhati. Sace pana kāsāye dhuraṃ nikkhipitvā odātaṃ nivāsetvā methunaṃ paṭisevitvā puna kāsāyāni nivāsetvā vassagaṇanādibhedaṃ vidhiṃ āpajjati, theyyasaṃvāsako hoti. Sāmaṇero saliṅge ṭhito methunādiassamaṇakaraṇadhammaṃ āpajjitvāpitheyyasaṃvāsako na hoti. Sacepi kāsāye saussāhova kāsāyāni apanetvā methunaṃ paṭisevitvā puna kāsāyāni nivāseti, neva theyyasaṃvāsako hoti. Sace pana kāsāye dhuraṃ nikkhipitvā naggo vā odātavattho vā [M 0.0150] methunasevanādīhi assamaṇo hutvā kāsāyaṃ nivāseti, theyyasaṃvāsako hoti.

A certain monk, while still zealous for the saffron robes, puts on a white garment, engages in sexual intercourse, then again puts on the saffron robes and undertakes the procedure with its distinctions such as the counting of years; this one also does not become one who lives in communion by theft; he receives only the going-forth. But if, having laid down the burden of the saffron robes, he puts on a white garment, engages in sexual intercourse, then again puts on the saffron robes and undertakes the procedure with its distinctions such as the counting of years, he becomes one who lives in communion by theft. A novice, while remaining in his own outward sign, even having committed an act that makes one not a recluse, such as sexual intercourse, does not become one who lives in communion by theft. Even if, while still zealous for the saffron robes, he removes the saffron robes, engages in sexual intercourse, and then again puts on the saffron robes, he does not become one who lives in communion by theft. But if, having laid down the burden of the saffron robes, being naked or wearing a white garment, he becomes not a recluse through acts such as engaging in sexual intercourse and then puts on the saffron robe, he becomes one who lives in communion by theft.

Sace gihibhāvaṃ patthayamāno kāsāyaṃ ovaṭṭikaṃ katvā aññena vā ākārena gihinivāsanena nivāseti “sobhati nu kho me gihiliṅgaṃ, na sobhatī”ti vīmaṃsanatthaṃ, rakkhati tāva. “Sobhatī”ti sampaṭicchitvā pana puna liṅgaṃ sādiyanto theyyasaṃvāsako hoti. Odātaṃ nivāsetvā vīmaṃsanasampaṭicchanesupi eseva nayo. Sace pana nivatthakāsāvassa upari odātaṃ nivāsetvā vīmaṃsati vā sampaṭicchati vā, rakkhatiyeva. Bhikkhuniyāpi eseva nayo. Sāpi gihibhāvaṃ patthayamānā sace kāsāyaṃ gihinivāsanaṃ nivāseti “sobhati nu kho me gihiliṅgaṃ, na sobhatī”ti vīmaṃsanatthaṃ, rakkhatiyeva. Sace “sobhatī”ti sampaṭicchati, na rakkhati. Odātaṃ nivāsetvā vīmaṃsanasampaṭicchanesupi eseva nayo. Nivatthakāsāyassa pana upari odātaṃ nivāsetvā vīmaṃsatu vā sampaṭicchatu vā, rakkhatiyeva.

If one, desiring the state of a householder, wears the saffron robe made into a lower garment or in some other way in the manner of a householder for the purpose of considering, 'I wonder, does the outward sign of a householder suit me, or does it not?', he is protected for the time being. But having accepted that 'it suits,' one who then delights in that outward sign becomes one who lives in communion by theft. This same principle applies also in the cases of considering and accepting after having put on a white garment. However, if, having put on a white garment over his already worn saffron robe, he either considers or accepts, he is indeed protected. For a bhikkhunī also, this is the same principle. If she, desiring the state of a householder, wears the saffron robe as a householder's garment for the purpose of considering, 'I wonder, does the outward sign of a householder suit me, or does it not?', she is indeed protected. If she accepts that 'it suits,' she is not protected. This same principle applies also in the cases of considering and accepting after having put on a white garment. However, having put on a white garment over her already worn saffron robe, whether she considers or accepts, she is indeed protected.

Sace koci vuḍḍhapabbajito vassāni agaṇetvā pāḷiyampi aṭṭhatvā ekapassena gantvā mahāpeḷādīsu kaṭacchunā ukkhitte bhattapiṇḍe pattaṃ upanāmetvā seno viya maṃsapesiṃ gahetvā gacchati, theyyasaṃvāsako na hoti, bhikkhuvassāni pana gaṇetvā gaṇhanto theyyasaṃvāsako hoti. Sayaṃ sāmaṇerova sāmaṇerapaṭipāṭiyā kūṭavassāni gaṇetvā gaṇhanto theyyasaṃvāsako na hoti. Bhikkhu bhikkhupaṭipāṭiyā kūṭavassāni gaṇetvā gaṇhanto bhaṇḍagghena kāretabbo.

If someone ordained in old age, without counting his years of seniority and without standing in line, goes to one side to the large containers and so on, presents his bowl to a lump of food scooped out with a ladle, and departs having taken it like a hawk seizing a piece of flesh, he is not one who lives in communion by theft. But one who takes it by counting the years of seniority of a bhikkhu is one who lives in communion by theft. If he, being only a novice, takes it by counting false years of seniority according to the order of novices, he is not one who lives in communion by theft. A bhikkhu who takes it by counting false years of seniority according to the order of bhikkhus should be made to pay its value.

139. Titthiyapakkantakoti titthiyesu pakkanto paviṭṭhoti titthiyapakkantako, sopi na pabbājetabbo. Tatrāyaṃ vinicchayo – upasampanno bhikkhu “titthiyo bhavissāmī”ti saliṅgeneva tesaṃ upassayaṃ gacchati, padavāre padavāre dukkaṭaṃ, tesaṃ liṅge ādinnamatte titthiyapakkantako [V 0.0145] hoti. Yopi sayameva “titthiyo bhavissa”nti kusacīrādīni nivāseti, titthiyapakkantako hotiyeva. Yo pana naggo nahāyanto attānaṃ oloketvā “sobhati me ājīvakabhāvo, ājīvako bhavissa”nti kāsāyāni anādāya naggo ājīvakānaṃ [M 0.0151] upassayaṃ gacchati, padavāre padavāre dukkaṭaṃ. Sace panassa antarāmagge hirottappaṃ uppajjati, dukkaṭāni desetvā muccati. Tesaṃ upassayaṃ gantvāpi tehi vā ovadito attanā vā “imesaṃ pabbajjā atidukkhā”ti disvā nivattantopi muccatiyeva. Sace pana “kiṃ tumhākaṃ pabbajjāya ukkaṭṭha”nti pucchitvā “kesamassuluñcanādīnī”ti vutto ekakesampi luñcāpeti, ukkuṭikappadhānādīni vā vattāni ādiyati, morapiñchādīni vā nivāseti, tesaṃ liṅgaṃ gaṇhāti, “ayaṃ pabbajjā seṭṭhā”ti seṭṭhabhāvaṃ vā upagacchati, na muccati, titthiyapakkantako hoti. Sace pana “sobhati nu kho me titthiyapabbajjā, nanu kho sobhatī”ti vīmaṃsanatthaṃ kusacīrādīni vā nivāseti, jaṭaṃ vā bandhati, khārikājaṃ vā ādiyati, yāva na sampaṭicchati laddhiṃ, tāva rakkhati, sampaṭicchitamatte titthiyapakkantako hoti. Acchinnacīvaro pana kusacīrādīni nivāsento rājabhayādīhi vā titthiyaliṅgaṃ gaṇhanto laddhiyā abhāvena neva titthiyapakkantako hoti. “Ayañca titthiyapakkantako nāma upasampannabhikkhunā kathito, tasmā sāmaṇero saliṅgena titthiyāyatanaṃ gatopi puna pabbajjañca upasampadañca labhatī”ti kurundiyaṃ vuttaṃ. Purimo pana theyyasaṃvāsako anupasampannena kathito, tasmā upasampanno kūṭavassaṃ gaṇentopi assamaṇo na hoti. Liṅge saussāho pārājikaṃ āpajjitvā bhikkhuvassādīni gaṇhantopi theyyasaṃvāsako na hoti.

139. A 'sectarian deserter' (titthiyapakkantaka) is one who has gone over to the sectarians or joined them. He too should not be given the going forth. Herein is the determination: A fully ordained monk who thinks, 'I will become a sectarian,' and goes to their dwelling place while still in his own proper attire, incurs a dukkaṭa offense at every step. The moment he adopts their outward sign, he becomes a sectarian deserter. Similarly, one who on his own, thinking, 'I will become a sectarian,' puts on grass and bark garments and the like, also becomes a sectarian deserter. If a monk, while bathing naked, looks at himself and thinks, 'The state of an Ājīvaka is splendid; I will become an Ājīvaka,' and without taking the saffron robes, goes naked to the Ājīvakas' dwelling, he incurs a dukkaṭa offense at every step. But if along the way shame and fear of wrongdoing arise in him, he is freed by confessing the dukkaṭa offenses. Even if he reaches their dwelling and, either being admonished by them or realizing on his own, 'Their going forth is exceedingly difficult,' and turns back, he is certainly freed. But if he asks them, 'What is excellent about your going forth?' and upon being told, 'The plucking out of hair and beard, and so on,' he has even a single hair plucked out, or takes up their practices such as the squatting exertion, or wears peacock feathers and the like, adopts their outward sign, or accepts its superiority, thinking, 'This going forth is excellent'—he is not freed and becomes a sectarian deserter. But if, for the purpose of investigation, he thinks, 'Does the sectarian going forth suit me, or does it not suit me?' and puts on grass and bark garments and the like, or ties his hair in a matted lock, or takes up a carrying-pole, as long as he does not accept their doctrine, he is protected; the moment he accepts it, he becomes a sectarian deserter. However, a monk whose robe has been stolen, who wears grass and bark garments and the like, or adopts a sectarian sign due to fear of the king and so on, does not become a sectarian deserter due to the absence of the doctrine. It is stated in the Kurundī commentary that 'this sectarian deserter is spoken of in reference to a fully ordained monk; therefore, even a novice who has gone to a sectarian dwelling while in his own proper attire can again receive both the going forth and higher ordination.' But the former, the thief-in-disguise, is spoken of in reference to a non-ordained person; therefore, even a fully ordained monk who reckons false seniority does not become a non-recluse.
