Nissāya vasantenapi alajjī nissāya na vasitabbaṃ. Vuttañhetaṃ “na, bhikkhave, alajjīnaṃ nissāya vatthabbaṃ, yo vaseyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (mahāva. 120). Ettha (mahāva. aṭṭha. 120) ca alajjīnanti upayogatthe sāmivacanaṃ, alajjipuggale nissāya na vasitabbanti vuttaṃ hoti. Tasmā navaṃ ṭhānaṃ gatena “ehi, bhikkhu, nissayaṃ gaṇhāhī”ti vuccamānenapi catūhapañcāhaṃ nissayadāyakassa lajjibhāvaṃ upaparikkhitvā nissayo gahetabbo. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, catūhapañcāhaṃ āgametuṃ yāva bhikkhusabhāgataṃ jānāmī”ti (mahāva. 120) hi vuttaṃ. Sace “thero [V 0.0162] lajjī”ti bhikkhūnaṃ santike sutvā āgatadivaseyeva gahetukāmo hoti, thero pana “āgamehi tāva, vasanto jānissasī”ti katipāhaṃ ācāraṃ upaparikkhitvā nissayaṃ deti, vaṭṭati, pakatiyā nissayagahaṇaṭṭhānaṃ gatena pana tadaheva gahetabbo, ekadivasampi parihāro natthi. Sace paṭhamayāme ācariyassa okāso natthi, okāsaṃ alabhanto “paccūsasamaye gahessāmī”ti sayati, aruṇaṃ uggatampi na jānāti, anāpatti. Sace pana “gaṇhissāmī”ti ābhogaṃ akatvā sayati, aruṇuggamane dukkaṭaṃ. Agatapubbaṃ ṭhānaṃ gatena dve tīṇi divasāni vasitvā gantukāmena anissitena vasitabbaṃ. “Sattāhaṃ vasissāmī”ti ālayaṃ karontena pana nissayo gahetabbo. Sace thero “kiṃ sattāhaṃ vasantassa nissayenā”ti vadati, paṭikkhittakālato paṭṭhāya laddhaparihāro hoti.

152. To whom should dependence be given, and to whom should it not be given? Here, dependence should be given to one who is conscientious. To the other, it should not be given, for it is said: “Bhikkhus, dependence should not be given to the shameless. Whoever should give it, commits an offense of wrong conduct.” Even one who is living in dependence should not live in dependence on a shameless person. For this was said: “Bhikkhus, one should not live in dependence on the shameless. Whoever should do so, commits an offense of wrong conduct.” And here, the word ‘alajjīnaṃ’ is a genitive case used in the sense of the accusative, meaning that it is said, “one should not live in dependence on shameless persons.” Therefore, when a bhikkhu has gone to a new place, even if he is told, “Come, bhikkhu, take dependence,” he should take dependence only after investigating the conscientiousness of the dependence-giver for four or five days. For it was said: “I allow, bhikkhus, to wait for four or five days until I know the bhikkhu’s suitability.” If, having heard from the bhikkhus that “the elder is conscientious,” he wishes to take dependence on the very day of his arrival, but the elder says, “Wait for now; while living here, you will come to know,” and gives dependence only after investigating his conduct for some days, it is allowable. However, by one who has gone to a place where dependence is customarily taken, it should be taken on that very day; there is no exemption even for a single day. If, during the first watch, the teacher has no opportunity, and one, not getting an opportunity, lies down thinking, “I will take it at dawn,” and does not know even when dawn has arisen, there is no offense. But if one lies down without making the mental advertence, “I will take it,” there is an offense of wrong conduct at the break of dawn. One who has gone to a place he has not been to before and who wishes to leave after staying for two or three days should live there without dependence. But one who has the desire, “I will stay for seven days,” should take dependence. If the elder says, “What is the use of dependence for you who are staying for only seven days?” then from the time of refusal, he has obtained an exemption.

“Anujānāmi[M 0.0170], bhikkhave, addhānamaggappaṭipannena bhikkhunā nissayaṃ alabhamānena anissitena vatthu”nti vacanato pana addhānamaggappaṭipanno sace attanā saddhiṃ addhānamaggappaṭipannaṃ nissayadāyakaṃ na labhati, evaṃ nissayaṃ alabhamānena anissitena bahūnipi divasāni gantuṃ vaṭṭati. Sace pubbe nissayaṃ gahetvā vutthapubbaṃ kiñci āvāsaṃ pavisati, ekarattaṃ vasantenapi nissayo gahetabbo. Antarāmagge vissamanto vā satthaṃ vā pariyesanto katipāhaṃ vasati, anāpatti. Antovasse pana nibaddhavāsaṃ vasitabbaṃ, nissayo ca gahetabbo. Nāvāya gacchantassa pana vassāne āgatepi nissayaṃ alabhantassa anāpatti. Sace antarāmagge gilāno hoti, nissayaṃ alabhamānena anissitena vasituṃ vaṭṭati.

“I allow, O bhikkhus, a monk who has set out on a long journey, if he does not obtain dependence, to dwell without dependence.” Because of this statement, if a monk who has set out on a long journey does not find a dependence-giver who has also set out on a long journey with him, it is proper for him, not obtaining dependence, to go without dependence for many days. If he enters any monastery where he has formerly dwelt having taken dependence, dependence must be taken even by one dwelling for only one night. If on the way he dwells for some days while resting or searching for a caravan, there is no offense. But during the Rains-residence, one must dwell in a fixed residence, and dependence must be taken. However, for one going by boat, even when the Rains-residence has arrived, there is no offense for one not obtaining dependence. If on the way he becomes ill, it is proper for him, not obtaining dependence, to dwell without dependence.

Gilānupaṭṭhākopi gilānena yāciyamāno anissito eva vasituṃ labhati. Vuttañhetaṃ “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, gilānena bhikkhunā nissayaṃ alabhamānena anissitena vatthuṃ, anujānāmi, bhikkhave, gilānupaṭṭhākena bhikkhunā nissayaṃ alabhamānena yāciyamānena anissitena vatthu”nti (mahāva. 121). Sace pana “yācāhi ma”nti vuccamānopi gilāno mānena na yācati, gantabbaṃ.

An attendant of the sick, if requested by the sick monk, may also dwell without dependence. For it has been said: “I allow, O bhikkhus, a sick monk, not obtaining dependence, to dwell without dependence. I allow, O bhikkhus, a monk attending the sick, not obtaining dependence, being requested, to dwell without dependence.” But if the sick monk, even when told by the attendant, “Request me,” does not request out of conceit, the attendant must depart.

“Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, āraññikena bhikkhunā phāsuvihāraṃ sallakkhentena nissayaṃ alabhamānena anissitena vatthuṃ ‘yadā patirūpo nissayadāyako āgacchissati, tadā tassa nissāya vasissāmī’”ti vacanato pana yattha vasantassa samathavipassanānaṃ paṭilābhavasena phāsu hoti, tādisaṃ phāsuvihāraṃ sallakkhentena nissayaṃ alabhamānena anissitena vatthabbaṃ. Imañca pana parihāraṃ neva sotāpanno, na sakadāgāmianāgāmiarahanto labhanti, na thāmagatassa [V 0.0163] samādhino vā vipassanāya vā lābhī, vissaṭṭhakammaṭṭhāne pana bālaputhujjane kathāva natthi. Yassa kho pana samatho vā vipassanā vā taruṇā hoti, ayaṃ imaṃ parihāraṃ labhati, pavāraṇāsaṅgahopi etasseva anuññāto. Tasmā iminā puggalena ācariye pavāretvā gatepi “yadā patirūponissayadāyako āgacchissati, taṃ nissāya vasissāmī”ti ābhogaṃ katvā puna yāva āsāḷhīpuṇṇamā, tāva anissitena vatthuṃ vaṭṭati. Sace pana āsāḷhīmāse ācariyo nāgacchati, yattha nissayo labbhati, tattha gantabbaṃ.

“I allow, monks, a forest-dwelling monk who, considering a comfortable dwelling, cannot obtain dependence, to dwell without dependence, thinking, ‘When a suitable giver of dependence arrives, I will live in dependence on him.’” Because of this statement, one who, considering a comfortable dwelling where ease is found through the attainment of serenity and insight, cannot obtain dependence, should dwell without dependence. However, this allowance is not obtained by a stream-enterer, a once-returner, a non-returner, or an Arahant, nor by one who has obtained concentration or insight that has reached a state of strength; as for a foolish worldling who has abandoned his meditation subject, there is nothing to be said. But a person whose serenity or insight is still tender obtains this allowance; the inclusion in the Pavāraṇā is also permitted for him alone. Therefore, even if the teacher has departed after having invited correction, it is proper for such a person, having made the intention, ‘When a suitable giver of dependence arrives, I will live in dependence on him,’ to dwell again without dependence until the full moon of Āsāḷhī. But if the teacher does not arrive in the month of Āsāḷhī, one must go where dependence can be obtained.

153. Kathaṃ [M 0.0171] gahito hotīti ettha upajjhāyassa santike tāva upajjhaṃ gaṇhantena ekaṃsaṃ uttarāsaṅgaṃ karitvā pāde vanditvā ukkuṭikaṃ nisīditvā añjaliṃ paggahetvā “upajjhāyo me, bhante, hohī”ti tikkhattuṃ vattabbaṃ. Evaṃ saddhivihārikena vutte sace upajjhāyo “sāhū”ti vā “lahū”ti vā “opāyika”nti vā “patirūpa”nti vā “pāsādikena sampādehī”ti vā kāyena viññāpeti, vācāya viññāpeti, kāyena vācāya viññāpeti, gahito hoti upajjhāyo. Idameva hettha upajjhāyaggahaṇaṃ, yadidaṃ upajjhāyassa imesu pañcasu padesu yassa kassaci padassa vācāya sāvanaṃ kāyena vā atthaviññāpananti. Keci pana “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchanaṃ sandhāya vadanti, na taṃ pamāṇaṃ. Āyācanadānamattena hi gahito hoti upajjhāyo, na ettha sampaṭicchanaṃ aṅgaṃ. Saddhivihārikenapi na kevalaṃ “iminā me padena upajjhāyo gahito”ti ñātuṃ vaṭṭati, “ajjatagge dāni thero mayhaṃ bhāro, ahampi therassa bhāro”ti idampi ñātuṃ vaṭṭati (mahāva. aṭṭha. 64). Vuttañhetaṃ –

153. How is a preceptor taken? Here, first, one who is taking a preceptor in the presence of the preceptor should arrange his upper robe over one shoulder, pay homage at the feet, sit squatting, raise his joined palms, and say three times: 'Venerable sir, be my preceptor.' When the co-resident has spoken thus, if the preceptor makes it known by body, or makes it known by speech, or makes it known by both body and speech, by saying 'Good,' or 'It is not a burden,' or 'It is my responsibility,' or 'It is fitting,' or 'Accomplish it with inspiring confidence,' then the preceptor is taken. This indeed is the taking of a preceptor here: that is, the making heard by speech of any of these five phrases from the preceptor, or the making known of the meaning by body. Some, however, speak with reference to acceptance by saying 'Good,' but that is not the standard. For the preceptor is taken merely by the act of requesting and giving; acceptance is not a factor here. It is not sufficient for the co-resident to know only, 'The preceptor has been taken by me with this phrase'; it is also proper to know this: 'From today onwards, the elder is my responsibility, and I too am the elder’s responsibility.' For it is said:

“Upajjhāyo, bhikkhave, saddhivihārikamhi puttacittaṃ upaṭṭhapessati, saddhivihāriko upajjhāyamhi pitucittaṃ upaṭṭhapessati, evaṃ te aññamaññaṃ sagāravā sappatissā sabhāgavuttino viharantā imasmiṃ dhammavinaye vuḍḍhiṃ virūḷhiṃ vepullaṃ āpajjissantī”ti (mahāva. 65).

“Monks, the preceptor should maintain the attitude of a son towards the co-resident, and the co-resident should maintain the attitude of a father towards the preceptor. Thus, dwelling with mutual respect, deference, and concordant practice, they will attain growth, development, and abundance in this Dhamma and Discipline.”

Ācariyassa santike nissayaggahaṇepi ayameva vinicchayo. Ayaṃ panettha viseso – ācariyassa santike nissayaṃ gaṇhantena ukkuṭikaṃ nisīditvā “ācariyo me, bhante, hohi, āyasmato nissāya vacchāmī”ti (mahāva. 77) tikkhattuṃ vattabbaṃ, sesaṃ vuttanayameva.

The same principle applies to taking dependence in the presence of a teacher. The difference here is this: when taking dependence in the presence of a teacher, one should sit squatting and say three times: “Venerable sir, be my teacher; I will live in dependence on the venerable one.” The rest is as stated before.

154. Kathaṃ [V 0.0164] paṭippassambhatīti ettha tāva upajjhāyamhā pañcahākārehi nissayapaṭippassaddhi veditabbā, ācariyamhā chahi ākārehi. Vuttañhetaṃ –

154. How does it cease? Here, first, the cessation of dependence from the preceptor should be known by five modes, and from the teacher by six modes. For this was said:

“Pañcimā, bhikkhave, nissayapaṭippassaddhiyo upajjhāyamhā. Upajjhāyo pakkanto vā hoti, vibbhanto vā, kālakato vā, pakkhasaṅkanto vā, āṇattiyeva pañcamī. Imā kho, bhikkhave, pañca nissayapaṭippassaddhiyo upajjhāyamhā.

“Monks, these are the five cessations of dependence from the preceptor: the preceptor has departed, or has disrobed, or has died, or has gone over to another faction; the command is the fifth. These, indeed, monks, are the five cessations of dependence from the preceptor.

Chayimā[M 0.0172], bhikkhave, nissayapaṭippassaddhiyo ācariyamhā. Ācariyo pakkanto vā hoti, vibbhanto vā, kālakato vā, pakkhasaṅkanto vā, āṇattiyeva pañcamī, upajjhāyena vā samodhānagato hoti. Imā kho, bhikkhave, cha nissayapaṭippassaddhiyo ācariyamhā”ti (mahāva. 83).

“Monks, these are the six cessations of dependence from a teacher: the teacher has departed, or has disrobed, or has died, or has gone over to another faction; the command is the fifth, or he has been united with the preceptor. These, indeed, monks, are the six cessations of dependence from a teacher.”

Tatrāyaṃ vinicchayo (mahāva. aṭṭha. 83) – pakkantoti disaṃ gato. Evaṃ gate ca pana tasmiṃ sace vihāre nissayadāyako atthi, yassa santike aññadāpi nissayo vā gahitapubbo hoti, yo vā ekasambhogaparibhogo, tassa santike nissayo gahetabbo, ekadivasampi parihāro natthi. Sace tādiso natthi, añño lajjī pesalo atthi, tassa pesalabhāvaṃ jānantena tadaheva nissayo yācitabbo. Sace deti, iccetaṃ kusalaṃ. Atha pana “tumhākaṃ upajjhāyo lahuṃ āgamissatī”ti pucchati, upajjhāyena ce tathā vuttaṃ, “āma, bhante”ti vattabbaṃ. Sace vadati “tena hi upajjhāyassa āgamanaṃ āgamethā”ti, vaṭṭati. Atha panassa pakatiyā pesalabhāvaṃ na jānāti, cattāri pañca divasāni tassa bhikkhussa sabhāgataṃ oloketvā okāsaṃ kāretvā nissayo gahetabbo. Sace pana vihāre nissayadāyako natthi, upajjhāyo ca “ahaṃ katipāhena āgamissāmi, mā ukkaṇṭhitthā”ti vatvā gato, yāva āgamanā parihāro labbhati, athāpi naṃ tattha manussā paricchinnakālato uttaripi pañca vā dasa vā divasāni vāsentiyeva, tena vihāraṃ pavatti pesetabbā “daharā mā ukkaṇṭhantu, ahaṃ asukadivasaṃ nāma āgamissāmī”ti, evampi parihāro labbhati. Atha āgacchato antarāmagge nadīpūrena vā corādīhi vā upaddavo hoti, thero udakosakkanaṃ vā āgameti, sahāye vā pariyesati, taṃ ce pavattiṃ daharā suṇanti, yāva āgamanā parihāro labbhati. Sace pana so “idhevāhaṃ vasissāmī”ti pahiṇati, parihāro natthi. Yattha nissayo labbhati, tattha gantabbaṃ. Vibbhante pana kālakate pakkhasaṅkante vā ekadivasampi parihāro natthi, yattha nissayo labbhati, tattha gantabbaṃ.

Herein is the determination (Mahāva. Aṭṭha. 83): 'Pakkanto' means gone to another region. When he has thus gone, if there is a giver of dependence in the monastery from whom one has previously taken dependence, or with whom one has common communion and use of requisites, dependence should be taken from him; there is no exemption even for a single day. If there is no such person, but there is another conscientious and amiable monk, knowing his amiable nature, one should request dependence from him on that very day. If he grants it, that is proper. But if he asks, 'Will your preceptor return soon?' and the preceptor has said so, one should reply, 'Yes, venerable sir.' If he says, 'Well then, wait for the preceptor’s return,' it is allowable. But if one does not know his natural amiable nature, one should observe that monk's good character for four or five days, create an opportunity, and then take dependence. But if there is no giver of dependence in the monastery, and the preceptor has gone after saying, 'I will return in a few days, do not be distressed,' an exemption is granted until his return. And if the people there have him stay for five or ten days even beyond the appointed time, he should send news to the monastery: 'Let the junior monks not be distressed, I will return on such-and-such a day.' Even in this case, an exemption is granted. Or if, while he is returning, there is a danger on the way from a flooded river or from thieves and so on, and the elder waits for the water to subside or seeks companions, and if the junior monks hear that news, an exemption is granted until his arrival. But if he sends word, 'I will live right here,' there is no exemption. One must go where dependence is obtainable. If he has disrobed, died, or gone over to another sect, there is no exemption even for a single day; one must go where dependence is obtainable.

Āṇattīti [M 0.0173][V 0.0165] pana nissayapaṇāmanā vuccati, tasmā “paṇāmemi ta”nti vā “mā idha paṭikkamī”ti vā “nīhara te pattacīvara”nti vā “nāhaṃ tayā upaṭṭhāpetabbo”ti vāti iminā pāḷinayena “mā maṃ gāmappavesanaṃ āpucchī”tiādinā pāḷimuttakanayena vā yo nissayapaṇāmanāya paṇāmito hoti, tena upajjhāyo khamāpetabbo. Sace āditova na khamati, daṇḍakammaṃ āharitvā tikkhattuṃ tāva sayameva khamāpetabbo. No ce khamati, tasmiṃ vihāre mahāthere gahetvā khamāpetabbo. No ce khamati, sāmantavihāre bhikkhū gahetvā khamāpetabbo. Sace evampi na khamati, aññattha gantvā upajjhāyassa sabhāgānaṃ santike vasitabbaṃ “appeva nāma ‘sabhāgānaṃ me santike vasatī’ti ñatvāpi khameyyā”ti. Sace evampi na khamati, tatreva vasitabbaṃ. Tatra ce dubbhikkhādidosena na sakkā hoti vasituṃ, taṃyeva vihāraṃ āgantvā aññassa santike nissayaṃ gahetvā vasituṃ vaṭṭati. Ayamāṇattiyaṃ vinicchayo.

Now, `āṇatti` is called the dismissal from dependence. Therefore, a resident pupil who has been dismissed from dependence, either by this method in the Pāḷi text, such as, 'I dismiss you,' or 'Do not enter here,' or 'Take out your bowl and robe,' or 'I am not to be attended by you,' or by a method not in the Pāḷi text, beginning with, 'Do not ask me for permission to enter the village'—that pupil must ask his preceptor for forgiveness. If from the very beginning he does not forgive, having undertaken a penance, he should ask for forgiveness by himself up to three times. If he still does not forgive, he should ask for forgiveness in the presence of the great elders in that monastery. If he still does not forgive, he should ask for forgiveness in the presence of the monks in a nearby monastery. If even then he does not forgive, he should go elsewhere and live in the presence of his preceptor's peers, thinking, 'Perhaps, upon knowing that I am living in the presence of his peers, he might forgive.' If even then he does not forgive, he should remain living there. If it is not possible to live there due to a fault such as famine, it is allowable for him to return to that same monastery and live, having taken dependence from another. This is the determination regarding `āṇatti`.

Ācariyamhā nissayapaṭippassaddhīsu ācariyo pakkanto vā hotīti ettha koci ācariyo āpucchitvā pakkamati, koci anāpucchitvā, antevāsikopi evameva. Tatra sace antevāsiko ācariyaṃ āpucchati “asukaṃ nāma, bhante, ṭhānaṃ gantuṃ icchāmi kenacideva karaṇīyenā”ti, ācariyena ca “kadā gamissasī”ti vutto “sāyanhe vā rattiṃ vā uṭṭhahitvā gamissāmī”ti vadati, ācariyopi “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchati, taṃ khaṇaṃyeva nissayo paṭippassambhati. Sace pana “bhante, asukaṃ nāma ṭhānaṃ gantukāmomhī”ti vutte ācariyo “asukasmiṃ nāma gāme piṇḍāya caritvā pacchā jānissasī”ti vadati, so ca “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchati, tato ce gato sugato. Sace pana na gacchati, nissayo na paṭippassambhati. Athāpi “gacchāmī”ti vutte ācariyena “mā tāva gaccha, rattiṃ mantetvā jānissāmā”ti vutto mantetvā gacchati, sugato. No ce gacchati, nissayo na paṭippassambhati. Ācariyaṃ anāpucchā pakkamantassa pana upacārasīmātikkame nissayo paṭippassambhati, antoupacārasīmato paṭinivattantassa na paṭippassambhati. Sace pana ācariyo antevāsikaṃ āpucchati “āvuso, asukaṃ nāma ṭhānaṃ gamissāmī”ti, antevāsikena ca “kadā”ti [M 0.0174] vutte “sāyanhe vā rattibhāge vā”ti vadati, antevāsikopi “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchati, taṃ khaṇaṃyeva nissayo paṭippassambhati, sace pana ācariyo “sve piṇḍāya caritvā gamissāmī”ti vadati, itaro ca “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchati, ekadivasaṃ tāva nissayo na paṭippassambhati, punadivase paṭippassaddho hoti. “Asukasmiṃ nāma gāme piṇḍāya caritvā jānissāmi mama gamanaṃ vā agamanaṃ vā”ti vatvā [V 0.0166] pana sace na gacchati, nissayo na paṭippassambhati. Athāpi “gacchāmī”ti vutte antevāsikena “mā tāva gacchatha, rattiṃ mantetvā jānissathā”ti vutto mantetvāpi na gacchati, nissayo na paṭippassambhati. Sace ubhopi ācariyantevāsikā kenacideva karaṇīyena bahisīmaṃ gacchanti, tato ce ācariyo gamiyacitte uppanne anāpucchāva gantvā dvinnaṃ leḍḍupātānaṃ antoyeva nivattati, nissayo na paṭippassambhati. Sace dve leḍḍupāte atikkamitvā nivattati, paṭippassaddho hoti. Ācariyupajjhāyā dve leḍḍupāte atikkamma aññasmiṃ vihāre vasanti, nissayo paṭippassambhati. Ācariye vibbhante kālakate pakkhasaṅkante ca taṃ khaṇaṃyeva paṭippassambhati.

In the cases of the cessation of dependence from a teacher: Herein, some teachers depart after informing, some depart without informing; the pupil is also just the same. Among them, if the pupil informs the teacher, saying, 'Venerable sir, I wish to go to such-and-such a place for some business,' and when asked by the teacher, 'When will you go?' the pupil replies, 'I will go in the evening or at night, having arisen,' and the teacher also accepts with 'Good,' the dependence ceases at that very moment. But if, when it is said, 'Venerable sir, I am desirous of going to such-and-such a place,' the teacher says, 'After going for alms in such-and-such a village, you will know afterwards,' and he accepts with 'Good,' then if he goes after that, it is a good going. But if he does not go, the dependence does not cease. Furthermore, if when he says, 'I will go,' he is told by the teacher, 'Do not go yet; having consulted at night, we will know,' and having consulted, he goes, it is a good going. If he does not go, the dependence does not cease. For one who departs without informing the teacher, the dependence ceases upon crossing the precinct boundary; for one who turns back from within the precinct boundary, it does not cease. But if the teacher informs the pupil, saying, 'Friend, I will go to such-and-such a place,' and when asked by the pupil, 'When?' he says, 'In the evening or in a part of the night,' and the pupil also accepts with 'Good,' the dependence ceases at that very moment. But if the teacher says, 'I will go tomorrow after going for alms,' and the other accepts with 'Good,' the dependence does not cease for one day; on the next day, it is ceased. But having said, 'After going for alms in such-and-such a village, I will know of my going or not going,' if he does not go, the dependence does not cease. Furthermore, if when he says, 'I will go,' he is told by the pupil, 'Do not go yet; having consulted at night, you will know,' and even having consulted, he does not go, the dependence does not cease. If both teacher and pupil go outside the boundary for some business, and if from there, upon a mind desirous of traveling arising, the teacher departs without informing and returns from within the distance of two clod-throws, the dependence does not cease. If, having crossed two clod-throws, he returns, it is ceased. If teachers and preceptors, having crossed two clod-throws, dwell in another monastery, the dependence ceases. When the teacher has become deranged, has passed away, or has gone over to another sect, the dependence ceases at that very moment.

Āṇattiyaṃ pana ācariyo muñcitukāmova hutvā nissayapaṇāmanāya paṇāmeti, antevāsiko ca “kiñcāpi maṃ ācariyo paṇāmeti, atha kho hadayena muduko”ti sālayo hoti, nissayo na paṭippassambhati. Sacepi āriyo sālayo, antevāsiko nirālayo “na dāni imaṃ nissāya vasissāmī”ti dhuraṃ nikkhipati, evampi na paṭippassambhati. Ubhinnaṃ sālayabhāve pana na paṭippassambhatiyeva, ubhinnaṃ dhuranikkhepena paṭippassambhati, paṇāmitena daṇḍakammaṃ āharitvā tikkhattuṃ khamāpetabbo. No ce khamati, upajjhāye vuttanayena paṭipajjitabbaṃ. Yathāpaññattaṃ pana ācariyupajjhāyavattaṃ paripūrentaṃ adhimattapemādipañcaṅgasamannāgataṃ antevāsikaṃ saddhivihārikaṃ vā paṇāmentassa dukkaṭaṃ, itaraṃ apaṇāmentassapi dukkaṭameva. Vuttañhetaṃ –

However, in the case of dismissal, a teacher, wishing to release the pupil, dismisses by means of dismissing the dependence. If the pupil, thinking, 'Although the teacher dismisses me, he is nevertheless gentle at heart,' remains affectionate, the dependence does not cease. And if the teacher is affectionate, but the pupil is unaffectionate and lays down the burden, thinking, 'I will no longer live in dependence on this teacher,' even so it does not cease. When there is affection on the part of both, it certainly does not cease; it ceases by the laying down of the burden by both. The dismissed pupil, having carried out the disciplinary action, should ask for forgiveness three times. If the teacher does not forgive, one should proceed in the manner stated regarding the preceptor. However, for a teacher or preceptor who dismisses a pupil or co-resident who is fulfilling the duties towards the teacher and preceptor as prescribed and is endowed with the five factors beginning with excessive affection, there is an offense of wrong-doing. For not dismissing the other, there is also an offense of wrong-doing. For it has been said:

“Na, bhikkhave, sammāvattanto paṇāmetabbo, yo paṇāmeyya, āpatti dukkaṭassa. Na ca, bhikkhave, asammāvattanto na paṇāmetabbo, yo na paṇāmeyya, āpatti dukkaṭassa (mahāva. 80).

“Monks, a pupil who is behaving rightly should not be dismissed. Whoever should dismiss one commits an offense of wrong-doing. And, monks, it is not that a pupil who is not behaving rightly should not be dismissed; he should indeed be dismissed. Whoever should not dismiss one commits an offense of wrong-doing.”

“Pañcahi[M 0.0175], bhikkhave, aṅgehi samannāgataṃ antevāsikaṃ apaṇāmento ācariyo sātisāro hoti, paṇāmento anatisāro hoti. Ācariyamhi nādhimattaṃ pemaṃ hoti, nādhimatto pasādo hoti, nādhimattā hirī hoti, nādhimatto gāravo hoti, nādhimattā bhāvanā hoti. Imehi kho, bhikkhave, pañcahaṅgehi samannāgataṃ antevāsikaṃ apaṇāmento ācariyo sātisāro hoti, paṇāmento anatisāro hoti (mahāva. 81).

“Monks, a teacher who does not dismiss a pupil endowed with five factors is at fault; one who dismisses him is not at fault. There is not excessive affection for the teacher, there is not excessive confidence, there is not excessive shame, there is not excessive respect, there is not excessive cultivation. Indeed, monks, a teacher who does not dismiss a pupil endowed with these five factors is at fault; one who dismisses him is not at fault.”

“Pañcahi[V 0.0167], bhikkhave, aṅgehi samannāgataṃ saddhivihārikaṃ apaṇāmento upajjhāyo sātisāro hoti, paṇāmento anatisāro hoti. Upajjhāyamhi nādhimattaṃ pemaṃ hoti, nādhimatto pasādo hoti, nādhimattā hirī hoti, nādhimatto gāravo hoti, nādhimattā bhāvanā hoti. Imehi kho, bhikkhave, pañcahaṅgehi samannāgataṃ saddhivihārikaṃ apaṇāmento upajjhāyo sātisāro hoti, paṇāmento anatisāro hotī”tiādi (mahāva. 68).

“Bhikkhus, a preceptor who does not dismiss a co-resident pupil endowed with five factors is at fault; one who dismisses him is not at fault. There is no excessive affection for the preceptor, no excessive confidence, no excessive moral shame, no excessive respect, no excessive development. Indeed, bhikkhus, a preceptor who does not dismiss a co-resident pupil endowed with these five factors is at fault; one who dismisses him is not at fault.”

Tattha (mahāva. aṭṭha. 68) nādhimattaṃ pemaṃ hotīti upajjhāyamhi adhimattaṃ gehassitapemaṃ na hoti. Nādhimattā bhāvanā hotīti adhimattā mettābhāvanā na hotīti attho.

Therein, the meaning of the phrase ‘there is no excessive affection’ should be understood thus: there is no excessive household-based affection for the preceptor. The meaning of the phrase ‘there is no excessive development’ should be understood thus: there is no excessive development of loving-kindness.

Upajjhāyena vā samodhānagatoti ettha (mahāva. aṭṭha. 83) dassanasavanavasena samodhānaṃ veditabbaṃ. Sace hi ācariyaṃ nissāya vasanto saddhivihāriko ekavihāre cetiyaṃ vā vandantaṃ, ekagāme vā piṇḍāya carantaṃ upajjhāyaṃ passati, nissayo paṭippassambhati. Upajjhāyo passati, saddhivihāriko na passati, na paṭippassambhati. Maggappaṭipannaṃ vā ākāsena vā gacchantaṃ upajjhāyaṃ disvā dūrattā “bhikkhū”ti jānāti, “upajjhāyo”ti na jānāti, na paṭippassambhati. Sace jānāti, paṭippassambhati. Uparipāsāde upajjhāyo vasati, heṭṭhā saddhivihāriko, taṃ adisvāva yāguṃ pivitvā paṭikkamati, āsanasālāya vā nisinnaṃ adisvāva ekamante bhuñjitvā pakkamati, dhammassavanamaṇḍape vā nisinnampi [M 0.0176] taṃ adisvāva dhammaṃ sutvā pakkamati, nissayo na paṭippassambhati. Evaṃ tāva dassanavasena samodhānaṃ veditabbaṃ. Savanavasena pana sace upajjhāyassa vihāre vā antaraghare vā dhammaṃ vā kathentassa anumodanaṃ vā karontassa saddaṃ sutvā “upajjhāyassa me saddo”ti sañjānāti, nissayo paṭippassambhati, asañjānantassa na paṭippassambhati. Ayaṃ samodhāne vinicchayo.

Here, 'associated with the preceptor' should be understood as association by way of seeing and hearing. If, for instance, a resident pupil living in dependence on a teacher sees the preceptor in the same monastery worshipping a shrine, or walking for alms in the same village, the dependence is suspended. If the preceptor sees, but the resident pupil does not see, the dependence is not suspended. If one sees the preceptor walking on a road or going through the air, but due to distance recognizes him only as 'a bhikkhu' and not as 'my preceptor,' the dependence is not suspended. But if one recognizes him, the dependence is suspended. If the preceptor is staying on an upper story and the resident pupil below, without seeing him, drinks gruel and departs; or without seeing him seated in the assembly hall, eats in a secluded spot and leaves; or without seeing him even when seated in the Dhamma-hearing pavilion, listens to the Dhamma and departs—in these cases, the dependence is not suspended. Thus, association by way of seeing should be understood. As for association by way of hearing: if, while in the monastery or inside a house, one hears the preceptor speaking the Dhamma or giving a blessing, and recognizes it as 'my preceptor’s voice,' the dependence is suspended. If one does not recognize it, the dependence is not suspended. This is the determination regarding association.

155. Nissāya kena vasitabbaṃ, kena na vasitabbanti ettha pana “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, byattena bhikkhunā paṭibalena pañca vassāni nissāya vatthuṃ, abyattena yāvajīva”nti (mahāva. 103) vacanato yo abyatto hoti, tena yāvajīvaṃ nissāyeva vasitabbaṃ. Sacāyaṃ (mahāva. aṭṭha. 103) vuḍḍhataraṃ ācariyaṃ na labhati, upasampadāya saṭṭhivasso vā sattativasso vā hoti, navakatarassapi byattassa santike ukkuṭikaṃ nisīditvā añjaliṃ paggahetvā “ācariyo me, āvuso, hoti, āyasmato nissāya vacchāmī”ti [V 0.0168] evaṃ tikkhattuṃ vatvā nissayo gahetabbova. Gāmappavesanaṃ āpucchantenapi ukkuṭikaṃ nisīditvā añjaliṃ paggahetvā “gāmappavesanaṃ āpucchāmi ācariyā”ti vattabbaṃ. Esa nayo sabbaāpucchanesu.

155. Here, as for by whom one should live in dependence and by whom one should not, it is said: “Bhikkhus, I allow a competent and capable bhikkhu to live in dependence for five years; for an incompetent one, for life.” Therefore, a bhikkhu who is incompetent must live in dependence for life. If such a bhikkhu does not find a more senior teacher, even if he is sixty or seventy years since his higher ordination, he must take dependence from even a more junior but competent bhikkhu, having sat down in the squatting posture, raised his hands in reverence, and said three times: “Venerable, be my teacher; I will live in dependence on the venerable one.” When asking leave to enter a village, one should also sit down in the squatting posture, raise one's hands in reverence, and say: “Teacher, I ask leave to enter the village.” This is the method for all instances of asking leave.

Yo pana byatto hoti upasampadāya pañcavasso, tena anissitena vatthuṃ vaṭṭati. Tasmā nissayamuccanakena (pāci. aṭṭha. 145-147) upasampadāya pañcavassena sabbantimena paricchedena dve mātikā paguṇā vācuggatā kattabbā, pakkhadivasesu dhammassavanatthāya suttantato cattāro bhāṇavārā, sampattānaṃ parisānaṃ parikathanatthāya andhakavinda(a. ni. 5.114) mahārāhulovāda(ma. ni. 2.113 ādayo) ambaṭṭha(daī. ni. 1.254 ādayo) sadiso eko kathāmaggo, saṅghabhattamaṅgalāmaṅgalesu anumodanatthāya tisso anumodanā, uposathapavāraṇādijānanatthaṃ kammākammavinicchayo, samaṇadhammakaraṇatthaṃ samādhivasena vā vipassanāvasena vā arahattapariyosānamekaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ, ettakaṃ uggahetabbaṃ. Ettāvatā hi ayaṃ bahussuto hoti cātuddiso, yattha katthaci attano issariyena vasituṃ labhati. Yaṃ pana vuttaṃ –

But a bhikkhu who is competent and is of five years' standing from his higher ordination is allowed to live without dependence. Therefore, a bhikkhu who is to be released from dependence, being of five years' standing from his higher ordination, must, as a bare minimum, make the two Mātikās fluent and learn them by heart. For the purpose of listening to the Dhamma on the observance days of the fortnight, four recitation sections from the Suttanta should be learned. For the purpose of discoursing to assemblies that have gathered, one line of discourse similar to the Andhakavinda, the Mahārāhulovāda, or the Ambaṭṭha should be learned. For the purpose of giving a blessing at Sangha-meals and on auspicious and inauspicious occasions, three types of blessings should be learned. For the purpose of knowing the Uposatha, Pavāraṇā, and so forth, the determination of what is a formal act and what is not a formal act should be learned. For the purpose of practicing the recluse's duties, one meditation subject culminating in Arahantship, either by way of concentration or by way of insight, should be learned. This much should be learned. For by this much, this person becomes very learned and unrestricted in the four directions; he is able to live wherever he pleases by his own authority. But as it was said—

“Pañcahi[M 0.0177], bhikkhave, aṅgehi samannāgatena bhikkhunā na anissitena vatthabbaṃ. Na asekkhena sīlakkhandhena samannāgato hoti, na asekkhena samādhikkhandhena… na asekkhena paññākkhandhena… na asekkhena vimuttikkhandhena… na asekkhena vimuttiñāṇadassanakkhandhena samannāgato hoti. Imehi kho, bhikkhave, pañcahaṅgehi samannāgatena bhikkhunā na anissitena vatthabbaṃ.

“Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu endowed with five factors should not live without dependence. He is not endowed with the aggregate of an adept's virtue; he is not endowed with the aggregate of an adept's concentration; he is not endowed with the aggregate of an adept's wisdom; he is not endowed with the aggregate of an adept's liberation; he is not endowed with the aggregate of an adept's knowledge and vision of liberation. Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu endowed with these five factors should not live without dependence.

“Aparehipi, bhikkhave, pañcahaṅgehi samannāgatena bhikkhunā na anissitena vatthabbaṃ. Assaddho hoti, ahiriko hoti, anottappī hoti, kusīto hoti, muṭṭhassati hoti. Imehi kho, bhikkhave, pañcahaṅgehi samannāgatena bhikkhunā na anissitena vatthabbaṃ.

“Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu endowed with another five factors should not live without dependence. He is faithless, shameless, without fear of wrongdoing, lazy, and of confused mindfulness. Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu endowed with these five factors should not live without dependence.

“Aparehipi, bhikkhave, pañcahaṅgehi samannāgatena bhikkhunā na anissitena vatthabbaṃ. Adhisīle sīlavipanno hoti, ajjhācāre ācāravipanno hoti, atidiṭṭhiyā diṭṭhivipanno hoti, appassuto hoti, duppañño hoti. Imehi kho, bhikkhave, pañcahaṅgehi samannāgatena bhikkhunā na anissitena vatthabbaṃ.

“Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu endowed with another five factors should not live without dependence. He is corrupt in higher virtue, corrupt in conduct, corrupt in view, has learned little, and is unwise. Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu endowed with these five factors should not live without dependence.

“Aparehipi[V 0.0169], bhikkhave, pañcahaṅgehi samannāgatena bhikkhunā na anissitena vatthabbaṃ. Āpattiṃ na jānāti, anāpattiṃ na jānāti, lahukaṃ āpattiṃ na jānāti, garukaṃ āpattiṃ na jānāti, ubhayāni kho panassa pātimokkhāni vitthārena na svāgatāni honti na suvibhattāni na suppavattīni na suvinicchitāni suttaso anubyañjanaso. Imehi kho, bhikkhave, pañcahaṅgehi samannāgatena bhikkhunā na anissitena vatthabbaṃ.

“Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu endowed with another five factors should not live without dependence. He does not know an offense, does not know what is not an offense, does not know a light offense, and does not know a heavy offense; and for this bhikkhu the two Pātimokkhas are not well-learned in detail, not well-analyzed, not well-mastered, and not well-decided upon rule by rule and phrase by phrase. Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu endowed with these five factors should not live without dependence.”

“Aparehipi, bhikkhave, pañcahaṅgehi samannāgatena bhikkhunā na anissitena vatthabbaṃ. Āpattiṃ na jānāti, anāpattiṃ na jānāti, lahukaṃ āpattiṃ na jānāti, garukaṃ āpattiṃ na jānāti, ūnapañcavasso hoti. Imehi kho, bhikkhave, pañcahaṅgehi samannāgatena bhikkhunā na anissitena vatthabba”nti (mahāva. 103). Etthāpi [M 0.0178] purimanayeneva ayuttavasena āpattiaṅgavasena ca paṭikkhepo katoti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

O monks, a monk endowed with another five factors should not live without dependence. He does not know an offense, he does not know what is not an offense, he does not know a light offense, he does not know a serious offense, and he is of less than five vassas. O monks, a monk endowed with these five factors indeed should not live without dependence. Here too, it should be understood that the prohibition is made by the previous method, on the basis of unsuitability and on the basis of the factor of offense.

Bālānaṃ pana abyattānaṃ disaṃgamikānaṃ antevāsikasaddhivihārikānaṃ anuññā na dātabbā. Sace denti, ācariyupajjhāyānaṃ dukkaṭaṃ. Te ce ananuññātā gacchanti, tesampi dukkaṭaṃ. Vuttañhetaṃ –

But permission should not be given to resident pupils and co-residents who are foolish, inexperienced, and going to another region. If they give it, there is a dukkaṭa offense for the teachers and preceptors. And if they go without being permitted, for them too, there is a dukkaṭa offense. For this has been said:

“Idha pana, bhikkhave, sambahulā bhikkhū bālā abyattā disaṃgamikā ācariyupajjhāye āpucchanti. Te, bhikkhave, ācariyupajjhāyehi pucchitabbā “kahaṃ gamissatha, kena saddhiṃ gamissathā”ti. Te ce, bhikkhave, bālā abyattā aññe bāle abyatte apadiseyyuṃ. Na, bhikkhave, ācariyupajjhāyehi anujānitabbā, anujāneyyuṃ ce, āpatti dukkaṭassa. Te ce, bhikkhave, bālā abyattā ananuññātā ācariyupajjhāyehi gaccheyyuṃ ce, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (mahāva. 163).

But here, O monks, many monks who are foolish and inexperienced and are going to another region ask leave of their teachers and preceptors. They, O monks, should be asked by their teachers and preceptors: 'Where will you go? With whom will you go?' If those foolish and inexperienced monks, O monks, should point to other foolish and inexperienced ones, they should not be given permission by their teachers and preceptors. If they should give permission, there is an offense of dukkaṭa. And if those foolish and inexperienced monks, O monks, should go without being permitted by their teachers and preceptors, there is an offense of dukkaṭa.

Iti pāḷimuttakavinayavinicchayasaṅgahe

Thus in the Pāḷimuttakavinayavinicchayasaṅgaha.

Nissayavinicchayakathā samattā.

The Discourse on the Decision Regarding Dependence is concluded.

24. Sīmāvinicchayakathā

24. 24. The Discourse on the Decision Regarding Boundaries

156. Sīmāti [V 0.0170] ettha (kaṅkhā. aṭṭha. nidānavaṇṇanā) sīmā nāmesā baddhasīmā abaddhasīmāti duvidhā hoti. Tattha ekādasa vipattisīmāyo atikkamitvā tividhasampattiyuttā nimittena nimittaṃ bandhitvā sammatā sīmā baddhasīmā nāma. Atikhuddakā, atimahatī, khaṇḍanimittā, chāyānimittā, animittā, bahisīme ṭhitasammatā, nadiyā sammatā, samudde sammatā, jātassare sammatā, sīmāya sīmaṃ sambhindantena sammatā, sīmāya sīmaṃ ajjhottharantena sammatāti imehi ekādasahi ākārehi sīmato kammāni vipajjantīti vacanato etā vipattisīmāyo nāma.

156. Herein (in the Nidāna section of the Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī Aṭṭhakathā), this which is called a sīmā is of two kinds: the established sīmā (baddhasīmā) and the unestablished sīmā (abaddhasīmā). Among these, the sīmā that is consecrated by connecting marker with marker, having avoided the eleven defective sīmās and being endowed with the threefold completeness, is called an established sīmā. The defective sīmās are: one that is too small, too large, with broken markers, with shadows as markers, without markers; one consecrated by those standing outside the sīmā, in a river, in the sea, in a natural lake; one consecrated by joining it with another sīmā; and one consecrated by overlapping another sīmā. Because it was stated, 'By these eleven types, acts from a sīmā are invalidated,' these are called defective sīmās.

Tattha atikhuddakā nāma yattha ekavīsati bhikkhū nisīdituṃ na sakkonti. Atimahatī nāma yā kesaggamattenapi tiyojanaṃ atikkamitvā sammatā. Khaṇḍanimittā [M 0.0179] nāma aghaṭitanimittā vuccati. Puratthimāya disāya nimittaṃ kittetvā anukkamena dakkhiṇāya disāya pacchimāya uttarāya disāya kittetvā puna puratthimāya disāya pubbakittitaṃ paṭikittetvā ṭhapetuṃ vaṭṭati, evaṃ akhaṇḍanimittā hoti. Sace pana anukkamena āharitvā uttarāya disāya nimittaṃ kittetvā tattheva ṭhapeti, khaṇḍanimittā hoti. Aparāpi khaṇḍanimittā nāma yā animittupagaṃ tacasārarukkhaṃ vā khāṇukaṃ vā paṃsupuñjaṃ vā vālukapuñjaṃ vā aññataraṃ antarā ekanimittaṃ katvā sammatā. Chāyānimittā nāma pabbatachāyādīnaṃ yaṃ kiñci chāyaṃ nimittaṃ katvā sammatā. Animittā nāma sabbena sabbaṃ nimittāni akittetvā sammatā. Bahisīme ṭhitasammatā nāma nimittāni kittetvā nimittānaṃ bahi ṭhitena sammatā. Nadiyā, samudde, jātassare sammatā nāma etesu nadiādīsu sammatā. Sā hi evaṃ sammatāpi “sabbā, bhikkhave, nadī asīmā, sabbo samuddo asīmo, sabbo jātassaro asīmo”ti (mahāva. 147) vacanato asammatāva hoti. Sīmāya sīmaṃ sambhindantena sammatā (mahāva. aṭṭha. 148) nāma attano sīmāya paresaṃ sīmaṃ sambhindantena sammatā. Sace hi porāṇakassa vihārassa puratthimāya disāya ambo ceva jambu cāti dve rukkhā aññamaññaṃ saṃsaṭṭhaviṭapā honti, tesu ambassa pacchimadisābhāge jambu, vihārasīmā ca jambuṃ antokatvā ambaṃ kittetvā baddhā hoti. Atha pacchā tassa vihārassa puratthimāya disāya vihāre kate sīmaṃ bandhantā bhikkhū taṃ ambaṃ antokatvā jambuṃ kittetvā bandhanti[V 0.0171], sīmāya sīmaṃ sambhinnā hoti. Tasmā sace paṭhamataraṃ katassa vihārassa sīmā asammatā hoti, sīmāya upacāro ṭhapetabbo. Sace sammatā hoti, pacchimakoṭiyā hatthamattā sīmantarikā ṭhapetabbā. Kurundiyaṃ “vidatthimattampi”, mahāpaccariyaṃ “caturaṅgulamattampi vaṭṭatī”ti vuttaṃ. Ekarukkhopi ca dvinnaṃ sīmānaṃ nimittaṃ hoti. So pana vaḍḍhanto sīmasaṅkaraṃ karoti, tasmā na kātabbo. Sīmāya sīmaṃ ajjhottharantena sammatā nāma attano sīmāya paresaṃ sīmaṃ ajjhottharantena sammatā. Sace hi paresaṃ baddhasīmaṃ sakalaṃ vā tassā padesaṃ vā antokatvā attano sīmaṃ sammannanti, sīmāya sīmaṃ ajjhottharitā nāma hoti. Bhikkhunīnaṃ pana sīmaṃ ajjhottharitvā antopi bhikkhūnaṃ sīmaṃ sammannituṃ vaṭṭati. Bhikkhunīnampi bhikkhūnaṃ sīmāya eseva [M 0.0180] nayo. Na hi te aññamaññassa kamme gaṇapūrakā honti, na kammavācaṃ vaggaṃ karonti. Iti imā ekādasa vipattisīmāyo atikkamitvā sīmā sammannitabbā.

Herein, 'too small' refers to a boundary wherein twenty-one monks cannot sit. 'Too large' refers to a boundary established exceeding three yojanas even by a hair's tip. 'With fragmented markers' is said to be a boundary with unconnected markers. Having announced the marker in the eastern direction, then successively in the southern, western, and northern directions, and then again re-announcing in the eastern direction the marker that was first announced, it is proper to establish it; thus it becomes a boundary with unbroken markers. But if, having proceeded successively, one announces the marker in the northern direction and establishes it right there, it becomes a boundary with fragmented markers. Another type of boundary with fragmented markers is one established by making a single marker in between out of something unsuitable as a marker, such as a tree with its core in the bark, a stump, a heap of earth, or a heap of sand. 'With a shadow as a marker' refers to a boundary established by making any shadow whatsoever, such as that of a mountain, into a marker. 'Without markers' refers to a boundary established without announcing any markers at all. 'Established by one standing outside the boundary' refers to a boundary established by one who is standing outside the markers after they have been announced. 'Established in a river, the ocean, or a natural lake' refers to a boundary established in these places, such as rivers. Indeed, even if so established, it is in fact unestablished because of the statement: 'Monks, every river is not a boundary, every ocean is not a boundary, every natural lake is not a boundary.' 'Established by joining a boundary with a boundary' refers to a boundary established by joining one's own boundary with another's boundary. For if, to the east of an ancient monastery, there are two trees—a mango and a rose apple—with intertwined branches, and the rose apple is to the west of the mango tree, and the monastery boundary was fixed by announcing the mango, having included the rose apple; and then later, when a monastery is built to the east of that monastery, if the monks fixing the boundary fix it by announcing the rose apple, having included that mango, the boundary has been joined with a boundary. Therefore, if the boundary of the first-established monastery is not yet established, a vicinity for the boundary should be left. If it is established, an interval between boundaries of a cubit's length should be left at the final edge. In the Kurundī it is said, 'even a span's length is permissible,' and in the Mahāpaccarī, 'even four finger-breadths are permissible.' Even a single tree can be the marker for two boundaries. However, as it grows, it causes a confusion of boundaries; therefore, it should not be made so. 'Established by overlapping a boundary with a boundary' refers to a boundary established by overlapping another's boundary with one's own boundary. For if they establish their own boundary by including, either entirely or in part, another's fixed boundary, it is called 'overlapping a boundary with a boundary.' However, it is permissible for monks to establish a boundary by overlapping a bhikkhunīs' boundary, even within it. For bhikkhunīs, too, this is the same method with regard to a bhikkhus' boundary. For they do not complete the quorum for each other's formal acts, nor do they render the formal proclamation invalid through factionalism. Thus, having avoided these eleven defective boundaries, a boundary should be established.

157. Tividhasampattiyuttā nāma nimittasampattiyā parisasampattiyā kammavācāsampattiyā ca yuttā. Tattha nimittasampattiyā yuttā nāma pabbatanimittaṃ pāsāṇanimittaṃ vananimittaṃ rukkhanimittaṃ magganimittaṃ vammikanimittaṃ nadīnimittaṃ udakanimittanti evaṃ vuttesu aṭṭhasu nimittesu tasmiṃ tasmiṃ disābhāge yathāladdhāni nimittupagāni nimittāni “puratthimāya disāya kiṃ nimittaṃ. Pabbato, bhante. Eso pabbato nimitta”ntiādinā nayena sammā kittetvā sammatā.

157. A sīmā endowed with threefold completeness is one endowed with completeness of the boundary marker, completeness of the assembly, and completeness of the formal act announcement. Therein, a sīmā endowed with completeness of the boundary marker is a sīmā agreed upon after having correctly proclaimed, by the method beginning with, 'What is the boundary marker in the eastern direction? A mountain, venerable sir. This mountain is the boundary marker,' the boundary markers suitable as such, as they are found in each and every directional area, from among the eight boundary markers thus spoken of: a mountain marker, a rock marker, a forest marker, a tree marker, a road marker, an anthill marker, a river marker, and a water marker.

Tatrāyaṃ vinicchayo (mahāva. aṭṭha. 138) – vinayadharena pucchitabbaṃ “puratthimāya disāya kiṃ nimitta”nti? “Pabbato, bhante”ti. Idaṃ pana upasampanno vā ācikkhatu anupasampanno vā, vaṭṭatiyeva. Puna vinayadharena “eso pabbato nimitta”nti evaṃ nimittaṃ kittetabbaṃ, “etaṃ pabbataṃ nimittaṃ karoma, karissāma, nimittaṃ kato, nimittaṃ hotu, hoti, bhavissatī”ti evaṃ pana kittetuṃ na vaṭṭati. Pāsāṇādīsupi eseva nayo. Puratthimāya disāya, puratthimāya anudisāya, dakkhiṇāya disāya, dakkhiṇāya anudisāya, pacchimāya disāya, pacchimāya anudisāya, uttarāya disāya, uttarāya anudisāya kiṃ nimittaṃ? Udakaṃ, bhante. Etaṃ udakaṃ nimittanti kittetabbaṃ. Ettha pana aṭṭhapetvā puna “puratthimāya disāya kiṃ nimittaṃ? Pabbato, bhante. Eso pabbato nimitta”nti evaṃ paṭhamaṃ kittitanimittaṃ kittetvāva ṭhapetabbaṃ. Evañhi nimittena nimittaṃ ghaṭitaṃ hoti, nimittāni sakiṃ [V 0.0172] kittitānipi kittitāneva honti. Andhakaṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana “tikkhattuṃ sīmamaṇḍalaṃ bandhantena nimittaṃ kittetabba”nti vuttaṃ.

Herein, this is the ascertainment: The Vinaya expert should ask, 'What is the boundary marker in the eastern direction?' It should be said, 'A mountain, venerable sir.' Now, this may be announced by one who is ordained or by one who is not ordained; it is indeed proper. Again, the Vinaya expert should proclaim the boundary marker thus, 'This mountain is the boundary marker.' However, it is not proper to proclaim thus: 'We make this mountain a boundary marker; we will make it; the boundary marker is made; let the boundary marker be; it is; it will be.' This same method applies also to rocks and so forth. For the eastern direction, the south-eastern intermediate direction, the southern direction, the south-western intermediate direction, the western direction, the north-western intermediate direction, the northern direction, and the north-eastern intermediate direction, one should ask, 'What is the boundary marker?' and it should be proclaimed, 'Water, venerable sir. This water is the boundary marker.' Here, however, not concluding there, one should again proclaim the first-proclaimed boundary marker and thus establish it, saying, 'What is the boundary marker in the eastern direction? A mountain, venerable sir. This mountain is the boundary marker.' For only in this way is a boundary marker connected with a boundary marker. And even if the boundary markers are proclaimed only once, they are indeed considered proclaimed. In the Andhakaṭṭhakathā, however, it is said: 'The boundary marker should be proclaimed three times by one connecting the sīmā-circle.'

158. Idāni nimittupagāni pabbatādīni veditabbāni – tividho pabbato suddhapaṃsupabbato suddhapāsāṇapabbato ubhayamissakoti. So tividhopi vaṭṭati, vālikarāsi pana na vaṭṭati. Itaropi hatthippamāṇato omakataro na vaṭṭati, hatthippamāṇato paṭṭhāya sineruppamāṇopi vaṭṭati. Sace catūsu disāsu cattāro tīsu vā tayo pabbatā honti[M 0.0181], catūhi vā tīhi vā pabbatanimittehi sammannitumpi vaṭṭati, dvīhi pana nimittehi ekena vā sammannituṃ na vaṭṭati. Ito paresu pāsāṇanimittādīsupi eseva nayo. Tasmā pabbatanimittaṃ karontena pucchitabbaṃ “ekābaddho, na ekābaddho”ti. Sace ekābaddho hoti, na kātabbo. Tañhi catūsu vā aṭṭhasu vā disāsu kittentenapi ekameva nimittaṃ kittitaṃ hoti, tasmā yo evaṃ cakkasaṇṭhānena vihārampi parikkhipitvā ṭhito pabbato, taṃ ekadisāya kittetvā aññāsu disāsu taṃ bahiddhā katvā anto aññāni nimittāni kittetabbāni. Sace pabbatassa tatiyabhāgaṃ vā upaḍḍhaṃ vā antosīmāya kattukāmā honti, pabbataṃ akittetvā yattakaṃ padesaṃ anto kattukāmā, tassa parato tasmiṃyeva pabbate jātarukkhavammikādīsu aññataraṃ nimittaṃ kittetabbaṃ. Sace ekayojanadviyojanappamāṇaṃ sabbaṃ pabbataṃ anto kattukāmā honti, pabbatassa parato bhūmiyaṃ jātarukkhavammikādīni nimittāni kittetabbāni.

158. Now, mountains and so forth, which are suitable as markers, should be understood. A mountain is of three kinds: a mountain of pure earth, a mountain of pure rock, or one of mixed earth and rock. All three types are suitable, but a heap of sand is not suitable. Also, a mountain smaller than the size of an elephant is not suitable; but from the size of an elephant upwards, even one the size of Mount Sineru is suitable. If there are four mountains in the four directions, or three mountains in three directions, it is suitable to designate the boundary with four or three mountain markers. However, it is not suitable to designate it with two markers, or with one. This same principle applies to other markers, such as rock markers and so forth. Therefore, when making a mountain a marker, one should ask, “Is it one continuous mass, or not one continuous mass?” If it is one continuous mass, it should not be made a marker. This is because even when delineating it in four or eight directions, only one single marker is delineated. Therefore, for a mountain that stands encircling the monastery like a wheel, one should delineate it in one direction and, in the other directions, exclude it by delineating other markers inside. If they wish to include a third part or a half of the mountain within the sīmā, without delineating the mountain itself, they should delineate as a marker any one among the trees, anthills, and so forth that have grown on that very mountain beyond the area they wish to include. If they wish to include the entire mountain—measuring one or two yojanas—within the boundary, markers such as trees, anthills, and so forth that have grown on the ground beyond the mountain should be delineated.

Pāsāṇanimitte ayaguḷopi pāsāṇasaṅkhyameva gacchati, tasmā yo koci pāsāṇo vaṭṭati. Pamāṇato pana hatthippamāṇo pabbatasaṅkhyaṃ gato, tasmā so na vaṭṭati, mahāgoṇamahāmahiṃsappamāṇo pana vaṭṭati. Heṭṭhimaparicchedena dvattiṃsapalaguḷapiṇḍappamāṇo vaṭṭati, tato khuddakataro iṭṭhakā vā mahantīpi na vaṭṭati, animittupagapāsāṇānaṃ rāsipi na vaṭṭati, pageva paṃsuvālukarāsi. Bhūmisamo khalamaṇḍalasadiso piṭṭhipāsāṇo vā bhūmito khāṇuko viya uṭṭhitapāsāṇo vā hoti, sopi pamāṇupago ce, vaṭṭati. Piṭṭhipāsāṇo atimahantopi pāsāṇasaṅkhyameva gacchati, tasmā sace mahato piṭṭhipāsāṇassa ekappadesaṃ antosīmāya kattukāmā honti, taṃ akittetvā tassupari añño pāsāṇo kittetabbo. Sace piṭṭhipāsāṇupari vihāraṃ karonti, vihāramajjhena vā piṭṭhipāsāṇo vinivijjhitvā gacchati, evarūpo piṭṭhipāsāṇo na vaṭṭati. Sace hi taṃ kittenti, nimittassa upari vihāro hoti, nimittañca [V 0.0173] nāma bahisīmāya hoti, vihāropi bahisīmāyaṃ āpajjati. Vihāraṃ parikkhipitvā ṭhitapiṭṭhipāsāṇo ekattha kittetvā aññattha na kittetabbo.

Regarding stone markers, even an iron ball is counted as a stone; therefore, any stone is suitable. In terms of size, however, one the size of an elephant is considered a mountain, and thus it is not suitable, but one the size of a large bull or buffalo is suitable. By the lower limit, a stone the size of a jaggery lump of thirty-two pala is suitable; one smaller than that is not suitable. A brick, even a large one, is also not suitable. A heap of stones unsuitable as markers is also not suitable, let alone a pile of earth or sand. A flat stone level with the ground, resembling a threshing floor, or a stone protruding from the ground like a post is also suitable, if it is of sufficient size. A flat stone, even if very large, is still counted as a stone. Therefore, if they wish to make a portion of a large flat stone part of the interior of the sīmā, they should not demarcate that flat stone but should demarcate another stone placed on top of it. If they build a monastery on top of a flat stone, or if the flat stone runs through the middle of the monastery, such a flat stone is not suitable. For if they demarcate it, the monastery would be on top of the marker, and a marker is by definition outside the sīmā; thus the monastery too would fall outside the sīmā. A flat stone that stands encircling a monastery should be demarcated on one side and not on another.

Vananimitte [M 0.0182] tiṇavanaṃ vā tacasāratālanāḷikerādirukkhavanaṃ vā na vaṭṭati, antosārānaṃ pana sākasālādīnaṃ antosāramissakānaṃ vā rukkhānaṃ vanaṃ vaṭṭati, tañca kho heṭṭhimaparicchedena catupañcarukkhamattampi, tato oraṃ na vaṭṭati, paraṃ yojanasatikampi vaṭṭati. Sace pana vanamajjhe vihāraṃ karonti, vanaṃ na kittetabbaṃ. Ekadesaṃ antosīmāya kātukāmehipi vanaṃ akittetvā tattha rukkhapāsāṇādayo kittetabbā. Vihāraṃ parikkhipitvā ṭhitavanaṃ ekattha kittetvā aññattha na kittetabbaṃ.

Regarding forest markers, a grass forest or a forest of trees with exterior heartwood, such as palmyra or coconut trees, is not suitable. However, a forest of trees with interior heartwood, such as teak and sal, or a forest of mixed trees with interior heartwood, is suitable. By the lower limit, even a group of four or five trees is suitable, but fewer than that is not suitable. Above that, even a forest spanning a hundred yojanas is suitable. If, however, they build a monastery in the middle of a forest, the forest should not be demarcated. Even by those who wish to make a portion of it the interior of the sīmā, the forest should not be demarcated; instead, the trees, stones, and so on in that place should be demarcated. A forest that stands encircling a monastery should be demarcated on one side and not on another.

Rukkhanimitte tacasāro tālanāḷikerādirukkho na vaṭṭati, antosāro jīvamānako antamaso ubbedhato aṭṭhaṅgulo pariṇāhato sūcidaṇḍakappamāṇopi vaṭṭati. Tato oraṃ na vaṭṭati, paraṃ dvādasayojano suppatiṭṭhitanigrodhopi vaṭṭati. Vaṃsanaḷakasarāvādīsu bījaṃ ropetvā vaḍḍhāpito pamāṇupagopi na vaṭṭati, tato apanetvā pana taṃ khaṇampi bhūmiyaṃ ropetvā koṭṭhakaṃ katvā udakaṃ āsiñcitvā kittetuṃ vaṭṭati. Navamūlasākhāniggamanaṃ akāraṇaṃ, khandhaṃ chinditvā ropite pana etaṃ yujjati. Kittentena ca “rukkho”tipi vattuṃ vaṭṭati “sākarukkho”tipi “sālarukkho”tipi. Ekābaddhaṃ pana suppatiṭṭhitanigrodhasadisaṃ ekattha kittetvā aññattha kittetuṃ na vaṭṭati.

Regarding a tree as a boundary marker, a tree with heartwood on the outside, such as a palmyra palm or coconut tree, is not suitable. A tree with heartwood on the inside, if it is alive, is suitable, even if it is at least eight finger-breadths in height and the size of a needle-shaft in circumference. Less than that is not suitable; more than that, even the Suppatiṭṭhita banyan tree of twelve yojanas is suitable. A tree grown from a seed planted in bamboo tubes, reed tubes, small pots, and so forth, even if it reaches the required size, is not suitable. However, having removed it from there, planted it in the ground even for a moment, made an enclosure, and poured water on it, it is then suitable to delineate it. The emergence of new roots and branches is not a necessary condition; however, if it is planted after having cut the trunk, this is fitting. And the delineator may say, 'a tree,' 'a teak tree,' or 'a sal tree.' However, for a continuous mass like the Suppatiṭṭhita banyan tree, having delineated it in one place, it is not suitable to delineate it in another place.

Magganimitte araññakhettanadītaḷākamaggādayo na vaṭṭanti, jaṅghamaggo vā sakaṭamaggo vā vaṭṭati. Yo nibbijjhitvā dve tīṇi gāmantarāni gacchati, yo pana jaṅghamaggasakaṭamaggato okkamitvā puna sakaṭamaggameva otarati, ye vā jaṅghamaggasakaṭamaggā avaḷañjā, te na vaṭṭanti, jaṅghasatthasakaṭasatthehi vaḷañjiyamānāyeva vaṭṭanti. Sace dve maggā nikkhamitvā pacchā sakaṭadhuramiva ekībhavanti, dvedhā bhinnaṭṭhāne vā sambandhaṭṭhāne vā sakiṃ kittetvā puna na kittetabbā. Ekābaddhanimittañhetaṃ hoti. Sace vihāraṃ parikkhipitvā cattāro maggā catūsu disāsu gacchanti, majjhe ekaṃ kittetvā aparaṃ kittetuṃ na vaṭṭati. Ekābaddhanimittañhetaṃ. Koṇaṃ nibbijjhitvā gataṃ pana parabhāge kittetuṃ vaṭṭati. Vihāramajjhena nibbijjhitvā gatamaggo pana na kittetabbo, kittite nimittassa upari vihāro hoti. Sace sakaṭamaggassa antimacakkamaggaṃ nimittaṃ karonti, maggo bahisīmāya hoti, sace bāhiracakkamaggaṃ nimittaṃ karonti, bāhiracakkamaggo bahisīmāya hoti[M 0.0183], sesaṃ antosīmaṃ bhajati. Maggaṃ kittentena “maggo [V 0.0174] pantho patho pajjo”tiādīsu dasasu yena kenaci nāmena ca kittetuṃ vaṭṭati, parikhāsaṇṭhānena vihāraṃ parikkhipitvā gatamaggo ekattha kittetvā aññattha kittetuṃ na vaṭṭati.

Regarding path-markers, paths such as those through forests, fields, rivers, or ponds are not suitable; a footpath or a cart-path is suitable. A path that cuts across and goes between two or three villages is also suitable. However, a path that deviates from a footpath or cart-path and then rejoins the cart-path, or footpaths and cart-paths that are not in use—these are not suitable. Only those that are in use by foot-travelers and cart-caravans are suitable. If two paths, having diverged, later merge like a cart’s yoke, having delineated it once at the point of divergence or at the point of connection, it should not be delineated again, for this is a single, connected marker. If, having encircled a monastery, four paths go in the four directions, having delineated one among them, it is not suitable to delineate another, for this is a single, connected marker. However, a path that cuts across a corner may be delineated in the other part. But a path that cuts across the middle of a monastery should not be delineated; if it is delineated, the monastery is above the marker. If they make the inner wheel-track of a cart-path the marker, the path is outside the boundary. If they make the outer wheel-track the marker, the outer wheel-track is outside the boundary, and the rest belongs within the boundary. When delineating a path, it is suitable to delineate it with any one of the ten names, such as 'maggo, pantho, patho, pajjo,' and so on. A path that goes encircling a monastery in the manner of a moat, having been delineated in one place, is not to be delineated elsewhere.

Vammikanimitte heṭṭhimaparicchedena taṃ divasaṃ jāto aṭṭhaṅgulubbedho govisāṇappamāṇopi vammiko vaṭṭati, tato oraṃ na vaṭṭati. Paraṃ himavantapabbatasadisopi vaṭṭati, vihāraṃ parikkhipitvā ṭhitaṃ pana ekābaddhaṃ ekattha kittetvā aññattha kittetuṃ na vaṭṭati.

Regarding anthill-markers, according to the lower limit, an anthill that has arisen on that very day, eight finger-breadths in height and the size of a cow's horn, is suitable. Less than that is not suitable. Beyond that, even one as large as the Himavant mountain is suitable. But an anthill that stands encircling a monastery, being a single connected mass, having been delineated in one place, is not to be delineated elsewhere.

Nadīnimitte yassā dhammikānaṃ rājūnaṃ kāle anvaḍḍhamāsaṃ anudasāhaṃ anupañcāhanti evaṃ deve vassante valāhakesu vigatamattesu sotaṃ pacchijjati, ayaṃ nadīsaṅkhyaṃ na gacchati. Yassā pana īdise suvuṭṭhikāle vassānassa cātumāse sotaṃ na pacchijjati, yattha titthena vā atitthena vā sikkhākaraṇīye āgatalakkhaṇena timaṇḍalaṃ paṭicchādetvā antaravāsakaṃ anukkhipitvā uttarantiyā bhikkhuniyā ekaṅguladvaṅgulamattampi antaravāsako temiyati, ayaṃ nadī sīmaṃ bandhantānaṃ nimittaṃ hoti. Bhikkhuniyā nadīpāragamanepi uposathādisaṅghakammakaraṇepi nadīpārasīmāsammannanepi ayameva nadī. Yā pana maggo viya sakaṭadhurasaṇṭhānena vā parikhāsaṇṭhānena vā vihāraṃ parikkhipitvā gatā, taṃ ekattha kittetvā aññattha kittetuṃ na vaṭṭati. Vihārassa catūsu disāsu aññamaññaṃ vinibbijjhitvā gate nadīcatukkepi eseva nayo. Asammissā nadiyo pana catassopi kittetuṃ vaṭṭati. Sace vatiṃ karonto viya rukkhapāde nikhaṇitvā vallipalālādīhi nadīsotaṃ rundhanti, udakaṃ ajjhottharitvā āvaraṇaṃ pavattatiyeva, nimittaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭati. Yathā pana udakaṃ na pavattati, evaṃ setumhi kate apavattamānā nadīnimittaṃ kātuṃ na vaṭṭati, pavattanaṭṭhāne nadīnimittaṃ, appavattanaṭṭhāne udakanimittaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭati. Yā pana dubbuṭṭhikāle vā gimhe vā nirudakabhāvena na pavattati, sā vaṭṭati. Mahānadito udakamātikaṃ nīharanti, sā kunnadīsadisā hutvā tīṇi sassāni sampādentī niccaṃ pavattati, kiñcāpi pavattati, nimittaṃ kātuṃ na vaṭṭati. Yā pana mūle mahānadito nīhatāpi kālantarena teneva nīhatamaggena nadiṃ bhinditvā sayaṃ gacchati, gacchantī parato susumārādisamākiṇṇā nāvādīhi sañcaritabbā nadī hoti, taṃ nimittaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭati.

Regarding a river-marker: a river whose stream is cut off even though it rains without fail every fortnight, every ten days, or every five days in the time of righteous kings, and the clouds have just dispersed, this does not count as a river. But a river whose stream is not cut off during such a time of good rain in the four months of the rainy season—where, whether at a ford or not at a ford, a bhikkhunī who is crossing with the characteristics of one undertaking the training, having covered her three circles and lifted her lower robe, has even a finger's or two fingers' breadth of her lower robe become wet—this river is a marker for those establishing a sīmā. This very river is the one for a bhikkhunī's crossing to the other side, for performing Sangha acts such as the Uposatha, and for determining the sīmā on the far side of the river. But as for a river that flows encircling a monastery like a road, or in the shape of a cart-pole, or in the shape of a moat, having declared it in one place, it is not proper to declare it in another. This same rule applies also to a four-fold river where the streams, having diverged from one another, flow in the four directions of the monastery. However, as for unmixed rivers, it is proper to declare all four. If they block the river stream with creepers, straw, and so forth, having planted stakes at the foot of trees as if making a fence, and the water, having flowed over the obstruction, indeed continues to flow, it is proper to make it a marker. But if a dam is made in such a way that the water does not flow, it is not proper to make a river-marker where it is not flowing. In the place where it flows, it is proper to make a river-marker; in the place where it does not flow, it is proper to make a water-marker. But a river that does not flow during a time of drought or in the hot season due to being without water, that one is allowable. If they lead out a main canal from a great river, and that canal, having become like a small river and making three crops successful, flows constantly—even though it flows, it is not proper to make it a marker. But as for a channel which, though originally led out from a great river, in time carves out a riverbed along that same course and flows by itself, and in flowing, afterwards becomes a river teeming with crocodiles and other creatures and is navigable by boats and so forth, it is proper to make that a marker.

Udakanimitte [M 0.0184] nirudakaṭṭhāne nāvāya vā cāṭiādīsu vā udakaṃ pūretvā udakanimittaṃ kittetuṃ na vaṭṭati, bhūmigatameva vaṭṭati. Tañca kho appavattanaudakaṃ āvāṭapokkharaṇītaḷaākajātassaraloṇisamuddādīsu ṭhitaṃ, aṭṭhitaṃ pana oghanadīudakavāhakamātikādīsu udakaṃ na vaṭṭati[V 0.0175]. Andhakaṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana “gambhīresu āvāṭādīsu ukkhepimaṃ udakaṃ nimittaṃ na kātabba”nti vuttaṃ, taṃ duvuttaṃ, attanomatimattameva. Ṭhitaṃ pana antamaso sūkarakhatāyapi gāmadārakānaṃ kīḷanavāpiyampi taṃ khaṇaññeva pathaviyaṃ āvāṭaṃ katvā kuṭehi āharitvā pūritaudakampi sace yāva kammavācāpariyosānā tiṭṭhati, appaṃ vā hotu bahuṃ vā, vaṭṭati. Tasmiṃ pana ṭhāne nimittasaññākaraṇatthaṃ pāsāṇavālikāpaṃsuādirāsi vā pāsāṇatthambho vā dārutthambho vā kātabbo. Taṃ kātuṃ kāretuñca bhikkhussa vaṭṭati, lābhasīmāyaṃ pana na vaṭṭati. Samānasaṃvāsakasīmā kassaci pīḷanaṃ na karoti, kevalaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ vinayakammameva sādheti, tasmā ettha vaṭṭati.

Regarding a water-marker: it is not permissible to proclaim a water-marker by filling a boat or a pot with water in a place without water; only water situated on the ground is permissible. And that water must be non-flowing; water that is stationary in pits, square ponds, reservoirs, natural lakes, salt-pits, or the ocean is permissible. But water that is not stationary, such as in torrents, rivers, and water-channels, is not permissible. In the Andhakaṭṭhakathā, however, it is said: 'In deep pits and so on, water that is drawn up should not be made a marker.' That is badly said; it is merely a personal opinion. But stationary water—even in a pig's trough or a village children's play-pond, or even water brought in pots and used to fill a pit dug in the ground at that very moment—if it remains until the conclusion of the formal act, whether it be little or much, it is permissible. In that place, however, for the purpose of making a sign for the marker, a pile of stones, sand, dust, and so on, or a stone pillar, or a wooden pillar should be made. It is permissible for a bhikkhu to do this or to have it done, but not in a gain-boundary. A boundary of common residence does not cause affliction to anyone; it merely accomplishes the Vinaya acts of the bhikkhus. Therefore, it is permissible here.

Imehi ca aṭṭhahi nimittehi asammissehipi aññamaññaṃ sammissehipi sīmā sammannituṃ vaṭṭatiyeva. Sā evaṃ sammannitvā bajjhamānā ekena dvīhi vā nimittehi abaddhā hoti, tīṇi pana ādiṃ katvā vuttappakārānaṃ nimittānaṃ satenapi baddhā hoti. Sā tīhi siṅghāṭakasaṇṭhānā hoti, catūhi caturassā vā siṅghāṭakaaḍḍhacandamudiṅgādisaṇṭhānā vā, tato adhikehi nānāsaṇṭhānā. Evaṃ vuttanayena nimittāni kittetvā sammatā “nimittasampattiyuttā”ti veditabbā.

And with these eight markers, whether unmixed or mixed with each other, it is indeed permissible to establish a boundary. That boundary, being established in this way, is not bound by one or two markers. But, beginning with three, it is bound even by a hundred of the aforementioned types of markers. With three markers, that boundary has the shape of a triangle; with four, it is quadrangular or has the shape of a crossroads, a half-moon, a drum, etc.; with more than these, it has various shapes. A boundary established by proclaiming the markers in the manner thus described should be known as 'endowed with the accomplishment of markers.'

159. Parisasampattiyuttā nāma sabbantimena paricchedena catūhi bhikkhūhi sannipatitvā yāvatikā tasmiṃ gāmakhette baddhasīmaṃ vā nadīsamuddajātassare vā anokkamitvā ṭhitā bhikkhū, te sabbe hatthapāse vā katvā chandaṃ vā āharitvā sammatā.

159. What is called 'endowed with the accomplishment of the assembly' is a boundary established when, as a minimum, four bhikkhus have gathered, and all bhikkhus who are present in that village-field—not having entered a bound sīmā, or a river, ocean, or natural lake—are included either by being brought within hand's reach or by having their consent brought.

160. Kammavācāsampattiyuttā nāma –

160. What is called 'endowed with the accomplishment of the formal act' is—

“Suṇātu me, bhante, saṅgho, yāvatā samantā nimittā kittitā, yadi saṅghassa pattakallaṃ, saṅgho etehi nimittehi sīmaṃ sammanneyya samānasaṃvāsaṃ ekūposathaṃ, esā ñatti.

“Venerable Sirs, may the Saṅgha hear me. As many as are the markers that have been proclaimed all around, if the time is right for the Saṅgha, the Saṅgha should, with these markers, authorize a sīmā for common residence and a single Uposatha. This is the motion.

“Suṇātu me, bhante, saṅgho, yāvatā samantā nimittā kittitā, saṅgho etehi nimittehi sīmaṃ sammannati samānasaṃvāsaṃ [M 0.0185] ekūposathaṃ, yassāyasmato khamati etehi nimittehi sīmāya sammuti samānasaṃvāsāya ekūposathāya, so tuṇhassa. Yassa nakkhamati, so bhāseyya.

“Venerable Sirs, may the Saṅgha hear me. As many as are the markers that have been proclaimed all around, the Saṅgha authorizes a sīmā with these markers for common residence and a single Uposatha. To whichever venerable one the authorization of the sīmā with these markers for common residence and a single Uposatha is agreeable, he should be silent. To whomever it is not agreeable, he should speak.

“Sammatā [V 0.0176] sīmā saṅghena etehi nimittehi samānasaṃvāsā ekūposathā, khamati saṅghassa, tasmā tuṇhī, evametaṃ dhārayāmī”ti (mahāva. 139) –

“The sīmā has been authorized by the Saṅgha with these markers for common residence and a single Uposatha. It is agreeable to the Saṅgha, therefore it is silent. Thus do I hold this.” (Mahāvagga 139) —

Evaṃ vuttāya parisuddhāya ñattidutiyakammavācāya sammatā. Kammavācāpariyosāne nimittānaṃ anto sīmā hoti, nimittāni sīmato bahi honti.

Thus it is authorized by a pure formal act preceded by a motion. At the conclusion of the formal act, the sīmā is inside the markers, and the markers are outside the sīmā.

161. Evaṃ baddhāya ca sīmāya ticīvarena vippavāsasukhatthaṃ daḷhīkammatthañca avippavāsasammuti kātabbā. Sā pana evaṃ kattabbā –

161. And when the sīmā has been bound in this way, an authorization of non-separation from the three robes should be made for the sake of convenience in being separated from them and for making the authorization firm. This, then, should be done as follows:

“Suṇātu me, bhante, saṅgho, yā sā saṅghena sīmā sammatā samānasaṃvāsā ekūposathā, yadi saṅghassa pattakallaṃ, saṅgho taṃ sīmaṃ ticīvarena avippavāsaṃ sammanneyya ṭhapetvā gāmañca gāmūpacārañca, esā ñatti.

Venerable Sirs, may the Saṅgha hear me. That sīmā which has been authorized by the Saṅgha for common residence and a single Uposatha—if the time is right for the Saṅgha, the Saṅgha should authorize that sīmā as one of non-separation from the three robes, excluding the village and the village precincts. This is the motion.

“Suṇātu me, bhante, saṅgho, yā sā saṅghena sīmā sammatā samānasaṃvāsā ekūposathā, saṅgho taṃ sīmaṃ ticīvarena avippavāsaṃ sammannati ṭhapetvā gāmañca gāmūpacārañca, yassāyasmato khamati etissā sīmāya ticīvarena avippavāsāya sammuti ṭhapetvā gāmañca gāmūpacārañca, so tuṇhassa. Yassa nakkhamati, so bhāseyya.

“Venerable sirs, may the Sangha hear me. That boundary which has been established by the Sangha for common residence and a single Uposatha—the Sangha establishes that boundary as being without separation from the three robes, excluding the village and its precincts. If the establishment of this boundary as being without separation from the three robes, excluding the village and its precincts, is agreeable to any venerable one, let him be silent. If it is not agreeable to anyone, let him speak.”

“Sammatā sā sīmā saṅghena ticīvarena avippavāsā ṭhapetvā gāmañca gāmūpacārañca, khamati saṅghassa, tasmā tuṇhī, evametaṃ dhārayāmī”ti (mahāva. 143).

“That boundary has been established by the Sangha as being without separation from the three robes, excluding the village and its precincts. It is agreeable to the Sangha, therefore it is silent. Thus I hold it.” (Mahāvagga 143).

Ettha (mahāva. aṭṭha. 144) ca nigamanagarānampi gāmeneva saṅgaho veditabbo. Gāmūpacāroti parikkhittassa parikkhepo, aparikkhittassa parikkhepokāso. Imesu pana gāmagāmūpacāresu adhiṭṭhitatecīvariko bhikkhu parihāraṃ na labhati. Ayañhi avippavāsasīmā “ṭhapetvā gāmañca gāmūpacārañcā”ti vuttattā gāmañca gāmūpacārañca [M 0.0186] na ottharati, samānasaṃvāsakasīmāva ottharati. Samānasaṃvāsakasīmā cettha attano dhammatāya gacchati, avippavāsasīmā pana yattha samānasaṃvāsakasīmā, tattheva gacchati. Na hi tassā visuṃ nimittakittanaṃ atthi, tattha sace avippavāsāya sammutikāle gāmo atthi, taṃ sā na ottharati[V 0.0177]. Sace pana sammatāya sīmāya pacchā gāmo nivisati, sopi sīmasaṅkhyaṃyeva gacchati. Yathā ca pacchā niviṭṭho, evaṃ paṭhamaṃ niviṭṭhassa pacchā vaḍḍhitappadesopi sīmasaṅkhyameva gacchati. Sace sīmāsammutikāle gehāni katāni, “pavisissāmā”ti ālayopi atthi, manussā pana appaviṭṭhā, porāṇakagāmaṃ vā sace gehameva chaḍḍetvā aññattha gatā, agāmoyeva esa, sīmā ottharati. Sace pana ekampi kulaṃ paviṭṭhaṃ vā agataṃ vā atthi, gāmoyeva, sīmā na ottharati. Ayamettha saṅkhepo.

Here (in the Mahāvagga Aṭṭhakathā 144), even market towns and cities should be understood as included under the term 'village.' The village precincts (gāmūpacāra) for an enclosed village is its enclosure; for an unenclosed village, it is the space for an enclosure. However, a bhikkhu who has determined his three robes does not obtain the exemption within these villages and village precincts. For this non-separation boundary (avippavāsasīmā), because it is stated, 'excepting the village and the village precincts,' does not extend over the village and the village precincts; only the boundary of common communion (samānasaṃvāsakasīmā) extends over them. Herein, the boundary of common communion proceeds according to its own nature, but the non-separation boundary proceeds only where the boundary of common communion is. Indeed, for that [non-separation boundary], there is no separate declaration of markers. In this matter, if a village exists at the time of agreeing upon the non-separation [boundary], that [boundary] does not extend over it. But if a village is established afterwards within the agreed-upon boundary, it too is counted as part of the boundary. And just as a village established afterwards is counted as part of the boundary, so too an area of a previously established village that has expanded afterwards is also counted as part of the boundary. If, at the time of agreeing upon the boundary, houses have been built and there is the intention, 'We will move in,' but people have not yet moved in, or if, in the case of an old village, they have abandoned only the houses and gone elsewhere, this is indeed not a village, and the boundary extends over it. But if even a single family has moved in or has not left, it is indeed a village, and the boundary does not extend over it. This is the summary herein.

162. Ayaṃ pana vitthāro (mahāva. aṭṭha. 138) sīmaṃ bandhitukāmena hi sāmantavihāresu bhikkhū tassa tassa vihārassa sīmāparicchedaṃ pucchitvā baddhasīmavihārānaṃ sīmāya sīmantarikaṃ, abaddhasīmavihārānaṃ sīmāya upacāraṃ ṭhapetvā disācārikabhikkhūnaṃ nissañcārasamaye sace ekasmiṃ gāmakhette sīmaṃ bandhitukāmā, ye tattha baddhasīmavihārā, tesu bhikkhūnaṃ “mayaṃ ajja sīmaṃ bandhissāma, tumhe sakasīmāya paricchedato mā nikkhamitthā”ti pesetabbaṃ. Ye abaddhasīmavihārā, tesu bhikkhū ekajjhaṃ sannipātetabbā, chandārahānaṃ chando āharāpetabbo. “Sace aññānipi gāmakhettāni antokātukāmā, tesu gāmesu ye bhikkhū vasanti, tehipi āgantabbaṃ, anāgacchantānaṃ chando āharitabbo”ti mahāsumatthero āha. Mahāpadumatthero pana “nānāgāmakhettāni nāma pāṭiyekkaṃ baddhasīmasadisāni, na tato chandapārisuddhi āgacchati, antonimittagatehi pana bhikkhūhi āgantabba”nti vatvā puna āha “samānasaṃvāsakasīmāsammannanakāle āgamanampi anāgamanampi vaṭṭati, avippavāsasīmāsammannanakāle pana antonimittagatehi āgantabbaṃ, anāgacchantānaṃ chando āharitabbo”ti.

162. Now, this is the detailed explanation: A monk who wishes to establish a boundary, having asked the monks in nearby monasteries about the boundary limits of each respective monastery, and having established a boundary-interval from the boundary of monasteries with an established boundary, and an approach-precinct from the boundary of monasteries without an established boundary, should establish the boundary at a time when the movement of monks wandering in the directions has ceased. If they wish to establish a boundary in a single village-field, a message should be sent to the monks in those monasteries with established boundaries there, saying: 'Today we will establish a boundary. Do not go out from the limit of your own boundary.' As for the monasteries without an established boundary, the monks in them should be assembled together, and the consent of those eligible to give consent should be brought. The Elder Mahāsuma said: 'If they also wish to include other village-fields within, the monks who dwell in those villages should also come. The consent of those not coming should be brought.' But the Elder Mahāpaduma said: 'Various village-fields, indeed, are like individually established boundaries; consent and purity do not come from there. But the monks who are within the boundary-markers should come.' He further said: 'At the time of establishing a boundary for common-communion, both coming and not coming are permissible. But at the time of establishing a boundary of non-separation, those within the boundary-markers should come. The consent of those not coming should be brought.'
