Among adzes and so forth, whichever adze is such that, apart from cutting tooth-sticks or scraping sugarcane, no other major work can be done with it, that is distributable. Any adze larger than that, made in any manner, is a heavy item indeed. An axe, however, even the small axe used by physicians for bloodletting, is a heavy item indeed. The ruling for a hatchet is the same as for an axe. However, one that is made in the manner of a weapon is not to be handled. A spade, even if only four finger-breadths in size, is a heavy item indeed. A chisel, whether it be square-mouthed or trough-mouthed, curved or straight—even one for piercing a broom handle—if it is attached to a handle, is a heavy item indeed. A chisel for hollowing a broom handle, however, if without a handle, is merely a blade. Any such chisel that can be put in a bag and carried around is distributable. An awl is also included under the category of a chisel. If people who have given adzes and other tools to the monastery have their homes burned down or plundered by thieves and say, 'Venerable sirs, give us the tools; we will restore them to their original state,' they are to be given. If they bring them back, they are not to be refused. Even if they do not bring them back, they are not to be asked for them.

Kammāratacchakāracundakāranaḷakāramaṇikārapattabandhakānaṃ adhikaraṇimuṭṭhikasaṇḍāsatulādīni sabbāni lohamayaupakaraṇāni saṅghe dinnakālato paṭṭhāya garubhaṇḍāni. Tipukoṭṭakasuvaṇṇakāracammakāraupakaraṇesupi eseva nayo. Ayaṃ pana viseso – tipukoṭṭakaupakaraṇesupi tipucchedanakasatthakaṃ, suvaṇṇakāraupakaraṇesu suvaṇṇacchedanakasatthakaṃ, cammakāraupakaraṇesu kataparikammacammacchedanakakhuddakasatthakanti imāni bhājanīyabhaṇḍāni. Nahāpitatunnakāraupakaraṇesupi ṭhapetvā mahākattariṃ mahāsaṇḍāsaṃ mahāpipphalikañca sabbaṃ bhājanīyaṃ, mahākattariādīni garubhaṇḍāni.

All iron implements of blacksmiths, carpenters, turners, reed-workers, jewelers, and bowl-menders—such as anvils, hammers, tongs, and scales—are heavy items from the time they are given to the Sangha. The same principle applies to the tools of tin-workers, goldsmiths, and leatherworkers. This, however, is the distinction: among the tools of tin-workers, the small knife for cutting tin; among the tools of goldsmiths, the small knife for cutting gold; and among the tools of leatherworkers, the small knife for cutting prepared leather—these are distributable items. As for the tools of barbers and tailors, excepting large scissors, large pincers, and a large bodkin, everything is distributable; the large scissors and so forth are heavy items.

Valliādīsu vettavalliādikā yā kāci aḍḍhabāhuppamāṇā valli saṅghassa dinnā vā tatthajātakā vā rakkhitagopitā garubhaṇḍaṃ hoti, sā saṅghakamme ca cetiyakamme ca kate sace atirekā hoti, puggalikakammepi upanetuṃ vaṭṭati. Arakkhitā pana garubhaṇḍameva na hoti. Suttamakacivākanāḷikerahīracammamayā rajjukā vā yottāni vā vāke ca nāḷikerahīre ca vaṭṭetvā katā ekavaṭṭā vā dvivaṭṭā vā saṅghassa dinnakālato paṭṭhāya garubhaṇḍaṃ. Suttaṃ pana avaṭṭetvā dinnaṃ makacivākanāḷikerahīrā ca bhājanīyā. Yehi panetāni rajjukayottādīni dinnāni honti, te attano karaṇīyena harantā na vāretabbā.

Among vines and so forth, any vine, such as a rattan vine, that has the measure of half an arm's length, whether given to the Sangha or grown in that Sanghika place, if it is protected and guarded by the Sangha, is a heavy item. If, after that vine has been used for Sangha work and for cetiya work, there is an excess, it is permissible to apply it even for an individual's work. However, if it is unprotected, it is not a heavy item. Ropes of thread, ropes of makacivāka grass, ropes of coconut fiber, or ropes made of leather, or straps, are heavy items. And those made by twisting or plaiting bark fibers and coconut fibers, whether single-twisted or double-twisted, are heavy items from the time they are given to the Sangha. But thread given without being twisted, and makacivāka grass fibers and coconut fibers, are distributable. Furthermore, the people by whom these ropes, straps, and so forth have been given, should not be prevented when taking them for their own necessary task.

Yo koci antamaso aṭṭhaṅgulasūcidaṇḍakamattopi veḷu saṅghassa dinno vā tatthajātako vā rakkhitagopito garubhaṇḍaṃ, sopi saṅghakamme ca cetiyakamme ca kate atireko puggalikakamme ca dātuṃ vaṭṭati. Pādagaṇhanakatelanāḷi pana kattarayaṭṭhi upāhanadaṇḍako chattadaṇḍako chattasalākāti idamettha bhājanīyabhaṇḍaṃ. Daḍḍhagehamanussā gaṇhitvā [M 0.0307] gacchantā na vāretabbā. Rakkhitagopitaṃ veḷuṃ gaṇhantena samakaṃ vā atirekaṃ vā thāvaraṃ antamaso taṃagghanakavallikāyapi phātikammaṃ katvā gahetabbo, phātikammaṃ akatvā gaṇhantena tattheva vaḷañjetabbo. Gamanakāle saṅghike āvāse ṭhapetvā gantabbaṃ, asatiyā gahetvā gatena pahiṇitvā dātabbo. Desantaragatena sampattavihāro saṅghikāvāse ṭhapetabbo.

Any piece of bamboo, even one measuring at least eight finger-breadths, the size of a stylus shaft, whether given to the Sangha or grown in that Sanghika land, if it is protected and guarded by the Sangha, is a heavy item. After that bamboo has been used for Sangha work and for cetiya work, it is permissible to give the excess for an individual's work also. However, an oil tube for anointing the feet, a walking stick, a stick for carrying sandals, an umbrella handle, and umbrella ribs—these here are distributable items. People whose houses have burned down, taking it and going, should not be prevented. By one taking the protected and guarded bamboo, a transaction should be made with a permanent item of equal or greater value, and then it should be taken; at the very least, a transaction should be made with a vine worth its price, and then it should be taken. By one who takes it without making a transaction, it should be used up in that very place. At the time of departure, it should be placed in a Sanghika dwelling before one goes. If one has taken it and gone through forgetfulness, one should have it sent back. By one who has gone to a distant place, it should be placed in the Sanghika dwelling of the monastery one has arrived at.

Tiṇanti [V 0.0285] muñjañca pabbajañca ṭhapetvā avasesaṃ yaṃ kiñci tiṇaṃ. Yattha pana tiṇaṃ natthi, tattha paṇṇehi chādenti, tasmā paṇṇampi tiṇeneva saṅgahitaṃ. Iti muñjādīsu yaṃ kiñci muṭṭhippamāṇaṃ tiṇaṃ tālapaṇṇādīsu ca ekapaṇṇampi saṅghassa dinnaṃ vā tatthajātakaṃ vā bahārāme saṅghassa tiṇavatthuto jātatiṇaṃ vā rakkhitagopitaṃ garubhaṇḍaṃ hoti, tampi saṅghakamme ca cetiyakamme ca kate atirekaṃ puggalikakamme dātuṃ vaṭṭati, daḍḍhagehamanussā gahetvā gacchantā na vāretabbā. Aṭṭhaṅgulappamāṇopi rittapotthako garubhaṇḍameva.

Grass is defined as any remaining grass after excluding muñja and pabbaja. Where there is no grass, they cover with leaves; therefore, leaves are also included under 'grass'. Thus, any grass the size of a handful from among muñja and the like, or even a single leaf from among palm leaves and the like, that is given to the Sangha, or grown in that place, or grass grown from the Sangha's grass-land outside the monastery, which is protected and guarded, is heavy property. That too, after work for the Sangha and work for a cetiya has been done, it is allowable to give the remainder for individual work. People from a burned house, taking and going, should not be prevented. Even an unwritten palm-leaf manuscript of the measure of eight finger-breadths is indeed heavy property.

Mattikā pakatimattikā vā hotu pañcavaṇṇā vā sudhā vā sajjurasakaṅguṭṭhasilesādīsu vā yaṃ kiñci dullabhaṭṭhāne ānetvā dinnaṃ tatthajātakaṃ vā, rakkhitagopitaṃ tālaphalapakkamattaṃ garubhaṇḍaṃ hoti, tampi saṅghakamme ca cetiyakamme ca niṭṭhite atirekaṃ puggalikakamme ca dātuṃ vaṭṭati, hiṅguhiṅgulakaharitālamanosilañjanāni pana bhājanīyabhaṇḍāni.

Clay, whether it be ordinary clay, or of five colors, or lime; or among resins, gums, glues, and the like, whatever is brought from a hard-to-get place and given, or is produced in that place—if it is protected and guarded, an amount the size of a ripe palm fruit is heavy property. That too, after work for the Sangha and work for a cetiya are finished, it is allowable to give the remainder for individual work. However, asafoetida, vermilion, orpiment, realgar, and collyrium are distributable property.

Dārubhaṇḍe “yo koci aṭṭhaṅgulasūcidaṇḍamattopi dārubhaṇḍako dārudullabhaṭṭhāne saṅghassa dinno vā tatthajātako vā rakkhitagopito, ayaṃ garubhaṇḍaṃ hotī”ti kurundiyaṃ vuttaṃ. Mahāaṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana sabbampi dāruveḷucammapāsāṇādivikatiṃ dārubhaṇḍena saṅgaṇhitvā āsandikato paṭṭhāya dārubhaṇḍe vinicchayo vutto. Tatrāyaṃ nayo – āsandiko sattaṅgo bhaddapīṭhaṃ pīṭhikā ekapādakapīṭhaṃ āmaṇḍakavaṇṭakapīṭhaṃ phalakaṃ kocchaṃ palālapīṭhanti imesu tāva yaṃ kiñci khuddakaṃ vā hotu mahantaṃ vā, saṅghassa dinnaṃ garubhaṇḍaṃ hoti. Palālapīṭhena cettha kadalipattādipīṭhānipi saṅgahitāni. Byagghacammaonaddhampi vāḷarūpaparikkhittaṃ ratanaparisibbitaṃ kocchaṃ garubhaṇḍameva, vaṅkaphalakaṃ dīghaphalakaṃ cīvaradhovanaphalakaṃ ghaṭṭanaphalakaṃ [M 0.0308] ghaṭṭanamuggaro dantakaṭṭhacchedanagaṇṭhikā daṇḍamuggaro ambaṇaṃ rajanadoṇi udakapaṭicchako dārumayo vā dantamayo vā veḷumayo vā sapādakopi apādakopi samuggo mañjūsā pādagaṇhanakato atirekappamāṇo karaṇḍo udakadoṇi udakakaṭāhaṃ uḷuṅko kaṭacchu pānīyasarāvaṃ pānīyasaṅkhoti etesupi yaṃ kiñci saṅghe dinnaṃ garubhaṇḍaṃ. Saṅkhathālakaṃ pana bhājanīyaṃ, tathā dārumayo udakatumbo.

Regarding wooden articles, in the Kurundī it is stated: “Any wooden article, even one the size of a stylus shaft eight finger-breadths long, which, in a place where wood is scarce, is given to the Sangha or has grown there and is guarded and protected—this is heavy property.” However, in the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā, having included all kinds of articles made of wood, bamboo, leather, stone, and the like under the term 'wooden articles', the analysis regarding wooden articles is stated beginning from the high seat. Therein, this is the method: Regarding a high seat, a seven-limbed seat, a cane seat, a small seat, a one-legged seat, a seat with legs round like castor-oil seeds, a board, a couch, and a straw seat—whatever among these is given to the Sangha, whether it be small or large, is heavy property. And here, by 'straw seat', seats made of banana leaves and the like are also included. A couch covered with tiger skin, surrounded by figures of beasts of prey, or adorned with jewels is indeed heavy property. A curved board, a long board, a robe-washing board, a board for smoothing robes, a beating mallet, a block for cutting tooth-sticks, a staff-mallet, a water trough, a dyeing vat, a receptacle for squeezed water—whether made of wood, ivory, or bamboo, with or without a base—a casket, a box, a basket of a size exceeding that which holds five betel quids, a water trough, a water cauldron, a scoop, a ladle, a drinking bowl, and a drinking conch-shell—among these also, whatever is given to the Sangha is heavy property. A conch-shell plate, however, is distributable; likewise, a wooden water gourd is distributable.

Pādakathalikamaṇḍalaṃ dārumayaṃ vā hotu coḷapaṇṇādimayaṃ vā, sabbaṃ garubhaṇḍaṃ. Ādhārako pattapidhānaṃ tālavaṇṭaṃ bījanī caṅkoṭakaṃ pacchi yaṭṭhisammuñjanī muṭṭhisammuñjanīti etesupi yaṃ kiñci khuddakaṃ vā hotu mahantaṃ vā, dāruveḷupaṇṇacammādīsu yena kenaci kataṃ garubhaṇḍameva. Thambhatulāsopānaphalakādīsu dārumayaṃ vā pāsāṇamayaṃ vā yaṃ kiñci gehasambhārarūpaṃ [V 0.0286] yo koci kaṭasārako yaṃ kiñci bhūmattharaṇaṃ yaṃ kiñci akappiyacammaṃ, sabbaṃ saṅghe dinnaṃ garubhaṇḍaṃ, bhūmattharaṇaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭati. Eḷakacammaṃ pana paccattharaṇagatikaṃ hoti, tampi garubhaṇḍameva. Kappiyacammāni bhājanīyāni. Kurundiyaṃ pana “sabbaṃ mañcappamāṇaṃ cammaṃ garubhaṇḍa”nti vuttaṃ.

A circular foot-wiper, whether made of wood, or of cloth, leaves, and so forth, is all heavy property. A bowl-stand, a bowl-cover, a round palm-leaf fan, a square fan, a flower basket, a basket, a broom with a handle, a hand-broom—among these, whatever item, whether small or large, made of anything such as wood, bamboo, leaves, or hide, is indeed heavy property. Among such things as pillars, beams, stairs, and planks, any kind of house-building material, whether made of wood or stone; any kind of rush mat; any kind of floor covering; any kind of hide from unsuitable flesh—all that is given to the Sangha is heavy property. It is allowable to make a floor covering. A sheep or goat hide, however, is of the nature of a coverlet; that too is indeed heavy property. Hides from suitable flesh are distributable. But in the Kurundī, it is said: 'All hide the size of a bed is heavy property.'

Udukkhalaṃ musalaṃ suppaṃ nisadaṃ nisadapoto pāsāṇadoṇi pāsāṇakaṭāhaṃ turivemabhastādi sabbaṃ pesakārādibhaṇḍaṃ sabbaṃ kasibhaṇḍaṃ sabbaṃ cakkayuttakaṃ yānaṃ garubhaṇḍameva. Mañcapādo mañcaaṭanī pīṭhapādo pīṭhaaṭanī vāsipharasuādīnaṃ daṇḍāti etesu yaṃ kiñci vippakatatacchanakammaṃ aniṭṭhitameva bhājanīyaṃ, tacchitamaṭṭhaṃ pana garubhaṇḍaṃ hoti. Anuññātavāsiyā pana daṇḍo chattamuṭṭhipaṇṇaṃ kattarayaṭṭhi upāhanā araṇisahitaṃ dhammakaraṇo pādagaṇhanakato anatirittaṃ āmalakatumbaṃ āmalakaghaṭo lābukatumbaṃ lābughaṭo visāṇakatumbanti sabbamevetaṃ bhājanīyaṃ, tato mahantataraṃ garubhaṇḍaṃ. Hatthidanto vā yaṃ kiñci visāṇaṃ vā atacchitaṃ yathāgatameva bhājanīyaṃ. Tehi katamañcapādādīsu purimasadisoyeva vinicchayo. Tacchitaniṭṭhitopi hiṅgukaraṇḍako gaṇṭhikā vidho añjanī añjanīsalākā udakapuñchanīti idaṃ sabbaṃ bhājanīyameva.

A mortar, a pestle, a winnowing basket, a grinding stone, a muller, a stone trough, a stone cauldron, a shuttle, a loom, leather bags, and so forth; all the equipment of weavers and the like; all farming equipment; any vehicle fitted with wheels—these are indeed heavy property. A bed leg, a bed frame, a chair leg, a chair frame, the handles of adzes, axes, and the like—among these, any roughly carved and unfinished work is divisible; but once carved and polished, it becomes heavy property. However, the handle of an allowed adze, palm-leaf for an umbrella-covering, a staff, sandals, a fire-drill set, a water-strainer, an āmalaka gourd not exceeding the capacity of five betel quids, an āmalaka pot, a gourd container, a gourd pot, and a horn container—all these are indeed divisible. Anything larger than that is heavy property. An elephant tusk or any kind of horn, uncarved and in its natural state, is indeed divisible. For bed legs and the like made from these, the ruling is the same as before. Even if carved and finished, an asafoetida casket, a belt-fastener, a bodkin, an ointment pot, an ointment applicator, and a water-wiper—all these are indeed divisible.

Mattikābhaṇḍe sabbaṃ manussānaṃ upabhogaparibhogaṃ ghaṭapīṭharādikulālabhājanaṃ pattakaṭāhaṃ aṅgārakaṭāhaṃ dhūmadānaṃ dīparukkhako dīpakapallikā [M 0.0309] cayaniṭṭhakā chadaniṭṭhakā thūpikāti saṅghassa dinnakālato paṭṭhāya garubhaṇḍaṃ, pādagaṇhanakato anatirittappamāṇo pana ghaṭako pattaṃ thālakaṃ kañcanako kuṇḍikāti idamettha bhājanīyabhaṇḍaṃ. Yathā ca mattikābhaṇḍe, evaṃ lohabhaṇḍepi kuṇḍikā bhājanīyakoṭṭhāsameva bhajatīti ayamettha anupubbikathā.

Regarding earthenware: all items for human use and enjoyment—such as pots, pot-lids, and other vessels made by potters; a pan for baking bowls, a charcoal pan, an incense burner, a lamp stand, a lamp cup, bricks for laying, roofing tiles, and finials—are heavy property from the time they are given to the Sangha. However, a small pot, a bowl, a plate, a drinking cup, and a water pitcher, having a size not exceeding that which holds five betel quids, are here divisible property. And just as with earthenware, so too with metal goods: a water pitcher falls into the very same category of divisible property. This here is the sequential discourse.

Iti pāḷimuttakavinayavinicchayasaṅgahe

Thus in the Pāḷimuttakavinayavinicchayasaṅgaha,

Garubhaṇḍavinicchayakathā samattā.

The Discourse on the Determination of Heavy Property is concluded.

31. Codanādivinicchayakathā

31. The Discourse on the Determination of Accusations, etc.

230. Codanādivinicchayoti [V 0.0287] ettha (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.385-6) pana codetuṃ ko labhati, ko na labhati? Dubbalacodakavacanaṃ tāva gahetvā koci na labhati. Dubbalacodako nāma sambahulesu kathāsallāpena nisinnesu eko ekaṃ ārabbha anodissakaṃ katvā pārājikavatthuṃ katheti, añño taṃ sutvā itarassa gantvā āroceti, so taṃ upasaṅkamitvā “tvaṃ kira maṃ idañcidañca vadasī”ti bhaṇati, so “nāhaṃ evarūpaṃ jānāmi, kathāpavattiyaṃ pana mayā anodissakaṃ katvā vuttamatthi. Sace ahaṃ tava imaṃ dukkhuppattiṃ jāneyyaṃ, ettakampi na katheyya”nti. Ayaṃ dubbalacodako. Tassetaṃ kathāsallāpaṃ gahetvā taṃ bhikkhuṃ koci codetuṃ na labhati, etaṃ pana aggahetvā sīlasampanno bhikkhu bhikkhuṃ vā bhikkhuniṃ vā, sīlasampannā ca bhikkhunī bhikkhunīmeva codetuṃ labhatīti mahāpadumatthero āha. Mahāsumatthero pana “pañcapi sahadhammikā labhantī”ti āha. Godattatthero “na koci na labhatī”ti vatvā “bhikkhussa sutvā codeti, bhikkhuniyā sutvā…pe… titthiyasāvakānaṃ sutvā codetī”ti idaṃ suttaṃ āhari. Tiṇṇampi therānaṃ vāde cuditakasseva paṭiññāya kāretabbo.

230. Furthermore, in this matter of the determination of accusations, etc., who is permitted to accuse, and who is not? First, taking the statement of a weak accuser, no one is permitted to accuse. A weak accuser is defined as follows: when many monks are seated engaged in conversation, one monk, concerning another, speaks of a pārājika matter without specifying anyone. Another monk, hearing this, goes and reports it to that other monk. That person then approaches the first monk and says, 'It is said that you say this and that about me.' The first monk replies, 'I do not know of such a matter. However, in the course of conversation, it was said by me without specifying anyone. If I had known of this arising of suffering for you, I would not have said even this much.' This is a weak accuser. Taking up this conversation of his, no one is permitted to accuse that monk. However, not taking this up, a monk endowed with virtue is permitted to accuse a monk or a nun, and a nun endowed with virtue is permitted to accuse only a nun—so said the Elder Mahāpaduma. The Elder Mahāsuma, however, said, 'The five kinds of co-religionists are permitted to accuse.' The Elder Godatta, having said, 'It is not the case that no one is not permitted,' brought forth this text: 'Having heard from a monk, one accuses; having heard from a nun… and so on… having heard from the disciples of heretics, one accuses.' In the opinion of all three elders, the matter should be proceeded with only by the acknowledgement of the accused.

Ayaṃ pana codanā nāma diṭṭhacodanā sutacodanā parisaṅkitacodanāti tividhā hoti. Aparāpi catubbidhā hoti sīlavipatticodanā ācāravipatticodanā diṭṭhivipatticodanā ājīvavipatticodanāti. Tattha garukānaṃ dvinnaṃ āpattikkhandhānaṃ vasena sīlavipatticodanā veditabbā[M 0.0310], avasesānaṃ vasena ācāravipatticodanā, micchādiṭṭhiantaggāhikadiṭṭhivasena diṭṭhivipatticodanā, ājīvahetu paññattānaṃ channaṃ sikkhāpadānaṃ vasena ājīvavipatticodanā veditabbā.

Furthermore, this thing called an accusation is of three kinds: an accusation based on what is seen, an accusation based on what is heard, and an accusation based on suspicion. It is also of four other kinds: an accusation of moral transgression, an accusation of transgression in conduct, an accusation of transgression in view, and an accusation of transgression in livelihood. Therein, an accusation of moral transgression is to be understood by way of the two grave classes of offenses. An accusation of transgression in conduct is to be understood by way of the remaining classes of offenses. An accusation of transgression in view is to be understood by way of wrong view and the view that grasps at extremes. An accusation of transgression in livelihood is to be understood by way of the six training rules laid down on account of livelihood.

Aparāpi catubbidhā hoti vatthusandassanā āpattisandassanā saṃvāsapaṭikkhepo sāmīcipaṭikkhepoti. Tattha vatthusandassanā nāma “tvaṃ methunaṃ dhammaṃ paṭisevi, adinnaṃ ādiyi, manussaṃ ghātayittha, abhūtaṃ ārocayitthā”ti evaṃ pavattā. Āpattisandassanā nāma “tvaṃ methunadhammapārājikāpattiṃ āpanno”tievamādinayappavattā. Saṃvāsapaṭikkhepo nāma “natthi tayā saddhiṃ uposatho vā pavāraṇā vā saṅghakammaṃ vā”ti evaṃ pavatto. Sāmīcipaṭikkhepo nāma [V 0.0288] abhivādanapaccuṭṭhānaañjalīkammabījanādikammānaṃ akaraṇaṃ. Taṃ paṭipāṭiyā vandanādīni karonto ekassa akatvā sesānaṃ karaṇakāle veditabbaṃ. Ettāvatāpi codanā nāma hoti. Yāgubhattādinā pana yaṃ icchati, taṃ āpucchati, na tāvatā codanā hoti.

It is also of four other kinds: pointing out the matter, pointing out the offense, rejection of communal living, and rejection of proper conduct. Herein, 'pointing out the matter' is an accusation that proceeds thus: “You engaged in sexual intercourse; you took what was not given; you killed a human being; you declared a non-existent attainment.” 'Pointing out the offense' is an accusation that proceeds according to the method beginning: “You have committed the Pārājika offense of sexual intercourse.” 'Rejection of communal living' is an accusation that proceeds thus: “There is no Uposatha, Pavāraṇā, or formal act of the Saṅgha with you.” 'Rejection of proper conduct' is the non-performance of acts such as bowing down, rising to greet, making the añjali gesture, fanning, and so forth. This should be understood as occurring when one who is performing acts of homage and so on in sequence, does not do so for one person while doing so for the others. Even by this much, it is called an accusation. However, with regard to things like rice-gruel and boiled rice, one invites whomever one wishes; by that alone, it is not an accusation.

Aparā pātimokkhaṭṭhapanakkhandhake (cūḷava. 387) “ekaṃ, bhikkhave, adhammikaṃ pātimokkhaṭṭhapanaṃ, ekaṃ dhammika”ntiādiṃ katvā yāva dasa adhammikāni pātimokkhaṭṭhapanāni, dasa dhammikānīti evaṃ adhammikā pañcapaññāsa, dhammikā pañcapaññāsāti dasuttarasataṃ codanā vuttā. Tā diṭṭhena codentassa dasuttarasataṃ, sutena codentassa dasuttarasataṃ, parisaṅkāya codentassa dasuttarasatanti tiṃsādhikāni tīṇi satāni honti. Tāni kāyena codentassa, vācāya codentassa, kāyavācāya codentassāti tiguṇāni katāni navutādhikāni nava satāni honti. Tāni attanā codentassapi parena codāpentassapi tattakānevāti vīsatiūnāni dve sahassāni honti. Puna diṭṭhādibhede samūlikāmūlikavasena anekasahassā codanā hontīti veditabbā.

Furthermore, in the Khandhaka on the Suspension of the Pātimokkha, beginning with the words, “Monks, there is one unrighteous suspension of the Pātimokkha and one righteous suspension,” up to “ten unrighteous suspensions of the Pātimokkha and ten righteous ones,” in this way fifty-five unrighteous and fifty-five righteous accusations are spoken of, totaling one hundred and ten. For one who accuses based on what is seen, there are one hundred and ten; for one who accuses based on what is heard, one hundred and ten; and for one who accuses based on suspicion, one hundred and ten—totaling three hundred and thirty. These, when made threefold for accusing by body, by speech, or by both body and speech, become nine hundred and ninety. These are just as many for one who accuses by oneself and for one who causes another to accuse, thus becoming one thousand nine hundred and eighty. Again, it should be understood that in the divisions of seen, heard, and suspected, by way of being rooted or unrooted, there come to be many thousands of accusations.

231. Vuttappabhedāsu pana imāsu codanāsu yāya kāyaci codanāya vasena saṅghamajjhe osaṭe vatthusmiṃ cuditakacodakā vattabbā “tumhe amhākaṃ vinicchayena tuṭṭhā bhavissathā”ti. Sace “bhavissāmā”ti [M 0.0311] vadanti, saṅghena taṃ adhikaraṇaṃ sampaṭicchitabbaṃ. Atha pana “vinicchinatha tāva, bhante, sace amhākaṃ khamissati, gaṇhissāmā”ti vadanti, “cetiyaṃ tāva vandathā”tiādīni vatvā dīghasuttaṃ katvā vissajjitabbaṃ. Te ce cirarattaṃ kilantā pakkantaparisā upacchinnapakkhā hutvā puna yācanti, yāvatatiyaṃ paṭikkhipitvā yadā nimmadā honti, tadā nesaṃ adhikaraṇaṃ vinicchinitabbaṃ. Vinicchinantehi ca sace alajjussannā hoti parisā, ubbāhikāya taṃ adhikaraṇaṃ vinicchinitabbaṃ. Sace bālussannā hoti parisā, “tumhākaṃ sabhāge vinayadhare pariyesathā”ti vinayadhare pariyesāpetvā yena dhammena yena vinayena yena satthusāsanena taṃ adhikaraṇaṃ vūpasammati, tathā taṃ adhikaraṇaṃ vūpasametabbaṃ.

231. Furthermore, among these accusations of the aforementioned types, when a matter is brought into the midst of the Saṅgha by means of any accusation whatsoever, the accused and the accuser should be told: “Will you be satisfied with our decision?” If they say, “We will be,” then the Saṅgha should accept that legal case. But if they say, “First decide, venerable sirs; if it is acceptable to us, we will accept it,” then, after saying such things as, “First pay homage to the shrine,” they should be dismissed by drawing out the matter. If, having become weary over a long time, with their assembly departed and their support cut off, they request again, they should be refused up to the third time. When they become free from pride, then their legal case should be decided. And by those deciding, if the assembly is full of shameless ones, that legal case should be decided by referral. If the assembly is full of foolish ones, having had them seek out those expert in the Vinaya by saying, “Seek out those expert in the Vinaya of your own group,” then by whichever Dhamma, by whichever Vinaya, by whichever teaching of the Teacher that legal case is settled, in that way should that legal case be settled.

Tattha ca dhammoti bhūtaṃ vatthu. Vinayoti codanā ceva sāraṇā ca. Satthusāsananti ñattisampadā ca anussāvanasampadā ca. Tasmā codakena vatthusmiṃ ārocite cuditako pucchitabbo “santametaṃ, no”ti. Evaṃ vatthuṃ upaparikkhitvā bhūtena vatthunā codetvā sāretvā ñattisampadāya ca anussāvanasampadāya ca taṃ adhikaraṇaṃ vūpasametabbaṃ. Tatra ce alajjī lajjiṃ codeti, so ca alajjī bālo hoti abyatto, nāssa nayo dātabbo, evaṃ pana vattabbo [V 0.0289] “kimhi naṃ codesī”ti. Addhā so vakkhati “kimidaṃ, bhante, kimhi naṃ nāmā”ti. “Tvaṃ kimhi nampi na jānāsi, na yuttaṃ tayā evarūpena bālena paraṃ codetu”nti uyyojetabbo, nāssa anuyogo dātabbo. Sace pana so alajjī paṇḍito hoti byatto, diṭṭhena vā sutena vā ajjhottharitvā sampādetuṃ sakkoti, etassa anuyogaṃ datvā lajjisseva paṭiññāya kammaṃ kātabbaṃ.

Herein, 'Dhamma' is the actual matter. 'Vinaya' is both accusation and reminding. 'The Teacher's instruction' is the accomplishment of the motion and the accomplishment of the proclamation. Therefore, when the accuser has announced the matter, the accused should be asked, 'Is this present, or not?' Having thus investigated the matter, that legal case should be settled by accusing and reminding based on the actual matter, and through the accomplishment of the motion and the accomplishment of the proclamation. If, in this case, a shameless monk accuses a conscientious one, and that shameless monk is foolish and unskilled, no procedure should be given to him. Instead, he should only be told, 'On what grounds do you accuse him?' Surely, he will say, 'Venerable sir, what is this thing called “on what grounds”?' He should be dismissed with the words, 'You do not even know “on what grounds”; it is not proper for such a fool as you to accuse another.' No inquiry should be given to him. But if that shameless monk is wise and skilled, and is able to overwhelm and establish the charge based on what was seen or heard, an inquiry should be given to him, and the formal act should be carried out based on the confession of the conscientious monk alone.

Sace lajjī alajjiṃ codeti, so ca lajjī bālo hoti abyatto, na sakkoti anuyogaṃ dātuṃ, tassa nayo dātabbo “kimhi naṃ codesi sīlavipattiyā vā ācāravipattiādīsu vā ekissā”ti. Kasmā pana imasseva evaṃ nayo dātabbo, na itarassāti, nanu na yuttaṃ vinayadharānaṃ agatigamananti? Na yuttameva. Idaṃ pana agatigamanaṃ na hoti, dhammānuggaho nāma eso. Alajjiniggahatthāya hi lajjipaggahatthāya ca sikkhāpadaṃ paññattaṃ. Tatra alajjī nayaṃ labhitvā ajjhottharanto ehiti, lajjī [M 0.0312] pana nayaṃ labhitvā diṭṭhe diṭṭhasantānena sute sutasantānena patiṭṭhāya kathessati, tasmā tassa dhammānuggaho vaṭṭati. Sace pana so lajjī paṇḍito hoti byatto, patiṭṭhāya katheti, alajjī ca “etampi natthi, etampi natthī”ti paṭiññaṃ na deti, alajjissa paṭiññāya eva kātabbaṃ.

If a conscientious monk accuses a shameless one, and that conscientious monk is a fool and unskilled, unable to follow up with an investigation, a procedure should be given to him: 'On what grounds do you accuse him? On a corruption of virtue, or on one among the corruptions of conduct and so on?' But why should this procedure be given only to him, and not to the other? Is it not improper for Vinaya experts to go on a wrong course? Indeed, it is improper. However, this is not going on a wrong course; this is called 'support through the Dhamma.' For the training rule was laid down for the suppression of the shameless and for the encouragement of the conscientious. Therein, the shameless one, having received the procedure, will come seeking to overwhelm. But the conscientious one, having received the procedure, will speak, being well-grounded, based on the continuity of what was seen and what was heard. Therefore, support through the Dhamma is proper for him. But if that conscientious one is wise and skilled, speaks being well-grounded, and the shameless one does not make an admission, saying, 'This too does not exist, and that too does not exist,' it should be dealt with according to the shameless one's denial.

Tadatthadīpanatthañca idaṃ vatthu veditabbaṃ – tipiṭakacūḷābhayatthero kira lohapāsādassa heṭṭhā bhikkhūnaṃ vinayaṃ kathetvā sāyanhasamaye vuṭṭhāti, tassa vuṭṭhānasamaye dve attapaccatthikā kathaṃ pavattesuṃ. Eko “etampi natthi, etampi natthī”ti paṭiññaṃ na deti, atha appāvasese paṭhamayāme therassa tasmiṃ puggale “ayaṃ patiṭṭhāya katheti, ayaṃ pana paṭiññaṃ na deti, bahūni ca vatthūni osaṭāni, addhā etaṃ kataṃ bhavissatī”ti asuddhaladdhi uppannā. Tato bījanīdaṇḍakena pādakathalikāya saññaṃ datvā “ahaṃ, āvuso, vinicchinituṃ ananucchaviko, aññena vinicchināpehī”ti āha. “Kasmā, bhante”ti? Thero tamatthaṃ ārocesi. Cuditakapuggalassa kāye ḍāho uṭṭhito, tato so theraṃ vanditvā “bhante, vinicchinituṃ anurūpena vinayadharena nāma tumhādiseneva bhavituṃ vaṭṭati, codakena ca īdiseneva bhavituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti vatvā setakāni nivāsetvā “ciraṃ kilamitāttha mayā”ti khamāpetvā pakkāmi.

And to illustrate that meaning, this story should be known. It is said that the Elder Tipiṭaka Cūḷābhaya, after teaching the Vinaya to the bhikkhus beneath the Lohapāsāda, rose in the evening. At the time of his rising, two bhikkhus who were adversaries began a dispute. One did not give an admission, saying, “This matter also does not exist; this matter also does not exist.” Then, when little remained of the first watch of the night, an opinion of ‘impure’ arose in the Elder concerning that person: “This one speaks haltingly, yet he does not give an admission, and many matters have been brought up; surely this deed must have been done.” Then, giving a sign on the footstool with his fan handle, he said, “Friends, I am not suitable to decide; have it decided by another.” When asked, “Why, venerable sir?” the Elder explained the matter. A burning sensation arose in the body of the accused person. Then, that person, having paid homage to the Elder, said, “Venerable sir, it is fitting that a Vinaya-holder suitable for deciding be one just like you, and it is fitting that the accuser be one just like this.” Having said this, he put on white clothes, asked for forgiveness, saying, “You have been troubled by me for a long time,” and departed.

Evaṃ lajjinā codiyamāno alajjī bahūsupi vatthūsu uppannesu paṭiññaṃ na deti, so neva “suddho”ti vattabbo, na “asuddho”ti, jīvamatako nāma āmakapūtiko nāma cesa. Sace panassa aññampi tādisaṃ vatthu uppajjati, na vinicchinitabbaṃ, tathā nāsitako bhavissati[V 0.0290]. Sace pana alajjīyeva alajjiṃ codeti, so vattabbo “āvuso, tava vacanenāyaṃ kiṃ sakkā vattu”nti. Itarampi tatheva vatvā “ubhopi ekasambhogaparibhogā hutvā jīvathā”ti uyyojetabbā. Sīlatthāya nesaṃ vinicchayo na kātabbo, pattacīvarapariveṇādiatthāya pana patirūpaṃ sakkhiṃ labhitvā kātabboti.

In this way, when a shameless one is accused by a conscientious one, even when many matters have arisen, he does not give an admission. He should be called neither ‘pure’ nor ‘impure’; he is called a ‘living corpse’ and ‘raw and putrid.’ And if another such matter arises for him, it should not be decided; he will be ruined in the same way. But if a shameless one accuses a shameless one, he, the accuser, should be told, “Friend, what can be said of this one by your word?” And having said the same to the other, the accused, they should be dismissed, saying, “Both of you, having common association and use, live on.” A decision should not be made for them for the sake of virtue. But for the sake of bowls, robes, monastic cells, and so on, it should be done after obtaining a suitable witness.

Atha lajjī lajjiṃ codeti, vivādo ca nesaṃ kismiñcideva appamattako hoti, saññāpetvā “mā evaṃ karothā”ti accayaṃ desāpetvā uyyojetabbā[M 0.0313]. Atha panettha cuditakena sahasā viraddhaṃ hoti, ādito paṭṭhāya alajjī nāma natthi. So ca pakkhānurakkhaṇatthāya paṭiññaṃ na deti, “mayaṃ saddahāma, mayaṃ saddahāmā”ti bahū uṭṭhahanti, so tesaṃ paṭiññāya ekavāraṃ dvevāraṃ suddho hotu, atha pana viraddhakālato paṭṭhāya ṭhāne na tiṭṭhati, vinicchayo na dātabbo.

Now, if a conscientious monk accuses another conscientious monk, and their dispute is over some trivial matter, they should be made to understand, saying, 'Do not act thus,' made to declare their fault, and then dismissed. But if, in this case, the accused has suddenly erred—though from the very beginning there is no one known as shameless—and he does not give an admission for the sake of protecting his faction, while many rise up saying, 'We believe, we believe,' let him be pure once or twice based on their admission. However, if from the time of the transgression onward he does not stand in the position of a conscientious one, a decision should not be given.

232. Adinnādānavatthuṃ vinicchinantena (pārā. aṭṭha. 1.92) pana pañcavīsati avahārā sādhukaṃ sallakkhetabbā. Tesu ca kusalena vinayadharena otiṇṇaṃ vatthuṃ sahasā avinicchinitvāva pañca ṭhānāni oloketabbāni, yāni sandhāya porāṇā āhu –

232. When judging a case of taking what is not given, the twenty-five modes of theft should be carefully considered. And a skilled Vinaya-holder, without hastily judging a case that has come before him, should examine five points, concerning which the ancients have said:

“Vatthuṃ kālañca desañca, agghaṃ paribhogapañcamaṃ;

Tulayitvā pañca ṭhānāni, dhāreyyatthaṃ vicakkhaṇo”ti. (pārā. aṭṭha. 1.92);

“The object, the time, the place, the value, and use as the fifth; having weighed these five points, the discerning one should understand the matter.”

Tattha vatthunti bhaṇḍaṃ. Avahārakena hi “mayā idaṃ nāma avahaṭa”nti vuttepi āpattiṃ anāropetvāva taṃ bhaṇḍaṃ “sasāmikaṃ vā asāmikaṃ vā”ti upaparikkhitabbaṃ. Sasāmikepi sāmikānaṃ sālayabhāvo vā nirālayabhāvo vā upaparikkhitabbo. Sace tesaṃ sālayakāle avahaṭaṃ, bhaṇḍaṃ agghāpetvā āpatti kātabbā. Sace nirālayakāle, pārājikena na kātabbā. Bhaṇḍasāmikesu pana bhaṇḍaṃ āharāpentesu bhaṇḍaṃ dātabbaṃ. Ayamettha sāmīci.

Therein, 'object' means the goods. Even if the one who took it says, 'I took such and such an item,' without first imposing an offense, those goods should be investigated as to whether they have an owner or are ownerless. Even in the case of having an owner, the owners' state of having attachment or no attachment should be investigated. If it was taken at a time when they had attachment, the goods should be valued and the offense applied. If at a time when they had no attachment, it should not be made a Pārājika offense. However, if the owners of the goods have them brought back, the goods should be given. This is the proper conduct here.

Imassa panatthassa dīpanatthamidaṃ vatthu – bhātiyarājakāle kira mahācetiyapūjāya dakkhiṇadisato eko bhikkhu sattahatthaṃ paṇḍukāsāvaṃ aṃse karitvā cetiyaṅgaṇaṃ pāvisi. Taṅkhaṇameva ca rājāpi cetiyavandanatthaṃ āgato. Tato ussāraṇāya vattamānāya mahājanasammaddo ahosi. Atha so bhikkhu janasammaddapīḷito aṃsato patantaṃ kāsāvaṃ adisvāva nikkhanto, nikkhamitvā [V 0.0291] kāsāvaṃ apassanto “ko īdise janasammadde kāsāvaṃ lacchati, na dāni taṃ mayha”nti dhuranikkhepaṃ katvā gato. Athañño bhikkhu pacchā āgacchanto taṃ kāsāvaṃ disvā theyyacittena gahetvā puna vippaṭisārī hutvā “assamaṇo dānimhi, vibbhamissāmī”ti citte uppanne “vinayadhare pucchitvā ñassāmī”ti cintesi.

And to illustrate this point, this story is told: It is said that during the reign of King Bhātiya, for paying homage at the great cetiya, a certain bhikkhu from the south entered the cetiya courtyard, carrying a seven-cubit, pale-yellow robe on his shoulder. And at that very moment, the king also arrived to pay homage to the cetiya. Then, while the ceremony was taking place, there was a great throng of people. Then that bhikkhu, pressed by the throng, departed without even seeing the robe falling from his shoulder. Having departed and not seeing the robe, he thought, 'Who could find a robe in such a throng? Now that robe is lost to me,' and having abandoned concern, he went away. Then another bhikkhu, coming later, saw that robe and, having taken it with a thieving mind, later felt remorse and, when the thought arose in his mind, 'Now I am no true monk; I will disrobe,' he thought, 'I will ask the Vinaya-holders and find out.'

Tena [M 0.0314] samayena cūḷasumanatthero nāma sabbapariyattidharo vinayācariyapāmokkho mahāvihāre paṭivasati. So bhikkhu theraṃ upasaṅkamitvā vanditvā okāsaṃ kāretvā attano kukkuccaṃ pucchi. Thero tena bhaṭṭhe janakāye pacchā āgantvā gahitabhāvaṃ ñatvā “atthi dāni ettha okāso”ti cintetvā āha “sace kāsāvasāmikaṃ bhikkhuṃ āneyyāsi, sakkā bhaveyya tava patiṭṭhā kātu”nti. Kathāhaṃ, bhante, taṃ dakkhissāmīti. Tahiṃ tahiṃ gantvā olokehīti. So pañcapi mahāvihāre oloketvā neva addakkhi. Tato naṃ thero pucchi “katarāya disāya bahū bhikkhū āgacchantī”ti? “Dakkhiṇadisāya, bhante”ti. Tena hi kāsāvaṃ dīghato ca tiriyañca minitvā ṭhapehi, ṭhapetvā dakkhiṇadisāya vihārapaṭipāṭiyā vicinitvā taṃ bhikkhuṃ ānehīti. So tathā katvā taṃ bhikkhuṃ disvā therassa santikaṃ ānesi. Thero pucchi “tavedaṃ kāsāva”nti? “Āma, bhante”ti. Kuhiṃ te pātitanti? So sabbaṃ ācikkhi. Thero tena kataṃ dhuranikkhepaṃ sutvā itaraṃ pucchi “tayā idaṃ kuhiṃ disvā gahita”nti? Sopi sabbaṃ ārocesi. Tato taṃ thero āha “sace te suddhacittena gahitaṃ abhavissa, anāpattiyeva te assa, theyyacittena pana gahitattā dukkaṭaṃ āpannosi, taṃ desetvā anāpattiko hoti, idañca kāsāvaṃ attano santakaṃ katvā etasseva bhikkhuno dehī”ti. So bhikkhu amateneva abhisitto varamassāsappatto ahosi. Evaṃ vatthu oloketabbaṃ.

At that time, an elder named Cūḷasumana, a master of all scriptures and foremost among Vinaya teachers, was residing at the Great Monastery. That bhikkhu approached the Elder, paid respects, requested an opportunity, and asked about his scruple. The Elder, knowing that it had been taken after the crowd had dispersed, thought, “Now there is a basis here,” and said, “If you can bring the bhikkhu who owns the robe, it might be possible to establish a basis for you.” “How, venerable sir, shall I see him?” “Go here and there and look.” He searched all five great monasteries but did not see him. Then the Elder asked him, “From which direction do many bhikkhus come?” “From the south, venerable sir.” “Then measure the robe lengthwise and widthwise, put it aside, and having put it aside, search along the row of monasteries to the south and bring that bhikkhu.” He did so and, having seen that bhikkhu, brought him to the Elder. The Elder asked, “Is this your robe?” “Yes, venerable sir.” “Where was it dropped by you?” He explained everything. The Elder, having heard about the abandoning of concern done by him, asked the other, “Where did you see and take this?” He too told everything. Then the Elder said to him, “If it had been taken by you with a pure mind, there would have been no offense for you. But since it was taken with a thieving mind, you have incurred a dukkaṭa offense. Having confessed that, you will be free of offense. And make this robe your own and give it to this very bhikkhu.” That bhikkhu was as if sprinkled with ambrosia and attained supreme consolation. Thus, the case should be examined.

Kāloti avahārakālo. Tadeva hi bhaṇḍaṃ kadāci appagghaṃ hoti, kadāci mahagghaṃ. Tasmā taṃ bhaṇḍaṃ yasmiṃ kāle avahaṭaṃ, tasmiṃyeva kāle yo tassa aggho hoti, tena agghena āpatti kāretabbā. Evaṃ kālo oloketabbo.

‘Time’ means the time of theft. For indeed, the same goods are sometimes of little value, and sometimes of great value. Therefore, at whatever time those goods were stolen, the offense should be determined according to the value that they had at that very time. Thus, time should be examined.

Desoti avahāradeso. Tañhi bhaṇḍaṃ yasmiṃ dese avahaṭaṃ, tasmiṃyeva dese yo tassa aggho hoti, tena agghena āpatti kāretabbā. Bhaṇḍuṭṭhānadese hi bhaṇḍaṃ appagghaṃ hoti, aññattha mahagghaṃ.

‘Place’ means the place of theft. For indeed, in whatever place those goods were stolen, the offense should be determined by the value they have in that very place. For goods are of little value in their place of origin, but of great value elsewhere.

Imassapi [V 0.0292] ca atthassa dīpanatthamidaṃ vatthu – antarasamudde kira eko bhikkhu susaṇṭhānaṃ nāḷikeraṃ labhitvā bhamaṃ āropetvā saṅkhathālakasadisaṃ manoramaṃ pānīyathālakaṃ katvā tattheva ṭhapetvā cetiyagiriṃ agamāsi[M 0.0315]. Añño bhikkhu antarasamuddaṃ gantvā tasmiṃ vihāre paṭivasanto taṃ thālakaṃ disvā theyyacittena gahetvā cetiyagirimeva āgato. Tassa tattha yāguṃ pivantassa taṃ thālakaṃ disvā thālakasāmiko bhikkhu āha “kuto te idaṃ laddha”nti. Antarasamuddato me ānītanti. So taṃ “netaṃ tava santakaṃ, theyyāya te gahita”nti saṅghamajjhaṃ ākaḍḍhi. Tattha ca vinicchayaṃ alabhitvā mahāvihāraṃ agamiṃsu, tattha ca bheriṃ paharāpetvā mahācetiyasamīpe sannipātaṃ katvā vinicchayaṃ ārabhiṃsu. Vinayadharattherā avahāraṃ saññāpesuṃ.

And to illustrate this meaning, this is the story: It is said that on an island in the middle of the ocean, a certain bhikkhu, having obtained a beautifully shaped coconut, placed it on a lathe and made a delightful drinking bowl resembling a conch-shell bowl. Having placed it right there, he went to Cetiyagiri. Another bhikkhu, having gone to the island in the middle of the ocean and while dwelling in that monastery, saw that bowl, and taking it with a thieving mind, came to Cetiyagiri itself. While he was drinking gruel there, the bhikkhu who owned the bowl saw it and asked, “From where did you get this?” When he said, “It was brought by me from the island in the middle of the ocean,” the owner dragged him into the midst of the Saṅgha, saying, “This is not your property; it was taken by you through theft.” And not obtaining a legal decision there, they went to the Mahāvihāra. And there, having caused the drum to be beaten and having convened an assembly near the Mahācetiya, they began the legal decision. The Elders who were masters of the Vinaya recognized it as a theft.

Tasmiñca sannipāte ābhidhammikagodattatthero nāma vinayakusalo hoti, so evamāha “iminā idaṃ thālakaṃ kuhiṃ avahaṭa”nti? “Antarasamudde avahaṭa”nti. Tattha taṃ kiṃ agghatīti. Na kiñci agghati. Tatra hi nāḷikeraṃ bhinditvā miñjaṃ khāditvā kapālaṃ chaḍḍeti, dāruatthaṃ pana pharatīti. Imassa bhikkhuno ettha hatthakammaṃ kiṃ agghatīti? Māsakaṃ vā ūnamāsakaṃ vāti. Atthi pana katthaci sammāsambuddhena māsake vā ūnamāsake vā pārājikaṃ paññattanti. Evaṃ vutte “sādhu sādhu, sukathitaṃ suvinicchita”nti ekasādhukāro ahosi. Tena ca samayena bhātiyarājāpi cetiyavandanatthaṃ nagarato nikkhanto taṃ saddaṃ sutvā “kiṃ ida”nti pucchitvā sabbaṃ paṭipāṭiyā sutvā nagare bheriṃ carāpesi “mayi sante bhikkhūnampi bhikkhunīnampi gihīnampi adhikaraṇaṃ ābhidhammikagodattattherena vinicchitaṃ suvinicchitaṃ, tassa vinicchaye atiṭṭhamānaṃ rājāṇāya ṭhapemī”ti. Evaṃ deso oloketabbo.

And at that gathering, there was an elder named Abhidhammika Godatta, skilled in the Vinaya, who said thus: “Where was this bowl stolen by this one?” “It was stolen on the island in the middle of the ocean.” “What is it worth there?” “It is worth nothing. For there, having broken a coconut, one eats the kernel and discards the shell; it serves only for the purpose of firewood.” “What is the value of this bhikkhu’s handiwork in this?” “A māsaka or less than a māsaka.” “But is there any instance where a pārājika for a māsaka or less than a māsaka has been laid down by the Perfectly Enlightened One?” When this was said, there arose a single cry of approval: “Good, good! Well-spoken, well-judged!” And at that time, King Bhātiya, having also left the city to venerate the cetiya, heard that sound and asked, “What is this?” After hearing the full account in order, he had a drum proclaimed in the city: “While I am present, any dispute of bhikkhus, bhikkhunīs, or laypeople decided by the Elder Abhidhammika Godatta is well-decided. Whoever does not abide by his decision, I will enforce it by royal authority.” Thus, the place should be examined.

Agghoti bhaṇḍaggho. Navabhaṇḍassa hi yo aggho hoti, so pacchā parihāyati. Yathā navadhoto patto aṭṭha vā dasa vā agghati, so pacchā bhinno vā chiddo vā āṇigaṇṭhikāhato vā appaggho hoti, tasmā na sabbadā bhaṇḍaṃ pakatiaggheneva kātabbanti. Evaṃ aggho oloketabbo.

‘Value’ means the value of the goods. For the value that new goods have, that later depreciates. Just as a newly fired bowl may be worth eight or ten, but later, if it is broken, or perforated, or damaged by a nail-knot, it becomes of little value; therefore, the goods should not always be valued at their original price. Thus, the value should be examined.

Paribhogoti bhaṇḍaparibhogo. Paribhogenapi hi vāsiādibhaṇḍassa aggho parihāyati. Tasmā evaṃ upaparikkhitabbaṃ – sace koci kassaci pādagghanakaṃ vāsiṃ harati, tatra vāsisāmiko pucchitabbo “tayā ayaṃ vāsi kittakena kītā”ti? “Pādena, bhante”ti. Kiṃ pana te kiṇitvāva ṭhapitā, udāhu naṃ vaḷañjesīti? Sace vadati “ekadivasaṃ me dantakaṭṭhaṃ [M 0.0316] vā rajanachalli vā pattapacanakadāru vā chinnaṃ, ghaṃsitvā vā nisitā”ti, athassa porāṇako [V 0.0293] aggho bhaṭṭhoti veditabbo. Yathā ca vāsiyā, evaṃ añjaniyā vā añjanisalākāya vā kuñcikāya vā palālena vā thusehi vā iṭṭhakacuṇṇena vā ekavāraṃ ghaṃsitvā dhovitamattenapi aggho bhassati. Tipumaṇḍalassa makaradantacchedanenapi parimajjanamattenapi, udakasāṭakassa sakiṃ nivāsanapārupanenapi paribhogasīsena aṃse vā sīse vā ṭhapanamattenapi, taṇḍulādīnaṃ papphoṭanenapi tato ekaṃ vā dve vā apanayanenapi antamaso ekaṃ pāsāṇasakkharaṃ uddharitvā chaḍḍitamattenapi, sappitelādīnaṃ bhājanantarapaavattanenapi antamaso tato makkhikaṃ vā kipillikaṃ vā uddharitvā chaḍḍitamattenapi, guḷapiṇḍakassa madhurabhāvajānanatthaṃ nakhena vijjhitvā aṇumattaṃ gahitamattenapi aggho bhassati. Tasmā yaṃ kiñci pādagghanakaṃ vuttanayeneva sāmikehi paribhogena ūnaṃ kataṃ hoti, na taṃ avahaṭo bhikkhu pārājikena kātabboti. Evaṃ aggho oloketabbo.

Usage (paribhoga) means the usage of goods. For indeed, even through usage, the value of goods such as an adze depreciates. Therefore, it should be investigated thus: if a certain bhikkhu steals another's adze worth a pāda, the owner of the adze should be asked, 'For how much was this adze bought by you?' 'For a pāda, venerable sir.' 'But was it just bought and kept by you, or did you use it?' If he says, 'For one day I cut a tooth-stick, or bark for dyeing robes, or firewood for baking a bowl with it, or it was sharpened by rubbing,' then it should be known that its former value is diminished. And just as with an adze, so too with an ointment pot, or an ointment applicator, or a key, even by merely rubbing and washing it once with straw, or with husks, or with brick dust, the value diminishes. Of a lead plate, the value diminishes even by merely cutting it in the shape of a makara's tooth or by merely wiping it. Of a water-cloth, the value diminishes even by wearing it as a lower or upper garment once, or by merely placing it on the shoulder or head by way of usage. Of rice and so on, the value diminishes even by merely winnowing it, or by removing one or two grains from it, or even by merely picking up and discarding a single stone or piece of gravel. Of ghee, oil, and so on, the value diminishes even by merely transferring it to another vessel, or even by merely picking up and discarding a fly or an ant from it. Of a lump of jaggery, the value diminishes even by merely piercing it with a fingernail to know its sweetness and taking a minute particle. Therefore, whatever item worth a pāda has been made to be of lesser value by the owners through usage in the way already described, a bhikkhu who has stolen it is not to be dealt with by a pārājika. Thus, the value should be examined.

Evaṃ imāni tulayitvā pañca ṭhānāni dhāreyya atthaṃ vicakkhaṇo, āpattiṃ vā anāpattiṃ vā garukaṃ vā lahukaṃ vā āpattiṃ yathāṭhāne ṭhapeyyāti. Tenāhu aṭṭhakathācariyā –

Thus, a discerning one, having weighed these five factors, should determine the case; he should place an offense or no offense, a grave or a light offense, in its proper place. Therefore, the commentary teachers said:

“Sikkhāpadaṃ samaṃ tena, aññaṃ kiñci na vijjati;

Anekanayavokiṇṇaṃ, gambhīratthavinicchayaṃ.

No other training rule whatsoever is found to be equal to it, which is replete with numerous methods and has a profound ascertainment of meaning.

“Tasmā vatthumhi otiṇṇe, bhikkhunā vinayaññunā;

Vinayānuggahenettha, karontena vinicchayaṃ.

Therefore, when a case has arisen, a judgment in this matter is to be made by a monk skilled in the Vinaya, for the support of the Vinaya.

“Pāḷiṃ aṭṭhakathañceva, sādhippāyamasesato;

Ogayha appamattena, karaṇīyo vinicchayo.

Having completely penetrated the Pāḷi and the Commentary along with their meaning, the judgment should be made with heedfulness.

“Āpattidassanussāho, na kattabbo kudācanaṃ;

Passissāmi anāpatti-miti kayirātha mānasaṃ.

An effort to see an offense should never be made; one should form the mental resolve: 'I shall see a non-offense.'

“Passitvāpi ca āpattiṃ, avatvāva punappunaṃ;

Vīmaṃsitvātha viññūhi, saṃsanditvā ca taṃ vade.

And even having seen an offense, without yet pronouncing it, one should declare it only after investigating it again and again and conferring with the wise.

“Kappiyepi [M 0.0317][V 0.0294] ca vatthusmiṃ, cittassa lahuvattino;

Vasena sāmaññaguṇā, cavantīdha puthujjanā.

Here, even in regard to an allowable object, the virtues of recluseship of ordinary people fall away due to the influence of a fickle mind.

“Tasmā paraparikkhāraṃ, āsīvisamivoragaṃ;

Aggiṃ viya ca sampassaṃ, nāmaseyya vicakkhaṇo”ti. (pārā. aṭṭha. 1.160-1 tatrāyaṃ anusāsanī);

Therefore, a discerning person, regarding another's requisite as like a venomous snake and like a fire, should not handle it. This is the instruction.

233. Uttarimanussadhammārocanaṃ vinicchinantena (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.197) pana “kiṃ te adhigataṃ. Kinti te adhigataṃ, kadā te adhigataṃ, kattha te adhigataṃ, katame te kilesā pahīnā, katamesaṃ tvaṃ dhammānaṃ lābhī”ti imāni cha ṭhānāni visodhetabbāni. Sace hi koci bhikkhu uttarimanussadhammādhigamaṃ byākareyya, na so ettāvatā sakkāro kātabbo, imesaṃ pana channaṃ ṭhānānaṃ sodhanatthaṃ evaṃ vattabbo “kiṃ te adhigataṃ, kiṃ jhānaṃ udāhu vimokkhādīsu aññatara”nti. Yo hi yena adhigato dhammo, so tassa pākaṭo hoti. Sace “idaṃ nāma me adhigata”nti vadati, tato “kinti te adhigata”nti pucchitabbo, “aniccalakkhaṇādīsu kiṃ dhuraṃ katvā aṭṭhatiṃsāya vā ārammaṇesu rūpārūpaajjhattabahiddhādibhedesu vā dhammesu kena mukhena abhinivisitvā”ti. Yo hi yassābhiniveso, so tassa pākaṭo hoti. Sace “ayaṃ nāma me abhiniveso, evaṃ mayā adhigata”nti vadati, tato “kadā te adhigata”nti pucchitabbo, “kiṃ pubbaṇhe, udāhu majjhanhikādīsu aññatarasmiṃ kāle”ti. Sabbesañhi attanā adhigatakālo pākaṭo hoti. Sace “amukasmiṃ nāma kāle adhigaka”nti vadati, tato “kattha te adhigata”nti pucchitabbo, “kiṃ divāṭṭhāne, udāhu rattiṭṭhānādīsu aññatarasmiṃ okāse”ti. Sabbesañhi attanā adhigatokāso pākaṭo hoti. Sace “amukasmiṃ nāma me okāse adhigata”nti vadati, tato “katame te kilesā pahīnā”ti pucchitabbo, “kiṃ paṭhamamaggavajjhā, udāhu dutiyādimaggavajjhā”ti. Sabbesañhi attanā adhigatamaggena pahīnā kilesā pākaṭā honti.

233. However, when investigating a declaration of a superhuman state, these six points should be clarified: 'What have you attained? How have you attained it? When did you attain it? Where did you attain it? Which defilements have you abandoned? Of which dhammas are you a recipient?' For if any monk declares an attainment of a superhuman state, he should not be honored merely on that account. But, to clarify these six points, he should be asked thus: 'What have you attained? Is it a jhāna or one of the liberations, etc.?' For whatever state one has attained, that is evident to him. If he says, 'I have attained such-and-such,' then he should be asked, 'How have you attained it? By focusing on which characteristic—impermanence, etc.—or by fixing attention on one of the thirty-eight objects, or by what approach among the dhammas distinguished as material and immaterial, internal and external, etc.?' For whatever his mental application was, that is evident to him. If he says, 'This was my mental application, and this is how I attained it,' then he should be asked, 'When did you attain it? Was it in the forenoon, or at one of the other times like midday, etc.?' For the time of one's own attainment is evident to everyone. If he says, 'I attained it at such-and-such a time,' then he should be asked, 'Where did you attain it? Was it in the day-quarters, or in some other place such as the night-quarters, etc.?' For the location of one's own attainment is evident to everyone. If he says, 'I attained it in such-and-such a place,' then he should be asked, 'Which defilements have you abandoned? Were they those eradicated by the first path, or by the second path, etc.?' For the defilements abandoned by the path one has attained are evident to everyone.

Sace “ime nāma me kilesā pahīnā”ti vadati, tato “katamesaṃ tvaṃ dhammānaṃ lābhī”ti pucchitabbo, “kiṃ sotāpattimaggassa, udāhu sakadāgāmimaggādīsu aññatarassā”ti. Sabbesañhi attanā adhigatadhammo pākaṭo [M 0.0318] hoti. Sace “imesaṃ nāmāhaṃ dhammānaṃ lābhī”ti vadati, ettāvatāpissa vacanaṃ na saddhātabbaṃ. Bahussutā hi uggahaparipucchākusalā bhikkhū imāni cha ṭhānāni sodhetuṃ sakkonti, imassa pana bhikkhuno āgamanapaṭipadā [V 0.0295] sodhetabbā. Yadi āgamanapaṭipadā na sujjhati, “imāya paṭipadāya lokuttaradhammo nāma na labbhatī”ti apanetabbo. Yadi panassa āgamanapaṭipadā sujjhati, dīgharattaṃ tīsu sikkhāsu appamatto jāgariyamanuyutto catūsu paccayesu alaggo ākāse pāṇisamena cetasā viharatīti paññāyati, tassa bhikkhuno byākaraṇaṃ paṭipadāya saddhiṃ saṃsandati. “Seyyathāpi nāma gaṅgodakaṃ yamunodakena saṃsandati sameti, evameva supaññattā tena bhagavatā sāvakānaṃ nibbānagāminī paṭipadā, saṃsandati nibbānañca paṭipadā cā”ti (dī. ni. 2.296) vuttasadisaṃ hoti. Apica kho na ettakenapi sakkāro kātabbo. Kasmā? Ekaccassa hi puthujjanassapi sato khīṇāsavassa paṭipattisadisā paṭipatti hoti, tasmā so bhikkhu tehi tehi upāyehi uttāsetabbo. Khīṇāsavassa nāma asaniyāpi matthake patamānāya bhayaṃ vā chambhitattaṃ vā lomahaṃso vā na hoti, puthujjanassa appamattakenapi hoti.

If he says, ‘These defilements have been abandoned by me,’ then he should be asked, ‘Which dhammas have you attained? Is it the path of stream-entry, or else one or another among the paths of once-returning and so on?’ For to everyone, the dhamma attained by oneself is manifest. If he says, ‘I have attained these dhammas,’ even with this much his word should not yet be believed. For learned monks, skilled in study and inquiry, are able to clarify these six points; however, this monk’s practice leading to attainment must be scrutinized. If the practice leading to attainment is not pure, he should be dismissed with the words, ‘By this practice, a supramundane dhamma is not obtained.’ But if his practice leading to attainment is pure—if it is apparent that for a long time he has dwelt diligently in the three trainings, devoted to wakefulness, unattached to the four requisites, and with a mind like the palm of the hand in the sky—then that monk’s declaration aligns with his practice. It becomes similar to what was said: ‘Just as the waters of the Ganges meet and merge with those of the Yamuna, so too does the well-proclaimed path leading to Nibbāna, taught by the Blessed One for his disciples, converge with Nibbāna itself.’ Moreover, honor should not be shown even for this much. Why? For even a certain ordinary person may have a practice similar to the practice of one whose cankers are destroyed. Therefore, that monk should be startled by various means. For one whose cankers are destroyed, there is no fear, trembling, or goosebumps even if a thunderbolt were to strike his head, but for an ordinary person, it would arise from the slightest thing.

Tatrimāni vatthūni (ma. ni. aṭṭha. 3.102) – dīghabhāṇakaabhayatthero kira ekaṃ piṇḍapātikaṃ pariggahetuṃ asakkonto daharassa saññaṃ adāsi. So taṃ nahāyamānaṃ kalyāṇīnadīmukhadvāre nimujjitvā pāde aggahesi. Piṇḍapātiko “kumbhīlo”ti saññāya mahāsaddamakāsi, tadā naṃ “puthujjano”ti jāniṃsu.

In this matter, these are the stories: It is said that the elder Abhaya, the Dīghabhāṇaka, being unable to investigate a certain alms-goer, gave a sign to a young monk. That young monk, diving down at the mouth of the Kalyāṇī river, seized the feet of that alms-goer who was bathing. The alms-goer, with the perception ‘It is a crocodile!’, made a loud cry. Then, they knew him to be an ordinary person.

Candamukhatissarājakāle pana mahāvihāre saṅghatthero khīṇāsavo dubbalacakkhuko vihāreyeva acchati. Rājā “theraṃ pariggaṇhissāmī”ti bhikkhūsu bhikkhācāraṃ gatesu appasaddo upasaṅkamitvā sappo viya pāde aggahesi. Thero silāthambho viya niccalo hutvā “ko etthā”ti āha. “Ahaṃ, bhante, tisso”ti? “Sugandhaṃ vāyasi no tissā”ti. Evaṃ khīṇāsavassa bhayaṃ nāma natthi.

But during the time of King Candamukha Tissa, the elder of the Saṅgha in the Mahāvihāra, a destroyer of the cankers who had weak eyes, was dwelling in the monastery itself. The king, thinking, ‘I will investigate the elder,’ approached quietly when the monks had gone on their alms-round and, like a snake, seized the elder’s feet. The elder, becoming as motionless as a stone pillar, said, ‘Who is here?’ ‘It is I, venerable sir, Tissa.’ The elder said, ‘You are very fragrant, Tissa!’ Thus, for one who has destroyed the cankers, there is no such thing as fear.

Ekacco pana puthujjanopi atisūro hoti nibbhayo. So rajanīyena ārammaṇena pariggaṇhitabbo. Vasabharājāpi ekaṃ theraṃ pariggaṇhamāno ghare nisīdāpetvā tassa santike badarasāḷavaṃ maddamāno [M 0.0319] nisīdi. Mahātherassa kheḷo calito, therassa puthujjanabhāvo āvibhūto. Khīṇāsavassa hi rasataṇhā nāma suppahīnā, dibbesupi rasesu nikanti nāma na hoti, tasmā imehi upāyehi pariggahetvā sacassa bhayaṃ vā chambhitattaṃ vā rasataṇhā vā uppajjati, “na ca tvaṃ arahā”ti apanetabbo. Sace pana abhīru acchambhī anutrāsī hutvā sīho viya nisīdati, dibbārammaṇepi nikantiṃ na janeti, ayaṃ bhikkhu sampannaveyyākaraṇo [V 0.0296] samantā rājarājamahāmattādīhi pesitaṃ sakkāraṃ arahatīti veditabbo. Evaṃ tāva uttarimanussadhammārocanaṃ vinicchinitabbaṃ.

Furthermore, a certain ordinary person may also be exceedingly brave and fearless. He should be investigated with a passion-arousing object. King Vasabha also, while investigating a certain elder, had him sit in the house and sat near him, crushing ripe jujubes. The great elder’s saliva flowed, and the elder’s state as an ordinary person became manifest. Indeed, for one who has destroyed the cankers, craving for tastes is well abandoned; there is no such thing as delight even in divine tastes. Therefore, having investigated with these means, if for him fear or stiffness or craving for tastes arises, he should be dismissed with the words, ‘You are not an Arahant.’ But if, being fearless, unstiffened, and unterrified, he sits like a lion and does not generate delight even in a divine object, this monk should be known as one whose declaration is accomplished and as worthy of the honor sent from all around by kings, great ministers, and others. Thus, in this way, the declaration of a superhuman state should be decided.

234. Sakale pana vinayavinicchaye (pārā. aṭṭha. 1.45) kosallaṃ patthayantena catubbidho vinayo jānitabbo.

234. However, by one who desires skill in the entire determination of the Vinaya, the fourfold Vinaya should be known.

Catubbidhañhi vinayaṃ, mahātherā mahiddhikā;

Nīharitvā pakāsesuṃ, dhammasaṅgāhakā purā.

For in ancient times, the great elders of great psychic power, the compilers of the Dhamma, extracted and expounded the fourfold Vinaya.

Katamaṃ catubbidhaṃ? Suttaṃ suttānulomaṃ ācariyavādaṃ attanomatinti. Yaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ “āhaccapadena kho, mahārāja, rasena ācariyavaṃsena adhippāyā”ti (mi. pa. 4.2.3). Ettha hi āhaccapadanti suttaṃ adhippetaṃ. Rasoti suttānulomaṃ. Ācariyavaṃsoti ācariyavādo. Adhippāyoti attanomati.

What is the fourfold? The Sutta, the Suttānuloma, the Ācariyavāda, and the Attanomati. Regarding this, it was said: “O great king, by the direct word, by the general principle, by the lineage of teachers, and by one’s own opinion.” Herein, ‘direct word’ (āhaccapada) is intended for the Sutta. ‘General principle’ (rasa) is for the Suttānuloma. ‘Lineage of teachers’ (ācariyavaṃsa) is for the Ācariyavāda. ‘One’s own opinion’ (adhippāya) is for the Attanomati.

Tattha suttaṃ nāma sakalavinayapiṭake pāḷi.

Therein, what is called ‘Sutta’ is the Pāḷi in the entire Vinaya Piṭaka.

Suttānulomaṃ nāma cattāro mahāpadesā. Ye bhagavatā evaṃ vuttā –

What is called ‘Suttānuloma’ are the four great references, which were spoken by the Blessed One thus:

“Yaṃ, bhikkhave, mayā ‘idaṃ na kappatī’ti appaṭikkhittaṃ, tañce akappiyaṃ anulometi, kappiyaṃ paṭibāhati, taṃ vo na kappati. Yaṃ, bhikkhave, mayā ‘idaṃ na kappatī’ti appaṭikkhittaṃ, tañce kappiyaṃ anulometi, akappiyaṃ paṭibāhati, taṃ vo kappati. Yaṃ, bhikkhave, mayā ‘idaṃ kappatī’ti ananuññātaṃ, taṃ ce akappiyaṃ anulometi, kappiyaṃ paṭibāhati, taṃ vo na kappati. Yaṃ, bhikkhave, mayā ‘idaṃ kappatī’ti ananuññātaṃ, tañce kappiyaṃ anulometi, akappiyaṃ paṭibāhati, taṃ vo kappatī”ti (mahāva. 305).

“Monks, whatever has not been rejected by me as ‘This is not allowable,’ should it conform to what is unallowable and contradict what is allowable, that is not allowable for you. Monks, whatever has not been rejected by me as ‘This is not allowable,’ should it conform to what is allowable and contradict what is unallowable, that is allowable for you. Monks, whatever has not been permitted by me as ‘This is allowable,’ should it conform to what is unallowable and contradict what is allowable, that is not allowable for you. Monks, whatever has not been permitted by me as ‘This is allowable,’ should it conform to what is allowable and contradict what is unallowable, that is allowable for you.”

Ācariyavādo [M 0.0320] nāma dhammasaṅgāhakehi pañcahi arahantasatehi ṭhapitā pāḷivinimuttā okkantavinicchayappavattā aṭṭhakathātanti.

What is called ‘Ācariyavāda’ is the lineage of the Aṭṭhakathā, established by the five hundred Arahant compilers of the Dhamma, which is separate from the Pāḷi and proceeds as an authoritative determination.

Attanomati [V 0.0297] nāma suttasuttānulomaācariyavāde muñcitvā anumānena attano anubuddhiyā nayaggāhena upaṭṭhitākārakathanaṃ.

What is called ‘Attanomati’ is, having set aside the Sutta, the Suttānuloma, and the Ācariyavāda, the stating of the matter as it presents itself through inference, according to one's own understanding, and by grasping a method.

Apica suttantābhidhammavinayaṭṭhakathāsu āgato sabbopi theravādo attanomati nāma. Taṃ pana attanomatiṃ gahetvā kathentena na daḷhaggāhaṃ gahetvā voharitabbaṃ, kāraṇaṃ sallakkhetvā atthena pāḷiṃ, pāḷiyā ca atthaṃ saṃsanditvā kathetabbaṃ, attanomati ācariyavāde otāretabbā. Sace tattha otarati ceva sameti ca, gahetabbā. Sace neva otarati na sameti, na gahetabbā. Ayañhi attanomati nāma sabbadubbalā, attanomatito ācariyavādo balavataro.

Furthermore, the entire Theravāda that is found in the commentaries on the Suttanta, Abhidhamma, and Vinaya is called 'one's own opinion' (attanomati). However, one who speaks taking that 'one's own opinion' should not speak holding a firm grasp. Having considered the reason, one should speak only after comparing the Pāḷi with the commentary, and the commentary with the Pāḷi. 'One's own opinion' should be checked against the teachers' tradition (ācariyavāda). If it fits and is consistent with it, it should be accepted. If it neither fits nor is consistent, it should not be accepted. For this 'one's own opinion' is the weakest of all; the teachers' tradition is stronger than 'one's own opinion'.

Ācariyavādopi suttānulome otāretabbo. Tattha otaranto samento eva gahetabbo, itaro na gahetabbo. Ācariyavādato hi suttānulomaṃ balavataraṃ.

The teachers' tradition should also be checked against the Suttānuloma. Therein, only that which fits and is consistent should be accepted; the other should not be accepted. For the Suttānuloma is stronger than the teachers' tradition.

Suttānulomampi sutte otāretabbaṃ. Tattha otarantaṃ samentameva gahetabbaṃ, itaraṃ na gahetabbaṃ. Suttānulomato hi suttameva balavataraṃ. Suttañhi appaṭivattiyaṃ kārakasaṅghasadisaṃ buddhānaṃ ṭhitakālasadisaṃ. Tasmā yadā dve bhikkhū sākacchanti, sakavādī suttaṃ gahetvā katheti, paravādī suttānulomaṃ. Tehi aññamaññaṃ khepaṃ vā garahaṃ vā akatvā suttānulomaṃ sutte otāretabbaṃ. Sace otarati sameti, gahetabbaṃ, no ce, na gahetabbaṃ, suttasmiṃyeva ṭhātabbaṃ. Athāyaṃ suttaṃ gahetvā katheti, paro ācariyavādaṃ. Tehipi aññamaññaṃ khepaṃ vā garahaṃ vā akatvā ācariyavādo sutte otāretabbo. Sace otarati sameti, gahetabbo. Anotaranto asamento ca gārayhācariyavādo na gahetabbo, suttasmiṃyeva ṭhātabbaṃ. Athāyaṃ suttaṃ gahetvā katheti, paro attanomatiṃ. Tehipi aññamaññaṃ khepaṃ vā garahaṃ vā akatvā attanomati sutte otāretabbā. Sace otarati sameti, gahetabbā, no ce, na gahetabbā, suttasmiṃyeva ṭhātabbaṃ.

The Suttānuloma should also be checked against the Sutta. Therein, only that which fits and is consistent should be accepted; the other should not be accepted. For the Sutta itself is stronger than the Suttānuloma. Indeed, the Sutta is irreversible, like the Saṅgha of the Councils, and like the time when the Buddhas were present. Therefore, when two monks are discussing, and the first proponent presents the Sutta while the other proponent presents the Suttānuloma, they should, without mutual disparagement or blame, check the Suttānuloma against the Sutta. If it fits and is consistent, it should be accepted; if not, it should not be accepted, and one should stand on the Sutta alone. Again, if the first proponent presents the Sutta while the other presents the teachers' tradition, they too, without mutual disparagement or blame, should check the teachers' tradition against the Sutta. If it fits and is consistent, it should be accepted. A blameworthy teachers' tradition that does not fit and is not consistent should not be accepted; one should stand on the Sutta alone. Again, if the first proponent presents the Sutta while the other presents 'one's own opinion', they too, without mutual disparagement or blame, should check 'one's own opinion' against the Sutta. If it fits and is consistent, it should be accepted; if not, it should not be accepted, and one should stand on the Sutta alone.

Athāyaṃ [M 0.0321] suttānulomaṃ gahetvā katheti, paro suttaṃ, suttānulome otāretabbaṃ. Sace otarati sameti, tisso saṅgītiyo āruḷhaṃ pāḷiāgataṃ paññāyati, gahetabbaṃ, no ce tathā paññāyati, na otarati na sameti, bāhirakasuttaṃ vā hoti siloko vā aññaṃ vā gārayhasuttaṃ guḷhavessantaraguḷhavinayavedallādīnaṃ aññatarato ābhataṃ, na gahetabbaṃ, suttānulomasmiṃyeva ṭhātabbaṃ. Athāyaṃ suttānulomaṃ gahetvā katheti, paro ācariyavādaṃ. Ācariyavādo [V 0.0298] suttānulome otāretabbo. Sace otarati sameti, gahetabbo. No ce, na gahetabbo, suttānulomeyeva ṭhātabbaṃ. Athāyaṃ suttānulomaṃ gahetvā katheti, paro attanomatiṃ. Attanomati suttānulome otāretabbā. Sace otarati sameti, gahetabbā. No ce, na gahetabbā, suttānulomeyeva ṭhātabbaṃ.

Then, if this proponent speaks taking up the Suttānuloma, and the other [cites] a Sutta, that Sutta should be checked against the Suttānuloma. If it conforms and agrees, it is known as being included in the three Councils and as having come down in the Pāḷi, and it should be accepted. If it is not known thus, does not conform, and does not agree, it is either an external Sutta, or a verse, or some other blameworthy Sutta brought from one of the suttas of the Mahāsaṅghika school, such as the Guḷhavessantara, Guḷhavinaya, and Guḷhavedalla; it should not be accepted. One should stand firm only in the Suttānuloma. Then, if this proponent speaks taking up the Suttānuloma, and the other [cites] a teacher's doctrine, that teacher's doctrine should be checked against the Suttānuloma. If it conforms and agrees, it should be accepted. If not, it should not be accepted; one should stand firm only in the Suttānuloma. Then, if this proponent speaks taking up the Suttānuloma, and the other [cites] a personal opinion, that personal opinion should be checked against the Suttānuloma. If it conforms and agrees, it should be accepted. If not, it should not be accepted; one should stand firm only in the Suttānuloma.

Athāyaṃ ācariyavādaṃ gahetvā katheti, paro suttaṃ. Suttaṃ ācariyavāde otāretabbaṃ. Sace otarati sameti, gahetabbaṃ. Itaraṃ gārayhasuttaṃ na gahetabbaṃ, ācariyavādeyeva ṭhātabbaṃ. Athāyaṃ ācariyavādaṃ gahetvā katheti, paro suttānulomaṃ. Suttānulomaṃ ācariyavāde otāretabbaṃ. Otarantaṃ samentameva gahetabbaṃ, itaraṃ na gahetabbaṃ, ācariyavādeyeva ṭhātabbaṃ. Athāyaṃ ācariyavādaṃ gahetvā katheti, paro attanomatiṃ. Attanomati ācariyavāde otāretabbā. Sace otarati sameti, gahetabbā. No ce, na gahetabbā, ācariyavādeyeva ṭhātabbaṃ.

Then, if this proponent speaks taking up the teacher's doctrine, and the other [cites] a Sutta, that Sutta should be checked against the teacher's doctrine. If it conforms and agrees, it should be accepted. The other—the blameworthy Sutta—should not be accepted; one should stand firm only in the teacher's doctrine. Then, if this proponent speaks taking up the teacher's doctrine, and the other [cites] the Suttānuloma, the Suttānuloma should be checked against the teacher's doctrine. Only that which conforms and agrees should be accepted; the other should not be accepted. One should stand firm only in the teacher's doctrine. Then, if this proponent speaks taking up the teacher's doctrine, and the other [cites] a personal opinion, that personal opinion should be checked against the teacher's doctrine. If it conforms and agrees, it should be accepted. If not, it should not be accepted; one should stand firm only in the teacher's doctrine.

Atha panāyaṃ attanomatiṃ gahetvā katheti, paro suttaṃ. Suttaṃ attanomatiyaṃ otāretabbaṃ. Sace otarati sameti, gahetabbaṃ. Itaraṃ gārayhasuttaṃ na gahetabbaṃ, attanomatiyameva ṭhātabbaṃ. Athāyaṃ attanomatiṃ gahetvā katheti, paro suttānulomaṃ. Suttānulomaṃ attanomatiyaṃ otāretabbaṃ. Otarantaṃ samentameva gahetabbaṃ, itaraṃ na gahetabbaṃ, attanomatiyameva ṭhātabbaṃ. Athāyaṃ attanomatiṃ gahetvā katheti, paro ācariyavādaṃ. Ācariyavādo attanomatiyaṃ otāretabbo. Sace otarati sameti, gahetabbo. Itaro gārayhācariyavādo na gahetabbo, attanomatiyameva [M 0.0322] ṭhātabbaṃ, attano gahaṇameva baliyaṃ kātabbaṃ. Sabbaṭṭhānesu ca khepo vā garahā vā na kātabbāti.

Furthermore, if one speaks taking up personal opinion, and another [cites] a sutta, that sutta should be checked against personal opinion. If it fits and agrees, it should be accepted. Otherwise, the blameworthy sutta should not be accepted; one should stand firm in personal opinion alone. Then, if one speaks taking up personal opinion, and another [cites] the Suttānuloma, the Suttānuloma should be checked against personal opinion. Only what fits and agrees should be accepted; otherwise, it should not be accepted. One should stand firm in personal opinion alone. Then, if one speaks taking up personal opinion, and another [cites] a teacher's doctrine, that teacher's doctrine should be checked against personal opinion. If it fits and agrees, it should be accepted. Otherwise, the blameworthy teacher's doctrine should not be accepted; one should stand firm in personal opinion alone, and one's own holding should be made strong. And in all places, neither disparagement nor blame should be made.

Atha panāyaṃ kappiyanti gahetvā katheti, paro akappiyanti, sutte ca suttānulome ca otāretabbaṃ. Sace kappiyaṃ hoti, kappiye ṭhātabbaṃ. Sace akappiyaṃ, akappiye ṭhātabbaṃ. Athāyaṃ tassa kappiyabhāvasādhakaṃ suttato bahuṃ kāraṇañca vinicchayañca dasseti, paro kāraṇaṃ na vindati, kappiyeva ṭhātabbaṃ. Atha paro tassa akappiyabhāvasādhakaṃ suttato bahuṃ kāraṇañca vinicchayañca dasseti, anena attano gahaṇanti katvā daḷhaṃ ādāya na ṭhātabbaṃ, “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchitvā akappiye eva ṭhātabbaṃ. Atha dvinnampi kāraṇacchāyā dissati, paṭikkhittabhāvoyeva sādhu, akappiye ṭhātabbaṃ. Vinayañhi patvā kappiyākappiyavicāraṇaṃ āgamma rundhitabbaṃ, gāḷhaṃ kattabbaṃ, sotaṃ pacchinditabbaṃ, garukabhāveyeva ṭhātabbaṃ.

Furthermore, if this one speaks, having taken a matter as 'allowable', and the other as 'unallowable', it should be compared with the Sutta and that which accords with the Sutta. If it is allowable, one should stand in what is allowable. If it is unallowable, one should stand in what is unallowable. Then, if this one demonstrates its state of being allowable with many reasons and judgments from the Sutta, and the other finds no reason, one should stand only in what is allowable. Then, if the other demonstrates its state of being unallowable with many reasons and judgments from the Sutta, this one should not stand, having taken it firmly, thinking 'this is my own view'; rather, having accepted it with 'Good!', one should stand only in what is unallowable. Then, if a semblance of a reason is seen for both, the state of being rejected is indeed better; one should stand in what is unallowable. For, having come to the Vinaya, based on the investigation of the allowable and unallowable, it should be obstructed, it should be made firm, the stream should be cut off; one should stand only in the state of being weighty.

Atha [V 0.0299] panāyaṃ akappiyanti gahetvā katheti, paro kappiyanti, sutte ca suttānulome ca otāretabbaṃ. Sace kappiyaṃ hoti, kappiye ṭhātabbaṃ. Sace akappiyaṃ, akappiye ṭhātabbaṃ. Athāyaṃ bahūhi suttavinicchayakāraṇehi akappiyabhāvaṃ dasseti, paro kāraṇaṃ na vindati, akappiye ṭhātabbaṃ. Atha paro bahūhi suttavinicchayakāraṇehi kappiyabhāvaṃ dasseti, ayaṃ kāraṇaṃ na vindati, kappiye ṭhātabbaṃ. Atha dvinnampi kāraṇacchāyā dissati, attano gahaṇaṃ na vissajjetabbaṃ. Yathā cāyaṃ kappiyākappiye akappiyakappiye ca vinicchayo vutto, evaṃ anāpattiāpattivāde āpattānāpattivāde ca, lahukagarukāpattivāde garukalahukāpattivāde cāpi vinicchayo veditabbo. Nāmamatteyeva hi ettha nānaṃ, yojanānaye nānaṃ natthi, tasmā na vitthāritaṃ.

Furthermore, if this one speaks, having taken a matter as 'unallowable', and the other as 'allowable', it should be compared with the Sutta and that which accords with the Sutta. If it is allowable, one should stand in what is allowable. If it is unallowable, one should stand in what is unallowable. Then, if this one demonstrates its state of being unallowable with many reasons for judgment from the Sutta, and the other finds no reason, one should stand in what is unallowable. Then, if the other demonstrates its state of being allowable with many reasons for judgment from the Sutta, and this one finds no reason, one should stand in what is allowable. Then, if a semblance of a reason is seen for both, one's own view should not be abandoned. And just as this judgment has been stated regarding the allowable and unallowable, and the unallowable and allowable, so too should the judgment be understood in a dispute about non-offense and offense, and offense and non-offense, and also in a dispute about a light and a serious offense, and a serious and a light offense. For here, the difference is only in name; there is no difference in the method of application. Therefore, it is not elaborated.

Evaṃ kappiyākappiyādivinicchaye uppanne yo suttasuttānulomaācariyavādaattanomatīsu atirekakāraṇaṃ labhati, tassa vāde ṭhātabbaṃ, sabbaso pana kāraṇavinicchayaṃ alabhantena suttaṃ na jahitabbaṃ, suttasmiṃyeva ṭhātabbanti. Evaṃ sakalavinayavinicchaye kosallaṃ patthayantena ayaṃ catubbidho vinayo jānitabbo.

Thus, when a judgment concerning the allowable, the unallowable, and so forth, has arisen, one should stand in the position of whoever obtains a superior reason among the Sutta, that which accords with the Sutta, the teachers' doctrine, and one's own opinion. However, one who does not in any way obtain a decisive reason should not abandon the Sutta; one should stand in the Sutta alone. Thus, by one desiring skill in all Vinaya judgments, this fourfold Vinaya should be known.

Imañca pana catubbidhaṃ vinayaṃ ñatvāpi vinayadharena puggalena tilakkhaṇasamannāgatena bhavitabbaṃ. Tīṇi hi vinayadharassa lakkhaṇāni icchitabbāni. Katamāni [M 0.0323] tīṇi? Suttañcassa svāgataṃ hoti suppavatti suvinicchitaṃ suttato anubyañjanasoti idamekaṃ lakkhaṇaṃ. Vinaye kho pana ṭhito hoti asaṃhīroti idaṃ dutiyaṃ. Ācariyaparamparā kho panassa suggahitā hoti sumanasikatā sūpadhāritāti idaṃ tatiyaṃ.

Furthermore, even having known this fourfold Vinaya, a person who is a Vinaya-holder should be endowed with three characteristics. Indeed, three characteristics are to be desired for a Vinaya-holder. What are the three? For him, the Sutta is well-received, well-practiced, and well-judged from the Sutta and from the detailed explanation—this is the first characteristic. Moreover, he is established in the Vinaya, unwavering—this is the second characteristic. Moreover, for him, the succession of teachers is well-grasped, well-attended to, and well-borne in mind—this is the third characteristic.

Tattha suttaṃ nāma sakalaṃ vinayapiṭakaṃ. Tadassa svāgataṃ hotīti suṭṭhu āgataṃ. Suppavattīti suṭṭhu pavattaṃ paguṇaṃ vācuggataṃ. Suvinicchitaṃ suttaso anubyañjanasoti pāḷito ca paripucchato ca aṭṭhakathāto ca suvinicchitaṃ hoti kaṅkhāchedanaṃ katvā uggahitaṃ. Vinaye kho pana ṭhito hotīti vinaye lajjibhāvena patiṭṭhito hoti. Alajjī hi bahussutopi samāno lābhagarukatāya tantiṃ visaṃvādetvā uddhammaṃ ubbinayaṃ satthusāsanaṃ dīpetvā sāsane mahantaṃ upaddavaṃ karoti, saṅghabhedampi saṅgharājimpi uppādeti. Lajjī pana kukkuccako sikkhākāmo jīvitahetupi tantiṃ avisaṃvādetvā dhammameva vinayameva dīpeti, satthusāsanaṃ garukaṃ katvā ṭhapeti. Tathā hi pubbe mahātherā tikkhattuṃ vācaṃ nicchāresuṃ “anāgate lajjī rakkhissati, lajjī [V 0.0300] rakkhissati, lajjī rakkhissatī”ti (pārā. aṭṭha. 1.45). Evaṃ yo lajjī, so vinayaṃ avijahanto avokkamanto lajjibhāveneva vinaye ṭhito hoti suppatiṭṭhitoti.

Here, 'sutta' means the entire Vinaya Piṭaka. 'It is well-received' means it has come properly. 'Well-practiced' means it is thoroughly practiced, proficient, and committed to memory. 'Well-judged from the Sutta and from the detailed explanation' means it is well-judged by means of the Pāḷi, by questioning, and by the commentaries, having been grasped after resolving doubts. 'Established in the Vinaya' means one is firmly grounded in the Vinaya through a sense of moral shame.
