Nāvābhiruhanasamaye [V 0.0389] “nāvaṃ abhiruhissāmī”ti bhuñjitabbaṃ, āruḷhena icchitaṭṭhānaṃ gantvāpi yāva na orohati, tāva bhuñjitabbaṃ, oruḷhena ekadivasaṃ bhuñjitabbaṃ.

At the time of embarking on a boat, one should partake thinking, 'I will embark on the boat.' Having embarked, one may partake for as long as one does not disembark, even after having reached the desired place. Having disembarked, one may partake for one day only.

Mahāsamayo nāma yattha dve tayo bhikkhū piṇḍāya caritvā yāpenti, antamaso catutthepi āgate na yāpenti, ayaṃ mahāsamayo. Yattha pana sataṃ vā sahassaṃ vā sannipatanti, tattha vattabbameva natthi, tasmā tādise kāle “mahāsamayo”ti adhiṭṭhahitvā bhuñjitabbaṃ.

A 'great occasion' is where two or three monks, having gone for alms, can sustain themselves, but at the very least, when a fourth arrives, they cannot sustain themselves—this is a great occasion. But where a hundred or a thousand gather, there is nothing even to be said; therefore, at such a time, one should partake, having determined it as 'a great occasion'.

Samaṇabhattasamayo nāma yo koci paribbājakasamāpanno bhattaṃ karoti, ayaṃ samaṇabhattasamayova. Tasmā sahadhammikesu vā titthiyesu vā aññatarena yena kenaci kate bhatte “samaṇabhattasamayo”ti bhuñjitabbaṃ. “Anāpatti samaye, dve tayo ekato bhuñjanti, piṇḍāya caritvā ekato sannipatitvā bhuñjanti, niccabhattaṃ, salākabhattaṃ, pakkhikaṃ, uposathikaṃ, pāṭipadikaṃ, pañca bhojanāni ṭhapetvā sabbattha anāpattī”ti (pāci. 220) vacanato yepi akappiyanimantanaṃ sādiyitvā dve vā tayo vā ekato gahetvā bhuñjanti, tesampi anāpatti.

The time of a meal for ascetics is when any person endowed with the appearance of a wandering ascetic prepares a meal; this is indeed the time of a meal for ascetics. Therefore, at a meal prepared by anyone whatsoever, whether among co-religionists or among sectarians, one should partake thinking, 'It is the time of a meal for ascetics.' As it is stated: 'There is no offense on an occasion of exception; when two or three eat together; when, having gone for alms, they gather and eat together; when eating a constant meal, a ticket meal, a fortnightly meal, an Uposatha meal, or a first-day-of-the-fortnight meal. Except for the five kinds of staple food, there is no offense in any case.' In accordance with this, even for those monks who, having consented to an improper invitation, take food and eat together in groups of two or three, for them also there is no offense.

Tattha animantitacatutthaṃ piṇḍapātikacatutthaṃ anupasampannacatutthaṃ pattacatutthaṃ gilānacatutthanti pañcannaṃ catutthānaṃ vasena vinicchayo veditabbo. Kathaṃ? Idhekacco cattāro bhikkhū “bhattaṃ gaṇhathā”ti nimanteti. Tesu tayo gatā, eko na gato. Upāsako “eko, bhante, thero kuhi”nti pucchati. Nāgato upāsakāti. So aññaṃ taṃkhaṇappattaṃ kañci “ehi, bhante”ti gharaṃ pavesetvā catunnampi bhattaṃ deti[M 0.0418], sabbesaṃ anāpatti. Kasmā? Gaṇapūrakassa animantitattā. Tayo eva hi tattha nimantitā gaṇhiṃsu, tehi gaṇo na pūrati, gaṇapūrako ca animantito, tena gaṇo bhijjatīti. Etaṃ animantitacatutthaṃ.

Herein, the ruling is to be understood by way of five cases concerning a fourth person: the uninvited-fourth, the alms-farer-fourth, the unordained-fourth, the bowl-fourth, and the sick-fourth. How? Here, a certain person invites four monks, saying, 'Accept the meal.' Three of them go, one does not. A lay follower asks, 'Venerable sir, where is the elder?' Upon being told, 'He has not come, lay follower,' he has another monk who happens to arrive at that moment enter the house, saying, 'Come, venerable sir,' and gives a meal to all four. There is no offense for any of them. Why? Because the one who completes the group was uninvited. For only three were invited there and accepted the meal; the group is not completed by them, and the one who completes the group is uninvited; therefore, the group is broken. This is the case of the uninvited-fourth.

Piṇḍapātikacatutthe nimantanakāle eko piṇḍapātiko hoti, so nādhivāseti, gamanavelāyaṃ pana “ehi bhante”ti vutte anadhivāsitattā anāgacchantampi “etha bhikkhaṃ lacchathā”ti gahetvā gacchanti, so taṃ gaṇaṃ bhindati, tasmā sabbesaṃ anāpatti.

In the case of the alms-farer-fourth, at the time of invitation, one monk is an alms-farer; he does not consent. But at the time of going, when told, 'Come, venerable sir,' even though he is not coming due to not having consented, they take him along, saying, 'Come, you will receive alms.' He breaks that group; therefore, there is no offense for any of them.

Anupasampannacatutthe sāmaṇerena saddhiṃ nimantitā honti, sopi gaṇaṃ bhindati.

In the case of the unordained-fourth, they are invited together with a novice, and he too breaks the group.

Pattacatutthe [V 0.0390] eko sayaṃ āgantvā pattaṃ peseti, evampi gaṇo bhijjati, tasmā sabbesaṃ anāpatti.

In the case of the bowl-fourth, one monk, without coming himself, sends his bowl. In this way too, the group is broken; therefore, there is no offense for any of them.

Gilānacatutthe gilānena saddhiṃ nimantitā honti, tattha gilānasseva anāpatti, itaresaṃ pana gaṇapūrako hoti. Na hi gilānena gaṇo bhijjati, tasmā tesaṃ āpatti. Mahāpaccariyaṃ pana avisesena vuttaṃ “samayaladdhako sayameva muccati, sesānaṃ gaṇapūrakattā āpattikaro hotī”ti. Tasmā cīvaradānasamayaladdhakādīnampi vasena catukkāni veditabbāni.

In the case of the sick-fourth, they are invited together with a sick monk. In that case, there is no offense for the sick monk alone, but for the others, he completes the group. For the group is not broken by the sick monk; therefore, for them there is an offense. However, in the Mahāpaccariya it is stated without distinction: 'One who has obtained an allowance for an occasion is himself exempt, but for the rest, because he completes the group, he causes them to incur an offense.' Therefore, the sets of four should also be understood in terms of those who have obtained an allowance for the robe-giving occasion and so on.

Sace pana adhivāsetvā gatesupi catūsu janesu eko paṇḍito bhikkhu “ahaṃ tumhākaṃ gaṇaṃ bhindissāmi, nimantanaṃ sādiyathā”ti vatvā yāgukhajjakāvasāne bhattatthāya pattaṃ gaṇhantānaṃ adatvā “ime tāva bhikkhū bhojetvā vissajjetha, ahaṃ pacchā anumodanaṃ katvā gamissāmī”ti nisinno, tesu bhutvā gatesu “detha, bhante, patta”nti upāsakena pattaṃ gahetvā bhatte dinne bhuñjitvā anumodanaṃ katvā gacchati, sabbesaṃ anāpatti. Pañcannañhi bhojanānaṃyeva vasena gaṇabhojane visaṅketaṃ natthi, odanena nimantetvā kummāsaṃ gaṇhantāpi āpajjanti, tāni ca tehi ekato na gahitāni, yāguādīhi pana visaṅketaṃ hoti, tāni tehi ekato gahitānīti evaṃ eko paṇḍito aññesampi anāpattiṃ karoti. Niccabhattanti dhuvabhattaṃ vuccati, “niccabhattaṃ gaṇhathā”ti vadanti, bahūnaṃ ekato gahetuṃ vaṭṭati. Salākabhattādīsupi eseva nayo.

If, however, even when four persons have consented and gone, one wise monk says, 'I will break up your group; please accept the invitation,' and at the end of the rice gruel and snacks, when the bowls are being taken for the meal, he does not give his, but sits down saying, 'First feed these monks and send them away; I will give the anumodanā afterward and leave'; and when they have eaten and gone, a lay supporter takes his bowl when told, 'Venerable sir, give your bowl,' and gives the meal, and the monk eats, gives the anumodanā, and departs—there is no offense for any of them. For, the breaking of an agreement regarding a group meal pertains only to the five staple foods. Even those who, having been invited for boiled rice, accept pulse gruel, incur an offense; and in this case, those staple foods were not accepted by them together. But with rice gruel and the like, a breaking of the agreement is effected, as those were accepted by them together. Thus, one wise monk causes there to be no offense for the others as well. 'Regular meal' is called a permanent meal. They say, 'Accept the regular meal'—it is allowable for many to accept it together. The same principle applies to ticket-food and the like.

2. “Paramparabhojane [M 0.0419] aññatra samayā pācittiya”nti (pāci. 222-223, 225) vuttaṃ paramparabhojanaṃ pana nimantanatoyeva pasavati. Yo hi “pañcannaṃ bhojanānaṃ aññatarena bhojanena bhattaṃ gaṇhathā”tiādinā nimantito taṃ ṭhapetvā aññaṃ pañcannaṃ bhojanānaṃ aññatarabhojanaṃ bhuñjati, tassetaṃ bhojanaṃ “paramparabhojana”nti vuccati. Evaṃ bhuñjantassa ṭhapetvā gilānasamayaṃ cīvaradānasamayaṃ cīvarakārasamayañca aññasmiṃ samaye pācittiyaṃ vuttaṃ, tasmā nimantanapaṭipāṭiyāva bhuñjitabbaṃ, na uppaṭipāṭiyā.

2. It is stated: 'Regarding eating in succession, except at an appropriate time, there is a pācittiya offense.' Now, eating in succession arises only from an invitation. For, if a monk is invited with such words as, 'Accept a meal with one of the five staple foods,' and, having set that food aside, he eats another of the five staple foods, this meal of his is called 'eating in succession.' For one who eats in this way, a pācittiya offense is stated for any other time, excepting the time of illness, the time of giving robes, and the time of making robes. Therefore, one should eat only according to the sequence of the invitation, not against the sequence.

“Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, vikappetvā paramparabhojanaṃ bhuñjitu”nti (pāci. 226) vacanato paṭhamanimantanaṃ aññassa vikappetvāpi paribhuñjituṃ vaṭṭati. Ayaṃ (pāci. aṭṭha. 226 ādayo) vikappanā nāma sammukhāpi parammukhāpi vaṭṭati. Sammukhā disvā “mayhaṃ bhattapaccāsaṃ tuyhaṃ vikappemī”ti vā “dammī”ti vā vatvā bhuñjitabbaṃ, adisvā pañcasu sahadhammikesu [V 0.0391] yassa kassaci nāmaṃ gahetvā “mayhaṃ bhattapaccāsaṃ itthannāmassa vikappemī”ti vā “dammī”ti vā vatvā bhuñjitabbaṃ. Dve tīṇi nimantanāni pana ekasmiṃ patte pakkhipitvā missetvā ekaṃ katvā bhuñjituṃ vaṭṭati. “Anāpatti dve tayo nimantane ekato bhuñjatī”ti (pāci. 229) hi vuttaṃ. Sace dve tīṇi kulāni nimantetvā ekasmiṃ ṭhāne nisīdāpetvā ito cito ca āharitvā bhattaṃ ākiranti, sūpabyañjanaṃ ākiranti, ekamissakaṃ hoti, etthāpi anāpatti.

“I allow, monks, to eat a successive meal after having designated it.” According to this statement, it is permissible to partake of a subsequent meal after designating the first invitation to another. This designation is permissible either face-to-face or in absentia. Face-to-face, upon seeing the person, one should say, “I designate my expectation of food to you,” or “I give it to you,” and then eat. If not seen, one should name any one among the five fellow Dhamma-practitioners and say, “I designate my expectation of food to so-and-so,” or “I give it to so-and-so,” and then eat. Furthermore, two or three invitations may be combined by placing them into a single bowl, mixing them, and eating them as one. For it is said, “There is no offense in eating two or three invitations together.” If two or three families invite and seat the monks in one place, bringing rice from here and there and pouring it together, and likewise with curries and side dishes, making it a single mixture—even in this case, there is no offense.

Sace pana mūlanimantanaṃ heṭṭhā hoti, pacchimaṃ pacchimaṃ upari, taṃ uparito paṭṭhāya bhuñjantassa āpatti, hatthaṃ pana anto pavesetvā paṭhamanimantanato ekampi kabaḷaṃ uddharitvā bhuttakālato paṭṭhāya yathā tathā vā bhuñjantassa anāpatti. “Sacepi tattha khīraṃ vā rasaṃ vā ākiranti, yena ajjhotthataṃ bhattaṃ ekarasaṃ hoti, koṭito paṭṭhāya bhuñjantassa anāpattī”ti mahāpaccariyaṃ vuttaṃ. Mahāaṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana vuttaṃ “khīrabhattaṃ vā rasabhattaṃ vā labhitvā nisinnassa tattheva aññepi khīrabhattaṃ vā rasabhattaṃ vā ākiranti, khīraṃ vā rasaṃ vā pivato anāpatti, bhuñjantena paṭhamaṃ laddhamaṃsakhaṇḍaṃ vā bhattapiṇḍaṃ vā mukhe pakkhipitvā koṭito paṭṭhāya bhuñjituṃ vaṭṭati. Sappipāyāsepi eseva nayo”ti.

If, however, the food from the original invitation is at the bottom and the food from each subsequent invitation is on top, for one who eats starting from the top, there is an offense. However, if one inserts the hand inside, takes out even a single morsel from the food of the first invitation, then from the time it is eaten, there is no offense for eating in any way whatsoever. In the Mahāpaccariya it is said: “Even if they pour milk or broth on that food, by which the covered food becomes of one taste, for one who eats starting from the edge, there is no offense.” But in the Mahāaṭṭhakathā it is said: “For one who has received milk-rice or broth-rice and is seated, if others then pour more milk-rice or broth-rice, or milk or broth, there is no offense in drinking the milk or broth. One who is eating, having first placed a piece of meat that was received or a lump of rice in the mouth, is permitted to eat starting from the edge. This same principle applies also to ghee-porridge.”

Mahāupāsako [M 0.0420] bhikkhuṃ nimanteti, tassa kulaṃ upagatassa upāsakopi tassa puttadārabhātubhaginiādayopi attano attano koṭṭhāsaṃ āharitvā patte pakkhipanti, “upāsakena paṭhamaṃ dinnaṃ abhuñjitvā pacchā laddhaṃ bhuñjantassa āpattī”ti mahāaṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttaṃ. Kurundaṭṭhakathāyaṃ “vaṭṭatī”ti vuttaṃ. Mahāpaccariyaṃ “sace pāṭekkaṃ pacanti, attano attano pakkabhattato āharitvā denti, tattha pacchā āhaṭaṃ paṭhamaṃ bhuñjantassa pācittiyaṃ. Yadi pana sabbesaṃ ekova pāko hoti, paramparabhojanaṃ na hotī”ti vuttaṃ. Mahāupāsako nimantetvā nisīdāpeti, añño manusso pattaṃ gaṇhāti, na dātabbaṃ. Kiṃ, bhante, na dethāti. Nanu upāsaka tayā nimantitamhāti. “Hotu, bhante, laddhaṃ laddhaṃ bhuñjathā”ti vadati, bhuñjituṃ vaṭṭati. “Aññena āharitvā bhatte dinne āpucchitvāpi bhuñjituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti kurundiyaṃ vuttaṃ.

A great lay supporter invites a bhikkhu. When the bhikkhu arrives at his home, the lay supporter, along with his children, wife, brothers, sisters, and others, each bring their own portions and place them in the bowl. It is said in the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā: “For one who eats what was received later without having first eaten what was given by the lay supporter, there is an offense.” In the Kurundaṭṭhakathā, it is said: “It is allowable.” In the Mahāpaccarī, it is said: “If they cook separately and, having brought from their own cooked rice, they give, in that case, for one who eats what was brought later first, there is a pācittiya offense. But if there is only one cooking for all of them, it is not sequential eating.” A great lay supporter invites and seats the bhikkhu, but another person takes the bowl; it should not be given. When asked, “Why, venerable sir, do you not give it?” it should be said, “Lay supporter, were we not invited by you?” If he says, “Let it be, venerable sir, eat whatever you receive,” it is allowable to eat. It is said in the Kurundī: “When food is brought and given by another, it is allowable to eat even after having asked the first donor.”

Anumodanaṃ katvā gacchantaṃ dhammaṃ sotukāmā “svepi, bhante, āgaccheyyāthā”ti sabbe nimantenti, punadivase āgantvā laddhaṃ laddhaṃ bhuñjituṃ vaṭṭati. Kasmā? Sabbehi nimantitattā. Ekopi bhikkhu piṇḍāya caranto bhattaṃ labhati, tamañño upāsako nimantetvā ghare [V 0.0392] nisīdāpeti, na ca tāva bhattaṃ sampajjati, sace so bhikkhu piṇḍāya caritvā laddhabhattaṃ bhuñjati, āpatti. Abhuñjitvā nisinne “kiṃ, bhante, na bhuñjasī”ti vutte “tayā nimantitattā”ti vatvā “laddhaṃ laddhaṃ bhuñjatha, bhante”ti vutte bhuñjituṃ vaṭṭati. Sakalena gāmena ekato hutvā nimantitassa yattha katthaci bhuñjato anāpatti. Pūgepi eseva nayo. “Anāpatti sakalena gāmena nimantito tasmiṃ gāme yattha katthaci bhuñjati, sakalena pūgena nimantito tasmiṃ pūge yattha katthaci bhuñjati, nimantiyamāno ‘bhikkhaṃ gahessāmī’ti bhaṇati, niccabhatte salākabhatte pakkhike uposathike pāṭipadike pañca bhojanāni ṭhapetvā sabbattha anāpattī”ti (pāci. 229) vuttaṃ.

Having given the anumodanā, those who wish to hear the Dhamma invite him as he departs, saying, “Venerable sir, please come again tomorrow too.” The next day, when he returns, it is allowable to eat whatever is received. Why? Because all have invited him. Even if a single bhikkhu, while going for alms, receives food, and another lay devotee invites him and has him sit in his house, but the meal is not yet ready—if that bhikkhu eats the food he obtained while going for alms, he incurs an offense. If he does not eat and remains seated, and when asked, “Venerable sir, why do you not eat?” he replies, “Because you invited me,” and when told, “Venerable sir, please eat whatever you have received,” it is then allowable for him to eat. For one who is invited by an entire village collectively, there is no offense in eating anywhere whatsoever. This same principle applies to a guild. It is said: “There is no offense if, having been invited by an entire village, one eats anywhere in that village; if, having been invited by an entire guild, one eats anywhere in that guild. If, while being invited, one says, ‘I will take almsfood,’ there is no offense in all cases, setting aside the five meals: a fixed-term meal, a ticket-meal, a fortnightly meal, an Uposatha-day meal, and a first-day-of-the-fortnight meal.”

Tattha nimantiyamāno bhikkhaṃ gahessāmīti bhaṇatīti ettha “bhattaṃ gaṇhā”ti nimantiyamāno “na mayhaṃ tava bhattenattho, bhikkhaṃ gaṇhissāmī”ti vadati, anāpattīti attho. Ettha pana mahāpadumatthero āha “evaṃ vadanto imasmiṃ sikkhāpade animantanaṃ kātuṃ sakkoti, bhuñjanatthāya [M 0.0421] pana okāso kato hotīti neva gaṇabhojanato, na cārittato muccatī”ti. Mahāsumatthero āha “yadaggena animantanaṃ kātuṃ sakkoti, tadaggena neva gaṇabhojanaṃ, na cārittaṃ hotī”ti.

Here, regarding the phrase ‘if, while being invited, one says, “I will take almsfood”’: when being invited with, “Take the meal,” if one responds, “I have no need of your meal; I will take almsfood,” there is no offense. This is the meaning. Here, however, the Elder Mahāpaduma said: “One who speaks thus is able to make it a non-invitation under this training rule, but an opportunity is made for the purpose of eating; thus, one is not freed from a group meal, nor from customary practice (cāritta).” The Elder Mahāsuma said: “To the extent that one is able to make it a non-invitation, to that extent, there is neither a group meal nor customary practice (cāritta).”

Tattha cārittanti –

Therein, as for customary practice (cāritta)—

“Yo pana bhikkhu nimantito sabhatto samāno santaṃ bhikkhuṃ anāpucchā purebhattaṃ vā pacchābhattaṃ vā kulesu cārittaṃ āpajjeyya aññatra samayā pācittiyaṃ. Tatthāyaṃ samayo cīvaradānasamayo cīvarakārasamayo. Ayaṃ tattha samayo”ti (pāci. 299) –

“Whatever bhikkhu, having been invited and having a meal, should, without informing a present bhikkhu, engage in visiting families either before or after the meal, except at the proper time, he incurs a pācittiya offense. Herein, this is the proper time: the time of giving robes and the time of making robes. This is the proper time in that case.”

Evamāgataṃ cārittasikkhāpadaṃ vuttaṃ. Iminā hi sikkhāpadena yo pañcannaṃ bhojanānaṃ aññatarena “bhattaṃ gaṇhathā”tiādinā akappiyanimantanena nimantito, teneva nimantanabhattena sabhatto samāno santaṃ bhikkhuṃ “ahaṃ itthannāmassa gharaṃ gacchāmī”ti vā “cārittaṃ āpajjāmī”ti vā īdisena vacanena anāpucchitvā yena bhattena nimantito, taṃ bhutvā vā abhutvā vā avītivatteyeva majjhanhike yasmiṃ kule nimantito, tato aññāni kulāni paviseyya, tassa vuttalakkhaṇaṃ duvidhampi samayaṃ ṭhapetvā aññattha pācittiyaṃ vuttaṃ. Tasmā akappiyanimantanena nimantiyamāno sace “bhikkhaṃ gaṇhissāmī”ti vadati, imināpi sikkhāpadena anāpatti.

Thus, the training rule on visiting (cāritta) has been stated. By this training rule, if a bhikkhu is invited with an improper invitation concerning one of the five kinds of foods—such as, ‘Take the meal’—and thereby has a meal from that invitation, and then, without informing a present bhikkhu by saying, ‘I am going to the house of so-and-so,’ or, ‘I will engage in visiting,’ he enters families other than the one where he was invited, whether having eaten that meal or not, before midday has passed; for him, setting aside the two kinds of specified proper times, a pācittiya offense is stated. Therefore, if, when being invited with an improper invitation, he says, ‘I will take almsfood,’ there is no offense under this training rule.

3. Santaṃ [V 0.0393] bhikkhuṃ anāpucchāti ettha (pāci. aṭṭha. 298) pana kittāvatā santo hoti, kittāvatā asanto? Antovihāre yattha ṭhitassa kulāni payirupāsanacittaṃ uppannaṃ, tato paṭṭhāya yaṃ passe vā abhimukhe vā passati, yassa sakkā hoti pakativacanena ārocetuṃ, ayaṃ santo nāma, ito cito ca pariyesitvā ārocanakiccaṃ pana natthi. Yo hi evaṃ pariyesitabbo, so asantoyeva. Apica antoupacārasīmāya bhikkhuṃ disvā “āpucchissāmī”ti gacchati. Tattha yaṃ passati, so āpucchitabbo. No ce passati, asantaṃ bhikkhuṃ anāpucchā paviṭṭho nāma hoti. Vikālagāmappavesanepi ayameva nayo.

3. Regarding the phrase, ‘without informing a present bhikkhu’: to what extent is a bhikkhu ‘present,’ and to what extent ‘not present’? When the thought to attend on families has arisen in a bhikkhu standing anywhere within the monastery, from that point on, any bhikkhu he sees at his side or in front, whom it is possible to inform with ordinary speech—this one is called ‘present.’ There is, however, no duty to inform after searching here and there. For a bhikkhu who must be searched for in this way is indeed ‘not present.’ Moreover, having seen a bhikkhu within the monastery's precincts, one goes thinking, ‘I will inform him.’ Whomever one sees there should be informed. If, however, one does not see anyone, one is said to have entered without informing a bhikkhu, as none was present. This same method applies also to entering a village at an improper time.

Sace [M 0.0422] (pāci. aṭṭha. 512) pana sambahulā kenaci kammena gāmaṃ pavisanti, “vikāle gāmappavesanaṃ āpucchāmī”ti sabbehi aññamaññaṃ āpucchitabbaṃ. Tasmiṃ gāme taṃ kammaṃ na sampajjatīti aññaṃ gāmaṃ gacchanti, gāmasatampi hotu, puna āpucchanakiccaṃ natthi. Sace pana ussāhaṃ paṭippassambhetvā vihāraṃ gacchantā antarā aññaṃ gāmaṃ pavisitukāmā honti, puna āpucchitabbameva. Kulaghare vā āsanasālāya vā bhattakiccaṃ katvā telabhikkhāya vā sappibhikkhāya vā caritukāmo hoti, sace passe bhikkhu atthi, āpucchitvā gantabbaṃ. Asante bhikkhumhi “natthī”ti gantabbaṃ, vīthiṃ otaritvā bhikkhuṃ passati, āpucchanakiccaṃ natthi, anāpucchitvāpi caritabbameva. Gāmamajjhena maggo hoti, tena gacchantassa “telādibhikkhāya carissāmī”ti citte uppanne sace passe bhikkhu atthi, āpucchitvā caritabbaṃ. Maggā anokkamma bhikkhāya carantassa pana āpucchanakiccaṃ natthi. Sace sīho vā byaggho vā āgacchati, megho vā uṭṭheti, añño vā koci upaddavo uppajjati, evarūpāsu āpadāsu anāpucchāpi bahigāmato antogāmaṃ pavisituṃ vaṭṭati.

If, however, several bhikkhus enter a village for some business, they should all ask leave of one another, saying, “I ask leave for entering the village at the wrong time.” If that business is not accomplished in that village and they go to another village—even if it be a hundred villages—there is no need to ask leave again. If, however, having pacified their effort, they are going to the monastery and on the way wish to enter another village, they must indeed ask leave again. Having finished the meal-duty in a family’s house or in a sitting-hall, if one wishes to go about for alms of oil or for alms of ghee, if there is a bhikkhu nearby, one should go after asking leave. If a bhikkhu is not present, one should go, thinking, “There is none.” Having gone down to the street, if one sees a bhikkhu, there is no need to ask leave; one may indeed go about even without asking leave. If there is a path through the middle of the village, and for one going by it the thought arises, “I will go about for alms of oil and so forth,” if there is a bhikkhu nearby, one should go about after asking leave. But for one going about for alms without deviating from the path, there is no need to ask leave. If a lion or a tiger approaches, or a cloud arises, or some other danger occurs, in such calamities it is permissible to enter a village from outside the village even without asking leave.

4. “Na ca, bhikkhave, abhinne sarīre paṃsukūlaṃ gahetabbaṃ, yo gaṇheyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (pārā. 137) vacanato abbhuṇhe allasarīre paṃsukūlaṃ na gahetabbaṃ, gaṇhanto dukkaṭaṃ āpajjati. Upaddavā ca tassa honti, bhinne pana gahetuṃ vaṭṭati.

4. “And, bhikkhus, a rag-robe should not be taken from an undecayed body. Whoever should take one, commits an offense of wrong-doing.” According to this statement, a rag-robe should not be taken from a fresh, wet body; one who takes it commits an offense of wrong-doing. And dangers arise for him. But from a decayed one, it is permissible to take.

Kittāvatā pana bhinnaṃ hoti? Kākakulalasoṇasiṅgālādīhi mukhatuṇḍakena vā dāṭhāya vā īsakaṃ phālitamattenapi. Yassa pana patato ghaṃsanena chavimattaṃ chinnaṃ hoti, cammaṃ acchinnaṃ, etaṃ abhinnameva, camme pana chinne bhinnaṃ. Yassapi sajīvakāleyeva pabhinnā gaṇḍakuṭṭhapīḷakā vā vaṇo vā hoti, idampi bhinnaṃ, tatiyadivasato pabhuti uddhumātakādibhāvena kuṇapabhāvaṃ upagatampi bhinnameva. Sabbena sabbaṃ pana abhinnepi susānagopakehi [V 0.0394] vā aññehi vā manussehi gāhāpetuṃ vaṭṭati. No ce aññaṃ labhati, satthakena vā kenaci vā vaṇaṃ katvā gahetabbaṃ. Visabhāgasarīre pana satiṃ upaṭṭhapetvā samaṇasaññaṃ uppādetvā sīse vā hatthapādapiṭṭhiyaṃ vā vaṇaṃ katvā gahetuṃ vaṭṭati.

To what extent is it considered 'broken'? It is considered 'broken' even by merely being slightly torn by the tip of the beak or a fang of crows, hawks, dogs, jackals, and so forth. However, if, from falling or friction, only the outer skin of a body is cut while the inner skin is not cut, it is indeed not broken; but when the inner skin is cut, it is 'broken'. And if a body, even while alive, has burst boils, leprosy sores, or abscesses, or has a wound, this too is considered 'broken'. A body that, from the third day onwards, has become bloated and has reached the state of a corpse, is also indeed 'broken'. However, even if it is entirely unbroken, it is permissible to have it taken by cemetery keepers or other people. If one does not find another person to do so, it should be taken after making a wound with a small knife or some other instrument. However, in the case of a body of the opposite sex, it is permissible to take it after making a wound on the head or on the back of the hand or foot, having established mindfulness and aroused the perception of a recluse.

5. Acchinnacīvarakena [M 0.0423] bhikkhunā kathaṃ paṭipajjitabbanti? “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, acchinnacīvarassa vā naṭṭhacīvarassa vā aññātakaṃ gahapatiṃ vā gahapatāniṃ vā cīvaraṃ viññāpetuṃ. Yaṃ āvāsaṃ paṭhamaṃ upagacchati, sace tattha hoti saṅghassa vihāracīvaraṃ vā uttarattharaṇaṃ vā bhūmattharaṇaṃ vā bhisicchavi vā, taṃ gahetvā pārupituṃ ‘labhitvā odahissāmī’ti. No ce hoti saṅghassa vihāracīvaraṃ vā uttarattharaṇaṃ vā bhūmattharaṇaṃ vā bhisicchavi vā, tiṇena vā paṇṇena vā paṭicchādetvā āgantabbaṃ, na tveva naggena āgantabbaṃ, yo āgaccheyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (pārā. 517) vacanato idha vuttanayena paṭipajjitabbaṃ.

5. How should a bhikkhu whose robe has been stolen proceed? ‘Bhikkhus, I allow a bhikkhu whose robe has been stolen or whose robe has been lost to request a robe from an unacquainted householder or householder's wife. Whatever dwelling he first approaches, if there is a monastery robe, or an upper covering, or a ground covering, or a bolster-cover belonging to the Sangha, he may take it and wear it, thinking, “When I obtain a robe, I will put this back.” If there is no monastery robe, or upper covering, or ground covering, or bolster-cover belonging to the Sangha, he should cover himself with grass or with leaves and then come; but he should certainly not come naked. Whichever bhikkhu should come naked commits an offense of wrong-doing.’ Therefore, one should proceed in the manner stated here.

Ayaṃ panettha anupubbakathā (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.517). Sace hi core passitvā daharā pattacīvarāni gahetvā palātā, corā therānaṃ nivāsanapārupanamattaṃyeva haritvā gacchanti, therehi neva tāva cīvaraṃ viññāpetabbaṃ, na sākhāpalāsaṃ bhañjitabbaṃ. Atha daharā sabbaṃ bhaṇḍakaṃ chaḍḍetvā palātā, corā therānañca nivāsanapārupanaṃ tañca bhaṇḍakaṃ haritvā gacchanti, daharehi āgantvā attano nivāsanapārupanāni na tāva therānaṃ dātabbāni. Na hi te anacchinnacīvarā attano atthāya sākhāpalāsaṃ bhañjituṃ labhanti, acchinnacīvarānaṃ pana atthāya labhanti. Acchinnacīvarāva attanopi paresampi atthāya labhanti, tasmā therehi vā sākhāpalāsaṃ bhañjitvā vākādīhi ganthetvā daharānaṃ dātabbaṃ, daharehi vā therānaṃ atthāya bhañjitvā ganthetvā tesaṃ hatthe datvā vā adatvā vā attanā nivāsetvā attano nivāsanapārupanāni therānaṃ dātabbāni, neva bhūtagāmapātabyatāya pācittiyaṃ hoti, na tesaṃ dhāraṇe dukkaṭaṃ.

Herein, this is the sequential explanation. If, upon seeing thieves, the junior bhikkhus take their bowls and robes and flee, and the thieves, having taken only the senior bhikkhus' lower and upper robes, depart, the senior bhikkhus should not yet request a robe, nor should a branch with leaves be broken. But if the junior bhikkhus, having abandoned all their belongings, flee, and the thieves, having taken both the senior bhikkhus' lower and upper robes and those belongings, depart, the junior bhikkhus, upon returning, should not yet give their own lower and upper robes to the senior bhikkhus. For those bhikkhus whose robes have not been taken are not permitted to break a branch with leaves for their own sake, but they are permitted to do so for the sake of those whose robes have been taken. Only those whose robes have been taken are permitted to do so for their own sake and for the sake of others. Therefore, either the senior bhikkhus should break a branch with leaves, tie it with bark fiber and so on, and give it to the junior bhikkhus; or the junior bhikkhus should break it for the sake of the senior bhikkhus, tie it, and then, whether having placed it in their hands or not, having worn it themselves, they should give their own lower and upper robes to the senior bhikkhus. There is no pācittiya offense for destroying plant life, nor is there a dukkaṭa offense for wearing them.

Sace antarāmagge rajakattharaṇaṃ vā hoti, aññe vā tādise manusse passanti, cīvaraṃ viññāpetabbaṃ. Yāni ca nesaṃ te vā viññattamanussā aññe vā sākhāpalāsanivāsane bhikkhū disvā ussāhajātā vatthāni denti, tāni sadasāni vā hontu adasāni vā nīlādinānāvaṇṇāni vā, kappiyānipi akappiyānipi sabbānipi acchinnacīvaraṭṭhāne ṭhitattā tesaṃ nivāsetuñca pārupituñca vaṭṭanti.

If on the way there is a dyer's spread, or if they see other such people, a robe should be requested. And whatever cloths are given by those people who were requested, or by others who become inspired upon seeing the monks wearing branches with leaves—whether they have a fringe or are without a fringe, whether they are of various colors such as dark blue and so forth, whether they are allowable or not allowable—all are permissible for them to wear as a lower garment and to wear as an upper garment, because they are in the position of one whose robe has been taken.

Vuttampihetaṃ [M 0.0424][V 0.0395] parivāre –

For this was also stated in the Parivāra:

“Akappakataṃ nāpi rajanāya rattaṃ,

Tena nivattho yenakāmaṃ vajeyya;

Na cassa hoti āpatti,

So ca dhammo sugatena desito;

Pañhāmesā kusalehi cintitā”ti. (pari. 481);

“Not made allowable, nor dyed with dye, clothed in that, one may go wherever one wishes; and there is no offense for them, that is the principle taught by the Well-Gone One; this question was pondered by the skillful.”

Ayañhi pañho acchinnacīvarakabhikkhuṃ sandhāya vutto. Atha pana titthiyehi samāgacchanti, te ca nesaṃ kusacīravākacīraphalakacīrāni denti, tānipi laddhiṃ aggahetvā nivāsetuṃ vaṭṭanti, nivāsetvāpi laddhi na gahetabbā.

Indeed, this question was stated concerning a monk who has been robbed of his robe. But then, should they travel together with sectarians, and those sectarians give them robes made of kusa grass, bark-fiber, or wooden strips, it is permissible to wear even those without adopting their views; and even having worn them, their views should not be adopted.

Yaṃ āvāsaṃ paṭhamaṃ upagacchanti, tattha vihāracīvarādīsu yaṃ atthi, taṃ anāpucchāpi gahetvā nivāsetuṃ vā pārupituṃ vā labhati. Tañca kho “labhitvā odahissāmi, puna ṭhapessāmī”ti adhippāyena, na mūlacchejjāya. Labhitvā ca pana ñātito vā upaṭṭhākato vā aññato vā kutoci pākatikameva kātabbaṃ. Videsagatena pana ekasmiṃ saṅghike āvāse saṅghikaparibhogena bhuñjanatthāya ṭhapetabbaṃ. Sacassa paribhogeneva taṃ jīrati vā nassati vā, gīvā na hoti. Sace pana etesaṃ vuttappakārānaṃ gihivatthādīnaṃ bhisicchavipariyantānaṃ kiñci na labhati, tena tiṇena vā paṇṇena vā paṭicchādetvā āgantabbanti.

Whatever monastery they first approach, whatever is available there among the monastery robes and so forth, they are permitted to take it even without asking permission, to wear as an under-robe or to drape over as an upper-robe. And this, indeed, should be with the intention, 'Having obtained a replacement, I will return this; I will put it back again,' not with the intention of permanent appropriation. And having obtained a replacement from relatives, from supporters, or from some other source, the original item should be restored. But by one who has gone to another region, it should be set aside in a communal monastery for use as communal property. If it wears out or is lost through his use, there is no liability. But if he does not obtain any of these aforementioned kinds of lay-cloths and so forth, ending with hide-rugs, then he should cover himself with grass or leaves and come.

6. “Na, bhikkhave, paṭibhānacittaṃ kārāpetabbaṃ itthirūpakaṃ purisarūpakaṃ, yo kārāpeyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (cūḷava. 299) vacanato itthipurisarūpaṃ kātuṃ vā kārāpetuṃ vā bhikkhuno na vaṭṭati. Na kevalaṃ (cūḷava. aṭṭha. 299) itthipurisarūpameva, tiracchānarūpampi antamaso gaṇḍuppādarūpaṃ bhikkhuno sayaṃ kātuṃ vā “karohī”ti vattuṃ vā na vaṭṭati, “upāsaka dvārapālaṃ karohī”ti vattumpi na labhati. Jātakapakaraṇaasadisadānādīni pana pasādanīyāni nibbidāpaṭisaṃyuttāni vā vatthūni parehi kārāpetuṃ labhati, mālākammādīni sayampi kātuṃ labhati.

6. “Monks, an artistic representation, a figure of a woman or a figure of a man, should not be caused to be made. Whoever should cause one to be made incurs an offense of wrong-doing.” Therefore, it is not proper for a monk to make a figure of a woman or a man, or to cause one to be made. It is not only a figure of a woman or a man; it is not proper for a monk to make even a figure of an animal—down to a figure of an earthworm—himself, or to say, “Make it.” He is not even permitted to say, “Lay supporter, make a door-guardian.” However, he is permitted to have others make inspiring figures, such as those depicting the Jātakas or the Asadisa-dāna, or narrative scenes connected with disenchantment. He is also permitted to make things like floral patterns himself.

7. “Na, bhikkhave, vippakatabhojano bhikkhu vuṭṭhāpetabbo, yo vuṭṭhāpeyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (cūḷava. 316) vacanato antaraghare (cūḷava. aṭṭha. 316) vā vihāre [M 0.0425] vā [V 0.0396] araññe vā yattha katthaci bhuñjamāno bhikkhu aniṭṭhite bhojane na vuṭṭhāpetabbo, antaraghare pacchā āgatena bhikkhaṃ gahetvā gantabbaṃ. Sace manussā vā bhikkhū vā “pavisathā”ti vadanti, “mayi pavisante bhikkhū uṭṭhahissantī”ti vattabbaṃ. “Etha, bhante, āsanaṃ atthī”ti vutte pana pavisitabbaṃ. Sace koci kiñci na vadati, āsanasālaṃ gantvā atisamīpaṃ agantvā sabhāgaṭṭhāne ṭhātabbaṃ. Okāse kate “pavisathā”ti vuttena pavisitabbaṃ. Sace pana yaṃ āsanaṃ tassa pāpuṇāti, tattha abhuñjanto bhikkhu nisinno hoti, taṃ uṭṭhāpetuṃ vaṭṭati. Yāgukhajjakādīsu pana yaṃ kiñci pivitvā khāditvā vā yāva añño āgacchati, tāva nisinnaṃ rittahatthampi uṭṭhāpetuṃ na vaṭṭati. Vippakatabhojanoyeva hi so hoti.

7. “O monks, a monk whose meal is unfinished should not be made to rise. Whoever should make him rise commits an offense of wrong-doing.” Therefore, whether within a village, in a monastery, or in a forest, in whatever place a monk is eating, he should not be made to rise when his meal is not finished. Within a village, one who has come later should take alms and depart. If people or monks say, ‘Enter,’ it should be said, ‘If I enter, the monks will rise.’ But when it is said, ‘Come, venerable sir, there is a seat,’ one should enter. If no one says anything, having gone to the seating hall, not going too close, one should stand in a suitable place. When an opportunity is made and one is told, ‘Enter,’ one should enter. But if a monk who is not eating is seated on a seat that another is entitled to, it is allowable to make him rise. However, in the case of gruel, snacks, and so on, having drunk or eaten anything, it is not allowable to make a monk who is seated until another arrives rise, even if his hands are empty. For he is indeed one whose meal is unfinished.

Sace pana āpattiṃ atikkamitvāpi vuṭṭhāpetiyeva, yaṃ so vuṭṭhāpeti, ayañca bhikkhu pavārito hoti, tena vattabbo “gaccha udakaṃ āharāhī”ti. Vuḍḍhataraṃ bhikkhuṃ āṇāpetuṃ idameva ekaṭṭhānaṃ. Sace so udakampi na āharati, sādhukaṃ sitthāni gilitvā vuḍḍhassa āsanaṃ dātabbaṃ. Vuttampi cetaṃ –

But if, even having transgressed the offense, one indeed makes him rise, and this monk who was made to rise has finished his meal, he is to be told, ‘Go, bring water.’ This is the one and only instance for commanding a more senior monk. If that monk does not bring water either, having properly swallowed the grains of rice, the seat should be given to the senior monk. And this has been said:

“Sace vuṭṭhāpeti, pavārito ca hoti, ‘gaccha udakaṃ āharā’ti vattabbo. Evañcetaṃ labhetha, iccetaṃ kusalaṃ. No ce labhetha, sādhukaṃ sitthāni gilitvā vuḍḍhassa āsanaṃ dātabbaṃ. Natvevāhaṃ, bhikkhave, ‘kenaci pariyāyena vuḍḍhatarassa bhikkhuno āsanaṃ paṭibāhitabba’nti vadāmi, yo paṭibāheyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (cūḷava. 316).

“If one makes him rise, and he has finished his meal, he is to be told, ‘Go, bring water.’ If one should obtain it thus, this is good. If one should not obtain it, having properly swallowed the grains of rice, the seat should be given to the senior one. O monks, I do not indeed say that ‘by any means whatsoever the seat of a more senior monk should be refused.’ Whoever should refuse it commits an offense of wrong-doing.”

8. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, navakena bhikkhunā uddisantena samake vā āsane nisīdituṃ uccatare vā dhammagāravena, therena bhikkhunā uddisāpentena samake vā āsane nisīdituṃ nīcatare vā dhammagāravenā”ti (cūḷava. 320) vacanato navakatarena bhikkhunā uddisantena uccatarepi āsane nisīdituṃ, vuḍḍhatarena bhikkhunā uddisāpentena nīcatarepi āsane nisīdituṃ vaṭṭati.

8. “O monks, I allow a junior monk, when teaching, to sit on a seat of equal height or, out of respect for the Dhamma, on a higher seat; and an elder monk, when receiving instruction, to sit on a seat of equal height or, out of respect for the Dhamma, on a lower seat.” Therefore, it is allowable for a more junior monk, when teaching, to sit even on a higher seat, and for a more senior monk, when receiving instruction, to sit even on a lower seat.

9. “Anujānāmi[M 0.0426], bhikkhave, tivassantarena saha nisīditu”nti (cūḷava. 320) vacanato tivassantarena bhikkhunā saddhiṃ ekāsane nisīdituṃ vaṭṭati. Tivassantaro (cūḷava. aṭṭha. 320) nāma yo dvīhi vassehi mahantataro vā daharataro vā hoti, yo pana ekena vassena [V 0.0397] mahantataro vā daharataro vā, yo vā samānavasso, tattha vattabbameva natthi, ime sabbe ekasmiṃ mañce vā pīṭhe vā dve dve hutvā nisīdituṃ labhanti. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, duvaggassa mañcaṃ duvaggassa pīṭha”nti (cūḷava. 320) hi vuttaṃ.

9. “I allow, bhikkhus, to sit together with one who is within three years of seniority.” Therefore, it is allowable for a bhikkhu to sit on the same seat with one who is within three years of seniority. “One within three years of seniority” means one who is either more senior or more junior by two years, or one who is more senior or more junior by one year, or one of the same seniority—in their case, there is nothing that needs to be said. All these may sit together two by two on the same bed or bench. For it is said: “I allow, bhikkhus, a bed for two, a bench for two.”

10. Yaṃ pana tiṇṇaṃ pahoti, taṃ saṃhārimaṃ vā hotu asaṃhārimaṃ vā, tathārūpe api phalakakhaṇḍe anupasampannenapi saddhiṃ nisīdituṃ vaṭṭati. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, yaṃ tiṇṇaṃ pahoti, ettakaṃ pacchimaṃ dīghāsana”nti (cūḷava. 320) hi vuttaṃ. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, ṭhapetvā paṇḍakaṃ mātugāmaṃ ubhatobyañjanakaṃ asamānāsanikehi saha dīghāsane nisīditu”nti (cūḷava. 320) vacanato pana dīghāsanepi paṇḍakādīhi saha nisīdituṃ na vaṭṭati.

10. Furthermore, on a seat that is sufficient for three—whether it be movable or immovable, even if it is a piece of board—it is allowable to sit together even with one who is not fully ordained. For it has been said: “Bhikkhus, that which is sufficient for three, I allow this much as the minimum for a long seat.” However, because of the saying: “Bhikkhus, excepting a eunuch, a woman, and one of both sexes, I allow sitting on a long seat together with those not on an equal seat,” it is not allowable to sit even on a long seat together with eunuchs and the others.

11. Gilānaṃ upaṭṭhahantena “natthi vo, bhikkhave, mātā, natthi pitā, ye vo upaṭṭhaheyyuṃ, tumhe ce, bhikkhave, aññamaññaṃ na upaṭṭhahissatha, atha ko carahi upaṭṭhahissati. Yo, bhikkhave, maṃ upaṭṭhaheyya, so gilānaṃ upaṭṭhaheyyā”ti (mahāva. 365) imaṃ bhagavato anusāsaniṃ anussarantena sakkaccaṃ upaṭṭhātabbo.

11. A sick person should be respectfully attended to by one who is attending, while repeatedly recollecting this instruction of the Blessed One: “Bhikkhus, you have no mother, you have no father, who might attend to you. If you, bhikkhus, do not attend to one another, then who will attend? Bhikkhus, whoever would attend to me, he should attend to the sick.”

Sace upajjhāyo hoti, upajjhāyena yāvajīvaṃ upaṭṭhātabbo, vuṭṭhānamassa āgametabbaṃ. Sace ācariyo hoti, ācariyena yāvajīvaṃ upaṭṭhātabbo, vuṭṭhānamassa āgametabbaṃ. Sace saddhivihāriko hoti, saddhivihārikena yāvajīvaṃ upaṭṭhātabbo, vuṭṭhānamassa āgametabbaṃ. Sace antevāsiko hoti, antevāsikena yāvajīvaṃ upaṭṭhātabbo, vuṭṭhānamassa āgametabbaṃ. Sace samānupajjhāyako hoti, samānupajjhāyakena yāvajīvaṃ upaṭṭhātabbo, vuṭṭhānamassa āgametabbaṃ. Sace samānācariyako hoti, samānācariyakena yāvajīvaṃ upaṭṭhātabbo, vuṭṭhānamassa āgametabbaṃ. Sace na hoti upajjhāyo vā ācariyo vā saddhivihāriko vā antevāsiko [M 0.0427] vā samānupajjhāyako vā samānācariyako vā, saṅghena upaṭṭhātabbo. No ce upaṭṭhaheyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (mahāva. 365) –

If he has a preceptor, he should be attended to by the preceptor for life, and his recovery should be awaited. If he has a teacher, he should be attended to by the teacher for life, and his recovery should be awaited. If he has a co-resident, he should be attended to by the co-resident for life, and his recovery should be awaited. If he has a resident pupil, he should be attended to by the resident pupil for life, and his recovery should be awaited. If he has one with the same preceptor, he should be attended to by the one with the same preceptor for life, and his recovery should be awaited. If he has one with the same teacher, he should be attended to by the one with the same teacher for life, and his recovery should be awaited. If he has neither a preceptor, nor a teacher, nor a co-resident, nor a resident pupil, nor one with the same preceptor, nor one with the same teacher, he should be attended to by the Sangha. If they do not attend, it is an offense of wrong-doing.

Vacanato yassa (mahāva. aṭṭha. 365) te upajjhāyādayo tasmiṃ vihāre natthi, āgantuko hoti ekacārikabhikkhu, saṅghassa bhāro, tasmā saṅghena upaṭṭhātabbo. No ce upaṭṭhaheyya, sakalassa saṅghassa āpatti. Vāraṃ ṭhapetvā jaggantesu pana yo attano vāre na jaggati, tasseva [V 0.0398] āpatti, saṅghattheropi vārato na muccati. Sace sakalo saṅgho ekassa bhāraṃ karoti, eko vā vattasampanno bhikkhu “ahameva jaggissāmī”ti jaggati, saṅgho āpattito muccati.

According to the statement, if for a sick bhikkhu those preceptors and so forth are not present in that monastery, and he is a visiting, solitary-faring bhikkhu, he is the responsibility of the Sangha. Therefore, he should be attended to by the Sangha. If they do not attend, it is an offense for the entire Sangha. However, among those attending by turns, whoever does not attend on his own turn, for him alone is the offense; even the elder of the Sangha is not exempt from his turn. If the entire Sangha assigns the responsibility to one bhikkhu, or if a bhikkhu accomplished in his duties attends, thinking, “I alone will attend,” the Sangha is freed from the offense.

Gilānena pana –

As for the sick person—

“Pañcahi, bhikkhave, aṅgehi samannāgato gilāno dūpaṭṭho hoti. Asappāyakārī hoti, sappāye mattaṃ na jānāti, bhesajjaṃ na paṭisevitā hoti, atthakāmassa gilānupaṭṭhākassa yathābhūtaṃ ābādhaṃ nāvikattā hoti ‘abhikkamantaṃ vā abhikkamatīti, paṭikkamantaṃ vā paṭikkamatīti, ṭhitaṃ vā ṭhito’ti, uppannānaṃ sārīrikānaṃ vedanānaṃ dukkhānaṃ tibbānaṃ kharānaṃ kaṭukānaṃ asātānaṃ amanāpānaṃ pāṇaharānaṃ anadhivāsakajātiko hotī”ti (mahāva. 366) –

“Bhikkhus, a sick person endowed with five factors is difficult to attend to. He does what is unsuitable; he does not know the measure in what is suitable; he does not take his medicine; he does not reveal his illness as it really is to an attendant who desires his welfare, saying, ‘It is increasing,’ when it is increasing, ‘It is decreasing,’ when it is decreasing, or ‘It is stable,’ when it is stable; and he is of a nature that cannot endure arisen bodily feelings that are painful, intense, harsh, sharp, disagreeable, unpleasant, and life-taking.”

Evaṃ vuttāni pañca ayuttaṅgāni ārakā parivajjetvā –

Having avoided from afar these five unsuitable factors thus stated—

“Pañcahi, bhikkhave, aṅgehi samannāgato gilāno sūpaṭṭho hoti. Sappāyakārī hoti, sappāye mattaṃ jānāti, bhesajjaṃ paṭisevitā hoti, atthakāmassa gilānupaṭṭhākassa yathābhūtaṃ ābādhaṃ āvikattā hoti ‘abhikkamantaṃ vā abhikkamatīti, paṭikkamantaṃ vā paṭikkamatīti, ṭhitaṃ vā ṭhito’ti, uppannānaṃ sārīrikānaṃ vedanānaṃ dukkhānaṃ tibbānaṃ kharānaṃ kaṭukānaṃ asātānaṃ amanāpānaṃ pāṇaharānaṃ adhivāsakajātiko hotī”ti (mahāva. 366) –

“Bhikkhus, a sick person endowed with five factors is easy to attend to. He does what is suitable; he knows the measure in what is suitable; he takes his medicine; he reveals his illness as it really is to an attendant who desires his welfare, saying, ‘It is increasing,’ when it is increasing, ‘It is decreasing,’ when it is decreasing, or ‘It is stable,’ when it is stable; and he is of a nature that can endure arisen bodily feelings that are painful, intense, harsh, sharp, disagreeable, unpleasant, and life-taking.”

Evaṃ vuttapañcaṅgasamannāgatena bhavitabbaṃ.

One should be endowed with the five factors thus stated.

Gilānupaṭṭhākena [M 0.0428] ca –

And as for the attendant of the sick—

“Pañcahi, bhikkhave, aṅgehi samannāgato gilānupaṭṭhāko nālaṃ gilānaṃ upaṭṭhātuṃ. Na paṭibalo hoti bhesajjaṃ saṃvidhātuṃ, sappāyāsappāyaṃ na jānāti, asappāyaṃ upanāmeti, sappāyaṃ apanāmeti, āmisantaro gilānaṃ upaṭṭhāti, no mettacitto, jegucchī hoti uccāraṃ vā passāvaṃ vā kheḷaṃ vā vantaṃ vā nīhātuṃ, na paṭibalo hoti [V 0.0399] gilānaṃ kālena kālaṃ dhammiyā kathāya sandassetuṃ samādapetuṃ samuttejetuṃ sampahaṃsetu”nti (mahāva. 366) –

“Bhikkhus, an attendant of the sick endowed with five factors is not fit to attend to the sick. He is not able to prepare medicine; he does not know what is suitable and unsuitable, offering what is unsuitable and removing what is suitable; he attends to the sick for material gain, not with a mind of loving-kindness; he is disgusted at removing feces, urine, saliva, or vomit; and he is not able from time to time to instruct, urge, rouse, and gladden the sick with a talk on the Dhamma.”

Evaṃ vuttāni pañca ayuttaṅgāni ārakā parivajjetvā –

Having avoided from afar these five unsuitable factors thus stated—

“Pañcahi, bhikkhave, aṅgehi samannāgato gilānupaṭṭhāko alaṃ gilānaṃ upaṭṭhātuṃ. Paṭibalo hoti bhesajjaṃ saṃvidhātuṃ, sappāyāsappāyaṃ jānāti, asappāyaṃ apanāmeti, sappāyaṃ upanāmeti, mettacitto gilānaṃ upaṭṭhāti, no āmisantaro, ajegucchī hoti uccāraṃ vā passāvaṃ vā kheḷaṃ vā vantaṃ vā nīhātuṃ, paṭibalo hoti gilānaṃ kālena kālaṃ dhammiyā kathāya sandassetuṃ samādapetuṃ samuttejetuṃ sampahaṃsetu”nti (mahāva. 366) –

Monks, a caregiver endowed with five qualities is fit to attend to the sick. They are capable of providing medicine, understand what is wholesome and unwholesome, remove what is unwholesome and provide what is wholesome, attend to the sick with a mind of loving-kindness, without an ulterior motive of material gain, are not disgusted when removing feces, urine, saliva, or vomit, and are capable of instructing, encouraging, inspiring, and gladdening the sick from time to time with a talk on the Dhamma.

Evaṃ vuttapañcaṅgasamannāgatena bhavitabbaṃ.

Thus, one should be endowed with the five stated factors.

12. Dhammiṃ kathaṃ karontena (mahāva. aṭṭha. 2.180) ca “sīlavā hi tvaṃ katakusalo, kasmā mīyamāno bhāyasi, nanu sīlavato saggo nāma maraṇamattapaṭibaddhoyevā”ti evaṃ gilānassa bhikkhuno maraṇavaṇṇo na saṃvaṇṇetabbo. Sace hi tassa saṃvaṇṇanaṃ sutvā āhārupacchedādinā upakkamena ekajavanavārāvasesepi āyusmiṃ antarā kālaṃ karoti, imināva mārito hoti. Paṇḍitena pana bhikkhunā iminā nayena anusiṭṭhi dātabbā “sīlavato nāma anacchariyā maggaphaluppatti, tasmā vihārādīsu āsattiṃ akatvā buddhagataṃ dhammagataṃ saṅghagataṃ kāyagatañca satiṃ upaṭṭhapetvā manasikāre appamādo kātabbo”ti. Maraṇavaṇṇepi saṃvaṇṇite so tāya saṃvaṇṇanāya kañci upakkamaṃ akatvā attano dhammatāya [M 0.0429] yathāyunā yathānusandhināva marati, tappaccayā saṃvaṇṇako āpattiyā na kāretabbo.

12. And when giving a Dhamma talk, one should not praise the virtues of death to a sick monk by saying, “You are indeed virtuous, one who has done wholesome deeds; why do you fear when you are dying? For one who is virtuous, is not the heavenly realm indeed just connected with the mere event of death?” For if, upon hearing such praise, he makes an effort by cutting off food and so forth and dies while even a single impulse-moment of life remains, he is considered to have been killed by this very person. Instead, a wise monk should give instruction in this way: “For one who is virtuous, the attainment of the path and fruit is not surprising. Therefore, without forming attachment to monasteries and so forth, one should establish mindfulness directed to the Buddha, the Dhamma, the Saṅgha, and the body, and practice heedfulness in attention.” Even if the virtues of death are praised and the sick monk, without making any effort on account of that praise, dies naturally in accordance with his lifespan and his karmic connection, on that account, the one who praised it should not be charged with an offense.

13. “Na ca, bhikkhave, attānaṃ pātetabbaṃ, yo pāteyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (pārā. 183) vacanato gilānena (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.182-183) bhikkhunāpi yena kenaci upakkamena antamaso āhārupacchedanenapi attā na māretabbo. Yopi gilāno vijjamāne bhesajje ca upaṭṭhākesu ca maritukāmo āhāraṃ upacchindati, dukkaṭameva. Yassa pana mahāābādho cirānubandho, bhikkhū upaṭṭhahantā kilamanti jigucchanti, “kadā nu kho gilānato [V 0.0400] muccissāmā”ti aṭṭīyanti. Sace so “ayaṃ attabhāvo paṭijaggiyamānopi na tiṭṭhati, bhikkhū ca kilamantī”ti āhāraṃ upacchindati, bhesajjaṃ na sevati, vaṭṭati. Yo pana “ayaṃ rogo kharo, āyusaṅkhārā na tiṭṭhanti, ayañca me visesādhigamo hatthappatto viya dissatī”ti upacchindati, vaṭṭatiyeva. Agilānassapi uppannasaṃvegassa “āhārapariyesanaṃ nāma papañco, kammaṭṭhānameva anuyuñjissāmī”ti kammaṭṭhānasīsena upacchindantassa vaṭṭati. Visesādhigamaṃ byākaritvā āhāraṃ upacchindati, na vaṭṭati. Sabhāgānañhi lajjībhikkhūnaṃ kathetuṃ vaṭṭati.

13. “And, monks, one should not destroy oneself. Whoever does so incurs an offense of dukkaṭa.” From this statement, even a sick monk should not kill himself by any means whatsoever, even by cutting off food. If a sick person, even when medicine and attendants are available, wishing to die, cuts off food, it is just a dukkaṭa offense. However, if someone has a severe and prolonged illness, and the monks attending him become weary, disgusted, and distressed, thinking, “When, oh when, shall we be free from this sick person?”—if he thinks, “This body will not survive even if tended to, and the monks are exhausted,” and cuts off food or does not take medicine, it is permissible. Furthermore, if he thinks, “This illness is severe, the life-formations do not last, and a special attainment appears as if it has come to hand,” and cuts off food, it is indeed permissible. Even for one who is not sick, but for whom a sense of spiritual urgency has arisen, and who thinks, “The seeking of food is proliferation; I will devote myself to the meditation subject,” and cuts off food with the meditation subject as the primary focus, it is permissible. But if one declares a special attainment and then cuts off food, it is not permissible. For it is permissible to speak of it to fellow, scrupulous monks.

14. “Na ca, bhikkhave, appaṭivekkhitvā āsane nisīditabbaṃ, yo nisīdeyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (pārā. 180) vacanato āsanaṃ anupaparikkhitvā na nisīditabbaṃ. Kīdisaṃ (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.180) pana āsanaṃ upaparikkhitabbaṃ, kīdisaṃ na upaparikkhitabbaṃ? Yaṃ suddhaṃ āsanameva hoti apaccattharaṇakaṃ, yañca āgantvā ṭhitānaṃ passataṃyeva attharīyati, taṃ na paccavekkhitabbaṃ, nisīdituṃ vaṭṭati. Yampi manussā sayaṃ hatthena akkamitvā “idha bhante nisīdathā”ti denti, tasmimpi vaṭṭati. Sacepi paṭhamameva āgantvāpi nisinnā pacchā uddhaṃ vā adho vā saṅkamanti, paṭivekkhaṇakiccaṃ natthi. Yampi tanukena vatthena yathā talaṃ dissati, evaṃ paṭicchannaṃ hoti, tasmimpi paṭivekkhaṇakiccaṃ natthi. Yaṃ pana paṭikacceva pāvārakojavādīhi atthataṃ hoti, taṃ hatthena parāmasitvā sallakkhetvā nisīditabbaṃ. Mahāpaccariyaṃ pana “ghanasāṭakenapi atthate yasmiṃ vali na paññāyati, taṃ na paṭivekkhitabba”nti vuttaṃ.

14. “And, monks, one should not sit down on a seat without first inspecting it. Whoever does so incurs an offense of dukkaṭa.” Therefore, a seat should not be sat upon without examining it. But what kind of seat should be examined, and what kind should not be examined? That which is simply a clean seat without a covering, and that which is spread out in the sight of those who have arrived and are standing—that should not be examined; it is permissible to sit. It is also permissible to sit on that which people themselves press down with their hand and offer, saying, “Venerable Sirs, sit here.” Also, if those who arrived first and are seated should afterwards move upwards or downwards, there is no need for examination. There is also no need for examination for that which is covered with a thin cloth so that the surface is visible. But that which has been spread beforehand with cloaks, rugs, and so forth, that should be touched with the hand and observed before sitting. However, in the Mahāpaccariya, it is said, “Even if it is covered with a thick cloth where no folds are apparent, that should not be examined.”

15. “Na[M 0.0430], bhikkhave, davāya silā paṭivijjhitabbā, yo paṭivijjheyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (pārā. 183) vacanato hasādhippāyena pāsāṇo na pavaṭṭetabbo. Na kevalañca (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.182-183) pāsāṇo, aññampi yaṃ kiñci dārukhaṇḍaṃ vā iṭṭhakakhaṇḍaṃ vā hatthena vā yantena vā paṭivijjhituṃ na vaṭṭati. Cetiyādīnaṃ atthāya pāsāṇādayo hasantā hasantā pavaṭṭentipi khipantipi ukkhipantipi, “kammasamayo”ti vaṭṭati, aññampi īdisaṃ navakammaṃ vā karontā bhaṇḍakaṃ vā dhovantā rukkhaṃ vā dhovanadaṇḍakaṃ vā ukkhipitvā paṭivijjhanti, vaṭṭati, bhattavissaggakālādīsu kāke vā soṇe vā kaṭṭhaṃ vā kathalaṃ vā khipitvā palāpenti, vaṭṭati.

15. “O monks, a stone should not be rolled for sport. Whoever should roll one, incurs an offense of dukkaṭa.” Therefore, a stone should not be rolled with the intention of amusement. And not only a stone, but it is also not proper to roll any other piece of wood or piece of brick by hand or by a device. For the purpose of cetiyas and so forth, if they roll, throw, or lift stones and so forth while laughing, it is permissible, considering it ‘a time for work.’ Also, if those doing other such new work or washing robes lift and throw a tree or a washing-stick, it is permissible. During the time of distributing food and so forth, if they throw a piece of wood or a potsherd to make crows or dogs flee, it is permissible.

16. “Na, bhikkhave, dāyo ālimpitabbo, yo ālimpeyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (cūḷava. 283) vacanato [V 0.0401] vane aggi na dātabbo. Sace (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.190) pana “etthantare yo koci satto maratū”ti aggiṃ deti, pārājikānantariyathullaccayapācittiyavatthūnaṃ anurūpato pārājikādīni akusalarāsi ca hoti. “Allatiṇavanappatayo ḍayhantū”ti aggiṃ dentassa pācittiyaṃ, “dabbūpakaraṇāni vinassantū”ti aggiṃ dentassa dukkaṭaṃ. “Khiḍḍādhippāyenapi dukkaṭa”nti saṅkhepaṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttaṃ. “Yaṃ kiñci allasukkhaṃ saindriyānindriyaṃ ḍayhatū”ti aggiṃ dentassa vatthuvasena pārājikathullaccayapācittiyadukkaṭāni veditabbāni.

16. “Bhikkhus, a forest fire is not to be set. Whoever should set one, incurs an offense of wrong-doing.” Therefore, a fire is not to be set in the forest. But if one sets a fire with the thought, ‘May any being whatsoever within this area die,’ then in accordance with the objects of defeat, of an act with immediate consequence, of a grave offense, and of expiation, the offenses of defeat and so forth, and a mass of demerit arise. For one who sets a fire thinking, ‘May the fresh grass and vegetation burn,’ there is an offense of expiation. For one who sets a fire thinking, ‘May the grass implements be destroyed,’ there is an offense of wrong-doing. In the Saṅkhepaṭṭhakathā it is said: “For one setting a fire even with the intention of sport, there is an offense of wrong-doing.” For one who sets a fire thinking, ‘May whatever is wet or dry, animate or inanimate, burn,’ the offenses of defeat, grave offense, expiation, and wrong-doing should be known according to the object.

Paṭaggidānaṃ pana parittakaraṇañca bhagavatā anuññātaṃ, tasmā araññe vanakammikehi vā dinnaṃ sayaṃ vā uṭṭhitaṃ aggiṃ āgacchantaṃ disvā “tiṇakuṭiyo mā vinassantū”ti tassa aggino paṭiaggiṃ dātuṃ vaṭṭati, yena saddhiṃ āgacchanto aggi ekato hutvā nirupādāno nibbāti. “Parittampi kātuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti tiṇakuṭikānaṃ samantā bhūmitacchanaṃ parikhākhaṇanaṃ vā, yathā āgato aggi upādānaṃ alabhitvā nibbāti, etañca sabbaṃ uṭṭhiteyeva aggismiṃ asati anupasampanne sayampi kātuṃ vaṭṭati. Anuṭṭhite pana anupasampannehi kappiyavohārena kāretabbaṃ, udakena pana nibbāpentehi appāṇakameva udakaṃ āsiñcitabbaṃ.

However, the setting of a counter-fire and the making of a protective barrier have been permitted by the Blessed One. Therefore, in the forest, upon seeing a fire set by forest workers or one that has arisen by itself approaching, it is permissible to set a counter-fire to that fire, thinking, ‘Let the grass-roofed huts not be destroyed,’ so that the approaching fire, having become one with it, is extinguished for lack of fuel. It is also permissible to make a protective barrier, such as leveling the ground or digging a trench around the grass-roofed huts, so that the approaching fire, not obtaining fuel, is extinguished. And all this, when a fire has already arisen and an unordained person is not present, it is permissible to do oneself. But when a fire has not yet arisen, it should be caused to be done by unordained persons using allowable speech. And those extinguishing with water should pour only water that is free of living beings.

17. Assaddhesu [M 0.0431] (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.181) micchādiṭṭhikulesu sakkaccaṃ paṇītabhojanaṃ labhitvā anupaparikkhitvā neva attanā paribhuñjitabbaṃ, na paresaṃ dātabbaṃ. Visamissampi hi tāni kulāni piṇḍapātaṃ denti. Yampi ābhidosikaṃ bhattaṃ vā khajjakaṃ vā tato labhati, tampi na paribhuñjitabbaṃ. Apihitavatthumpi hi sappavicchikādīhi adhisayitaṃ chaḍḍanīyadhammaṃ tāni kulāni denti. Gandhahaliddādimakkhitopi tato piṇḍapāto na gahetabbo. Sarīre rogaṭṭhānāni puñchitvā ṭhapitabhattampi hi tāni dātabbaṃ maññantīti.

17. Having received respectfully prepared, excellent food from faithless families of wrong view, without examining it, it should neither be consumed by oneself nor given to others. For those families may offer almsfood even mixed with poison. Whatever stale food or snacks one obtains from them, that too should not be consumed. For those families may offer even an uncovered item, which is to be discarded, having been lain upon by snakes, scorpions, and so forth. Even almsfood smeared with perfumes, turmeric, and so forth should not be accepted from them. For they might think it proper to offer food that has been placed after wiping diseased parts of their bodies.

18. “Anāpatti, bhikkhave, gopakassa dāne”ti (pārā. 156) vuttaṃ. Tattha (pārā. aṭṭha. 1.156) kataraṃ gopakadānaṃ vaṭṭati, kataraṃ na vaṭṭati? Mahāsumatthero tāva āha “yaṃ gopakassa paricchinditvā dinnaṃ hoti ‘ettakaṃ divase divase gaṇhā’ti, tadeva vaṭṭati, tato uttari na vaṭṭatī”ti. Mahāpadumatthero panāha “kiṃ gopakānaṃ paṇṇaṃ āropetvā nimittasaññaṃ vā katvā dinnaṃ atthi, etesaṃ hatthe vissaṭṭhakassa ete issarā, tasmā yaṃ denti, taṃ bahukampi vaṭṭatī”ti. Kurundaṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana vuttaṃ “manussānaṃ ārāmaṃ vā aññaṃ vā phalāphalaṃ dārakā rakkhanti, tehi dinnaṃ vaṭṭati, āharāpetvā pana na gahetabbaṃ. Saṅghike pana cetiyassa [V 0.0402] santake ca keṇiyā gahetvā rakkhantasseva dānaṃ vaṭṭati, vetanena rakkhantassa attano bhāgamattaṃ vaṭṭatī”ti. Mahāpaccariyaṃ pana “yaṃ gihīnaṃ ārāmarakkhakā bhikkhūnaṃ denti, etampi vaṭṭati. Bhikkhusaṅghassa ārāmagopakā yaṃ attano bhatiyā khaṇḍitvā denti, etaṃ vaṭṭati. Yopi upaḍḍhārāmaṃ vā kecideva rukkhe vā bhatiṃ labhitvā rakkhati, tassapi attano sampattarukkhatoyeva dātuṃ vaṭṭati, keṇiyā gahetvā rakkhantassa pana sabbampi vaṭṭatī”ti vuttaṃ. Etaṃ pana sabbaṃ byañjanato nānaṃ, atthato ekameva, tasmā adhippāyaṃ ñatvā gahetabbaṃ.

18. “There is no offense, Bhikkhus, in an offering from a park-keeper,” it is said. In this context, which offering from a park-keeper is allowable, and which is not? The Elder Mahāsuma, for his part, stated: “Whatever is given to the park-keeper after it has been demarcated with the instruction, ‘Take this much each day,’ that alone is allowable; anything beyond that is not allowable.” However, the Elder Mahāpaduma stated: “Is there anything given to park-keepers after affixing a leaf or making a sign as a mark? They are masters of what has been released into their hands; therefore, whatever they give, even if a large amount, is allowable.” But in the Kurundaṭṭhakathā, it is stated: “When children guard a park of laypeople or other fruits, major and minor, what is given by them is allowable, but having it brought, it should not be accepted. In the case of what belongs to the Saṅgha or a cetiya, the offering of one who guards it after having purchased it is allowable. For one who guards for a wage, only his own share is allowable.” However, in the Mahāpaccariya, it is said: “Whatever the park-keepers of laypeople give to the bhikkhus, that too is allowable. If the park-keepers of the Saṅgha of bhikkhus give something, having deducted it from their own wage, that is allowable. And whoever guards half a park or only certain trees, having received a wage, for him too, it is allowable to give only from the trees that have fallen to his share. But for one who guards after having purchased it, even all of it is allowable.” All this, however, is different in letter but one and the same in meaning; therefore, it should be understood by discerning the intention.

Apicettha ayampi vinicchayo veditabbo (pārā. aṭṭha. 1.156) – yattha āvāsikā āgantukānaṃ na denti, phalavāre ca sampatte aññesaṃ abhāvaṃ disvā corikāya attanāva khādanti, tattha āgantukehi ghaṇṭiṃ paharitvā bhājetvā paribhuñjituṃ vaṭṭati. Yattha pana āvāsikā rukkhe rakkhitvā phalavāre sampatte bhājetvā khādanti, catūsu paccayesu sammā upanenti, anissarā [M 0.0432] tattha āgantukā. Yepi rukkhā cīvaratthāya niyametvā dinnā, tesupi āgantukā anissarā. Esa nayo sesapaccayatthāya niyametvā dinnepi. Ye pana tathā aniyametvā āvāsikā ca te rakkhitvā gopetvā corikāya paribhuñjanti, na tesu āvāsikānaṃ katikāya ṭhātabbaṃ. Ye phalaparibhogatthāya dinnā, āvāsikā ca ne rakkhitvā gopetvā sammā upanenti, tesuyeva tesaṃ katikāya ṭhātabbaṃ. Mahāpaccariyaṃ pana vuttaṃ “catunnaṃ paccayānaṃ niyametvā dinnaṃ theyyacittena paribhuñjanto bhaṇḍaṃ agghāpetvā kāretabbo, paribhogavasena bhājetvā paribhuñjantassa bhaṇḍadeyyaṃ. Yaṃ panettha senāsanatthāya niyamitaṃ, taṃ paribhogavaseneva bhājetvā paribhuñjantassa thullaccayañca bhaṇḍadeyyañcā”ti.

Furthermore, here this legal decision should also be understood: where resident bhikkhus do not give to visiting bhikkhus, and when the turn for distributing fruit arrives, seeing that others are absent, they consume it themselves by stealth; there it is allowable for the visiting bhikkhus to strike the gong, divide the fruit, and partake of it. But where resident bhikkhus guard the trees and, when the turn for distributing fruit arrives, divide and consume it, and properly provide the four requisites, the visiting bhikkhus have no authority there. Also, regarding trees that have been designated and given for the purpose of robes, the visiting bhikkhus have no authority. This same principle applies to things designated and given for the purpose of the other requisites. However, regarding those trees which, without being so designated, the resident bhikkhus guard, protect, and consume by stealth, one should not abide by the agreement of those resident bhikkhus. Regarding those trees given for the purpose of partaking of the fruit, if the resident bhikkhus guard, protect, and properly provide them, only in that case should one abide by their agreement. In the Mahāpaccarī, however, it is stated: ‘A bhikkhu who partakes with a thieving mind of what has been designated for the four requisites should be made to pay the value of the goods. For one who partakes after dividing it by way of consumption, there is payment for the goods. As for what among these has been designated for the purpose of lodging, for one who partakes of it after dividing it only by way of consumption, there is a grave offense and payment for the goods.’

Odissa cīvaratthāya dinnaṃ cīvareyeva upanetabbaṃ. Sace dubbhikkhaṃ hoti, bhikkhū piṇḍapātena kilamanti, cīvaraṃ pana sulabhaṃ, saṅghasuṭṭhutāya apalokanakammaṃ katvā piṇḍapātepi upanetuṃ vaṭṭati. Senāsanena gilānapaccayena vā kilamantesu saṅghasuṭṭhutāya apalokanakammaṃ katvā tadatthāyapi upanetuṃ vaṭṭati. Odissa piṇḍapātatthāya ca gilānapaccayatthāya ca dinnepi eseva nayo. Odissa senāsanatthāya dinnaṃ pana garubhaṇḍaṃ hoti, taṃ rakkhitvā gopetvā tadatthameva upanetabbaṃ. Sace pana dubbhikkhaṃ hoti, bhikkhū piṇḍapātena na yāpenti, ettha rājarogacorabhayādīhi aññattha gacchantānaṃ vihārā palujjanti, tālanāḷikerādike vināsenti, senāsanapaccayaṃ pana nissāya yāpetuṃ sakkā hoti, evarūpe kāle senāsanaṃ vissajjetvāpi senāsanajagganatthāya paribhogo bhagavatā anuññāto. Tasmā ekaṃ vā dve vā varasenāsanāni ṭhapetvā [V 0.0403] itarāni lāmakakoṭiyā piṇḍapātatthāya vissajjetuṃ vaṭṭanti, mūlavatthucchedaṃ pana katvā na upanetabbaṃ.

What is specifically designated for robes should be applied only for robes. If there is a famine, and the monks are distressed by lack of almsfood, but robes are easily obtained, having performed an act of announcement for the welfare of the Sangha, it is permissible to apply it for almsfood as well. If monks are distressed due to lodging or requisites for the sick, having performed an act of announcement for the welfare of the Sangha, it is permissible to apply it for those purposes too. This same principle applies when something is specifically designated for almsfood or for requisites for the sick. However, what is given specifically for lodging is a heavy item; it should be guarded and protected and applied only for that purpose. But if there is a famine and the monks cannot subsist on almsfood, and in that place, due to dangers from kings, disease, thieves, and so on, the monasteries of those going elsewhere are ruined and their palm, coconut, and other trees are destroyed, yet it is possible to subsist by relying on the requisite of lodging—in such a time, its use for the sake of maintaining the lodging, even by disposing of the lodging, has been permitted by the Blessed One. Therefore, having set aside one or two excellent lodgings, it is permissible to dispose of the others, beginning with the inferior ones, for the sake of almsfood. However, it should not be applied by destroying the original property.

Yo pana ārāmo catupaccayatthāya niyametvā dinno, tattha apalokanakammaṃ na kātabbaṃ. Yena paccayena pana ūnaṃ, tadatthaṃ upanetuṃ vaṭṭati, ārāmo paṭijaggitabbo, vetanaṃ datvāpi jaggāpetuṃ vaṭṭati. Ye pana vetanaṃ labhitvā ārāmeyeva gehaṃ katvā vasantā rakkhanti, te ce āgatānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ nāḷikeraṃ vā tālapakkaṃ vā denti, yaṃ tesaṃ saṅghena anuññātaṃ hoti “divase divase ettakaṃ nāma khādathā”ti, tadeva [M 0.0433] te dātuṃ labhanti, tato uttari tesaṃ dentānampi gahetuṃ na vaṭṭanti. Yo pana ārāmaṃ keṇiyā gahetvā saṅghassa catupaccayatthāya kappiyabhaṇḍameva deti, ayaṃ bahukampi dātuṃ labhati. Cetiyassa padīpatthāya vā khaṇḍaphullapaṭisaṅkharaṇatthāya vā dinnaārāmopi jaggitabbo, vetanaṃ datvāpi jaggāpetabbo. Vetanañca panettha cetiyasantakampi saṅghasantakampi dātuṃ vaṭṭati. Etampi ārāmaṃ vetanena tattheva vasitvā rakkhantānañca keṇiyā gahetvā kappiyabhaṇḍadāyakānañca tatthajātakaphaladānaṃ vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ.

However, for a monastery that has been given, having been designated for the sake of the four requisites, an act of announcement is not to be performed therein. If any of the requisites are lacking, it is allowable to apply it for that purpose. The monastery is to be maintained, and it is also permissible to hire someone for wages to maintain it. Those who, having received wages, build houses within the monastery grounds and live there to guard it—if they offer coconuts or ripe palm fruits to arriving monks, they may give only what the Sangha has permitted them, saying, “Eat this much each day.” Beyond that, even if they offer more, it is not permissible for the monks to accept it. However, one who, having acquired the monastery by purchase, provides only allowable goods for the Sangha’s four requisites, such a person is permitted to give even a great deal. A monastery given for the purpose of a lamp for a shrine or for repairing broken and dilapidated parts should also be maintained, and it is permissible to hire someone for wages to maintain it. Here, wages may be given from what belongs to the shrine as well as what belongs to the Sangha. Similarly, regarding this monastery, the giving of fruits produced there by those who guard it while living there for wages, and by those who, having acquired it by purchase, provide allowable goods, should be understood in the same way as previously explained.

19. Dhammikarakkhaṃ (pāci. aṭṭha. 679) yācantena atītaṃ anāgataṃ vā ārabbha odissa ācikkhituṃ na vaṭṭati. Atītañhi ārabbha atthi odissa ācikkhanā, atthi anodissa ācikkhanā, anāgataṃ ārabbhapi atthi odissa ācikkhanā, atthi anodissa ācikkhanā. Kathaṃ atītaṃ ārabbha odissa ācikkhanā hoti? Bhikkhūnaṃ vihāre gāmadārakā vā dhuttādayo vā ye keci anācāraṃ ācaranti, rukkhaṃ vā chindanti, phalāphalaṃ vā haranti, parikkhāre vā acchindanti, bhikkhu vohārike upasaṅkamitvā “amhākaṃ vihāre idaṃ nāma kata”nti vadati. “Kenā”ti vutte “asukena ca asukena cā”ti ācikkhati. Evaṃ atītaṃ ārabbha odissa ācikkhanā hoti, sā na vaṭṭati. Tañce sutvā te vohārikā tesaṃ daṇḍaṃ karonti, sabbaṃ bhikkhussa gīvā hoti, “daṇḍaṃ gaṇhissantī”ti adhippāyepi sati gīvāyeva hoti. Sace pana “tassa daṇḍaṃ gaṇhathā”ti vadati, pañcamāsakamatte gahite pārājikaṃ hoti. “Kenā”ti vutte pana “asukenāti vattuṃ amhākaṃ na vaṭṭati, tumheyeva jānissatha. Kevalañhi mayaṃ rakkhaṃ yācāma, taṃ no detha, avahaṭabhaṇḍañca āharāpethā”ti vattabbaṃ. Evaṃ anodissa ācikkhanā hoti, sā vaṭṭati. Evaṃ vutte sacepi te vohārikā kārake gavesitvā tesaṃ daṇḍaṃ karonti, sabbasāpateyyepi gahite bhikkhuno neva gīvā, na āpatti. Parikkhāraṃ harante disvā tesaṃ anatthakāmatāya “coro [V 0.0404] coro”ti vattumpi na vaṭṭati. Evaṃ vuttepi hi yaṃ tesaṃ daṇḍaṃ karonti, sabbaṃ bhikkhuno gīvā hoti. Attano vacanakaraṃ pana “iminā me parikkhāro gahito, taṃ āharāpehi, mā cassa daṇḍaṃ karohī”ti [M 0.0434] vattuṃ vaṭṭati. Dāsadāsīvāpiādīnampi atthāya aḍḍaṃ karonti ayaṃ akappiyaaḍḍo nāma, na vaṭṭati.

19. When requesting righteous protection, it is not allowable to report concerning a past or future event by specifying individuals. Indeed, concerning the past, there is reporting by specifying and reporting without specifying; concerning the future, there is also reporting by specifying and reporting without specifying. How is there reporting concerning the past by specifying? In the monks' monastery, village boys, rogues, or whoever else may commit misconduct: they may cut down a tree, take fruit, or forcibly take requisites. A monk, having approached the judicial officers, says, “In our monastery, such-and-such a deed was done.” When asked, “By whom?” he reports, “By so-and-so and so-and-so.” This is reporting concerning the past by specifying; it is not allowable. If, having heard this, those judicial officers impose a punishment on them, the entire responsibility is the monk's. Even if there is only the intention, “They will impose a punishment,” the responsibility is still his. But if he says, “Impose a punishment on him,” when a fine of the value of five māsakas is taken, a pārājika offense is incurred. But when asked, “By whom?” it should be said: “It is not allowable for us to say by whom; you yourselves will find out. We are merely requesting protection; give that to us, and have the stolen goods returned.” This is reporting without specifying; it is allowable. When it is said thus, even if those judicial officers, having sought out the perpetrators, impose a punishment on them, and even if all their property is taken, it is not the monk's responsibility, nor is there an offense. Seeing those taking a requisite, it is not allowable to say, “Thief! Thief!” with the wish for their harm. For even when it is said thus, whatever punishment they impose on them, the entire responsibility is the monk's. However, to one who does one's bidding, it is allowable to say: “My requisite was taken by this person; have it brought back, and do not impose a punishment on him.” Even for the sake of male and female slaves, reservoirs, and so on, if they impose a fine, this is called an 'unallowable fine'; it is not allowable.

Kathaṃ anāgataṃ ārabbha odissa ācikkhanā hoti? Vuttanayeneva parehi anācārādīsu katesu bhikkhu vohārike evaṃ vadati “amhākaṃ vihāre idañcidañca karonti, rakkhaṃ no detha āyatiṃ akaraṇatthāyā”ti. “Kena evaṃ kata”nti vutte ca “asukena ca asukena cā”ti ācikkhati. Evaṃ anāgataṃ ārabbha odissa ācikkhanā hoti, sāpi na vaṭṭati. Tesañhi daṇḍe kate purimanayeneva sabbaṃ bhikkhussa gīvā, sesaṃ purimasadisameva. Sace vohārikā “bhikkhūnaṃ vihāre evarūpaṃ anācāraṃ karontānaṃ imaṃ nāma daṇḍaṃ karomā”ti bheriṃ carāpetvā āṇāya atiṭṭhamāne pariyesitvā daṇḍaṃ karonti, bhikkhuno neva gīvā, na āpatti. Vihārasīmāya rukkhādīni chindantānaṃ vāsipharasuādīni gahetvā pāsāṇehi koṭṭenti, na vaṭṭati. Sace dhārā bhijjati, kārāpetvā dātabbā. Upadhāvitvā tesaṃ parikkhāre gaṇhanti, tampi na kātabbaṃ. Lahuparivattañhi cittaṃ, theyyacetanāya uppannāya mūlacchejjampi gaccheyya.

How is reporting by specifying with regard to the future done? In the same way as before, when others have committed misconduct, a monk tells the authorities: “In our monastery, such and such things are being done. Give us protection so that they will not do it again in the future.” When asked, “By whom was this done?” he replies, “By so-and-so and so-and-so.” Thus, reporting by specifying with regard to the future occurs, but even this is not permissible. For if punishment is inflicted on them, all the blame falls on the monk as before, and the rest is similar to the previous case. If the authorities, intending to punish those who commit such misconduct in the monks’ monastery, proclaim an order by beating a drum and then, after searching, inflict punishment on those who do not abide by the order, there is neither responsibility nor an offense for the monk. It is not permissible to take the adzes, axes, and so on from those who are cutting trees and so on within the monastery boundary and strike the tools with stones. If a blade breaks, it should be repaired and given back. Chasing after them and seizing their belongings—that too should not be done. For the mind is quick to change, and if an intention of theft arises, it could lead even to an offense entailing expulsion.

20. Uccāraṃ vā passāvaṃ vā saṅkāraṃ vā vighāsaṃ vā tirokuṭṭe vā tiropākāre vā chaḍḍetuṃ vā chaḍḍāpetuṃ vā na vaṭṭati. Cattāripi (pāci. aṭṭha. 826) vatthūni ekapayogena chaḍḍentassa ekameva dukkaṭaṃ, pāṭekkaṃ chaḍḍentassa vatthugaṇanāya dukkaṭāni. Āṇattiyampi eseva nayo. Dantakaṭṭhachaḍḍanepi dukkaṭameva. Oloketvā vā avalañje vā uccārādīni chaḍḍentassa anāpatti. Yampi manussānaṃ upabhogaparibhogaṃ ropimaṃ khettaṃ hotu nāḷikerādiārāmo vā, tatthāpi yattha katthaci ropimaharitaṭṭhāne etāni vatthūni chaḍḍetuṃ na vaṭṭati. Chaḍḍentassa purimanayeneva āpattibhedo veditabbo. Khette vā ārāme vā nisīditvā bhuñjamāno ucchuādīni vā khādamāno gacchanto ucchiṭṭhodakacalakādīni haritaṭṭhāne chaḍḍeti, antamaso udakaṃ pivitvā matthakacchinnanāḷikerampi chaḍḍeti, dukkaṭaṃ. Kasitaṭṭhāne nikkhittabīje aṅkure uṭṭhitepi avuṭṭhitepi dukkaṭameva. Anikkhittabījesu pana khettakoṇādīsu vā asañjātaropimesu khettamariyādādīsu vā chaḍḍetuṃ vaṭṭati, manussānaṃ kacavarachaḍḍanaṭṭhānepi vaṭṭati. Manussesu [M 0.0435] sassaṃ uddharitvā gatesu chaḍḍitakhettaṃ nāma hoti, tattha vaṭṭati. Yattha pana “lāyitampi pubbaṇṇādi puna uṭṭhahissatī”ti rakkhanti, tattha na vaṭṭati.

20. It is not allowable to discard or to cause to be discarded feces, urine, rubbish, or leftovers beyond a wall or a fence. For the four substances, discarding them with a single effort incurs one offense of wrong conduct; discarding them separately incurs offenses of wrong conduct according to the number of items. This same method applies to giving an order. Even in the case of discarding a tooth-stick, it is an offense of wrong conduct. There is no offense for one who discards feces and so on after looking, or in a place not used by people. Whatever cultivated field or coconut grove, etc., is for the use and enjoyment of humans, it is not allowable to discard these items in any planted green place there. For one who discards, the distinction of offenses should be understood according to the previous method. If one, while sitting and eating in a field or a grove, or while chewing sugarcane and so on and walking, discards leftover water, scraps, and so on in a green place; or at the very least, after drinking the water, discards a coconut with its top cut off, it is an offense of wrong conduct. On plowed land where seeds have been sown, whether sprouts have emerged or not, it is an offense of wrong conduct. However, it is allowable to discard in corners of fields where seeds have not been sown, or on unplanted field boundaries, and so on, or in a place where people discard rubbish. When people have harvested the crop and departed, it is called an abandoned field; there it is allowable. But where they guard it, thinking, 'Even though reaped, the early grain and so on will sprout again,' there it is not allowable.
