21. “Na[V 0.0405], bhikkhave, nahāyamānena bhikkhunā rukkhe kāyo ugghaṃsetabbo, yo ugghaṃseyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (cūḷava. 243) vacanato nahāyantena (cūḷava. aṭṭha. 243 ādayo) rukkhe vā nahānatitthe nikhanitvā ṭhapitatthambhe vā iṭṭhakasilādārukuṭṭānaṃ aññatarasmiṃ kuṭṭe vā kāyo na ghaṃsetabbo.

21. “Monks, a monk who is bathing should not rub his body against a tree. Whoever should do so, commits an offense of wrong conduct.” Therefore, while bathing, one should not rub one's body against a tree, a pillar dug in and set up at a bathing place, or any wall made of brick, stone, or wood.

“Na, bhikkhave, aṭṭāne nahāyitabbaṃ, yo nahāyeyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (cūḷava. 243) vacanato aṭṭānepi nahāyituṃ na vaṭṭati. Aṭṭānaṃ nāma rukkhaṃ phalakaṃ viya tacchetvā aṭṭhapadākārena rājiyo chinditvā nahānatitthe nikhananti, tattha cuṇṇāni ākiritvā manussā kāyaṃ ghaṃsanti.

“Monks, one should not bathe on a scrubbing board. Whoever does so, commits an offense of wrong conduct.” Thus, it is not permissible to bathe on a scrubbing board. A scrubbing board is a wooden board, planed like a plank, into which grooves are carved in the pattern of a checkerboard; they embed it in a bathing place, and people sprinkle powder on it to scrub their bodies.

“Na, bhikkhave, gandhabbahatthakena nahāyitabbaṃ, yo nahāyeyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (cūḷva. 243) vacanato nahānatitthe ṭhapitena dārumayahatthena cuṇṇāni gahetvā manussā sarīraṃ ghaṃsanti, tena nahāyituṃ na vaṭṭati.

“Monks, one should not bathe with a wooden hand. Whoever does so, commits an offense of wrong conduct.” Thus, it is not permissible to bathe with a hand made of wood that is placed at a bathing place, with which people take powders and scrub their bodies.

“Na, bhikkhave, kuruvindakasuttiyā nahāyitabbaṃ, yo nahāyeyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (cūḷava. 243) vacanato kuruvindakasuttiyāpi nahāyituṃ na vaṭṭati. Kuruvindakasutti nāma kuruvindakapāsāṇacuṇṇāni lākhāya bandhitvā kataguḷikakalāpako vuccati, yaṃ ubhosu antesu gahetvā sarīraṃ ghaṃsanti.

“Monks, one should not bathe using a string of rubbing balls. Whoever should do so, commits an offense of wrong conduct.” Thus, it is not permissible to bathe using a string of rubbing balls. A string of rubbing balls is said to be a rope of balls made by binding touchstone powder with lac, which they hold at both ends and rub on the body.

“Na, bhikkhave, viggayha parikammaṃ kārāpetabbaṃ, yo kārāpeyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (cūḷava. 243) vacanato aññamaññaṃ sarīrena ghaṃsituṃ na vaṭṭati.

“Monks, one should not have the body scrubbed by rubbing against another. Whoever should have it done, commits an offense of wrong conduct.” Therefore, it is not permissible to rub bodies against one another.

“Na, bhikkhave, mallakena nahāyitabbaṃ, yo nahāyeyya, āpatti dukkaṭassa. Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, gilānassa akatamallaka”nti (cūḷava. 243-244) vacanato makaradaṇḍake chinditvā mallakamūlasaṇṭhānena kataṃ “mallaka”nti vuccati, idaṃ gilānassapi na vaṭṭati. Akatamallakaṃ nāma dante acchinditvā kataṃ, idaṃ agilānassa na vaṭṭati, iṭṭhakakhaṇḍaṃ pana kapālakhaṇḍaṃ vā vaṭṭati.

“Monks, a back-scrubber should not be used for bathing; whoever does so, commits an offense of wrong conduct. I allow, monks, a back-scrubber without teeth for the sick.” Thus, what is called a “back-scrubber,” which has crocodile-teeth patterns carved into it, is not permissible even for the sick. A back-scrubber without teeth is one made without carving teeth; this is not permissible for one who is not sick. However, a piece of brick or a potsherd is permissible.

“Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, ukkāsikaṃ puthupāṇika”nti (cūḷava. 244) vacanato ukkāsikaṃ puthupāṇikañca vaṭṭati. Ukkāsikaṃ nāma vatthavaṭṭi, tasmā nahāyantassa [M 0.0436] yassa kassaci [V 0.0406] nahānasāṭakavaṭṭiyā piṭṭhiṃ ghaṃsituṃ vaṭṭati. Puthupāṇikanti hatthaparikammaṃ vuccati, tasmā sabbesaṃ hatthena piṭṭhiparikammaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭati.

“Monks, I allow a twisted cloth and scrubbing with the hand.” Therefore, a twisted cloth and scrubbing with the hand are allowable. A twisted cloth is called an ‘ukkāsika’; therefore, it is allowable for any monk who is bathing to rub his back with a twisted bathing cloth. Scrubbing with the hand is called ‘puthupāṇika’; therefore, it is allowable for all to scrub their backs with their hands.

Idaṃ panettha nahānavattaṃ – udakatitthaṃ gantvā yattha vā tattha vā cīvaraṃ nikkhipitvā vegena ṭhitakeneva na otaritabbaṃ, sabbadisā pana oloketvā vivittabhāvaṃ ñatvā khāṇugumbalatādīni vavatthapetvā tikkhattuṃ ukkāsitvā avakujja ṭhitena uttarāsaṅgacīvaraṃ apanetvā pasāretabbaṃ, kāyabandhanaṃ mocetvā cīvarapiṭṭheyeva ṭhapetabbaṃ. Sace udakasāṭikā natthi, udakante ukkuṭikaṃ nisīditvā nivāsanaṃ mocetvā sace ninnaṭṭhānaṃ atthi, ātape pasāretabbaṃ. No ce atthi, saṃharitvā ṭhapetabbaṃ. Otarantena saṇikaṃ nābhippamāṇamattaṃ otaritvā vīciṃ anuṭṭhapentena saddaṃ akarontena nivattitvā āgatadisābhimukhena nimujjitabbaṃ, evaṃ cīvaraṃ rakkhitaṃ hoti. Ummujjantenapi saddaṃ akarontena saṇikaṃ ummujjitvā nahānapariyosāne udakante ukkuṭikena nisīditvā nivāsanaṃ parikkhipitvā uṭṭhāya suparimaṇḍalaṃ nivāsetvā kāyabandhanaṃ bandhitvā cīvaraṃ pārupitvāva ṭhātabbaṃ.

Herein is the duty for bathing: Having gone to a bathing place and placed the robe here or there, one should not descend hastily while standing. But having looked in all directions, having ascertained the seclusion, having noted the location of stumps, bushes, creepers, and so on, having cleared the throat three times, then while standing, the upper robe should be removed and spread out upside down. Having untied the waistband, it should be placed upon the surface of the robe itself. If there is no bathing cloth, having sat squatting at the water's edge and removed the lower garment, if there is a low-lying place, it should be spread out in the sun. If there is not, it should be folded and put away. When descending, one should descend slowly to a depth not exceeding the navel, not making waves arise, not making a sound, and having turned back, one should submerge facing the direction from which one came. Thus the robe is protected. When emerging also, not making a sound, one should emerge slowly. At the end of bathing, having sat squatting at the water's edge, having taken up the lower garment, having stood up, having put on the lower garment neatly all around, having tied the waistband, one should stand only after having put on the upper robe.

22. “Na, bhikkhave, vallikā dhāretabbā… na pāmaṅgo dhāretabbo… na kaṇṭhasuttakaṃ dhāretabbaṃ… na kaṭisuttakaṃ dhāretabbaṃ… na ovaṭṭikaṃ dhāretabbaṃ… na kāyūraṃ dhāretabbaṃ… na hatthābharaṇaṃ dhāretabbaṃ… na aṅgulimuddikā dhāretabbā, yo dhāreyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (cūḷava. 245) vacanato kaṇṇapiḷandhanādi yaṃ kiñci ābharaṇaṃ na vaṭṭati. Tattha (cūḷava. aṭṭha. 245) vallikāti kaṇṇato nikkhantamuttolambakādīnaṃ etaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Na kevalañca vallikā eva, yaṃ kiñci kaṇṇapiḷandhanaṃ antamaso tālapaṇṇampi na vaṭṭati. Pāmaṅganti yaṃ kiñci palambakasuttaṃ. Kaṇṭhasuttakanti yaṃ kiñci gīvūpagaṃ ābharaṇaṃ. Kaṭisuttakanti yaṃ kiñci kaṭipiḷandhanaṃ, antamaso suttatantumattampi. Ovaṭṭikanti valayaṃ. Kāyūrādīni pākaṭāneva.

22. “Bhikkhus, a vallikā should not be worn… a pāmaṅga should not be worn… a kaṇṭhasuttaka should not be worn… a kaṭisuttaka should not be worn… an ovaṭṭika should not be worn… a kāyūra should not be worn… a hand ornament should not be worn… a finger ring should not be worn. Whoever should wear one, commits an offence of wrong-doing.” Thus, any kind of ornament, such as ear adornments, is not allowable. Therein, ‘vallikā’ is a designation for dangling pearl ornaments and the like that hang from the ear. Not only a vallikā, but any ear adornment whatsoever, even a palm leaf, is not allowable. ‘Pāmaṅga’ means any kind of hanging thread for the head. ‘Kaṇṭhasuttaka’ refers to any neck ornament. ‘Kaṭisuttaka’ means any waist adornment, even a mere thread. ‘Ovaṭṭika’ is a bracelet. Kāyūra and the others are well-known.

23. “Na, bhikkhave, dīghā kesā dhāretabbā, yo dhāreyya, āpatti dukkaṭassa. Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, dvemāsikaṃ vā duvaṅgulaṃ vā”ti (cūḷava. 246) vacanato [M 0.0437] sace kesā antodvemāse dvaṅgulaṃ pāpuṇanti, antodvemāseyeva chinditabbā, dvaṅgulehi atikkāmetuṃ na vaṭṭati. Sacepi na dīghā, dvemāsato ekadivasampi atikkāmetuṃ na labhatiyeva. Ubhayathāpi ukkaṭṭhaparicchedova vutto, tato oraṃ pana na vaṭṭanabhāvo nāma natthi.

23. “Bhikkhus, long hair should not be kept. Whoever should keep it, commits an offence of wrong-doing. I allow, bhikkhus, hair of two months' growth or two finger-breadths' length.” In accordance with this, if hair reaches two finger-breadths within two months, it must be cut within those two months; it is not allowable to exceed two finger-breadths. Even if it is not long, one is not allowed to exceed two months by even a single day. In both cases, only the maximum limit is stated; there is no such thing as a prohibition against it being less than that.

“Na[V 0.0407], bhikkhave, kattarikāya kesā chedāpetabbā, yo chedāpeyya, āpatti dukkaṭassa. Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, ābādhapaccayā kattarikāya kese chedāpetu”nti (cūḷava. 275) vacanato ābādhaṃ vinā kattarikāya kese chedāpetuṃ na vaṭṭati.

“Bhikkhus, one should not have one's hair cut with scissors. Whoever should have it cut, commits an offence of wrong-doing. I allow, bhikkhus, one to have one's hair cut with scissors on account of illness.” Thus, without illness, it is not allowable to have one's hair cut with scissors.

“Na, bhikkhave, kocchena kesā osaṇṭhetabbā… na phaṇakena kesā osaṇṭhetabbā… na hatthaphaṇakena kesā osaṇṭhetabbā… na sitthatelakena kesā osaṇṭhetabbā… na udakatelakena kesā osaṇṭhetabbā, yo osaṇṭheyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (cūḷava. 246) vacanato maṇḍanatthāya kocchādīhi kesā na osaṇṭhetabbā, uddhalomena pana anulomanipātanatthaṃ hatthaṃ temetvā sīsaṃ puñchitabbaṃ, uṇhābhitattarajasirānampi allahatthena puñchituṃ vaṭṭati.

“Bhikkhus, hair is not to be dressed with a boar's bristle brush… not with a comb… not with a hand-comb… not with beeswax oil… not with oil mixed with water. Whoever should dress it, commits an offence of wrong-doing.” In accordance with this, hair is not to be dressed with a boar's bristle brush and the like for the purpose of adornment. However, for a bhikkhu whose hair stands up, in order to make it lie down smoothly, the head should be wiped after moistening the hand. It is also allowable for one whose head is afflicted by heat and has dust on it to wipe it with a wet hand.

24. “Na, bhikkhave, ādāse vā udakapatte vā mukhanimittaṃ oloketabbaṃ, yo olokeyya, āpatti dukkaṭassa. Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, ābādhapaccayā ādāse vā udakapatte vā mukhanimittaṃ oloketu”nti (cūḷava. 247) vacanato ābādhaṃ vinā ādāse vā udakapatte vā mukhaṃ na oloketabbaṃ. Ettha ca kaṃsapattādīnipi yesu mukhanimittaṃ paññāyati, sabbāni ādāsasaṅkhameva gacchanti, kañjiyādīnipi ca udakapattasaṅkhameva. Tasmā yattha katthaci olokentassa dukkaṭaṃ. Ābādhapaccayā pana “sañchavi nu kho me vaṇo, udāhu na tāvā”ti jānanatthaṃ vaṭṭati, “jiṇṇo nu khomhi, no”ti evaṃ āyusaṅkhāraṃ olokanatthampi vaṭṭatīti vuttaṃ.

24. “Bhikkhus, the reflection of one's face is not to be looked at in a mirror or a water vessel; whoever should look, commits an offence of wrong-doing. I allow, O bhikkhus, to look at the reflection of one's face in a mirror or a water vessel on account of illness.” In accordance with this, without illness, the face is not to be looked at in a mirror or a water vessel. And here, even bronze bowls and the like in which the reflection of the face appears, all are included under the category of ‘mirror’; and rice gruel and the like are included under the category of ‘water vessel’. Therefore, for one who looks in any such place, it is an offence of wrong-doing. However, on account of illness, it is allowable for the purpose of knowing, “Is the skin of my wound normal now, or not yet?” It is also said that it is allowable to look for the purpose of observing the signs of aging, thinking, “Am I now old, or not?”

“Na, bhikkhave, mukhaṃ ālimpitabbaṃ… na mukhaṃ ummadditabbaṃ… na mukhaṃ cuṇṇetabbaṃ… na manosilikāya mukhaṃ lañchetabbaṃ… na aṅgarāgo kātabbo… na mukharāgo kātabbo… na aṅgarāgamukharāgo kātabbo, yo kareyya, āpatti dukkaṭassa[M 0.0438]. Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, ābādhapaccayā mukhaṃ ālimpitu”nti (cūḷava. 247) vacanato ābādhaṃ vinā mukhavilimpanādi na kātabbaṃ.

“Bhikkhus, the face is not to be smeared… the face is not to be massaged… the face is not to be powdered… the face is not to be marked with red arsenic… coloring the limbs is not to be done… coloring the lips is not to be done… both coloring the limbs and coloring the lips are not to be done. Whoever should do so, commits an offence of wrong-doing. I allow, O bhikkhus, to smear the face on account of illness.” In accordance with this, without illness, smearing the face and the like is not to be done.

25. “Na, bhikkhave, naccaṃ vā gītaṃ vā vāditaṃ vā dassanāya gantabbaṃ, yo gaccheyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (cūḷava. 248) vacanato naccādiṃ dassanāya na gantabbaṃ. Ettha (pāci. aṭṭha. 835) ca naccanti naṭādayo vā naccantu soṇḍā vā antamaso morasūvamakkaṭādayopi, sabbametaṃ naccameva, tasmā antamaso moranaccampi dassanāya [V 0.0408] gacchantassa dukkaṭaṃ. Sayampi naccantassa vā naccāpentassa vā dukkaṭameva. Gītanti naṭādīnaṃ vā gītaṃ hotu ariyānaṃ parinibbānakāle ratanattayaguṇūpasañhitaṃ sādhukīḷitagītaṃ vā asaññatabhikkhūnaṃ dhammabhāṇakagītaṃ vā antamaso dantagītampi, “yaṃ gāyissāmā”ti pubbabhāge okūjantā karonti, sabbametaṃ gītameva, sayaṃ gāyantassapi gāyāpentassapi dukkaṭameva.

25. “Bhikkhus, one should not go to see dancing, singing, or instrumental music. Whoever goes incurs an offence of wrong conduct.” (Cūḷavagga 248) Therefore, one should not go to see dancing and so forth. Here (Pācittiya Commentary 835), as for dancing, whether dancers and the like dance, or drunkards dance, or even peacocks, parrots, monkeys, and the like, all this is just dancing. Therefore, for one who goes to see even a peacock dance, it is an offence of wrong conduct. For one who dances oneself or causes others to dance, it is also just an offence of wrong conduct. As for singing, whether it is the singing of dancers and the like, or the singing well-performed as an offering associated with the qualities of the Triple Gem at the time of the noble ones’ parinibbāna, or the Dhamma-reciting singing of unrestrained bhikkhus, or even whistling—that which they do by humming in the preliminary stage, thinking, “We will sing”—all this is just singing. For one who sings oneself or causes others to sing, it is also just an offence of wrong conduct.

“Pañcime, bhikkhave, ādīnavā āyatakena gītassarena dhammaṃ gāyantassa. Attanāpi tasmiṃ sare sārajjati, parepi tasmiṃ sare sārajjanti, gahapatikāpi ujjhāyanti, sarakuttimpi nikāmayamānassa samādhissa bhaṅgo hoti, pacchimā janatā diṭṭhānugatiṃ āpajjati. Ime kho, bhikkhave, pañca ādīnavā āyatakena gītassarena dhammaṃ gāyantassa. Na, bhikkhave, āyatakena gītassarena dhammo gāyitabbo, yo gāyeyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (cūḷava. 249) –

“Bhikkhus, there are these five disadvantages for one who chants the Dhamma with a drawn-out musical voice. He himself becomes infatuated with that sound, others also become infatuated with that sound, householders complain, concentration is broken for one desiring a refined sound, and later generations adopt the practice. These, bhikkhus, are the five disadvantages for one who chants the Dhamma with a drawn-out musical voice. The Dhamma should not be chanted with a drawn-out musical voice. Whoever chants it incurs an offence of wrong conduct.” (Cūḷavagga 249)

Vacanato āyatakena gītassarena dhammopi na gāyitabbo.

According to this statement, the Dhamma also should not be chanted with a drawn-out musical voice.

Āyatako (cūḷava. aṭṭha. 249) nāma gītassaro taṃ taṃ vattaṃ bhinditvā akkharāni vināsetvā pavatto. Dhamme pana suttantavattaṃ nāma atthi, jātakavattaṃ nāma atthi, gāthāvattaṃ nāma atthi, taṃ vināsetvā atidīghaṃ kātuṃ na vaṭṭati, caturassena vattena parimaṇḍalāni padabyañjanāni dassetabbāni. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, sarabhañña”nti (cūḷava. 249) vacanato pana sarena dhammaṃ bhaṇituṃ vaṭṭati. Sarabhaññe kira taraṅgavattadhotakavattagalitavattādīni dvattiṃsa vattāni atthi, tesu yaṃ icchati, taṃ kātuṃ labhati. Sabbesaṃ padabyañjanaṃ avināsetvā vikāraṃ [M 0.0439] akatvā samaṇasāruppena caturassena nayena pavattanaṃyeva lakkhaṇaṃ.

What is called `āyatako` (Cūḷavagga Commentary 249) is a singing voice that proceeds by breaking the respective rhythm and destroying the syllables. However, in the Dhamma, there is the rhythm of the Suttantas, the rhythm of the Jātakas, and the rhythm of the verses. It is not permissible to destroy these and make them excessively long. The words and phrases should be presented in a well-rounded manner with a balanced rhythm. From the statement, 'I allow, bhikkhus, intoning recitation (sarabhañña)' (Cūḷavagga 249), it is permissible to recite the Dhamma with a melodious voice. In intoning recitation, it is said there are thirty-two rhythms, such as the wave-like rhythm, the rhythm like washing a garment, and the flowing rhythm. Among these, one is permitted to perform whichever one desires. The characteristic is to proceed without destroying any of the words and phrases, without making distortions, in a balanced manner that is befitting a recluse.

Vāditaṃ nāma tantibaddhādivādanīyabhaṇḍaṃ vāditaṃ vā hotu kuṭabherivāditaṃ vā antamaso udakabherivāditampi, sabbametaṃ na vaṭṭati. Yaṃ pana niṭṭhubhanto vā sāsaṅke vā ṭhito accharikaṃ vā phoṭeti, pāṇiṃ vā paharati, tattha anāpatti, sabbaṃ antarārāme ṭhitassa passato anāpatti, passissāmīti vihārato vihāraṃ gacchantassa āpattiyeva. Āsanasālāyaṃ nisinno passati, anāpatti. Passissāmīti uṭṭhahitvā gacchato āpatti, vīthiyaṃ ṭhatvā gīvaṃ parivattetvā passatopi āpattiyeva. Salākabhattādīnaṃ vā atthāya aññena vā kenaci karaṇīyena gantvā gataṭṭhāne passati vā suṇāti vā, anāpatti. Āpadāsu tādisena upaddavena [V 0.0409] upadduto samajjaṭṭhānaṃ pavisati, evaṃ pavisitvā passantassa suṇantassa vā anāpatti. “Cetiyassa upahāraṃ detha upāsakā”ti vattumpi, “tumhākaṃ cetiyassa upahāraṃ karomā”ti vutte sampaṭicchitumpi na labhati. “Tumhākaṃ cetiyassa upaṭṭhānaṃ karomā”ti vutte pana “upaṭṭhānakaraṇaṃ nāma sundara”nti vattuṃ vaṭṭati.

Instrumental music refers to the playing of an instrument such as one bound with strings. Whether it is this, or playing a pot-drum, or even playing a water-drum—all of this is not permissible. However, if one spits, or stands in a place that causes revulsion, or snaps the fingers, or claps the hands, there is no offense. In all cases, for one standing within the monastery and watching, there is no offense. But if one thinks, “I will watch,” and goes from one dwelling to another, it is an offense. If one sits in the assembly hall and watches, there is no offense. If one rises thinking, “I will watch,” and goes, it is an offense. Even standing in the street and turning one’s neck to watch is an offense. If one goes for the sake of distributing meal tickets or for some other duty, and sees or hears while at that place, there is no offense. In times of danger, if one is afflicted by such a danger and enters a place of entertainment, there is no offense for seeing or hearing after having entered in this way. It is not permitted even to say, “Lay devotees, give offerings to the shrine,” nor, when they say, “We are making offerings to your shrine,” is it permitted to accept. But if they say, “We are attending to your shrine,” it is permissible to say, “Attending to the shrine is a fine thing.”

26. “Na, bhikkhave, attano aṅgajātaṃ chetabbaṃ, yo chindeyya, āpatti thullaccayassā”ti (cūḷava. 251) vacanato aṅgajātaṃ (cūḷava. 251) chindantassa thullaccayaṃ, aññaṃ pana kaṇṇanāsāaṅguliādiṃ yaṃ kiñci chindantassa tādisaṃ vā dukkhaṃ uppādentassa dukkaṭaṃ. Ahikīṭadaṭṭhādīsu pana aññābādhapaccayā vā lohitaṃ vā mocentassa chindantassa vā anāpatti.

26. “Bhikkhus, one should not cut off one’s own genitals. Whoever should do so, there is an offense of thullaccaya.” Thus, for one who cuts off the genitals, there is an offense of thullaccaya. But for one who cuts off anything else, such as the ears, nose, fingers, etc., or for one who causes similar pain, there is an offense of wrong-doing. However, in cases such as being bitten by a snake or an insect, there is no offense. Furthermore, for one who lets blood or cuts on account of another illness, there is no offense.

27. “Na, bhikkhave, gihīnaṃ uttarimanussadhammaṃ iddhipāṭihāriyaṃ dassetabbaṃ, yo dasseyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (cūḷava. 252) vacanato gihīnaṃ vikubbaniddhiṃ dassetuṃ na vaṭṭati, adhiṭṭhāniddhi pana appaṭikkhittā.

27. “Bhikkhus, superhuman qualities and displays of psychic power should not be shown to laypeople. Whoever should do so, there is an offense of wrong-doing.” Thus, it is not permissible to display transformative psychic power to laypeople, but the power of resolution is not prohibited.

28. “Na, bhikkhave, sovaṇṇamayo patto dhāretabbo…pe… na rūpiyamayo…pe… na maṇimayo…pe… na veḷuriyamayo…pe… na phalikamayo…pe… na kaṃsamayo…pe… na kācamayo…pe… na tipumayo …pe… na sīsamayo…pe… na tambalohamayo patto dhāretabbo, yo dhāreyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (cūḷava. 252) vacanato suvaṇṇamayādipatto [M 0.0440] na vaṭṭati. Sacepi gihī bhattagge suvaṇṇataṭṭikādīsu byañjanaṃ katvā upanāmenti, āmasitumpi na vaṭṭati. Phalikamayakācamayakaṃsamayāni pana taṭṭikādīni bhājanāni puggalikaparibhogeneva na vaṭṭanti, saṅghikaparibhogena vā gihivikaṭāni vā vaṭṭanti. Tambalohamayopi pattoyeva na vaṭṭati, thālakaṃ pana vaṭṭati. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, dve patte ayopattaṃ mattikāpatta”nti (cūḷava. 252) dveyeva ca pattā anuññātā.

28. “Bhikkhus, a bowl made of gold should not be used… nor one made of silver… nor one made of a gem… nor one made of beryl… nor one made of crystal… nor one made of bronze… nor one made of glass… nor one made of tin… nor one made of lead… nor one made of copper should be used. Whoever should use one, there is an offense of wrong-doing.” Therefore, a bowl made of gold and the like is not allowable. Even if laypeople, having prepared curry in golden plates and so forth in the refectory, should offer it, it is not allowable even to touch it. However, vessels such as plates made of crystal, glass, or bronze are not allowable only for personal use; they are allowable for the use of the Sangha or as the property of laypeople. Only a bowl made of copper is not allowable, but a plate is allowable. “Bhikkhus, I allow two bowls: an iron bowl and a clay bowl.” Thus, only two bowls are allowed.

“Na, bhikkhave, tumbakaṭāhe piṇḍāya caritabbaṃ, yo careyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (cūḷava. 255) vacanato lābukaṭāhaṃ pariharituṃ na vaṭṭati, taṃ labhitvā pana tāvakālikaṃ paribhuñjituṃ vaṭṭati. Ghaṭikaṭāhepi eseva nayo.

“Bhikkhus, one should not go for alms with a gourd bowl; whoever should do so, commits an offense of wrong-doing.” Therefore, it is not allowable to carry a gourd bowl; however, having obtained one, it is allowable to use it temporarily. This same principle applies also to a pot bowl.

“Na[V 0.0410], bhikkhave, chavasīsapatto dhāretabbo, yo dhāreyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (cūḷava. 255) vacanato chavasīsamayopi patto na vaṭṭati.

“Bhikkhus, a bowl made from a human skull should not be used; whoever should use one, commits an offense of wrong-doing.” Therefore, a bowl made from a human skull is also not allowable.

“Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, pattādhāraka”nti (cūḷava. 254) vacanato bhūmidārudaṇḍavaalavettādīhi kate bhūmiādhārake dārudaṇḍaādhārake ca pattaṃ ṭhapetuṃ vaṭṭati. Ettha ca “bhūmiādhārake tayo daṇḍādhārake dve patte uparūpari ṭhapetuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti kurundiyaṃ vuttaṃ. Mahāaṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana vuttaṃ “bhūmiādhārake tiṇṇaṃ pattānaṃ anokāso, dve ṭhapetuṃ vaṭṭati. Dāruādhārakadaṇḍādhārakesupi susajjitesu eseva nayo. Bhamakoṭisadiso pana dāruādhārako tīhi daṇḍakehi baddho, daṇḍādhārako ca ekassapi pattassa anokāso, tattha ṭhapetvāpi hatthena gahetvāva nisīditabbaṃ, bhūmiyaṃ pana nikkujjitvā ekameva ṭhapetabba”nti.

Because it is said, “Bhikkhus, I allow a bowl-stand,” it is allowable to place a bowl on a ground-stand or a wooden-rod-stand made from earth, wood, ivory, creepers, cane, and so on. And in this connection, it is said in the Kurundī: “On a ground-stand, it is allowable to place three bowls one above the other; on a rod-stand, two bowls.” In the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā, however, it is said: “On a ground-stand, there is no room for three bowls; it is allowable to place two. This is also the method for well-made wooden-stands and rod-stands. But a wooden stand resembling the head of a lathe, and a rod-stand bound with three rods, have no room for even a single bowl. On such a stand, even after placing the bowl, one must sit holding it by hand. On the ground, however, only one bowl should be placed overturned.”

“Na, bhikkhave, miḍḍhante patto nikkhipitabbo, yo nikkhipeyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (cūḷava. 254) vacanato ālindakamiḍḍhikādīnaṃ ante ṭhapetuṃ na vaṭṭati. Sace pana parivattetvā tattheva patiṭṭhāti, evarūpāya vitthiṇṇāya miḍḍhikāya ṭhapetuṃ vaṭṭati.

“Bhikkhus, a bowl is not to be placed on the edge of an inner wall’s ledge; whoever should place it there, commits an offense of wrong-doing.” Therefore, it is not allowable to place it on the edge of an inner ledge such as a veranda molding. If, however, having been turned over, it stands firm in that very place, it is allowable to place it on such a wide ledge.

“Na, bhikkhave, paribhaṇḍante patto nikkhipitabbo, yo nikkhipeyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (cūḷava. 254) vacanato bāhirapasse katāya tanukamiḍḍhikāya antepi eseva nayo. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, coḷaka”nti (cūḷava. 254) vacanato coḷakaṃ [M 0.0441] pattharitvā tattha ṭhapetuṃ vaṭṭati. Tasmiṃ pana asati kaṭasārake vā taṭṭikāya vā mattikāya vā paribhaṇḍakatāya bhūmiyā yattha na dussati, tathārūpāya vālikāya vā ṭhapetuṃ vaṭṭati. Paṃsurajādīsu pana kharabhūmiyaṃ vā ṭhapentassa dukkaṭaṃ.

“Bhikkhus, a bowl is not to be placed on the edge of an outer wall’s ledge; whoever should place it there, commits an offense of wrong-doing.” Therefore, this same principle applies to the edge of a thin ledge made on an outer wall. Because it is said, “Bhikkhus, I allow a piece of cloth,” it is allowable to place the bowl there after spreading out a piece of cloth. But if that is not available, it is allowable to place it on a kaṭasāra mat, on a wickerwork tray, on ground that has been prepared with clay where it will not be damaged, or on sand of such a kind. But for one who places it on dust, dirt, and so on, or on rough ground, there is an offense of wrong-doing.

“Na, bhikkhave, patto laggetabbo, yo laggeyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (cūḷava. 254) vacanato nāgadantādīsu yattha katthaci laggetuṃ na vaṭṭati, cīvaravaṃsepi bandhitvā ṭhapetuṃ na vaṭṭati.

“Bhikkhus, a bowl should not be hung; whoever should hang it, commits an offense of wrong-doing.” Accordingly, it is not allowable to hang it on things such as elephant-tusk pegs, or in any place whatsoever. Even on a robe-rack, it is not allowable to place it there having tied it.

“Na, bhikkhave, mañce patto nikkhipitabbo, yo nikkhipeyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (cūḷava. 254) vacanato bhaṇḍakaṭṭhapanatthameva vā kataṃ hotu nisīdanasayanatthaṃ vā, yattha katthaci mañce vā pīṭhe vā ṭhapentassa dukkaṭaṃ, aññena pana bhaṇḍakena saddhiṃ bandhitvā ṭhapetuṃ, aṭaniyaṃ bandhitvā olambituṃ vā vaṭṭati, bandhitvāpi upari ṭhapetuṃ na vaṭṭatiyeva. Sace [V 0.0411] pana mañco vā pīṭhaṃ vā ukkhipitvā cīvaravaṃsādīsu aṭṭakacchannena ṭhapitaṃ hoti, tattha ṭhapetuṃ vaṭṭati. Aṃsavaṭṭanakena aṃsakūṭe laggetvā aṅke ṭhapetuṃ vaṭṭati, chatte bhattapūropi aṃsakūṭe laggitapattopi ṭhapetuṃ na vaṭṭati. Bhaṇḍakena pana saddhiṃ bandhitvā aṭṭakaṃ katvā vā ṭhapite yo koci ṭhapetuṃ vaṭṭati.

“Bhikkhus, a bowl should not be placed on a bed; whoever should place it, commits an offense of wrong-doing.” Accordingly, whether it is made for the purpose of placing belongings or for sitting and lying down, for one who places a bowl on any bed or stool whatsoever, there is an offense of wrong-doing. However, it is allowable to place it having tied it together with other belongings, or to hang it down having tied it to a rack. Even having tied it, it is certainly not allowable to place it on top. If, however, a bed or stool is lifted and placed on a robe-rack or the like in the manner of a platform, it is allowable to place the bowl there. It is allowable to place it on the lap, having hung it on the shoulder-tip with a shoulder strap. On an umbrella, it is not allowable to place a bowl full of food, nor a bowl hung on the shoulder-tip. However, on an umbrella that has been set up by tying it together with belongings or by making it into a stand, it is allowable to place any bowl whatsoever.

“Na, bhikkhave, pattahatthena kavāṭaṃ paṇāmetabbaṃ, yo paṇāmeyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (cūḷava. 255) vacanato pattahatthena kavāṭaṃ na paṇāmetabbaṃ. Ettha ca na kevalaṃ yassa patto hatthe, so eva pattahattho. Na kevalañca kavāṭameva paṇāmetuṃ na labhati, apica kho pana hatthe vā piṭṭhipāde vā yattha yatthaci sarīrāvayave pattasmiṃ sati hatthena vā pādena vā sīsena vā yena kenaci sarīrāvayavena kavāṭaṃ vā paṇāmetuṃ ghaṭikaṃ vā ukkhipituṃ sūciṃ vā kuñcikāya avāpurituṃ na labhati, aṃsakūṭe pana pattaṃ laggetvā yathāsukhaṃ avāpurituṃ labhati.

“Bhikkhus, a door-leaf should not be pushed open by one with a bowl in hand; whoever should push it open, commits an offense of wrong-doing.” Accordingly, a door-leaf should not be pushed open by one with a bowl in hand. And in this context, it is not only one who has a bowl in his hand who is ‘one with a bowl in hand.’ And it is not only a door-leaf that one is not permitted to push open. But rather, when a bowl is on the hand, on the top of the foot, or on any bodily limb whatsoever, one is not permitted to push open a door-leaf, or to lift a bolt or a pin, or to open with a key, using the hand, the foot, the head, or any bodily limb whatsoever. However, having hung the bowl on the shoulder-tip, one is permitted to open as one pleases.

“Na, bhikkhave, calakāni vā aṭṭhikāni vā ucchiṭṭhodakaṃ vā pattena nīharitabbaṃ, yo nīhareyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (cūḷava. 255) vacanato calakādīni pattena nīharituṃ na vaṭṭati. Ettha ca calakānīti cabbetvā apaviddhāmisāni. Aṭṭhikānīti macchamaṃsaaakāni. Ucchiṭṭhodakanti mukhavikkhālitodakaṃ. Etesu yaṃ kiñci pattena nīharantassa dukkaṭaṃ. Pattaṃ paṭiggahaṃ katvā hatthaṃ dhovitumpi [M 0.0442] na labhati. Hatthadhotapādadhotaudakampi patte ākiritvā nīharituṃ na vaṭṭati, anucchiṭṭhaṃ suddhapattaṃ ucchiṭṭhahatthena gaṇhituṃ na vaṭṭati, vāmahatthena panettha udakaṃ āsiñcitvā ekaṃ udakagaṇḍusaṃ gahetvā ucchiṭṭhahatthena gaṇhituṃ vaṭṭati. Ettāvatāpi hi so ucchiṭṭhapatto hoti, hatthaṃ pana bahiudakena vikkhāletvā gahetuṃ vaṭṭati. Macchamaṃsaphalāphalādīni ca khādanto yaṃ tattha aṭṭhiṃ vā calakaṃ vā chaḍḍetukāmo hoti, taṃ patte ṭhapetuṃ na labhati. Yaṃ pana paṭikhāditukāmo hoti, taṃ patte ṭhapetuṃ labhati. Aṭṭhikakaṇṭakādīni tattheva katvā hatthena luñcitvā khādituṃ vaṭṭati. Mukhato nīhaṭaṃ pana yaṃ kiñci puna khāditukāmo patte ṭhapetuṃ na labhati, siṅgiveranāḷikerakhaṇḍādīni ḍaṃsitvā puna ṭhapetuṃ labhati.

“Monks, scraps, bones, or water used for rinsing should not be removed with the bowl. Whoever removes them incurs an offense of wrongdoing.” Therefore, it is not permissible to remove scraps and so forth with the bowl. Herein, ‘scraps’ are pieces of food that have been chewed and discarded. ‘Bones’ are fish bones and meat bones. ‘Water used for rinsing’ is water for rinsing the mouth. For one who removes any of these with the bowl, there is an offense of wrongdoing. It is not permissible to use the bowl as a receptacle for washing one's hands. It is also not permissible to pour water used for washing hands or feet into the bowl and remove it. A clean bowl that has no leftovers should not be taken with a hand that has touched leftovers. However, it is permissible to pour water into it with the left hand, take a single mouthful of water, and then take the bowl with the hand that has touched leftovers. For by this much, that bowl becomes a bowl that has touched leftovers. As for the hand, however, it is permissible to wash it with water outside and then take the bowl. And when eating fish, meat, fruits, and so forth, if one wishes to discard any bone or scrap that is there, one is not permitted to place it in the bowl. But whatever one wishes to eat again, one is permitted to place in the bowl. It is permissible to separate flesh from bones, thorns, and so forth with the hand right there in the bowl and eat it. However, whatever is taken from the mouth, one is not permitted to place it in the bowl if one wishes to eat it again. One is permitted to bite things like pieces of fresh ginger or coconut and place them back again.

29. “Na ca, bhikkhave, sabbapaṃsukūlikena bhavitabbaṃ, yo bhaveyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (cūḷava. 255) vacanato sabbapaṃsukūlikena na bhavitabbaṃ. Ettha pana cīvarañca mañcapīṭhañca paṃsukūlaṃ vaṭṭati, ajjhoharaṇīyaṃ pana dinnameva gahetabbaṃ.

29. “Monks, one should not be one who uses refuse-rag material for everything; if one were, there is an offense of wrongdoing.” Therefore, one should not be one who uses refuse-rag material for everything. Here, however, it is permissible for robes, beds, and chairs to be from refuse material, but as for that which is to be ingested, only what is given should be accepted.

30. “Na[V 0.0412], bhikkhave, addhānamaggappaṭipannena bhikkhunā parissāvanaṃ yāciyamānena na dātabbaṃ, yo na dadeyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (cūḷava. 259) vacanato aparissāvanakassa (cūḷava. aṭṭha. 259) yācamānassa parissāvanaṃ adātuṃ na vaṭṭati. Yo pana attano hatthe parissāvane vijjamānepi yācati, tassa na akāmā dātabbaṃ.

30. “Monks, a monk traveling on a road should not refuse a water-strainer when asked for it. He who would not give it commits an offense of wrongdoing.” Therefore, it is not allowable to refuse a water-strainer to a monk who asks for one and is without it. However, as for one who asks even while a water-strainer is in his own hand, it need not be given against one's will.

“Na ca, bhikkhave, aparissāvanakena bhikkhunā addhānamaggo paṭipajjitabbo, yo paṭipajjeyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (cūḷava. 259) vacanato aparissāvanakena maggo na gantabbo. Sacepi na hoti parissāvanaṃ vā dhammakaraṇaṃ vā, saṅghāṭikaṇṇo adhiṭṭhātabbo “iminā parissāvetvā pivissāmī”ti.

“Monks, a monk should not undertake a journey on the road without a water-strainer. If he does, there is an offense of wrongdoing.” Thus, one should not travel on the road without a water-strainer. Even if there is no water-strainer or other straining device available, a corner of the outer robe should be designated with the thought, “I will drink after straining with this.”

“Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, daṇḍaparissāvana”nti (cūḷava. 259) vacanato daṇḍaparissāvanampi vaṭṭati. Daṇḍaparissāvanaṃ nāma yattha rajakānaṃ khāraparissāvanaṃ viya catūsu pādesu baddhanisseṇikāya sāṭakaṃ bandhitvā majjhe daṇḍake udakaṃ āsiñcanti, taṃ ubhopi koṭṭhāse pūretvā parissāvati.

“Monks, I allow a stick water-strainer.” Thus, a stick water-strainer is permissible. A stick water-strainer is this: like the lye-strainer of washermen, a cloth is tied to a frame with four legs and rungs, and water is poured onto the cloth in the middle. It fills both sections and then strains.

“Anujānāmi[M 0.0443], bhikkhave, ottharaka”nti (cūḷava. 259) vacanato ottharakaṃ parissāvanampi vaṭṭati. Ottharakaṃ nāma yaṃ udake ottharitvā ghaṭakena udakaṃ gaṇhanti, tañhi catūsu daṇḍakesu vatthaṃ bandhitvā udake cattāro khāṇuke nikhanitvā tesu bandhitvā sabbapariyante udakato mocetvā majjhe ottharitvā ghaṭena udakaṃ gaṇhanti.

“Monks, I allow an ‘ottharaka’ (immersed strainer).” Thus, an ‘ottharaka’ strainer is also permissible. An ‘ottharaka’ is that which, having been immersed in water, is used to draw water with a small pot. For this, a cloth is tied to four sticks, or four posts are driven into the water and the cloth is tied to them. Having kept all the edges free from the water, the cloth is pressed down in the middle, and water is drawn with a pot.

31. “Na, bhikkhave, naggena naggo abhivādetabbo, yo abhivādeyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”tiādivacanato (cūḷava. 261) na naggena naggo abhivādetabbo, na naggena abhivādetabbaṃ, na naggena naggo abhivādāpetabbo, na naggena abhivādāpetabbaṃ, na naggena naggassa parikammaṃ kātabbaṃ, na naggena naggassa dātabbaṃ, na naggena paṭiggahetabbaṃ, na naggena khāditabbaṃ, na naggena bhuñjitabbaṃ, na naggena sāyitabbaṃ, na naggena pātabbaṃ.

31. Because of the statement beginning: “Monks, a naked person should not pay homage to a naked person. Whoever should pay homage, it is an offense of wrongdoing,” a naked person should not pay homage to a naked person; a naked person should not pay homage; a naked person should not cause a naked person to pay homage; a naked person should not cause homage to be paid; a naked person should not perform a service for a naked person; a naked person should not give to a naked person; a naked person should not receive; a naked person should not chew; a naked person should not eat; a naked person should not taste; a naked person should not drink.

“Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, tisso paṭicchādiyo jantāgharapaṭicchādiṃ udakapaṭicchādiṃ vatthapaṭicchādi”nti (cūḷava. 261) vacanato tisso paṭicchādiyo vaṭṭanti. Ettha ca jantāgharapaṭicchādi udakapaṭicchādi ca parikammaṃ karontasseva vaṭṭati, sesesu abhivādanādīsu na vaṭṭati. Vatthapaṭicchādi pana sabbakammesu vaṭṭati.

“Monks, I allow three coverings: the covering of a sweat-house, the covering of water, and the covering of a cloth.” Therefore, the three coverings are allowable. And here, the covering of a sweat-house and the covering of water are allowable only for one who is scrubbing the body; they are not allowable in other instances such as paying homage. The covering of a cloth, however, is allowable in all actions.

32. “Na[V 0.0413], bhikkhave, pupphābhikiṇṇesu sayanesu sayitabbaṃ, yo saseyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (cūḷava. 264) vacanato pupphehi santhatesu sayanesu na sayitabbaṃ, gandhagandhaṃ pana gahetvā kavāṭe pañcaṅguliṃ dātuṃ vaṭṭati pupphaṃ gahetvā vihāre ekamantaṃ nikkhipituṃ.

32. “Monks, one should not lie on beds strewn with flowers; whoever should lie down, it is an offense of wrongdoing.” Therefore, one should not lie on beds covered with flowers. However, it is allowable to take a fragrant substance and apply a five-fingered mark to a door-leaf, and it is allowable to take a flower and place it to one side in the monastery.

33. “Na, bhikkhave, āsittakūpadhāne bhuñjitabbaṃ, yo bhuñjeyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (cūḷava. 264) vacanato āsittakūpadhāne ṭhapetvā na bhuñjitabbaṃ. Āsittakūpadhānanti tambalohena vā rajatena vā katāya peḷāya etaṃ adhivacanaṃ, paṭikkhittattā pana dārumayāpi na vaṭṭati.

33. “Monks, one should not eat from an inlaid container; whoever should eat, it is an offense of wrongdoing.” Therefore, one should not eat having placed food in an inlaid container. ‘Inlaid container’ (āsittakūpadhāna) is a designation for a box made of copper or silver. But because it is rejected, even one made of wood is not allowable.

34. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, maḷorika”nti (cūḷava. 264) vacanato maḷorikāya ṭhapetvā bhuñjituṃ vaṭṭati. Maḷorikāti daṇḍādhārako vuccati. Yaṭṭhiādhārakapaṇṇādhārakapacchikapīṭhādīnipi ettheva paviṭṭhāni. Ādhārakasaṅkhepagamanato hi paṭṭhāya chiddaṃ viddhampi aviddhampi vaṭṭatiyeva.

34. Because of the text, ‘Monks, I allow a maḷorikā,’ it is permissible to eat after placing the bowl on a maḷorikā. Maḷorikā is called a staff-support. Stands made of bamboo sticks, stands made of leaves, small baskets, stools, and so on are also included herein. Indeed, from its being reckoned as a stand, it is permissible whether it has a hole pierced through it or not.

35. “Na[M 0.0444], bhikkhave, ekabhājane bhuñjitabbaṃ, yo bhuñjeyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti(cūḷava. 264) ādivacanato na ekabhājane bhuñjitabbaṃ, na ekathālake pātabbaṃ. Sace pana eko bhikkhu bhājanato phalaṃ vā pūpaṃ vā gahetvā gacchati, tasmiṃ apagate itarassa sesakaṃ bhuñjituṃ vaṭṭati, itarassapi tasmiṃ khīṇe puna gahetuṃ vaṭṭati.

35. Because of the initial text, ‘Monks, one should not eat from a single dish; whoever does so incurs an offense of wrongdoing,’ one should not eat from a single dish, nor drink from a single bowl. But if one monk takes fruit or cake from a dish and goes away, when he has departed, it is permissible for the other to eat the remainder. And for that other one, when that portion is finished, it is permissible to take more again.

“Na, bhikkhave, ekamañce tuvaṭṭitabbaṃ, yo tuvaṭṭeyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti(cūḷava. 264) ādivacanato na ekamañce nipajjitabbaṃ, na ekattharaṇe nipajjitabbaṃ. Vavatthānaṃ pana dassetvā majjhe kāsāvaṃ vā kattarayaṭṭhiṃ vā antamaso kāyabandhanampi ṭhapetvā nipajjantānaṃ anāpatti. Ekapāvuraṇehi ekattharaṇapāvuraṇehi ca na nipajjitabbaṃ. Ekaṃ attharaṇañceva pāvuraṇañca etesanti ekattharaṇapāvuraṇā. Saṃhārimānaṃ pāvārattharaṇakaṭasārakādīnaṃ ekaṃ antaṃ attharitvā ekaṃ pārupitvā nipajjantānametaṃ adhivacanaṃ.

Because of the initial text, ‘Monks, one should not lie down on a single bed; whoever does so incurs an offense of wrongdoing,’ one should not lie down on a single bed, nor lie down on a single spread. However, for those lying down, there is no offense after having shown a boundary by placing in the middle a robe, a walking stick, or at the very least, even a waistband. And one should not lie down with a single covering or with a single spread-and-covering. ‘Those with a single spread-and-covering’ are they for whom there is one spread and covering. This is a designation for those who lie down using one end of a foldable item—such as a cloak, a spread, or a mat—as a spread and covering themselves with the other end.

36. “Na, bhikkhave, celappaṭikā akkamitabbā, yo akkameyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (cūḷava. 268) vacanato na celasanthāro akkamitabbo, “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, gihīnaṃ maṅgalatthāya yāciyamānena celappaṭikaṃ akkamitu”nti (cūḷava. 268) vacanato pana kāci itthī (cūḷava. aṭṭha. 268) apagatagabbhā vā hoti garugabbhā vā, evarūpesu [V 0.0414] ṭhānesu maṅgalatthāya yāciyamānena akkamituṃ vaṭṭati. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, dhotapādakaṃ akkamitu”nti (cūḷava. 268) vacanato pādadhovanaṭṭhāne dhotehi pādehi akkamanatthāya atthatapaccattharaṇaṃ akkamituṃ vaṭṭati.

36. Because of the text, ‘Monks, a cloth covering should not be stepped on; whoever should step on it commits an offense of wrongdoing,’ a cloth spread should not be stepped on. However, because of the text, ‘Monks, I allow one who is requested by laypeople for an auspicious purpose to step on a cloth covering,’ it is permissible to step on it when requested for an auspicious purpose in such cases where a woman has lost a pregnancy or is heavily pregnant. Because of the text, ‘Monks, I allow stepping with washed feet,’ it is permissible to step on a covering that is spread in a place for washing feet for the purpose of stepping on it with washed feet.

37. “Na, bhikkhave, katakaṃ paribhuñjitabbaṃ, yo paribhuñjeyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (cūḷava. 269) vacanato katakaṃ na vaṭṭati. Katakaṃ nāma padumakaṇṇikākāraṃ pādaghaṃsanatthaṃ kaṇṭake uṭṭhāpetvā kataṃ. Taṃ vaṭṭaṃ vā hotu caturassādibhedaṃ vā, bāhulikānuyogattā paṭikkhittameva, neva paṭiggahetuṃ, na paribhuñjituṃ vaṭṭati. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, tisso pādaghaṃsaniyo sakkharaṃ kathalaṃ samuddapheṇaka”nti (cūḷava. 269) vacanato sakkharādīhi pādaghaṃsanaṃ vaṭṭati. Sakkharāti pāsāṇo vuccati, pāsāṇapheṇakopi vaṭṭatiyeva.

37. Because of the text, ‘Monks, a kataka should not be used; whoever should use one commits an offense of wrongdoing,’ a kataka is not allowable. A kataka is something made for the purpose of scrubbing the feet by raising spikes in the shape of a lotus pericarp. Whether it is round or has other shapes such as square, it is rejected on account of its leading to luxurious living. It is not allowable to receive it, nor is it allowable to use it. Because of the text, ‘Monks, I allow three kinds of foot-scrubbers: gravel, a potsherd, and sea-foam,’ foot-scrubbing with gravel and the like is allowable. By sakkhara is meant stone; stone-foam is also allowable.

38. “Na[M 0.0445], bhikkhave, cāmaribījanī dhāretabbā, yo dhāreyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (cūḷava. 269) vacanato cāmarivālehi katabījanī na vaṭṭati. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, makasabījaniṃ. Anujānāmi bhikkhave tisso bījaniyo vākamayaṃ usīramayaṃ morapiñchamayaṃ. Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, vidhūpanañca tālavaṇṭañcā”ti (cūḷava. 269) vacanato makasabījanīādi vaṭṭati. Tattha vidhūpananti bījanī vuccati. Tālavaṇṭaṃ pana tālapaṇṇehi vā kataṃ hotu veḷudantavilīvehi vā morapiñchehi vā cammavikatīhi vā, sabbaṃ vaṭṭati. Makasabījanī dantamayavisāṇamayadaṇḍakāpi vaṭṭati. Vākamayabījaniyā ketakapārohakuntālapaṇṇādimayāpi saṅgahitā.

38. Because of the text, ‘Monks, a chowrie fan is not to be used; whoever should use one incurs an offense of wrongdoing,’ a fan made with the hairs of the chowrie is not allowable. Because of the text, ‘I allow, monks, a fly-whisk. I allow, monks, three kinds of fans: one made of bark-fiber, one made of usīra root, and one made of peacock feathers. I allow, monks, a square fan and a round palm-leaf fan,’ a fly-whisk and so on are allowable. Therein, ‘vidhūpana’ is called a square fan. As for a round palm-leaf fan, whether it is made of palm leaves, or of strips of bamboo or ivory, or of peacock feathers, or of leather cuttings, all is allowable. A fly-whisk, even with a handle made of ivory or horn, is allowable. Under the category of a fan made of bark-fiber, those made of ketaka shoots, kuntāla palm leaves, and so on, are also included.

39. “Na, bhikkhave, chattaṃ dhāretabbaṃ, yo dhāreyya, āpatti dukkaṭassa. Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, gilānassa chatta”nti (cūḷava. 270) vacanato agilānena chattaṃ na dhāretabbaṃ. Yassa pana kāyaḍāho vā pittakopo vā hoti cakkhu vā dubbalaṃ, añño vā koci ābādho vinā chattena uppajjati, tassa gāme vā araññe vā chattaṃ vaṭṭati. Vasse pana cīvaraguttatthampi vāḷamigacorabhayesu attaguttatthampi vaṭṭati, ekapaṇṇacchattaṃ pana sabbattheva vaṭṭati. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, agilānenapi ārāme ārāmūpacāre chattaṃ dhāretu”nti (cūḷava. 270) vacanato pana agilānassapi ārāmaārāmūpacāresu chattaṃ dhāretuṃ vaṭṭati.

39. Because of the text, ‘Monks, an umbrella is not to be carried; whoever should carry one incurs an offense of wrongdoing. I allow, monks, an umbrella for one who is sick,’ an umbrella is not to be carried by one who is not sick. For whichever monk, however, there is burning of the body or a disturbance of the bile, or the eyes are weak, or some other illness arises without an umbrella, for that monk an umbrella is allowable in a village or in a forest. But in the rainy season, it is allowable for the purpose of protecting the robe, and in situations of danger from savage beasts and thieves, also for the purpose of protecting oneself. An umbrella made of a single leaf, however, is allowable everywhere. Because of the text, ‘I allow, monks, even for one who is not sick to carry an umbrella in the monastery and in the monastery precincts,’ it is allowable even for one who is not sick to carry an umbrella in the monastery and its precincts.

40. “Na, bhikkhave, dīghā nakhā dhāretabbā, yo dhāreyya, āpatti dukkaṭassa. Anujānāmi[V 0.0415], bhikkhave, maṃsappamāṇena nakhaṃ chinditu”nti (cūḷava. 274) vacanato dīghā nakhā chinditabbā. “Na, bhikkhave, vīsatimaṭṭhaṃ kārāpetabbaṃ, yo kārāpeyya, āpatti dukkaṭassa. Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, malamattaṃ apakaḍḍhitu”nti (cūḷava. 274) vacanato vīsatipi nakhe likhitamaṭṭhe kārāpetuṃ na vaṭṭati, nakhato malamattaṃ pana apakaḍḍhituṃ vaṭṭati.

40. Because of the text, ‘Monks, long nails are not to be kept; whoever should keep them incurs an offense of wrongdoing. I allow, monks, the nail to be cut to the measure of the flesh,’ long nails are to be cut. Because of the text, ‘Monks, the grooming of the twenty nails is not to be caused to be done; whoever should cause it to be done incurs an offense of wrongdoing. I allow, monks, only the dirt to be scraped out,’ it is not allowable to cause the twenty nails to be groomed by scraping and polishing; however, it is allowable to scrape out only the dirt from the nails.

“Na, bhikkhave, sambādhe lomaṃ saṃharāpetabbaṃ, yo saṃharāpeyya, āpatti dukkaṭassa. Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, ābādhapaccayā sambādhe lomaṃ saṃharāpetu”nti (cūḷava. 275) vacanato gaṇḍavaṇādiābādhaṃ vinā sambādhe lomaṃ saṃharāpetuṃ na vaṭṭati. “Na, bhikkhave, dīghaṃ nāsikālomaṃ dhāretabbaṃ, yo [M 0.0446] dhāreyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (cūḷava. 275) vacanato saṇḍāsena nāsikālomaṃ saṃharāpetuṃ vaṭṭati. Sakkharādīhi nāsikālomaṃ gāhāpanepi āpatti natthi, anurakkhaṇatthaṃ pana “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, saṇḍāsa”nti (cūḷava. 275) saṇḍāso anuññāto. “Na, bhikkhave, palitaṃ gāhāpetabbaṃ, yo gāhāpeyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (cūḷava. 275) vacanato palitaṃ gāhāpetuṃ na vaṭṭati. Yaṃ pana bhamukāya vā nalāṭe vā dāṭhikāya vā uggantvā bībhacchaṃ hutvā ṭhitaṃ, tādisaṃ lomaṃ palitaṃ vā apalitaṃ vā gāhāpetuṃ vaṭṭati.

“Monks, hair in the private parts is not to be caused to be removed. Whoever should cause it to be removed, there is an offense of wrong-doing. I allow, monks, hair in the private parts to be caused to be removed on account of illness.” Therefore, without an illness such as a boil or a sore, it is not allowable to cause hair in the private parts to be removed. “Monks, long nose-hair is not to be kept. Whoever should keep it, there is an offense of wrong-doing.” Therefore, it is allowable to cause nose-hair to be removed with tweezers. There is no offense even in causing nose-hair to be removed with gravel and so forth; however, for the sake of protection, “I allow, monks, tweezers,” thus tweezers are allowed. “Monks, gray hair is not to be caused to be plucked. Whoever should cause it to be plucked, there is an offense of wrong-doing.” Therefore, it is not allowable to cause gray hair to be plucked. However, if hair grows on the eyebrows, forehead, or jaw and becomes unsightly, it is allowable to cause such hair—whether gray or not—to be plucked.

41. “Na, bhikkhave, akāyabandhanena gāmo pavisitabbo, yo paviseyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (cūḷava. 278) vacanato akāyabandhanena gāmo na pavisitabbo, abandhitvā nikkhamantena yattha sarati, tattha bandhitabbaṃ. “Āsanasālāya bandhissāmī”ti gantuṃ vaṭṭati, saritvā yāva na bandhati, na tāva piṇḍāya caritabbaṃ.

41. “Monks, a village should not be entered without a waistband. Whoever should enter incurs an offense of wrong-doing.” Thus, a village should not be entered without a waistband. When going out without having tied it, it should be tied wherever one remembers. It is allowable to go thinking, ‘I will tie it in the assembly hall,’ but after remembering, one should not walk for alms until it is tied.

42. “Na, bhikkhave, gihinivatthaṃ nivāsetabbaṃ, yo nivāseyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti(cūḷava. 280) ādivacanato hatthisoṇḍādivasena gihinivatthaṃ na nivāsetabbaṃ, setapaṭapārutādivasena na gihipārutaṃ pārupitabbaṃ, mallakammakarādayo viya kacchaṃ bandhitvā na nivāsetabbaṃ. Evaṃ nivāsetuṃ gilānassapi maggappaṭipannassapi na vaṭṭati. Yampi maggaṃ gacchantā ekaṃ vā dve vā koṇe ukkhipitvā antaravāsakassa upari lagganti, anto vā ekaṃ kāsāvaṃ tathā nivāsetvā bahi aparaṃ nivāsenti, sabbaṃ na vaṭṭati. Gilāno pana antokāsāvassa ovaṭṭikaṃ dassetvā aparaṃ upari nivāsetuṃ labhati, agilānena dve nivāsentena saguṇaṃ katvā nivāsetabbāni.

42. “Monks, one should not wear clothing like a householder. Whoever wears it incurs an offense of wrong-doing.” From this and similar statements, one should not wear householder’s clothing in the manner of an elephant’s trunk, etc.; nor should one wrap oneself like a householder, in the manner of those who wear white cloth, etc.; nor should one wear the lower robe by tucking it in like wrestlers, laborers, and so on. It is not allowable to wear it in this manner, even for the sick or for one who is on a journey. And also, when monks going on a journey lift up one or two corners and attach them upon the inner robe, or wear one ochre robe inside in that way and wear another outside—all of that is not allowable. A sick person, however, is allowed to wear another robe over the inner ochre robe, showing its fold. A healthy person, when wearing two robes, should wear them having made them doubled.

43. “Na[V 0.0416], bhikkhave, ubhatokājaṃ haritabbaṃ, yo hareyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (cūḷava. 281) vacanato ubhatokājaṃ harituṃ na vaṭṭati. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, ekatokājaṃ antarākājaṃ sīsabhāraṃ khandhabhāraṃ kaṭibhāraṃ olambaka”nti vacanato ekatokājādiṃ harituṃ vaṭṭati.

43. “Monks, a carrying pole with a load on both ends should not be carried. Whoever should carry it incurs an offense of wrong-doing.” Thus, it is not allowable to carry a carrying pole with a load on both ends. “I allow, monks, a carrying pole with a load on one end, a load carried in the middle, a head-load, a shoulder-load, a hip-load, or a hanging load.” Thus, it is allowable to carry a carrying pole with a load on one end and so on.

44. “Na, bhikkhave, dīghaṃ dantakaṭṭhaṃ khāditabbaṃ, yo khādeyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (cūḷava. 282) vacanato na dīghaṃ dantakaṭṭhaṃ khāditabbaṃ. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, aṭṭhaṅgulaparamaṃ [M 0.0447] dantakaṭṭhaṃ. Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, caturaṅgulapacchimaṃ dantakaṭṭha”nti (cūḷava. 282) vacanato manussānaṃ pamāṇaṅgulena aṭṭhaṅgulaparamaṃ caturaṅgulapacchimañca dantakaṭṭhaṃ khāditabbaṃ.

44. “Monks, a long tooth-stick should not be chewed. Whoever should chew it incurs an offense of wrong-doing.” Thus, a long tooth-stick should not be chewed. “I allow, monks, a tooth-stick of at most eight finger-breadths. I allow, monks, a tooth-stick of at least four finger-breadths.” Thus, a tooth-stick of at most eight finger-breadths and of at least four finger-breadths, according to human finger measurements, may be chewed.

45. “Na, bhikkhave, rukkho abhiruhitabbo, yo abhiruheyya, āpatti dukkaṭassa. Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, sati karaṇīye porisaṃ rukkhaṃ abhiruhituṃ āpadāsu yāvadattha”nti (cūḷava. 284) vacanato na rukkhaṃ abhiruhitabbaṃ, sukkhakaṭṭhagahaṇādikicce pana sati purisappamāṇaṃ abhiruhituṃ vaṭṭati. Āpadāsūti vāḷamigādayo vā disvā maggamūḷho vā disā oloketukāmo hutvā davaḍāhaṃ vā udakoghaṃ vā āgacchantaṃ disvā atiuccampi rukkhaṃ ārohituṃ vaṭṭati.

45. “Monks, a tree should not be climbed. Whoever should climb it incurs an offense of wrong-doing. I allow, monks, when there is a need, to climb a tree to a man’s height, and in emergencies, as far as is necessary.” Thus, a tree should not be climbed. However, when there is a need for tasks like gathering dry wood, it is allowable to climb to a man’s height. In emergencies—such as seeing beasts of prey, or being lost on the path and wishing to survey the directions, or seeing an approaching forest fire or flood—it is allowable to climb even a very tall tree.

46. “Na, bhikkhave, buddhavacanaṃ chandaso āropetabbaṃ, yo āropeyya, āpatti dukkaṭassa. Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, sakāya niruttiyā buddhavacanaṃ pariyāpuṇitu”nti (cūḷava. 285) vacanato vedaṃ viya buddhavacanaṃ sakkaṭabhāsāya vācanāmaggaṃ ārocetuṃ na vaṭṭati, sakāya pana māgadhikāya niruttiyā pariyāpuṇitabbaṃ.

46. “Monks, the word of the Buddha should not be rendered into Sanskrit. Whoever should do so incurs an offense of wrong-doing. I allow, monks, to learn the word of the Buddha in your own language.” Thus, it is not allowable to render the word of the Buddha into the Sanskrit language as one would the Vedas; rather, it should be learned in one’s own Magadhan language.

47. “Na, bhikkhave, lokāyataṃ pariyāpuṇitabbaṃ, yo pariyāpuṇeyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti(caūḷava. 286) ādivacanato lokāyatasaṅkhātaṃ “sabbaṃ ucchiṭṭhaṃ, sabbaṃ anucchiṭṭhaṃ, seto kāko, kāḷo bako iminā ca iminā ca kāraṇenā”ti evamādiniratthakakāraṇapaṭisaṃyuttaṃ titthiyasatthaṃ neva pariyāpuṇitabbaṃ, na parassa vācetabbaṃ. Na ca tiracchānavijjā pariyāpuṇitabbā, na parassa vācetabbā.

47. “Monks, Lokāyata should not be studied. Whoever should study it incurs an offense of wrong-doing.” From this and similar statements, the sectarian doctrines known as Lokāyata, which are associated with meaningless reasons such as ‘everything is leftover, everything is not leftover, the crow is white, the heron is black, and for this and that reason,’ should neither be studied nor taught to others. And base arts should not be studied, nor should they be taught to others.

48. “Na, bhikkhave, khipite ‘jīvā’ti vattabbo, yo vadeyya, āpatti dukkaṭassa. Anujānāmi[V 0.0417], bhikkhave, gihīnaṃ ‘jīvatha bhante’ti vuccamānena ‘ciraṃ jīvā’ti vattu”nti (cūḷava. 288) vacanato khipite “jīvā”ti na vattabbaṃ, gihinā pana “jīvathā”ti vuccamānena “ciraṃ jīvā”ti vattuṃ vaṭṭati.

48. “Monks, when one sneezes, one should not say, ‘May you live long’; whoever should say so incurs an offense of wrong-doing. I allow, monks, for one who is told by laypeople, ‘May you live, venerable sirs,’ to say, ‘May you live long.’” According to this, when one sneezes, one should not say, ‘May you live long.’ But when told by a layperson, ‘May you live,’ it is permissible to say, ‘May you live long.’

49. “Na, bhikkhave, lasuṇaṃ khāditabbaṃ, yo khādeyya, āpatti dukkaṭassa. Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, ābādhapaccayā lasuṇaṃ khāditu”nti (cūḷava. 289) vacanato ābādhaṃ [M 0.0448] vinā lasuṇaṃ khādituṃ na vaṭṭati, sūpasampākādīsu (pāci. aṭṭha. 797) pakkhittaṃ pana vaṭṭati. Tañhi paccamānesu muggasūpādīsu vā macchamaṃsavikatiyā vā tele vā badarasāḷavādīsu vā ambilasākādīsu vā uttaribhaṅgesu vā yattha katthaci antamaso yāgubhattepi pakkhittaṃ vaṭṭati.

49. “Monks, garlic should not be eaten. Whoever should eat it incurs an offense of wrong-doing. I allow, monks, that garlic be eaten on account of illness.” According to this, it is not permissible to eat garlic without illness, but it is permissible when it is added in the preparation of soups and so forth. Indeed, it is permissible when added to mung bean soup and so forth while being cooked, or to preparations of fish and meat, or to oil, or to dishes of jujube and so forth, or to sour greens and so forth, or to side dishes, or wherever it is added, even in rice-gruel and cooked rice.

50. “Na, bhikkhave, adhotehi pādehi senāsanaṃ akkamitabbaṃ, yo akkameyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (cūḷava. 324) vacanato adhotehi pādehi mañcapīṭhādisenāsanaṃ parikammakatā vā bhūmi na akkamitabbā. “Na, bhikkhave, allehi pādehi senāsanaṃ akkamitabbaṃ, yo akkameyya āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (cūḷava. 324) vacanato yehi (cūḷava. aṭṭha. 324) akkantaṭṭhāne udakaṃ paññāyati, evarūpehi allapādehi paribhaṇḍakatā bhūmi vā senāsanaṃ vā na akkamitabbaṃ. Sace pana udakasinehamattameva paññāyati, na udakaṃ, vaṭṭati. Pādapuñchaniṃ pana allapādehipi akkamituṃ vaṭṭatiyeva. “Na, bhikkhave, saupāhanena senāsanaṃ akkamitabbaṃ, yo akkameyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (cūḷava. 324) vacanato dhotapādehi akkamitabbaṭṭhānaṃ saupāhanena akkamituṃ na vaṭṭati.

50. “Monks, a lodging should not be stepped upon with unwashed feet. Whoever should step upon it incurs an offense of wrong-doing.” According to this, a lodging such as a bed or bench, or prepared ground, should not be stepped upon with unwashed feet. “Monks, a lodging should not be stepped upon with wet feet. Whoever should step upon it incurs an offense of wrong-doing.” According to this, prepared ground or a lodging should not be stepped upon with such wet feet that water is apparent in the place stepped upon. But if only the moisture of water is apparent, and not the water itself, it is permissible. However, it is indeed permissible to step upon a foot-wiper even with wet feet. “Monks, a lodging should not be stepped upon while wearing footwear. Whoever should step upon it incurs an offense of wrong-doing.” According to this, a place that should be stepped upon with washed feet should not be stepped upon while wearing footwear.

“Na, bhikkhave, parikammakatāya bhūmiyā niṭṭhubhitabbaṃ, yo niṭṭhubheyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (cūḷava. 324) vacanato parikammakatāya bhūmiyā na niṭṭhubhitabbaṃ. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, kheḷamallaka”nti (cūḷava. 324) evaṃ anuññāte kheḷamallake niṭṭhubhitabbaṃ. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, coḷakena paliveṭhetu”nti (cūḷava. 324) vacanato sudhābhūmiyā vā paribhaṇḍabhūmiyā vā mañcapīṭhaṃ nikkhipantena sace taṭṭikā vā kaṭasārako vā natthi, coḷakena mañcapīṭhānaṃ pādā veṭhetabbā, tasmiṃ asati paṇṇampi attharituṃ vaṭṭati, kiñci anattharitvā ṭhapentassa pana dukkaṭaṃ. Yadi pana tattha nevāsikā anatthatāya bhūmiyāpi ṭhapenti, adhotapādehipi vaḷañjenti, tatheva vaḷañjetuṃ vaṭṭati.

“Monks, one should not spit on a prepared floor. Whoever should spit incurs an offense of wrong-doing.” According to this, one should not spit on a prepared floor. “I allow, monks, a spittoon.” Thus, when a spittoon is allowed, one should spit into the spittoon. “I allow, monks, to wrap with a coarse cloth.” According to this, when placing a bed or a bench on a plastered floor or a finished floor, if there is no mat or rug, the legs of the beds and benches should be wrapped with a coarse cloth. If that is not available, it is permissible to spread even leaves. For one who places them without spreading anything, however, there is an offense of wrong-doing. But if the resident monks there place them even on a floor without a covering, and use it with unwashed feet, it is permissible to use it in that same way.

“Na[V 0.0418], bhikkhave, parikammakatā bhitti apassetabbā, yo apasseyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (cūḷava. 324) vacanato parikammakatā bhitti setabhitti vā hotu cittakammakatā vā, na apassetabbā. Na kevalañca bhittimeva, dvārampi vātapānampi apassenaphalakampi pāsāṇatthambhampi rukkhatthambhampi cīvarena vā yena kenaci appaṭicchādetvā apassituṃ na labhati. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave[M 0.0449], paccattharitvā nipajjitu”nti (cūḷava. 325) vacanato pana dhotapādehi akkamitabbaṃ, paribhaṇḍakataṃ bhūmiṃ vā bhūmattharaṇaṃ senāsanaṃ vā saṅghikamañcapīṭhaṃ vā attano santakena paccattharaṇena paccattharitvāva nipajjitabbaṃ. Sace niddāyatopi paccattharaṇe saṅkuṭite koci sarīrāvayavo mañcaṃ vā pīṭhaṃ vā phusati, āpattiyeva, lomesu pana phusantesu lomagaṇanāya āpattiyo. Paribhogasīsena apassayantassapi eseva nayo. Hatthatalapādatalehi pana phusituṃ akkamituṃ vā vaṭṭati, mañcaṃ vā pīṭhaṃ vā harantassa kāye paṭihaññati, anāpatti.

“Monks, a prepared wall should not be leaned against. Whoever should lean against it incurs an offense of wrong-doing.” According to this, a prepared wall, whether it be a whitewashed wall or a painted wall, should not be leaned against. And not only a wall; one is not allowed to lean against a door, a window, a shutter, a stone pillar, or a wooden pillar without first covering it with a robe or with some other cloth. However, because of the statement, “Monks, I allow you to lie down after spreading a covering,” one should lie down on a prepared floor, a ground-covering lodging, or a communal bed or bench—which are to be stepped upon with washed feet—only after spreading one's own covering over it. If, while one is asleep, the covering gets rolled up and any part of the body touches the bed or bench, it is an offense of wrong-doing. But if the hairs touch, there are offenses according to the number of hairs. For one who leans against it for the purpose of use, this is the very same rule. However, it is permissible to touch or to step with the palms of the hands or the soles of the feet. If a bed or a bench strikes the body of one who is carrying it, there is no offense.

51. “Dasayime, bhikkhave, avandiyā. Pureupasampannena pacchupasampanno avandiyo, anupasampanno avandiyo, nānāsaṃvāsako vuḍḍhataro adhammavādī avandiyo, mātugāmo avandiyo, paṇḍako avandiyo, pārivāsiko avandiyo, mūlāyapaṭikassanāraho avandiyo, mānattāraho avandiyo, mānattacāriko avandiyo, abbhānāraho avandiyo”ti (cūḷava. 312) vacanato ime dasa avandiyāti veditabbā.

51. “Monks, these ten are not to be venerated. A later ordained monk is not to be venerated by an earlier ordained monk; an unordained person is not to be venerated; an older monk of a different communion who speaks contrary to the Dhamma is not to be venerated; a woman is not to be venerated; a paṇḍaka is not to be venerated; one undergoing probation is not to be venerated; one deserving to be sent back to the beginning is not to be venerated; one deserving penance is not to be venerated; one undertaking penance is not to be venerated; one deserving reinstatement is not to be venerated.” According to this, these ten are to be known as those who are not to be venerated.

“Pacchupasampannena pureupasampanno vandiyo, nānāsaṃvāsako vuḍḍhataro dhammavādī vandiyo, tathāgato arahaṃ sammāsambuddho vandiyo”ti (cūḷava. 312) – vacanato ime tayo vanditabbā.

“An earlier ordained monk is to be venerated by a later ordained monk; an older monk of a different communion who speaks in accordance with the Dhamma is to be venerated; the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, is to be venerated.” According to this, these three are to be venerated.

52. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, tīṇi tūlāni rukkhatūlaṃ latātūlaṃ poṭakītūla”nti (cūḷava. 297) vacanato imāni tīṇi tūlāni kappiyāni. Tattha (cūḷava. aṭṭha. 297) rukkhatūlanti simbalirukkhādīnaṃ yesaṃ kesañci rukkhānaṃ tūlaṃ. Latātūlanti khīravalliādīnaṃ yāsaṃ kāsañci vallīnaṃ tūlaṃ. Poṭakītūlanti poṭakītiṇādīnaṃ yesaṃ kesañci tiṇajātikānaṃ antamaso ucchunaḷādīnampi tūlaṃ. Etehi tīhi sabbabhūtagāmā saṅgahitā honti. Rukkhavallitiṇajātiyo hi muñcitvā añño bhūtagāmo nāma natthi, tasmā yassa kassaci bhūtagāmassa tūlaṃ bimbohane vaṭṭati. Bhisiṃ pana pāpuṇitvā sabbametaṃ akappiyatūlanti vuccati. Na kevalañca bimbohane etaṃ tūlameva, haṃsamorādīnaṃ sabbasakuṇānaṃ sīhādīnaṃ [V 0.0419] sabbacatuppadānañca lomampi vaṭṭati, piyaṅgupupphabakulapupphādīnaṃ pana yaṃ kiñci pupphaṃ na vaṭṭati. Tamālapattaṃ suddhameva [M 0.0450] na vaṭṭati, missakaṃ pana vaṭṭati, bhisīnaṃ anuññātaṃ pañcavidhaṃ uṇṇāditūlampi vaṭṭati.

52. “I allow, monks, three kinds of stuffing: tree stuffing, vine stuffing, and poṭakī stuffing.” (Cūḷavagga 297) According to this statement, these three kinds of stuffing are allowable. Therein (Cūḷavagga Aṭṭhakathā, 297), ‘tree stuffing’ is the stuffing from any trees whatsoever, such as the silk-cotton tree and so on. ‘Vine stuffing’ is the stuffing from any vines whatsoever, such as the milk vine and so on. ‘Poṭakī stuffing’ is the stuffing from any kind of grass whatsoever, such as poṭakī grass and so on, down to even that of sugarcane and reeds. By these three, all plant life is included. For, apart from the kinds of trees, vines, and grasses, there is no other so-called plant life. Therefore, the stuffing of any plant life whatsoever is allowable for a pillow. However, when it comes to a bolster, all of this is called unallowable stuffing. And not only is this stuffing allowable for a pillow, but the down of all birds, such as geese and peacocks, and the hair of all quadrupeds, such as lions, are also allowable. However, any flower whatsoever, such as the piyaṅgu flower, the bakula flower, and so on, is not allowable. The tamāla leaf by itself is not allowable, but when mixed, it is allowable. For bolsters, the five kinds of allowed stuffing, beginning with wool, are also allowable.

53. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, pañca bhisiyo uṇṇabhisiṃ coḷabhisiṃ vākabhisiṃ tiṇabhisiṃ paṇṇabhisi”nti (cūḷava. 297) vacanato pañcahi uṇṇādīhi pūritā pañca bhisiyo anuññātā. Tūlagaṇanāya hi etāsaṃ gaṇanā vuttā. Tattha uṇṇaggahaṇena na kevalaṃ eḷakalomameva gahitaṃ, ṭhapetvā pana manussalomaṃ yaṃ kiñci kappiyākappiyamaṃsajātīnaṃ pakkhicatuppadānaṃ lomaṃ sabbaṃ idha uṇṇaggahaṇeneva gahitaṃ. Tasmā channaṃ cīvarānaṃ channaṃ anulomacīvarānañca aññatarena bhisicchaviṃ katvā taṃ sabbaṃ pakkhipitvā bhisiṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭati. Eḷakalomāni pana apakkhipitvā kambalameva catugguṇaṃ pañcaguṇaṃ vā pakkhipitvā katāpi uṇṇabhisisaṅkhyameva gacchati.

53. “I allow, monks, five kinds of mattresses: a wool mattress, a cloth mattress, a bark-fiber mattress, a grass mattress, and a leaf mattress.” (Cūḷavagga 297) In accordance with this statement, five kinds of mattresses, filled with wool and the other materials, are permitted. Indeed, their enumeration is stated according to the count of the stuffing. Herein, by the term ‘wool,’ not only sheep’s wool is taken, but, excepting human hair, any hair from creatures with permissible or impermissible flesh, birds, or quadrupeds—all this is taken here by the term ‘wool.’ Therefore, it is permissible to make a mattress by making a mattress cover from any one of the six robes or the six suitable robes, and stuffing it with all such material. However, even if one is made without stuffing it with sheep’s wool, but by stuffing it with a blanket folded four or five times, it still falls under the category of a wool mattress.

Coḷabhisiādīsu yaṃ kiñci navacoḷaṃ vā purāṇacoḷaṃ vā saṃharitvā anto pakkhipitvā vā katā coḷabhisi. Yaṃ kiñci vākaṃ pakkhipitvā katā vākabhisi. Yaṃ kiñci tiṇaṃ pakkhipitvā katā tiṇabhisi. Aññatra suddhatamālapattā yaṃ kiñci paṇṇaṃ pakkhipitvā katā paṇṇabhisīti veditabbā. Tamālapattaṃ pana aññena missameva vaṭṭati. Suddhaṃ na vaṭṭati. Yaṃ panetaṃ uṇṇādipañcavidhaṃ tūlaṃ bhisiyaṃ vaṭṭati, taṃ masūrakepi vaṭṭatīti kurundiyaṃ vuttaṃ. Etena masūrakaṃ paribhuñjituṃ vaṭṭatīti siddhaṃ hoti. Bhisiyā pamāṇaniyamo natthi, mañcabhisi pīṭhabhisi bhūmattharaṇabhisi caṅkamanabhisi pādapuñchanabhisīti etāsaṃ anurūpato sallakkhetvā attano rucivasena pamāṇaṃ kātabbaṃ. Bimbohanaṃ pana pamāṇayuttameva vaṭṭati.

Regarding cloth mattresses and so forth: a cloth mattress is one made by gathering and stuffing inside any new cloth or old cloth. One made by stuffing it with any bark-fiber is a bark-fiber mattress. One made by stuffing it with any grass is a grass mattress. It should be understood that a leaf mattress is one made by stuffing it with any kind of leaf, except for pure tamāla leaves. However, tamāla leaves are permissible only when mixed with other leaves; pure, they are not permissible. Furthermore, those five kinds of stuffing, beginning with wool, which are permissible for a mattress, are also permissible for a leather mattress—so it is said in the Kurundī. By this, it is established that it is permissible to use a leather mattress. There is no fixed measurement for a mattress; having considered what is appropriate for bed mattresses, seat mattresses, floor-covering mattresses, walking-path mattresses, and foot-wiping mattresses, the size should be made according to one’s own preference. A pillow, however, is only permissible when it is of the proper size.

54. “Na, bhikkhave, aḍḍhakāyikāni bimbohanāni dhāretabbāni, yo dhāreyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (cūḷava. 297) yesu kaṭito paṭṭhāya yāva sīsaṃ upadahanti, tādisāni upaḍḍhakāyappamāṇāni bimbohanāni paṭikkhipitvā “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, sīsappamāṇaṃ bimbohana”nti (cūḷava. 297) sīsappamāṇaṃ anuññātaṃ. Sīsappamāṇaṃ nāma yassa vitthārato tīsu kaṇṇesu dvinnaṃ kaṇṇānaṃ antaraṃ miniyamānaṃ vidatthi ceva caturaṅgulañca hoti, majjhaṭṭhānaṃ muṭṭhiratanaṃ hoti. “Dīghato pana diyaḍḍharatanaṃ vā dviratanaṃ vā”ti kurundiyaṃ vuttaṃ. Ayaṃ sīsappamāṇassa ukkaṭṭhaparicchedo, ito uddhaṃ na vaṭṭati, heṭṭhā vaṭṭati[M 0.0451]. Agilānassa sīsūpadhānañca [V 0.0420] pādūpadhānañcāti dvayameva vaṭṭati, gilānassa bimbohanāni santharitvā upari paccattharaṇaṃ datvā nipajjitumpi vaṭṭati. “Yāni pana bhisīnaṃ anuññātāni pañca kappiyatūlāni, tehi bimbohanaṃ mahantampi vaṭṭatī”ti phussadevatthero āha. Vinayadharaupatissatthero pana “bimbohanaṃ karissāmīti kappiyatūlaṃ vā akappiyatūlaṃ vā pakkhipitvā karontassa pamāṇameva vaṭṭatī”ti āha.

54. “Monks, half-body pillows should not be kept. Whoever should keep one, commits an offense of wrong-doing.” (Cūḷavagga 297) Having prohibited such pillows which support from the waist up to the head, those pillows approximating half the body in size, He said: “I allow, monks, a pillow the size of the head.” (Cūḷavagga 297) A head-sized pillow is permitted. A head-sized pillow is defined as one whose width, when the distance between two corners is measured at three points, is a span and four fingers, and the central part is a fist-cubit. “In length, it should be one and a half cubits or two cubits,” as stated in the Kurundī. This is the upper limit for a head-sized pillow; anything above this is not permissible, but anything below it is. For one who is not ill, only a head-pillow and a foot-pillow are permissible. For one who is ill, it is also permissible to spread out pillows, place a covering on top, and lie down. “A pillow made with the five kinds of allowable stuffing permitted for cushions is allowable, even if it is large,” said the Elder Phussadeva. However, the Elder Upatissa, an expert in the Vinaya, said, “For one who intends to make a pillow, whether stuffing it with permitted or unpermitted stuffing, only the prescribed size is permissible.”

55. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, āsandika”nti (cūḷava. 297) vacanato caturassapīṭhasaṅkhāto āsandiko vaṭṭati, so ca “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, uccakampi āsandika”nti (cūḷava. 297) vacanato aṭṭhaṅgulato uccapādakopi vaṭṭati. Ekatobhāgena dīghapīṭhameva hi aṭṭhaṅgulato uccapādakaṃ na vaṭṭati, tasmā caturassapīṭhaṃ pamāṇātikkantampi vaṭṭati. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, sattaṅga”nti (cūḷava. 297) vacanato tīsu disāsu apassayaṃ katvā katamañcopi vaṭṭati. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, uccakampi sattaṅga”nti (cūḷava. 297) vacanato ayampi pamāṇātikkanto ca vaṭṭati. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, bhaddapīṭha”ntiādinā (cūḷava. 297) pāḷiyaṃ anuññātaṃ vettamayapīṭhaṃ pilotikābaddhapīṭhaṃ dārupaṭṭikāya upari pāde ṭhapetvā bhojanaphalakaṃ viya kataṃ eḷakapādapīṭhaṃ āmalakākārena yojitaṃ bahupādakaṃ āmaṇḍakavaṭṭikapīṭhaṃ palālapīṭhaṃ phalakapīṭhañca pāḷiyaṃ anāgatañca aññampi yaṃ kiñci dārumayapīṭhaṃ vaṭṭati.

55. “I allow, monks, an āsandika,” (Cūḷavagga 297); from this statement, an āsandika, which is designated as a square stool, is allowable. And because of the statement, “I allow, monks, even a high āsandika,” (Cūḷavagga 297), it is also allowable with legs higher than eight finger-breadths. Indeed, it is only a long seat with legs higher than eight finger-breadths that is not allowable; therefore, a square stool is allowable even if it exceeds the measurement. Because of the statement, “I allow, monks, a sattaṅga,” (Cūḷavagga 297), a couch made with supports on three sides is also allowable. Because of the statement, “I allow, monks, even a high sattaṅga,” (Cūḷavagga 297), this too is allowable even if it exceeds the measurement. By the Pāḷi text beginning, “I allow, monks, a bhaddapīṭha,” etc., (Cūḷavagga 297), the following are permitted: a seat made of wicker, a seat bound with coarse cloth, a stool made like a dining table by placing legs upon a wooden plank base, a goat-foot seat, a many-legged seat with legs fitted in the shape of an emblic myrobalan, a seat with many turned legs shaped like emblic myrobalans, a straw seat, and a plank seat. Furthermore, any other wooden seat whatsoever that is not mentioned in the Pāḷi is allowable.

“Na, bhikkhave, ucce mañce sayitabbaṃ, yo sayeyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (cūḷava. 297) vacanato pamaṇātikkante mañce sayantassa dukkaṭaṃ, taṃ pana karontassa kārāpentassa ca chedanakaṃ pācittiyaṃ. Aññena kataṃ paṭilabhitvā paribhuñjantena chinditvā paribhuñjitabbaṃ. Sace na chinditukāmo hoti, bhūmiyaṃ nikhanitvā pamāṇaṃ upari dasseti, uttānakaṃ vā katvā paribhuñjati, ukkhipitvā tulāsaṅghāṭe ṭhapetvā aṭṭaṃ katvā paribhuñjati, vaṭṭati. “Na, bhikkhave, uccā mañcapaṭipādakā dhāretabbā, yo dhāreyya, āpatti dukkaṭassa. Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, aṭṭhaṅgulaparamaṃ mañcapaṭipādaka”nti (cūḷava. 297) vacanato manussānaṃ pamāṇaṅgulena aṭṭhaṅgulaparamova mañcapaṭipādako vaṭṭati, tato uddhaṃ na vaṭṭati.

“Monks, one should not lie on a high bed. Whoever does so, commits an offense of wrong-doing.” (Cūḷavagga 297) According to this, lying on a bed that exceeds the limit is an offense of wrong-doing. However, for one who makes it or has it made, there is a pācittiya offense requiring it to be cut down. Having received a bed made by another, it should be cut down before being used. If one does not wish to cut it, one may bury it in the ground showing the proper measure above; or, laying it flat, one may use it; or, having lifted it and placed it on a trestle, and having made a platform, one may use it; this is allowable. “Monks, high bed-legs should not be kept. Whoever keeps them, commits an offense of wrong-doing. I allow, monks, a bed-leg of at most eight finger-breadths.” (Cūḷavagga 297) According to this, a bed-leg of at most eight finger-breadths, measured by the standard finger-breadth of humans, is allowable. Beyond that is not allowable.

56. “Na[M 0.0452], bhikkhave, uccāsayanamahāsayanāni dhāretabbāni, seyyathidaṃ, āsandi pallaṅko gonako cittako paṭikā paṭalikā tūlikā vikatikā uddalomi ekantalomi kaṭṭissaṃ koseyyaṃ kuttakaṃ hatthattharaṃ assattharaṃ rathattharaṃ ajinapaveṇī kadalimigapavarapaccattharaṇaṃ sauttaracchadaṃ [V 0.0421] ubhatolohitakūpadhānaṃ, yo dhāreyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (mahāva. 254) vacanato uccāsayanamahāsayanāni na vaṭṭanti. Tattha (mahāva. aṭṭha. 254) uccāsayanaṃ nāma pamāṇātikkantaṃ mañcaṃ. Mahāsayanaṃ nāma akappiyattharaṇaṃ. Āsandiādīsu āsandīti pamāṇātikkantāsanaṃ. Pallaṅkoti pādesu vāḷarūpāni ṭhapetvā kato. Gonakoti dīghalomako mahākojavo. Caturaṅgulādhikāni kira tassa lomāni. Cittakoti ratanacitrauṇṇāmayattharako. Paṭikāti uṇṇāmayo setattharako. Paṭalikāti ghanapupphako uṇṇāmayalomattharako, yo “āmalakapaṭo”tipi vuccati. Tūlikāti pakatitūlikāyeva. Vikatikāti sīhabyagghādirūpavicitro uṇṇāmayattharako. Uddalomīti ekato uggatalomaṃ uṇṇāmayattharaṇaṃ. Ekantalomīti ubhato uggatalomaṃ uṇṇāmayattharaṇaṃ. Kaṭṭissanti ratanaparisibbitaṃ koseyyakaṭṭissamayaṃ paccattharaṇaṃ. Koseyyanti ratanaparisibbitaṃ kosiyasuttamayaṃ paccattharaṇaṃ, suddhakoseyyaṃ pana vaṭṭati.

56. “Monks, high beds and luxurious beds should not be used. These are: a long-legged chair exceeding the standard measure; a couch with animal figures on its legs; a large, long-fleeced, black woolen rug; a woolen spread variegated with figures of wild animals; a white woolen spread; a red woolen spread with thick floral designs; a cotton-filled mattress; a woolen spread variegated with figures of lions, tigers, and so on; a woolen spread with fleece on one side; a woolen spread with fleece on both sides; a spread of silk interwoven with gold thread; a silken spread embroidered with gold; a woolen spread large enough for sixteen dancing girls; an elephant saddle-blanket; a horse saddle-blanket; a chariot-rug; a spread of black antelope skins sewn together in layers; an excellent spread made of the hide of the kadali deer; a bed with a red canopy; and a bed with red pillows at both ends. Whoever should use these, commits an offense of wrong-doing.” (Mahāvagga 254) Thus, high and luxurious beds are not allowable. Therein (Mahāvagga Aṭṭhakathā 254), a ‘high bed’ means a couch that exceeds the standard measure. A ‘luxurious bed’ means an unallowable spread.
