Among these: ‘Āsandī’ means a long-legged seat that exceeds the standard measure. ‘Pallaṅka’ is a couch made by placing figures of wild animals on its legs. ‘Gonaka’ is a large carpet with long fleece; its fleece, it is said, is longer than four finger-breadths. ‘Cittaka’ is a woolen spread variegated with figures of wild animals. ‘Paṭikā’ is a white woolen spread. ‘Paṭalikā’ is a red-colored woolen spread with thick floral designs, which is also called an ‘āmalaka cloth.’ ‘Tūlikā’ is just an ordinary cotton-filled mattress. ‘Vikatikā’ is a woolen spread variegated with figures of lions, tigers, and so on. ‘Uddalomī’ is a woolen spread with fleece rising on one side. ‘Ekantalomī’ is a woolen spread with fleece rising on both sides. ‘Kaṭṭissaṃ’ is a spread made of silk interwoven with gold thread and embroidered with gold. ‘Koseyya’ is a spread made of silk thread, embroidered with gold; however, a spread made of pure silk is allowable.

Kuttakanti soḷasannaṃ nāṭakitthīnaṃ ṭhatvā naccanayoggaṃ uṇṇāmayattharaṇaṃ. Hatthattharaassattharā hatthiassapiṭṭhīsu attharaṇakaattharaṇā eva. Rathattharepi eseva nayo. Ajinapaveṇīti ajinacammehi mañcappamāṇena sibbitvā katā paveṇī. Kadalimigapavarapaccattharaṇanti kadalimigacammaṃ nāma atthi, tena kataṃ pavarapaccattharaṇanti attho. Taṃ kira setavatthassa upari kadalimigacammaṃ pattharitvā sibbitvā karonti. Sauttaracchadanti saha uttaracchadena, uparibaddhena rattavitānena saddhinti attho. Setavitānampi heṭṭhā akappiyapaccattharaṇe sati na vaṭṭati, asati pana vaṭṭati. Ubhatolohitakūpadhānanti sīsūpadhānañca pādūpadhānañcāti mañcassa ubhatolohitakūpadhānaṃ, etaṃ na kappati. Yaṃ pana ekameva upadhānaṃ ubhosu passesu rattaṃ vā hotu padumavaṇṇaṃ vā vicitraṃ vā, sace pamāṇayuttaṃ, vaṭṭati, mahāupadhānaṃ pana paṭikkhittaṃ. Gonakādīni (cūḷava. aṭṭha. 320) saṅghikavihāre vā [M 0.0453] puggalikavihāre vā mañcapīṭhakesu attharitvā paribhuñjituṃ na vaṭṭanti, dhammāsane pana gihivikatanīhārena labbhanti, tatrāpi nipajjituṃ na vaṭṭati.

A Kuttaka is a woolen spread suitable for sixteen dancing girls to stand and dance upon. Elephant and horse coverings are simply coverings for the backs of elephants and horses. The same method applies to chariot coverings. An Ajinapaveṇī is a fine spread made by stitching together skins of black antelope to the size of a bed. Kadalimigapavarapaccattharaṇa means an excellent spread made from the skin of a kadali deer. A white canopy is also not allowable when there is an unallowable spread underneath it; if there is not, however, it is allowable. Ubhatolohitakūpadhāna means having a head-cushion and a foot-cushion for a bed; this is not allowable. However, a single cushion that is red, lotus-colored, or variegated on both sides is allowable if it is of proper size; but an oversized cushion is rejected. Items like the Gonaka are not allowable to be spread on beds or chairs for use in a monastery belonging to the Sangha or to an individual. However, on a Dhamma seat, they are allowable when spread by laypeople, but even there, it is not allowable to lie down.

“Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, ṭhapetvā tīṇi āsandiṃ pallaṅkaṃ tūlikaṃ gihivikataṃ abhinisīdituṃ, na tveva abhinipajjitu”nti (cūḷava. 314) – vacanato āsandādittayaṃ ṭhapetvā avasesesu gonakādīsu gihivikatesu dhammāsane vā bhattagge vā antaraghare vā nisīdituṃ vaṭṭati, nipajjituṃ na vaṭṭati. Tūlonaddhaṃ pana mañcapīṭhaṃ bhattagge antaraghareyeva nisīdituṃ [V 0.0422] vaṭṭati, tatthāpi nipajjituṃ vaṭṭati. Tūlonaddhaṃ pana mañcapīṭhaṃ kārāpentassapi uddālanakaṃ pācittiyaṃ.

“Monks, I allow you to sit upon furnishings belonging to laypeople, setting aside three things—a high seat, a couch, and a stuffed mattress; but I certainly do not allow you to lie down upon them.” According to this, setting aside those three, the high seat and so on, it is allowable to sit on the remaining items belonging to laypeople, such as Gonaka rugs, whether on a Dhamma seat, in a dining hall, or inside a house, but it is not allowable to lie down. However, it is allowable to sit on a bed or chair stuffed with cotton only in a dining hall or inside a house, and it is also allowable to lie down there. But for one who has a bed or chair stuffed with cotton made, there is a Pācittiya offense requiring the removal of the stuffing.

“Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, onaddhamañcaṃ onaddhapīṭha”nti (cūḷava. 297) vacanato pana cammādīhi onaddhaṃ mañcapīṭhaṃ vaṭṭati. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, pāvāraṃ. Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, koseyyapāvāraṃ. Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, kojavaṃ. Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, kambala”nti (mahāva. 337-338) – vacanato pāvārādīni saṅghikāni vā hontu puggalikāni vā, yathāsukhaṃ vihāre vā antaraghare vā yattha katthaci paribhuñjituṃ vaṭṭanti. Kojavaṃ panettha pakatikojavameva vaṭṭati, mahāpiṭṭhiyakojavaṃ na vaṭṭati.

“O monks, I allow a couch interwoven with straps and a chair interwoven with straps.” According to this statement, a couch or chair covered with leather and so forth is allowable. “O monks, I allow a mantle. O monks, I allow a silk mantle. O monks, I allow a rug. O monks, I allow a blanket.” According to this statement, mantles and so forth, whether they belong to the Sangha or to an individual, are allowable to be used as one pleases, whether in a monastery or inside a house, anywhere at all. However, in this matter, only an ordinary rug is allowable; a rug for a great elephant saddle is not allowable.

“Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, sabbaṃ pāsādaparibhoga”nti (cūḷava. 320) vacanato suvaṇṇarajatādivicitrāni (cūḷava. aṭṭha. 320) kavāṭāni mañcapīṭhāni tālavaṇṭāni suvaṇṇarajatayoni pānīyaghaṭapānīyasarāvāni, yaṃ kiñci cittakammakataṃ, sabbaṃ senāsanaparibhoge vaṭṭati. “Pāsādassa dāsidāsaṃ khettavatthuṃ gomahiṃsaṃ demā”ti vadanti, pāṭekkaṃ gahaṇakiccaṃ natthi, pāsāde paṭiggahite paṭiggahitameva hoti.

“O monks, I allow all furnishings of a storied building.” According to this statement, door-leaves adorned with gold, silver, and so forth; couches and chairs; palm-leaf fans; water pots and drinking cups made of gold and silver—whatever is artistically made—all are allowable as furnishings for a lodging. If they say, “We give female slaves, male slaves, fields, land, cattle, and buffaloes to the storied building,” there is no need for a separate act of acceptance; when the storied building is accepted, they are indeed accepted.

“Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, ekapalāsikaṃ upāhanaṃ… na, bhikkhave, diguṇā upāhanā dhāretabbā… na tiguṇā upāhanā dhāretabbā… na guṇaṅguṇūpāhanā dhāretabbā… yo dhāreyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (mahāva. 245) – vacanato ekapaṭalāyeva upāhanā vaṭṭati, dvipaṭalā pana tipaṭalā na vaṭṭatiyeva. Guṇaṅguṇūpāhanā (mahāva. aṭṭha. 245) nāma catupaṭalato paṭṭhāya vuccati, sā pana majjhimadeseyeva na vaṭṭati. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, sabbapaccantimesu janapadesu guṇaṅguṇūpāhana”nti (mahāva. 259) – vacanato paccantimesu janapadesu guṇaṅguṇūpāhanā [M 0.0454] navā vā hotu paribhuttā vā, vaṭṭati. Majjhimadese pana “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, omukkaṃ guṇaṅguṇūpāhanaṃ. Na, bhikkhave, navā guṇaṅguṇūpāhanā dhāretabbā, yo dhāreyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (mahāva. 247) vacanato paṭimuñcitvā apanītā paribhuttāyeva guṇaṅguṇūpāhanā vaṭṭati, aparibhuttā paṭikkhittāyeva. Ekapaṭalā pana paribhuttā vā hotu aparibhuttā vā, sabbattha vaṭṭati. Ettha ca manussacammaṃ ṭhapetvā yena kenaci cammena katā upāhanā vaṭṭati. Upāhanakosakasatthakakosakakuñcikakosakesupi eseva nayo.

“Bhikkhus, I allow a single-layered sandal… Bhikkhus, double-layered sandals should not be worn… Triple-layered sandals should not be worn… Multi-layered sandals should not be worn… Whoever should wear them, commits an offense of wrong-doing.” According to this statement, only single-layered sandals are permissible, while double-layered or triple-layered ones are not permissible at all. Multi-layered sandals are so-called starting from four layers, but these are not permissible in the Middle Country. “Bhikkhus, I allow multi-layered sandals in all border regions.” According to this statement, in the border regions, multi-layered sandals, whether new or used, are permissible. However, in the Middle Country, “Bhikkhus, I allow multi-layered sandals that have been put on and taken off. Bhikkhus, new multi-layered sandals should not be worn; whoever should wear them, commits an offense of wrong-doing.” According to this, only used multi-layered sandals that have been put on and taken off are permissible; unused ones are prohibited. Single-layered sandals, however, whether used or unused, are permissible everywhere. And here, excepting human leather, sandals made from any kind of leather are permissible. This same principle applies also to sandal cases, small knife cases, and key cases.

“Na[V 0.0423], bhikkhave, sabbanīlikā upāhanā dhāretabbā… na sabbapītikā upāhanā dhāretabbā… na sabbalohitikā upāhanā dhāretabbā… na sabbamañjiṭṭhikā upāhanā dhāretabbā… na sabbakaṇhā upāhanā dhāretabbā… na sabbamahāraṅgarattā upāhanā dhāretabbā. Na sabbamahānāmarattā upāhanā dhāretabbā, yo dhāreyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (mahāva. 246) – vacanato sabbanīlikādi upāhanā na vaṭṭati. Ettha ca nīlikā umāpupphavaṇṇā hoti. Pītikā kaṇikārapupphavaṇṇā… lohitikā jayasumanapupphavaṇṇā… mañjiṭṭhikā mañjiṭṭhavaṇṇā eva… kaṇhā addāriṭṭhakavaṇṇā… mahāraṅgarattā satapadipiṭṭhivaṇṇā… mahānāmarattā sambhinnavaṇṇā hoti paṇḍupalāsavaṇṇā. Kurundiyaṃ pana “padumapupphavaṇṇā”ti vuttaṃ. Etāsu yaṃ kiñci labhitvā rajanaṃ coḷakena puñchitvā vaṇṇaṃ bhinditvā dhāretuṃ vaṭṭati, appamattakepi bhinne vaṭṭatiyeva.

“Monks, all-blue sandals should not be worn… all-yellow sandals should not be worn… all-red sandals should not be worn… all-madder-colored sandals should not be worn… all-black sandals should not be worn… all-mahāraṅga-dyed sandals should not be worn. All-mahānāma-dyed sandals should not be worn. Whoever should wear them, commits an offense of wrong-doing.” Thus, sandals that are entirely blue and so on are not allowable. Herein, ‘blue’ is the color of the umā flower. ‘Yellow’ is the color of the kaṇikāra flower… ‘Red’ is the color of the jayasumana flower… ‘Madder-colored’ is the color of madder itself… ‘Black’ is the color of a fresh soap-nut… ‘Mahāraṅga-dyed’ is the color of a centipede’s back… ‘Mahānāma-dyed’ is a mixed color, the color of a withered leaf. But in the Kurundī, it is said to be “the color of a lotus flower.” Having obtained any of these, it is allowable to wear them after wiping them with a dyed cloth and thus breaking the color. Even if it is broken only slightly, it is indeed allowable.

“Na, bhikkhave, nīlakavaddhikā upāhanā dhāretabbā… na pītakavaddhikā upāhanā dhāretabbā… na lohitakavaddhikā upāhanā dhāretabbā… na mañjiṭṭhikavaddhikā upāhanā dhāretabbā… na kaṇhavaddhikā upāhanā dhāretabbā… na mahāraṅgarattavaddhikā upāhanā dhāretabbā… na mahānāmarattavaddhikā upāhanā dhāretabbā… yo dhāreyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (mahāva. 246) – vacanato yāsaṃ vaddhāyeva nīlādivaṇṇā honti, tāpi na vaṭṭanti, vaṇṇabhedaṃ pana katvā dhāretuṃ vaṭṭati.

“Monks, sandals with blue straps should not be worn… sandals with yellow straps should not be worn… sandals with red straps should not be worn… sandals with madder-colored straps should not be worn… sandals with black straps should not be worn… sandals with mahāraṅga-dyed straps should not be worn… sandals with mahānāma-dyed straps should not be worn. Whoever should wear them, commits an offense of wrong-doing.” Thus, those sandals whose straps alone are of blue and other such colors are also not allowable. But it is allowable to wear them after breaking the color.

“Na, bhikkhave, khallakabaddhā upāhanā dhāretabbā… na puṭabaddhā upāhanā dhāretabbā… na pāliguṇṭhimā upāhanā dhāretabbā… na tūlapuṇṇikā upāhanā dhāretabbā… na tittirapattikā upāhanā dhāretabbā… na meṇḍavisāṇavaddhikā [M 0.0455] upāhanā dhāretabbā… na ajavisāṇavaddhikā upāhanā dhāretabbā… na vicchikāḷikā upāhanā dhāretabbā… na morapiñchaparisibbitā upāhanā dhāretabbā… na citrā upāhanā dhāretabbā, yo dhāreyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (mahāva. 246) – vacanato khallakabaddhādi upāhanāpi na vaṭṭati. Tattha khallakabaddhāti paṇhipidhānatthaṃ tale khallakaṃ bandhitvā katā. Puṭabaddhāti yonakaupāhanā vuccati, yā yāva jaṅghato sabbapādaṃ paṭicchādeti. Pāliguṇṭhimāti paliguṇṭhitvā katā, upari pādamattameva paṭicchādeti, na jaṅghaṃ. Tūlapuṇṇikāti tūlapicunā pūretvā katā. Tittirapattikāti tittirapattasadisā vicitrabaddhā. Meṇḍavisāṇavaddhikāti kaṇṇikaṭṭhāne meṇḍakasiṅgasaṇṭhāne vaddhe yojetvā katā. Ajavisāṇavaddhikādīsupi eseva nayo, vicchikāḷikāpi tattheva vicchikanaṅguṭṭhasaṇṭhāne vaddhe yojetvā katā. Morapiñchaparisibbitāti talesu [V 0.0424] vā vaddhesu vā morapiñchehi suttakasadisehi parisibbitā. Citrāti vicitrā. Etāsu yaṃ kiñci labhitvā sace tāni khallakādīni apanetvā sakkā honti vaḷañjituṃ, vaḷañjetabbā. Tesu pana sati vaḷañjantassa dukkaṭaṃ.

“Bhikkhus, shoes with heel coverings should not be worn… pouch-bound shoes should not be worn… wrapped-around shoes should not be worn… cotton-stuffed shoes should not be worn… shoes with partridge-wing patterns should not be worn… shoes with ram's-horn straps should not be worn… shoes with goat's-horn straps should not be worn… shoes with scorpion-tail straps should not be worn… shoes sewn with peacock feathers should not be worn… ornate shoes should not be worn. Whoever should wear them, commits an offense of wrong-doing” (Mahāvagga 246) — therefore, shoes with heel coverings and the like are not allowable. Therein, ‘khallakabaddhā’ are those made by fastening a covering to the sole in order to cover the heel. ‘Puṭabaddhā’ are called Yonaka shoes; they are those which cover the entire foot up to the shin. ‘Pāliguṇṭhimā’ are those made by wrapping; they cover only the foot, not the shin. ‘Tūlapuṇṇikā’ are those made by stuffing them full with cotton wool. ‘Tittirapattikā’ are those with variegated straps resembling partridge wings. ‘Meṇḍavisāṇavaddhikā’ are those made by attaching straps shaped like a ram's horn at the opening. The same method applies to ‘ajavisāṇavaddhikā’ and the like. ‘Vicchikāḷikā’ are also made by attaching straps shaped like a scorpion's tail at that same place. ‘Morapiñchaparisibbitā’ are those sewn on the soles or straps with the thread-like quills of peacock feathers. ‘Citrā’ means ornate. Among these, if any are obtained and it is possible to use them after removing those features such as heel-coverings, they may be used. However, for one who uses them while those features are present, there is an offense of wrong-doing.

“Na, bhikkhave, sīhacammaparikkhaṭā upāhanā dhāretabbā… na byagghacammaparikkhaṭā upāhanā dhāretabbā… na dīpicammaparikkhaṭā upāhanā dhāretabbā… na ajinacammaparikkhaṭā upāhanā dhāretabbā… na uddacammaparikkhaṭā upāhanā dhāretabbā… na majjāracammaparikkhaṭā upāhanā dhāretabbā… na kāḷakacammaparikkhaṭā upāhanā dhāretabbā… na luvakacammaparikkhaṭā upāhanā dhāretabbā, yo dhāreyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (mahāva. 246) – vacanato sīhacammādiparikkhaṭāpi upāhanā na vaṭṭati. Tattha sīhacammaparikkhaṭā nāma pariyantesu cīvare anuvātaṃ viya sīhacammaṃ yojetvā katā. Esa nayo sabbattha. Luvakacammaparikkhaṭāti pakkhibiḷālacammaparikkhaṭā. Etāsupi yā kāci taṃ cammaṃ apanetvā dhāretabbā.

“Bhikkhus, shoes trimmed with lion skin are not to be worn… shoes trimmed with tiger skin are not to be worn… shoes trimmed with leopard skin are not to be worn… shoes trimmed with the skin of a black deer with its hair are not to be worn… shoes trimmed with otter skin are not to be worn… shoes trimmed with cat skin are not to be worn… shoes trimmed with black squirrel skin are not to be worn… shoes trimmed with mongoose skin are not to be worn. Whoever should wear them, it is an offense of wrong-doing.” Therefore, shoes trimmed with lion skin and so forth are not allowable. Herein, ‘shoes trimmed with lion skin’ means those made by attaching lion skin to the edges, like a border on a robe. This is the method in all cases. ‘Shoes trimmed with mongoose skin’ means shoes trimmed with the skin of a mongoose (pakkhibiḷāla). Among these also, whichever shoes are obtained, they are to be worn after removing that skin.

“Na, bhikkhave, kaṭṭhapādukā dhāretabbā… na tālapattapādukā… na veḷupattapādukā, na tiṇapādukā… na muñjapādukā, na pabbajapādukā… na hintālapādukā, na kamalapādukā… na kambalapādukā… na sovaṇṇapādukā… na rūpiyamayā pādukā… na maṇimayā… na veḷuriyamayā… na phalikamayā [M 0.0456]… na kaṃsamayā… na kācamayā… na tipumayā… na sīsamayā… na tambalohamayā… na kāci saṅkamanīyā pādukā dhāretabbā, yo dhāreyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (mahāva. 250-251) – vacanato yena kenaci tiṇena vā aññena vā katā yā kāci saṅkamanīyā pādukā na dhāretabbā. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, tisso pādukā dhuvaṭṭhāniyā asaṅkamanīyāyo, vaccapādukaṃ passāvapādukaṃ ācamanapāduka”nti (mahāva. 251) – vacanato pana bhūmiyaṃ suppatiṭṭhitā niccalā asaṃhāriyā vaccapādukādī tisso pādukā paribhuñjituṃ vaṭṭanti.

“Bhikkhus, wooden sandals are not to be worn… palm-leaf sandals… bamboo sandals, grass sandals… muñja-grass sandals, sandals of pabbaja grass… hintāla-palm sandals, sandals made with a grass called kamala… woolen sandals… golden sandals… sandals made of silver… made of jewels… made of beryl… made of crystal… made of bronze… made of glass… made of tin… made of lead… made of copper… no movable sandals whatsoever are to be worn. Whoever should wear them, it is an offense of wrong-doing.” Therefore, any movable sandals whatsoever, made of any kind of grass or of another material, are not to be worn. “Bhikkhus, I allow three sandals that are in a permanent place, immovable: a toilet sandal, a urinal sandal, and a sandal for cleansing.” Therefore, the three sandals beginning with the toilet sandal, which are well-established on the ground, unshaking, and not to be carried away, are allowable to be used.

“Na, bhikkhave, saupāhanena gāmo pavisitabbo, yo paviseyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (mahāva. 259) vacanato saupāhanena gāmo na pavisitabbo. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, gilānena bhikkhunā saupāhanena gāmaṃ pavisitu”nti (mahāva. 256) vacanato pana yassa pādā vā phālitā pādakhīlā vā ābādho pādā vā dukkhā honti, yo na sakkoti anupāhano gāmaṃ pavisituṃ, evarūpena gilānena saupāhanena gāmaṃ pavisituṃ vaṭṭati. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, ajjhārāme upāhanaṃ dhāretuṃ ukkaṃ padīpaṃ kattaradaṇḍa”nti [V 0.0425] (mahāva. 249) vacanato ajjhārāme agilānassapi upāhanaṃ dhāretuṃ vaṭṭati.

“Bhikkhus, a village is not to be entered with shoes. Whoever should enter, commits an offense of wrong-doing.” In accordance with this (Mahāvagga 259), a village is not to be entered with shoes. “Bhikkhus, I allow a sick bhikkhu to enter a village with shoes.” In accordance with this (Mahāvagga 256), for a bhikkhu whose feet are cracked, or who has a disease of foot-spikes, or whose feet are painful, who is unable to enter a village without shoes—for such a sick bhikkhu, it is allowable to enter a village with shoes. “Bhikkhus, I allow the wearing of shoes, a torch, a lamp, and a walking stick within the monastery.” In accordance with this (Mahāvagga 249), it is allowable even for a bhikkhu who is not sick to wear shoes within the monastery.

“Na, bhikkhave, ācariyesu ācariyamattesu upajjhāyesu upajjhāyamattesu anupāhanesu caṅkamamānesu saupāhanena caṅkamitabbaṃ, yo caṅkameyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (mahāva. 248) – vacanato ācariyādīsu anupāhanesu caṅkamantesu saupāhanena na caṅkamitabbaṃ. Ettha (mahāva. aṭṭha. 248) ca pabbajjācariyo upasampadācariyo nissayācariyo uddesācariyoti ime cattāropi idha ācariyā eva. Avassikassa chabbasso ācariyamatto. So hi catuvassakāle taṃ nissāya vacchati. Evaṃ ekavassassa sattavasso, duvassassa aṭṭhavasso, tivassassa navavasso, catuvassassa dasavassoti imepi ācariyamattā eva. Upajjhāyassa sandiṭṭhasambhattā pana sahāyabhikkhū, ye vā pana keci dasavassehi mahantatarā, te sabbepi upajjhāyamattā nāma. Ettakesu bhikkhūsu anupāhanesu caṅkamantesu saupāhanassa caṅkamato āpatti.

“Bhikkhus, one should not walk with footwear when teachers, those like teachers, preceptors, and those like preceptors are walking without footwear. Whoever should do so, commits an offense of wrong-doing.” In accordance with this (Mahāvagga 248), when teachers and so forth are walking without footwear, one should not walk with footwear. Herein (Mahāvagga Aṭṭha. 248), the Going-Forth Teacher, the Higher-Ordination Teacher, the Dependence Teacher, and the Instruction Teacher—these four are indeed teachers in this context. For a bhikkhu with no rains-retreats, a bhikkhu with six rains-retreats is one who is like a teacher. For, at the time of his fourth rains-retreat, he will live in dependence on him. Similarly, for a bhikkhu of one rains-retreat, a bhikkhu of seven rains-retreats; for a bhikkhu of two rains-retreats, a bhikkhu of eight rains-retreats; for a bhikkhu of three rains-retreats, a bhikkhu of nine rains-retreats; and for a bhikkhu of four rains-retreats, a bhikkhu of ten rains-retreats—these too are ones who are like teachers. However, the preceptor’s associates and companions are companion bhikkhus. Or, whoever are more senior than those of ten rains-retreats, all of them are called ‘ones who are like a preceptor.’ When these many bhikkhus are walking without footwear, for one who walks with footwear, there is an offense.

“Na[M 0.0457], bhikkhave, mahācammāni dhāretabbāni sīhacammaṃ byagghacammaṃ dīpicammaṃ, yo dhāreyya, āpatti dukkaṭassa”. “Na, bhikkhave, gocammaṃ dhāretabbaṃ, yo dhāreyya, āpatti dukkaṭassa”. “Na, bhikkhave, kiñci cammaṃ dhāretabbaṃ, yo dhāreyya, āpattidukkaṭassā”ti (mahāva. 255) – vacanato majjhimadese sīhacammādi yaṃ kiñci cammaṃ gahetvā pariharituṃ na vaṭṭati. Sīhacammādīnañca pariharaṇeyeva paṭikkhepo kato. Bhūmattharaṇavasena pana aññattha anīharantena yaṃ kiñci cammaṃ paribhuñjituṃ vaṭṭati.

“Bhikkhus, large hides—a lion hide, a tiger hide, a leopard hide—are not to be used. Whoever should use one, commits an offense of wrong-doing.” “Bhikkhus, a cowhide is not to be used. Whoever should use it, commits an offense of wrong-doing.” “Bhikkhus, any hide whatsoever is not to be used. Whoever should use it, commits an offense of wrong-doing” (Mahāvagga 255). In accordance with this, in the Middle Country, it is not allowable to take and carry about any hide whatsoever, such as a lion hide. And the prohibition is made only regarding the carrying about of lion hides and so on. However, it is allowable for one who does not carry it to another place to use any hide whatsoever as a ground covering.

“Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, sabbapaccantimesu janapadesu cammāni attharaṇāni eḷakacammaṃ ajacammaṃ migacamma”nti (mahāva. 259) vacanako pana paccantimesu janapadesu yaṃ kiñci (mahāva. aṭṭha. 259) eḷakacammañca ajacammañca attharitvā nipajjituṃ vā nisīdituṃ vā vaṭṭati. Migacamme eṇimigo vātamigo pasadamigo kuruṅgamigo migamātuko rohitamigoti etesaṃyeva cammāni vaṭṭanti, aññesaṃ pana –

“Bhikkhus, in all border districts, I allow hide coverings: sheepskin, goatskin, and deerskin” (Mahāvagga 259). By this utterance, however, in border districts, it is allowable to spread out and lie down or sit on any sheepskin and goatskin. Regarding deerskin, only the hides of these are allowable: the eṇi deer, the vāta deer, the pasada deer, the kuruṅga deer, the migamātuka deer, and the rohita deer; but of others—

Makkaṭo kāḷasīho ca, sarabho kadalīmigo;

Ye ca vāḷamigā keci, tesaṃ cammaṃ na vaṭṭati.

The monkey and the black lion, the sarabha, the plantain deer; and whatever fierce animals there are, their hide is not allowable.

Tattha [V 0.0426] vāḷamigāti sīhabyagghaacchataracchā. Na kevalañca eteyeva, yesaṃ vā pana cammaṃ vaṭṭatīti vuttaṃ, te ṭhapetvā avasesā antamaso gomahiṃsasasabiḷārādayopi sabbe imasmiṃ atthe “vāḷamigā”tveva veditabbā. Etesañhi sabbesaṃ pana cammaṃ na vaṭṭati.

Therein, ‘fierce animals’ means lions, tigers, bears, and hyenas. And not only these, but setting aside those animals whose hide is said to be allowable, all the rest—even down to cows, buffaloes, rabbits, cats, and so on—should all be understood in this context only as ‘fierce animals.’ Indeed, the hide of all of these is not allowable.

“Na, bhikkhave, yānena yāyitabbaṃ, yo yāyeyya, āpatti dukkaṭassa. Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, gilānassa yāna”nti (mahāva. 253) vacanato agilānena bhikkhunā yānena na gantabbaṃ. Kataraṃ pana yānaṃ kappati, kataraṃ na kappatīti? “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, purisayuttaṃ hatthavaṭṭakaṃ. Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, sivikaṃ pāṭaṅki”nti (mahāva. 253) vacanato purisayuttaṃ hatthavaṭṭakaṃ sivikā pāṭaṅkī ca vaṭṭati. Ettha ca purisayuttaṃ itthisārathi vā hotu purisasārathi vā, vaṭṭati, dhenuyuttaṃ pana na vaṭṭati. Hatthavaṭṭakaṃ pana itthiyo vā vaṭṭentu purisā vā, vaṭṭatiyeva.

“Bhikkhus, one should not travel by vehicle. Whoever does so commits an offense of wrong-doing. Bhikkhus, I allow a vehicle for the sick” (Mahāvagga 253). Thus, a bhikkhu who is not sick should not travel by vehicle. But which vehicle is allowable, and which is not? “Bhikkhus, I allow a vehicle yoked with a male animal and a hand-drawn vehicle. Bhikkhus, I allow a palanquin and a sedan chair” (Mahāvagga 253). Thus, a vehicle yoked with a male animal, a hand-drawn vehicle, a palanquin, and a sedan chair are allowable. Here, regarding the vehicle yoked with a male animal, whether it has a female driver or a male driver, it is allowable. However, a vehicle yoked with a cow is not allowable. As for the hand-drawn vehicle, whether women or men draw it, it is indeed allowable.

57. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, ahatānaṃ dussānaṃ ahatakappānaṃ diguṇaṃ saṅghāṭiṃ ekacciyaṃ uttarāsaṅgaṃ ekacciyaṃ antaravāsakaṃ, utuddhaṭānaṃ dussānaṃ catugguṇaṃ [M 0.0458] saṅghāṭiṃ diguṇaṃ uttarāsaṅgaṃ diguṇaṃ antaravāsakaṃ, paṃsukūle yāvadatthaṃ, pāpaṇike ussāho karaṇīyo”ti (mahāva. 348) vacanato adhotānaṃ (mahāva. aṭṭha. 348) ekavāraṃ dhotānañca vatthānaṃ dupaṭṭā saṅghāṭi kātabbā, uttarāsaṅgo antaravāsako ca ekapaṭṭo kātabbo. Utuddhaṭānaṃ pana hatavatthānaṃ pilotikānaṃ saṅghāṭi catugguṇā kātabbā, uttarāsaṅgo antaravāsako ca dupaṭṭo kātabbo, paṃsukūle pana yathāruci kātabbaṃ. Antarāpaṇato patitapilotikacīvarepi ussāho karaṇīyo, pariyesanā kātabbā, paricchedo pana natthi, paṭṭasatampi vaṭṭati. Sabbamidaṃ sādiyantassa bhikkhuno vuttaṃ. Tīsu pana cīvaresu dve vā ekaṃ vā chinditvā kātabbaṃ. Sace nappahoti, āgantukapattaṃ dātabbaṃ. Āgantukapattañhi appahonake anuññātaṃ. Vuttañhetaṃ –

57. “Bhikkhus, for new, unwashed cloths and for cloths like them, I allow a double-layered outer robe, a single-layered upper robe, and a single-layered lower robe; for cloths worn out from being kept for a long time, a quadruple-layered outer robe, a double-layered upper robe, and a double-layered lower robe. For a rag-robe, as much as is needed. Effort should be made to acquire worn-out cloth from the market-place” (Mahāvagga 348). Thus, for unwashed cloth and cloth washed once, the outer robe should be made double-layered, while the upper robe and lower robe should be single-layered. For cloths worn out from being kept for a long time and for tattered cloths, the outer robe should be made quadruple-layered, and the upper robe and lower robe should be double-layered. As for a rag-robe, it may be made according to one’s liking. Even for worn-out robe-cloth fallen from within the market-place, effort should be made; it should be sought after. There is no limit—even a hundred layers are allowable. All this is said for a bhikkhu who accepts this. But of the three robes, two or one should be made by cutting. If it is not sufficient, an additional patch should be applied. For an additional patch is allowed when there is not enough. As it has been said—

“Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, dve chinnakāni ekaṃ acchinnakanti. Dve chinnakāni ekaṃ acchinnakaṃ nappahoti. Bhagavato etamatthaṃ ārocesuṃ. Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, dve acchinnakāni ekaṃ chinnakanti. Dve acchinnakāni ekaṃ chinnakaṃ nappahoti. Bhagavato etamatthaṃ ārocesuṃ. Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, anvādhikampi āropetuṃ. Na ca, bhikkhave, sabbaṃ acchinnakaṃ dhāretabbaṃ, yo dhāreyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (mahāva. 360).

“I allow, Bhikkhus, two cut robes and one uncut robe. Two cut robes and one uncut robe are not sufficient. They reported this matter to the Blessed One. I allow, Bhikkhus, two uncut robes and one cut robe. Two uncut robes and one cut robe are not sufficient. They reported this matter to the Blessed One. I allow, Bhikkhus, to apply even an additional patch. And, Bhikkhus, an entirely uncut robe should not be worn; whoever should wear one, commits an offense of wrong-doing.”

Tasmā [V 0.0427] sace pahoti āgantukapattaṃ, na vaṭṭati, chinditabbameva.

Therefore, if there is sufficient cloth, an additional patch is not allowable; it must be cut.

“Na, bhikkhave, potthako nivāsetabbo, yo nivāseyya, āpatti dukkaṭassa. Na, bhikkhave, sabbanīlakāni cīvarāni dhāretabbāni… na sabbapītakāni… na sabbalohitakāni… na sabbamañjiṭṭhakāni… na sabbakaṇhāni… na sabbamahāraṅgarattāni… na sabbamahānāmarattāni… na acchinnadasāni… na dīghadasāni… na pupphadasāni… na phaladasāni cīvarāni dhāretabbāni… na kañcukaṃ… na tirīṭakaṃ… na veṭhanaṃ dhāretabbaṃ, yo dhāreyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (mahāva. 371-372) – vacanato potthakādīni na dhāretabbāni. Tattha (mahāva. aṭṭha. 371-372) potthakoti makacimayo vuccati, akkadussakadalidussaerakadussānipi potthakagatikāneva. Sabbanīlakādīni rajanaṃ dhovitvā puna rajitvā dhāretabbāni. Na sakkā ce honti dhovituṃ, paccattharaṇāni vā kātabbāni. Tipaṭṭacīvarassa vā majjhe dātabbāni. Tesaṃ [M 0.0459] vaṇṇanānattaṃ upāhanāsu vuttanayameva. Acchinnadasadīghadasāni dasā chinditvā dhāretabbāni. Kañcukaṃ labhitvā phāletvā rajitvā paribhuñjituṃ vaṭṭati. Veṭhanepi eseva nayo. Tirīṭakaṃ pana rukkhacchallimayaṃ, taṃ pādapuñchaniṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭati.

“Monks, a `potthaka` [robe of woven fibers] should not be worn; whoever should wear one, there is an offense of wrong-doing. Monks, robes that are entirely blue should not be worn… nor entirely yellow… nor entirely red… nor entirely crimson… nor entirely black… nor entirely of `mahāraṅga` dye… nor entirely of `mahānāma` dye… nor robes with uncut fringes… nor robes with long fringes… nor robes with flower-like fringes… nor robes with fruit-like fringes should be worn… nor a tunic… nor a garment of tree bark… nor a turban should be worn; whoever should wear one, there is an offense of wrong-doing.” Therefore, `potthaka` and the like should not be worn. Therein, `potthaka` is said to be a robe made of `makaci` fiber. Cloth made from `akkā` fiber, banana fiber, and `eraka` grass fiber are also of the same nature as a `potthaka`. The dye of all-blue robes and the like should be washed out, and they should be dyed again before being worn. If they cannot be washed, they should be made into ground-sheets, or they should be placed in the middle of a three-layered robe. The variety of their colors is to be treated according to the method stated in the section on footwear. As for robes with uncut fringes and long fringes, the fringes should be cut before they are worn. Having obtained a tunic, it is allowable to tear it up, dye it, and then use it. For a turban, this is the same method. A `tirīṭaka`, however, is made of tree bark; it is allowable to make it into a foot-wiping cloth.

58. “Na, bhikkhave, adhammakammaṃ kātabbaṃ, yo kareyya, āpatti dukkaṭassa. Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, adhammakamme kayiramāne paṭikkositu”nti (mahāva. 154) vacanato adhammakammaṃ na kātabbaṃ, kayiramānañca nivāretabbaṃ. Nivārentehi ca “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, catūhi pañcahi paṭikkosituṃ, dvīhi tīhi diṭṭhiṃ āvikātuṃ, ekena adhiṭṭhātuṃ ‘na metaṃ khamatī”ti (mahāva. 154) vacanato yattha nivārentassa bhikkhuno upaddavaṃ karonti, tattha ekakena na nivāretabbaṃ. Sace cattāro pañca vā honti, nivāretabbaṃ. Sace pana dve vā tayo vā honti, “adhammakammaṃ idaṃ, na metaṃ khamatī”ti evaṃ aññassa santike attano diṭṭhi āvikātabbā. Sace ekova hoti, “na metaṃ khamatī”ti adhiṭṭhātabbaṃ. Sabbañcetaṃ tesaṃ anupaddavatthāya vuttaṃ.

58. “Monks, an act against the Dhamma should not be done. Whoever does so incurs an offense of wrong-doing. I allow, monks, that when an act against the Dhamma is being done, it should be opposed.” Because of this statement, an act against the Dhamma should not be done, and when it is being done, it should be prevented. And by those who would prevent it: “I allow, monks, for four or five to oppose, for two or three to declare their view, and for one to resolve, ‘This is not agreeable to me.’” Because of this statement, where they would cause trouble for the monk who is preventing it, it should not be prevented by one alone. If there are four or five, it should be prevented. But if there are two or three, one’s view should be declared in the presence of another thus: “This is an act against the Dhamma; this is not agreeable to me.” If there is only one, one should resolve: “This is not agreeable to me.” And all this has been said for their freedom from trouble.

59. “Na, bhikkhave, anokāsakato bhikkhu āpattiyā codetabbo, yo codeyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (mahāva. 153) vacanato codentena “karotu me āyasmā okāsaṃ, ahaṃ taṃ vattukāmo”ti evaṃ okāsaṃ kārāpetvā codetabbo. Adhippāyabhedo panettha veditabbo (mahāva. aṭṭha. 2.389). Ayañhi adhippāyo nāma cāvanādhippāyo akkosādhippāyo [V 0.0428] kammādhippāyo vuṭṭhānādhippāyo uposathapavāraṇaṭṭhapanādhippāyo anuvijjanādhippāyo dhammakathādhippāyoti anekavidho. Tattha purimesu catūsu adhippāyesu okāsaṃ akārāpentassa dukkaṭaṃ, okāsaṃ kārāpetvāpi sammukhā amūlakena pārājikena codentassa saṅghādiseso, amūlakena saṅghādisesena codentassa pācittiyaṃ, amūlikāya ācāravipattiyā codentassa dukkaṭaṃ, akkosādhippāyena vadantassa pācittiyaṃ. Asammukhā pana sattahipi āpattikkhandhehi vadantassa dukkaṭaṃ, asammukhā eva sattavidhampi kammaṃ karontassa dukkaṭameva. Kurundiyaṃ pana “vuṭṭhānādhippāyena ‘tvaṃ imaṃ nāma āpattiṃ āpanno, taṃ paṭikarohī’ti [M 0.0460] vadantassa okāsakiccaṃ natthī”ti vuttaṃ. Uposathapavāraṇaṃ ṭhapentassapi okāsakammaṃ natthi, ṭhapanakhettaṃ pana jānitabbaṃ “suṇātu me, bhante, saṅgho, ajjuposatho pannaraso, yadi saṅghassa pattakallaṃ, saṅgho uposathaṃ kare”ti.

59. “Monks, a monk should not be accused of an offense without being given an opportunity. If one accuses without opportunity, one incurs an offense of wrong-doing” (Mahāvagga 153). Therefore, the accuser should first request, “Venerable, please grant me the opportunity; I wish to speak to you,” and only after obtaining permission should the accusation be made. Here, the distinction of intention must be understood (Mahāvagga Aṭṭhakathā 2.389). For intention here is of many kinds: the intention to cause to fall away, the intention to insult, the intention for disciplinary action, the intention to make one rise from an offense, the intention to suspend the Uposatha or Pavāraṇā, the intention to investigate, or the intention to discuss the Dhamma. In the first four kinds of intention, if one does not request permission, it is a wrong-doing. Even if permission is obtained, falsely accusing someone to their face of a Pārājika offense entails a Saṅghādisesa offense. Falsely accusing someone to their face of a Saṅghādisesa offense entails a Pācittiya offense. Falsely accusing someone to their face of a corruption of conduct entails a wrong-doing. Speaking with the intention to insult entails a Pācittiya offense. Furthermore, if one speaks about someone in their absence regarding any of the seven groups of offenses, it is a wrong-doing. Similarly, performing any of the seven kinds of disciplinary actions in someone’s absence is also a wrong-doing. However, in the Kurundī, it is stated: “When speaking with the intention to make one rise from an offense, saying, ‘You have committed such-and-such an offense; make amends for it,’ there is no need to request permission.” Likewise, when suspending the Uposatha or Pavāraṇā, there is no need for a formal request. However, the occasion for the suspension should be known, [which is during the announcement]: “Venerable Sirs, may the Saṅgha listen to me. Today is the fifteenth day, the Uposatha. If it is convenient for the Saṅgha, may the Saṅgha observe the Uposatha.”

Etasmiñhi re-kāre anatikkanteyeva ṭhapetuṃ labbhati, tato paraṃ pana yya-kāre patte na labbhati. Esa nayo pavāraṇāya.

For in this case, the suspension is permitted only before the syllable 're' has been passed over; however, once the syllable 'yya' has been reached, it is not permitted. This is the method for the Pavāraṇā.

Anuvijjakassapi osaṭe vatthusmiṃ “atthetaṃ tavā”ti anuvijjanādhippāyena vadantassa okāsakammaṃ natthi. Dhammakathikassapi dhammāsane nisīditvā “yo idañcidañca karoti, ayaṃ bhikkhu assamaṇo”tiādinā nayena anodissa dhammaṃ kathentassa okāsakammaṃ natthi. Sace pana odissa niyametvā “asuko ca asuko ca assamaṇo anupāsako”ti katheti, dhammāsanato orohitvā āpattiṃ desetvā gantabbaṃ. “Na, bhikkhave, suddhānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ anāpattikānaṃ avatthusmiṃ akāraṇe okāso kārāpetabbo, yo kārāpeyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (mahāva. 153) vacanato suddhānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ akāraṇe vatthusmiṃ okāso na kāretabbo. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, puggalaṃ tulayitvā okāsaṃ kātu”nti (mahāva. 153) vacanato “bhūtameva nu kho āpattiṃ vadati, abhūta”nti evaṃ upaparikkhitvā okāso kātabbo.

For an investigating Vinaya-expert also, when the matter is presented, there is no [need for] requesting permission for one who says, with the intention of investigating, 'Does this matter [of accusation] exist for you?'. For a Dhamma-preacher also, having sat on the Dhamma-seat, there is no [need for] requesting permission for one who preaches the Dhamma without specifying anyone, by the method of saying, 'Whatever monk does such-and-such, this monk is not a recluse,' and so on. If, however, having specified and defined, he says, 'So-and-so and so-and-so are not recluses, not true followers,' he should descend from the Dhamma-seat, confess the offense, and depart. Because of the text: 'Monks, for pure monks who are without offense, permission should not be requested without a basis, without a cause. Whoever should cause it to be requested, there is an offense of wrong-doing,' permission should not be requested for pure monks in a matter without a cause. Because of the text: 'I allow, monks, that permission be requested after weighing the person,' permission should be requested after investigating thus: 'Does he speak of an offense that is indeed true, or one that is untrue?'

60. “Na, bhikkhave, saddhādeyyaṃ vinipātetabbaṃ, yo vinipāteyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (mahāva. 361) vacanato saddhādeyyaṃ na vinipātetabbaṃ. Ṭhapetvā mātāpitaro (mahāva. aṭṭha. 361) sesañātīnaṃ dentopi vinipātetiyeva, mātāpitaro pana rajje ṭhitāpi patthayanti, dātabbaṃ.

60. Because of the text: ‘Monks, a gift of faith should not be wasted; whoever should waste it, there is an offense of wrong-doing,’ a gift of faith should not be wasted. Except for one’s mother and father, even one who gives to other relatives indeed wastes it. But as for one’s mother and father, even if they are established in a kingdom, they desire it; it should be given.

61. “Na[V 0.0429], bhikkhave, santaruttarena gāmo pavisitabbo, yo paviseyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (mahāva. 362) vacanato santaruttarena gāmo na pavisitabbo.

61. Because of the text: ‘Monks, a village should not be entered with only the inner and upper robes; whoever should enter, there is an offense of wrong-doing,’ a village should not be entered with only the inner and upper robes.

62. “Pañcime, bhikkhave, paccayā saṅghāṭiyā nikkhepāya. Gilāno vā hoti, vassikasaṅketaṃ vā hoti, nadīpāragataṃ vā hoti, aggaḷaguttivihāro vā hoti, atthatakathinaṃ vā hoti. Ime kho, bhikkhave, pañca paccayā saṅghāṭiyā nikkhepāyā”ti (mahāva. 362) – vacanato pana gahetvā [M 0.0461] gantuṃ asamattho gilāno vā hoti, vassikasaṅketādīsu vā aññataraṃ kāraṇaṃ, evarūpesu paccayesu saṅghāṭiṃ aggaḷaguttivihāre ṭhapetvā santaruttarena gantuṃ vaṭṭati. Sabbesveva hi etesu gilānavassikasaṅketanadīpāragamanaatthatakathinabhāvesu aggaḷaguttiyeva pamāṇaṃ, gutte eva vihāre nikkhipitvā bahi gantuṃ vaṭṭati, nāgutte. Āraññakassa pana vihāro na sugutto hoti, tena bhaṇḍukkhalikāya pakkhipitvā pāsāṇasusirarukkhasusirādīsu supaṭicchannesu ṭhapetvā gantabbaṃ. Uttarāsaṅgaantaravāsakānaṃ nikkhepepi imeyeva pañca paccayā veditabbā.

62. “Monks, these are the five conditions for setting aside the outer robe. One is sick, or it is the four-month period of the rains, or one has gone to the other side of a river, or the monastery is secured by a bolt, or the kaṭhina has been spread. These, monks, are the five conditions for setting aside the outer robe.” According to this, if a monk is sick and unable to take it and go, or if there is another reason such as the four-month period of the rains, under such conditions, it is permissible to leave the outer robe in a monastery secured by a bolt and to go wearing only the lower and upper robes. Indeed, in all these situations—being sick, the four-month period of the rains, going to the other side of a river, and the spreading of the kaṭhina—security by a bolt is the standard. One may set it aside and go outside only in a secure monastery, not in an insecure one. For a forest-dwelling monk, however, the monastery is not well-secured. That monk should place it in a cloth-bundle and store it in a well-concealed place, such as a rock crevice or tree hollow, before departing. These same five conditions should also be understood for setting aside the upper robe and the lower robe.

63. “Na, bhikkhave, sambādhassa sāmantā dvaṅgulā satthakammaṃ vā vatthikammaṃ vā kārāpetabbaṃ, yo kārāpeyya, āpatti thullaccayassā”ti (mahāva. 279) vacanato yathāparicchinne okāse (mahāva. aṭṭha. 279) yena kenaci satthena vā sūciyā vā kaṇṭakena vā sattikāya vā pāsāṇasakkhalikāya vā nakhena vā chindanaṃ vā phālanaṃ vā vijjhanaṃ vā lekhanaṃ vā na kātabbaṃ, sabbañhetaṃ satthakammameva hoti. Yena kenaci pana cammena vā vatthena vā vatthipīḷanampi na kātabbaṃ, sabbañhetaṃ vatthikammameva hoti. Ettha ca “sambādhassa sāmantā dvaṅgulā”ti idaṃ satthakammaṃyeva sandhāya vuttaṃ, vatthikammaṃ pana sambādheyeva paṭikkhittaṃ. Tattha pana khāraṃ vā dātuṃ yena kenaci rajjukena vā bandhituṃ vaṭṭati, yadi tena chijjati, succhinnaṃ. Aṇḍavuḍḍhirogepi satthakammaṃ na vaṭṭati, tasmā “aṇḍaṃ phāletvā bījāni uddharitvā arogaṃ karissāmī”ti na kātabbaṃ, aggitāpanabhesajjalepanesu pana paṭikkhepo natthi. Vaccamagge bhesajjamakkhitā ādānavaṭṭi vā veḷunāḷikā vā vaṭṭati, yāya khārakammaṃ vā karonti, telaṃ vā pavesenti.

63. “Monks, a surgical operation or an enema procedure should not be performed within two fingerbreadths of a private part. Whoever should have it performed commits a grave offense.” According to this, in the defined area, cutting, splitting, piercing, or scraping should not be done with any kind of knife, needle, thorn, small spear, stone splinter, or fingernail, for all this is indeed a surgical operation. Furthermore, the pressing of an enema with any kind of leather or cloth should not be done, for all this is indeed an enema procedure. And here, this statement, “within two fingerbreadths of a private part,” is said with reference only to a surgical operation, but an enema procedure is prohibited in the private part itself. In that place, however, it is allowable to apply a caustic solution or to bind with any kind of small cord; if it is severed by this, it is well-severed. In the case of a disease of scrotal swelling, too, a surgical operation is not allowable; therefore, it should not be done thinking, “I will cure him by splitting the scrotum and removing the testicles.” However, there is no prohibition on heating with fire and the application of medicine. In the anal passage, a medicine-smeared inserted wick or a small bamboo tube is allowable, by which a caustic treatment is performed or oil is introduced.

64. “Na, bhikkhave, nahāpitapubbena khurabhaṇḍaṃ pariharitabbaṃ, yo parihareyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (mahāva. 303) vacanato nahāpitapubbena (mahāva. aṭṭha. 303) khurabhaṇḍaṃ gahetvā pariharituṃ na vaṭṭati, aññassa santakena pana kese chedetuṃ vaṭṭati. Sace vetanaṃ [V 0.0430] gahetvā chindati, na vaṭṭati. Yo anahāpitapubbo, tasseva pariharituṃ vaṭṭati, taṃ vā aññaṃ vā gahetvā kese chedetumpi vaṭṭati.

64. “Monks, barber’s tools should not be carried by one who was formerly a barber. Whoever should carry them commits an offense of wrong-doing.” According to this, it is not allowable for one who was formerly a barber to take and carry barber’s tools; however, it is allowable to cut another’s hair with tools belonging to someone else. If he cuts hair after taking payment, it is not allowable. For a monk who was not formerly a barber, it is allowable for him to carry them. And taking his own tools or another’s, it is also allowable for him to cut hair.

65. “Saṅghikāni[M 0.0462], bhikkhave, bījāni puggalikāya bhūmiyā ropitāni bhāgaṃ datvā paribhuñjitabbāni. Puggalikāni bījāni saṅghikāya bhūmiyā ropitāni bhāgaṃ datvā paribhuñjitabbānī”ti (mahāva. 304) – vacanato puggalikāya bhūmiyā saṅghikesu bījesu ropitesu saṅghikāya bhūmiyā vā puggalikesu bījesu ropitesu dasamabhāgaṃ datvā paribhuñjitabbaṃ. Idaṃ kira jambudīpe porāṇakacārittaṃ, tasmā dasa koṭṭhāse katvā eko koṭṭhāso bhūmisāmikānaṃ dātabbo.

65. “Monks, seeds belonging to the Sangha, when planted on individual land, are to be enjoyed after giving a share. Individual seeds, when planted on Sangha land, are to be enjoyed after giving a share.” According to this, when seeds belonging to the Sangha are planted on individual land, or when individual seeds are planted on Sangha land, they are to be enjoyed after giving a tenth share. This, it is said, is the ancient custom in Jambudīpa. Therefore, having made ten portions, one portion is to be given to the owners of the land.

66. “Santi, bhikkhave, maggā kantārā appodakā appabhakkhā, na sukarā apātheyyena gantuṃ. Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, pātheyyaṃ pariyesituṃ. Taṇḍulo taṇḍulatthikena, muggo muggatthikena, māso māsatthikena, loṇaṃ loṇatthikena, guḷo guḷatthikena, telaṃ telatthikena, sappi sappitthikenā”ti (mahāva. 299) – vacanato tādisaṃ kantāraṃ nittharantena pātheyyaṃ pariyesituṃ vaṭṭati. Kathaṃ pana pariyesitabbanti? Sace (mahāva. aṭṭha. 296) kecisayameva ñatvā denti, iccetaṃ kusalaṃ. No ce denti, ñātipavāritaṭṭhānato vā bhikkhācāravattena vā pariyesitabbaṃ. Tathā alabhantena aññātikaappavāritaṭṭhānato yācitvāpi gahetabbaṃ. Ekadivasena gamanīye magge ekabhattatthāya pariyesitabbaṃ. Dīghe addhāne yattakena kantāraṃ nittharati, tattakaṃ pariyesitabbaṃ.

66. “Monks, there are roads that are wildernesses, with little water and little food, not easy to traverse without provisions. I allow you, monks, to seek provisions. One who needs rice may seek rice; one who needs black gram, black gram; one who needs beans, beans; one who needs salt, salt; one who needs jaggery, jaggery; one who needs oil, oil; one who needs ghee, ghee.” According to this, for one crossing such a wilderness, it is proper to seek provisions. But how are they to be sought? If some, knowing for themselves, give, this is good. If they do not give, they should be sought from relatives, from an invited place, or by the practice of the alms-round. If not obtaining them in this way, they may be taken even after asking from an uninvited place of non-relatives. On a journey to be travelled in a single day, provisions should be sought for one meal. On a long journey, as much as is needed to cross the wilderness should be sought.

67. “Yaṃ, bhikkhave, mayā ‘idaṃ na kappatī’ti appaṭikkhittaṃ, tañce akappiyaṃ anulometi, kappiyaṃ paṭibāhati, taṃ vo na kappati. Yaṃ, bhikkhave, mayā ‘idaṃ na kappatī’ti appaṭikkhittaṃ, tañce kappiyaṃ anulometi, akappiyaṃ paṭibāhati, taṃ vo kappati. Yaṃ, bhikkhave, mayā ‘idaṃ kappatī’ti ananuññātaṃ, tañce akappiyaṃ anulometi, kappiyaṃ paṭibāhati, taṃ vo na kappati. Yaṃ, bhikkhave, mayā ‘idaṃ kappatī’ti ananuññātaṃ, tañce kappiyaṃ anulometi, akappiyaṃ paṭibāhati, taṃ vo kappatī”ti (mahāva. 305) – ime cattāro mahāpadese bhagavā bhikkhūnaṃ nayaggahaṇatthāya āha. Tattha dhammasaṅgāhakattherā suttaṃ gahetvā parimaddantā idaṃ addasaṃsu. “Ṭhapetvā dhaññaphalarasa”nti satta dhaññarasāni “pacchābhattaṃ na kappatī”ti paṭikkhittāni[M 0.0463]. Tālanāḷikerapanasalabujaalābukumbhaṇḍapussaphalatipusaphalaeḷālukāni nava mahāphalāni sabbañca aparaṇṇaṃ dhaññagatikameva. Taṃ kiñcāpi na paṭikkhittaṃ[V 0.0431], atha kho akappiyaṃ anulometi, tasmā pacchābhattaṃ na kappati. Aṭṭha pānāni anuññātāni, avasesāni vettatintiṇikamātuluṅgakapiṭṭhakosambakaramandādikhuddakaphalapānāni aṭṭhapānagatikāneva. Tāni kiñcāpi na anuññātāni, atha kho kappiyaṃ anulomenti, tasmā kappanti. Ṭhapetvā hi sānulomaṃ dhaññaphalarasaṃ aññaṃ phalapānaṃ nāma akappiyaṃ natthi, sabbaṃ yāmakālikaṃyevāti kurundiyaṃ vuttaṃ.

67. “Bhikkhus, that which has not been rejected by me, saying, ‘This is not allowable,’ if it conforms to the unallowable and obstructs the allowable, that is not allowable for you. Bhikkhus, that which has not been rejected by me, saying, ‘This is not allowable,’ if it conforms to the allowable and obstructs the unallowable, that is allowable for you. Bhikkhus, that which has not been permitted by me, saying, ‘This is allowable,’ if it conforms to the unallowable and obstructs the allowable, that is not allowable for you. Bhikkhus, that which has not been permitted by me, saying, ‘This is allowable,’ if it conforms to the allowable and obstructs the unallowable, that is allowable for you.” The Blessed One spoke these four Great Authorities for the bhikkhus to grasp the method. Therein, the elder monks who compiled the Dhamma, having taken up the Sutta and examined it, saw this: By the words, ‘Excluding the juice of grain-fruit,’ the seven grain juices were rejected, saying, ‘They are not allowable after midday.’ The nine great fruits—tāla (palmyra palm), nāḷikera (coconut), panasa (jackfruit), labuja (breadfruit), alābu (bottle gourd), kumbhaṇḍa (pumpkin), pussaphala (snake gourd), tipusaphala (cucumber), and eḷāluka (muskmelon)—and all other pulses are of the same nature as grain. Although these were not rejected, they conform to the unallowable; therefore, they are not allowable after midday. Eight kinds of drinks were permitted. The remaining drinks from small fruits, such as vetta (rattan), tintiṇika (tamarind), mātuluṅga (citron), kapiṭṭha (wood apple), kosamba (neem), karamanda (carissa), and so on, are of the same nature as the eight drinks. Although these were not permitted, they conform to the allowable; therefore, they are allowable. Indeed, excluding grain-fruit juice and that which conforms to it, there is no other fruit drink that is unallowable; all are indeed allowable for the watch (yāmakālika). Thus it is said in the Kurundī.

Bhagavatā – “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, cha cīvarāni khomaṃ kappāsikaṃ koseyyaṃ kambalaṃ sāṇaṃ bhaṅga”nti (mahāva. 339) cha cīvarāni anuññātāni, dhammasaṅgāhakattherehi tesaṃ anulomāni dukūlaṃ pattuṇṇaṃ cīnapaṭṭaṃ somārapaṭṭaṃ iddhimayaṃ devadattiyanti aparāni cha anuññātāni. Tattha pattuṇṇanti pattuṇṇadese pāṇakehi sañjātavatthaṃ. Dve paṭāni desanāmeneva vuttāni. Tīṇi koseyyassa anulomāni, dukūlaṃ sāṇassa, itarāni dve kappāsikassa vā sabbesaṃ vā.

By the Blessed One, it was said: “I allow, bhikkhus, six kinds of robes: linen, cotton, silk, wool, hemp, and coarse cloth.” Thus, six kinds of robes were allowed. By the Elder Compilers of the Dhamma, another six were allowed in conformity with these: fine cloth, Pattuṇṇa cloth, Chinese cloth, Somāra cloth, cloth made by psychic power, and cloth given by devas. Therein, 'Pattuṇṇa cloth' is cloth produced by insects in the Pattuṇṇa region. Two cloths are spoken of by the name of their region. Three are in conformity with silk, fine cloth with hemp, and the other two with cotton or with all six.

Bhagavatā ekādasa patte paṭikkhipitvā dve pattā anuññātā lohapatto ca mattikāpatto ca. Lohathālakaṃ mattikāthālakaṃ tambalohathālakanti tesaṃyeva anulomāni. Bhagavatā tayo tumbā anuññātā lohatumbo kaṭṭhatumbo phalatumboti. Kuṇḍikā kañcanako udakatumboti tesaṃyeva anulomāni. Kurundiyaṃ pana “pānīyasaṅkhapānīyasarāvakānaṃ ete anulomā”ti vuttaṃ. Paṭṭikā sūkarantanti dve kāyabandhanāni anuññātāni. Dussapaṭṭena rajjukena ca katakāyabandhanāni tesaṃyeva anulomāni. Setacchattaṃ kilañjacchattaṃ paṇṇacchattanti tīṇi chattāni anuññātāni. Ekapaṇṇacchattaṃ tesaṃyeva anulomanti iminā nayena pāḷiñca aṭṭhakathañca anupekkhitvā aññānipi kappiyākappiyānaṃ anulomāni vinayadharena veditabbāni.

By the Blessed One, having rejected eleven kinds of bowls, two bowls were allowed: an iron bowl and an earthen bowl. An iron dish, an earthen dish, and a copper dish—these are in conformity with only those bowls. By the Blessed One, three kinds of gourds were allowed: an iron gourd, a wooden gourd, and a fruit gourd. A water pot, a golden water pot, and a water gourd—these are in conformity with only those. But in the Kurundī it is said: “These are in conformity with drinking conches and small drinking cups.” A flat waistband and a waistband with a chisel-like weave—two kinds of waistbands were allowed. Waistbands made with a cloth strip and a rope are in conformity with only those. A white parasol, a red parasol, and a leaf parasol—three kinds of parasols were allowed. A single-leaf parasol is in conformity with only those. In this way, having examined the Pāḷi and the commentary, other things in conformity with what is allowable and unallowable should be known by one who is versed in the Vinaya.

68. Vinayadharo (pāci. aṭṭha. 438) ca puggalo vinayapariyattimūlake pañcānisaṃse chānisaṃse sattānisaṃse aṭṭhānisaṃse navānisaṃse dasānisaṃse ekādasānisaṃse [M 0.0464] labhati. Katame pañcānisaṃse labhati? Attano sīlakkhandhaguttiādike. Vuttañhetaṃ –

68. A person who is a Vinaya-holder, having the study of the Vinaya as their basis, obtains five advantages, six advantages, seven advantages, eight advantages, nine advantages, ten advantages, and eleven advantages. What five advantages does one obtain? Protection of one’s own aggregate of morality, and so on. For it was said:

“Pañcime, bhikkhave, ānisaṃsā vinayadhare puggale. Attano sīlakkhandho sugutto hoti surakkhito, kukkuccapakatānaṃ paṭisaraṇaṃ hoti, visārado saṅghamajjhe voharati, paccatthike sahadhammena suniggahitaṃ niggaṇhāti, saddhammaṭṭhitiyā paṭipanno hotī”ti (pari. 325).

“Bhikkhus, there are these five benefits in a person who is an expert in the Vinaya. His own aggregate of virtue is well-guarded and well-protected. He is a refuge for those afflicted by remorse. Being confident, he speaks in the midst of the Saṅgha. He thoroughly restrains adversaries in accordance with the Dhamma and with reason. He is one who practices for the stability of the good Dhamma.”

Kathamassa [V 0.0432] attano sīlakkhandho sugutto hoti surakkhito? Idhekacco bhikkhu āpattiṃ āpajjanto chahākārehi āpajjati alajjitā, aññāṇatā, kukkuccapakatatā, akappiye kappiyasaññitā, kappiye akappiyasaññitā, satisammosā. Kathaṃ alajjitāya āpajjati? Akappiyabhāvaṃ jānantoyeva madditvā vītikkamaṃ karoti. Vuttampi cetaṃ –

How is his own aggregate of virtue well-guarded and well-protected? Here, a certain bhikkhu incurs an offense in six ways: through shamelessness, through ignorance, through being afflicted by scruples, through perceiving what is unallowable as allowable, through perceiving what is allowable as unallowable, and through a lapse of mindfulness. How does one incur an offense through shamelessness? Knowing full well that it is unallowable, he disregards this and commits the transgression. And this has been said:

“Sañcicca āpattiṃ āpajjati, āpattiṃ parigūhati;

Agatigamanañca gacchati, ediso vuccati alajjipuggalo”ti. (pari. 359);

“Knowingly, one incurs an offense; one conceals the offense; and one goes on a wrong course—such a person is called a shameless person.”

Kathaṃ aññāṇatāya āpajjati? Aññāṇapuggalo hi mando momūho kattabbākattabbaṃ ajānanto akattabbaṃ karoti, kattabbaṃ virādheti. Evaṃ aññāṇatāya āpajjati. Kathaṃ kukkuccapakatatāya āpajjati? Kappiyākappiyaṃ nissāya kukkucce uppanne vinayadharaṃ pucchitvā kappiyaṃ ce, kattabbaṃ siyā, akappiyaṃ ce, na kattabbaṃ, ayaṃ pana “vaṭṭatī”ti madditvā vītikkamatiyeva. Evaṃ kukkuccapakatatāya āpajjati.

How does one incur an offense through ignorance? An ignorant person, being dull and greatly confused, not knowing what should be done and what should not be done, does what should not be done and neglects what should be done. Thus, one incurs an offense through ignorance. How does one incur an offense through being afflicted by scruples? When scruples arise concerning what is allowable and unallowable, one should ask an expert in the Vinaya; if it is allowable, it should be done, and if it is unallowable, it should not be done. This person, however, thinking, “It is permissible,” disregards this and transgresses indeed. Thus, one incurs an offense through being afflicted by scruples.

Kathaṃ akappiye kappiyasaññitāya āpajjati? Acchamaṃsaṃ “sūkaramaṃsa”nti khādati, dīpimaṃsaṃ “migamaṃsa”nti khādati, akappiyabhojanaṃ “kappiyabhojana”nti bhuñjati, vikāle kālasaññāya bhuñjati, akappiyapānakaṃ “kappiyapānaka”nti pivati. Evaṃ akappiye kappiyasaññitāya āpajjati. Kathaṃ kappiye akappiyasaññitāya āpajjati? Sūkaramaṃsaṃ “acchamaṃsa”nti khādati, migamaṃsaṃ “dīpimaṃsa”nti khādati, kappiyabhojanaṃ “akappiyabhojana”nti bhuñjati, kāle vikālasaññāya bhuñjati, kappiyapānakaṃ “akappiyapānaka”nti pivati. Evaṃ kappiye akappiyasaññitāya āpajjati. Kathaṃ satisammosā [M 0.0465] āpajjati? Sahaseyyacīvaravippavāsabhesajjacīvarakālātikkamanapaccayā āpattiṃ satisammosā āpajjati. Evamidhekacco bhikkhu imehi chahi ākārehi āpattiṃ āpajjati.

How does one incur an offense regarding what is unallowable, through the perception that it is allowable? One eats bear's flesh thinking it is pork; one eats leopard's flesh thinking it is deer's flesh; one consumes unallowable food thinking it is allowable food; one consumes at the wrong time with the perception that it is the right time; one drinks an unallowable drink thinking it is an allowable drink. Thus, one incurs an offense regarding what is unallowable, through the perception that it is allowable. How does one incur an offense regarding what is allowable, through the perception that it is unallowable? One eats pork thinking it is bear's flesh; one eats deer's flesh thinking it is leopard's flesh; one consumes allowable food thinking it is unallowable food; one consumes at the right time with the perception that it is the wrong time; one drinks an allowable drink thinking it is an unallowable drink. Thus, one incurs an offense regarding what is allowable, through the perception that it is unallowable. How does one incur an offense through a lapse of mindfulness? Due to causes related to sleeping together, being separated from one's robes, medicine, and letting the time for robes pass, one incurs an offense through a lapse of mindfulness. Thus, in this Dispensation, a certain bhikkhu incurs an offense in these six ways.

Vinayadharo pana imehi chahākārehi āpattiṃ na āpajjati. Kathaṃ lajjitāya nāpajjati? So hi “passatha bho, ayaṃ kappiyākappiyaṃ jānantoyeva paṇṇattivītikkamaṃ karotī”ti imaṃ parūpavādaṃ rakkhantopi nāpajjati. Evaṃ lajjitāya nāpajjati, sahasā āpannampi desanāgāminiṃ desetvā vuṭṭhānagāminiyā vuṭṭhahitvā suddhante patiṭṭhāti. Tato –

A Vinaya-expert, however, does not incur an offense in these six ways. How does one not incur an offense through conscientiousness? Because that Vinaya-expert, while guarding against this reproach from others, 'Sirs, look! This Vinaya-expert, while knowing what is allowable and unallowable, commits a transgression of the rule,' does not incur an offense. Thus, one does not incur an offense through conscientiousness. Even if one has inadvertently incurred an offense that is expiated by confession, having confessed it, and for one that is expiated by rehabilitation, having been rehabilitated, one is established in a pure state. Therefore—

“Sañcicca [V 0.0433] āpattiṃ nāpajjati, āpattiṃ na parigūhati;

Agatigamanañca na gacchati, ediso vuccati lajjipuggalo”ti. (pari. 359) –

“One does not deliberately incur an offense; one does not conceal an offense; and one does not go on a wrong course. Such a person is called a conscientious person.”

Imasmiṃ lajjibhāve patiṭṭhitova hoti.

In this state of conscientiousness, one is indeed established.

Kathaṃ ñāṇatāya nāpajjati? So hi kappiyākappiyaṃ jānāti, tasmā kappiyaṃyeva karoti, akappiyaṃ na karoti. Evaṃ ñāṇatāya nāpajjati. Kathaṃ akukkuccapakatatāya nāpajjati? Kappiyākappiyaṃ nissāya kukkucce uppanne vatthuṃ oloketvā mātikaṃ padabhājanaṃ antarāpattiṃ anāpattiṃ oloketvā kappiyaṃ ce hoti, karoti, akappiyaṃ ce, na karoti. Evaṃ akukkuccapakatatāya nāpajjati. Kathaṃ akappiye kappiyasaññitādīhi nāpajjati? So hi kappiyākappiyaṃ jānāti, tasmā akappiye kappiyasaññī na hoti, kappiye akappiyasaññī na hoti, suppatiṭṭhitā cassa sati hoti, adhiṭṭhātabbaṃ adhiṭṭheti, vikappetabbaṃ vikappeti. Iti imehi chahi ākārehi āpattiṃ nāpajjati. Anāpajjanto akhaṇḍasīlo hoti, parisuddhasīlo hoti. Evamassa attano sīlakkhandho sugutto hoti surakkhito.

How does one not incur an offense through knowledge? Because that person knows what is allowable and unallowable, therefore they do only what is allowable and do not do what is unallowable. Thus, through knowledge, one does not incur an offense. How does one not incur an offense through being free from scruples? When scruples arise concerning what is allowable and unallowable, having examined the case, and having examined the Mātika, the Padabhājana, the intermediate offenses, and non-offenses, if it is allowable, they do it; if it is unallowable, they do not do it. Thus, through being free from scruples, one does not incur an offense. How does one not incur an offense through perceptions such as perceiving the unallowable as allowable? Because that person knows what is allowable and unallowable, therefore they do not perceive the unallowable as allowable, nor do they perceive the allowable as unallowable. And their mindfulness is well-established; they determine what should be determined, and they share what should be shared. Thus, in these six ways, they do not incur an offense. Not incurring an offense, they are of unbroken virtue, they are of pure virtue. Thus, for that person, their own aggregate of virtue is well-guarded and well-protected.

Kathaṃ kukkuccapakatānaṃ paṭisaraṇaṃ hoti? Tiroraṭṭhesu tirojanapadesu ca uppannakukkuccā bhikkhū “asukasmiṃ kira vihāre vinayadharo vasatī”ti dūratova tassa santikaṃ āgantvā kukkuccaṃ pucchanti. So tehi katassa kammassa vatthuṃ oloketvā āpattānāpattigarukalahukādibhedaṃ sallakkhetvā desanāgāminiṃ desāpetvā, vuṭṭhānagāminiyā vuṭṭhāpetvā suddhante patiṭṭhāpeti. Evaṃ kukkuccapakatānaṃ paṭisaraṇaṃ hoti.

How are they a refuge for those beset by scruples? In foreign countries and in regions outside the district, bhikkhus in whom scruples have arisen, thinking, 'It is said that a Vinaya-expert lives in such-and-such a monastery,' come from afar to their presence and ask about their scruples. That Vinaya-expert, having examined the basis of the deed done by those bhikkhus and having considered the distinctions such as offense and non-offense, serious and light, makes them confess an offense that is cleared by confession, and rehabilitates them from an offense that is cleared by rehabilitation, establishing them in the sphere of purity. Thus, they are a refuge for those beset by scruples.

Visārado [M 0.0466] saṅghamajjhe voharatīti avinayadharassa hi saṅghamajjhe kathentassa bhayaṃ sārajjaṃ okkamati, vinayadharassa taṃ na hoti. Kasmā? “Evaṃ kathentassa doso hoti, evaṃ na doso”ti ñatvā kathanato.

Being confident, they speak in the midst of the Saṅgha. For indeed, when one who is not a Vinaya-expert speaks in the midst of the Saṅgha, fear and diffidence arise; but for a Vinaya-expert, that does not happen. Why? Because they speak having known: 'Speaking thus, there is a fault; speaking thus, there is no fault.'

Paccatthike sahadhammena suniggahitaṃ niggaṇhātīti ettha dvidhā paccatthikā nāma attapaccatthikā ca sāsanapaccatthikā ca. Tattha mettiyabhūmajakā ca bhikkhū vaḍḍho ca licchavī amūlakena antimavatthunā codesuṃ, ime attapaccatthikā nāma. Ye pana aññepi dussīlā pāpadhammā[V 0.0434], sabbete attapaccatthikā. Viparītadassanā pana ariṭṭhabhikkhukaṇṭakasāmaṇeravesālikavajjiputtakā parūpahāraaññāṇakaṅkhāvitaraṇādivādā mahāsaṅghikādayo ca abuddhasāsanaṃ “buddhasāsana”nti vatvā katapaggahā sāsanapaccatthikā nāma. Te sabbepi sahadhammena sahakāraṇena vacanena yathā taṃ asaddhammaṃ patiṭṭhāpetuṃ na sakkonti, evaṃ suniggahitaṃ katvā niggaṇhāti.

Here, concerning the phrase 'one restrains enemies well with the Dhamma,' enemies are of two kinds: personal enemies and enemies of the Dispensation. Among these, the monks Mettiya and Bhūmajaka, and the Licchavi Vaḍḍha, accused others with a baseless grave offense; these are called personal enemies. And all others who are immoral and of evil character are also personal enemies. But those with wrong views, such as the monk Ariṭṭha, the novice Kaṇṭaka, the Vajjiputtakas of Vesālī, and the Mahāsaṅghikas and others who hold such views as that an Arahant can have a seminal emission, can have ignorance, and can have doubt—who, having declared what is not the Buddha’s Dispensation to be 'the Buddha’s Dispensation,' have taken up such a stand—these are called enemies of the Dispensation. All of them, by means of the Dhamma and with reasoned speech, are so thoroughly refuted that they cannot establish that false Dhamma; thus, one restrains them.

Saddhammaṭṭhitiyā paṭipanno hotīti ettha pana tividho saddhammo pariyattipaṭipattiadhigamavasena. Tattha tepiṭakaṃ buddhavacanaṃ pariyattisaddhammo nāma. Terasa dhutaguṇā cuddasa khandhakavattāni dveasīti mahāvattānīti ayaṃ paṭipattisaddhammo nāma. Cattāro maggā ca cattāri phalāni ca, ayaṃ adhigamasaddhammo nāma.

Here, concerning the phrase 'one who practices for the stability of the true Dhamma,' the true Dhamma is threefold by way of textual study, practice, and realization. Among these, the Buddha’s words in the three Piṭakas are called the true Dhamma of textual study. The thirteen ascetic practices, the fourteen duties pertaining to the Khandhakas, and the eighty-two great observances—these are called the true Dhamma of practice. The four paths and the four fruits—these are called the true Dhamma of realization.

Tattha keci therā “yo vo, ānanda, mayā dhammo ca vinayo ca desito paññatto, so vo mamaccayena satthā”ti iminā suttena (dī. ni. 2.216) “sāsanassa pariyatti mūla”nti vadanti. Keci therā “ime ca subhadda bhikkhū sammā vihareyyuṃ, asuñño loko arahantehi assā”ti iminā suttena (dī. ni. 2.214) “sāsanassa paṭipatti mūla”nti vatvā “yāva pañca bhikkhū sammāpaṭipannā saṃvijjanti, tāva sāsanaṃ ṭhitaṃ hotī”ti āhaṃsu. Itare pana therā “pariyattiyā antarahitāya suppaṭipannassapi dhammābhisamayo natthī”ti vatvā āhaṃsu “sacepi pañca bhikkhū cattāri pārājikāni rakkhakā honti, te saddhe kulaputte pabbājetvā paccantime janapade upasampādetvā dasavaggaṃ gaṇaṃ pūretvā majjhimajanapade upasampadaṃ karissanti, etenupāyena vīsativaggaṃ saṅghaṃ pūretvā attanopi abbhānakammaṃ katvā sāsanaṃ vuddhiṃ virūḷhiṃ [M 0.0467] gamayissanti. Evamayaṃ vinayadharo tividhassapi saddhammassa ciraṭṭhitiyā paṭipanno hotī”ti. Evamayaṃ vinayadharo ime tāva pañcānisaṃse paṭilabhatīti veditabbo.

In this regard, some elders say, based on the sutta passage, 'Ānanda, the Dhamma and Vinaya I have taught and laid down for you shall be your teacher after my passing,' that 'the scriptural learning is the root of the Dispensation.' Some elders say, based on the sutta passage, 'Subhadda, if these monks live rightly, the world will not be empty of arahants,' that 'practice is the root of the Dispensation,' and they declare, 'As long as even five monks practice rightly, the Dispensation remains established.' But other elders say, 'When the scriptural learning has disappeared, even for one who is of good practice, there is no realization of the Dhamma,' and they declare, 'Even if there are five monks who are guardians of the four Pārājika offenses, they, having given the going forth to faithful sons of good families and having conferred the higher ordination in a border district, thereby completing a group of ten, will perform the higher ordination in the middle country. By this method, having completed a Saṅgha of twenty and having performed the act of rehabilitation for themselves, they will cause the Dispensation to attain growth and expansion. Thus, this Vinaya-expert is one who practices for the long-lastingness of the threefold good Dhamma.' In this way, it should be understood that this Vinaya-expert obtains these five benefits.

Katame chānisaṃse labhatīti? Tassādheyyo uposatho pavāraṇā saṅghakammaṃ pabbajjā upasampadā, nissayaṃ deti, sāmaṇeraṃ upaṭṭhāpeti. Yepi ime cātuddasiko, pannarasiko, sāmaggiuposatho, saṅghe uposatho, gaṇe uposatho, puggale uposatho, suttuddeso, pārisuddhi, adhiṭṭhānauposathoti nava uposathā, sabbe te vinayadharāyattā, yāpi ca imā cātuddasikā, pannarasikā, sāmaggipavāraṇā, saṅghe pavāraṇā, gaṇe pavāraṇā, puggale pavāraṇā, tevācikā pavāraṇā[V 0.0435], dvevācikā pavāraṇā, samānavassikā pavāraṇāti nava pavāraṇā, tāpi vinayadharāyattā eva, tassa santakā, so tāsaṃ sāmī.

What six benefits does he gain? The Uposatha, Pavāraṇā, acts of the Sangha, going forth, and higher ordination are dependent on him; he gives dependence, and he has a novice attend upon him. All these—the Uposatha on the fourteenth day, on the fifteenth day, the harmonious Uposatha, the Uposatha in the Sangha, the Uposatha in a group, the Uposatha of an individual, the recitation of the Pātimokkha, the Uposatha by purification, and the Uposatha by determination—these nine Uposathas are dependent on the Vinaya-holder. Similarly, the Pavāraṇā on the fourteenth day, on the fifteenth day, the harmonious Pavāraṇā, the Pavāraṇā in the Sangha, the Pavāraṇā in a group, the Pavāraṇā of an individual, the Pavāraṇā with three recitations, the Pavāraṇā with two recitations, and the Pavāraṇā of those of the same rains-residence—these nine Pavāraṇās are also dependent on the Vinaya-holder. They are his property; he is their master.

Yānipi imāni apalokanakammaṃ ñattikammaṃ ñattidutiyakammaṃ ñatticatutthakammanti cattāri saṅghakammāni, yā cāyaṃ upajjhāyena hutvā kulaputtānaṃ pabbajjā ca upasampadā ca kātabbā, ayampi vinayadharāyattāva. Na hi añño dvipiṭakadharopi evaṃ kātuṃ labhati, so eva nissayaṃ deti, sāmaṇeraṃ upaṭṭhāpeti, añño neva nissayaṃ dātuṃ labhati, na sāmaṇeraṃ upaṭṭhāpetuṃ. Teneva “na, bhikkhave, ekena dve sāmaṇerā upaṭṭhāpetabbā, yo upaṭṭhāpeyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (mahāva. 101) paṭikkhipitvā puna anujānantenapi “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, byattena bhikkhunā ekena dve sāmaṇere upaṭṭhāpetuṃ, yāvatake vā pana ussahati ovadituṃ anusāsituṃ, tāvatake upaṭṭhāpetu”nti (mahāva. 105) byattasseva sāmaṇerupaṭṭhāpanaṃ anuññātaṃ. Sāmaṇerupaṭṭhāpanaṃ paccāsīsanto pana vinayadharassa santike upajjhaṃ gāhāpetvā vattapaṭipattiṃ sādituṃ labhati. Ettha ca nissayadānañceva sāmaṇerupaṭṭhānañca ekamaṅgaṃ. Iti imesu chasu ānisaṃsesu ekena saddhiṃ purimāni pañca cha honti. Dvīhi saddhiṃ satta, tīhi saddhiṃ aṭṭha, catūhi saddhiṃ nava, pañcahi saddhiṃ dasa, sabbehipetehi saddhiṃ ekādasāti evaṃ vinayadharo puggalo pañca cha satta aṭṭha nava dasa ekādasa ca ānisaṃse labhatīti veditabbo.

These four Sangha acts—the act of announcement (apalokanakamma), the act of motion (ñattikamma), the act of motion followed by one announcement (ñattidutiyakamma), and the act of motion followed by three announcements (ñatticatutthakamma)—are dependent on the Vinaya-holder. And this too—the going forth and the higher ordination of sons of good family, which must be performed by a preceptor—is likewise dependent on the Vinaya-holder. For indeed, no other, even one who has mastered the two Piṭakas, is able to do so. Only he gives dependence (nissaya); only he has a novice attend upon him. Another is neither able to give dependence nor to have a novice attend upon him. For that very reason, having first prohibited it, saying: 'Monks, two novices are not to be attended upon by one monk. Whoever should have them attend, there is an offense of wrong conduct,' and then permitting it again, saying: 'I allow, monks, for two novices to be attended upon by one competent monk, or as many as he is able to instruct and admonish, so many may he have attend upon him,' the attendance of a novice was permitted only to a competent one. However, one who desires the attendance of a novice is able, by having a preceptor appointed in the presence of a Vinaya-holder, to fulfill the duties and observances. And here, the giving of dependence and the attendance of a novice are a single factor. Thus, among these six benefits, the preceding five together with one become six. With two, they become seven; with three, eight; with four, nine; with five, ten; with all of these, they become eleven. In this way, it should be understood that a person who is a Vinaya-holder obtains five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten, and eleven benefits.

Mahānisaṃsamiccevaṃ[M 0.0468], kosallaṃ vinaye sadā;

Patthentenettha kātabbo, abhiyogo punappunanti.

Thus, by one who always desires skill in the Vinaya, which has great benefits, exertion should be made herein again and again.

Iti pāḷimuttakavinayavinicchayasaṅgahe

Thus in the Pāḷimuttakavinayavinicchayasaṅgaha.

Pakiṇṇakavinicchayakathā samattā.

The Discourse on Miscellaneous Decisions is completed.

Niṭṭhito cāyaṃ pāḷimuttakavinayavinicchayasaṅgaho.

And this Pāḷimuttakavinayavinicchayasaṅgaha is completed.

Nigamanakathā

The Concluding Discourse

Ajjhesito narindena, sohaṃ parakkamabāhunā;

Saddhammaṭṭhitikāmena, sāsanujjotakārinā.

That I was requested by the king, Parakkamabāhu, who desires the stability of the good Dhamma and who causes the Dispensation to shine.

Teneva [V 0.0436] kārite ramme, pāsādasatamaṇḍite;

Nānādumagaṇākiṇṇe, bhāvanābhiratālaye.

In that delightful abode built by him, adorned with hundreds of mansions, teeming with various kinds of trees, a dwelling for those who delight in meditation;

Sītalūdakasampanne, vasaṃ jetavane imaṃ;

Vinayasaṅgahaṃ sāraṃ, akāsi yoginaṃ hitaṃ.

Dwelling in this Jetavana, endowed with cool shade and water, I composed this Vinayasaṅgaha, which is an essence, for the welfare of yogis.

Yaṃ siddhaṃ iminā puññaṃ, yañcaññaṃ pasutaṃ mayā;

Etena puññakammena, dutiye attasambhave.

Whatever merit has been accomplished by this work, and whatever other merit has been accumulated by me, by this meritorious deed, in a second existence,

Tāvatiṃse pamodento, sīlācāraguṇe rato;

Alaggo pañcakāmesu, patvāna paṭhamaṃ phalaṃ.

rejoicing in Tāvatiṃsa, delighting in the virtue of moral conduct, unattached to the five sense pleasures, having become a devaputta and having attained the first fruit,

Antime attabhāvamhi, metteyyaṃ munipuṅgavaṃ;

Lokaggapuggalaṃ nāthaṃ, sabbasattahite rataṃ.

in my final existence, may I see Metteyya, the chief of sages, the foremost individual in the world, the protector, who delights in the welfare of all beings.

Disvāna tassa dhīrassa, sutvā saddhammadesanaṃ;

Adhigantvā phalaṃ aggaṃ, sobheyyaṃ jinasāsananti.

Having seen that wise one, having heard his teaching of the true Dhamma, and having attained the highest fruit, may I adorn the Dispensation of the Conqueror.

Vinayasaṅgaha-aṭṭhakathā niṭṭhitā.

The Vinayasaṅgaha Commentary is completed.
